t: Alert List — Suspicious virtual asset trading platforms category
sl: SFC · Alert List — Suspicious virtual asset trading platforms category (2026)
s: This is the SFC's running public register of entities it has flagged as suspicious, captured on the snapshot date. It groups names into categories such as suspicious virtual-asset trading platforms, fake regulators, unlicensed firms and phishing attempts. Rows are added and removed continuously, so the file is a point-in-time capture rather than a fixed publication. Most listed names have no formal enforcement outcome attached; inclusion just signals the SFC has received complaints or spotted impersonation activity. The virtual-asset sub-list is dominated by copycat sites impersonating licensed exchange brand names.
w: This is useful as one input to sanctions and fraud screening of counterparties and customer-named platforms. But it changes daily and carries no due-process explanation, so it cannot be the sole basis for a due-diligence decision.
k: The register sorts flagged names into several buckets, including one specifically for suspicious virtual-asset trading platforms.
Suspicious virtual asset trading platforms heading
Recent virtual-asset entries are dominated by look-alike domains copying a licensed platform's brand name, suggesting active phishing/impersonation campaigns rather than new unlicensed exchanges.
Suspicious virtual asset trading platforms table, entries dated Jul-Sep 2026
A separate 'unlicensed entities' bucket includes at least one digital-token-related fund/issuance name.
Unlicensed entities table, 'Vajra Fund / Vajra Issuance Limited' row
The page states each name is described only under headings such as 'type' and 'add date'; no reasoning or evidence is published alongside a listing.
table column headers throughout

t: HKIB Annual Banking Conference: Bank of Tomorrow: Transform to Excellence – Regulatory Update by HKMA
sl: HKMA · HKIB Annual Banking Conference: Bank of Tomorrow: Transform to… (2026)
s: This is Deputy Chief Executive Arthur Yuen's slide deck for a 25 September 2026 regulatory keynote. It is structured around four themes: governing agentic AI, engineering technology resilience, building trusted tokenisation, and fostering data excellence. On tokenisation, it presents the Supervisory Incubator for DLT as the launchpad for business-model transformation. It raises the open question of which roles banks can play as trusted intermediaries alongside smart contracts and AI agents. On resilience, it reports a first Quantum Preparedness Index score of 2.3 out of 10, with a target of full sectoral readiness by 2030. It also reports GenAI Sandbox++ growth to 36 use cases across 30 institutions and 27 tech partners.
w: This signals HKMA's current supervisory priorities on AI governance, quantum-readiness timelines and tokenisation roles for banks, ahead of formal circulars. The accountability principle -- 'delegating authority does not delegate accountability' -- is directly relevant to any bank deploying agentic AI in digital-asset workflows.
k: The deck sets out an AI action spectrum from 'Assist', which retrieves information, through 'Recommend' and 'Decide', to 'Act', which carries out actions using approved tools. It makes clear that handing authority to AI systems doesn't hand off accountability too. The Board and senior management stay answerable throughout the whole action chain.
slide 5 & 7

The GenAI Sandbox programme grew across three cohorts. The 2024 first cohort of GenAI Sandbox had 10 banks, 4 tech partners and 15 use cases. The 2025 second cohort of GenAI Sandbox had 20 banks, 14 tech partners and 27 use cases. The 2026 first cohort of the renamed GenAI Sandbox++ had 30 financial institutions, 27 tech partners and 36 use cases, reflecting a shift toward cross-sector agentic AI end-to-end processes.
slide 6

HKMA's first Quantum Preparedness Index (QPI) score is 2.3 out of 10. Banks that have transition plans report an expected implementation time of 5.6 years, against an HKMA objective of full sectoral readiness by 2030.
slide 11

Banks should secure their own and critical service providers' cyber fundamentals, and frontier AI-driven cyber risks should not be underestimated even as cyber risk management fundamentals remain the 'gold standard'.
slide 10
The Supervisory Incubator for DLT is presented as a 'launchpad' enabling real-value, real-transaction business-model transformation trials for banks.
slide 14

The deck poses an open question on 'who is authorised to move value' in a tokenised ecosystem involving smart contract guardrails, trusted transaction rails and AI agents. This frames potential bank roles as still under exploration.
slide 15

Data Excellence is framed around a 'GRID' model: Granularity, Reliability, Ingenuity, Discoverability. Granular Data Reporting (GDR) 3.0 is aimed at moving from aggregated template-based reporting to data-point-centric submissions, described as 'report once, use multiple'.
slide 17-18
95% fintech adoption was reported among surveyed banks, but 41% cited high-quality data as an adoption challenge.
slide 17
rg: Slide deck with minimal running text; review slides 5-7 (AI governance and accountability), 10-11 (cyber and quantum) and 14-15 (tokenisation), which carry the substantive content. Slides 1-4 and 16-19 are largely agenda and branding.

t: Review of the Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners
sl: HKMA · Review of the Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners (2026)
s: The HKMA reviewed the ECF, the bank staff qualification framework launched in 2014 with ten workstreams including Compliance, Fintech, AML/CFT and Cybersecurity. It proposes five changes: a single common Core Level for all practitioners, one consolidated Professional Level qualification per workstream, and shorter experience requirements. It also proposes letting practitioners keep certificates after changing roles if continuing training is met, and fewer overlapping qualifications. Industry feedback gathered through HKAB and HKIB committees was broadly supportive but stressed smooth transition. A three-phase roadmap runs from mid-2028 to 2030, with HKIB to set transition arrangements and courses and the HKMA to issue new ECF guidance. Specific competency standards will be revised in a later phase.
w: Relevant to planning qualifications for digital asset compliance staff: the separate Fintech/DLT certificates will be merged and certificates will become portable. No near-term compliance obligation arises.
k: The review follows the August 2025 'Capacity Building for Future Banking, 2026-2030' study and its ASCEND action plan.
Executive summary, p.5
Core Level becomes one common, non-workstream module; completing it also gives HKIB Certified Banker Stage I.
Enhancement 2, pp.6, 16
Each of the ten workstreams (including Fintech and Compliance) will have one consolidated Professional Level qualification.
Enhancements 1 and 5, pp.6-7, 19
Experience: one year at an AI in Hong Kong for Core; three years for Professional, at least two in the workstream.
Enhancement 3, p.18
Holders may keep certificates after moving roles, provided they meet continuing professional development (CPD) requirements.
Enhancement 4, p.18
Direct entry to the Professional Level without first taking Core will be allowed.
Figure 3, p.8; Box 1, p.21
Today the Fintech workstream alone has six separate qualifications, including one on distributed ledger technology.
Figure 4, p.14
Implementation is phased from mid-2028 to 2030: HKIB transition arrangements and new courses, and new HKMA ECF guidance.
Section 4, Figure 5, p.23
rg: Read the executive summary (pp.5-8) and roadmap (p.23); skip methodology.

t: The Chief Executive's 2026 Policy Address
sl: Government · The Chief Executive's 2026 Policy Address (2026)
s: This is the Chief Executive's annual policy speech to the legislature, setting government priorities across many areas. Within the finance chapter, it lists a cluster of digital-asset initiatives that regulators and market bodies are pursuing over the coming years. These include a test of putting Exchange Fund Bills on a distributed ledger, and a new digital-asset settlement platform at the clearing house CMU OmniClear. They also include wider bond tokenisation work, and a blockchain-based tokenisation platform at the exchange operator. It also flags planned moves to widen virtual-asset licensing coverage, let licensed trading venues offer regulated stablecoins, and expand tokenised bank deposits and a wholesale digital-currency settlement pilot. A separate customs-led programme will build systems to analyse digital-asset transactions for anti-money-laundering purposes by 2029.
w: None of this creates a binding rule yet -- it is a statement of government direction, so no immediate compliance action is required. It does flag several workstreams a compliance head should put on a watchlist. These include wider virtual-asset licensing and stablecoin trading permissions for licensed venues, and a new SFC custody surveillance system that will touch custodians the bank may rely on. It also flags the central bank's own tokenised-deposit and wholesale digital-currency pilots that the bank's treasury or product teams may be asked to join.
k: The central bank will trial running Exchange Fund Bills on distributed-ledger technology by the end of the year, aimed at letting banks manage these instruments around the clock.
para 35(ii)
A cross-agency group will start a second round of legal review on how distributed-ledger technology can be used in capital markets, working with the finance bureau.
para 35(iii)
The clearing entity CMU OmniClear will stand up a new digital-asset platform this year to handle issuance and settlement of digital bonds in one place.
para 35(iv)
The stock exchange operator is building a blockchain platform covering several asset types, already used for carbon credits, and will add tokenised commodity warehouse receipts next year.
para 46(v)
The securities regulator will widen virtual-asset licensing coverage and put out clearer rules so virtual-asset firms know what compliance is expected of them.
para 49(i)
The securities regulator will update its rules for tokenised investment products so licensed venues can offer tokenised gold and similar real-world assets, plus new product types.
para 49(ii)
The securities regulator plans to let licensed virtual-asset trading venues offer regulated stablecoins, and let those tokens be used to settle tokenised money-market funds.
para 49(iii)
The central bank intends to add round-the-clock settlement using a wholesale digital-currency pilot (EnsembleTX) by roughly year-end, and keep looking for new uses of tokenised bank deposits.
para 50

The securities regulator will begin operating a system to watch over digital-asset custody arrangements sometime in the year's second half. It will also switch on a separate big-data surveillance tool for market abuse and money laundering in 2027.
para 51(iii)
The central bank will keep testing new uses for tokenised deposits, including a Mainland trade-finance pilot meant to finish transactions before year-end.
para 99

Customs authorities plan a second phase, targeted for 2029, of two new systems: one to analyse digital-asset transactions and one for anti-money-laundering analytics. These feed into a wider financial-crime data platform.
Annex (I) New Indicators, item 209
rg: Read paragraphs 34-52, pp.22-28, the fintech and capital-markets tokenisation measures, and Annex (I) New Indicators, item 209, p.112, the AML digital-asset analytics system. Skip the remaining roughly 370 paragraphs on national security, housing, healthcare and other non-financial topics.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC)
sl: HKMA · Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) (2026)
s: This is the central bank's standing web page pulling together its whole central-bank digital currency workstream. It walks through the wholesale line of work, starting with an early proof of concept in 2017. This runs through joint cross-border trials with Thailand, a wider multi-country bridge project, and a tokenised-deposit initiative called Project Ensemble. It then covers a separate retail-facing strand, exploring a possible Hong Kong dollar digital currency for individuals and firms, including two rounds of public feedback and two pilot phases. The page states plainly that the authority has not yet decided whether or when to launch a retail digital currency. It will instead put its near-term effort into the wholesale, institutional side. It links out to the underlying reports, whitepapers and pilot summaries that give the detail behind each project name.
w: This page is the compliance head's map of every named HKMA digital-money initiative the bank may be asked to join or reference. It confirms there is still no live retail digital Hong Kong dollar and no firm launch date, so no new consumer-facing obligations arise from it yet. It does flag that tokenised deposits and cross-border wholesale settlement are the areas moving fastest, which is where the bank's treasury and payments teams are most likely to be approached next.
k: The authority is putting near-term priority on a digital currency built for banks and other institutions rather than one for consumers. It is keeping the option open to extend it to retail use later.
para 1 (e-HKD for financial institutions intro)

The wholesale work began in 2017 as a proof of concept with the three banknote-issuing banks, then extended cross-border with Thailand. It later added mainland China, the UAE and the BIS innovation arm, under the name mBridge.
Project Inthanon-LionRock / Project mBridge sections

A newer strand, Project Ensemble, launched in 2024 to build shared settlement rails for tokenised bank deposits and other tokenised assets. It moved from a sandbox into a live pilot called Ensemble TX, with named participating banks.
Project Ensemble / Ensemble TX sections

An architecture community of market participants was set up in 2024 to help agree common technical standards. This is so that tokenised deposits, tokenised assets and any future digital Hong Kong dollar can work together.
Project Ensemble Architecture Community section

On the retail side, two rounds of market feedback and two pilot phases with industry were completed, with reports in 2023 and 2025. The authority then concluded that, for now, the bigger near-term value lies in the wholesale space rather than a retail digital Hong Kong dollar.
e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 1 / Phase 2 sections

No decision has been taken on whether, or when, a retail digital Hong Kong dollar would actually be launched. Preparatory legal, policy and technical groundwork is being completed instead, expected by the first half of 2026.
'Policy Stance and Three-Rail Approach' section

The authority also ran two earlier joint research projects on a possible retail digital currency with the Bank for International Settlements and other central banks. One project looked at a two-tier prototype, and the other at giving private firms direct access to a central-bank ledger.
'Collaborative Projects' section (Project Aurum, Project Sela)
rg: Read the wholesale and retail section headers and their opening paragraphs first. Skip the speech and press-release listings and the academic expert-group member table at the bottom, which are not substantive.

t: SFC-HKMA Joint Survey on the Sale of Non-exchange-traded Investment Products 2025
sl: HKMA/SFC · SFC-HKMA Joint Survey on the Sale of Non-exchange-traded Investment… (2026)
s: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) run this survey each year. It measures sales of unlisted investment products by licensed corporations (LCs) and by banks registered as registered institutions (RIs) during 2025. It covers sales to non-professional investors, individual professional investors and some corporate professional investors. Total sales rose 63% to a record HK$9.9 trillion, and RIs made 62% of them. Funds and structured products drove the growth, and money market funds were the most popular fund type. Online channels reached 21% of sales. The survey excludes exchange-traded funds (ETFs), listed products and bank-issued currency and interest-rate linked instruments. It reports no virtual asset product category.
w: Registered institutions made 62% of unlisted investment product sales in 2025. This survey shows the scale and the online shift of the bank wealth channel. The regulators say they use the data to spot risks in intermediaries' selling (para 2).
k: The survey covers 2025 sales by 2,611 surveyed firms (2,502 LCs and 109 RIs), with over 99% responding; 67 RIs reported selling investment products.
para 1, 6
Exchange-traded funds, listed securities, insurance products and bank-issued currency and interest-rate linked instruments sold by RIs are outside the survey.
para 4
Total transaction value rose 63% to HK$9.9 trillion; RIs accounted for 62% and LCs 38%.
para 7
Collective investment schemes (CIS) rose 85% to HK$4.1 trillion and structured products 53% to HK$3.9 trillion, together over 80% of activity.
para 8
Clients completing at least one trade rose 33% to more than 1.6 million.
para 9
Online sales were 21% of the total, up from 17%, and 122 firms (including 36 RIs) sold through online platforms.
para 14, 51
Sales staff reached a record 20,126, including 13,808 relevant individuals at RIs.
para 24

t: Digital Banks (list of digital banks, as at 31 August 2026)
sl: HKMA · Digital Banks (list of digital banks, as at 31… (2026)

The webpage defines a digital bank as one that delivers banking services mainly or only through the internet or other electronic channels. It says digital banks follow the same supervisory requirements as conventional banks. Some requirements are adapted to their business models on a risk-based, technology-neutral basis. Digital banks were earlier called virtual banks, and the HKMA renamed its authorization guideline in October 2024.

t: Quarterly Report April-June 2026
sl: SFC · Quarterly Report April-June 2026 (2026)
s: This Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) quarterly report covers 1 April to 30 June 2026, the first quarter of its 2026-27 financial year. On digital assets, it reports 13 licensed virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs), with six more applications under review. It reports 11 virtual asset (VA) spot exchange-traded funds (ETFs) with a combined value of US$451 million. Fifteen tokenised retail products held HK$10.3 billion in their tokenised classes. In May 2026, the SFC and the Government's Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) published joint conclusions on regulating VA advisory and management services. The SFC says it aims to put a bill for the VA dealing, custody, advisory and management regimes into the Legislative Council (LegCo) in 2026. It also notes an April pilot that lets tokenised SFC-authorised funds trade on licensed VATPs.

t: Circular to licensed corporations, SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities Mitigating risks in receiving deposits through simplified eDDA arrangements
sl: SFC · licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities Mitigating… (2026)
s: The SFC highlights risks in licensed firms' use of simplified Electronic Direct Debit Authorisation (eDDA) arrangements for receiving client trading-account deposits. Under simplified eDDA, the firm, as payee, initiates a client's bank debit setup based on client-provided pre-authorisation, rather than the client initiating it via their own bank. Key risks are impersonation/unauthorised eDDA setup using stolen bank details, and financial exposure from indemnities the firm gives its bank against claims from fraudulent or erroneous setups. The circular requires firms to review their simplified-eDDA arrangements, assess risk, and implement mitigation measures before processing new setup requests, including verifying bank account ownership (e.g. via a one-off small-value transfer) and verifying identification information consistency, declining/withholding processing on unresolved red flags (e.g. deposits immediately converted to virtual assets and withdrawn), imposing transaction limits or withholding periods, and disclosing eDDA settings to clients with their consent. Where risks cannot be adequately mitigated, firms should switch to alternative deposit arrangements.
w: This circular binds SFC-licensed corporations and VASPs as eDDA payees, not the bank as the account-holding institution. A compliance head should treat its red-flag list -- especially rapid VA conversion after a new eDDA setup -- as a template for the bank's own deposit-fraud monitoring. This is because the bank's customer accounts are the ones being debited.
k: Under simplified eDDA, the licensed firm, as payee, initiates the setup request based on client-provided pre-authorisation and bank details, rather than the client initiating via their own bank (standard eDDA). Firms bear primary responsibility for ensuring proper authorisation where the payer bank does not require account-owner confirmation.
paras 2-6
Firms may be required to indemnify their bank against losses from fraudulent or erroneous eDDA setup requests/deposits.
para 5

Before processing new simplified eDDA setup requests, firms should ascertain bank account ownership. This can be done by assessing the payer bank's authentication process, or via a one-off small-value transfer verified against the account holder's name. Firms should also verify identification information consistency with firm records.
para 10

Firms should decline or withhold processing where verification cannot be satisfied or red flags are detected. Red flags include repeated setup failures, frequent or large deposits without rationale, and deposits inconsistent with client profile. They also include a new eDDA setup followed by whitelisting a new VA wallet address, or vice versa, and deposits quickly converted to virtual assets and withdrawn.
para 11

Suspicious transactions must be promptly investigated and, where warranted, reported to the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit or Anti-Deception Coordination Centre (HKPF). They must also be notified to the SFC per Code of Conduct para 12.5 or VATP Guidelines para 16.7, where applicable.
para 11, footnotes 7-8

Clients onboarded via 'online onboarding using a designated bank account in Hong Kong' should not have their initial deposit accepted via simplified eDDA. This is unless the firm can confirm the account owner has given their consent to that setup.
para 10, footnote 5
Firms should consider supplementary measures such as transaction amount/frequency limits, withholding periods after deposits, and step-up authentication.
para 12
Where risks cannot be adequately mitigated, firms should switch to other ways of taking deposits, such as standard eDDA or bank transfers.
para 13
Firms should disclose eDDA settings (limits, expiry) to clients, obtain consent, and remind clients to monitor their linked bank accounts for irregularities.
paras 14-15
rg: Read paras 1-6 for the mechanism and risk, then paras 9-13, the operative risk-assessment and mitigation requirements, as the core compliance content. Paras 14-17 are disclosure and administrative wrap-up.

t: FSTB responds to media enquiries regarding preferential tax regime for carried interest
sl: FSTB · FSTB responds to media enquiries regarding preferential tax regime… (2026)
s: This reply of 12 August 2026 from the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) was republished on the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) website. It explains the carried interest part of the 2026 tax bill on funds, family offices and carried interest. The bill proposes that the concession cover other profits of eligible funds, not only private equity. A business trading with its own capital for its own account is not a fund, so pay from it would not qualify. Eligible carried interest must be linked to fund performance, set by the fund's governing agreement and non-discretionary. It must be earned for investment management services in Hong Kong. The Legislative Council (LegCo) Bills Committee had finished clause-by-clause scrutiny. The Government aimed to resume the second reading debate in the second half of 2026. If passed, the measures would apply from the 2025/26 year of assessment.
w: It confirms the bill was still before LegCo in August 2026. It also shows the Government separates funds from own-account trading businesses for this tax concession.
k: The carried interest concession would cover other profits of eligible funds, not just private equity.
para 3
A business trading or holding assets with its own capital for its own account is not a fund, so its staff pay would not qualify.
para 3
Eligible carried interest must depend on fund performance, follow the governing agreement and be non-discretionary, and be earned for investment management services provided in Hong Kong.
para 4
Clause-by-clause examination was complete, and the Government targeted resuming second reading in the second half of 2026.
para 6
If passed, the measures would apply from the 2025/26 year of assessment, and the IRD would issue administrative guidance where needed.

t: Digital Bond Grant Scheme
sl: HKMA · Digital Bond Grant Scheme (2026)
s: This is a one-page HKMA summary flyer for the Digital Bond Grant Scheme (DBGS), a subsidy for issuing bonds on distributed ledger technology (DLT) in Hong Kong. It states it is for reference only, and points to a separate full Guideline for binding terms. A bond meeting only the basic conditions -- issued in Hong Kong, plus either genuine local DLT-team presence or issuance on the CMU's own DLT platform -- qualifies for a half grant. That half grant is up to HK$1.25 million, covering half of eligible costs. Meeting four extra conditions as well raises the cap to a full HK$2.5 million grant. Those conditions are an independent DLT platform provider, a minimum HK$1 billion issuance size, and at least five unrelated investors at issuance. The last condition is a listing on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong or an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP). Eligible costs named are Hong Kong-based DLT platform, legal, listing, arranger and audit fees, plus CMU lodging and clearing fees.
w: A bank arranging, underwriting or issuing tokenised/digital bonds in Hong Kong can weigh this cost subsidy in DLT-platform and listing-venue choices. Compliance must still check the full Guideline, not captured in this text, for binding eligibility and application terms before relying on the flyer's figures.
k: The scheme reimburses half of eligible issuance costs, capped at HK$1.25 million, once only the basic conditions are met.
p.1 (flyer text, left column)
A higher cap of HK$2.5 million applies only if the basic conditions and all four additional conditions are satisfied.
p.1 (flyer text, right column)
One basic condition is that the bond is issued in Hong Kong.
p.1, 'Basic Requirements' (a)
The other basic condition, met either way, is that the DLT development/operations team has a real Hong Kong footprint, or the bond runs on the CMU's own DLT platform.
p.1, 'Basic Requirements' (b)
An additional condition requires the DLT platform provider to be unrelated to (not an associate of) the bond issuer.
p.1, 'Additional Requirements' (a)
Another additional condition sets a minimum issuance size of HK$1 billion equivalent.
p.1, 'Additional Requirements' (b)
A further additional condition requires at least five investors at issuance who are not connected to the issuer or the DLT platform provider.
p.1, 'Additional Requirements' (c)
The last additional condition requires listing either on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong or on an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform.
p.1, 'Additional Requirements' (d)
Costs the grant can reimburse span Hong Kong-based DLT platform, legal, arranger and audit fees, exchange/VATP listing fees, and CMU fees for lodging and clearing the bond.
p.1, 'Eligible Expenses'
rg: The whole one-page flyer is short enough to read in full; do not treat it as the authoritative source — the linked full Guideline (not in this text) governs actual applications.

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism (1) FATF Statement on High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action (2) FATF Statement on Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring (3) Outcomes from the FATF Plenary, 17-19 June 2026
sl: SFC · licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities -… (2026)
s: This is a routine SFC anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) relay of the Financial Action Task Force's (FATF) 19 June 2026 statements. It covers the Call for Action list: countermeasures against North Korea and Iran, and extra due diligence for Myanmar. It also covers the Increased Monitoring list: Bosnia and Herzegovina and Iraq added; Algeria and Namibia removed. It also relays selected results from the FATF Plenary of 17-19 June 2026. These include a new report on public/private information-sharing partnerships, and a public consultation on cross-border payment transparency guidance under Recommendation 16, closing 21 August 2026. They also include a report on terrorist financing through social media, messaging, and streaming platforms, and a coming report on underground banking and hawala misuse. Further results are the seventh targeted update on how FATF's virtual asset and Virtual Asset Service Provider (VASP) standards are being applied. There is also a new targeted report on money-laundering, terrorist-financing, and proliferation-financing risk in decentralised finance (DeFi) platforms. Licensed corporations, VASPs, and associated entities are reminded to apply enhanced due diligence and the special high-risk-jurisdiction rules in the AML Guideline.
w: Most of this is a routine jurisdictional-risk update for AML/CFT screening. But the item on the coming FATF virtual asset and DeFi reports flags future SFC or HKMA guidance that a bank's digital-asset AML program should watch for.
k: FATF calls for countermeasures against North Korea and Iran, and for due diligence proportionate to risk in Myanmar's case. This has been in place since October 2022, with countermeasures to be considered if there is no progress by October 2026.
section (1)
FATF's Increased Monitoring list was updated: Bosnia and Herzegovina and Iraq were added; Algeria and Namibia were removed.
section (2)

Firms are reminded to pay particular attention and take extra care with business relationships and transactions tied to higher-risk jurisdictions. They should apply the special high-risk rules under paragraphs 4.9 and 4.13 of the AML Guideline.
final substantive para, footnote 10

The FATF Plenary, held 17-19 June 2026, approved a seventh targeted update on how its virtual asset and VASP standards are being applied. It also approved a new targeted report on DeFi platforms' money-laundering, terrorist-financing, and proliferation-financing risk, both due to be published later.
section (3)(e)
A public consultation on new guidance for cross-border payment transparency under Recommendation 16 closes on 21 August 2026.
section (3)(b)
rg: This is a routine FATF list relay. The jurisdiction lists (sections 1-2) can be skimmed for country names and changes. Section (3)(e), on the VA/VASP and DeFi FATF reports, is the only forward-looking item of note for digital-asset purposes.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - EvergreenHub: Navigating Bond Tokenisation  Digital Bond Knowledge Repository
sl: HKMA · EvergreenHub: Navigating Bond Tokenisation  Digital Bond Knowledge Repository (2026)
s: EvergreenHub is HKMA's reference repository on Project Evergreen and Hong Kong's tokenised bond market. It recounts three Government tokenised green bond issuances: the Feb 2023 proof-of-concept and the Feb 2024 first multi-currency digital bond. The third is the Nov 2025 record HK$10bn issuance integrating e-CNY/e-HKD settlement. It also lists ongoing HKMA efforts: consistent tokenised government bond supply, financial infrastructure interoperability, and the Tokenised Bond Expert Group. Other efforts include the DLT legal-framework review with FSTB, and the Digital Bond Grant Scheme, a subsidy of up to HK$2.5 million per eligible digital bond issuance.
w: This is a central reference hub for any bank considering acting as arranger, dealer or DLT platform provider on a tokenised bond in Hong Kong, including the DBGS subsidy scheme. It links to the underlying HKMA 'Bond Tokenisation in Hong Kong' report, separately registered as id a0b44be27c40, that sets out the legal deal-structuring analysis.
k: The Government's first tokenised green bond, in February 2023, proved compatibility with Hong Kong's legal and regulatory framework, and completed a full bond lifecycle on DLT, from issuance to redemption. It also shortened primary settlement from typical T+5 to T+1.
'Feb 2023' section
The second issuance, in February 2024, broke new ground as the world's first digital bond spanning multiple currencies (HKD, RMB, USD, EUR), worth around HK$6 billion equivalent.
'Feb 2024' section

The third issuance, in November 2025, set a new record, raising more than HK$10 billion across four currency tranches, with over HK$130 billion in subscriptions. It stretched tenor out to five years, and became the first to settle via tokenised central bank money -- e-HKD and e-CNY -- for its HKD and RMB tranches.
'Nov 2025' section
The HKMA's Digital Bond Grant Scheme pays up to HK$2.5 million per qualifying digital bond issued in Hong Kong (see separate registry entry for the Guideline, id 5a0563de8142).
'Digital Bond Grant Scheme' section
HKMA is exploring legal framework enhancements for DLT adoption in the fixed income market jointly with FSTB (see the related 29 June 2026 press release, id 279f10054c6e).
'Continue to scale tokenisation' section
rg: Read the three issuance summaries (2023/2024/2025) and the Digital Bond Grant Scheme paragraph; the page's substantial site-navigation boilerplate and long video/podcast list can be skipped.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers
sl: HKMA · Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers (2026)
s: This is the HKMA's standing web page for the stablecoin issuer licensing regime, which took effect on 1 August 2025 under the Stablecoins Ordinance. It links to the licensee register, the Explanatory Note on licensing, the Supervisory Guideline, the AML/CFT Guideline, and the full history of discussion papers, consultations and conclusions that preceded the regime. It also lists related press releases and speeches, including confirmation that the first licences were granted on 10 April 2026. The page is a navigation hub rather than a source of new obligations in itself.
w: This page is the fastest way for compliance to confirm who currently holds a Hong Kong stablecoin issuer licence, and to reach the current versions of the binding guidelines. This matters both for a bank's own potential issuance plans and for due diligence on any stablecoin issuer counterparty.
k: Issuing a fiat-referenced stablecoin has been a licensable activity in Hong Kong since 1 August 2025, when the Stablecoins Ordinance regime started operating.
body text, p.1
The page hosts the Register of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers, which the public can check for who currently holds a licence.
'Register of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers' section, p.1
Firms interested in applying are told to read the Explanatory Note and are invited to contact HKMA early for informal discussion before applying.
'Licensing for Stablecoin Issuers' section, p.1
HKMA has published a general supervisory guideline and a dedicated AML/CFT guideline setting out its regulatory expectations for licensees.
'Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers' section, p.1
The first stablecoin issuer licences were announced as granted on 10 April 2026, roughly eight months after the regime began.
press release list entry '10 Apr 2026', p.1
A sandbox for prospective stablecoin issuers was launched in March 2024 and its participants were announced in July 2024, well before the ordinance itself came into force.
press release list entries 'Mar 2024' and 'Jul 2024', p.1
rg: Read the whole page once; it is short. Use it mainly as an index to the Explanatory Note, the two guidelines and the register, rather than for substantive rules.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Complaints about Licensed Stablecoin Issuers
sl: HKMA · Complaints about Licensed Stablecoin Issuers (2026)
s: This HKMA consumer-facing webpage explains how a customer can complain about a licensed stablecoin issuer. It states that the Stablecoins Ordinance obliges every licensed issuer to run a redress process that meets set quality standards. It also names a designated officer at each issuer to receive complaints, with a contact list attached. If an issuer does not resolve a complaint, or misconduct is suspected, the customer can escalate to HKMA, which logs, reviews and refers the case, and writes back with an outcome. HKMA is explicit that it stays out of the underlying commercial dispute and does not order compensation. A 7-business-day first-response target and minimal personal-data rules are also set out. The page was last revised 13 July 2026.
w: It sets the baseline consumer-redress standard a bank must meet if it, or an affiliate, becomes a licensed stablecoin issuer. It confirms HKMA will not compel compensation, so any redress promise to customers is the issuer's own commitment, not a regulator-backed guarantee.
k: Under the Stablecoins Ordinance, each licensed stablecoin issuer must operate a complaints and redress process that is easy to reach, fairly run, timely and well-recorded.
Section 'Lodging Complaint with Licensed Stablecoin Issuers', p.1
Every licensed issuer has a named officer or unit responsible for taking in customer complaints, with contact details on a companion list.
Section 'Lodging Complaint with Licensed Stablecoin Issuers', p.1
A customer may bring a complaint to HKMA once the issuer has failed to fix it, or where the customer thinks staff or the issuer acted improperly.
Section 'Lodging Complaint with the HKMA', p.1
HKMA's process for an escalated case is: acknowledge receipt, assess it, pass it to the issuer as needed, then write to the complainant once handling is finished.
Section 'Lodging Complaint with the HKMA', p.1
HKMA will not second-guess an issuer's business choices, settle a dispute between issuer and customer, or direct an issuer to pay compensation.
Section 'Lodging Complaint with the HKMA', p.1
Giving personal data beyond name and a way to be contacted is optional for a complainant.
Section 'Lodging Complaint with the HKMA', p.1
HKMA targets a first substantive reply within 7 working days of validating a complaint or enquiry it receives.
Section 'Performance Pledge', p.1
rg: Read the two short body sections ('Lodging Complaint with Licensed Stablecoin Issuers' and 'Lodging Complaint with the HKMA'); skip the site navigation menu text at the top, which is boilerplate.

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Cybersecurity Webinar
sl: SFC · licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities -… (2026)
s: This is an administrative SFC circular inviting licensed corporations, SFC-licensed VASPs and associated entities to nominate staff to attend one of two free Cybersecurity Webinar sessions. Nominees could include management, compliance and IT staff, and system vendor representatives. The sessions, in English and Cantonese, ran on 30 July 2026 via Zoom, covering the cyber threat landscape and the SFC's expectations under its AI-enabled cyberattack circular. Enrolment (max three representatives per firm, one form per firm) was due by 24 July 2026 via a linked online form, allocated first-come-first-served.

k: SFC hosted two Cybersecurity Webinar sessions (English 15:00-16:15, Cantonese 16:30-17:45) on 30 July 2026 via Zoom.
page 1 body; Appendix
Webinar objectives: raise awareness of AI-enabled cyberattack threats and share SFC expectations/guidance/practical measures under the related circular.

Each firm should submit only one enrolment form, with a maximum of three representatives, by 24 July 2026, allocated first-come-first-served.

t: SFC mandates phishing-resistant authentication methods for internet brokers and VATPs to protect client accounts
sl: SFC · SFC mandates phishing-resistant authentication methods for internet brokers and… (2026)
s: This SFC press release announces the same-day circular (26EC35). It requires internet brokers and VATPs to adopt phishing-resistant authentication, such as passkeys or bound devices, for client login and device binding. They must also cease using OTPs within 12 months of the circular, or immediately for large internet brokers. It quotes Dr Eric Yip, SFC Executive Director of Intermediaries, on the need for holistic prevention, detection, response and education measures. It reiterates that senior management is ultimately accountable, and that the SFC will hold firms accountable for client losses from control lapses. It also reminds investors to adopt safe practices and report suspected compromises immediately.
w: This formally binds internet brokers and VATPs, not RIs, to phase out OTP authentication in favour of phishing-resistant methods. The bank should treat it as a benchmark for its own client-authentication controls, and as a due-diligence checkpoint for any VATP or internet-broker counterparty's account-security posture.
k: SFC circular requires internet brokers and VATPs to stop relying on OTPs when handling client login and device binding, because of the risks involved and the existence of sturdier alternatives.
para 2

Phishing-resistant login/device-binding authentication needs to go live promptly, and in any case within 12 months of when the circular was issued; large internet brokers are expected to move immediately.
para 3

Firms should also implement monitoring/surveillance for suspicious login, trading and withdrawal activity, notify clients of key account events, respond promptly to hacking incidents, and regularly alert clients to phishing risks.
para 4
SFC will hold senior management accountable for client losses arising from control lapses.
para 6
SFC first strongly encouraged (not mandated) LCs to stop using OTPs in its 6 February 2025 cybersecurity review circular; this July 2026 circular converts that into a mandatory requirement.
Notes
rg: Short press release (15 short paragraphs plus notes); read in full. It is a condensed public summary of circular 26EC35 (SFC ref 26EC35 / id 724f4d9f786e in this batch), which carries the full compliance detail.

t: Circular to licensed corporations and SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers Implementing (i) robust authentication methods to reduce and mitigate hacking risks from phishing attacks and (ii) adequate monitoring and surveillance measures to identify suspicious activities
sl: SFC · licensed virtual asset service providers Implementing (i) robust authentication… (2026)
s: The SFC expects internet brokers and SFC-licensed VASPs, currently meaning VATPs, to adopt phishing-resistant authentication, such as passkeys or robust device binding, for client login and device registration. It also expects them to implement effective monitoring and surveillance to detect suspicious account activity. This follows large-scale SMS phishing campaigns in 2025 that used man-in-the-middle attacks to intercept OTPs. OTP (email/SMS) is explicitly no longer considered phishing-resistant and should not be used for login/device-binding authentication. Firms are expected to implement robust authentication solutions no later than 8 July 2027, which is 12 months from the circular date, with large internet brokers expected to implement immediately. Other expected enhancements, such as monitoring and client awareness, should be made immediately or as soon as practicable. Clients generally may not bind more than three passkeys/devices without additional assessment. Senior management -- the Manager-in-Charge of Overall Management and Oversight, together with the MIC-IT -- is accountable. Firms failing to prevent large-scale unauthorised transactions after a hacking incident will be held accountable by the SFC for client losses. An Appendix gives detailed acceptable authentication examples including passkeys and device-binding verification methods.
w: This is a direct, dated cyber-governance expectation for the bank's SFC-licensed corporation or VASP entity. Named senior managers are accountable, and OTP should be phased out as a login factor. The SFC has stated it will hold the firm liable for client losses from hacking if controls are inadequate.
k: The SFC expects internet brokers and SFC-licensed VASPs to adopt robust, phishing-resistant authentication for client login and device binding, and to implement effective monitoring/surveillance for suspicious activity.
para 1
The SFC regards OTP (whether by email or SMS) as falling short of a phishing-resistant authentication method, and says firms should not rely on it for login or device-binding steps.
para 7
Passkeys (FIDO-certified, public-key based) and robustly-verified device binding are the two acceptable authentication methods described; existing bound devices need not be re-registered.
paras 5, 8
Generally, firms shouldn't let clients register above three passkeys, or above three devices, unless they've done extra checks for the request.
para 10
Session idle timeout should generally be limited to within 30 minutes and clients should not be allowed to disable session timeout, absent justified and monitored exceptions.
para 11

Internet brokers and VASPs are expected to alert clients right away about successful logins and other high-risk account activity. This covers logins from new devices, device binding, or passkey creation or revocation, using more than one communication channel.
para 13
Internet brokers and VASPs should report hacking incidents to the SFC immediately and conduct root cause analysis with remedial action.
para 18

Internet brokers and VASPs are expected to implement robust authentication solutions as soon as practicable, and no later than 8 July 2027, which is 12 months from the circular. Large internet brokers are expected to implement immediately.
para 21(c)
Firms unable to meet the 12-month implementation deadline should immediately notify their case officer-in-charge.
para 23

Senior management -- in particular the Manager-in-Charge of Overall Management and Oversight, together with the MIC-IT -- bears ultimate responsibility for overseeing these safeguards and keeping client accounts properly protected.
para 24

If a firm doesn't put in place sufficient controls to stop, catch and halt large-scale unauthorised transactions after a hacking incident, the SFC will hold that firm accountable. The firm will be held accountable for the resulting client losses.
para 25
rg: Read paras 1-3 (background and 2025 phishing incidents), and paras 21-25 (implementation timeline and management accountability), as most consequential. The Appendix's passkey and device-binding examples (paras 1-6) are useful implementation reference, but can be skimmed once the two acceptable methods are understood.

t: Asset and Wealth Management Activities Survey 2025
sl: SFC · Asset and Wealth Management Activities Survey 2025 (2026)
s: This is the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) annual survey of Hong Kong's asset and wealth management industry. It gives figures as at 31 December 2025 and was published in July 2026. Total assets under management (AUM) rose 20% to a record HK$42,202 billion. Net fund inflows rose 193% to HK$2,065 billion. Private banking and private wealth management, served by licensed corporations and by banks registered with the SFC, grew 24% to HK$12,945 billion. The report notes that SFC-authorised virtual asset (VA) funds may now stake, and that three VA spot exchange-traded funds (ETFs) were staking by December 2025. It also gives staff numbers, including 8,752 private banking and wealth staff reported by registered institutions (RIs).
w: This is the official sizing of the wealth market in which banks distribute funds, including VA funds and ETFs. It also gives staffing figures for registered institutions. The figures are survey data as at 31 December 2025, not forecasts.
k: Hong Kong's total assets under management rose 20% to HK$42,202 billion at end-2025, a record above the 2021 peak.
Section I, para 1
Net fund inflows rose 193% to HK$2,065 billion in 2025, the third straight year of growth.
Section I, para 1
Private banking and private wealth management assets, served by licensed corporations (LCs) and RIs, rose 24% to HK$12,945 billion, with net inflows up 79% to HK$686 billion.
Section I, para 5
After an April 2025 SFC update, authorised VA funds may stake. The SFC approved two VA spot ETFs for staking, and three were doing so by December 2025.
Section IV, para 28
Hong Kong-listed ETFs and leveraged and inverse products reached HK$618.7 billion market value at end-2025, up 33.7%.
Section IV, para 26
The report cites an InvestHK-commissioned study counting over 3,380 single-family offices at end-2025, with interest in digital assets among alternatives.
Section IV, paras 30-31 and fn 4
Firms licensed for asset management (Type 9) rose 7% to 2,358 and licensed individuals 5% to 15,747.
Section VI, paras 43-44
Industry headcount rose 5% to 56,557; about 51% of respondents plan to hire in the coming year.
Section VI, paras 46, 49
47 RIs reported private banking or wealth business, and RIs reported 8,752 staff in that segment.
Section VI, para 45 and fn 1, para 50

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - FSTB and HKMA to further unlock potential of distributed ledger technology in Hong Kong's fixed income market
sl: FSTB/HKMA · FSTB and HKMA to further unlock potential of distributed… (2026)
s: FSTB and HKMA announced conclusion of the first phase of a joint review on wider DLT adoption in Hong Kong's fixed income market. It found the existing legal and regulatory environment already flexible enough for tokenised bond issuances. The Companies Registry issued FAQs confirming a DLT-based register of debenture holders can satisfy Companies Ordinance record-keeping requirements. A second phase, starting in the second half of 2026, will examine legislative enhancements such as electronic execution of tokenised bond issuance documents. It will also look at concepts of possession and transfer for tokenised fixed income instruments.
w: Confirms a primary-source legal clarification -- DLT-based debenture registers satisfy Companies Ordinance record-keeping -- directly relevant to any bank acting as issuer, arranger or registrar for tokenised bonds. It also flags upcoming legislative changes on electronic execution and possession/transfer of tokenised instruments to track.
k: The Companies Registry issued FAQs confirming that a register of debenture holders maintained using DLT can be deemed to fulfil the record-keeping requirements of the Companies Ordinance (Cap. 622).
'Issuing clarifications on DLT record keeping' section

The review's first-phase findings conclude that Hong Kong already has legal and regulatory settings flexible enough to support tokenised bond issuances. This is shown by three landmark Government issuances and a growing number of corporate tokenised bond deals.
opening paragraph

A second phase of the review (second half of 2026) will examine legal enhancements including electronic execution of tokenised bond issuance documents (e.g. recognising electronic signatures for trust creation) and concepts of possession/transfer for tokenised fixed income instruments.
'Next phase' section

The Government's tokenised bond issuance in November 2025 was, at that point, the largest digital bond anywhere in the world. It was also the first to weave in tokenised central bank money -- specifically e-HKD and e-CNY -- as part of the settlement.
Eddie Yue quote
rg: Short release; read in full.

t: FSTB and HKMA to further unlock potential of distributed ledger technology in Hong Kong's fixed income market
sl: FSTB/HKMA · FSTB and HKMA to further unlock potential of distributed… (2026)
s: FSTB and HKMA concluded the first phase of a review into using distributed ledger technology (DLT) more widely for Hong Kong's fixed-income market. They found the existing legal and regulatory setup is already flexible enough for tokenised bond issuances. As an immediate step, the Companies Registry issued FAQs confirming that a DLT-maintained register of debenture holders satisfies the Companies Ordinance's record-keeping requirements. A second-phase legislative review starting in the second half of 2026 will examine electronic execution of tokenised bond issuance documents and legal concepts of possession/transfer for tokenised fixed-income instruments.

It also flags upcoming legal changes, such as electronic signatures and possession/transfer concepts, relevant to bond documentation and custody processes.
k: The Companies Registry issued FAQs confirming that a register of debenture holders maintained using distributed ledger technology satisfies the record-keeping requirements of the Companies Ordinance (Cap. 622).
section 'Issuing clarifications on DLT record keeping'

The review's first-phase finding is that Hong Kong already has legal and regulatory arrangements flexible enough to support tokenised bond issuances. This is shown by three government tokenised bond issuances and a rising volume of corporate issuance, including from Asian and Middle Eastern issuers.
section 'First-phase findings and enhancements'

A second-phase legislative review beginning in the second half of 2026 will examine electronic execution and signatures for tokenised bond and fund trust issuance documents. It will also examine legal concepts of possession and transfer for tokenised fixed-income instruments.

The most recent government tokenised bond issuance, in November 2025, was, back then, the largest digital bond in the world. It was also the first to weave in tokenised central bank money, in both e-HKD and e-CNY form.
quote from HKMA Chief Executive
rg: Read the whole release; it is short and entirely on-topic. The FAQ itself sits on the Companies Registry website (linked, not part of this text) and was not separately fetched.

t: LCQ11: Management of stablecoins
sl: Government · LCQ11: Management of stablecoins (2026)
s: A Legislative Council written question-and-answer session where the Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury describes how the government sees stablecoin risk to banks and the public. He confirms two bank-linked groups now hold stablecoin issuer licences and expects launches around mid-to-late 2026. He explains reserve-asset placement rules, cross-border enforcement steps against unlicensed issuers, and plans for a bill covering virtual-asset dealing, custody, advisory and management services later in the year.
w: Confirms which two licensed stablecoin issuers are entering the market and the government's reserve-asset and enforcement expectations. This is useful context for the bank's own due diligence on any issuer relationship, and for anticipating the incoming VA-services bill.
k: Two institutions with a banking background received HKMA stablecoin issuer licences, with market launch expected between mid and late 2026.
Reply, para 2
Licensed issuers must hold reserve assets such as bank deposits and high-quality liquid debt, placed with banks located in Hong Kong.

Only entities regulated under the Stablecoins Ordinance may lawfully offer stablecoins to the Hong Kong public; other acquisitions carry no statutory protection.
Reply, part (3)
The HKMA has been sending letters to unregulated stablecoin-offering businesses explaining legal requirements and may refer persistent cases to police or prosecutors.
Reply, part (3)
A bill to regulate virtual-asset dealing, custody, advisory and management providers, covering stablecoins among other tokens, is planned for introduction to the Legislative Council later this year.
Reply, part (3)

t: SFC Annual Report 2025-26
sl: SFC · SFC Annual Report 2025-26 (2026)
s: This Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) annual report covers the year to 31 March 2026. It reviews SFC work under its ASPIRe digital asset roadmap, which has five pillars: Access, Safeguards, Products, Infrastructure and Relationships. It records two joint consultations with the Government's Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB). The first was on licensing virtual asset (VA) dealing and custody providers. The second was on extending licensing to VA advisory and management, with a bill planned for 2026. New permissions include shared order books with overseas affiliates, affiliate market makers, staking and VA margin financing. With the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the SFC also issued guidance on off-platform trading. At year-end there were 12 licensed virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs), 11 VA spot exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and 13 tokenised retail products. Project Ensemble moved to its EnsembleTX pilot in November 2025.
w: This is the SFC's own year-end record of which VA activities are now allowed and how big the market is. Some items involve intermediaries, including banks, directly: the joint HKMA-SFC guidance on off-platform VA trading and on client subscriptions and redemptions paid in VAs. It also records the planned VA dealing and custody regimes and the EnsembleTX pilot for tokenised deposits.
k: The SFC and FSTB consulted in 2025 on licensing VA dealing and custody providers, then consulted in late 2025 on adding VA advisory and management, and plan a 2026 bill.
p.64, 'Access'; Strategic Priority 3, p.12
From November 2025 licensed VATPs may pool orders with overseas affiliates in a shared order book, and affiliates may act as market makers.
p.64, 'Increasing market accessibility'
Twelve VATPs were licensed at 31 March 2026, with seven applications under review, four from deemed applicants.
The SFC clarified minimum custody requirements for VATPs, covering governance, cold wallet set-up, use of outside providers and live threat monitoring.
p.65, 'Safeguards'
By 31 March 2026 there were 11 SFC-authorised VA spot ETFs, three permitted to stake through licensed VATPs, and two VATPs offering staking.
p.65, 'Products'
VA brokers may offer VA financing to securities margin clients with strong credit and collateral, subject to safeguards.
p.65, 'Products'
With the HKMA, the SFC issued guidance letting intermediaries use VATPs' off-platform trading services and clarifying subscriptions and redemptions paid in VAs.
p.65, 'Products'
VATPs may now list VAs for professional investors, and HKMA-licensed stablecoins, without a 12-month track record, and may distribute tokenised securities.
p.65, 'Products'
The Government confirmed that the stamp duty waiver for transfers of Hong Kong-listed ETFs extends to tokenised ETFs.
p.65, 'Driving tokenised products'

t: Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Preferential Tax Regimes for Funds, Family-owned Investment Holding Vehicles and Carried Interest) Bill 2026 gazetted
sl: Government · Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Preferential Tax Regimes for Funds, Family-owned… (2026)
s: This Government press release announces that a tax bill was published in the Gazette on 12 June 2026. The bill proposes wider tax breaks for privately offered funds, for family-owned investment holding vehicles (FIHVs) run by eligible single family offices, and for carried interest. It proposes a wider definition of fund, more qualifying investments, removal of the 5% cap on incidental transactions, and relaxed rules for special purpose entities. It also proposes better carried interest rules. The unified funds regime would gain a tax reporting mechanism and economic substance requirements. A Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) spokesperson said the changes would complement Hong Kong's development in areas including digital assets. First reading in the Legislative Council (LegCo) was set for 24 June 2026.
w: The bill proposes tax changes for Hong Kong funds, family-office vehicles and carried interest, and the FSTB links them to Hong Kong's digital asset development. As of 25 September 2026 it is a bill, not law.
k: The bill seeks better tax treatment for private funds, family-office FIHVs and fund managers' carried interest.

t: HKMC's HK$12 billion inaugural public digital bond issuance
sl: Other · HKMC's HK$12 billion inaugural public digital bond issuance (2026)
s: Hong Kong Mortgage Corporation (HKMC) announced pricing of its first-ever digital bond issuance, worth about HK$12 billion in total. It was split into three tranches: a 2-year piece of HK$6 billion, a 5-year piece of HK$2.5 billion, and a 3-year CNH tranche of CNH 3 billion. It was issued under HKMC's US$30 billion Medium Term Note Programme and priced on 10 June 2026. It is called the largest digital bond deal in the world so far, and the first from a Hong Kong public-sector issuer. The five-year HKD tranche also stands as the longest-tenor HKD digital bond to date. The bonds are digitally created and settled on the Central Moneymarkets Unit's (CMU) distributed ledger technology (DLT) platform, linked to Euroclear and Clearstream, using the HSBC Orion digital-assets platform. The settlement cycle was shortened from 5 to 3 business days. The annex lists full deal terms, including ratings, yields, listing venue, and the 16 banks acting as Joint Global Coordinators, Bookrunners, or Lead Managers.
w: This is informational rather than a source of obligations. A compliance head should note the operating model it sets: CMU's DLT platform and the shortened T+3 cycle. It is relevant if the bank acts as arranger or dealer on future digital bond deals.
k: HKMC's first digital bond issuance totals around HK$12 billion equivalent, priced 10 June 2026, under HKMC's US$30 billion Medium Term Note Programme.
para 1

It is called the world's biggest digital bond deal to date, and HKMC is the first Hong Kong public-sector body to issue digital bonds. The 5-year HKD tranche is the longest-tenor HKD digital bond ever.
para 2

The bonds are digitally created on a DLT platform that the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU) operates, and which also functions as their clearing and settlement system.
para 4

t: LCQ6: Development and regulation of stablecoins
sl: FSTB · LCQ6: Development and regulation of stablecoins (2026)
s: In this Legislative Council reply, the government confirmed the HKMA received 36 applications during the initial application window under the Stablecoins Ordinance. It granted licences to two entities in April 2026, with business launch of their regulated stablecoins expected around mid-2026. Officials stated the HKMA has begun engaging remaining applicants but has made no decision on further licence numbers or timing. They stressed the overall licensing threshold will stay high and that any additional licences will remain very limited in number. The two licensed issuers are already participating in HKMA's central bank digital currency and tokenised deposit pilots, including EnsembleTX. Their proposed use cases include enabling real-time on-chain tokenised-asset transactions.
w: This confirms the licensed stablecoin market will stay extremely narrow: 2 of 36 applicants so far, officially described as staying 'very limited'. This matters directly for counterparty concentration risk if the bank plans to distribute, hold, or settle in a Hong Kong-regulated stablecoin.
k: 36 applications were received by the HKMA during the initial application window under the Stablecoins Ordinance, of which two entities were granted licences in April 2026.
Reply, para 1

The two licensed issuers must complete technology-platform testing, reserve-asset management and safekeeping arrangements, price-stabilisation mechanisms and redemption arrangements before commercial launch. Government expects launch as early as mid-2026, based on the issuers' own plans.
Reply (1)

HKMA evaluates remaining stablecoin licence applicants against three criteria: practical and feasible use cases contributing to the ecosystem, and a robust and sustainable business model, including risk-management capability. The third criterion is compliance with Hong Kong and other relevant jurisdictions' laws.
Reply (2)

t: HKMA establishes Tokenised Bond Expert Group
sl: HKMA · HKMA establishes Tokenised Bond Expert Group (2026)
s: The HKMA announced the formation of a Tokenised Bond Expert Group (TBEG). It brings together industry representatives from financial institutions, legal advisers, financial infrastructure and technology providers, and industry associations. The purpose is to push forward the growth and scale-up of tokenised bonds in Hong Kong. The Expert Group held its first discussion session in May 2026, exchanging views on Hong Kong's legal and regulatory regime as applied to tokenised bond issuance and transactions. Feedback is feeding into HKMA's continuing collaboration with the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) to explore potential regime enhancements, which will be announced separately. The release also recaps HKMA's tokenised bond track record since a 2021 BIS Innovation Hub proof-of-concept. This includes three landmark government tokenised bond issuances: the 2023 green bond, the 2024 multi-currency bond, and the 2025 digital bond integrating e-CNY and e-HKD. It also covers ongoing initiatives such as the Digital Bond Grant Scheme and EvergreenHub knowledge repository.
w: This is context for a compliance head: it signals Hong Kong's tokenised bond regime is under active, industry-consultative review. This review will eventually shape the bank's role as issuer, dealer or infrastructure provider, but no concrete rule change exists yet.

t: SPM CRP-1: update on cryptoassets classification conditions
sl: HKMA · SPM CRP-1: update on cryptoassets classification conditions (2026)
s: CRP-1 sets extra conditions before a cryptoasset on a permissionless blockchain can be treated as Group 1 for capital. t: Circular to licensed corporations, SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities Enhanced cybersecurity measures to address evolving risks arising from artificial intelligence-enabled cyberattacks
sl: SFC · licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities Enhanced… (2026)
s: This SFC circular alerts licensed corporations, licensed VATPs and associated entities (licensed firms) to heightened cyberattack risk from frontier AI models. Such models can identify and chain vulnerabilities, execute multi-step autonomous attacks, and lower the barrier for phishing, social engineering and deepfake impersonation. It reminds firms that senior leaders, including the Manager-in-Charge of IT, carry ultimate responsibility for cybersecurity risk. It sets out five areas firms should review and strengthen: patching and vulnerability management, access and privilege controls (zero-trust design), and detection and monitoring. The other two areas are third-party supply chain risk management, and incident response and recovery. Firms using AI language models must also apply the core principles from the SFC's November 2024 generative-AI circular. They must also comply with notification requirements for high-risk AI use cases under the Securities and Futures (Licensing and Registration) (Information) Rules. An Appendix gives non-exhaustive illustrative examples of controls for each of the five areas.
w: This is addressed to LCs and SFC-licensed VASPs, not RIs, so it does not bind the bank directly. Its AI-enabled cyberattack guidance is still a useful benchmark for the bank's own cybersecurity framework, and a diligence reference when assessing a VATP counterparty's resilience.
k: Senior management, including the MIC-IT, bears ultimate responsibility for handling the firm's cybersecurity risk. The MIC-IT should make sure changes to the cybersecurity framework get properly reviewed, approved and rolled out promptly.
para 3
Licensed firms should assess preparedness for AI-enabled cyberattacks and address vulnerabilities, seeking IT security expert advice as necessary.
para 3

Firms should maintain an accurate, up-to-date technology asset inventory identifying externally exposed and business-critical components, updated enough for same-day prioritisation when new vulnerabilities emerge.
para 6

Firms should enforce least-privilege/zero-trust access design, treat external/untrusted inputs (apps, emails, documents, webpages) as potentially adversarial, and require maker-checker sign-off before carrying out high-impact actions.
paras 10-11

Firms using AI language models -- internal, group, third-party or open-source -- should ensure associated cyber risks are addressed per the November 2024 generative-AI circular. These risks include adversarial attacks, data leakage and system prompt override. Firms deploying such models for high-risk use cases must also meet the notification duties set out in the Securities and Futures (Licensing and Registration) (Information) Rules.
para 8, footnotes 3-5
Firms should strengthen third-party supply-chain risk governance, including initial/ongoing assessment of third-party service providers for AI-enabled cyberattack risk.
para 13
Firms should establish escalation/reporting mechanisms and pre-planned containment/exploit-interruption strategies, since AI-enabled attacks may outpace traditional detection-and-response.
para 15
LCs engaged in electronic trading and VATPs must back up their business records along with client and transaction data at least once a day.
para 17, footnote 8
Firms are required to give the SFC prompt notice of any material cybersecurity incident or attack, per Code of Conduct para 12.5(e) and VATP Guidelines paras 16.7(b)-(c).
para 18
The circular's Appendix sets out illustrative, non-exhaustive control measures for the five areas; firms should scale measures to their nature, scale, complexity and risk exposure.
para 3-19 framing; Appendix text not captured in the fetched source

t: Keynote Speech at Hong Kong Digital Finance Summit 2026
sl: HKMA · Keynote Speech at Hong Kong Digital Finance Summit 2026 (2026)
s: In this policy-framing keynote, the HKMA distinguishes three categories of digital asset: speculative crypto-assets (SFC's remit), tokenised real-world assets, and 'tokenised money' (CBDCs, tokenised bank deposits, stablecoins). It also sets out three HKMA responsibilities: providing central bank money in new forms, setting guardrails for private-sector innovation, and building interoperable common infrastructure. It reviews a decade of HKMA digital-money work, including e-HKD, mBridge, tokenised green bonds, the Stablecoins Ordinance and the April 2026 first two stablecoin licences, and Project Ensemble/EnsembleTX. It previews an upcoming Ensemble Use Case Report and Ensemble Taxonomy. It states HKMA now prioritises wholesale e-HKD over retail, and flags 'digital twin' reconciliation burden and platform fragmentation as the two main remaining structural challenges to tokenisation.
w: This is HKMA's clearest recent statement of its three-part regulatory philosophy for digital money, and its confirmation that wholesale e-HKD, not retail, is now the near-term priority. This should directly shape how a bank sequences its own tokenised-deposit, stablecoin and CBDC-interoperability roadmap and Project Ensemble engagement.
k: HKMA distinguishes three categories of digital asset: (1) speculative crypto-assets like Bitcoin, regulated by the SFC for investor protection and market integrity. The second is tokenisation of real-world assets, such as bonds, funds and receivables, which is a market-infrastructure question. The third (3) is 'tokenised money' -- CBDCs, tokenised commercial bank deposits and stablecoins -- which are new means of payment, not investment instruments.
'The Digital Finance Landscape' section

HKMA defines three responsibilities in digital finance: providing central bank money in new forms to anchor trust and singleness of money, and setting guardrails for responsible private-sector innovation. It also intends to build common, interoperable infrastructure as a public good.
'The Role for Central Banking Institution' section

Now that Phase 2 of the e-HKD Pilot Programme is done, HKMA judges that wholesale use cases matter more right now than retail ones for e-HKD. This is given how developed Hong Kong's retail payments already are.
'A Decade of Progress' section

The Government's third tokenised green bond issuance, in November 2025, raised roughly HK$10 billion in total across four currencies, drawing subscriptions above HK$130 billion. It was the world's first digital bond to use tokenised central bank money -- e-HKD and e-CNY -- for settlement.
'A Decade of Progress' section

HKMA confirms the April 2026 grant of stablecoin issuer licences to two entities, and states it expects regulated stablecoins to launch in Hong Kong within the next few months. It is keeping the licensing threshold high and the number of additional licences very limited.
'A Decade of Progress' section

In November 2025, Project Ensemble entered its pilot phase for real-value transactions, branded 'Ensemble TX'. This allows participating banks to settle tokenised assets against tokenised deposits on a delivery-versus-payment (DvP) basis.
'The third area—infrastructure' section
HKMA will soon publish an Ensemble Use Case Report and an Ensemble Taxonomy -- a common set of terms built jointly with the Ensemble Architectural Community -- to support interoperability standards.
'The Road Ahead' section

Most tokenised assets today follow a 'digital twin' model, where the off-chain register remains primary and the token is a mirrored claim. This delivers efficiency gains but relocates, rather than eliminates, reconciliation burden. The end-state goal is 'digitally native' issuance, where the token itself is the primary ownership record.
'The Road Ahead' section
The immediate next step for Ensemble TX is to extend it to support settlement of tokenised deposits in central bank digital currency, enabling continuous 24/7 settlement.
'The Road Ahead' section, closing paragraphs

Ensemble TX's initial infrastructure is built on the Ensemble Interoperability Layer, drawing on Hong Kong's existing RTGS system for interbank settlement. It is described as a pragmatic first step rather than the end-state architecture.
'The Road Ahead' section
rg: Read 'The Digital Finance Landscape' and 'The Role for Central Banking Institution' sections first for the policy taxonomy. Then read 'A Decade of Progress' for concrete milestones and 'The Road Ahead' for the digital-twin and fragmentation challenges; the speech has no page or paragraph numbering.

t: Circular on provision of Relevant Stablecoin service by virtual asset trading platforms and licensed corporations
sl: SFC · provision of Relevant Stablecoin service by virtual asset trading… (2026)
s: This SFC circular clarifies how the VATP Guidelines and the Joint Circular on intermediaries' virtual asset activities apply to 'Relevant Stablecoins' - specified stablecoins under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) issued by an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer and authorised under that licence. Because Relevant Stablecoins are already subject to HKMA reserve-backing and redemption oversight, the SFC removes or relaxes several VATP/intermediary requirements that otherwise apply to virtual assets generally. The liquidity/index requirements for retail-tradable tokens, the client virtual-asset-knowledge assessment (for Relevant-Stablecoin-only clients). Inclusion of Relevant Stablecoin holdings in a client's virtual asset exposure limit. Suitability requirements still apply when a VATP or LC solicits or recommends a Relevant Stablecoin. The circular also permits licensed corporations to partner directly with HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers (not only VATPs) and to hold client Relevant Stablecoins in segregated accounts at the issuer itself. Removes the prior requirement that retail VA dealing go only through an omnibus account with a platform not subject to a professional-investor-only condition. Revised VATP licensing conditions and updated Appendix 6/7 terms and conditions (clean and tracked-changes versions) are attached.
w: This directly shapes how the bank, as a Registered Institution, can onboard, disclose, and distribute HKMA-licensed Relevant Stablecoins. Including a new option to custody them directly at the issuer -- while confirming suitability rules still apply whenever the bank solicits or recommends one.
k: Relevant Stablecoins are specified stablecoins under s.4 of the Stablecoins Ordinance issued by an HKMA-licensed issuer and authorised under that licence. The circular does not apply to other stablecoins.
para 2
The retail-tradability liquidity and index requirements (VATP Guidelines paras 7.7-7.8. Joint Circular paras 20(a)(iv) and 28) need not be applied to Relevant Stablecoins.
para 4
VATPs and LCs must disclose material information on a Relevant Stablecoin's stabilisation mechanism and redemption arrangements.
para 5

VA-knowledge assessment is not required for clients who are provided Relevant-Stablecoin-only services. Firms must still assess a non-Relevant-Stablecoin-only client's VA knowledge even if that client ends up trading only Relevant Stablecoins.
para 6, footnote 7
Client holdings of Relevant Stablecoins need not be counted toward the client's virtual asset exposure limit.
para 7

A Relevant Stablecoin is treated as a non-complex product. If a VATP/LC solicits or recommends one, ordinary suitability requirements apply and commission rebates must not be the primary basis for the recommendation.
para 8
Licensed corporations may now partner directly with an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer (not only a VATP) to provide dealing services in that issuer's Relevant Stablecoin.
para 9
Joint Circular paragraph 20(a)(iii). Required retail VA dealing via an omnibus account with a platform not subject to a professional-investor-only condition, is removed.
para 10, footnote 11

Licensed corporations may now hold clients' Relevant Stablecoins in segregated accounts maintained with the relevant HKMA-licensed issuer itself (which provides custody with client-asset segregation). Not only with VATPs or authorized financial institutions.
para 11

VATPs and LCs don't need the SFC's prior written approval to admit a Relevant Stablecoin for trading. They must give the SFC written notice ahead of time whenever they plan to admit, suspend or remove one.
para 12
Firms must review and update internal policies, procedures and disclosures to comply with the circular.
para 13

Revised VATP licensing condition removes the 12-month track record requirement for Relevant Stablecoins and disapplies VATP Guidelines paras 7.7(b). 7.8 and 16.4 to them. Para 9.4 is disapplied where a licensee serves Relevant-Stablecoin-only clients.
Appendix 1, amended licensing condition
