t: Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions providing virtual asset dealing services and virtual asset advisory services
sl: HKMA/SFC · Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for… (2026)
s: This May 2026 consolidated text sets the conditions the SFC imposes (in consultation with the HKMA for banks) on firms that broker or advise on VAs. Part I covers introducing clients and dealing through omnibus accounts, and Part II covers advice. The May 2026 edits add HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers alongside SFC-licensed platforms as permitted venues for licensed stablecoins. They also create lighter paths for 'stablecoin-only' clients: no VA knowledge test, no VA exposure limit, no generic VA risk warnings, and suitability based on the client's use case. It also embeds VA financing as defined in the SFC's 11 February 2026 circular, with statement, record and custody provisions for VA collateral. Other rules such as client identity, contract notes, custody through segregated accounts, staking, record keeping and reporting of material breaches continue.
w: These conditions are imposed on a bank's SFC registration and are what HKMA and SFC examiners test for VA brokerage and advice. Compliance should update onboarding, suitability, disclosure and custody procedures for stablecoin-only accounts and for VA financing.
k: Introducing agents may only introduce clients to SFC-licensed platforms, or (new) directly to an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer for that issuer's own coins. They must not relay orders or hold client assets.

Omnibus dealing is allowed only through accounts with SFC-licensed platforms, or with the licensed issuer for its own stablecoin.
Part I, omnibus conditions (a), p.6; T&C para 4.1, p.10
Clients normally must be the firm's Type 1 (securities dealing) clients, but an RI offering stablecoin-only dealing need not limit service to Type 1 clients.
Part I, omnibus conditions (b)(i)-(ii), p.6
Retail clients may trade only VAs the platform or issuer offers to retail investors.
para 4.1, p.10
Trades need pre-funding unless the firm does securities margin financing and these terms sit on its Type 1 registration (enabling VA financing).
No yield arrangements on client VAs other than the permitted staking under Part VIII.
para 4.4, p.10
Discretionary accounts may put under 10% of gross asset value into VAs.
para 4.7, p.11
Recommended VAs for retail should be large-cap (in two qualifying indices from independent providers) and retail-available, except that licensed stablecoins are exempt from the liquidity test.
para 4.8 and Notes 1-2, pp.11-12
Advice on licensed stablecoins to non-institutional clients should rest on analysis of the client's use case and avoid rebates as the main driver.
footnote 3, p.11
Firms should detect red flags of manipulation and notify the SFC, and also the HKMA if a licensed stablecoin was involved.

VA knowledge test, risk profiling and exposure limits apply to non-institutional clients. Clearly separated stablecoin-only accounts are exempt from the knowledge test and exposure limit, and licensed stablecoin holdings are excluded from exposure counts.
paras 6.1-6.4A and footnote 7, pp.12-13
Firms should identify who originates each instruction and who benefits, and keep those records in Hong Kong before effecting trades.

t: Terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions which manage portfolios that invest in virtual assets
sl: HKMA/SFC · Terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions… (2026)
s: These May 2026 terms apply to an LC or RI managing a fund or discretionary account that meets the VA 'de minimis threshold'. That threshold is a stated VA objective, or an intention to hold 10% or more of gross asset value in VAs. They cover custody of fund assets (independent custodian or self-custody, due diligence on custodians, custody agreements and disclosure), valuation and record keeping. They also cover audits, investor disclosures and reporting to the SFC and, for banks, the HKMA. Schedules add discretionary-account rules, counterparty and cyber risk controls and example risk disclosures. The May 2026 edits carve out licensed stablecoins. Where the VA portion is only such coins, generic VA risk examples and the knowledge test for discretionary clients fall away, and the retail liquidity test does not apply to them. The companion circular also says an RI whose portfolios hold licensed stablecoins but no other VAs does not need Type 9 registration.
w: If the bank's private banking or asset management runs VA-exposed portfolios above the threshold, these terms apply through its registration and require HKMA reporting. The stablecoin carve-outs let cash-management style mandates in licensed stablecoins run with lighter onboarding.
k: The terms bite when a portfolio's stated objective is VA investment or it intends to put 10% or more of gross asset value (GAV) into VAs.
Part I, 'de minimis threshold', p.3
A mainly-securities fund that drifts over 10% only through price rises is not caught if it is taking steps to reduce. If the breach looks lasting, the SFC and (for banks) the HKMA should be alerted.
Part I, pp.3-4
Fund assets go to a functionally independent custodian and are segregated; there should be controls for new platform/custodian accounts, IP and wallet whitelisting and asset transfers.
The manager should choose and document the custody arrangement, weighing access speed, security and the custodian's ability to compensate losses.
para 4.3, pp.6-7
Self-custody requires independent custody staff, trust-style segregation and adequate insurance.

Custodian selection should consider track record, regulatory status, segregation through the chain, financial resources and insurance, cyber controls and sub-custodian oversight; prefer a regulated custodian and consider more than one.
para 4.7 and Note, pp.7-8
A formal custody agreement should set the custodian's scope of responsibility and liability, and be monitored.
Disclose custody arrangements, including split across custodians where more than 10% of GAV sits with one custodian or in self-custody.
Keep records at least seven years (two years for order records) and appoint an auditor able to verify VA existence, ownership and valuation.
Generic VA risk examples in Schedule 4 do not apply where the VA portion consists solely of licensed stablecoins.
para 6.1A, p.11
Report material non-compliance promptly and give at least 7 business days' notice of significant business changes to the SFC and, for banks, the HKMA.
Discretionary clients (non-institutional) need a VA knowledge check, except where the VA portion of the mandate is licensed stablecoins only.
Schedule 2, paras 1-1A, p.16
rg: Read the de minimis definition (pp.3-4), custody paras 4.1-4.12 and Schedule 2. Schedule 1 lists code carve-outs and can be skimmed.

t: Virtual asset-related activities in relation to relevant stablecoins issued by licensed stablecoin issuers
sl: HKMA · Virtual asset-related activities in relation to relevant stablecoins issued… (2026)
s: This is a 27 May 2026 HKMA letter to all registered institutions, formulated jointly with the SFC. It eases how the existing VA Joint Circular regime applies where the virtual asset is a 'Relevant Stablecoin' issued under a Stablecoins Ordinance licence. It removes several retail-protection frictions for Relevant-Stablecoin-only activity: the VA knowledge test, VA exposure-limit counting, high-liquidity and complex-product presumptions, and standard VA warning statements. It keeps core suitability, disclosure and conduct duties, and requires advance notice to HKMA and SFC before starting such activities.
w: Gives the bank a materially lighter conduct regime for licensed HK stablecoins specifically, but conditions it on advance HKMA/SFC notification, ring-fenced client handling, and continued suitability/disclosure discipline.
k: The circular sets HKMA guidance for RIs' dealing, advisory, asset-management and product-distribution activities where the virtual asset is a Stablecoins-Ordinance-licensed 'Relevant Stablecoin'. It was issued jointly with SFC guidance to licensed corporations.
opening paragraph, p.1

VA activities are currently governed by the Dec 2023 Joint Circular and the Sep 2025 supplemental circular. After the Stablecoins Ordinance commenced on 1 Aug 2025, HKMA and SFC reviewed how those circulars should apply to Relevant Stablecoins, given their different, currency-pegged payment-token risk profile.
Background, p.1-2

The circular appends corresponding updates to the Joint Circular's Appendix 6 (dealing/advisory terms and conditions, now Appendix A1) and Appendix 7 (portfolio management terms and conditions, now Appendix A2).
Detailed guidance, p.2

None of this applies to stablecoins that are not Relevant Stablecoins, or to AIs that are not RIs. It also does not apply to an HKMA-licensed issuer's dealings in its own stablecoin, since issuers face separate HKMA standards.
footnote 3, p.2
RIs may now provide Relevant Stablecoin dealing services by partnering with either an SFC-licensed VATP or the HKMA-licensed issuer of that stablecoin.
para (1), p.3

RIs may partner with a VATP that carries a professional-investor-only licensing condition to serve retail clients indirectly. The RI must make sure retail clients trade only in tokens the VATP has cleared for retail use. As a result, paragraph 20(a)(iii) of the Joint Circular no longer applies.
para (1), p.3
RIs offering Relevant-Stablecoin-only dealing services no longer need Type 1 (dealing in securities) registration, and are not limited to Type 1 clients. The conduct terms in Appendix A1 still apply.
para (2), p.3

For clients whose accounts are clearly ring-fenced as Relevant-Stablecoin-only, RIs need not run the standard VA knowledge test. RIs should still consider why the client wants the stablecoin, i.e. its use case.
para (3)(a), p.4
A client's Relevant Stablecoin holdings need not be counted toward the VA exposure limit normally required for retail (non-institutional, non-qualified) clients.
RIs may deal in Relevant Stablecoins through the issuer itself, and the 'high liquidity' requirement that otherwise applies to VAs offered to retail clients does not apply to Relevant Stablecoins.
para (3)(c), p.5
RIs may receive and process client withdrawals of Relevant Stablecoins via segregated client accounts held with the HKMA-licensed issuer, which itself keeps client assets segregated from its own.
para (4), p.5
RIs should disclose material information on a Relevant Stablecoin's stabilisation mechanism and redemption arrangements when providing dealing services.
para (5), p.5
rg: Read the whole letter (9 pages); the Roman-numeral headings (I-IV) map to dealing, portfolio management, advisory and distribution respectively.

t: Circular on SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets
sl: SFC · SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets (2026)
s: This revised SFC circular supersedes the 7 April 2025 version. It sets the requirements under which the SFC will authorise public investment funds with more than 10% NAV exposure to virtual assets (VA Funds). The SFC authorises these funds under sections 104-105 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), including VA-related activities such as staking these funds may undertake. It does not apply to exposure to Relevant Stablecoins or tokenised deposits, which are instead covered by FAQs on the UT Code. Requirements cover eligible management companies and eligible underlying VA, which must be accessible to the Hong Kong public on SFC-licensed VATPs. They also cover investment strategy limits, such as no leverage and VA futures only on conventional regulated exchanges. Transaction and custody channels must be SFC-licensed VATPs or qualifying AIs, meeting custody standards for cold storage, segregation and key management. Requirements also cover valuation methodology and disclosure obligations. Funds seeking more than 10% VA exposure, or wishing to engage in staking or other VA-related activities, require prior SFC consultation and approval.
w: As the current, in-force circular, this directly governs the custody and transaction-channel standards a bank AI must meet to provide VA custody to an SFC-authorised fund. It confirms stablecoin and tokenised-deposit fund exposure is regulated separately from this over-10% NAV VA-fund framework.
k: Circular governs SFC authorisation of public funds with VA exposure exceeding 10% of NAV under ss.104-105 SFO.
para 1
Requirements do not apply to fund exposure to Relevant Stablecoins (HKMA-licensed, SO-authorised) or tokenised deposits; see UT Code FAQs Q20G instead.
para 2
This is a revised circular, superseding the earlier Circular on SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets, which was issued on 7 April 2025.
para 3
VA Funds are limited to investing in VA tokens -- whether directly, or indirectly through exposure -- that Hong Kong residents can already trade on SFC-licensed VATPs.
para 11
At the fund level, VA Funds are not permitted to take on leveraged exposure to VA.
para 15
Spot VA transactions/acquisitions must be through SFC-licensed VATPs or qualifying authorized institutions (or subsidiaries of locally incorporated AIs).
para 17

Custody should be delegated only to an SFC-licensed VATP, a qualifying AI or subsidiary meeting HKMA VA custody standards, or another SFC-acceptable entity. Firms should mainly use cold-wallet storage and keep hot-wallet holdings to a minimum. Seeds and private keys should be kept in Hong Kong with restricted access, anti-collusion measures such as multi-signature or key sharding, and backups.
paras 20-21
Valuation of spot VA should use an indexing approach based on trade volume across major VA trading platforms via a reputable benchmark index provider.
para 22
Offering documents/KFS should disclose VA exposure investment limits and key risks (price, custody, cybersecurity, fork risk for spot; roll cost/operational risk for futures).
paras 24-25

Under the ASPIRe roadmap, the SFC may let VA Funds take part in staking and other VA-linked activities, through SFC-licensed VATPs or qualifying AIs. This is subject to guiding principles on investment consistency, internal controls, due diligence, disclosure, investor notice, and reporting of VA committed to such activities.
para 28
Funds seeking >10% VA exposure, existing funds moving to >10%, or funds wanting to engage in staking/other VA activities require prior SFC consultation and approval.
para 31
Recognised Jurisdiction Schemes (incl. UCITS) and mutual-recognition-of-funds arrangements are generally exempt from these requirements, except the prior consultation/approval requirement.
para 30, footnote 1
rg: Read paras 1-3 for scope and supersession, then paras 17-21 (custody and transactions) and para 28 (staking) as the most operationally significant sections for a bank. Paras 22-27 (valuation, disclosure, distribution) are more standard fund-governance detail.

t: Updated Guidance on Expected Standards on Provision of Custodial Services for Digital Assets by Authorized Institutions
sl: HKMA · Updated Guidance on Expected Standards on Provision of Custodial… (2026)
s: This Annex lists 26 expectations for banks and their local subsidiaries that hold digital assets for clients, grouped under governance, segregation, safeguarding, outsourcing, disclosure, records, ongoing monitoring and staking. Compared with the 2024 version, it adds detailed wallet-operation controls. These include cold-wallet whitelists with system checks on every transfer, no smart contracts in cold wallets on public chains, and dedicated signing devices. It also adds air-gapped integrity checks, anti-blind-signing, code-management segregation of duties and 24/7 security monitoring. The fixed 50%/100% insurance or compensation footnote is gone; instead the bank is liable for losses attributable to it and must hold adequate financial resources, which may include insurance. The 98% cold-storage rule for VAs and the Hong Kong key-location rule stay. A new carve-out lets an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer, with HKMA consent, hold keys for its own coins in Hong Kong or another accepted location. A licensed stablecoin issuer is added as a permitted custody delegate, and third-party transfers are allowed for payments and settlement where controls exist. The separate AML section of 2024 no longer appears.
w: This is the paragraph list HKMA will test custody against. Compliance needs a line-by-line gap analysis, especially for the new wallet-operation controls in paras 10-11 and 23-25. This includes the move from a fixed insurance percentage to liability plus adequate financial resources, and any plan to use a licensed stablecoin issuer as custodian.
k: Scope: client-held crypto-based assets (VAs, tokenised securities, other tokenised assets) at AIs and local AIs' subsidiaries; limited purpose tokens and proprietary holdings excluded. Banks that also deal in the VAs must also follow the dealing rules, e.g. on third-party transfers.
Preamble and footnotes 1-5, p.1
Before launch, run a full risk assessment and set policies and controls; board and senior management oversee risk before and after launch.
para 1, p.1
Resource the business with skilled people; train staff at the outset and continuously, with in-depth training for transaction signers on verification and handling exceptions (signer training is new).
paras 2-3, p.2
Set written roles, responsibilities and reporting lines, and manage conflicts of interest across the bank and affiliates.
para 4, p.2
Maintain contingency and disaster recovery plans and now also run drills for emergency and business continuity scenarios.
para 5, p.2
Keep client assets in segregated client accounts and wallet addresses, apart from the bank's own, so creditors cannot reach them in insolvency or resolution.
para 6 and footnote 6, p.2
Do not transfer title to, lend, pledge or encumber client assets except for settlement or fees owed, with prior explicit written client consent, or where law requires.
para 7, p.3
Controls may be risk-based by network type; new text notes permissioned tokens with smart-contract access controls may allow recovery of lost assets.
para 9, p.3
Written procedures should cover access authorisation plus detection of intrusion into critical wallet infrastructure (cold vault, signing devices, databases, production binaries, code repositories).
para 10, first bullet, p.4
New: system-enforced controls should block unauthorised cold-wallet transfers, using whitelists with tight oversight of changes and systematic verification of each transaction.
para 10, second bullet, p.4
New: procedures for handling security alerts and incidents by severity level with matching response protocols.
para 10, fourth bullet, p.4
For client VAs the para 11 controls are generally required; for other digital assets a risk-based approach is allowed, with extra caution for permissionless tokens on public permissionless chains.
para 11 (chapeau), p.4
rg: Read paras 10-11 (safeguarding controls, pp.3-7) and 14-17 (outsourcing, pp.8-9) first, then 23-25 (monitoring). Paras 1-7 and 20-22 largely repeat the 2024 text.

t: Guidance on Offering of Financing for Virtual Asset Dealing, Shared Order Book, and Client Virtual Asset Withdrawals
sl: HKMA · Guidance on Offering of Financing for Virtual Asset Dealing,… (2026)
s: This is a 27 May 2026 HKMA letter to all registered institutions (RIs). It sets the standards under which RIs may offer margin financing for VA dealing, give clients agency access to a VATP's shared order book, and permit client VA withdrawals. It largely extends to RIs the standards the SFC set for licensed VA brokers on 11 February 2026. Eligible VA financing collateral is capped to bitcoin, ether and HKMA-licensed stablecoins, with prudent haircuts. Such loans get no capital credit for the VA collateral itself under the Banking (Capital) Rules.
w: This sets the precise conditions, collateral list, haircuts and controls a bank must have in place to lawfully offer VA-backed margin lending. It confirms such exposures earn the bank no capital relief for the VA collateral itself.
k: Before the SFC's 11 Feb 2026 circular, licensed corporations and RIs were barred from providing any financing for clients to buy VA. This ban was under paragraph 4.3 of the omnibus-account Terms and Conditions.
Background, p.1-2

That SFC circular now lets VA brokers under omnibus-account arrangements with SFC-licensed VATPs offer margin financing for VA dealing to clients with strong credit profiles and sufficient collateral.
Background, p.2
HKMA is letting RIs providing VA dealing services offer the same kind of VA financing, provided they meet standards equivalent to those the SFC set for VA brokers.
HKMA's guidance for RIs, p.2
VA financing may only be extended to a margin client based on the client's financial capability and on securities and/or VA collateral the client has posted.
para (1), p.2
Only the RI's existing securities margin-financing clients are eligible for VA financing.
para (2), p.2
An RI is not expected to raise a client's credit limit just because VA financing is now offered. It should factor in the price volatility of non-fiat assets when assessing financial capability.

Where a client's VA holdings feed into that assessment, the RI should weigh VA quality, volatility and price-gap risk. It should also weigh valuation and liquidity sustainability, and digital-asset sector concentration, including operator or treasury-company shares. It should also weigh asset-specific risk such as infrastructure failure, correlation with equities in stress, and likely deterioration of repayment ability. For corporates, it should weigh related-party VA exposure too.

The circular notes VAs have a limited track record through systemic shocks, and can fall sharply within a day or across days. VAs tend to move together across the VA sector in stress, and leverage from margin lending or derivatives can amplify losses.
para (3), p.3
An RI should carefully consider whether relying on VA as loan collateral is prudent at all, given these risks.
para (4), p.3
Eligible VA collateral is limited to bitcoin, ether, and stablecoins issued by HKMA-licensed issuers under the Stablecoins Ordinance ('Relevant Stablecoins'), with a prudent haircut applied.
A minimum 60% haircut applies to the market value of bitcoin and ether collateral; HKMA can revise this haircut later, giving RIs prior notice.
footnote 5 and para (4), p.4

An RI relying on VA collateral should document its risk-assessment methodology in its margin lending policy, and set and monitor acceptable credit exposure accordingly. It should also keep the operational capability to track VA collateral volatility in real time and act promptly.
rg: Read the whole letter; it is short (6 pages). Pay particular attention to paras (3)-(9) on the financing/collateral controls.

t: Updated Guidance on Provision of Custodial Services for Digital Assets
sl: HKMA · Updated Guidance on Provision of Custodial Services for Digital… (2026)
s: The HKMA tells all authorized institutions (AIs, i.e. banks) that it has refreshed its expectations for holding digital assets on behalf of clients. The review reflects market and technology change and the start of the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656). The refreshed standards sit in an Annex and allow arrangements proportionate to each asset's features and risks. They cover assets received as a virtual asset (VA) intermediary, through tokenised product distribution, or in a standalone custody business, and also reach subsidiaries of locally incorporated banks. Banks planning to start must discuss with the HKMA first; banks already active must review and upgrade their controls. The letter replaces the February 2024 circular.

k: 'Digital assets' covers crypto-based assets such as VAs, tokenised securities and other tokenised assets, and also the keys, seeds and backups used to access them.
footnote 1, p.1
Limited purpose digital tokens and the bank's or its group's own (proprietary) holdings are out of scope.
footnote 1, p.1

t: Consultation Conclusions: Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Advisory Service Providers and Virtual Asset Management Service Providers
sl: FSTB/SFC · Consultation Conclusions: Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Advisory… (2026)
s: This paper finalises how Hong Kong will licence virtual asset (VA) advisory services (modelled on Type 4) and VA management/discretionary services (modelled on Type 9). Both regimes are activity-based and technology-neutral. They catch AI-generated advice, robo-advisers and copy-trading, and they capture the substance of an activity regardless of labels like 'education'. VA management has no de minimis threshold — any discretionary VA exposure triggers licensing. VA management firms may appoint SFC- or overseas-regulated custodians of their choice for private funds (no mandatory SFC-custodian-only rule). Though self-custody of hard-to-place tokens will be subject to new SFC-prescribed safeguards. No deeming/grandfathering will be offered when the regimes commence, though an expedited track exists for firms already vetted. A single bill covering dealing, custodian, advisory and management regimes is targeted for the Legislative Council in 2026.
w: This settles the two remaining pieces of Hong Kong's VA-intermediary framework relevant to any bank providing digital-asset advice or discretionary management. The no-de-minimis rule means even a token amount of client VA exposure triggers licensing. The confirmation that private-fund custodians need not be SFC-regulated gives more counterparty flexibility than the parallel dealing-services regime.
k: VA advisory and VA management licensing look to the substance of the activity, not its label — content marketed as 'education'. 'research' or 'trading signals' is regulated if it in substance advises on acquiring or disposing of VAs.
paras 6, 8

Both regimes are technology-neutral. Providing an algorithm or AI language model that generates VA advice, or a robo-adviser that makes discretionary VA investment decisions, counts as providing the regulated service.
paras 9, 40

Advising on tokenised securities, or on derivatives or structured products referencing VAs, generally falls under existing SFO licences (Type 4/5/11) rather than the new VA advisory regime. This is because the statutory VA definition excludes securities and futures contracts.
paras 11-12

Advising on a client's combined VA-and-securities portfolio is not treated as wholly incidental to a Type 4 securities licence. A separate VA advisory licence is still required for the VA component, even if delivered alongside securities advice.
para 21

The SFC is separately reviewing finfluencer activity across both the SFO and the new VA regimes, having observed undisclosed conflicts of interest and 'education'-labelled promotion of specific VAs. A dedicated consultation may follow.
para 18

VA advisory service providers get a tiered capital baseline. This is HK$100,000 minimum liquid capital if not holding client assets, otherwise HK$5 million paid-up capital plus HK$3 million liquid capital, matching Type 4 treatment. Dual Type 4/VA-advisory licensees are not subject to double capital requirements.
paras 25-26
VA management has no de minimis threshold. Any portfolio with discretionary VA exposure, however small, requires a licence, matching the 'no de minimis' approach under Type 9.
para 32
A VA management licensee that deals in VAs solely to service its own fund management (e.g. converting subscription proceeds to VAs) is exempt from also needing a separate VA dealing licence.
para 38

Private VA fund managers retain flexibility to appoint any qualified custodian globally (not restricted to SFC-regulated custodians) for the funds they manage, mirroring existing Type 9 treatment. The SFC will however prescribe specific safeguards where a manager self-custodies tokens lacking any supporting custodian.
paras 56-57

No deeming or grandfathering arrangement will be offered. Both regimes take full effect on the commencement date, with an expedited approval track for firms already assessed by SFC or HKMA. Existing RA9 managers below the old VA de minimis threshold must either seek a licence or wind down their VA management activity in an orderly way by commencement.

The VA dealing, advisory and management regimes will operate as standalone AMLO licensing regimes. These replace the current practice of imposing VA-related terms and conditions on SFO licensees under the Joint Circular, whose existing requirements become the new regimes' baseline.
para 62
Both regimes prohibit actively marketing VA advisory or management services to the Hong Kong public from anywhere in the world without an SFC licence or registration.
para 70
rg: Read paras 1-52 (Sections A-D) for scope, technology-neutrality and capital rules; read paras 53-57 (custody, Question 7) closely if the bank runs or advises VA funds. Skim licensing fees and skip the respondent annex.

t: Consultation Conclusions on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Advisory Service Providers and Virtual Asset Management Service Providers
sl: FSTB/SFC · Consultation Conclusions on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset… (2026)
s: FSTB and SFC conclude the further consultation (closed January 2026) on separate AMLO licensing regimes. These cover VA advisory services (modelled on SFO Type 4) and VA management services (modelled on SFO Type 9). The scope is technology-neutral, covering AI/algorithm-driven advice and discretionary robo-management, and excludes advice or management confined to tokenised securities (which stays under the SFO). No de minimis threshold applies to VA management. Private funds managing VAs will retain flexibility to appoint qualified custodians globally rather than being restricted to SFC-regulated VA custodians. Though the SFC plans to set strict rules for VA management firms that hold client tokens themselves because no qualified custodian is available. No deeming/grandfathering arrangement will be given; a bill is targeted for the Legislative Council in 2026.
w: This finalises the scope, exemptions and custody flexibility for any bank-affiliated VA advisory or fund/portfolio management activity. Including the important carve-out that Relevant Stablecoins dealt in by SFC-licensed intermediaries don't need separate VA licences. That private VA funds are not forced into SFC-regulated custodians only.
k: VA advisory services scope covers giving advice, or issuing analyses or reports, on whether, which, when or on what terms VAs should be acquired or disposed of. The assessment turns on substance, not labels like 'educational content' or 'trading signals'.

Mirror/copy trading that provides trading signals for others to replicate constitutes VA advisory. If execution is also provided, that constitutes VA dealing, and if trades are executed on a discretionary basis, that also involves VA management.
para 8, p.5

Technology tools, such as algorithms or AI language models, that generate specific VA recommendations for others' use amount to VA advisory services. Tools that merely filter factual information for self-directed research do not.
para 9-10, p.5

Advice on a client's portfolio comprising both VAs and securities is not treated as 'wholly incidental' to RA4 (securities advisory). VA advice requires a separate VA advisory licence even when given concurrently with securities advice.
para 21, p.7-8

The SFC is separately reviewing finfluencer activity across both the SFO and the new VA regimes. Citing concerns about undisclosed conflicts of interest and 'education'-labelled promotion of specific VAs.
para 18, p.6-7
No de minimis threshold will apply to VA management. Any entity managing a portfolio with any VA exposure needs a licence or registration, mirroring the VA dealing/custodian regimes' approach.

A VA management licensee can deal in VAs purely to support its VA management work, for example turning subscribed VAs into cash before investing. In that case it will not also need a VA dealing licence.
para 38, p.11

SFC-licensed or registered intermediaries dealing in 'Relevant Stablecoins' (specified stablecoins issued by HKMA-licensed issuers) will be exempt from needing separate VA service provider licences for those SFO activities.
para 39, p.11

Private funds retain flexibility to appoint qualified VA custodians globally (not restricted to SFC-regulated custodians) for VAs held by the funds, mirroring existing RA9 treatment. However, the SFC intends to impose strict conditions where a VA management service provider holds client tokens itself because no qualified custodian exists for them.

Financial resources requirements for VA advisory and VA management providers mirror RA4/RA9. This is HK$100,000 minimum liquid capital if not holding client assets, otherwise HK$5 million paid-up capital plus HK$3 million liquid capital. Dual RA4/RA9-and-VA licensees are not subject to double capital requirements but must meet the highest applicable requirement.

There will be no deeming or grandfathering for firms already providing VA advisory or VA management services. Both new regimes become fully effective on the statute's commencement date, though the timing of commencement will factor in transition needs.

The VA Dealing, VA Advisory and VA Management Regimes will run as standalone regimes under the AMLO. This takes over from today's approach of attaching terms and conditions to SFO licences for intermediaries under the Joint Circular, whose existing requirements will become the regimes' baseline.
rg: Read Section A (VA Advisory scope, p.4-8) and Section C (VA Management scope, p.9-12) for the definitional boundaries. Then the custody discussion under Question 7 (para 53-57, p.13-14) and the transitional/other-comments sections (p.15-18). Skip the Annex list of respondents (p.19-20).

t: FSTB and SFC conclude consultations on virtual asset advisory and management regimes
sl: FSTB · FSTB and SFC conclude consultations on virtual asset advisory… (2026)
s: The Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB), together with the SFC. Issued their conclusions on the plan to license providers of virtual asset (VA) advisory and VA management services, after getting broad support across 51 responses. Following the 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle, the new regimes will be aligned respectively with Type 4, which covers advising on securities. Type 9, which covers asset management, regulated activities under the SFO. The FSTB and SFC will finalise legislation under the AMLO, aiming to bring a bill to the Legislative Council (LegCo) in 2026. Together with the already-concluded VA dealing and custodian regimes, this completes the planned set of new VA intermediary licences envisioned in the FSTB's Policy Statement 2.0 (June 2025). That statement covers VA trading platforms, stablecoin issuers, dealing, custody, advisory and management.
w: This confirms the scope (matching Type 4 and Type 9 rules) of the coming VA advisory and management licensing regimes, headed for a 2026 bill. The bank's licensed representative (RI) arm should track this and think about talking to the SFC early if it advises on or manages VA portfolios.
k: 51 responses came in from a wide range of stakeholders on the further consultation for the VA advisory and management regimes, with broad market support.
Note 2, p.1

The VA advisory regime will align with Type 4 (advising on securities), and the VA management regime with Type 9 (asset management). Both regulated-activity categories under the SFO -- following the 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle.
para 2, p.1
The FSTB and SFC will finalise legislation under the AMLO (Cap. 615) for these new regimes, aiming to bring a bill to LegCo in 2026.
para 3, p.1

This wraps up the fourth and final piece of a set of new VA intermediary regimes (dealing, custody, advisory, management). Together with the existing VATP and stablecoin issuer licences are meant to cover the key parts of Hong Kong's digital asset ecosystem under Policy Statement 2.0 (June 2025).
paras 4-5, p.1
Firms already offering, or planning to offer, VA advisory and management services are strongly urged to start talking with the SFC well before they apply.
para 6, p.1
rg: Short press release; read in full for the policy conclusion; the detailed consultation conclusions paper (with the Annex list of 51 respondents) is referenced but not included in this document.

t: FSTB and SFC publish consultation conclusions on legislative proposals for regulating virtual asset advisory and management services
sl: FSTB/SFC · FSTB and SFC publish consultation conclusions on legislative proposals… (2026)
s: FSTB and the SFC published the conclusions of the one-month consultation on licensing regimes for virtual asset (VA) advisory and VA management service providers. Modelled respectively on the Type 4 and Type 9 regimes under the Securities and Futures Ordinance. Of 51 submissions, most supported the proposals. Officials frame this as completing the legal-framework coverage across the full digital-asset value chain — trading platforms, stablecoin issuers. The now-finalised dealing, custodian, advisory and management regimes — with a single bill targeted for the Legislative Council within the year. The operative detail is in the companion consultation-conclusions paper, summarised separately.
w: This confirms the government is now finalising all four new VA intermediary licensing tracks together in one bill. A bank offering or planning to offer VA advice or discretionary VA management should treat this timeline as the point to firm up its licensing strategy.
k: 51 submissions were received on the further consultation covering VA advisory and VA management services, most supporting the proposed regimes.
para 2 (main text)
The VA advisory regime will track the scope of Type 4 (advising on securities) and the VA management regime will track Type 9 (asset management) under the Securities and Futures Ordinance.
para 3 (main text)

Officials describe the dealing, custodian, advisory and management regimes together as completing coverage of the key nodes of Hong Kong's digital-asset ecosystem. Alongside the existing VATP and stablecoin issuer licensing regimes.
para 4 (main text)
A single bill covering the VA dealing, custodian, advisory and management regimes is targeted for introduction into the Legislative Council within the year.
para 5 (main text)

t: Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amended Common Reporting Standard) Bill 2026
sl: LegCo · Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amended Common… (2026)
s: This bill amends the Inland Revenue Ordinance to insert a new Part 8B creating Hong Kong's CARF reporting regime and to update the Common Reporting Standard rules. It defines Hong Kong Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Providers (HKRCASPs), sets nexus, due-diligence, registration and reporting duties. Creates new offences and penalties, including a financial-penalty alternative to prosecution.
w: This is the actual legal text underlying the IRD's CARF summary. Compliance should use it (not just the webpage) to confirm exact offence thresholds, the 'reasonable excuse' defence. That outsourcing to a service provider does not remove the bank's own liability.
k: Part 2 of the Ordinance (the CARF rules) starts on 1 January 2027; Part 3 (amended CRS) starts on 1 January 2028. The rest starts on gazettal.
A new Part 8B (sections 50M-50Y) sets out interpretation, nexus rules, registration duty, due diligence, and reporting duties for HKRCASPs.
Clause 3, Part 8B, p.C192 onward
An HKRCASP that fails to register, carry out due diligence. Or file a return without reasonable excuse commits an offence punishable by a fine at Level 3.
New s.80R(1) and (3), p.C325
For registration, reporting, and certain notice failures, a continuing daily fine of $500 applies after conviction for each day the offence continues.
For a due-diligence breach, the court can instead fine $1,000 multiplied by the number of affected crypto-asset users and controlling persons. If that is higher than the standard fine.
A person who knowingly or recklessly gives a misleading, false or incorrect self-certification commits a separate offence with a Level 3 fine.
New s.80(2ZD)-(2ZE), p.C325
An administrative financial-penalty mechanism is created as an alternative to prosecution. With a right to make written representations and to appeal to the Board of Review.
New ss.82E-82F, p.C351-C359
Engaging a third-party service provider to carry out CARF duties does not by itself excuse an HKRCASP from an offence for failing to register. Do due diligence, or report.
rg: Read Clause 1 (commencement) and new sections 50M, 50O-50R (duties) and 80R-82F (offences/penalties); skip the bilingual formatting and page-number front matter.

t: Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amended Common Reporting Standard) Bill 2026 to be gazetted
sl: FSTB · Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amended Common… (2026)
s: The government announced that a bill implementing the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) and the updated Common Reporting Standard (CRS) would be gazetted 22 May 2026. It would be tabled for first reading in the Legislative Council on 3 June. CARF requires crypto-asset service providers with a Hong Kong reporting nexus to register with the Inland Revenue Department. They must comply with due diligence, filing and record-keeping duties, taking effect the year after passage. Sharing tax data automatically on crypto-asset dealings with partner jurisdictions, alongside the amended CRS, are both targeted to start in 2028.
w: Once enacted, this will impose direct crypto-asset tax-reporting registration and due-diligence duties on the bank wherever it. Or an affiliate, qualifies as a crypto-asset service provider with a Hong Kong nexus. Compliance should start scoping which of the bank's digital-asset activities will trigger CARF registration ahead of the 2027 effective date.
k: The bill was to be gazetted on 22 May 2026 and introduced to the Legislative Council for first reading on 3 June 2026.
para 1 (main text)

CARF will be implemented the year following the bill, from 2027. Crypto-asset service providers with a Hong Kong reporting nexus must register with the Inland Revenue Department and meet due diligence, return-filing and record-keeping duties.
para 4 (main text)

Hong Kong aims to start swapping tax data on crypto-asset dealings with partner jurisdictions automatically, from 2028. It also aims to roll out the amended Common Reporting Standard from the same year, depending on those jurisdictions' own readiness.
para 4 (main text)

A public consultation ran from December of the prior year to February of the Budget year. Stakeholders, including the financial and crypto-asset sectors, generally supported the proposals, and their feedback informed the bill's drafting.
para 5 (main text)
The Inland Revenue Department will issue guidance and provide technical support to help industry adapt to the new requirements.
para 6 (main text)
rg: Short press release; read in full.

t: Annex: Proposed Amendments to the Banking (Capital) Rules (Cap. 155L)
sl: HKMA · Annex: Proposed Amendments to the Banking (Capital) Rules (2026)
s: This annex sets out illustrative drafting for proposed BCR amendments. Most items concern CET1 capital-base deductions and Basel technical updates with no VA link. The stablecoin/crypto-relevant items would: define a new BCR category of 'other regulated financial institution' covering entities such as HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers. Generally exclude such subsidiaries from an AI's consolidated capital-ratio calculation (subject to HKMA override); confirm that carrying on a licensed stablecoin activity counts as an activity ancillary to banking. Add specific default-risk-exposure rules for hedged 'group 2b cryptoasset derivative contracts'; and remove cryptoassets from the BCR's list of assets treated as low-risk 'cash items'.
w: If enacted, clarifies how the bank must capital-treat any stablecoin-issuer subsidiary (deduction rather than consolidation. Generally) and confirms cryptoassets get no 'cash item' capital relief, plus specific rules for hedged crypto-derivative counterparty exposure.
k: A new BCR term, 'other regulated financial institution', would be created to cover licensed entities such as HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers, distinct from banks, insurers and securities firms.
Item 5, p.9

An AI's stablecoin-issuer or other-regulated-financial-institution subsidiary would generally be left out of the AI's consolidated capital-adequacy-ratio calculation. The exception is if HKMA decides on reasonable grounds it is prudent to include it.

In deciding whether to include such a subsidiary in consolidation, HKMA may weigh several things. These are the subsidiary's business and activities, its size and financial significance to the AI, the risks it poses to the AI, and any other relevant factor.

The BCR's 'financial sector entity' definition would be clarified to expressly cover activities ancillary to banking listed in the Banking Ordinance's Fourteenth Schedule. The drafters confirm carrying on a licensed stablecoin activity falls within this.
Item 7, p.11

An AI's stablecoin-issuer or other-regulated-financial-institution subsidiary may have a capital shortfall it fails to fix in time. If so, HKMA could require that shortfall to be deducted from the AI's own CET1 capital.
Item 8, p.12

A new rule would set out how to calculate default-risk exposure on 'group 2b cryptoasset derivative contracts' when an AI hedges the counterparty credit risk with a guarantee or credit derivative. Mirroring the general hedging-recognition mechanics proposed elsewhere in the annex.
Cryptoassets would be removed from the definition of 'cash item' in Part 6 of the BCR. This means they can no longer be treated as a low-risk cash-equivalent exposure for capital purposes.
rg: Skip the general CET1/ECAI/technical-amendment items. Read Items 5-9 (stablecoin-issuer subsidiary capital treatment, p.9-12), Item 19 (crypto derivative hedging, p.28-29) and Item 45 (cash-item definition, p.50-51).

t: HKMA Annual Report 2025 - International Financial Centre
sl: HKMA · HKMA Annual Report 2025 - International Financial Centre (2026)
s: This is the International Financial Centre chapter of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) Annual Report 2025. It reviews the HKMA's fintech and market-development work in 2025. It records the launch of the Fintech 2030 strategy, whose four pillars are known as DART: data and payments, artificial intelligence (AI), resilience and tokenisation. It describes the November 2025 launch of EnsembleTX, for settling real-value deals with tokenised deposits. It records the end of Phase 2 of the e-HKD (Hong Kong's central bank digital currency) pilot, with a new focus on wholesale use by financial institutions. It also covers the Government's third tokenised bond and plans to issue tokenised bonds regularly. On stablecoins, it notes that the Stablecoins Ordinance took effect on 1 August 2025. The HKMA set a high bar for licences and announced the first two licensed issuers in April 2026.
w: This is the HKMA's own account of where tokenised deposits, e-HKD, tokenised bonds and stablecoin licensing stood at end-2025. It frames which bank digital-asset projects the HKMA is actively supporting.
k: The HKMA unveiled Fintech 2030 in November 2025 with four pillars (data and payments, AI, resilience, tokenisation) and more than 40 initiatives.
p.133, 'Fintech 2030' and Figure A

EnsembleTX, the pilot phase of Project Ensemble, launched in November 2025. It supports settling real-value deals in tokenised deposits. It starts with tokenised money market fund deals and real-time liquidity and treasury management.
p.137, 'Project Ensemble'
After e-HKD Pilot Phase 2 ended in October 2025, the HKMA said it would prioritise e-HKD for financial institutions in wholesale settings while keeping retail readiness.
p.137, 'Project e-HKD+'
The Government's third tokenised bond, in November 2025, was described as the largest digital bond offering and the first to settle with tokenised central bank money (e-CNY and e-HKD).
p.125, 'Navigating bond tokenisation'
The 2025-26 Budget announced regular tokenised government bond issuance, and the HKMA is reviewing the legal framework for tokenised bonds with the Government.

The Legislative Council (LegCo) passed the Stablecoins Bill in May 2025. The Ordinance took effect on 1 August 2025. The HKMA issued its supervisory guideline and its anti-money laundering guideline for issuers beforehand.
p.138, 'New regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers'

The HKMA set a high bar for stablecoin licences: compliance, viable use cases and prudent operation. It began taking applications in August 2025 and announced the first two licensed issuers in April 2026.
The HKMA led the Financial Stability Board's thematic review of how jurisdictions implement the global crypto-asset framework.
rg: Read pp.133 (Fintech 2030), 137 (Ensemble, e-HKD) and 138 (stablecoins); p.125 covers tokenised bonds. The rest of the chapter covers payments, market infrastructure and research.

t: HKMA Annual Report 2025 - Banking Stability
sl: HKMA · HKMA Annual Report 2025 - Banking Stability (2026)
s: This is the Banking Stability chapter of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) Annual Report 2025. It reviews bank supervision in 2025. For digital assets, it records April 2025 HKMA guidance on banks offering staking as part of custody. It records a September 2025 supplemental joint circular with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC). That circular lets intermediaries offer staking and use the off-platform trading services of SFC-licensed platforms. The HKMA, the Government and the SFC are also developing statutory regimes for virtual asset (VA) dealing and custody. The Basel crypto-asset capital and disclosure standards took effect in Hong Kong on 1 January 2026, through changes to the banking capital, disclosure and exposure-limit rules. The chapter also reports twice as many anti-money laundering on-site examinations, wider artificial intelligence (AI) use in transaction monitoring, and a longer engagement period for itinerant professionals.
w: It confirms the HKMA supervises banks' digital-asset activities through thematic reviews, and that crypto capital and disclosure rules now bind banks from 1 January 2026. It also lists the 2025 staking and off-platform trading permissions a bank's VA business can use.
k: In April 2025 the HKMA set out standards for banks offering VA staking as part of custody services.
p.86, 'Wealth management and MPF-related businesses'
A September 2025 supplemental joint HKMA-SFC circular let intermediaries offer staking and use SFC-licensed platforms' off-platform VA trading services.
The HKMA is working with the Government and SFC on statutory regimes for VA dealing and custody services.
The HKMA stepped up surveillance of crypto firms falsely claiming to be banks, in breach of the Banking Ordinance.
Thematic work in 2025 covered banks' digital asset-related activities among other conduct topics, within 24 on-site examinations and 509 thematic reviews.
The Basel crypto-asset exposure and disclosure standards took effect in Hong Kong on 1 January 2026 via changes to the Banking (Capital), (Disclosure) and (Exposure Limits) Rules.

HKMA on-site examinations of banks' anti-money laundering controls doubled from 14 in 2024 to 28 in 2025.

Banks' implementation plans show that more than 30% of banks with significant Hong Kong operations already use AI in transaction monitoring. The plans indicate this will rise above 80% over the next two years.
RIs may now engage itinerant professionals for up to 45 days a year, up from 30.

t: Beware of tokens purported to be associated with licensed stablecoin issuers

t: Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products
sl: SFC · tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products (2026)
s: This SFC circular (revised 20 April 2026) sets the rules for turning SFC-authorised investment products. Authorised under Part IV of the SFO for public sale in Hong Kong -- into tokenised form. Using a 'see-through' approach, SFC allows primary dealing (buying and selling units) in tokenised versions of SFC-authorised products. As long as the underlying product still meets every authorisation rule, plus extra safeguards for tokenisation-specific risks. Record-keeping, cybersecurity, avoiding open public blockchains, smart-contract integrity, disclosure, distributor regulation, and staff competence. Secondary trading of these tokenised products on SFC-licensed VATPs is allowed separately, under a companion circular. New tokenised products, or big changes to how tokenisation works, need SFC consultation and approval first.
w: This rule applies to the fund or product-provider entity, not directly to the bank as an authorized institution. But if the bank distributes or structures tokenised SFC-authorised products through its licensed corporation or fund arm, a compliance head must make sure smart-contract audits, staff competence. Blockchain controls are all in place, and that SFC has been consulted beforehand.
k: The SFC will permit subscription and redemption (primary dealing) in tokenised versions of SFC-authorised investment products. This applies provided the underlying product satisfies all standard authorisation rules, along with extra safeguards specific to tokenisation.
para 5, p.1

Trading tokenised SFC-authorised investment products in the secondary market on an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform is permitted too. This is provided rules on fair pricing, orderly trading, liquidity and disclosure are met, as detailed in the companion 'Circular on secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products'.
para 6, p.1
Product Providers stay fully responsible for running the tokenisation arrangement soundly and for keeping ownership records, even if parts of the work are outsourced.
para 10, p.2
Tokenised SFC-authorised investment products are not expected to be issued as bearer instruments.
para 11 and footnote 2, p.2
Product Providers should avoid open, permissionless public blockchain networks unless extra controls -- such as a permissioned token -- are added.
para 13, p.2

If SFC asks, Product Providers must show their operations are sound. They must get independent audit or verification of the tokenisation setup and smart-contract integrity, and obtain a satisfactory legal opinion to back their application.
paras 14-16, p.2

Offering documents must clearly explain the tokenisation setup. This includes whether settlement is final off-chain or on-chain, how tokens represent ownership, and the risks involved: cybersecurity, system outages, undiscovered technical flaws, and a changing regulatory landscape.
para 17, p.3

Anyone distributing tokenised products, including a Product Provider selling its own products, must be a regulated intermediary (an SFC-licensed corporation or registered institution) following existing conduct, onboarding and suitability rules.
para 18, p.3
Product Providers must confirm at least one staff member has the relevant experience to run or oversee the tokenisation setup and manage the new ownership and technology risks.
para 19, p.3
New tokenised products need SFC consultation before authorisation. Tokenising an existing product, or making a major change to how tokenisation works, may also need prior approval.
paras 20-21, p.3
rg: Read Section A (background, paras 2-7) for context, then Section B (paras 8-19) in full as the binding requirements. Section C (paras 20-22) covers the prior consultation/approval process. The document shows 'Amended' markers indicating this is a revised version.

t: Circular on secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products
sl: SFC · secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products (2026)
s: This SFC circular lays out the conditions for permitting public secondary trading, on SFC-licensed VATPs, of Tokenised Products — tokenised SFC-authorised investment products, mainly open-ended funds. It should be read together with the Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products and the Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities. It covers on-platform trading rules, fair-pricing controls including a mandatory Price Deviation Alert measured against indicative net asset value (NAV). Liquidity requirements (at least one market maker, with 3 months' notice before ending that role. And appointed SFC-licensed distributors), detailed disclosure duties in offering documents and Key Facts Statements (KFS). Prior SFC consultation or approval for new or existing tokenised products and for major changes to trading arrangements.
w: This directly binds the bank as a Registered Institution if it sells tokenised SFC-authorised funds or connects clients to secondary trading of them on VATPs. It creates Price Deviation Alert, risk-disclosure, and advance-notification duties to both SFC and, at the same time, HKMA.
k: Secondary trading of Tokenised Products can be offered to retail investors through on-platform. On-screen auto-matching trading on SFC-licensed VATPs, following the existing VATP Guidelines' trading rules and risk controls.
paras 8-9, p.2

SFC-licensed VATPs must run a Price Deviation Alert that warns investors when the trade price would move significantly away from the product's real-time or near real-time indicative NAV. Plus controls such as trading bands and cooling-off periods to guard against sharp price swings and manipulation.
para 12, p.2
Product Providers should make their best effort to line up at least one market maker per Tokenised Product. Give at least 3 months' notice before ending that arrangement.
para 15(a), p.3

Distributors appointed for Tokenised Products need to hold SFC licences (as corporations or registered institutions). Normally take care of creation and redemption requests coming from third-party investors.
para 15(c), p.3

Offering documents, including the Key Facts Statement, must clearly disclose the risks of secondary trading. Liquidity, price deviation, price differences across trading channels, and reliance on the market maker. Along with how the trading channel works, market-making arrangements and incentives, and any conflicts of interest if a market maker is an affiliated entity.
para 19, p.4-5

SFC-licensed VATPs and Connecting Brokers must maintain online tools that display real-time or near-real-time indicative NAV. Refreshed no less often than every 15 seconds while trading is underway, together with the last NAV. Must obtain client confirmation of understanding the risks before allowing secondary-market trades.
para 20(b)-(c), p.5

Product Providers must immediately tell SFC and investors if dealing in a Tokenised Product stops or is suspended. Or if market-making activity stops, is disrupted, or is suspended. Including an assessment of the impact and a plan to fix or manage the situation.
para 22, p.5

New tokenised products need prior SFC consultation before authorisation. Adding tokenisation or secondary-trading features to an existing SFC-authorised product needs both prior consultation and approval.
paras 23-24, p.5
Registered institutions doing secondary trading of Tokenised Products must also notify HKMA, following the Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities.
footnote 13, p.6
rg: Read Section A (background, paras 1-6, p.1) then Section B in full (paras 7-22, p.2-6) as the operative requirements. Section C (paras 23-28, p.5-6) covers the prior consultation process, important for registered institutions needing dual SFC/HKMA notification.

t: SFC unveils new regulatory framework to allow secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products
sl: SFC · SFC unveils new regulatory framework to allow secondary trading… (2026)
s: SFC rolled out a fresh set of rules, in a same-day circular, to pilot secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised funds (mainly open-ended funds) on SFC-licensed VATPs. Over-the-counter deals are looked at case by case. It builds on the tokenisation framework SFC first put in place through two circulars dated 2 November 2023. By March 2026, Hong Kong had 13 such tokenised products on the market. Their combined tokenised-class assets under management (AUM) had grown roughly seven times over within a year, reaching $10.7 billion. The plan is to let trading run around the clock, beyond normal market hours, potentially helped along by licensed stablecoins and tokenised deposits. The first products under the scheme are likely to be tokenised money-market funds.
w: This sets out a framework for VATPs and fund issuers, not a direct bank obligation. A compliance head should track it as it shapes how the bank's tokenised fund products could achieve round-the-clock secondary trading through regulated stablecoins and tokenised deposits.
k: SFC first put its tokenisation framework in place via two circulars dated 2 November 2023. These were the 'Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products' and the 'Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities'.
Note 1, p.1
By March 2026, Hong Kong had 13 tokenised products on public sale. Their combined tokenised-class AUM had grown roughly seven times over within a year, reaching $10.7 billion.
para 3, p.1

The new scheme aims to let tokenised open-ended funds trade around the clock. This may be helped by licensed stablecoins (fiat-referenced stablecoins approved under the Stablecoins Ordinance) and tokenised deposits, to keep liquidity flowing at all hours.
para 4 and Note 2, p.1
Trading mainly happens on SFC-licensed VATPs under this scheme, though SFC may also weigh up over-the-counter secondary-trading setups on an individual basis.
para 2, p.1
New safeguards cover fair pricing, orderly trading, liquidity, and disclosure, drawing on lessons from exchange-traded fund (ETF) trading and SFC-licensed VATP systems.
para 4, p.1
The first products likely to launch under this scheme are tokenised money-market funds. SFC plans to review how things go before widening the range of products covered.
para 6, p.1
Firms that issue these products, and intermediaries such as SFC-licensed VATPs, are encouraged to consult the SFC or give notice before undertaking work connected to this framework.
para 7, p.1
rg: Short press release; read in full; cross-reference the same-day circular 26EC23 for the binding rules.

t: Speech by FS at Hong Kong Web3 Festival 2026 (English only) (with photos/video)
sl: Government · Speech by FS at Hong Kong Web3 Festival 2026… (2026)
s: The Financial Secretary set out Hong Kong's policy approach to the convergence of Web3, tokenisation and AI. Reaffirming 'same activity, same risks, same regulation' and a dual regulatory mandate of prudent oversight plus market facilitation. He confirmed that two stablecoin issuer licences had been granted earlier that month. Described more than US$2 billion in tokenised green and infrastructure bonds issued to date with issuance now regularised. Referenced EnsembleTX (launched the previous November) which lets participants put tokenised deposits to work in money-market-fund dealings and treasury management. He flagged three cross-cutting risks from AI-driven Web3 activity — settlement speed keeping pace with machine-speed transactions, maintaining human control over autonomous AI agents. Keeping regulation and accountability current — and announced a new Committee on AI+ and Industry Development Strategy that will cover the Web3/AI intersection.
w: This is a useful confirmation that only two stablecoin issuer licences existed as of the speech date. It flags coming AI-governance expectations (predictability, traceability, human override) that compliance should anticipate extending to any AI-agent-driven digital-asset activity the bank builds or relies on.
k: Two stablecoin issuer licences had been granted earlier in the month the speech was given (April 2026).
section 'Hong Kong's vision and pathway'
Hong Kong has carried out several rounds of tokenised green and infrastructure bond issuance worth more than US$2 billion in total. This is now a regular programme rather than a one-off effort.
section 'Hong Kong's vision and pathway'
EnsembleTX, launched under Project Ensemble the previous November, lets market participants use tokenised deposits for money-market-fund transactions and real-time liquidity/treasury management.
section 'Hong Kong's vision and pathway'

The Financial Secretary identifies three policy challenges from AI-driven Web3 activity: keeping settlement infrastructure and cross-border standards at machine speed. Ensuring autonomous AI agents remain predictable, traceable and open to human intervention; and keeping regulation/accountability frameworks current as activity spans platforms.
section 'The issues to be addressed'
A new Committee on AI+ and Industry Development Strategy, flagged in the 2026-27 Budget. Will treat the Web3/AI intersection as one of its focus areas.
section 'Hong Kong's vision and pathway'
rg: Read the whole speech; it is short. The operative policy content is concentrated in 'The issues to be addressed' and 'Hong Kong's vision and pathway'; the opening and closing remarks are ceremonial.

t: Robust development of the regulated stablecoin ecosystem in Hong Kong
sl: HKMA · Robust development of the regulated stablecoin ecosystem in Hong… (2026)
s: HKMA announced its first two stablecoin issuer licences under the Stablecoins Ordinance: Anchorpoint Financial Limited — jointly owned by Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong), HKT and Animoca Brands — and HSBC. Both will initially issue HKD-referenced stablecoins for cross-border payments, local payments, tokenised asset trading settlement and other programmable use cases. HKMA received 36 first-batch applications by the 30 September 2025 deadline and assessed them mainly on risk-management capability and viable use cases. Licensees must complete technology and risk-management preparatory work before launch, expected mid-to-second-half of 2026, and will face ongoing on-site/off-site supervision. HKMA signalled the overall number of licences will remain very limited given high licensing thresholds.
w: This is the first concrete market outcome of the Stablecoins Ordinance and directly names one bank counterparty (HSBC) now licensed to issue regulated stablecoins. Relevant for counterparty due diligence on any regulated-stablecoin product, payments partnership, or as a competitive-landscape reference given the very limited number of licences signalled.
k: HKMA granted the first two stablecoin issuer licences under the Stablecoins Ordinance to two firms. One is Anchorpoint Financial Limited, owned jointly by Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong), HKT and Animoca Brands. The other is The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited (HSBC).
para 1

HKMA received 36 applications in the first batch by the 30 September 2025 deadline. These were assessed chiefly on (1) applicants' risk-management capability and compliance commitment, and (2) their ability to propose distinct, viable use cases.
para 3-4

Both licensees plan to initially issue HKD-referenced stablecoins for cross-border payments, local payments, tokenised asset trading settlement, and other programmable use cases such as conditional payments and supply chain financing.
'Use cases and strategic priorities' section

Licensed issuers must implement robust risk-management measures. These cover fiat reserve asset safekeeping, price stabilisation, redemption arrangements and technology risk mitigation, plus AML controls including blockchain analytics tools and holder identity verification (directly or via reliable third parties).
'Risk management measures' section

Prior to launch, licensees must complete preparatory work including technology platform and systems testing and implementation of risk-management measures and HR arrangements. Regulated stablecoins are expected to launch in mid-to-second-half of 2026.
'Follow-up work' section
Once the regulated stablecoins launch, HKMA plans continuous oversight -- a mix of site visits, remote reviews, independent assessments, and direct contact with licensees' senior leadership.
'Follow-up work' section

HKMA signalled the licensing threshold will remain high and the overall number of licences granted, even if more are approved later, will remain very limited. This reflects stablecoin activity risk, user protection needs and market capacity considerations.
final paragraphs
rg: Read in full; it is the primary source for the first two HKD stablecoin licensees and their planned use cases and ongoing supervisory approach.

t: Granting of stablecoin issuer licences
sl: HKMA · Granting of stablecoin issuer licences (2026)
s: The HKMA announced that the Monetary Authority had licensed two firms, Anchorpoint Financial Limited and HSBC, as stablecoin issuers under the Stablecoins Ordinance, with licences effective the same day. Based on their business plans, the licensees intend to finish preparation and launch business in the coming months. The HKMA keeps a public Register of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers and warns the public to only get or use stablecoins through regulated channels. Staying alert for fraud claiming ties to the licensees.
w: This licence grant is a direct matter. An Authorized Institution is now a licensed stablecoin issuer under the Stablecoins Ordinance, so its business-plan promises to the HKMA become live commitments. It is also the benchmark precedent for any other bank weighing the same licence.
k: Under the Stablecoins Ordinance, the HKMA licensed two firms -- Anchorpoint Financial Limited and HSBC -- to issue stablecoins, with effect from 10 April 2026.
para 1, p.1
According to their business plans, the licensees intend to finish the needed preparation and launch business within the coming few months.
para 2, p.1
The HKMA keeps a public Register of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers, listing licensee names, addresses, email contacts, and other details.
para 4, p.1
The public is reminded to only acquire or use stablecoins through regulated channels, and to check a licensee's legitimacy through the HKMA's Register.
para 5, p.1
rg: Short press release; read in full.

t: LCQ18: Development of digital Renminbi and stablecoins
sl: FSTB · LCQ18: Development of digital Renminbi and stablecoins (2026)
s: In a written Legislative Council reply, the Financial Secretary's Bureau gave an update on the cross-boundary e-CNY (digital Renminbi) pilot with the People's Bank of China. E-CNY wallet issuance by Mainland institutions has grown to five. 18 local banks now support top-ups via the Faster Payment System, roughly 80,000 wallets were registered as of end-January 2026. Around 5,200 local merchants now accept e-CNY. On stablecoins, the reply confirms the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) took effect 1 August 2025 and reiterates that stablecoins, e-CNY and tokenised deposits are expected to develop with differentiated roles. Determined largely by market forces rather than official design.
w: This confirms the e-CNY pilot remains small in absolute scale in Hong Kong and that government policy is explicitly leaving stablecoin-versus-CBDC-versus-tokenised-deposit positioning to the market. Is useful context when a bank weighs which of these payment rails to prioritise.
k: By the close of January 2026. Roughly 80,000 e-CNY wallets tied to Hong Kong mobile numbers had been set up in total, per PBoC data.
Reply (1)
Local retail merchants taking e-CNY payments have grown in number from about 300 at the pilot's start to roughly 5,200 now.
Reply (1)
18 local banks now participate in e-CNY wallet top-ups via the Faster Payment System, up from 17 at the pilot's start.
Reply (1)
The government confirms the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) took effect on 1 August 2025, introducing a licensing regime for regulated stablecoin activities.
Question (3), Reply (3)

Officials expect stablecoins, e-CNY and tokenised deposits to develop with differentiated roles based on their distinct characteristics and market forces. Rather than a government-directed allocation.
Reply (3)
rg: Read the full reply; it is short and entirely on-topic, no boilerplate to skip.

t: Consultation: revised SPM module CA-G-5 “Supervisory Review Process” |  | Annex: Supervisory Review Process (Consultation)

s: This is the HKMA's landing page and cover letter for a consultation, opened 19 March 2026 and closed 23 April 2026. On a revised Supervisory Policy Manual module CA-G-5 covering the Pillar 2 supervisory review process. The full draft module is the attached PDF. The bulk of the module is general capital-adequacy supervisory methodology; only a small part touches cryptoassets. No conclusions document is included in this batch.

k: HKMA wrote to the banking industry on 19 March 2026 to consult on a revised version of SPM module CA-G-5.

Consultation Open/Close Date fields
