t: Strategic innovation drives growth of Hong Kong's listing and digital asset markets: SFC Quarterly Report
sl: SFC · Strategic innovation drives growth of Hong Kong's listing and… (2026)
s: The SFC's Quarterly Report (covering Q4 2025 / full-year 2025) highlights Hong Kong becoming the world's top IPO venue (over $280 billion raised in 2025) and growth in the digital asset ecosystem. SFC-authorised tokenised retail money market funds' AUM grew to $8.66 billion by December 2025 (up 14% quarter-on-quarter). Hong Kong's 11 listed virtual asset spot ETFs (Asia's first, introduced 2024) reached total market capitalisation of over $5.4 billion, up 142% since launch. It also reports broader capital market metrics (Stock Connect volumes, licence applications, ETF/L&I market cap growth. Fund flows) and investor protection actions, including the SFC's first custodial sentence against an unlicensed finfluencer.
w: An SFC quarterly market report giving no bank obligations, but useful board-level context on the scale and growth of Hong Kong's tokenised fund and VA ETF market. On rising SFC licence-application volumes.
k: Hong Kong became the world's top IPO venue in 2025, raising over $280 billion. The Technology Enterprises Channel (TECH) received 119 IPO applications (73 biotech, 46 specialist technology) since its May 2025 launch through December.
paras 1-2, p.1
SFC-authorised tokenised retail money market funds' AUM grew to $8.66 billion as of December 2025, up 14% from a quarter ago.
para 4, p.1
There are 11 virtual asset spot ETFs listed in Hong Kong (Asia's first, launched in 2024). Their combined market value has jumped 142% since listing, passing $5.4 billion.
para 4, p.1

Combined market value of SFC-authorised ETFs and leveraged-and-inverse (L&I) products rose 33.7% year-on-year to $618.7 billion by December 2025. The segment drew $9.2 billion in net inflows last quarter and made up 14% of Hong Kong's market turnover.
para 5, p.1
The SFC received 9,637 licence applications in 2025: 9,338 from individuals and 299 from corporations. This was a 17% increase from 2024.
para (b), p.1
The SFC won its first case resulting in a jail term for a finfluencer who lacked a licence and offered paid investment tips on social media.
para (c), p.1
rg: Read paras 1-6 for headline digital-asset and IPO figures; the 'Other highlights' bullet list (Stock Connect, licensing, enforcement, anti-scam outreach) is supplementary context.

t: Supervisory Policy Manual CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process V.78 – 19.12.2025 Consultation
sl: HKMA · Supervisory Policy Manual CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process V.78 –… (2026)
s: This is the draft revised text of SPM module CA-G-5 on the Pillar 2 supervisory review process, out for consultation from 19 March to 23 April 2026. It is a broad module on how the HKMA assesses an authorized institution's capital adequacy and risk management. Cryptoasset-specific content is limited to two short passages on supervisory tools for crypto-related risk deficiencies and on board oversight of new/complex activities. A separate existing module, CRP-1, covers cryptoasset classification and is only cross-referenced here, not reproduced.
w: Confirms the HKMA's toolkit for crypto-related capital or risk-management gaps is discretionary and case-by-case. That board-level understanding of crypto activities is an explicit supervisory expectation to be evidenced.
k: Where an AI has capital-adequacy or risk-management shortcomings tied to cryptoasset activities, the HKMA can respond with capital add-ons. Provisioning for foreseeable crypto losses, activity limits, or other mitigation, chosen case by case.
para 3.6.6

Boards and senior management are expected to fully understand firm-wide risks. Cryptoasset activity is named as an example (alongside originate-to-distribute and securitisation) of a new or complex activity they must grasp.
para 4.2.8

The module's reference list shows a separate, already-existing SPM module, CRP-1 ‘Classification of cryptoassets’. Filed under a dedicated ‘Cryptoassets’ category alongside interest-rate and market-risk modules.
module index, p.90
rg: Skip the general Pillar 2 methodology. Read only para 3.6.6 (p.52), para 4.2.8 (p.62), and the module index (p.90) for the cryptoasset-relevant content.

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism (1) FATF Statement on High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action (2) FATF Statement on Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring (3) Outcomes from the FATF Plenary, 11-13 February 2026
sl: SFC · licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities -… (2026)
s: This SFC circular relays the FATF's February 2026 statements identifying DPRK and Iran as jurisdictions subject to a call for countermeasures. Myanmar as subject to enhanced due diligence (with countermeasures to be considered if no progress by June 2026). The updated list of jurisdictions under increased monitoring adds Kuwait and Papua New Guinea. It also flags three FATF Plenary (11-13 February 2026) outputs of particular relevance to VA-related firms. A paper on cyber-enabled fraud (published 24 February 2026), a report on offshore virtual asset service provider risks (published 11 March 2026). A targeted report on stablecoins and unhosted wallets illicit-finance risks (published 3 March 2026).
w: The stablecoin/unhosted-wallet and offshore VASP FATF reports flagged here are directly relevant to a bank's stablecoin and VA AML risk assessments and travel-rule/unhosted-wallet controls. The DPRK/Iran call-for-action list must feed sanctions screening for VA transactions specifically.
k: FATF reiterates calls for countermeasures against DPRK given continued AML/CFT deficiencies and proliferation financing risks linked to increased DPRK connectivity with the international financial system.
FATF calls for effective countermeasures against Iran. Citing non-compliant ratification of the Palermo and TF Conventions and continuing failure to address its action plan since 2016.

Myanmar remains subject to a FATF call for enhanced due diligence proportionate to risk. The FATF says it will weigh countermeasures should this situation still lack meaningful improvement come June 2026.
The FATF's updated list of Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring adds Kuwait and Papua New Guinea.

Among FATF's listed countermeasures, one option is capping or cutting off dealings and money movements. Including in virtual assets -- with persons or entities tied to the flagged jurisdiction, applied according to risk.
footnote 4, p.2

FATF approved publication of a targeted report (3 March 2026) on stablecoins and unhosted wallets. Highlighting illicit finance risks from criminals' misuse of stablecoins via peer-to-peer transactions through unhosted wallets, with recommended controls.
para (c), p.3

FATF approved publication of a report (11 March 2026) on understanding and mitigating risks of offshore virtual asset service providers. Examining how regulatory/supervisory gaps are exploited by criminals.
para (b), p.3

Licensed firms are reminded to exercise extra care and apply special high-risk-situation requirements (per paras 4.9 and 4.13 of the AML/CFT Guideline). This applies to business relationships and transactions with higher-risk jurisdictions generally, beyond the specifically listed ones.
p.3, footnote 10
rg: This is a routine FATF-relay circular. Skim the jurisdiction lists (largely boilerplate) but read part (3) on FATF Plenary outcomes (p.3) closely. As it points to substantive new reports on stablecoins/unhosted wallets and offshore VASPs.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Opening Remarks at “Tokenisation: Banking the Future”
sl: HKMA · Opening Remarks at “Tokenisation: Banking the Future” (2026)
s: Deputy Chief Executive Arthur Yuen's opening remarks (event held 9 March 2026) frame DLT's transformative effect on bank liquidity through three concepts. 'novel', 'smart' and 'trusted' liquidity -- and position banks as trusted intermediaries bridging traditional and digital finance. The speech announces that HKMA is issuing, the same day. A circular that asks banks to review their business models strategically in light of digital transformation (see the separate registry entry for that circular, id 3ec5b269b5dc).
w: Directly previews the HKMA circular (see 3ec5b269b5dc) requiring the bank's board to endorse a formal digital-transformation strategic business plan within six months. Frames the regulator's rationale for expecting banks to act as trusted intermediaries in tokenisation.
k: DLT is described as unlocking three new forms of liquidity. 'Novel Liquidity' (tokenising previously illiquid assets like corporate loans, carbon credits and IP), 'Smart Liquidity' (smart-contract automation compressing settlement time). 'Trusted Liquidity' (banks as trusted intermediaries verifying underlying assets and smart contract integrity).
paras on Novel/Smart/Trusted Liquidity, p.1

The same day, HKMA is issuing a circular that calls on banks to strategically review their business models in response to digital transformation. Covering product offerings, revenue models, customer engagement, risk management frameworks and operational processes.
'Call for Action' paragraph, p.1
The strategic review is meant to steer how banks navigate the next five years as DLT, AI, cloud and high-performance computing reshape business models.
'Call for Action' paragraph, p.1
rg: Read in full (short); the circular referenced (footnote 3) is the operative document and is separately registered (id 3ec5b269b5dc).

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Welcoming Remarks at “Tokenisation: Banking the Future”
sl: HKMA · Welcoming Remarks at “Tokenisation: Banking the Future” (2026)
s: In welcoming remarks (event held 9 March 2026) to about 60 banks. The HKMA's Financial Infrastructure department frames tokenisation as central to 'Fintech 2030' and updates on Project Ensemble and the Supervisory Incubator for DLT. EnsembleTX entered pilot phase in November 2025, enabling real-value transactions in tokenised deposits and digital assets. From 2026, HKMA plans to onboard more banks, add use cases and enhance EnsembleTX. The speech calls on banks to take proactive steps to capture tokenisation opportunities.
w: Signals HKMA's expectation that banks actively engage with Project Ensemble/EnsembleTX and the Supervisory Incubator for DLT. Foreshadowing the same-day strategic-review circular issued to the paired speech's parent event.
k: The event was jointly organised by HKMA's Banking Supervision Department (regulator) and Financial Infrastructure Department (infrastructure provider) to engage both regulatory and technical experts with about 60 banks.
para 3, p.1
EnsembleTX entered its pilot phase in November 2025. Enabling market participants to conduct real-value transactions in tokenised deposits and digital assets for liquidity and investment management.
para 6, p.1

Starting in 2026, HKMA intends to grow the tokenisation ecosystem, with priorities that include bringing in more banks, developing further use cases, driving wider adoption. Improving EnsembleTX to keep up with market needs.
para 7, p.1
HKMA urged banks to take proactive steps to capture the opportunities of tokenisation, citing early global adoption of products such as tokenised money market funds.
para 8, p.1

t: Strategic Review of Business Models amid Digital Transformation
sl: HKMA · Strategic Review of Business Models amid Digital Transformation (2026)
s: This HKMA circular (reference B1/15C, dated 9 March 2026, signed by Deputy Chief Executive Arthur Yuen) tells banks to actively rethink their long-term business models. This is in light of digitalisation, distributed ledger technology (DLT), agentic artificial intelligence (AI), and cloud or high-performance computing. It refers to the HKMA's Fintech Promotion Blueprint under 'Fintech 2030'. It asks each bank's board to oversee and approve a formal strategic business plan covering these changes, within six months of the circular. A bank may optionally use the Supervisory Incubator for DLT to test new business models. It confirms banks must still discuss any new digital-asset activity with the HKMA before launching it.
w: This creates a specific, dated board-level task — a strategic plan covering DLT and digital transformation. Due within six months — and restates the standing rule that any new digital-asset activity must be discussed with the HKMA first. Compliance needs to track and calendar both.
k: Digitalisation, especially the spread of distributed ledger technology (DLT), is reshaping customer expectations and the financial landscape. The HKMA says agentic AI, cloud computing and high-performance computing are speeding up this shift.
letter body, para 2

The HKMA expects each Authorized Institution's Board of Directors to oversee and approve, within six months of the circular's date, a formal strategic business plan covering these technology shifts. This spans products, revenue models, customer engagement, risk management and operations where relevant.
letter body, para 4
As part of that plan, a bank may choose to run small, real-world trials through the HKMA's Supervisory Incubator for DLT to test new business models.
letter body, para 4
Some Authorized Institutions will be asked to submit their strategic business plans through the HKMA's Survey Tool.
letter body, para 4
As is already the practice, banks entering new digital-asset activities are still expected to talk through their plans with the HKMA before launching.
letter body, para 5
rg: Read the full two-page letter; it is short and entirely about the strategic business-plan expectation and DLT-related digital transformation.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Shanghai Data Bureau, and National Technology Innovation Center for Blockchain sign MOU to strengthen Shanghai-Hong Kong co-operation in digitised cargo trade and finance (with photo)

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Shanghai Data Bureau, and National Technology Innovation Center for Blockchain sign MoU to strengthen Shanghai-Hong Kong cooperation in digitised cargo trade and finance
sl: HKMA · Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Shanghai Data Bureau, and National… (2026)
s: HKMA, together with two Mainland partners. The Shanghai Data Bureau (SDB) and NTICBC (the National Technology Innovation Center for Blockchain). Signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) aimed at deepening Shanghai-Hong Kong ties in digitised cargo trade and finance. Under the deal, the three sides will jointly look into digital-technology uses, weigh up building a cross-border platform, and, through that platform. Open up cross-border financial cooperation while separately looking at electronic bills of lading (eBL) under Project Ensemble. They will also study how trade finance could move faster using cargo and trade data. Linking to the Commercial Data Interchange (CDI) on one side and Cargo X on the other.

k: HKMA joined the Shanghai Data Bureau (SDB) and NTICBC (the National Technology Innovation Center for Blockchain) in signing an MoU on Shanghai-Hong Kong cooperation over digitised cargo trade and finance.
para 1, p.1
The three sides will jointly research digital-technology uses in cargo trade and finance, and weigh up building a cross-border platform.
para 2, p.1
That platform is meant to open up cross-border financial cooperation and, separately, look at electronic bills of lading (eBL) under Project Ensemble.
para 2, p.1
The parties will also study how trade finance could move faster. Using cargo and trade data linked to the Commercial Data Interchange (CDI) and to Cargo X.

t: Guideline on Minimum Criteria for Authorization
sl: HKMA · Guideline on Minimum Criteria for Authorization (2026)
s: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) issued this statutory guideline under Banking Ordinance (BO) section 16(10). It explains how the HKMA reads the Seventh Schedule criteria for becoming and staying an authorized institution. The criteria apply continuously, look forward and cover the whole institution. So a later failure can be a ground for revoking authorization. The guideline sets out how the HKMA judges the fitness of directors, chief executives (CEs), alternate CEs, executive officers (EOs) and controllers. It also says when the HKMA may meet candidates face to face. It states board-independence expectations and the seniority test for EOs of banks registered with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC). This version, dated 27 February 2026, replaces the version of 22 July 2022.
w: This is the HKMA's rulebook for approving the senior people a compliance head may one day become: CE, alternate CE, director or EO. It sets the EO seniority test that the HKMA expects any SFO-regulated bank desk, including a digital-asset desk, to meet, and the fitness factors the HKMA may probe in interview.
k: The authorization criteria keep applying after licensing, and failing them can lead to revocation at the HKMA's discretion.
para 4(a)
Controllers include indirect controllers and anyone controlling 10% or more of voting power, with over 50% making a majority shareholder controller.
para 9
Directors, CEs and alternates of a Hong Kong-incorporated AI, and the Hong Kong CE of an overseas bank, need HKMA approval under BO s.71 and must be fit and proper.
para 12

The HKMA expects independent non-executive directors (INEDs) to make up one-third of the board or three members, whichever is higher. This applies to Hong Kong-incorporated licensed banks, and to restricted licence banks (RLBs) and deposit-taking companies (DTCs) designated as systemically important. At least two INEDs should have an accounting, banking or financial background.
para 13
Fitness depends on the role: a person may suit one position but not another with different duties, and time commitment is also weighed.
para 15
The HKMA may meet candidates for director, CE, alternate CE or EO face to face to test their knowledge of Hong Kong banking and key rules.
para 16
The level of probity expected is broadly the same whatever the position.
para 18
Each registered bank must appoint at least two EOs per regulated activity under BO s.71D; the HKMA is the front-line supervisor and gives consent under s.71C.
para 23-24
For EO fitness, the HKMA applies SFO s.129 and the SFC's Fit and Proper Guidelines, Guidelines on Competence and CPT requirements.
para 25
An EO should generally be the most senior person in the regulated activity and no more than one rank below a CE, alternate CE, director or s.72B manager.
para 27
The more influence a controller has, the higher the fitness bar; would-be majority controllers must present detailed plans for the bank.
rg: For career and approvals, read paras 10-33 (fitness of directors, CEs, EOs and controllers). Paras 1-6 explain how the criteria work; later paragraphs cover capital, liquidity and other criteria.

t: The 2026-27 Budget — Speech by the Financial Secretary
sl: Government · The 2026-27 Budget — Speech by the Financial Secretary (2026)
s: In the digital-asset section of the 2026-27 Budget Speech, the Financial Secretary confirmed plans to introduce a bill in 2026 licensing digital asset dealing and custodian service providers. Noted the first batch of stablecoin issuer licences would be issued the following month. The SFC will look to widen liquidity and product access for professional investors and set up an accelerator for market innovation. Separately, an Inland Revenue amendment bill will implement the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and the amended Common Reporting Standard within two years. The HKMA's CMU OmniClear will launch a digital asset platform in 2026 to support digital bond issuance and settlement, alongside continued rollout of Project Ensemble's tokenised-deposit pilot (EnsembleTX).
w: The speech confirms government-level timelines the bank should track against its own build plans. The dealing/custodian licensing bill, first stablecoin-issuer licences. The CARF tax-reporting bill all land or advance in 2026, and CMU OmniClear's new digital asset platform signals where institutional tokenised-bond settlement infrastructure is heading.
k: A bill to establish licensing regimes for digital asset dealing and custodian service providers will be introduced in 2026.
para 104
The first batch of stablecoin issuer licences (under the existing licensing regime for fiat-referenced stablecoin issuers) was due to be issued the month after the speech.
para 105

The SFC intends to broaden digital-asset market liquidity and product/service offerings for professional investors, subject to sufficient investor protection. Will set up an accelerator to speed up market innovation.
para 106
Government will issue guidelines clarifying that debenture-holder registers may be kept as a distributed ledger, to support tokenisation of bond issuance and trading.
para 107

The Government plans to bring a bill amending the Inland Revenue Ordinance to adopt the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and the OECD's updated Common Reporting Standard. This is planned sometime in the year's first six months, with the two-year rollout starting after that.
para 108

Project Ensemble's pilot phase, EnsembleTX (launched the previous November), lets industry participants transact in tokenised deposits and digital assets in a controlled pilot environment. The HKMA will keep upgrading it toward 24/7 settlement and cross-market interoperability standards.
para 109

CMU OmniClear will launch a digital asset platform in 2026 to support issuance and settlement of digital bonds. With plans to extend it to other digital assets and link with regional tokenisation platforms.
para 114

The Government will widen family-office tax concessions to treat digital assets. Along with precious metals and specified commodities. As qualifying investments, through a bill due in the year's first six months, aiming to take effect from the 2025/26 year of assessment.
para 98

The Government issued a third batch of tokenised government bonds (HK$10 billion) in Q4 of the prior year. Settled with an option for tokenised central bank money. Will continue regular tokenised bond issuance, with HKMA encouraging further digital bond issuance via the Digital Bond Grant Scheme.
para 97
rg: Skip most of the 180+ page speech. Go straight to paras 96-115 (pp.37-42), the 'Develop Fintech and Financial Infrastructure' and adjacent bond-market/asset-management subsections, which contain every digital-asset-relevant passage.

t: SFC launches trading initiatives to boost digital asset market vibrancy in Hong Kong
sl: SFC · SFC launches trading initiatives to boost digital asset market… (2026)
s: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) announced three initiatives on the same day, aimed at boosting liquidity in Hong Kong's digital asset market under the ASPIRe roadmap. First, virtual asset (VA) brokers may offer financing to securities margin clients, under a circular covering VA financing and shared order book access. Second, for the first time, the SFC issued a high-level framework letting licensed virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs) build leveraged perpetual contracts. This is limited to professional investors, and covers product design, disclosure and operating controls. Third, affiliates of licensed VATPs may now act as market makers on those platforms, subject to safeguards against conflicts of interest, under a separate circular on affiliated market makers.
w: This widens what SFC-licensed VA brokers and VATPs may offer, such as margin financing, leveraged perpetual contracts, and affiliated market makers. The bank is not directly bound, but compliance should weigh the new leverage and conflict-of-interest risks when reviewing any VATP or VA broker counterparty.
k: VA brokers can now offer financing to their securities margin clients, as long as collateral is sufficient and strong investor protections are in place. This lets creditworthy margin clients trade more VA.
para 2, p.1

For the first time, the SFC issued a high-level framework for licensed VATPs to build leveraged perpetual contracts. These are offered only to professional investors, with clear product design, disclosure and strong operating controls.
para 3, p.1
Affiliates of licensed VATPs may now act as market makers on those same platforms, as long as strong safeguards limit conflicts of interest.
para 4, p.1
These three initiatives carry out the SFC's ASPIRe roadmap goal of widening the range of products and services and improving liquidity.
para 2, p.1
rg: Short press release; read in full, then cross-reference the same-day circulars 26EC5 (VA financing/shared order book) and 26EC6 (affiliated market makers) for detail. The perpetual contracts framework referenced in Note 3 is a separate document not included in this batch.

t: A high-level framework for virtual asset perpetual contracts offering by virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · A high-level framework for virtual asset perpetual contracts offering… (2026)
s: The SFC set out, at a high level, the conditions under which its licensed virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs) may offer perpetual contracts (Perps) — leveraged. No-expiry derivatives whose price tracks a reference virtual asset via periodic funding payments. Perps may only be offered to professional investors and only over spot assets already tradable by retail clients on the platform, or an IOSCO-compliant index of such assets. The framework prescribes margining, valuation, liquidation and disclosure standards, and requires margin to be posted in fiat, HKMA-regulated stablecoins or tokenised deposits only, with no credit extended for margin. Platform operators are invited to bring proposed Perp structures to the SFC for discussion before launch.
w: If the bank's clients trade Perps via an SFC-licensed VATP, compliance should confirm the platform is following this framework. This matters especially for the professional-investor gate and the HKMA-regulated-collateral rule, before treating any related exposure as within the regulated perimeter for due-diligence purposes.
k: Perpetual contracts may only be offered to professional investors, not retail clients, and only after the platform assesses each client's derivatives knowledge under the Code of Conduct.
section 'Eligible investors and reference assets'
A Perp's reference asset must already be tradable in spot form by retail clients on the same platform, or must be an index of such assets compliant with IOSCO benchmark principles.
section 'Eligible investors and reference assets'
Margin collateral is restricted to fiat currency, or to stablecoins or tokenised deposits that are HKMA-regulated; platforms may not extend credit for margin.
section 'Margin arrangements and loss allocation management'

Platforms must maintain a pre-defined loss-allocation hierarchy (order-book liquidation, backstop liquidity, reserve/insurance fund, auto-deleveraging, other last resort) and disclose the triggers for each to clients.
section 'Margin arrangements and loss allocation management'
Funding-rate payments between long and short position holders must occur at least once every 24 hours, following methodologies that are transparent, verifiable, and calculated in real time.
section 'Trading and settlement'

Pricing references (mark price, index) must draw on multiple independent sources to reduce single-entity manipulation risk, with disclosed compilation methodology and contingency/failover arrangements.
section 'Trading and settlement'

If the insurance fund is depleted or unavailable, platforms must promptly notify all open-position clients and warn that auto-deleveraging may follow. A post-event report is required within 24 hours of any auto-deleveraging.
section 'Margin arrangements and loss allocation management'
Platforms should implement real-time cross-market surveillance covering both spot and Perp trading to catch manipulation patterns specific to Perps.
section 'Market surveillance'
The SFC frames this as an initial, high-level framework that may be refined, and operators are encouraged to bring proposed Perp structures to the SFC for discussion before offering them.
section 'Way forward'
rg: Read the whole document; it is short (one page of continuous text) with no page or paragraph numbering, organised by section headings from 'Scope of application' through 'Disclosure requirements'.

t: Circular on licensed corporations providing virtual asset dealing services (1) to offer financing for virtual asset dealing and access to shared order book, and (2) to safeguard client virtual assets relating to withdrawals
sl: SFC · licensed corporations providing virtual asset dealing services (1) to… (2026)
s: The SFC lets VA brokers (licensed corporations dealing in VAs through omnibus accounts at licensed platforms) that already run securities margin financing lend to margin clients for VA trades. Credit must rest on the client's financial capacity and on securities and a narrow set of VA collateral: bitcoin and ether only, with a haircut of at least 60%. Brokers must assess VA-specific risks, monitor collateral in real time, apply existing margin-lending rules and not reuse VA collateral. The circular also sets conditions for agency trading on shared order books linked to overseas affiliates, including explicit opt-in for retail clients. Requires stronger controls where brokers let clients withdraw VAs. The HKMA circulated this same SFC circular to registered institutions (RIs) as an attachment to its own circular dated 27 May 2026. The HKMA circular's own covering text was not captured in the fetched source for this entry, so any bank-specific modifications (e.g. to eligible collateral or capital treatment) it may make are not verified here.
w: The fetched text for this entry is the SFC circular itself. The HKMA is confirmed (via the BRDR listing) to have issued it to RIs on 27 May 2026. The HKMA cover circular's own substantive text was not fetched, so compliance should obtain and read that HKMA circular directly rather than assume it mirrors the SFC terms.
k: Before this, firms were barred from giving clients credit to buy VAs; the SFC now allows it as a first step under its ASPIRe roadmap.
paras 2-3, p.1
Financing is limited to existing securities margin clients and based on their financial capacity plus posted collateral.
paras 4-5, p.1
Firms should not raise credit limits just because VA financing is available, and should weigh VA-specific risks when counting VAs toward net worth.
para 6(a)-(g), pp.1-2
VA collateral is limited to bitcoin and ether with a haircut of at least 60%, which the SFC may revise on notice.
para 7, p.2
Firms relying on VA collateral must document methods in the margin policy and monitor collateral volatility in real time.
para 8, p.2
Value collateral using prices on the platform where the client's orders execute, with a contingency plan for platform outages.
para 9, p.2
Existing margin rules extend to VA financing; VA collateral cannot be repledged or reused except on client default.
para 10(a)-(c), p.3
Where the loan exceeds collateral value or margin calls go unpaid, stop further advances and VA purchases and review limits.
para 11, p.3
Until capital rules are revised, VA collateral gets a 100% haircut under the Financial Resources Rules.
para 14, p.3
Agency trading on a shared order book needs a prior risk assessment (conflicts, settlement, failure scenarios, reserves, client recourse) and clear disclosure.
para 16, p.4
Retail clients may access a shared order book only after the overseas risks are prominently explained and they expressly opt in.
para 17, p.4
Where clients can withdraw VAs, brokers must harden authentication and access, monitor around the clock with escalation and suspension. Work with platforms on withdrawal limits and blocking.
paras 19-20, pp.4-5
rg: Read paras 4-11 (financing), 16-17 (shared order book) and 19-20 (withdrawals). Para 14 on capital applies to LCs only.

t: Circular on licensed corporations providing virtual asset dealing services (1) to offer financing for virtual asset dealing and access to shared order book, and (2) to safeguard client virtual assets relating to withdrawals
sl: SFC · licensed corporations providing virtual asset dealing services (1) to… (2026)
s: This SFC circular relaxes the prior prohibition on financial accommodation for VA dealing. Permitting VA brokers (licensed corporations providing VA dealing services under an omnibus account arrangement) that already conduct securities margin financing to extend VA financing to margin clients. Subject to strict conditions. Eligible VA collateral limited to bitcoin and ether with a haircut of 60% or more, extension of existing Securities Margin Financing Guidelines controls, and specific credit-risk factors to assess. It also lets VA brokers act as agent on a Shared Order Book that matches orders across affiliated VATPs. This is subject to risk assessment and, for retail clients, explicit risk disclosure and opt-in. Finally, it sets expected controls for VA brokers offering client VA withdrawal functionality, given the added cyber/operational risk of fraudulent withdrawal instructions.
w: This binds the bank's SFC-licensed VA-dealing subsidiary directly. It sets credit-risk, collateral-eligibility and withdrawal-security controls the compliance head must build into the bank's VA brokerage product design before any VA-collateralised margin lending goes live.
k: VA brokers engaging in securities margin financing may now extend VA financing to margin clients, based on financial capability plus securities and/or VA collateral. This relaxes the prior blanket prohibition on financial accommodation for VA dealing.
paras 2-4, p.1

Eligible VA clients for financing are limited to the broker's existing securities margin financing clients. Brokers must not increase a client's credit limit solely because VA financing becomes available.
paras 5-6, p.1-2
If VA collateral is used as credit risk mitigation, it must be limited to bitcoin and ether only, with a prudent haircut of 60% or more applied to its market value.
para 7, p.2
Until a planned consultation revises capital requirements, VA collateral must be treated with a full 100% haircut, per the Securities and Futures (Financial Resources) Rules.
para 14, p.3
VA brokers must not repledge, reuse or create encumbrance over VA collateral other than to enforce it upon client default.
para 10(c), p.3

VA brokers may conduct agency trading on a Shared Order Book (cross-platform order matching among affiliate VATPs). Before doing so, they must assess conflicts of interest, the settlement mechanism, failed-settlement or default processes, risk mitigation measures, and client protection or recourse.

Retail clients may only access the Shared Order Book if the broker has explained the additional overseas-jurisdiction risks (including potentially lower client protection) and the client has expressly elected to participate.
para 17, p.4

VA brokers offering client VA withdrawal functionality must implement robust authentication and access controls, plus continuous monitoring with incident escalation. They must also collaborate with VATP operators on withdrawal limits and suspicious-withdrawal detection, given the risk of fraudulent withdrawal instructions from a compromised broker system.
rg: Read paras 1-14 (VA financing) and paras 18-20 (withdrawal safeguards) closely. Paras 15-17 (Shared Order Book) are secondary if the bank's VA broker does not use shared order books.

t: Circular on permitting virtual asset trading platform operators to accept affiliated market makers
sl: SFC · permitting virtual asset trading platform operators to accept affiliated… (2026)
s: This SFC circular permits SFC-licensed VATP operators, for the first time as a general policy rather than case-by-case, to allow an affiliated company (an affiliated market maker. AFMM) to conduct market making on their platform, in order to address subdued VATP liquidity under Pillar A (Access) of the ASPIRe roadmap. Permission is conditional on effective conflicts-of-interest controls (functional independence, information barriers, client order priority, post-trade AFMM trade identification. Disclosure of preferential treatment), binding Terms and Conditions imposed on the operator's licence (set out in an Appendix). A mandatory prior notification to the SFC accompanied by an independent professional firm's compliance report, signed off by the Manager-in-Charge of Overall Management Oversight (MIC OMO).
w: This binds VATPs, not the bank directly. If the bank's VATP-affiliated entity wants to market-make on its own platform, a compliance head must ensure the conflicts-of-interest. Disclosure and SFC pre-notification framework here is fully built before commencing.
k: Under the current VATP Guidelines (para 13.3), a Platform Operator's group companies are generally barred from proprietary trading through the Platform Operator, except where the SFC permits it case-by-case. This circular sets a general framework to permit an AFMM to market-make.
para 4, p.1
A Platform Operator must ensure the AFMM is functionally independent, with organisational and administrative segregation from the Platform Operator's operating environment.
para 7(a) and Appendix para 1(a), p.1-2

Platform operators must make sure client orders rank ahead of AFMM orders whenever they trade at the same price. They must also be able to flag which trades in post-trade data were executed by the AFMM.
para 7(e)-(f), p.2
The Platform Operator must disclose to clients the AFMM's presence and role, any preferential treatment in pre-trade transparency/order placing/execution, and associated risks.
para 7(g), p.2
At least one Responsible Officer or MIC must be designated to oversee conflicts of interest management regarding the AFMM.
para 7(c), p.2

Before allowing AFMM market making, the Platform Operator must notify the SFC in writing and submit an independent professional firm's report confirming the effectiveness of its Terms and Conditions compliance controls.
para 9, p.2

The MIC of Overall Management Oversight (MIC OMO) must sign the notification to the SFC, confirming that compliance policies are in place. They must also pledge to immediately halt AFMM market making the moment a breach affects clients significantly, in the SFC's judgement.
para 10, p.2

The AFMM must get the same technical access as other market makers get, including market data feeds, connectivity, and order types. Its orders and trades must be captured in the operator's market surveillance systems.
Appendix paras 1(g), 2, p.1-2
The Platform Operator must immediately report to the SFC any actual or potential material breach of the Terms and Conditions, or any regulatory or law enforcement action against the AFMM.
Appendix para 3, p.2
Compliance with the AFMM Terms and Conditions must be covered in the Platform Operator's annual independent professional firm review reported to the SFC.
Appendix para 4, p.2
rg: Read the main circular (paras 1-11) for the policy rationale and notification process, then the Appendix Terms and Conditions in full as they are the binding licence conditions.

t: SFC convenes third Digital Asset Consultative Panel meeting
sl: SFC · SFC convenes third Digital Asset Consultative Panel meeting (2026)
s: The SFC held the third meeting of its Digital Asset Consultative Panel (DACP). A forum where the SFC's licensed virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs) come together to discuss upcoming regulatory developments. Participants discussed initiatives to strengthen the digital asset ecosystem, including steps to boost liquidity on licensed VATPs and widen the range of products and services. The DACP is chaired by Dr Eric Yip, the SFC's Executive Director of Intermediaries, and works under Pillar Re (Relationships) of the ASPIRe roadmap.
w: This signals the SFC's ongoing industry-engagement channel (DACP). Previewing coming liquidity and product-expansion steps for licensed VATPs — useful for anticipating future circulars, such as those on shared order books and financing.
k: The SFC held the third DACP meeting with SFC-licensed VATPs to discuss coming digital asset regulatory developments.
para 1, p.1
Topics discussed included regulatory steps to boost liquidity on licensed VATPs and to widen product and service offerings.
para 2, p.1
The DACP works in line with Pillar Re (Relationships) of the SFC's ASPIRe roadmap, supporting ongoing collaboration with licensed VATPs.
para 4, p.1
rg: Short press release; read in full (under 1 page).

t: HKMA unveils Fintech Promotion Blueprint: From adoption to advancement
sl: HKMA · HKMA unveils Fintech Promotion Blueprint: From adoption to advancement (2026)
s: The HKMA published its Fintech Promotion Blueprint under the 'Fintech 2030' strategy, focused on more sophisticated applications of AI and distributed ledger technology (DLT). Enabled by high-performance computing (HPC), with Data Excellence and Cyber Resilience as foundational pillars. Four flagship projects were announced: a Quantum Preparedness Index to assess banks' post-quantum cryptography readiness; a New Risk Data Strategy to strengthen bank data governance and infrastructure. A Fintech Cybersecurity Baseline for fintech solution providers to streamline bank due-diligence; and Competency Development Support for fintech users. The Blueprint also introduces FiNETech events, innovation competitions, a revamped Fintech Connect matching platform, and workshops, responding to challenges identified in the HKMA's Tech Maturity Stock-take.
w: Non-binding today. A compliance head should still track the Quantum Preparedness Index and the Fintech Cybersecurity Baseline. Both are likely future supervisory expectations relevant to any DLT-enabled digital-asset product's technology and vendor risk management.
k: The Blueprint sits under 'Fintech 2030' and is structured around three tactical dimensions: Ecosystem Collaboration, Technological Advancement, and Talent and Outreach, with Data Excellence and Cyber Resilience as foundational pillars.
paras 2-3, p.1

The HKMA plans to build a Quantum Preparedness Index. This gauges how ready the banking sector is for Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), giving both a snapshot of where things stand now and a measurable target over several years.
para 5, p.1
A New Risk Data Strategy will enhance banks' data management capabilities and data governance frameworks to support advanced AI/DLT analytics and expand the HKMA's Granular Data Reporting initiative.
para 6, p.1

A new industry-led Fintech Cybersecurity Baseline will be established with industry experts for fintech solution providers using AI/DLT, to improve due-diligence efficiency for banks onboarding fintech partners.
para 7, p.1
Competency development support will provide practical guidance to enhance skills of general fintech users, with a focus on 'human-machine interaction' capability.
para 8, p.1

The Blueprint responds to challenges identified in the HKMA's Tech Maturity Stock-take via FiNETech events, responsible innovation competitions, a revamped Fintech Connect matching platform, and practical workshops.
para 9, p.1
rg: Short press release (about 1 page); read in full for the four flagship projects; the full Blueprint PDF attachment gives the detailed initiatives.

t: SFC and UAE's Capital Market Authority sign milestone MoU to strengthen cross-border digital asset collaboration
sl: SFC · SFC and UAE's Capital Market Authority sign milestone MoU… (2026)
s: The SFC and the UAE's Capital Market Authority (CMA) signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to deepen cross-border regulatory teamwork on digital-asset matters. The SFC's first agreement with an overseas regulator focused specifically on supervising regulated digital-asset firms. The MoU sets up a framework for the two regulators to consult each other and share information when overseeing cross-border digital-asset entities, under the SFC's ASPIRe roadmap. It follows and expands on a Mutual Recognition of Funds MoU the two regulators signed in September 2025, and was announced alongside an industry event on UAE fund distribution.
w: Shows Hong Kong and the UAE stepping up cooperation on supervising digital-asset businesses -- worth noting for a bank with UAE ties or plans for cross-border digital-asset activity.
k: This is the SFC's first agreement with a foreign regulator built specifically for joint supervision of regulated digital-asset entities.
para 2, p.1
The MoU sets up a channel for the two regulators to consult each other and exchange information to help supervise digital-asset firms operating across both markets.
para 2, p.1
CMA CEO H.E. Waleed Saeed Al Awadhi and SFC CEO Ms Julia Leung signed the agreement, with SFC Chairman Dr Kelvin Wong present.
para 3, p.1
This digital-asset MoU builds on an earlier fund-recognition agreement the two regulators signed in September 2025. Lets each side's public funds be offered in the other's market.
para 6 and Note 3, p.1
rg: Read in full; short press release with quotes; notes provide background only.

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism Transition to the new suspicious transaction reporting platform
sl: SFC · licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities -… (2026)
s: This SFC circular tells licensed corporations, SFC-licensed virtual-asset service providers and their associated entities about a platform switch. The Joint Financial Intelligence Unit (JFIU) is switching from the STREAMS platform to the new STREAMS 2 platform for filing suspicious transaction reports (STRs), effective 2 February 2026. It sets out the three allowed submission methods: XML file, uploading a set PDF form, or a web form. It also covers account sign-up steps, and a blackout window from midnight on 28 January 2026 to 9am on 2 February 2026. During that window, any urgent STR must go straight to the JFIU by email, phone or fax.
w: This is a firm operational deadline for the bank's SFC-licensed corporation or trading-platform subsidiary, not for the bank itself as an Authorized Institution (AI). Files STRs under a separate HKMA AML/CFT channel. The Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO) should confirm which entity's filings this switch affects before 2 February 2026.
k: From 2 February 2026, STREAMS 2 becomes the only way to file STRs, replacing the old STREAMS platform.
Licensed firms must file STRs on STREAMS 2 using one of three formats. These are XML format (needs a Hongkong Post e-Cert), a preset PDF form upload (also needs an e-Cert), or the web-based STR form.
Licensed firms should sign up for STREAMS 2 accounts by sending a registration form to the JFIU by email, so they can file promptly.
STREAMS stops taking submissions from midnight on 28 January 2026, and STREAMS 2 starts taking them again at 9am on 2 February 2026. This gap is the blackout window.
para (a), p.2
During the blackout window, urgent STRs must go straight to the JFIU by email, phone (2866 3366) or fax (2529 4013).
para (b), p.2
All STRs filed earlier through STREAMS will move over to STREAMS 2, including any consent status attached to them.
para (c), p.2
Firms planning to file via XML must follow the JFIU's XML format and arrange a test with the JFIU as soon as possible.
para (d), p.2
Any STR sent to the JFIU by a channel other than STREAMS 2 after the switch must be re-filed through STREAMS 2.
footnote 2, p.1
rg: Read in full; it is a short two-page operational circular with a clear timeline.

t: SFC reprimands and fines Saxo Capital Markets HK Limited $4 million for regulatory breaches over distribution of virtual asset-related products
sl: SFC · SFC reprimands and fines Saxo Capital Markets HK Limited… (2026)
s: The SFC reprimanded Saxo Capital Markets HK Limited (SCMHK) and imposed a HK$4 million fine. The fine was for selling 32 unauthorised virtual-asset (VA) funds and VA-related products to retail and professional clients through its online trading platform. This ran over roughly four years, from late 2018 to late 2022, in breach of two SFC circulars that limit such products to professional investors.
w: This SFC enforcement case against an online broker equivalent to a Registered Institution (RI), for selling VA products to retail clients without suitability checks. Knowledge tests or warnings, gives a useful benchmark for the bank's own online product-identification and suitability controls. Shows the value of self-reporting.
k: SCMHK was fined HK$4 million and reprimanded for selling VA products to retail and professional investor (PI) clients. Breaching 2018 and 2022 circulars that limit such products to professional investors.
para 1, p.1

During the relevant period (1 November 2018 to 25 November 2022), SCMHK executed 1,446 trades across 32 VA products. Including 21 exchange-traded derivatives, on behalf of six individual PIs plus 130 retail clients.
para 3, p.1
SCMHK never checked whether clients understood VA products or gave enough VA-specific information and warnings before executing trades, breaching circular guidance.
para 4, p.1

SCMHK had no dedicated due-diligence process for VA products and instead relied on a flawed group-wide check that missed all 32 products as VA-related. They went to every client regardless of PI status.
para 5, p.1
The SFC found SCMHK failed to check whether complex VA products suited each client and failed to give enough risk and feature information plus warnings on its online platform.
paras 7-8, p.1
For 87 clients who traded exchange-traded derivative VA products, SCMHK failed to properly check and record their derivatives knowledge.
para 9, p.1
The breaches involved two instruments. The Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the SFC, together with the Guidelines on Online Distribution and Advisory Platforms.
para 10, p.1

Factors reducing the penalty: SCMHK reported itself, voluntarily paid clients back, stopped regulated activities from 28 February 2025, cooperated, and had a clean disciplinary history. The misconduct lasting over four years counted against it.
para 12, p.1
rg: Read the full release; it is a concise enforcement summary with no sections to skip.

t: Consultation Conclusions on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Custodian Service Providers
sl: FSTB/SFC · Consultation Conclusions on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset… (2025)
s: The FSTB and SFC conclude their June 2025 consultation on a new AMLO licensing regime for virtual asset (VA) custodian services. The scope targets entities that safekeep private keys or similar instruments enabling transfer of client VAs (a technology-neutral test), not entities with a purely administrative or delegated oversight role. HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers custodying only their own issued stablecoins are exempt. Custody of tokenised securities is out of scope because 'virtual asset' under the AMLO excludes securities. Baseline financial resources requirements mirror Type 13 (depositary) licensees: HK$10 million minimum paid-up capital and HK$3 million minimum liquid capital. No deeming arrangement will be provided; a bill is planned for the Legislative Council in 2026.
w: This defines the future licensing perimeter and capital/individual-licensing standards for any VA custody function the bank or its associated entities perform. Sets the due-diligence bar the bank should expect of any third-party VA custodian it appoints as a counterparty.
k: VA custodian licensing will cover entities that safekeep private keys or similar instruments enabling transfer of client virtual assets. This is a technology-neutral definition covering MPC, HSM and other key-management models case by case.
para 6-7, p.5

Trustees or fund managers who merely delegate custody to a third-party VA custodian, without holding keys themselves, will not require a VA custodian licence. Their role is treated as administrative or contractual, similar to a securities trustee.
para 8, p.5
Custody of tokenised securities is outside the VA custodian licensing regime because the AMLO's definition of 'virtual asset' excludes securities and futures contracts.
para 12, p.6
Stablecoin issuers licensed by HKMA under the Stablecoins Ordinance are exempt from VA custodian licensing when they custody only the stablecoins they themselves issue for their clients.
para 34, p.11

SFC-regulated VA custodians may draw on overseas group resources and infrastructure without that group entity needing its own licence. This applies as long as the SFC-regulated entity can still move client assets on its own, without needing the overseas entity's agreement. The overseas group entities must not actively market themselves as VA custodians to Hong Kong.
para 16, p.8

Individual licensing (or being engaged as a relevant individual) will apply to senior managers overseeing custody, and to anyone able to directly access private keys or to start or approve VA transfers. It also covers participants in multi-signature or threshold-signing arrangements, and anyone with access to key generation, storage or recovery systems. Staff doing purely clerical work are excluded.
VA custodians will be permitted to offer staking services, subject to the same safeguards as the SFC's existing staking guidance for VATPs (7 April 2025 circular).

No restriction is being imposed on which types of VA a custodian may hold. Custodians must perform robust due diligence, including a token admission committee process similar to the VATP Guidelines' due diligence framework, and can also custody tokenised securities.
para 40, p.13

Baseline financial resources rules require at least HK$10 million in paid-up share capital and at least HK$3 million in required liquid capital, matching Type 13 (depositary services) licensed corporations. Banks, however, stay subject to their existing HKMA capital rules instead.
para 42, p.14

The SFC will build custody regulatory requirements on the existing VATP Guidelines Chapter X (Custody of Client Assets) as the baseline. This includes its 15 August 2025 circular on custody of virtual assets.
para 44, p.15

No deeming or grandfathering arrangement will be given. The regime takes full effect on the statutory commencement date, though the Government and SFC will consider an appropriate commencement date allowing time for market participants to adjust.

A faster approval track will be available for associated entities of SFC-licensed VATPs, and for banks. It also covers subsidiaries of locally incorporated banks that the SFC or HKMA has already assessed for VA custody activity.
rg: Read the Introduction (p.3) and the scope/response sections (paras 5-35, p.5-12) for who needs a licence. Then the financial resources (paras 41-42, p.13-14) and transitional arrangement (paras 45-52, p.15-17) sections. Skip the Annex list of respondents (p.20-21).

t: FSTB and SFC publish consultation conclusions on legislative proposals for regulating virtual asset dealing and custodian services
sl: FSTB/SFC · FSTB and SFC publish consultation conclusions on legislative proposals… (2025)
s: The government and the SFC announced the outcome of two 2025 consultations on how to license virtual-asset dealing and virtual-asset custody businesses. Most respondents backed extending regulation beyond the existing trading-platform regime. At the same time, the two bodies opened a fresh one-month consultation on separate licensing tracks for virtual asset advisory and virtual asset management services, closing 23 January 2026. Officials aim to bring a single bill covering all these regimes to the Legislative Council in 2026. The full detail sits in two companion papers, summarised as separate registry entries.
w: This is the clearest signal yet that Hong Kong will regulate the full VA intermediary chain, not just exchanges. A bank's compliance function should start mapping which of its VA-related activities (dealing, custody, advice, fund management) will each need a separate licence.
k: The dealing-services licensing model will largely mirror the existing Type 1 (dealing in securities) regime under the Securities and Futures Ordinance.
para 4 (main text)
Custodian licensing will center on the safekeeping of private keys, since that is seen as the core custody risk.
para 4 (main text)
A new, separate one-month consultation on VA advisory and VA management licensing opened the same day and runs to 23 January 2026.
para 6 (main text)
Government intends to introduce a single bill covering the dealing, custodian, advisory and management regimes into the Legislative Council during 2026.
para 9 (main text)
rg: Read this press release for the headline outcome and dates; go to the two attached consultation-conclusions papers for the operative detail bankers need.

t: Consultation Conclusions Legislative Proposal to Regulate Dealing in Virtual Assets and Further Public Consultation Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Advisory Service Providers and Virtual Asset Management Service Providers
sl: FSTB · Consultation Conclusions Legislative Proposal to Regulate Dealing in Virtual… (2025)
s: The FSTB and SFC publish conclusions on their June 2025 consultation on a licensing regime for VA dealing services under the AMLO. Confirming the scope will align with Type 1 regulated activity. Custody of client VAs must be with SFC-regulated VA custodians, baseline capital requirements will mirror Type 1 licensed corporations (HK$5 million paid-up capital. Up to HK$3 million liquid capital), no deeming/transitional arrangement will be given. An expedited approval process will apply to existing SFC-licensed VATPs, LCs and RIs already dealing in VAs. In the same paper, Section B launches a further consultation (comments due 23 January 2026). It proposes new licensing regimes for VA advisory service providers (referencing Type 4) and VA management service providers (referencing Type 9). This includes proposed definitions, exemptions, no de minimis threshold for VA management, and indicative financial resources requirements. A bill covering VA dealing, advisory and management services is targeted for introduction to LegCo in 2026.
w: These are the finalised (VA dealing) and further-consulted (VA advisory/management) terms a compliance head must plan the bank's registration and custody-arrangement strategy around. Including the bank-only registration pathway for advisory/management services and the absence of grandfathering.
k: VA dealing service scope will be aligned with Type 1 (dealing in securities) under the SFO. Limb (b) of the original proposed definition covering VA derivatives/structured products has been removed to avoid duplicative licensing.
paras 3-5, p.5-6
Payment service providers offering VA conversion services that amount to acquiring/disposing of VAs may need a licence even if VA transactions are incidental to cross-border settlement.
para 4, p.5
Issuers holding an HKMA stablecoin licence, when carrying out regulated stablecoin activity, will not need to also hold a licence under the VA dealing regime.
para 11, p.6

The SFC will require VA dealers to keep client VAs in custody exclusively with custodian service providers regulated by the SFC. Turning down proposals to also permit overseas-regulated custodians given how early-stage this regime still is.
para 26, p.9

Baseline financial resources for VA dealing service providers. At least HK$5 million in paid-up share capital. Required liquid capital that can reach HK$3 million according to the firm's business model, matching Type 1 licensed corporations. The SFC keeps the flexibility to demand excess liquid capital equal to at least 12 months of operating expenses.
para 29, p.10

No deeming/transitional arrangement will be granted to existing VA dealing service providers. The regime takes full effect on the commencement date, though SFC-licensed VATPs. LCs and RIs already dealing in VAs qualify for an expedited approval process.
paras 31, 36, p.11
Persons not licensed/registered with the SFC will be prohibited from actively marketing VA dealing services to the Hong Kong public. Whether based in Hong Kong or elsewhere.
para 40, p.12

Section B of the further consultation proposes licensing VA advisory providers (modelled on Type 4) and VA management providers (modelled on Type 9) under the AMLO. Only banks would register rather than be licensed for VA advisory or management services. The HKMA does not anticipate its licensed stablecoin issuers or SVFs offering these services.
paras 52, 58 and footnotes 9-10, p.15-16

No de minimis threshold is proposed for VA management licensing - any entity managing a portfolio that invests in VAs. Regardless of amount, needs a licence or registration, to prevent regulatory arbitrage.
paras 60-61, p.17

Proposed baseline financial resources for firms providing VA advisory or VA management services. HK$5 million in paid-up capital. Minimum liquid capital of HK$100,000 if they hold no client assets or HK$3 million if they do, mirroring the Type 4/Type 9 rules.
Comments on the further consultation (VA advisory and VA management regimes) are due by 23 January 2026.
para 72, p.19
rg: Read the Introduction (p.3-4) for context, then Section A responses (paras 3-48, p.5-14) for the finalised VA dealing regime. Section B (paras 50-72, p.15-19) for the new advisory/management proposals. Skip the Annex list of respondents (p.20-21).

t: Consultation Conclusions: Legislative Proposal to Regulate Dealing in Virtual Assets, and Further Public Consultation: Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Advisory Service Providers and Virtual Asset Management Service Providers
sl: FSTB/SFC · Consultation Conclusions: Legislative Proposal to Regulate Dealing in Virtual… (2025)
s: This paper closes out the mid-2025 consultation on licensing virtual asset (VA) dealing services and, in the same document. Opens a fresh consultation proposing separate licences for VA advisory and VA management services. Modelled on the Type 1, Type 4 and Type 9 regimes under the Securities and Futures Ordinance. VA dealing will be licensed on an activity basis regardless of purpose, catching even payment firms that convert VAs incidentally. Licensed VA dealers will generally be required to hold client VAs only with SFC-regulated VA custodians, and no grandfathering (deeming) will be offered when the regime starts. A bill is targeted for introduction into the Legislative Council in 2026.
w: If the bank runs, or wants to run, VA dealing, advisory or discretionary VA management for clients. This paper is the clearest current statement of what capital, custody-outsourcing and marketing rules to expect. It confirms banks (uniquely among non-SFC entities) may register rather than seek a full SFC licence for advisory/management.
k: VA dealing services will be defined to track the existing Type 1 (dealing in securities) activity definition under the Securities and Futures Ordinance. Catching anyone who, as a business, makes or induces agreements to acquire, dispose of, subscribe for or underwrite virtual assets.
para 3
Payment service providers whose services include converting virtual assets can be caught as VA dealers even where the VA leg is incidental to a payment or settlement purpose.
para 4
Tokenised-securities-only dealing is excluded, because the statutory definition of virtual asset under the AMLO carves out securities and futures contracts.
para 6
HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers doing only their own licensed stablecoin activity will be exempt from needing a separate VA dealing licence.
para 11
SFC-regulated VA dealers will be required to custody client virtual assets with SFC-regulated VA custodian service providers rather than overseas custodians. At least while the regime is new.
para 26

A licensed VA dealing service provider's baseline financial resources will be paid-up share capital of at least HK$5 million. With required liquid capital that can rise as high as HK$3 million, matching the standard for Type 1 licensed corporations.
para 29
No deeming/grandfathering arrangement will apply — existing VA dealing firms must be licensed by the commencement date or must stop operating on that date.
para 31
Firms already offering these services are urged to contact the SFC or HKMA early to access an expedited licensing/registration track.
para 33
Unlicensed persons will be prohibited from actively marketing VA dealing services to the Hong Kong public, wherever the marketer is based.
para 40

New: a further one-month consultation proposes separate VA advisory and VA management licences (mirroring Types 4 and 9). Only open to banks by way of registration rather than any AI/RI generally. Comments due 23 January 2026.
rg: Read paras 1-49 (Section A) for the dealing-services conclusions, especially paras 3-27 on scope and custody. Read Section B (paras 50-72) for the new advisory/management proposals; skip the respondent list annex.

t: Consultation Conclusions on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Dealing in Virtual Assets and Further Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Advisory Service Providers and Virtual Asset Management Service Providers
sl: FSTB/SFC · Consultation Conclusions on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Dealing in… (2025)
s: The FSTB and SFC report back on their mid-2025 consultation about licensing virtual asset (VA) dealing under the AMLO. Open a further round of consultation (which closed January 2026) on two new licence types for VA advisory and VA fund/portfolio management. Built on the existing SFO Type 4 and Type 9 regimes. VA dealing will be scoped like ordinary securities dealing, with no transition period letting existing providers carry on unlicensed. Firms already licensed by HKMA to issue stablecoins do not need a separate VA dealing licence for that stablecoin business. A bill covering all these regimes is due before the Legislative Council in 2026.
w: This defines the forthcoming AMLO licensing perimeter for VA dealing, advisory and management activities that the bank's own or affiliated entities. Its VATP/custodian counterparties, will need to comply with. The no-deeming-arrangement decision means any bank-linked entity providing these services must pre-engage the SFC/HKMA now to avoid a forced business halt on commencement.
k: VA dealing will be defined the same way as ordinary securities dealing under the SFO. Making or offering deals, or inducing someone else to deal, to buy, sell, subscribe for or underwrite virtual assets.
para 3, p.5

Payment service providers whose VA-conversion activity meets the VA dealing definition (e.g. offering conversion services) may need to be licensed or registered, even if VA use is incidental to cross-border settlement.
para 4, p.5-6
Stablecoin issuers licensed by HKMA under the Stablecoins Ordinance are exempt from the VA dealing licence for their regulated stablecoin activity.
para 11, p.6
Firms dealing in VAs for clients on the SFC's watch will, for now. Only be allowed to hold those client assets with an SFC-regulated VA custodian. Not a custodian regulated somewhere else.
para 26, p.9
VA dealers will face the same capital rules as ordinary securities dealers. HK$5 million paid-up capital, with liquid capital that can reach as much as HK$3 million according to the business model.
para 29, p.10
Existing VA dealers get no transition window -- once the new law takes effect, anyone still unlicensed must stop dealing in VAs that day.
An expedited approval process will apply to SFC-licensed VATPs and existing licensed corporations/registered institutions already providing VA dealing services.
para 36, p.11
Anyone without an SFC licence or registration may not actively market VA dealing services to people in Hong Kong. Regardless of whether the marketing originates inside or outside Hong Kong.
para 40, p.12

Two new licensing regimes are proposed (further consultation, closing 23 January 2026). VA advisory services (modelled on SFO Type 4) and VA management services (modelled on SFO Type 9). Each requiring SFC licensing/registration subject to a fit-and-proper test.

Banks alone will be able to register with the SFC for VA advisory or VA management services rather than needing a full licence. The HKMA does not expect its licensed stablecoin issuers or stored value facilities to offer these services.
footnote 9 & 10, p.15-17

The proposed VA management licence deliberately has no minimum-exposure carve-out. Any firm running a portfolio with even a small slice in VAs needs a licence, a stricter line than some other markets' portfolio-percentage thresholds.
para 60, p.17

Capital rules proposed for VA advisers and VA managers copy the existing Type 4/Type 9 bands. HK$5 million paid-up capital, plus liquid capital of either HK$100,000 (no client assets held) or HK$3 million.
rg: Read Section A intro (p.3-4) and the 'Response' paragraphs for scope, custody, financial resources and transitional arrangement (paras 3-49, p.5-14) first. Section B (p.15-19) covers the new VA advisory/VA management proposals; skip the Annex list of respondents (p.20-21).

t: Consultation Conclusions: Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Custodian Services
sl: FSTB/SFC · Consultation Conclusions: Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Custodian… (2025)
s: This paper sets out how Hong Kong will licence virtual asset (VA) custodian services. The licence will attach to whoever actually safekeeps private keys or equivalent instruments — the entity able to move client VAs — not to trustees or fund managers who merely delegate custody onward. Individuals with real control over signing or key access, but not clerical staff, will need an individual licence or accreditation. No grandfathering will be offered when the regime commences, but an expedited process exists for entities already vetted by SFC or HKMA. HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers custodying only their own stablecoins are exempt.
w: This defines exactly which of the bank's VA-custody-adjacent functions will need a licence (key-holding entities) versus which will not (trustees, delegating fund managers). Sets the individual-licensing net compliance must apply to staff with real key or signing access.
k: A VA custodian service licence is needed only by the entity that can safekeep or independently transfer client virtual assets via private keys or similar instruments. Entities that merely delegate custody to a licensed custodian (e.g. fund trustees) do not need a separate custodian licence.
paras 6-8

Whether a technology provider (e.g. An MPC service) needs a licence turns on whether it can unilaterally move client assets. Providers whose clients can independently reconstruct keys or move assets without the provider generally do not need one.
para 11
Custody of tokenised securities (as opposed to virtual assets) falls outside this licensing regime because the statutory VA definition excludes securities and futures contracts.
para 12

An overseas group entity supporting a Hong Kong SFC-regulated custodian's infrastructure need not itself be separately licensed. Provided the Hong Kong entity retains sole ability to move client assets and the overseas entity does not itself market custody services to the Hong Kong public.
para 16

Individual licensing (or accreditation as a relevant individual) will be required for senior management overseeing custody. Anyone with direct access to private keys or authority to approve transfers, multi-signature participants. Those with access to key generation/recovery systems. Purely clerical staff are excluded.
paras 25-26

A licensed VA custodian's baseline financial resources will be paid-up share capital of at least HK$10 million and liquid capital of at least HK$3 million. Matching the Type 13 (depositary services) standard, though banks rely instead on their existing HKMA capital rules.
para 42
No deeming/grandfathering arrangement will apply. The regime takes full effect on the commencement date, though an expedited approval track is available for entities already assessed by SFC or HKMA.
paras 48, 51
HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers custodying only the stablecoins they themselves issue for their own clients are exempt from needing a separate VA custodian licence.
para 34

SFC intends to use the VATP Guidelines' Chapter X custody standards (including the existing 98/2 cold/hot storage benchmark referenced by respondents) as the baseline for the new custodian regulatory requirements.
para 44 (referencing 98/2 ratio raised in para 43(a))
Licensed VA custodians will be permitted to offer staking services, subject to safeguards similar to those already required of VATPs offering staking.
para 37
rg: Read paras 1-35 (Scope) closely for the private-key test and exemptions, and paras 15-28 on individual licensing; skim paras 36-64 on allowed activities, fees and appeals. Skip the annex of respondents.

t: FSTB and SFC conclude consultations on virtual asset dealer and custodian regimes, further consult on two new regimes
sl: FSTB · FSTB and SFC conclude consultations on virtual asset dealer… (2025)
s: This press release announces that the FSTB and SFC have finished reviewing the mid-2025 VA dealing and VA custodian consultations and will move ahead with both licensing regimes. Citing broad market support (over 190 responses) under the ASPIRe roadmap's 'Access' pillar. VA dealers will be regulated in a way that tracks Type 1 (securities dealing). VA custodians will be regulated around how they keep client VAs' private keys safe within Hong Kong. At the same time, a further consultation was launched on new VA advisory and VA management service provider regimes, with comments due 23 January 2026. A bill covering all these regimes is targeted for introduction to LegCo in 2026.
w: This confirms Hong Kong's VA regulatory perimeter is expanding into dealing, custody, advisory and management as separately licensable activities under one forthcoming bill. A compliance head should map which of the bank's activities will need which licence and start SFC pre-application discussions early.
k: FSTB and SFC will proceed with legislative proposals for VA dealer and VA custodian regimes following broad market support.
para 2, p.1
The VA dealer regime will closely track the Type 1 (dealing in securities) regulated activity set out in the SFO, with comparable exemptions being considered.
para 3, p.1
The VA custodian regime will centre on the risks of keeping client VAs' private keys secure within Hong Kong.
para 3, p.1
Interested parties are encouraged to initiate pre-application discussions with the SFC to prepare for the proposed regimes.
para 4, p.1
Further consultation launched the same day on new VA advisory and VA management service provider regimes, modelled on comparable securities-market regulation.
para 5, p.1
Over 190 responses were received across the two original consultations (VA dealer and VA custodian).
Note 2, p.1
Comments on the VA advisor and manager regimes further consultation are due to FSTB or SFC by 23 January 2026.
final note, p.1
FSTB and SFC intend to finalise legislative proposals under the AMLO (Cap. 615) and introduce a bill into LegCo in 2026.
Note 3, p.1
rg: Short press release; read in full (about 1 page); notes at the end give background context only.

t: Supervisory Policy Manual CR-G-8: Large Exposures and Risk Concentrations
sl: HKMA · Supervisory Policy Manual CR-G-8: Large Exposures and Risk Concentrations (2025)
s: CR-G-8 is a general SPM module (V.5, effective 19 Dec 2025) explaining how banks value exposures for the statutory large-exposure limits. These limits sit under the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules (BELR) Part 7. Most of it covers ordinary credit, derivative and securities-financing exposures and does not mention cryptoassets. A dedicated set of paragraphs was added covering how cryptoasset-related exposures are valued for large-exposure purposes, cross-referring to the new Banking (Capital) Rules cryptoasset provisions.
w: Confirms that cryptoasset exposures are not simply folded into existing large-exposure valuation methods. They sit under a separate BELR division, and the HKMA has reserved a case-by-case power to override the standard valuation approach for individual banks.
k: For large-exposure valuation, ordinary (non-cryptoasset) exposures are valued under Part 7 Divisions 4 and 5. Cryptoasset-related exposures get their own valuation regime under a new Division 5A.

Division 5A covers both credit-counterparty-risk and non-credit-counterparty-risk cryptoasset exposures. A bank must first identify the counterparty for each exposure, using the same counterparty identification already done for the capital-rules cryptoasset calculation.

How Division 5A applies to a given cryptoasset exposure depends on which definitional limb it falls under. It also depends on whether the underlying is a group 1a, 1b, 2a or 2b cryptoasset, and whether it sits in the banking or trading book.

In some cases a bank must apply the ordinary Division 5 valuation rules to certain non-credit-counterparty-risk cryptoasset exposures. In others it can reuse the valuation it already produced for capital purposes.

Because cryptoassets and their underlying technology and markets are still new and changing, the HKMA can prescribe a different valuation methodology than the standard one in the BELR. It does this by written notice to one or more banks.
rg: Read paras 2.8.1 and 2.8.8-2.8.12 (pages 18-21); skip the surrounding general discussion of sovereign concentration risk and standard derivative/SFT valuation.

t: Overview of Capital Adequacy Regime for Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions
sl: HKMA · Overview of Capital Adequacy Regime for Locally Incorporated Authorized… (2025)

It is a navigation page; the substantive text is the attached PDF, captured separately in this registry. The page shows CA-G-1's full version history back to 2008.
