t: Supervisory Policy Manual CA-G-5: Supervisory Review Process
sl: HKMA · Supervisory Policy Manual CA-G-5: Supervisory Review Process (2025)
s: CA-G-5 is a large, general SPM module (V.7, effective 19 Dec 2025). It explains how the HKMA's Pillar 2 Supervisory Review Process sets bank-specific capital add-ons on top of the minimum ratio. Most of the module is generic (governance expectations, ICAAP, stress testing) and does not mention cryptoassets. Two passages were added for the cryptoasset standard. One is a paragraph on how the HKMA may respond to capital or risk-management shortfalls tied to cryptoasset activities. The other is a reminder that boards must understand cryptoasset-related risks as part of firm-wide risk oversight. A companion cross-reference lists the new CRP-1 'Classification of Cryptoassets' module.
w: This confirms the HKMA treats cryptoasset activity as a distinct trigger for extra Pillar 2 capital or provisioning if a bank's controls are not yet mature. It expects that judgement to be made at board level, not left to a trading desk.
k: Because cryptoasset business is new and still developing, the HKMA may respond to related capital or risk-control gaps in several ways. These include temporary capital add-ons, requiring provisions against foreseeable cryptoasset losses, imposing exposure limits, or other mitigation measures.
para 3.6.6

As part of sound firm-wide risk management, the board and senior management should fully understand risks tied to new or complex activities, giving cryptoasset activities as one worked example alongside securitisation.
para 4.2.8
The module's own list of related SPM modules confirms a new module, CRP-1 'Classification of Cryptoassets', now sits alongside the credit, liquidity and market-risk modules.
Appendix listing, p.91
rg: Read only paras 3.6.6 and 4.2.8 (pages 53 and 63); the rest of this 300-page module is generic Pillar 2/ICAAP/stress-testing guidance unrelated to cryptoassets.

t: Cryptoassets standard: gazettal of revised SPM modules and code of practice
sl: HKMA · Cryptoassets standard: gazettal of revised SPM modules and code… (2025)
s: This is the operative HKMA circular (19 Dec 2025, Ref B1/15C etc.) announcing that the Monetary Authority has gazetted eight revised SPM modules and one revised code of practice. These are statutory guidelines or code under the Banking Ordinance. The stated purpose is to implement locally the Basel Committee's standard on the prudential treatment of banks' cryptoasset exposures. This is done via the Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2025 and consequential changes in the Banking (Exposure Limits) (Amendment) Rules 2025. All nine instruments take effect 1 January 2026.
w: This is the umbrella circular that gives every other module in this batch its legal basis and go-live date. Compliance should treat 1 January 2026 as the hard date by which crypto capital, large-exposure, major-acquisition, liquidity and market/CVA risk provisions all became binding statutory guidance.
k: The Monetary Authority has, by notice in the Gazette, issued eight revised SPM modules as statutory guidelines under sections 7(3) or 16(10) of the Banking Ordinance. It also issued a revised code of practice under section 97M(1). These are CA-G-1, CA-G-5, CR-G-8, CR-G-9, CR-L-5, LM-1, MR-1, MR-2, and the Banking (Exposure Limits) Code.
letter body, para 1

The revisions primarily implement the Basel Committee's standard on the prudential treatment of banks' cryptoasset exposures. This is given effect through the Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2025, plus consequential amendments in the Banking (Exposure Limits) (Amendment) Rules 2025.
letter body, para 2
All the revised modules and the code of practice take effect on 1 January 2026 and are accessible via the HKMA's Banking Regulatory Document Repository or the Supervisory Communication Website.
letter body, para 3
rg: Read the full two-page letter; it is short and entirely about the cryptoasset standard package.

t: CA-G-1 Overview of Capital Adequacy Regime for Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions
sl: HKMA · CA-G-1 Overview of Capital Adequacy Regime for Locally Incorporated… (2025)
s: CA-G-1 is the HKMA's master overview module explaining how a locally incorporated bank works out its capital adequacy ratio and leverage ratio, covering capital composition, buffers. The whole risk-weighting framework. This gazetted version (effective from the module's structure, aligned to the 1 January 2026 package) adds cryptoasset exposures throughout. A new section 8.7 on credit risk for tokenised assets and stablecoins, cross-references to the market-risk and CVA modules for crypto trading positions. A clarification that a cryptoasset exposure is never treated as an intangible asset for capital-deduction purposes. It formally replaces the fourth edition of CA-G-1 dated 29 November 2024.
w: This is the current, citable master reference for how any cryptoasset exposure on the bank's books feeds into its regulatory capital ratio. Compliance should map any crypto product against these classification-driven rules before onboarding it.
k: A cryptoasset exposure is not counted as an intangible asset for the purpose of deducting contingent items from a bank's capital base.
para 6.6.1, footnote 17
A new Part 12 was added to the risk-weighting framework, dedicated to calculating risk-weighted amounts for cryptoasset exposures.
para 8.1.1 (structure list); para 8.1.4
Tokenised traditional assets held in the banking book (Group 1a) are generally risk-weighted the same way as the underlying traditional asset would be.
para 8.7.1
For stablecoin-type tokens (Group 1b) held in the banking book. A bank must separately calculate the credit risk of the referenced asset and the credit risk that the redeemer defaults.
para 8.7.2
Where only some holders can redeem a Group 1b token directly. Extra credit risk applies depending on whether the bank is a redeeming member or must rely on a member to redeem on its behalf.
para 8.7.2(b)
The riskiest token category, Group 2b. Is subject to a fixed conservative capital treatment set in the Banking (Capital) Rules rather than a bespoke risk calculation.
para 8.7.3
A large or domestic systemically important bank faces an additional capital add-on once its ratio of Group 2 cryptoasset exposures to total capital passes a prescribed limit.
para 8.7.4(d)
For trading-book market risk, crypto positions must use one of three specified methods, with the internal models approach barred for Group 2a tokens. Detailed rules sit in module MR-1.
para 8.9.13

For CVA risk, crypto trades generally follow the same rules as trades on non-tokenised assets. Except that the standardised CVA approach cannot be used for Group 2a token trades. Detailed rules sit in module MR-2.
para 8.9.14
rg: Read section 8.7 (paras 8.7.1-8.7.4, pages 47-48) for the core credit-risk treatment. Plus the short crypto cross-references in paras 8.9.13-8.9.14 (page 52) and footnote 17 (page 23) on capital deductions. The rest of the module is general, non-crypto background.

t: Supervisory Policy Manual MR-2: CVA Risk Capital Charge
sl: HKMA · Supervisory Policy Manual MR-2: CVA Risk Capital Charge (2025)
s: MR-2 is a general SPM module (V.2, effective 19 Dec 2025) on calculating credit valuation adjustment (CVA) risk capital charges for derivatives and securities-financing transactions (SFTs). It adds a dedicated section 4, 'Cryptoasset exposures', applying the CVA framework to derivatives and material fair-valued SFTs referencing group 1a. 1b, 2a and 2b cryptoassets, with different treatment for each group.
w: This sets out exactly when a crypto derivatives desk can use the more capital-efficient SA-CVA model versus being forced onto the basic approach. Confirms the HKMA treats the least-mature cryptoasset bucket (group 2b) with a blunt, very high risk weight rather than a modelled charge.
k: Derivatives and SFTs on group 1a (tokenised) cryptoassets generally get the same CVA capital treatment as the equivalent non-tokenised traditional asset would receive.
para 4.2.1

A bank must independently assess the tokenised asset itself against the module's eligibility criteria (including liquidity characteristics). It cannot simply inherit the treatment of the underlying traditional asset, because differing liquidity between the two can create extra basis risk.
para 4.2.2

If there is not enough data to model the liquidity-driven basis risk between a tokenised asset and its traditional equivalent. The simpler basic approach (BA-CVA) must be used instead of the standardised approach (SA-CVA).
para 4.2.2
Derivatives on group 1b cryptoassets (stablecoins) get the same CVA capital treatment as derivatives on the traditional assets they reference.
para 4.2.3
Group 2a cryptoassets follow the module's requirements generally. Except that SA-CVA is not permitted for derivatives or fair-valued SFTs referencing them — only the basic approach applies.
para 4.3.1

Group 2b cryptoasset CVA risk is generally already captured by the conservative 1,250% risk-weight treatment, so no separate CVA calculation is needed. If credit risk for such an exposure is not already assessed at 1,250%. The bank must instead apply that conservative treatment for CVA risk specifically.
Fair-valued SFTs collateralised by cryptoassets are only brought into the CVA charge if the HKMA determines the resulting CVA risk is material.
para 4.3.3
rg: Read section 4 in full (pages 43-45, paras 4.1.1-4.3.3); the rest of the module is the general CVA framework for traditional derivatives and SFTs.

t: Supervisory Policy Manual LM-1: Regulatory Framework for Supervision of Liquidity Risk
sl: HKMA · Supervisory Policy Manual LM-1: Regulatory Framework for Supervision of… (2025)
s: LM-1 is a broad Supervisory Policy Manual (SPM) module (version 5, effective 19 December 2025) covering the HKMA's approach to supervising liquidity risk. Including the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) and Core Funding Ratio (CFR). It adds a short new section 5.9 and a large new Annex 3 explaining how cryptoasset exposures. Tokenised assets, stablecoins and other cryptoassets -- are treated for liquidity purposes, splitting category 1 and category 2 institutions and leaving central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) out of the annex's scope.
w: This is the clearest statement yet from the HKMA on how stablecoins and tokenised assets must be modelled in a bank's LCR and NSFR calculations. It puts direct liquidity-outflow consequences on a bank that issues or helps redeem stablecoins. Compliance needs this built into treasury's liquidity models and data feeds.
k: Cryptoasset exposures should generally get the same treatment as traditional exposures carrying the same economic risk, for LCR, NSFR, LMR and CFR purposes.
para 5.9.1
Because cryptoasset exposures can carry extra risk and there isn't much historical data yet, more detailed liquidity treatment is spelled out separately in Annex 3.
para 5.9.2
Annex 3's cryptoasset rules do not cover CBDCs. CBDCs are generally treated like physical banknotes and coins of the issuing jurisdiction, subject to each CBDC's own features and legal standing.
para 5.9.3

A cryptoasset cannot count as a high-quality liquid asset (HQLA), or as a liquefiable asset for category 2 institutions. The only exception is a group 1a cryptoasset that tokenises a traditional asset already eligible as HQLA. Even then, both the token and the underlying asset must meet all the usual eligibility tests.
Annex 3, paras 1 and 12

If a bank has issued group 1a cryptoassets that meet the tokenised-claim conditions, it must treat the resulting liabilities as deposits or unsecured funding. The exact outflow or inflow treatment depends on whether holders can be identified and whether the cryptoasset is mainly used to make payments.
Annex 3, para 4

Stablecoins -- defined here as group 1b cryptoassets, plus some group 2 cryptoassets meeting similar stability tests -- are treated like non-HQLA debt securities. An issuing bank must assume full redemption within the LCR window. The exception is when the backing assets independently qualify as HQLA; then the earliest possible redemption date sets the inflow or outflow treatment.
Annex 3, paras 6-7
A bank holding a stablecoin must treat it as a non-HQLA debt security and generally apply a 0% inflow rate, adjusted if the stablecoin has a set remaining maturity.
Annex 3, para 7

Other cryptoassets split into two kinds. Group 1a cryptoassets that don't qualify as HQLA follow the treatment of whatever traditional asset they represent. Other group 2 cryptoassets get a full 100% run-off or required-collateral treatment under the CFR, and no inflow credit under the LMR.
Annex 3, paras 8 and 16

The HKMA can decide a particular cryptoasset carries extra liquidity risk, say because of its technical design or the bank's role as holder or issuer. It can then demand extra safeguards. These include protecting the bank's own liquidity when it issues, or is a key service provider helping redeem, certain stablecoins.
Annex 3, para 9 and footnote 84

Derivatives linked to a cryptoasset are explicitly covered by the Annex 3 rules, not carved out. The same is true of secured funding or lending using cryptoassets as collateral, cryptoasset collateral swaps, and committed facilities to lend cryptoassets.
Annex 3, para 10
rg: Read para 5.9 (page 65) for the general principle, then Annex 3 in full (around page 78 onward. Paras 1-16+) for the detailed tokenised-claim, stablecoin and other-cryptoasset treatment. Skip the surrounding generic LCR/NSFR calculation mechanics.

t: Supervisory Policy Manual MR-1: Market Risk Capital Charge
sl: HKMA · Supervisory Policy Manual MR-1: Market Risk Capital Charge (2025)
s: MR-1 is a large, general SPM module (V.2, effective 19 Dec 2025) on calculating market risk capital charges under the simplified standardised (SSTM). Full standardised (STM) and internal-models (IMA) approaches. It adds a dedicated section 6, 'Cryptoasset exposures', covering how each approach treats group 1 (tokenised assets and stablecoins) and group 2a cryptoassets. Plus a trading-book/banking-book boundary rule for cryptoasset reclassifications and a footnote excluding cryptoasset exposures from the market-risk de-minimis exemption.
w: This is where the bulk of a bank's market-risk capital methodology work for any crypto trading book will sit. It dictates classification-dependent decomposition, hedging recognition. A harder capital treatment (100% net position, no IMA) for the riskier group 2a bucket. Plus an explicit ban on the small-book market-risk exemption once any cryptoasset exposure exists.
k: A bank with any cryptoasset exposure cannot use the market-risk de-minimis exemption that smaller trading books would otherwise qualify for.
footnote 80 to para 6.1.1

Under SSTM, group 1 cryptoasset positions are converted to HKD at spot price. They are mapped to the same risk category (interest rate, equity, FX or commodities) as the traditional asset they represent or reference. Netting and hedging are recognised between a tokenised or stablecoin instrument and its traditional-asset equivalent.
para 6.1.2

Under STM, a tokenised instrument (group 1a) or stablecoin (group 1b) is broken down using the same risk factors that apply to the traditional asset it represents or references. Sensitivities are matched inside the existing risk classes.
para 6.1.4
The IMA may be used for group 1 cryptoassets but is not permitted for instruments referencing group 2 cryptoassets.
para 6.1.9

Where a group 1b cryptoasset (stablecoin) carries redeemer default risk or redemption-intermediary risk, that risk must be captured under the credit-risk capital framework rather than market risk. This applies across the SSTM, STM and IMA approaches.
Group 2a cryptoassets must sit in the trading book and get a modified, standalone SSTM or STM treatment with limited hedging recognition. The IMA cannot be used for them.
For each group 2a cryptoasset, the position-risk capital requirement is 100% of the net position, calculated with a formula that only gives 65% offset credit between long and short positions.

Group 2b cryptoassets are not subject to this market-risk capital charge at all. Instead they get the conservative treatment (a flat risk weight covering credit and market risk together, including CVA risk) under a separate capital-rules provision.
footnote 81 to para 6.2.1

Book transfers of an instrument can be triggered by a cryptoasset's reclassification under the new CRP-1 classification module (paras 2.1.2-2.1.3 of CRP-1). Such a transfer is not treated as a discretionary trading or banking-book switch. So it escapes the usual capital surcharge for such switches.
footnote 13 to para 2.1.14
rg: Read section 6 in full (pages 150-155ish, paras 6.1.1-6.2.28) plus footnote 13 on page 14 for the boundary/reclassification carve-out. The rest of this ~300-page module is standard SSTM/STM/IMA mechanics for traditional instruments.

t: Public consultation on implementation of Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and amendments in relation to Common Reporting Standard launched
sl: FSTB · Public consultation on implementation of Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and… (2025)
s: The government launched a public consultation on implementing the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) and related amendments to the Common Reporting Standard (CRS) in Hong Kong. Both will be enacted via changes to the Inland Revenue Ordinance (Cap. 112). CARF, published by the OECD in 2023, lets partner jurisdictions automatically swap tax data on crypto-asset transactions with each other. The government plans to finish the local legislative amendments within the coming year, aiming to start CARF information exchange from 2028 and the newly amended CRS from 2029. Proposed changes also include mandatory registration for relevant financial institutions and higher penalties, partly in response to an OECD peer review of Hong Kong's CRS framework. The consultation runs to 6 February 2026.
w: This is the launch notice for the CARF/CRS consultation. It flags the 2028 start date and the proposal for mandatory registration and higher penalties. Both bear directly on any bank group entity that is a reporting financial institution for crypto-asset transactions. See the fuller consultation paper entry for detail.
k: The government will amend the Inland Revenue Ordinance (Cap. 112) to implement the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and the newly amended Common Reporting Standard.
para 4
The government targets completing the legislative amendments within the coming year, starting automatic exchange of crypto-asset tax information from 2028 and the newly amended CRS from 2029.
para 5
Proposed amendments include mandatory registration for relevant financial institutions and increased penalty levels, partly to address an ongoing OECD peer review of Hong Kong's CRS administration.
para 6
The public consultation covers reporting procedures, record-keeping requirements, and penalties and enforcement, and closes for comments on 6 February 2026.
para 7
rg: Read paragraphs 4-7 for the substance; paragraphs 1-3 are OECD/CRS background that can be skimmed. Cross-refer to the full consultation paper (id 275d5cc93a88) for detail.

t: Implementation of Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amendments in Relation to Common Reporting Standard in Hong Kong
sl: FSTB · Implementation of Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amendments in Relation… (2025)
s: This joint FSTB/Inland Revenue Department consultation paper sets out legislative proposals for Hong Kong. It would bring the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) and an amended Common Reporting Standard (CRS) into the Inland Revenue Ordinance. It defines who counts as a Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Provider (RCASP), what crypto-asset transactions must be reported, and what due diligence RCASPs must run on customers. It also proposes mandatory RCASP registration, record-keeping, enforcement powers, and a tiered penalty regime modelled on existing CRS sanctions. Separately, it proposes amending CRS itself so it also covers certain digital financial products. It excludes CBDCs (central bank digital currencies) and specified electronic money products, which fall under CARF instead. It also proposes strengthening CRS's own administrative framework (mandatory RFI registration, higher penalties) in response to an OECD peer review. It sets a phased implementation timeline running from 2027 through the first CARF information exchange in 2028 and first amended-CRS exchange in 2029, and invites comments by 6 February 2026.
w: If the bank or a group entity executes crypto-asset exchange transactions or operates a trading platform for customers, it will likely be an RCASP. It will face new mandatory registration, customer due diligence, and reporting duties from 2027, with real penalties for non-compliance. Banks that are already CRS Reporting Financial Institutions must also plan for dual CARF/CRS reporting on the same crypto-asset disposals under the government's proposed default treatment.
k: A Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Provider (RCASP) is any business executing crypto-asset exchange transactions or transfers for customers, or making available a trading platform (including certain decentralised platforms). RCASPs will have to register, run customer due diligence and report transaction data to the Inland Revenue Department.

Crypto-assets that cannot be used for payment or investment are outside CARF's reporting scope. So are central bank digital currencies and specified electronic money products, though CBDCs and some e-money products fall under the amended CRS instead.
para 1.5, p.7

RCASPs must obtain customer self-certifications to determine tax residency, cross-checked against AML/KYC information. For existing customers, self-certifications must be obtained within twelve months of CARF taking effect in Hong Kong.
para 1.15 and footnote 18, p.13-14

All RCASPs with any nexus to Hong Kong must register on the IRD's CARF Portal, whether or not they have information to report. Registration is proposed to run from September 2027 and be completed by end-December 2027 or end-January 2028, depending on when the nexus arose.
para 2.8 and Chapter 6 timeline, p.20 and p.48

RCASPs must keep due diligence and reporting records for at least six years. They must tell IRD within one month if the business is dissolved or terminated, with the obligation to preserve records falling on former directors if the RCASP is dissolved.

Proposed penalties for RCASP non-compliance range from a HK$10,000 fine for failing to register or file a return. The maximum is a HK$100,000 fine plus three years' imprisonment on indictment for knowingly providing false information with intent to defraud. An administrative-penalty alternative to prosecution is also proposed.

Entities that are both RCASPs and Reporting Financial Institutions (RFIs) will, under the proposed default treatment, have to report the same crypto-asset sale or redemption proceeds twice. They must report under both CARF and the amended CRS, and will not be allowed to report only once.

The government proposes introducing mandatory registration and a stronger penalty regime for CRS-reporting financial institutions generally. This responds to an OECD peer review finding gaps in how Hong Kong identifies reporting financial institutions and enforces the existing CRS regime.

Implementation is phased. RCASP due diligence starts January 2027, and RCASP registration starts from September 2027. First CARF returns are filed by RCASPs in June 2028, with first CARF information exchange with partner jurisdictions in September 2028. Amended-CRS due diligence starts January 2028, with first exchange in September 2029.
Chapter 6 implementation table, p.44-45
rg: Read the Executive Summary (p.1-4) and Chapter 1 (RCASP scope, transactions, due diligence, p.5-21). Also read the penalty and timeline sections of Chapter 2 (p.23-26) and Chapter 6's implementation table (p.44-45). Chapters 3 and 5's treaty and administrative detail, and Annex C, can be skimmed unless drafting a formal consultation response.

t: Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau: Fintech

t: Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework: Frequently Asked Questions (Last updated December 2025)
sl: Other · Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework: Frequently Asked Questions (2025)
s: This is the OECD's own FAQ on interpreting CARF, hosted by IRD as background reading rather than a Hong Kong-specific document. It clarifies edge cases such as branch nexus, retail payment reporting thresholds, staking/wrapped-token treatment, NFT exclusions, and how tokenised traditional financial assets are treated.
w: These OECD interpretive answers will likely shape how Hong Kong's own CARF rules are applied in practice. Compliance can use them to pressure-test edge cases (staking, tokenised securities, NFTs), even though the document itself is not a Hong Kong legal instrument.
k: A retail payment transfer above USD 50,000 made as agent for the customer must be reported as a separate 'Reportable Retail Payment Transaction' category.
Section II, Q1, p.2
Moving crypto into a staking contract and receiving a matching tokenised version back counts as a reportable exchange transaction.
Section IV, Q2, p.4-5

An NFT is excluded from reporting only if it does not represent a financial asset and is not marketed as an investment. It must also not be an AML/KYC (anti-money laundering / know-your-customer) virtual asset under FATF rules. On top of that, it must have low value and trading volume (illustratively, under USD 200 and no meaningful trading).
Section IV, Q5, p.6

A tokenised traditional financial asset is NOT treated as a reportable crypto-asset if it can only be held or transferred through custodial accounts at regulated custodians, i.e. it is not truly disintermediated.
Section IV, Q6, p.6-7
rg: Skim Section headers only; read Section II Q1 (retail payments) and Section IV Q2, Q5, Q6 (staking, NFTs, tokenised assets) as the parts most relevant to a bank's product set.

t: CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process
sl: HKMA · CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process (2025)
s: This statutory guideline sets out how the HKMA runs the Pillar 2 supervisory review process, including how it may adjust a bank's individual capital requirement above the regulatory minimum. Version 7 adds a dedicated paragraph on cryptoassets. Because crypto activities and their risks are still new and evolving, the HKMA may respond to capital or risk-management shortcomings tied to crypto. It may use capital add-ons, provisioning requirements, activity limits, or other mitigation measures. Separately, the module's general Pillar 2 governance guidance now lists cryptoasset activity alongside securitisation as an example of a complex activity. The board and senior management must understand this as part of firm-wide risk oversight.
w: Compliance should flag that examiners can now raise Pillar 2 capital or impose activity limits specifically because of crypto risk-management gaps. Any internal audit or risk-management finding on crypto should be remediated before a supervisory review cycle.
k: Because crypto risks are new and still developing, the HKMA may use any of four supervisory tools where it sees capital or risk-management gaps tied to a bank's crypto activity. These are extra capital add-ons, requiring provisions for foreseeable and estimable crypto losses, imposing activity limits, or other mitigation measures.
para 3.6.6

The board and senior management should understand firm-wide risks from complex or new activities. Crypto is now named alongside securitisation and 'originate-to-distribute' lending as an example. They should also set firm-wide prudential limits consistent with the bank's risk appetite.
para 4.2.8
A dedicated SPM module, CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets, is now listed in this module's index of related modules under a new 'Cryptoassets' heading.
module index, 'Cryptoassets' heading
rg: Read para 3.6.6 (p.52-53) and para 4.2.8 (p.63) for the crypto-specific text. The rest of the module is the general Pillar 2/SRP framework and can be skimmed unless capital planning is in scope.

t: CR-G-8 Large Exposures and Risk Concentrations
sl: HKMA · CR-G-8 Large Exposures and Risk Concentrations (2025)
s: CR-G-8 version 5 is a statutory guideline under Banking Ordinance s.16(10). It explains how locally incorporated AIs apply the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules (BELR) on single-counterparty, equity and land exposures. The crypto change is a new part of section 2.8: cryptoasset-related exposures are valued under a new Division 5A of BELR Part 7. Only crypto exposures that carry a counterparty's default risk count toward large exposure limits; pure holdings without counterparty risk are disregarded. The bank identifies counterparties as it already does for capital purposes. Valuation depends on the exposure type, its Group 1a/1b/2a/2b classification and whether it sits in the banking or trading book. The rest of the module restates existing limits, board oversight and breach notification duties that apply equally to crypto-related counterparty exposures.
w: Exposures to crypto counterparties, such as a stablecoin issuer, custodian or derivative counterparty, now count toward the bank's large exposure limits under a dedicated valuation method. Compliance must make sure limit monitoring and breach notification cover these crypto-linked counterparties.
k: The module is a statutory guideline and applies to AIs incorporated in Hong Kong; overseas-incorporated AIs still report large exposures of their Hong Kong operation.
Cover (Classification; Application)
A large exposure is any exposure to one counterparty or linked group equal to or above 10% of Tier 1 capital.
para 1.1.5
The statutory ceiling on exposure to a single counterparty or linked group is 25% of Tier 1 capital. Local global systemically important banks face a 15% cap toward other such groups.
Crypto-related exposures are valued under BELR Part 7 Division 5A, separately from ordinary exposures in Divisions 4 and 5.

For crypto exposures that carry counterparty default risk, the bank must first identify each counterparty or linked group, reusing the counterparty identification already done for capital, then value each under Division 5A.
para 2.8.9
Crypto exposures with no counterparty credit or default risk are ignored when measuring large exposures.
footnote 13 (Rule 48(1)(ba))
Which valuation rule applies depends on the exposure category in the Rule 2(1) definition, the asset's Group 1a/1b/2a/2b classification, and banking versus trading book.
para 2.8.10 and footnote 14
Some crypto exposures borrow Division 5 methods (for example Group 1a banking book items). Others reuse capital-rule figures for credit or default risk or jump-to-default amounts.
para 2.8.11 and footnotes 15-17
Because crypto markets change fast, the Monetary Authority may set a different valuation method for one or more AIs by written notice under BELR Rule 77A(2).
para 2.8.12
Any breach of statutory or HKMA-set limits should be reported to the HKMA as soon as practicable, with an impact assessment and a rectification plan.
para 6.1.1
A notifiable breach must be reported in writing with details of the limit, timing, cause and remediation; suspected breaches should be flagged before the investigation ends.
Failing to meet a prescribed notification or remedial action requirement is an offence for the AI and its directors, chief executives and managers.
para 6.4.1
rg: Read paras 2.8.1 and 2.8.8-2.8.12 for the crypto valuation rules, then section 6 on breach notification. The rest restates the existing large exposure framework.

t: LM-1 Regulatory Framework for Supervision of Liquidity Risk
sl: HKMA · LM-1 Regulatory Framework for Supervision of Liquidity Risk (2025)
s: LM-1 version 5 is a statutory guideline on applying the Banking (Liquidity) Rules (BLR). It covers the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR), Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) and Core Funding Ratio (CFR). The crypto additions are section 5.9 and a new Annex 3. Crypto exposures generally follow the treatment of traditional exposures with equivalent economic risk, but Annex 3 sets specific rules. Only Group 1a tokenised versions of eligible assets can count as high-quality liquid assets (HQLA). Bank-issued tokenised claims can be treated as deposits, stablecoins are treated like non-HQLA debt securities, and Group 2 cryptoassets get the harshest treatment. The HKMA may impose stricter treatment for any cryptoasset with extra liquidity risk, and CBDCs are excluded.
w: If the bank issues tokenised deposits or a stablecoin, or holds either, Annex 3 sets how they hit the LCR and NSFR. The holder-identification test for tokenised deposits and the 100% outflow for issued stablecoins are the points most likely to affect product design and compliance sign-off.
k: Crypto exposures, whether assets, liabilities or contingent items, should generally be treated like traditional exposures with economically equivalent risk across LCR, NSFR, LMR and CFR.
para 5.9.1
Annex 3 adds crypto-specific rules because of extra risks and thin historical data. CBDCs are outside Annex 3 and are generally treated like the issuing jurisdiction's notes and coins.

A cryptoasset can count as HQLA only if it is a Group 1a token of an eligible asset class, and both the traditional and tokenised forms meet the HQLA criteria. It must also meet operational requirements, for example an established ledger and a deep market.
Annex 3, para 1 and footnote 95

An issuing bank may treat its tokenised claims (Group 1a, redeemable at par in fiat, backed by the bank's own balance sheet) as deposits or unsecured funding. If the bank cannot identify holders at all times, it must treat them as other unsecured wholesale funding, and they can never count as stable retail deposits.
Annex 3, para 4
Tokenised claims used mainly for payment within an operational relationship with wholesale customers follow the operational deposit treatment.
Annex 3, para 4 (fourth bullet)

A bank holding tokenised deposits issued by another AI or a regulated bank treats them like unsecured loans to financial institutions. No inflow is recognised if they cannot be redeemed within 30 days.
Annex 3, para 5
Stablecoins in this annex are Group 1b coins, plus fully collateralised Group 2 coins that fail only the redemption test because of notice periods or fixed terms.
Annex 3, para 6

A bank that issues a stablecoin redeemable within the LCR period must apply a 100% outflow rate, unless the backing assets would qualify as HQLA apart from encumbrance. The segregated backing assets count as pledge under the NSFR.
Annex 3, para 7 (issuer bullets)

A bank holding a stablecoin treats it as non-HQLA debt, generally with a 0% LCR inflow and an 85% NSFR required stable funding factor. This falls to 50% if it matures within 12 months into fiat. Issuer redemption options are assumed not exercised.
Annex 3, para 7 (holder bullets)
Group 1a tokens that are not HQLA follow their traditional equivalent. Any extra liquidity risk from the token form, such as delayed cash flows from the infrastructure, must be reflected.
Annex 3, para 8(a)

Other Group 2 cryptoassets held get a 100% NSFR required stable funding factor and no LCR inflow. Unsecured crypto borrowings due within the LCR period take a 100% outflow unless covered by the bank's own unencumbered stock, and crypto-denominated funding gets 0% available stable funding.
Annex 3, para 8(b)
The HKMA may impose stricter treatment where a cryptoasset carries extra liquidity or contingent risk, for example the need to support redemptions of a stablecoin the bank issues or services.
Annex 3, para 9 and footnotes 97-98
rg: Go straight to section 5.9 (p.67) and Annex 3 (pp.91-98). The rest of the module is the general liquidity framework and can be skipped for crypto purposes.

t: Code of Practice for the Purposes of Providing Guidance in Respect of the Provisions of Rules 20(4)(b), 37(2) and (3) and 41 of the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules (Chapter 155S)
sl: HKMA · Code of Practice for the Purposes of Providing Guidance… (2025)
s: Known as the Banking (Exposure Limits) Code, this statutory code of practice interprets three specific rules under the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules. It covers how to judge whether a third-party data provider is 'competent and reliable' for valuing collective investment scheme exposures. It also covers what counts as a bank's self-use land, and when two counterparties are 'economically dependent' on each other for large-exposure grouping purposes. It took effect 1 January 2026. Despite being bundled into the November 2025 cryptoassets standard package, the code's own text contains no cryptoasset-specific rule. It appears to be a general large-exposures code amended and reissued alongside the crypto package rather than a crypto-specific instrument.
w: This code governs how the bank groups connected counterparties for its large-exposure limits generally. Compliance should note it is not crypto-specific despite arriving in the crypto package. It does not change how crypto counterparty exposures are treated beyond the ordinary economic-dependence tests.
k: To decide if a market data provider is competent and reliable for equity-exposure valuation under rule 20(4)(b), a bank should weigh several factors. These are the provider's market standing, financial strength, service capacity, track record, and contingency arrangements.
para 3(2)(a)-(e)

The code defines when one counterparty is 'economically dependent' on another for grouping purposes under rule 41. It lists seven specific tests, such as 50%+ of receipts coming from the other party or shared reliance on the same funding source.
para 6(4)(a)-(g)

A bank may rely in good faith on information a counterparty provides about its own economic dependence, as long as it does not conflict with information the bank otherwise holds. The bank should actively request this information during credit reviews and when granting new facilities.
para 6(2)

Where Entity A depends economically on Entity B, the bank has to fold Entity A into Entity B's linked-counterparty group. However, that does not automatically mean Entity B belongs in Entity A's group too, unless Entity B independently satisfies the grouping criteria.
para 6(5)
rg: Read paras 3 and 6 (pages 4-12) for the two live guidance items. Para 5A on self-use land premises is a narrow, low-relevance point and paras 4, 5 and 7 are repealed and can be skipped.

t: CR-L-5 Major Acquisitions and Investments: BELR Part 3
sl: HKMA · CR-L-5 Major Acquisitions and Investments: BELR Part 3 (2025)
s: CR-L-5 version 3 is a statutory guideline about acquiring share capital in a company. It explains when a locally incorporated AI needs the Monetary Authority's prior written consent, which is needed once the stake is worth 5% or more of its Tier 1 capital. The crypto change is a footnote: under BELR Rule 21(2), a cryptoasset that carries the economic substance of equity ownership counts as share capital for these rules. The module also covers exemptions (debt recovery, underwriting, insurance business, trading book below a threshold), application content, grounds for refusal, conditions, revocation and a one-month advance notice for other significant acquisitions.
w: A bank taking a stake in a digital asset business, or holding tokens that represent equity, may need prior HKMA consent at the 5% of Tier 1 level. A strategic crypto investment that changes the bank's business line may need a month's advance notice even below that level.
k: A locally incorporated AI should not acquire shares in a company worth 5% or more of its Tier 1 capital without the Monetary Authority's written consent. This also covers setting up a company.
para 1.1
Tokens that give the economic substance of equity ownership count as share capital for this consent regime.
para 2.1.3, footnote 1 (BELR Rule 21(2))
The 5% test uses book value at acquisition plus any unpaid amount, normally against the previous quarter-end Tier 1 figure.
Exemptions cover debt recovery, underwriting for up to seven working days, insurance business meeting set conditions, and trading book holdings whose assessment amount is below 5% of Tier 1.
para 2.2.1
The rule applies on a solo and consolidated basis, so acquisitions through a consolidated subsidiary also need consent.
para 2.3.1
AIs should approach the HKMA early and file a written notice with details such as value, capital impact, funding, business plan and the target's regulation.
para 2.5.1
Consent may be refused, conditioned or revoked if depositors' interests would be threatened; the AI gets a chance to make representations first.

AIs are expected to give at least one month's notice of other acquisitions with significant effect. Examples include entering a new line of business or cutting the capital ratio by around 0.5% or more.
rg: Read para 1.1, footnote 1 on page 3 and paras 2.5 and 2.9; the deemed-consent transition in 2.4 is historical.

t: Cryptoassets standard: SPM modules, code of practice, disclosure templates and tables, and banking returns
sl: HKMA · Cryptoassets standard: SPM modules, code of practice, disclosure templates… (2025)
s: This HKMA circular finalises a package of capital, disclosure and reporting changes for Hong Kong's new cryptoasset prudential standard. The changes follow several rounds of industry consultation. It finalises a new module, CRP-1 (classification of cryptoassets), plus revisions to nine other Supervisory Policy Manual (SPM) modules and a code of practice. All of these take effect on 1 January 2026, alongside related Banking (Capital), (Disclosure) and (Exposure Limits) amendment rules. It also issues a revised disclosure package with a new crypto-specific disclosure part, and confirms new banking return templates. A six-month transitional easement lets banks with no cryptoasset exposure on 1 January 2026 keep using the old return templates until 30 June 2026.
w: This is the master document setting the effective date and transitional relief for the entire crypto capital, disclosure and reporting package. Compliance needs it to plan the 1 January 2026 go-live and decide whether the bank qualifies for the six-month reporting transition.
k: Ten SPM modules/code items (listed (a) to (j)) were finalised and take effect on 1 January 2026, implementing three sets of Banking Ordinance amendment rules due to commence the same day.
p.1, 'SPM modules and code of practice'

Compared with the consultation draft, the HKMA further clarified how central bank digital currencies are treated for prudential purposes. It also eased the process for classifying tokenised traditional assets, both in module CRP-1.
p.2, bullet 1
The HKMA clarified that moving a position between books purely because of a cryptoasset reclassification is not treated as a book switch. So it does not trigger the usual capital surcharge in MR-1.
p.2, bullet 2
A revised standard disclosure package, including a new Part XII for cryptoasset exposures, takes effect for any reporting period ending after 1 January 2026.
p.2-3, 'Disclosure templates and tables'
Seven new or revised banking return templates, including capital adequacy, market risk/CVA, liquidity, leverage and large exposures returns, were scheduled for release in December 2025.
p.3, 'Banking returns' list (a)-(g)
Banks with no cryptoasset exposure as of 1 January 2026 may keep using the old return templates for six months, until 30 June 2026, for four of the listed returns.
p.3-4, transitional arrangement paragraph
Even banks using the transitional easement must still apply the revised completion instructions for unrelated miscellaneous changes in the capital adequacy ratio return from 1 January 2026.
p.3, footnote 4

A bank that gains cryptoasset exposure after 1 January 2026 may agree a temporary alternative reporting arrangement with the HKMA. The same option is open to a transitional bank not yet ready to switch return formats. The arrangement covers the period 31 January to 30 June 2026.
p.4, first full paragraph
rg: Read the full four-page letter; it is short. Pay closest attention to the commencement date, the list of ten finalised modules, and the transitional-arrangement paragraphs on pages 3-4.

t: MR-1 Market Risk Capital Charge
sl: HKMA · MR-1 Market Risk Capital Charge (2025)
s: MR-1 is the HKMA's Supervisory Policy Manual module telling locally incorporated banks how to work out the capital charge for market risk. A new section 6, added for the cryptoassets standard, sets out how each of the four cryptoasset categories defined in module CRP-1 must be handled. Group 1a tokens (tokenised traditional assets) and Group 1b tokens (asset-referenced coins such as stablecoins) are mapped onto the risk factors of the asset they represent or reference. So they mostly ride on the existing framework. Group 2a tokens get their own separate risk bucket with no diversification benefit against other assets, and cannot use a bank's internal model. Group 2b tokens fall outside market-risk rules altogether. Instead they pick up the flat, punitive treatment set in the credit-risk rules.
w: This module tells compliance exactly how trading-book crypto and stablecoin positions must be classified and capitalised. It shows that most crypto trading exposures cost more capital than an equivalent traditional position, because diversification and netting benefits are restricted or removed.
k: Before applying any market-risk method, a bank must first sort each crypto position into Group 1a, 1b, 2a or 2b using module CRP-1.
para 6.1.1, footnote 79
A bank holding any cryptoasset exposure loses access to the small-portfolio (de-minimis) exemption from market-risk capital rules, even if the position is tiny.
para 6.1.1, footnote 80
For Group 1a tokens, hedging and netting against the underlying traditional asset is allowed provided both are mapped to the same risk category.
para 6.1.2
For Group 1b tokens (e.g. stablecoins), the credit risk that the redeemer or an intermediary fails to honour redemption is capitalised separately under the credit-risk rules, not under market risk.
Banks using the internal models approach cannot use it at all for Group 2a tokens; only the two standardised methods are allowed for that group.
para 6.1.9
For Group 2a tokens, positions in the same coin held on different exchanges cannot be netted against each other; long and short amounts must be kept separate.
para 6.2.6
The formula for a Group 2a token's net position only lets 65% of the smaller of the long/short side offset the larger side, so full netting is not available.
para 6.2.7
The capital charge for a Group 2a token's position risk is simply 100% of that net position, added up across all such tokens with no diversification credit.
Options on a Group 2a token must be valued with a scenario (matrix) method. This moves the price and volatility by up to 100% each way; simpler option methods are banned for these tokens.
para 6.2.10

A footnote confirms that when a bank moves a position between the banking book and trading book purely because of a CRP-1 reclassification, this is not treated as a book-switch. It does not trigger the usual capital surcharge for switching.
para 6.1.1, footnote 79, p.151; also para 2.1.15 with footnote 13, p.14
rg: Read section 6 (paragraphs 6.1-6.2, pages 151-160) in full. The earlier sections 1-5 are the general, non-crypto market-risk framework and can be skimmed unless a cross-reference sends you there.

t: CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets
sl: HKMA · CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets (2025)
s: This is the HKMA Banking Regulatory Document Repository (BRDR) index page for the new Supervisory Policy Manual (SPM) module CRP-1. t: MR-2 CVA Risk Capital Charge
sl: HKMA · MR-2 CVA Risk Capital Charge (2025)
s: MR-2 tells banks how to compute the capital charge for CVA risk, the risk that a derivative counterparty's credit quality worsens before a trade settles. A new section 4 extends this to crypto derivatives and to securities-financing trades collateralised by cryptoassets. Group 1a and 1b tokens are broadly treated like the traditional asset they represent, though a bank must separately check the tokenised version for extra liquidity mismatch risk. Group 2a tokens can use most CVA methods except the advanced standardised approach. Group 2b tokens skip CVA calculation entirely and instead get the same flat, punitive capital charge used for their credit risk.
w: This module sets how much extra capital a bank's derivatives desk needs to hold against counterparty credit-spread risk on crypto trades. It also flags that the harshest, 1,250% treatment applies automatically to the riskiest token category, with no modelling option.
k: Derivatives and securities-financing trades on Group 1a tokens are generally capitalised the same way as trades on the underlying traditional asset.
para 4.2.1
A bank must assess the tokenised asset in its own right, not simply assume it qualifies for the same treatment as the traditional asset it copies, because liquidity can differ.
para 4.2.2

If a bank cannot get enough data to model the liquidity difference between a tokenised asset and its traditional counterpart, it must fall back to the simpler basic CVA approach. It cannot use the standardised approach instead.
para 4.2.2
Derivatives on Group 1b tokens (stablecoin-type instruments) follow the same CVA treatment as trades on non-tokenised assets.
para 4.2.3
For Group 2a tokens, every CVA method applies except the standardised CVA approach, which is off-limits for these instruments.
para 4.3.1
Group 2b token exposures do not get a separate CVA calculation; they instead carry the same conservative 1,250% risk weight used for their credit risk.
para 4.3.2
Securities-financing trades collateralised by Group 2b tokens only attract a CVA charge if the HKMA decides that CVA risk on those trades is material.
para 4.3.3
rg: Read section 4 (paragraphs 4.1-4.3, pages 44-46) in full; sections 1-3 cover the general, non-crypto CVA framework and can be skimmed for background only.

t: Annex 4: Standard Disclosure Templates and Tables
sl: HKMA · Annex 4: Standard Disclosure Templates and Tables (2025)
s: This is the full set of Pillar 3 public disclosure templates and tables that locally incorporated banks must use, updated to add a new Part XII covering cryptoasset exposures. Part XII adds four items. Table CAEA is a narrative on the bank's crypto activities and risk approach. Template CAE1 covers exposure amounts and risk-weighted assets by cryptoasset group. Template CAE2 covers accounting classification of crypto holdings. Template CAE3 covers liquidity metrics for crypto exposures, for banks designated as category 1 institutions. Crypto exposures must also feed into the ordinary credit-risk, market-risk and liquidity templates elsewhere in the package, not only the dedicated crypto tables. Frequency ranges from annual (Table CAEA) to semi-annual (CAE1-3), and formats are mostly flexible rather than fixed.
w: These are the actual public disclosure formats the bank's Pillar 3 report team must build from January 2026 onward, whenever the bank has any crypto exposure. Compliance needs to confirm finance and risk teams have mapped internal data to every CAE1-3 field and the CAEA narrative before the first reporting cycle.
k: Table CAEA requires an annual narrative naming the bank's crypto-related activities. These include holding crypto directly, trading for clients, equity stakes in crypto exchanges or fund managers, or issuing crypto liabilities, and whether the bank acts as a redemption intermediary.
Table CAEA, point (a)
The same narrative must cover how each crypto activity feeds into credit, market, operational and liquidity risk, the mitigation policies applied, and the most significant current and emerging risks.
Table CAEA, points (b),(d),(e)
For group 1 cryptoassets, the bank must explain, using public information only, how it assessed each of the four BCR classification conditions.
Table CAEA, point (f)

Template CAE1 breaks out total exposure, exposure at default, and risk-weighted assets separately for group 1a, 1b, 2a and 2b cryptoassets. It splits these by credit risk and market risk columns, on a semi-annual basis.
Template CAE1, table and columns (a)-(f)

A bank must add extra rows for any individual stablecoin or unbacked cryptoasset that is 'material' under the template's own test. Broadly, that means the bank's group 2 exposure ratio is at or above 0.3% and that single asset is over 5% of all group 2 holdings.
Template CAE1, points to note (iii)(a)-(b)

Template CAE1 also captures how close a bank is to the group 2 (unbacked/algorithmic) cryptoasset concentration limits. It must show any exposure or RWA once the 1% of Tier 1 capital threshold is crossed, and total RWA once the 2% cap is breached.
Template CAE1, rows 6-10

The bank must separately state the total market value of client cryptoassets it holds in custody, broken down by tokenised traditional assets, stablecoins, and other crypto, as narrative accompanying CAE1.
Template CAE1, 'Accompanying narrative'

Template CAE2 shows how crypto holdings and crypto liabilities are booked on the balance sheet: cash, financial assets by measurement basis, and intangibles. This is split again by the four crypto groups, on a semi-annual basis.
Template CAE2

Template CAE3 reports the liquidity-coverage-ratio haircuts, inflow and outflow rates, and net-stable-funding factors applied to each crypto category. It is required semi-annually, only from banks designated as category 1 liquidity institutions with crypto exposure.
Template CAE3

Group 1 and group 2 crypto exposures reported in the crypto-specific templates must also be folded into the bank's ordinary templates elsewhere in the package. This includes the credit-risk, market-risk and liquidity disclosure templates. Doing so avoids double-counting confusion.
Template CAE1, points to note (ii); Template CAE2, point to note (i)
rg: Read only Part XII (pages 210-219) plus the points-to-note. The rest of the 220-page document is unrelated Basel III disclosure templates and can be skipped.

t: CR-G-9 Exposures to Connected Parties
sl: HKMA · CR-G-9 Exposures to Connected Parties (2025)
s: CR-G-9 version 5 is a statutory guideline under Banking Ordinance s.7(3) on how locally incorporated AIs identify, limit and control exposures to connected parties under BELR Part 8. The text does not mention cryptoassets directly. It appears in the package because connected-party exposures are valued the same way as Part 7 large exposures, which now include the new crypto valuation rules. It sets the aggregate and single connected-party limits, arm's-length dealing, board oversight, independent monitoring and breach reporting.
w: If the bank's group holds crypto-related positions with an affiliate or a firm linked to its directors or controllers, those exposures fall under connected-party limits and arm's-length rules. The module itself adds no crypto-specific duty.
k: AIs should deal with connected parties at arm's length, and the same impartiality applies to non-lending dealings such as asset sales and service contracts.
Breaching a Rule 87 limit is a notifiable event; the AI must tell the Monetary Authority as soon as practicable after it knows or should know.
para 1.1.3
Connected parties include directors, credit approvers, controllers and their relatives, plus firms and unlisted companies in which they hold key roles.
para 2.1.1
The aggregate connected-party exposure ratio must not exceed 15% of Tier 1 capital. Exposure to a single connected natural person is capped at the lower of HK$20 million or 5% of Tier 1.
Connected-party exposures are valued in the same way as Part 7 counterparty exposures, subject to Part 8 adjustments, and only the portion not covered by recognised credit risk mitigation counts.
para 2.3.1
The board should understand the legal limits, approve a connected-party policy and ensure systems exist to monitor and control these exposures.
A designated independent unit should monitor connected-party exposures, and internal audit should review them regularly.
Figures in the large exposures return, MA(BS)28, and the compliance certificate, MA(BS)1F(a), must be accurate, and limit breaches reported promptly.
rg: Read paras 2.2-2.3 for limits and valuation and 4.2 for reporting; the rest restates existing connected-lending controls.

t: CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets
sl: HKMA · CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets (2025)
s: CRP-1 is a new, non-statutory SPM guidance note (Version 1, dated 1 January 2026). It explains how AIs sort their cryptoasset exposures into prudential groups, under the HKMA's implementation of the Basel cryptoasset standard. A cryptoasset reaches Group 1 only if it passes four classification conditions. Group 1a covers tokenised traditional assets and Group 1b covers stablecoins with an effective stabilisation mechanism, while everything else falls into Group 2. Group 2 is split into Group 2a (limited hedge recognition, if three hedging recognition criteria are met) and Group 2b (no hedge recognition). The module sets extra safeguards for assets on permissionless blockchains, requires HKMA notification and agreement before any new cryptoasset can leave Group 2b, and lets the HKMA override a bank's classification. The Banking (Capital) Rules (BCR), Part 12, carry the legal requirements and prevail over the module in any conflict.
w: Every crypto or tokenised exposure the bank takes needs a documented classification, including tokenised deposits, bonds, stablecoins and crypto ETFs. Any new asset type needs an HKMA notification and sits in punitive Group 2b until the HKMA agrees otherwise. Compliance should own the notification and evidence trail, because missing it means full-capital treatment and supervisory override.
k: CRP-1 is guidance, not statute: a new non-statutory guidance note that applies to every AI from 1 January 2026.
Cover page (Classification; Application)
The legal rules on classification conditions, initial approval and later reclassification sit in BCR Part 12. If CRP-1 and the BCR differ, the BCR wins.
para 1.1.4

A cryptoasset is a digital store of value that relies mainly on cryptography and distributed ledger technology (DLT). It can be used to pay, invest or access goods and services. Securities issued on DLT are in scope; securities on centrally run electronic registers are not.
Central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) sit outside the standard and are generally treated like the fiat money of the issuing central bank.
para 1.2.3 and footnote 4
Group 1 requires all four classification conditions. Group 1a is tokenised traditional assets; Group 1b is stablecoins with an effective stabilisation mechanism. Anything not in Group 1 is Group 2.

Group 1 assets get the same capital, liquidity and other treatment as the underlying traditional asset. The HKMA may add an infrastructure risk add-on, which starts at zero but can be raised if weaknesses are seen in the underlying technology.
para 1.3.2 and footnote 5

Group 2 covers all unbacked cryptoassets, plus tokenised assets and stablecoins that fail the conditions, and attracts full capitalisation. Hedging recognition criteria split it into Group 2a (some hedging recognised) and Group 2b (none).
para 1.3.3
Look-through: funds such as Group 2b cryptoasset ETFs, entities whose value derives mainly from Group 2b assets, and equity, derivative or short positions in them are all treated as Group 2b.
para 1.3.3, footnote 6
The standard and CRP-1 took effect on 1 January 2026. Any cryptoasset exposure held before that date must sit in Group 2b until the HKMA agrees the bank's classification assessment.

Classification is a continuing duty. AIs must have policies, procedures, governance, staff and IT able to assess cryptoasset risk, and must fully document the evidence for each classification and give it to the HKMA on request.
para 2.1.1

Before acquiring a new type of cryptoasset, an AI must notify the HKMA and hold it as Group 2b until the HKMA agrees any better classification. A first Bitcoin spot or derivative trade triggers notification; Bitcoin futures after existing spot exposure do not.
para 2.1.2 and footnote 7

If an agreed Group 1a, 1b or 2a asset stops meeting its conditions or criteria, the AI must drop it to Group 2b at once until it complies again. Later purchases take the last assessed classification. Moving back up from Group 2b needs HKMA agreement.
rg: Read sections 1.3-1.4 and 2.1 first (group structure, effective date, notification and reclassification process), then section 2.6 for permissionless chains and section 3 for Group 2a thresholds. Paragraphs 2.2.6-2.2.9 on reserve quality matter mainly when assessing a specific stablecoin.

t: CA-G-1 Overview of Capital Adequacy Regime for Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions
sl: HKMA · CA-G-1 Overview of Capital Adequacy Regime for Locally Incorporated… (2025)
s: This is a near-final version of CA-G-1, the HKMA's master overview module for how locally incorporated banks calculate their capital adequacy ratio. It adds a new Part 12 and section 8.7 covering how cryptoasset exposures feed into credit-risk-weighted assets. It also adds crypto-specific points on market risk, CVA (credit valuation adjustment) risk and regulatory capital deductions. Its cover page still carries an unfilled placeholder date, showing it was published just ahead of formal gazettal. The text is almost identical to the gazetted version issued three weeks later. It is treated here as a superseded interim copy; see the gazetted entry for the current text and full key points.
w: This draft shows the shape of the final capital-adequacy overview module ahead of gazettal, but compliance should rely on the later gazetted text for citation purposes.
k: A new Part 12 was added to the risk-weighting framework specifically for calculating risk-weighted amounts of cryptoasset exposures.
para 8.1.1 (structure list)
For regulatory capital deduction purposes, a cryptoasset exposure is not treated as an intangible asset, so it is not automatically deducted from capital the way goodwill is.
footnote 17

t: CA-D-1 Guideline on the Application of the Banking (Disclosure) Rules
sl: HKMA · CA-D-1 Guideline on the Application of the Banking (Disclosure)… (2025)
s: This non-statutory guideline explains how banks should interpret and apply the Banking (Disclosure) Rules. Version 5, effective 1 January 2026, adds interpretive guidance for the new cryptoasset disclosure requirements introduced alongside the standard templates. These are an annual narrative table on crypto activities and liquidity risk (linked to sections 103(4A) and (4B)). There is also a semi-annual template on liquidity requirements for crypto exposures for category 1 institutions (linked to sections 16ZQK and 103AC). It sets out which of the new crypto disclosures are mandatory only for banks that actually have cryptoasset exposure, and cross-references the standard templates annex for the exact format.
w: This is the interpretive rulebook compliance should use alongside the raw templates to decide exactly which crypto disclosure items apply, to whom, and how often, before the first 2026 reporting cycle.
k: The new crypto liquidity narrative (Table CAEA) is only required from a bank if it has cryptoasset exposures that create liquidity risk. It applies to Hong Kong-incorporated and overseas-incorporated banks alike.
para 12.2.4

Banks designated as category 1 liquidity institutions with cryptoasset exposure must file the semi-annual liquidity-requirements-for-crypto template (Template CAE3) under section 16ZQK (local banks) or 103AC (overseas-incorporated banks).
para 12.2.4

A summary table maps each liquidity disclosure item to who must make it, on what frequency, and in what format. The crypto liquidity narrative is annual and flexible in format, while the crypto liquidity template is semi-annual and fixed format.
para 12.14.2, items (b) and (f)
For the standard templates generally (including the new crypto ones), a bank must follow the associated explanatory notes issued by the HKMA rather than relying on the BDR text alone.
para 2.1
The guideline is interpretive only - if it conflicts with the Banking (Disclosure) Rules themselves, the Rules prevail, and this text is not a substitute for the bank obtaining its own legal advice.
para 2.2
rg: Read paras 12.2.4-12.2.5 and the summary table at 12.14.2 (pages 40-53). The rest of the module covers ordinary non-crypto disclosure mechanics and can be skimmed.

t: Supporting Artificial Intelligence Adoption in AML/CFT
sl: HKMA · Supporting Artificial Intelligence Adoption in AML/CFT (2025)
s: This HKMA letter to all authorized institutions follows up a September 2024 letter on using artificial intelligence for suspicious-activity monitoring. It reports that 48 banks assessed the idea, over 30% already use AI in monitoring, and most of the rest expect adoption to exceed 80% within one to two years. The HKMA is running workshops on AI monitoring approaches. Because more banks plan to offer crypto-asset-related services, it is adding a workshop specifically on money-laundering and terrorist-financing risk management for that area.
w: Signals that the HKMA now expects AI-based AML/CFT monitoring to be near-universal within two years and is building crypto-specific AML training. A bank expanding into crypto services should plan to attend and align its transaction-monitoring roadmap.
k: 48 authorized institutions responded to the HKMA's earlier request to assess the feasibility of using AI for transaction monitoring.
para 2, p.1
More than 30% of authorized institutions had already adopted AI in their monitoring systems, with most others aiming to push the adoption rate above 80% within 12-24 months.
para 2, p.1

A growing number of authorized institutions plan to offer crypto-asset-related services. Because of this, the HKMA is adding a dedicated workshop on money-laundering and terrorist-financing risk management for that business line.
para 4, p.2
The HKMA will keep tracking each bank's AI-adoption implementation plan and reviewing the effectiveness of transaction-monitoring systems.
para 6, p.2
rg: Read in full; it is two pages with no numbered paragraphs beyond the natural paragraph breaks used as locators here.

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism Detection and prevention of potential layering activities in money laundering
sl: SFC · licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities -… (2025)
s: This SFC circular alerts licensed corporations, SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities to an emerging pattern of layering activities in money laundering. This pattern is characterised by frequent, swift fund/VA deposits and withdrawals with little or no trading. It sets out red flags drawn from the AML/CFT Guideline and Hong Kong Police Force intelligence, including scam-related proceeds being converted to VAs and withdrawn to unhosted wallets. It reiterates regulatory expectations that firms implement robust transaction monitoring, screen VA transactions and wallet addresses, and establish bank account/wallet address registration or whitelisting mechanisms. It warns of supervisory and enforcement action, including licence conditions, suspension or revocation, for firms that fail to detect and prevent such activity.
w: This circular's AML/CFT obligations bind licensed corporations and SFC-licensed VA service providers, not the bank directly (the bank's governing text is the HKMA AML/CFT Guideline). Compliance should use its layering red flags as reference indicators for the bank's own monitoring and be alert when client fund flows touch LC/VATP accounts exhibiting these patterns.
k: Licensed firms are reminded that strict AML/CFT compliance is both a legal obligation and essential to safeguarding operational and systemic integrity.
para 2, p.1

Typical layering pattern: frequent, scattered small/odd-amount deposits from multiple bank accounts, later withdrawn to the client's own (sometimes different) bank accounts. There is no or minimal trading, and accounts going inactive afterward.
para 7, p.2
Scam proceeds are being layered through licensed firms via bank transfers, some converted to VAs and withdrawn to unhosted wallets, to obscure fund flows.
para 8, p.2

Licensed firms must put in place transaction-monitoring systems that are robust and effective, scaled to their transaction volume and ML/TF risk. They must also apply extra vigilance when handling deposits and withdrawals.

Firms should establish a registration mechanism for client bank accounts and a whitelisting mechanism for VA wallet addresses, verifying ownership (for example, micropayment test, message signing test). They should avoid sole reliance on client-provided documents.
para 20(a), p.6

Whenever a registered bank account or whitelisted wallet address is added or replaced, senior management should review and approve it, applying a risk-sensitive approach. This can be the MIC of AML/CFT, the compliance officer, or the MLRO.
para 20(c), p.7
Clients may not share bank accounts or wallet addresses with each other. This bar covers ones that were previously removed or replaced too, except where an account is jointly owned.
para 20(d) and fn.12, p.7
Firms should consider limiting withdrawals to the accounts/wallets from which funds/VAs were originally deposited and implementing a withdrawal holding period (for example, one to two days).
para 23(a)-(b), p.7
VA transactions and wallet addresses should be screened using blockchain analytical tools before and, on a risk-sensitive basis, after transactions to identify illicit-linked addresses.
para 17, p.5-6

SFC will not hesitate to use powers under the SFO and AMLO against firms and senior management (directors, ROs, MIC, MLRO) for AML/CFT failures. This includes licence conditions, business restrictions, suspension/revocation, fines and reprimands.
para 25, p.8
rg: Read paras 5-23 (the red flags and expected controls); paras 1-4 and 24-26 are framing/contact boilerplate and can be skimmed.

t: Annex A - Tokenised Deposit Banks# of EnsembleTX

w: Identifies which banks are first movers in real-value tokenised deposit settlement via EnsembleTX. Useful for competitor/peer benchmarking and for counterparty due diligence if the bank transacts with any of these institutions' tokenised deposits.
k: Seven banks are named as Tokenised Deposit Banks under EnsembleTX: Bank of China (Hong Kong), China Construction Bank (Asia), Fubon Bank (Hong Kong) and Fusion Bank. The other three are Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong), Bank of East Asia, and HSBC.

A 'Tokenised Deposit Bank' is defined as a bank that will (1) make tokenised deposits available to Hong Kong customers. It will also (2) use EnsembleTX to settle interbank tokenised-deposit transactions on a real-value basis.
footnote, p.1
rg: One page; skim only.

t: HKMA announces new phase of Project Ensemble to support real-value transactions in tokenised deposits and digital assets
sl: HKMA · HKMA announces new phase of Project Ensemble to support… (2025)
s: The HKMA launched EnsembleTX, the pilot phase of Project Ensemble, moving from the proof-of-concept Ensemble Sandbox (running since August 2024) to real-value transactions in tokenised deposits and digital assets. Seven named commercial banks will issue tokenised deposits to customers and settle interbank tokenised deposit transactions through EnsembleTX, alongside other named industry pioneers. The pilot's initial focus is tokenised money market fund transactions and real-time liquidity/treasury management. EnsembleTX runs throughout 2026, starting with interbank settlement via the existing HKD Real Time Gross Settlement system, before being upgraded to round-the-clock settlement in tokenised central bank money. The SFC is a partner in the Ensemble Architecture Community.

t: HKMA introduces HKEX as strategic shareholder in CMU OmniClear Holdings Limited (with photo)
sl: HKMA · HKMA introduces HKEX as strategic shareholder in CMU OmniClear… (2025)
s: The HKMA announced a deal under which Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) is to acquire a 20% stake in CMU OmniClear Holdings Limited. CMU OmniClear Holdings is the holding company the HKMA's Exchange Fund set up in October 2025 to own CMU OmniClear Limited. CMU OmniClear operates the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU), Hong Kong's central securities depository system, on the HKMA's behalf. After the deal, the Exchange Fund will hold 80% and HKEX 20%. The stated goal is to grow CMU into a broader, multi-asset-class central securities depository, supporting settlement and collateral services across a wider range of asset classes. The HKMA confirmed it remains the legal owner and system operator of CMU under the Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance.
w: CMU underpins settlement of Hong Kong government tokenised/digital bonds and other securities a bank may custody or trade. This ownership restructuring is background context for assessing the CMU infrastructure a bank relies on, but creates no new bank obligation.
k: HKEX is acquiring a 20% stake in CMU OmniClear Holdings Limited by subscribing for new shares; after completion the Exchange Fund will hold 80% and HKEX 20%.

CMU OmniClear Limited, which operates Hong Kong's Central Moneymarkets Unit central securities depository, was established in 2024. Its holding company CMU OmniClear Holdings was set up by the Exchange Fund in October 2025.

t: HKMA introduces HKEX as a strategic shareholder in CMU OmniClear Holdings Limited

s: HKMA announced that HKEX will become a strategic shareholder in CMU OmniClear Holdings Limited, buying a 20% stake through a new share subscription (the Exchange Fund keeps the other 80%). This is to help build up Hong Kong's central securities depository (CSD) infrastructure and its fixed income and currencies (FIC) market. CMU OmniClear Holdings was set up in October 2025 by the Exchange Fund to wholly own CMU OmniClear Limited, which runs the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU) system on HKMA's behalf. As of end-September 2025, CMU held around HK$5 trillion equivalent in assets under custody. HKMA stays the owner and system operator of CMU under the Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance.

t: HKSAR Government’s Third Digital Green Bonds Offering
sl: HKMA · HKSAR Government’s Third Digital Green Bonds Offering (2025)
s: The HKSAR Government announced pricing of its third digital green bond issuance (~HK$10 billion equivalent across HKD, RMB, USD and EUR tranches) on the HSBC Orion platform, cleared via CMU. It is the first digital bond anywhere to bring tokenised central bank money, e-CNY and e-HKD, into how it settles. It reached a record size for a digital bond with over HK$130 billion in total subscriptions, and stretched its tenor to 5 years. It also used Digital Token Identifiers (DTIs) plus wider ICMA Bond Data Taxonomy coverage. It is the first issuance since the Government's Policy Statement 2.0, which commits to making tokenised Government bond issuance a regular practice.
w: Names the bank (or its peers) as direct participants. Platform provider, joint coordinators, settlement agents. In a HK$10 billion tokenised bond issuance settling partly via tokenised central bank money, giving compliance a live template for tokenised-deposit/CBDC settlement operational and counterparty risk.
k: This is the first digital bond issuance anywhere to bring tokenised central bank money (e-CNY and e-HKD) into its settlement process. This runs alongside the traditional settlement rails, for the HKD and RMB tranches.
para 4, p.1
The issuance size hit a record HK$10 billion, drawing total subscriptions above HK$130 billion, the biggest digital bond deal seen anywhere so far. Its tenor stretched to as long as 5 years.
para 5, p.1
Digital Token Identifiers (DTIs, ISO 24165) were obtained for all tranches and linked to ISINs and the issuer's LEI. ICMA Bond Data Taxonomy adoption was expanded versus the second issuance.
paras 6-7, p.1

This is the first tokenised bond issuance following the Government's Policy Statement 2.0 on Development of Digital Assets in Hong Kong, which commits to regularising issuance of tokenised Government bonds.
Secretary for FS&T quote, p.1
Settlement cycle is T+1. Clearing and settlement via CMU (operated by the HKMA) with linkage to Euroclear and Clearstream. Governing law is Hong Kong law. Listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.
'Key features' table, p.1
rg: Read paragraphs 1-7 (the narrative, pp.1) plus the 'Key features' table; the extensive banker/law-firm quotes are promotional and can be skimmed.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - The HKMA Unveils “Fintech 2030” at the Hong Kong FinTech Week 2025
sl: HKMA · The HKMA Unveils “Fintech 2030” at the Hong Kong… (2025)
s: The HKMA announced its 'Fintech 2030' strategy, succeeding the earlier 'Fintech 2025' plan. It is built around four pillars called DART: Next-generation Data and payment infrastructure, an AI-for-banks strategy, technology/quantum Resilience, and Tokenisation of finance. Over 40 initiatives are planned. On tokenisation specifically, the HKMA says it will keep issuing tokenised government bonds and explore tokenising Exchange Fund papers. It will also launch the Project Ensemble pilot for real-value transactions, and support settlement via e-HKD, tokenised deposits and regulated stablecoins.
w: Sets the top-level policy frame (tokenisation as one of four strategic pillars) that later HKMA circulars, the Supervisory Incubator for DLT, and Project Ensemble initiatives sit under. Useful context when briefing the board on why HKMA is pushing tokenisation strategic reviews.
k: Fintech 2030 is organised around four pillars nicknamed 'DART': Data and payment infrastructure, AI (the 'AI2 Strategy' for banks), technology/quantum Resilience, and Tokenisation of finance.

On tokenisation specifically, the HKMA says it will keep issuing tokenised government bonds and explore tokenising Exchange Fund papers. It will also launch the Project Ensemble pilot for real-value transactions, and support settlement via e-HKD, tokenised deposits and regulated stablecoins.

t: Appendix II — Amended licensing condition permitting distribution and/or custody services beyond own-platform trading (to the Circular on expansion of products and services of virtual asset trading platforms)

This comes together with a matching widening of the defined 'Relevant Activities' under the VATP Guidelines.
