t: Appendix III — Amended licensing condition permitting trust/client accounts with third-party custodians for distribution activities (to the Circular on expansion of products and services of virtual asset trading platforms)
sl: SFC · Appendix III — Amended licensing condition permitting trust/client accounts… (2025)
s: Amended licensing condition letting a VATP depart from VATP Guidelines paragraph 10.1 (which would otherwise require client assets to be held on trust solely through the licensee's own Associated Entity). It can hold trust/client accounts in its own name with the custodian(s) of investment products it distributes that are linked to digital assets and/or tokenised securities. This is subject to applicable law and regulation.

t: Circular on expansion of products and services of virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · expansion of products and services of virtual asset trading… (2025)
s: Under Pillar P (Products) of the ASPIRe roadmap, this circular widens what SFC-licensed VATPs may offer. (i) drops the 12-month track-record requirement for virtual assets sold to professional investors, and for stablecoins from HKMA-licensed issuers sold to retail investors. That 12-month rule still applies when other virtual assets are offered to retail clients. (ii) lets VATPs sell digital-asset-related products and tokenised securities and hold client assets in trust/client accounts with third-party custodians for that purpose. And (iii) lets VATPs' associated entities custody digital assets not traded on their own platform, subject to conditions.
w: This binds VATPs, not the bank. It opens a new distribution channel (VATPs distributing bank-originated tokenised securities) and broadens VATP-affiliated custody scope, both relevant to a compliance head evaluating new partnership structures.
k: The 12-month track record requirement no longer applies to virtual assets (including stablecoins) offered to professional investors, nor to stablecoins issued by an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer offered to retail investors. It still applies to retail offerings of other virtual assets.
paras 5-6, p.2
VATPs must still perform reasonable due diligence on all virtual assets before admission and disclose where a professional-investor-only asset has less than a 12-month track record.
para 6(a)-(b), p.2
The 12-month track-record rule is entirely inapplicable to tokenised securities and other digital securities.
para 7, p.2

VATPs may apply to amend standard licensing conditions to explicitly permit distribution of digital asset-related products and tokenised securities. They may also apply to open trust/client accounts in the VATP's own name with the custodian of the distributed product.
para 8, p.2

VATPs (via associated entities) may now apply to provide custody services for digital assets not made available for trading on their own platform -- previously disallowed under existing licensing conditions.
paras 10-11, p.3

VATPs still awaiting completion of the second-phase assessment may nonetheless be allowed to custody tokenised securities where the SFC agrees individually. They must finish that assessment before they can custody other digital assets not traded on their platform.
para 13, p.3

s: This appendix gives the exact wording of an amended licence condition that removes the 12-month track-record requirement in the trading-platform guidelines (para 7.6(c)). This applies to (1) virtual assets that only professional investors can trade and (2) specific stablecoins issued by HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers. It also requires trading platforms to tell clients on their website and app which professional-investor-only assets lack a 12-month track record, and to give clearer risk warnings for them.

The licensee must tell clients, on its website and app, which professional-investor-only virtual assets lack a 12-month track record and give them extra risk warnings.
full text, p.1

t: Circular on shared liquidity by virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · shared liquidity by virtual asset trading platforms (2025)
s: Under Pillar A (Access) of the ASPIRe roadmap, this circular lets SFC-licensed VATP operators link their order books with affiliated overseas trading platform operators (OVATPs) through a 'Shared Order Book'. This pools client orders into one combined liquidity pool. It sets rules for eligible OVATPs, trading and settlement risk management, and preventing market misconduct. Settlement risk management includes delivery-versus-payment (DVP) settlement, an Unsettled Trade Limit, a reserve fund, and compensation arrangements. It also requires mandatory prior written SFC approval, with detailed terms and conditions in the appendix (id fda3c03f239d).
w: This binds the affiliated VATP, not the bank directly, but a compliance head overseeing a bank-affiliated VATP group should treat these as the requirements to meet. FATF-aligned overseas affiliate regulation, a funded Hong Kong reserve, and prior SFC approval -- before that VATP shares order-book liquidity.
k: An OVATP wanting to join a Shared Order Book should be based somewhere that belongs to the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), or to an FATF-style regional body. Its rules should broadly match FATF and IOSCO recommendations for crypto/digital-asset markets on market abuse and safeguarding client assets.
para 7, p.1-2

The Shared Order Book should only take fully pre-funded orders, settled through delivery-versus-payment (DVP), with settlement happening at least once a day and during the day too. This keeps unsettled exposure within a set Unsettled Trade Limit.

Platform Operators must keep a Hong Kong reserve fund, held on trust, sized at no less than the Unsettled Trade Limit, to cover client losses from failed settlements. They must also keep insurance or compensation cover for Settlement Assets no less than required under VATP Guidelines para 10.22.
paras 16-17, p.3
Retail clients can only use a Shared Order Book if the extra cross-border risks, including possibly weaker client protection overseas, are clearly disclosed and the client chooses to take part.
para 25, p.4
Platform Operators should obtain prior written SFC approval before running a Shared Order Book, and conditions will be imposed through licence terms.
paras 26-27, p.4
rg: Read the main circular body (pp.1-4) for the policy rationale and headline requirements. The appended Terms and Conditions (id fda3c03f239d) contain the enforceable in force detail and should be read alongside it.

The Shared Order Book circular (Pillar A - Access) and the products/services expansion circular (Pillar P - Products). It highlights that Platform Operators may now combine orders with affiliated overseas platforms. Separately, they may offer VAs without a 12-month track record to professional investors and HKMA-licensed stablecoins. They may also distribute tokenised securities/digital asset investment products and offer wider custody services.

Summarises that the two same-day circulars implement Pillar A (Access) and Pillar P (Products) of the ASPIRe roadmap respectively.

t: Terms and conditions for operating a Shared Order Book (Appendix to the Circular on shared liquidity by virtual asset trading platforms)
sl: SFC · Terms and conditions for operating a Shared Order Book (2025)
s: These are the detailed, licence-imposed terms and conditions supporting the shared-liquidity circular. They define eligibility (the Other Virtual Asset Trading Platform (OVATP) must be a 'related corporation' under section 53ZRC of the AMLO), what Shared Order Book Rules must cover, and trading operations. They also define settlement controls, which cover delivery-versus-payment, netting, and Unsettled Trade Limit factors. They also cover default management, compensation and reserve fund mechanics, and steps to prevent market misconduct. They set a 7-year record-keeping duty, client disclosures, and mandatory reporting of incidents and regulatory changes to the SFC.

The reserve fund should be kept, in fiat currency unless the SFC agrees otherwise, across one or more segregated accounts at an authorized financial institution. It must be at least as large as the Unsettled Trade Limit.
paras 33-35, pp.4-5
Records must be retained for at least 7 years, enough detail to rebuild the complete history of every order, trade, settlement, surveillance alert, and incident response.
para 44, p.6

A Platform Operator should tell the SFC without delay about any actual or suspected serious breach, or any regulatory action taken against the OVATP or its Designated Custodian. It should also report any serious adverse event, or any possible regulatory change that could affect them.
para 50, pp.7-8
A Platform Operator should keep a contingency plan ready to pause order matching with the OVATP and isolate its own client orders if there is a serious disruption.

t: Appointments to Stablecoin Review Tribunal
sl: Government · Appointments to Stablecoin Review Tribunal (2025)
s: This announcement confirms that the Chief Executive appointed a Chairperson and six panel members to the Stablecoin Review Tribunal, each for a three-year term starting 1 November 2025. The Tribunal is established under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) to hear appeals against specified decisions made by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority under that Ordinance. A government spokesman described the Tribunal as a safeguard to keep the Monetary Authority's stablecoin-related regulatory decisions reasonable and fair.
w: If a bank group entity ever becomes, or deals with, a licensed stablecoin issuer and disputes an HKMA decision, this Tribunal is now operational and is the appeal route to know about.
k: The Stablecoin Review Tribunal was formally staffed with a Chairperson and six panel members, each appointed for a three-year term from 1 November 2025 to 31 October 2028.

The Tribunal's function is to review specified Hong Kong Monetary Authority decisions made under the Stablecoins Ordinance, upon receiving an appeal.
para 4

t: HKMA completes e-HKD Pilot Programme and outlines future direction of e-HKD
sl: HKMA · HKMA completes e-HKD Pilot Programme and outlines future direction… (2025)
s: The HKMA announced the publication of the 'e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 2 Report,' presenting findings from 11 industry pilot groups and the HKMA's updated policy stance. The report compares e-HKD with tokenised deposits and finds the public sees them similarly, given trust in Hong Kong's banking system. The near-term e-HKD priority is now wholesale payments rather than retail. Policy, legal, and technical groundwork for a possible future retail use will be finished by the first half of 2026. The HKMA will also publish shared token standards for programmability, coming out of the e-HKD Industry Forum.
w: For a compliance head, this signals the HKMA's near-term e-HKD focus is wholesale, not retail. The bank need not rush retail e-HKD readiness, though wholesale and tokenised-deposit engagement stays relevant.
k: The HKMA has concluded that the near-term priority for e-HKD is wholesale payments, rather than retail use, at this stage. This includes cross-border settlement and support for the tokenisation ecosystem.
para 4, p.1

Groundwork on policy, law, and technology for a possible future retail extension of e-HKD will be finished by the first half of 2026. Whether and when any actual extension happens depends on international developments, technology, and market needs.
para 5, p.1
The HKMA will publish a set of shared token standards to support wider use of programmability in digital money, as an outcome of the e-HKD Industry Forum.
para 6, p.1
A key Phase 2 finding: the public sees e-HKD and tokenised deposits in a similar light, given high trust in Hong Kong's banking system.
para 3, p.1
rg: Read in full (short); pairs with the full Phase 2 Report (attachment bdefe7fc69d4) for detailed findings and design considerations.

t: e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 2 Report
sl: HKMA · e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 2 Report (2025)
s: The HKMA's full Phase 2 Report on the e-HKD Pilot Programme (part of Project e-HKD+) documents 11 industry pilot groups' work. This work is grouped into three areas: tokenised-asset settlement, programmable-money use cases, and payments while offline. It was carried out after Phase 1 finished in October 2023. The report concludes that e-HKD and tokenised deposits deliver comparable retail benefits, and that commercial banks lean slightly toward tokenised deposits (lower cost of capital, faster time-to-market, customer stickiness). It also sets out key design considerations, such as interoperability, programmability, privacy, identity, convertibility, and reliability/performance, for any future retail e-HKD. The HKMA's resulting policy stance prioritises wholesale e-HKD development, treating retail extension as a longer-term, conditional option.
w: No obligation attaches. This informs a compliance head's input on whether the bank should prioritise tokenised-deposit infrastructure over e-HKD integration. It also flags concrete constraints, such as privacy-cost trade-offs and throughput limits, relevant to any DLT settlement build.
k: Commercial banks leaned slightly toward tokenised deposits rather than e-HKD, pointing to a lower cost of capital under fractional banking and more design flexibility with a shorter time-to-market. Commercial banks also cited stronger customer stickiness as a reason to favour tokenised deposits.
Executive Summary, p.2 (doc p.2)

A natively 'programmable e-HKD' with explicit spending conditions risks undermining fungibility and the 'singleness of money'. Purpose-bound money (PBM)/programmable payments are preferred alternatives that preserve fungibility.
Section 4, 'Programmability', p.30 (doc p.29-30)

Privacy-enhancing technologies (ZKPs via Zeto and Anonymous Zether) improved privacy with similar settlement times but increased gas fees up to 320 times versus no PETs. A tiered privacy model (basic for low-value, advanced PETs for high-value/high-risk) is recommended.
Section 4, 'Privacy', p.31, and footnote 38

Public DLTs such as Ethereum Layer 1 currently manage only roughly 15-30 transactions each second, a throughput limit for high-volume retail e-HKD use. The HKMA does not rule out public DLTs but flags a need for further optimisation.
Section 4, 'Reliability and Performance', p.33
HKMA will prioritise e-HKD development for financial institutions (wholesale); a sustainable private-sector business model for retail e-HKD has not yet been identified.
Section 5, 'Path Forward', p.34

Digital identity: pilots tested a digital identity framework using verifiable credentials (VCs) and unique identifiers (UIDs) issued by a trusted authority, cryptographically verified before each signed transaction.
Section 4, 'Identity', p.32
rg: Read the Executive Summary (p.2), Section 4 Design Considerations (pp.28-33) and Section 5 Path Forward (p.34) first — these carry the policy conclusions. Section 2 (pilot structure) and Section 3 (detailed findings by theme, pp.18-27) can be skimmed for specific use-case detail as needed.

t: List of e-HKD Industry Forum Members
sl: HKMA · List of e-HKD Industry Forum Members (2025)
s: This is a one-page membership list for the HKMA's e-HKD Industry Forum, naming three co-lead banks (Bank of China (Hong Kong), DBS Bank (Hong Kong), HSBC), six member firms. The HKMA as facilitator. It carries no obligations or policy content of its own.
w: Purely informational membership roster; useful only to identify which banks are already engaged with HKMA on e-HKD/tokenisation standard-setting.
k: The e-HKD Industry Forum has three co-lead banks: Bank of China (Hong Kong), DBS Bank (Hong Kong) and HSBC.
Member firms as of the list date include Aptos Labs, Boston Consulting Group, China Construction Bank (Asia), Forms Syntron Information (HK), Hang Seng Bank, and Mastercard Asia/Pacific.
rg: One page; skim only.

t: e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 2 Report
sl: HKMA · e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 2 Report (2025)
s: This HKMA report presents the findings of Phase 2 of the e-HKD Pilot Programme. Eleven industry pilot groups tested e-HKD and tokenised deposits across three areas: settling tokenised assets, programmable-money features, and offline payments. It compares e-HKD against privately-issued digital money, especially tokenised deposits, and finds banks generally prefer tokenised deposits for cost-of-capital and design-flexibility reasons. It concludes that most of the programmability and settlement benefits come from smart contracts rather than from the choice of settlement medium. It also concludes that a viable business case for a retail e-HKD has not yet emerged. The HKMA states it will prioritise e-HKD development for wholesale (interbank) use. It will continue preparatory legal, policy and technical groundwork for a possible retail extension by the first half of 2026, without committing to launch retail e-HKD.
w: This is the HKMA's own account of why it is not yet committing to retail e-HKD. It explains the regulator's current thinking on tokenised deposits versus CBDC. Directly relevant background for a bank's own tokenised-deposit and digital-money product strategy and for engaging with the HKMA's e-HKD Industry Forum and Supervisory Incubator for DLT.
k: Phase 2 involved eleven groups of firms trialling e-HKD and tokenised-deposit use cases in three areas: settling tokenised assets, programmable-money features, and offline payments.
Executive Summary, p.6

Commercial banks leaned slightly toward tokenised deposits rather than e-HKD, pointing to a lower cost of capital under fractional banking, greater design flexibility, and stronger customer stickiness.
Executive Summary, p.6

The HKMA will prioritise developing e-HKD for wholesale (interbank) use. It will keep preparing the policy, legal and technical groundwork to allow a possible retail extension, with that preparatory work targeted for completion in 2026. This is not a decision to launch retail e-HKD.
Executive Summary p.6 / Section 5 Path Forward, p.34

Gains from programmability (smart contracts) were found to come mainly from the smart-contract layer itself, not from whether the settlement medium is e-HKD or tokenised deposits. So e-HKD offers no unique programmability advantage.
Section 3.1.2, p.20

Achieving same-day (T+0) settlement of tokenised funds requires on-chain net asset values calculated close to real time, and wider native on-chain tokenisation rather than mere 'digital twins'. It would need a major redesign of core banking infrastructure, not just a new settlement medium.
Section 3.1.1, p.20

Privacy-enhancing technologies (zero-knowledge proofs such as Zeto and Anonymous Zether) improved transaction privacy. They increased gas fees by up to 320 times versus transactions without such technology, creating a cost/privacy trade-off for any future e-HKD design.
Section 4 Privacy, p.31

About 35% of surveyed respondents in one pilot said they would be less likely to use e-HKD for routine payments. They cited concern about the central bank's potential access to personal and transaction data.
Section 3.2.1, p.25

For offline payments, survey data showed limited appetite. 48% of respondents said Hong Kong's existing offline payment options, used by about 98% of the population, already meet their needs. 68% of merchants expected fees in line with current merchant fees, making cost recovery for an offline e-HKD difficult.
Section 3.1.3, p.22-23

The e-HKD Industry Forum, formed December 2024, includes a Programmability Working Group of nine firms, co-led by BOCHK, DBS and HSBC. This group is developing common token standards, due to be published separately by the first half of 2026.
Section 2.4, p.16
The report recommends an account-based balance model over a UTXO model for any future offline e-HKD, because it needs less local device storage and simpler synchronisation.
Section 3.1.3, p.24

Design considerations flagged as critical for any retail e-HKD include interoperability across DLT networks and tiered privacy. Tiered privacy means basic privacy for low-value transactions and stronger privacy-enhancing technology for high-value or high-risk ones. Other design considerations include a digital identity/verifiable-credential framework, and non-interest-bearing design to avoid competing with bank deposits.
Section 4, p.28-33

The report notes that if e-HKD is extended to retail, holding limits and non-interest-bearing design are being considered. This is to reduce the risk of large-scale deposit outflow from banks during stress.
Section 3.2.3, p.26-27
rg: Read the Executive Summary (p.6) and Section 5 Path Forward (p.34) first for the bottom line. Skim Section 3 (Findings) for the tokenised-deposits-vs-e-HKD comparison. The glossary and pilot fact-sheet appendix (p.36-44) can be skipped.

t: Updated Guidance on Registration in Respect of Regulated Activities under the Securities and Futures Ordinance and Controls to Ensure Fitness and Properness of Staff
sl: HKMA · Updated Guidance on Registration in Respect of Regulated Activities… (2025)
s: This Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) circular to all authorized institutions (AIs) gathers the still-valid guidance on three topics in one place. These are registration with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), executive officer (EO) consent, and the HKMA register of bank securities staff. The HKMA says it adds no new standards. It replaces 14 older circulars listed in its Annex 5. It reminds banks that reference checks on new hires should ask about dismissals, forced resignations and internal conduct investigations. It also reminds banks to follow the Mandatory Reference Checking (MRC) Scheme. Banks should answer other banks' reference requests within a reasonable time. A separate annex covers due diligence on all potential employees, including past terminations and fraud or dishonesty convictions.
w: This is the current HKMA playbook for staffing any SFO-regulated digital-asset activity at a bank: EO consent, register entries and hiring checks. It replaces older circulars, so policies citing them need updating.
k: Under the securities law, anyone carrying on regulated activities has to be licensed by or registered with the SFC, unless an exemption applies. A bank that intends to do so should apply to become a registered institution (RI) and appoint at least two EOs for each activity.
p.1, para 2
The HKMA expects a bank to enter other staff doing regulated work on the HKMA register before they perform any regulated function.
p.1, para 2
The circular consolidates existing guidance and introduces no new regulatory standards; superseded circulars are listed in Annex 5.
p.2, para 1; p.3
Reference checks on a proposed registered employee should cover dismissals, requests to resign and internal investigations or discipline for conduct.
p.2, para 2
Banks should respond clearly and within a reasonable time to other banks' requests for information on former staff, using MRC timelines as a guide.
p.2, para 3

The HKMA reminds banks that they need to ensure all their employees are fit and proper, not just EOs and registered staff. This includes thorough due diligence on job candidates' past terminations and criminal convictions (Annex 4).
p.2, para 5
rg: The three-page letter is quick; the operative detail is in Annex 1 (registration, EOs, HKMA register), Annex 2 (fitness controls, unregistered dealing) and Annex 4 (pre-hire checks).

t: Annex 1 - Guidance on registration related matters (with Annexes 2 to 5)
sl: HKMA · Annex 1 - Guidance on registration related matters (2025)
s: These annexes support the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) circular of 27 October 2025. They give the working detail for banks that are, or want to become, registered institutions (RIs) with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC). Annex 1 covers how to apply for registration and how the HKMA advises the SFC. It also covers consent for executive officers (EOs), provisional consent, and keeping the HKMA register of securities staff up to date. Annex 2 covers controls to keep registered staff fit and proper and to prevent unregistered dealing. Annex 4 sets pre-hire checks for all employees. These include the Banking Ordinance (BO) bar on hiring people with fraud or dishonesty convictions without HKMA consent. Annex 5 lists the older HKMA circulars that the package replaces.
w: These annexes are the step-by-step checklist for adding a VA-related regulated activity, appointing EOs and keeping the HKMA register accurate. Annex 4's conviction and termination checks apply to every hire into a digital-asset team.
k: A bank must apply to the HKMA for consent to at least two EOs per proposed activity no later than it applies to the SFC for registration.
Annex 1, Part I, 'Application for registration as RIs'
The HKMA assesses registration applicants on experience, management, controls and resources, may ask for an Independent Assurance Report, and may recommend conditions such as limits on scope.
Annex 1, Part I, 'Assessment of an application to become an RI'
Banks should tell the HKMA in advance of planned registration applications.
Annex 1, Part I, 'Assessment of an application to become an RI'
No one may act as an EO before written HKMA consent; the applicant must show fitness and sufficient authority.
Annex 1, Part II, 'Application to become an EO'
At least one EO per activity should be a CE, alternate CE, director or s.72B manager, and any other EO no more than one rank below that level.
Annex 1, Part II, 'Assessment of an application to become an EO'
The HKMA may grant provisional EO consent under BO s.71E pending background checks, if depositors and investors are not prejudiced.
Annex 1, Part II, 'Application for provisional consent'
An EO needs fresh consent before supervising an extra regulated activity.
Annex 1, Part II, item (b)

The RI should tell the HKMA about changes to EO information, including an EO leaving, within seven business days. The RI is also required to tell the SFC and the HKMA whether it started an internal investigation into the person in the six months before the EO role ended.
Annex 1, Part II, items (c)-(d)
Relevant individuals who stop being fit and proper, for example by failing to pass the local regulatory paper in time, should be promptly removed from the HKMA register.
Annex 1, Part III

The HKMA expects banks to have controls against unregistered dealing. Staff should report suspected cases to compliance at once. Where there are reasonable grounds to believe it happened, the bank should stop the practice at once and report in writing to the HKMA as soon as practicable.
Annex 2, 'Prohibition of unregistered dealing'
Before hiring, banks should ask about past terminations and fraud or dishonesty convictions, including spent ones; such a person cannot be employed without written HKMA consent under BO s.73(1)(b).
Annex 4, items (1)-(2)
rg: Read Annex 1 Parts I-II (pp.1-7) and Annex 4 (p.19) first; Annex 1 Part III and Annex 2 cover register mechanics and ongoing controls. Annex 3 lists other applicable guidelines and Annex 5 lists superseded circulars.

t: Supervisory Policy Manual CA-G-1: Overview of Capital Adequacy Regime for Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions (Version 5 - consultation draft)
sl: HKMA · Supervisory Policy Manual CA-G-1: Overview of Capital Adequacy Regime… (2025)
s: This draft module explains, at a general level, how the HKMA supervises the capital adequacy of locally incorporated banks. It covers solo and consolidated capital ratios, the leverage ratio, capital buffers and the risk-weighting framework. The version put out for consultation adds a new subsection setting out, in outline, how cryptoasset exposures are folded into the existing credit-risk capital-charge methodology. This subsection references the detailed cryptoasset capital rules set out elsewhere in the Banking (Capital) Rules.
w: This is the overview-level anchor for the bank's cryptoasset capital charge. The compliance head needs it to confirm the bank's capital model correctly separates Group 1a, 1b and 2 cryptoasset exposures and applies the right add-ons. The line-by-line formulas sit in the underlying capital rules and CRP-1 classification guideline.
k: A bank's capital adequacy ratio and leverage ratio must be calculated in line with the Banking (Capital) Rules. The MA can impose bank-specific minimum ratios above the regulatory minimum.
For a tokenised traditional asset (Group 1a cryptoasset) held in the banking book, the bank applies the same capital treatment as it would to the underlying asset.

For a Group 1b cryptoasset, held in the banking book, the bank must separately capitalise the credit risk of the reference asset. For example, a reference-asset-backed token such as certain stablecoins counts as Group 1b. The bank must also capitalise the credit risk of the entity performing redemption.

Where only some token holders can redeem directly with the issuer, a member bank must also capitalise the risk that it may have to buy the token from non-member holders. A non-member bank must instead capitalise its credit risk on the members.
Riskier tokens that do not meet the Group 1 classification tests (Group 2b cryptoassets) get a conservative capital treatment set by a separate Banking (Capital) Rules provision.

Extra capital add-ons apply for Group 1b assets held in the trading book, an infrastructure-risk add-on for Group 1 assets, a further add-on for Group 2a stablecoin exposures. A concentration add-on for global or domestic systemically important banks whose Group 2 cryptoasset exposure exceeds a prescribed limit.
rg: Read section 8.7 (pages 47-49) closely. Sections 1-7 and 9-15 are the pre-existing general capital-adequacy overview and only need a skim for context.

t: LegCo Secretariat releases Policy Pulse on "Latest developments in fintech and digital assets in Hong Kong"

t: LCQ21: e-CNY wallets
sl: Government · LCQ21: e-CNY wallets (2025)
s: This is a written Legislative Council question-and-answer about digital yuan (e-CNY) wallets in Hong Kong. A lawmaker asked about uptake statistics, merchant acceptance, transaction limits, and cross-border settlement under Project mBridge. The Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury replied that the HKMA does not itself hold e-CNY wallet usage statistics, since Mainland operating institutions run the wallets. He confirmed possible future increases to wallet limits are still under discussion with the People's Bank of China, with no fixed timetable. He also gave an update on mBridge reaching a Minimum Viable Product stage in June 2024.
w: Confirms there is no official Hong Kong data on e-CNY wallet adoption a bank can rely on for market sizing. That mBridge fee-setting is left to participating banks' own commercial judgement, which matters for any bank already connected to mBridge.
k: The HKMA does not compile statistics on how many Hong Kong residents have set up e-CNY wallets or how often they use them, because Mainland institutions operate the wallets.
reply (1)-(2)

The Legislator's question states the current e-CNY wallet limits as RMB 2,000 per transaction and RMB 50,000 per year. The Government's reply does not dispute this and says only that a possible relaxation is still being discussed with the People's Bank of China, with no confirmed date.
Question (3); reply (3) and (5)
Project mBridge reached its Minimum Viable Product stage in June 2024 and now forms part of Hong Kong's financial market infrastructure, with participating banks setting their own service fees.
reply (4)

The government plans to keep expanding e-CNY application scenarios, and separately plans to keep expanding mBridge's public- and private-sector participation, but gave no fixed rollout timetable for either.
reply (3), (4) and (5)

t: Supplemental joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Supplemental joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities (2025)
s: This circular updates the original December 2023 SFC-HKMA Joint Circular on intermediaries' virtual-asset activities, easing several requirements after a market review while keeping investor protection. It lets intermediaries offer staking through segregated accounts, allows VA trades via a licensed platform's off-platform service, and clarifies that VA-funded subscriptions/redemptions are not 'dealing' services. It also drops certain suitability and disclosure steps for institutional and qualified corporate professional investors. Separate guidance on HKMA-licensed stablecoin activities is still to come.
w: As an RI, the bank reaches this circular through HKMA's frontline supervision. It now permits staking and simplifies VA-funded subscriptions for the bank's clients, but only inside tightly controlled, pre-notified arrangements.
k: Intermediaries. Licensed corporations and registered institutions. Can now offer staking to existing virtual-asset clients. Only via segregated accounts held at an SFC-licensed trading platform, at an authorized institution, or at that institution's subsidiary.
paras 4-5
Staking is defined as locking up a client's virtual assets in a proof-of-stake blockchain's validation process to earn and pass on rewards.
para 4

Intermediaries may now execute client virtual-asset trades through a licensed platform's off-platform trading service, after removing the earlier restriction in clause 4.2 of the Terms and Conditions.
para 6

Clients paying for or receiving investment-product subscriptions/redemptions in virtual assets are not treated as using a 'dealing' service. The intermediary must still tell the regulators in advance, hold the assets at a licensed platform or authorized institution, and apply the AML travel-rule chapter to those movements.
para 7

The net-worth suitability check for clients of VA-exposed products. The requirement to give a VA-futures-specific risk warning, no longer apply to institutional and qualified corporate professional investors.
paras 8-9

Intermediaries must tell the SFC (and HKMA where relevant) in advance before. Changing the type of clients they serve, first letting clients deposit/withdraw virtual assets, first offering staking, first allowing VA-funded subscriptions/redemptions, or making other material changes to their VA activities.
para 10
Guidance specific to activities involving stablecoins issued under HKMA's own licensing regime is not yet published and will follow separately.
para 2
rg: Read paras 4-10 in full — they are the in force changes; para 1-3 is background on why the update was made.

t: Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions providing virtual asset dealing services and virtual asset advisory services (Appendix A to the Supplemental Joint Circular)
sl: SFC/HKMA · Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for… (2025)
s: The full, consolidated Terms and Conditions (September 2025 version, Appendix 6) governing licensed corporations/registered institutions providing VA dealing services (via omnibus account with an SFC-licensed platform) and VA advisory services. Covers interpretation, applicable codes/guidelines, financial soundness (12 months' operating expenses in excess liquid capital), operational controls, market-abuse prevention, and extensive client-facing duties (KYC, suitability, disclosure, contract notes/statements/receipts). It also covers custody of client assets and money, a new Part VIII on staking, record keeping, auditor reporting, conflicts of interest, and ongoing SFC/HKMA reporting obligations.
w: This is the current master terms and conditions for the bank's VA dealing and advisory activities as a registered institution. It directly sets the capital buffer, segregated-custody and new staking-disclosure obligations a compliance head must have live controls for, not merely track for the future.
k: A licensed corporation must keep, in Hong Kong, liquid capital in excess of its own actual operating expenses for a rolling 12-month period. This is over and above the ordinary Financial Resources Rules requirement.

Client virtual assets must be held on trust in segregated 'VA Segregated Account(s)' with an SFC-licensed platform or a qualifying authorized financial institution. Withdrawals must go directly to the client from that account.
Discretionary account managers may only invest less than 10% of a client's account gross asset value in virtual assets where VA trading authority is ancillary to a securities discretionary mandate.

New Part VIII (Staking): intermediaries may only stake client VAs via an SFC-licensed platform or authorized financial institution ('Staking Service Provider') with the necessary regulatory approval, or after discussion with HKMA. They must disclose staking risks (slashing, lock-up, validator risk) and obtain client acknowledgement.

A licensed corporation should not engage in VA market making on an execution venue, for example an SFC-licensed platform, through which it also provides Relevant VA Dealing services to clients. This is a conflicts-of-interest restriction.

Auditors must report annually on whether adequate custody control systems were in place and whether the firm complied with the Custody and Record Keeping parts and the financial soundness requirement.

Standard mandatory risk disclosures to retail clients include that VAs may not be 'property' under law and are not covered by the Investor Compensation Fund. They also include that VAs are not legal tender, and transactions may be irreversible.
rg: Read Part VII (Custody, p.20) and the new Part VIII (Staking, p.24) closely as the most operationally significant sections for a bank. Parts I-VI (client-facing conduct rules, pp.7-19) are largely a restatement of existing Code of Conduct-style obligations mapped onto VA activities. They can be skimmed once familiar with the Code of Conduct.

t: Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions providing virtual asset dealing services and virtual asset advisory services (Appendix A to the Supplemental Joint Circular, September 2025)
sl: HKMA/SFC · Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for… (2025)
s: This is the September 2025 set of licensing conditions that the SFC and HKMA impose on banks and brokers that deal in or advise on virtual assets. Part I covers two dealing models. Acting purely as an introducer to an SFC-licensed trading platform, and running client trades through the firm's own omnibus account at such a platform. Part II covers advisory services. The document sets client-classification, suitability, disclosure, custody, record-keeping and reporting standards, and for the first time gives detailed conditions for staking services offered to clients.
w: These are the actual licensing conditions a bank's registered-institution business must comply with for virtual asset dealing, advisory and staking, covering custody, suitability, disclosure and reporting duties owed to both regulators.
k: A firm that only introduces clients to an SFC-licensed platform must not hold client money or virtual assets itself and must use a written client agreement describing its limited role.
Part I, intro (a)-(c), p.4
A firm running an omnibus account must keep at least 12 months of operating expenses as excess liquid capital in Hong Kong, on top of the normal Financial Resources Rules.
para 3.1, p.8

Retail clients may only trade virtual assets through an omnibus account at a platform that itself is allowed to serve retail investors. They may only trade in tokens that platform makes available to retail investors.
para 4.1, p.9
The firm must not offer clients any financing to buy virtual assets, and should try to stop group companies doing so too.
para 4.3, p.9

Recommended virtual assets for retail clients must be liquid enough to appear in at least two independent, IOSCO-consistent market indices. They must also be tradable for retail investors on the platform used.
Client virtual assets must be held on trust in a segregated account at either an SFC-licensed platform or an authorized institution (or its subsidiary) that meets HKMA's expected custody standards.
para 7.1(a), p.20

A firm may stake client virtual assets only via a Staking Service Provider that is either an SFC-licensed platform or an authorized institution. This is only once that provider holds the necessary SFC clearance or has discussed the service with the HKMA.

Clients must be told the risks specific to staking, such as slashing, lock-up delays, validator hacking and legal uncertainty over their interest in staked assets. They must sign an acknowledgement of those risks before staking, unless they are institutional or qualified professional investors.
Records on client virtual assets, money, orders and staking must be kept for at least seven years, with contract notes/receipts kept for at least two years.
Any actual or suspected material breach of these terms must be reported to the SFC, and also to the HKMA if the firm is a registered institution, as soon as practicable.

For advisory services, a firm must assess a client's virtual-asset knowledge and risk tolerance before advising, and train clients lacking knowledge. It may only recommend liquid, index-qualifying tokens to retail clients.
Part II, paras 3.1-3.5, p.35-36
rg: Read Part I paras 4 (Operations), 6 (Dealing with clients), 7 (Custody) and 8 (Staking) closely. The Schedule 1 list of applied SFC codes and Part II (advisory) can be skimmed since they largely mirror Part I's suitability logic.

t: Supplemental joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities
sl: SFC/HKMA · Supplemental joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities (2025)
s: This circular adds to the SFC and HKMA's 22 December 2023 Joint Circular on intermediaries' virtual asset (VA)-related activities, bringing in relaxations after industry feedback. It lets intermediaries offer staking services to clients through SFC-licensed platforms or authorized financial institutions (AIs), and allows trade execution through off-platform virtual asset trading platform (VATP) services. It also clarifies that subscribing to or redeeming investment products using virtual assets is not itself a VA dealing service. It exempts institutional or qualified corporate professional investors from certain net-worth and risk-disclosure rules. Separate guidance on activities involving HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers is promised. Updated Terms and Conditions (Appendix 6) come with this circular.
w: As an update to the Joint Circular that reaches the bank through the HKMA, this circular relaxes some rules, such as off-platform trading and staking. It also adds new advance-notice duties for staking, VA-funded subscriptions and redemptions, and other material changes to VA-related activities.
k: Intermediaries can now offer clients staking services. This is only via segregated accounts kept at an SFC-licensed trading platform, at an authorized financial institution, or at a subsidiary of a locally incorporated authorized institution.
para 5

A licensed corporation or registered institution can now route a client's virtual-asset dealing trade through an SFC-licensed platform's own off-platform trading service. The earlier restriction in clause 4.2 of the prior Terms and Conditions has been dropped as a result.
para 6

Clients subscribing to or redeeming investment products using virtual assets, or making in-kind subscriptions or redemptions of VA funds, are not treated as receiving VA dealing services. This applies as long as advance notice and custody conditions are met.
para 7
The net-worth rule in paragraph 6.2 of the Joint Circular no longer applies to clients who are institutional professional investors or qualified corporate professional investors.
para 8
The requirement to give risk disclosure statements for VA futures contracts (Joint Circular paragraph 13) no longer applies to institutional or qualified corporate professional investors.
para 9

Intermediaries must tell the SFC, and the HKMA where relevant, in advance of material changes. These include a client's first deposit or withdrawal, first staking service, or first subscription or redemption using VA.
para 10
Separate guidance specific to activities involving HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) will come later.
para 11
rg: Read the full 3-page body. The Appendices, Appendix A clean T&Cs and Appendix B tracked-changes T&Cs, are the detailed in-force rules. They should be read via the separate T&C attachment records rather than in full duplicate here.

t: 2025 Policy Address
sl: Government · 2025 Policy Address (2025)
s: The Chief Executive's 2025 Policy Address is a wide-ranging annual government speech. Only its digital-asset/fintech passages are captured here (paragraphs 97, 103-104, 110-111 and Annex item 22, on pages 39-43 and 97). It confirms continuation of Project Ensemble, including encouraging banks to issue tokenised deposits and settle tokenised money market funds, plus regularising government tokenised bond issuance. It confirms the government is implementing a stablecoin issuer licensing regime. The government is also drafting legislative proposals for a new licensing regime covering digital asset dealing and custodian service providers, with a bill targeted for the Legislative Council in 2026. It also notes the SFC is exploring wider digital asset products for professional investors, and plans automated reporting and surveillance tools. It also notes a tokenised-gold investment product initiative, and a pilot use of tokenised deposits in commodity trade finance with Brazil's central bank.
w: This is the clearest, highest-level government confirmation that Hong Kong will pass legislation in 2026 to license digital asset dealing and custody businesses. This adds to the stablecoin regime already in force. A bank's digital asset business plan and licensing roadmap should track this bill.
k: The government will support issuers in launching tokenised gold as a new investment vehicle, as part of building Hong Kong into a regional gold trading and storage hub.
para 97(iv), p.39
The HKMA will keep advancing Project Ensemble, encouraging commercial banks to issue tokenised deposits and to settle tokenised money market fund transactions using tokenised deposits.
para 103, p.40
The HKMA will help the government regularise (make routine) the issuance of tokenised government bonds, and will encourage banks to strengthen risk management via the supervisory sandbox.
para 103, p.40

The government is implementing the licensing regime for stablecoin issuers and is separately drafting legislative proposals for new licensing regimes covering digital asset dealing and custodian service providers.
para 104, p.41

The SFC is looking at whether professional investors could be given access to a broader menu of digital asset products and services, conditional on adequate investor safeguards. The SFC will also bring in automated reporting and data-surveillance tools against digital asset risks.
para 104, p.41
A pilot with Banco Central do Brazil will test tokenised deposits and electronic bills of lading to support international commodity trade finance.
para 111(iii), p.43
The government commits to bringing a bill to the Legislative Council in 2026 that would set up licensing for firms dealing in digital assets and providing digital asset custody.
Annex, item 22, p.97
rg: Read only paragraphs 97(iv), 103-104 and 111(iii) on pages 39-43, plus Annex item 22 on page 97. Skip the rest of this 90+ page general policy speech, which covers unrelated topics (housing, healthcare, trade, shipping, etc).

t: SB-1 Supervision of Regulated Activities of SFC-Registered Authorized Institutions
sl: HKMA · SB-1 Supervision of Regulated Activities of SFC-Registered Authorized Institutions (2025)
s: SB-1 sets out how HKMA supervises the day-to-day conduct of an AI's SFC-registered activities once it becomes a Registered Institution (RI). It explains HKMA's role as frontline supervisor working alongside the SFC, the mandatory appointment and registration of executive officers and relevant individuals, HKMA's tiered response to control deficiencies and misconduct. The events an RI must proactively report — including any plan to start or change virtual-asset-related activities.
w: This is the core rulebook for how HKMA actually supervises the bank's RI status day to day. It covers who must be appointed, what must be pre-notified before touching virtual assets, and how the bank's people and licence can be disciplined.
k: Once an AI is registered by the SFC to carry on a regulated activity, it becomes a Registered Institution (RI). The HKMA acts as the RI's frontline day-to-day supervisor while the SFC keeps overall regulatory responsibility and can rely on HKMA's supervision.
para 2.1.3

An RI must have a minimum of two executive officers responsible for the direct supervision of each of its regulated activities. Each needs the HKMA's prior written consent, with at least one available at all times per activity.

Every 'relevant individual' who performs a regulated function for an RI must be entered in the HKMA Register before starting that work. Any change to their registered details must be notified within 7 business days.

HKMA uses a three-step, risk-based approach to deficiencies. It first shares good practice, then requires corrective action or an independent review for control weaknesses. Finally, it moves to disciplinary or enforcement action where there is a prima facie case of misconduct or unfitness.
HKMA generally expects an RI to meet the same conduct standards the SFC applies to licensed corporations, and can add extra investor-protection requirements specific to the banking context.

For anti-money-laundering purposes, RIs and their AI associated entities must follow the HKMA's AML/CFT Guideline for Authorized Institutions. They must also take into account specific parts of the SFC's own AML/CFT guideline, including its virtual-asset chapter, for definitions and provisions relevant to securities-sector business.
para 4.16.1

An RI should tell the SFC and HKMA before it starts any virtual-asset activities, such as dealing, advisory or asset-management services in VA products. It should also tell them before changing how it runs those activities, including changes to the kinds of clients it serves.
para 5.6

An RI must give at least 7 business days' advance notice before ceasing a regulated activity or changing its address for carrying one on. It must also notify certain changes to relevant individuals' backgrounds within 7 business days of becoming aware of them.
paras 5.1, 5.5

Both HKMA and SFC can discipline a relevant individual or executive officer found guilty of misconduct or no longer fit and proper. This can include removing them from the HKMA Register or withdrawing an executive officer's consent, with a right of appeal to the Securities and Futures Appeals Tribunal.
paras 6.3, 6.7
rg: Read section 2 (HKMA/SFC framework), 4.3 (executive officers and relevant individuals), 4.16 (AML) and 5 (event reporting, especially para 5.6 on virtual assets) closely. Sections 4.8-4.14 on specific product/activity codes can be skimmed unless the bank runs those specific activities.

t: LCQ10: Regulation of digital assets
sl: FSTB · LCQ10: Regulation of digital assets (2025)
s: A written Legislative Council reply clarifies who may lawfully offer a stablecoin under the Stablecoins Ordinance, in response to concerns that virtual-asset OTC shops were exploiting grey areas. It confirms only five categories of 'permitted offeror' may offer a specified stablecoin. Licensed stablecoin issuers, SFC-licensed virtual-asset service providers, stored-value-facility licensees, SFC Type 1-licensed corporations, and authorised institutions (banks). Virtual-asset OTC trading institutions are not permitted offerors and cannot offer stablecoins to any investor type. It also confirms no stablecoin issuer had yet been licensed as of the reply date. That the licensing timetable for the dealing/custodian regimes would be announced after the consultation (closed August 29, 2025) is digested.
w: This is a core compliance reference. It confirms the bank, as an authorised institution, is itself one of only five categories of entity legally permitted to offer a stablecoin. It also confirms that a range of common counterparties, such as VA OTC shops, are explicitly barred from doing so. The bank should build this fact into its own product-distribution and counterparty-screening rules.
k: Only five types of 'permitted offeror' may offer a specified stablecoin. Licensed stablecoin issuers, SFC-licensed virtual-asset service providers, stored-value-facility licensees, SFC Type 1-licensed corporations, and authorised institutions.
reply (1), para 2
Permitted offerors may offer a regulated (HKMA-licensed-issuer) stablecoin to both retail and professional investors, but an unregulated stablecoin may only be offered to professional investors.
reply (1), para 2

Because virtual-asset OTC trading institutions do not qualify as permitted offerors, they are barred from selling any specified stablecoin to any investor type, whether or not that stablecoin is itself regulated.
reply (1), para 3
As of this reply, the HKMA had not licensed any stablecoin issuer, so members of the public acquiring any stablecoin currently bear their own risk.
reply (2), para 1
The FSTB and SFC are still formulating details of the dealing/custodian licensing regimes based on consultation feedback and will announce a legislative timetable in due course.
reply (3), para 2
rg: Read reply (1) in full for the permitted-offeror list and OTC-shop exclusion; replies (2) and (3) are shorter status updates.

t: Supervisory Policy Manual LM-1: Regulatory Framework for Supervision of Liquidity Risk (draft V.5)
sl: HKMA · Supervisory Policy Manual LM-1: Regulatory Framework for Supervision of… (2025)
s: This is a statutory guideline under section 7(3) of the Banking Ordinance, in draft form. It adds a new section 5.9 and Annex 3 on cryptoassets to the HKMA's existing liquidity-risk supervision module. It tells authorized institutions how cryptoasset exposures should be folded into the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) and Core Funding Ratio (CFR). The default principle is to treat a cryptoasset the same as the traditional asset or liability it economically resembles, unless it carries extra risk from its digital form. The draft sets specific rules for three buckets: tokenised claims that are a legal claim on the bank, stablecoins, and all other cryptoassets. It also reserves the HKMA's right to apply tougher treatment case by case.
w: This module is the primary rulebook compliance would use to determine how any cryptoasset custody, trading, issuance or tokenised-deposit activity affects the bank's regulatory liquidity ratios. It directly drives the new lines in Form MA(BS)1E.
k: As a baseline, cryptoasset exposures should get the same LCR/NSFR/LMR/CFR treatment as an economically equivalent traditional exposure, because of their extra risk and limited track record.
para 5.9.1-5.9.2 (footnote 78-79 define 'cryptoasset' and 'cryptoasset exposure')

A cryptoasset can only count as a high-quality liquid asset (HQLA) if it is a 'group 1a' tokenised version of an already-eligible traditional asset. Both the token and the underlying asset must meet all the usual HQLA conditions. The token must also meet extra operational conditions, for example living on a well-established ledger with an active, sizable market so it can be sold quickly with little loss of value.
Annex 3, paras 1-1(b) and footnote 95

A bank may issue tokens that are a direct, par-value redeemable claim on it, backed one-to-one by a matching pool of assets. It can then treat the resulting liability like ordinary deposits or unsecured funding, but only from the earliest date holders could demand redemption. It only gets the favourable retail/small-business rate if the bank can always identify the token holders.
Annex 3, para 4

Stablecoins a bank issues get a 100% LCR outflow rate if redeemable within the LCR window. This does not apply if they are fully backed by HQLA-eligible assets; then the more favourable secured-funding outflow rates may apply instead.
Annex 3, para 7

Stablecoins a bank holds, rather than issues, are treated as ordinary non-HQLA debt securities. This generally means a 0% LCR inflow rate and an 85% NSFR required-stable-funding factor. A lower 50% factor can apply if the maturity is short and it will convert to fiat within 12 months.
Annex 3, para 7

Any other cryptoasset the bank holds or has borrowed gets the harshest treatment: no LCR inflow recognition and a 100% NSFR funding requirement. It also gets a 100% outflow rate if the bank owes the asset back to a counterparty.
Annex 3, para 8(b)

The HKMA can impose stricter LCR/NSFR treatment for a specific cryptoasset if the asset carries extra liquidity risk, or if the bank has contingent exposure from issuing or trading it. For example, the bank might feel pressure to support redemptions to protect its reputation.
para 9 and footnote 98
The same tokenised-claim, stablecoin and 'other cryptoasset' logic carries over largely unchanged to the Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (for category 2 institutions) and the Core Funding Ratio.
paras 11-17
rg: Read section 5.9 (p.65) as the summary, then Annex 3 in full (pp.88-94); skip the unchanged core LCR/LMR mechanics elsewhere in the module.

t: Supervisory Policy Manual MR-2: CVA Risk Capital Charge (V.2 - Consultation)
sl: HKMA · Supervisory Policy Manual MR-2: CVA Risk Capital Charge (2025)
s: This draft statutory guideline adds a new section 4 on cryptoassets to the module covering credit valuation adjustment (CVA) risk capital. CVA is the capital a bank must hold against the risk that a derivative counterparty's credit quality worsens. Derivatives and securities-financing transactions referencing tokenised traditional assets or stablecoins (groups 1a/1b) are generally treated the same as instruments on the underlying traditional asset. A bank must still separately check the token's own liquidity behaviour rather than assuming it matches the original asset. Group 2a cryptoasset derivatives cannot use the more risk-sensitive standardised CVA approach at all. Group 2b exposures are folded into an existing, very conservative flat risk-weight treatment with no extra CVA calculation.
w: Sets the capital a derivatives or securities-financing desk must hold for counterparty credit-quality risk on any cryptoasset-referencing trade. It also confirms less-standard tokens cannot use the more capital-efficient standardised method.
k: Derivatives and financing trades on group 1a tokenised assets are generally charged CVA capital the same way as trades on the non-tokenised version of the asset.
para 4.2.1

A bank must independently assess the tokenised asset itself against this module's tests. It cannot simply assume the token qualifies for a treatment just because the underlying traditional asset does, because liquidity behaviour can differ between the two.
para 4.2.2
If there is not enough data to model how those liquidity differences affect the tokenised asset's value, the standardised CVA approach cannot be used. The basic approach applies instead.
para 4.2.2
Group 2a cryptoasset derivatives and securities-financing trades must use the basic CVA approach. The standardised approach is not permitted for them.
para 4.3.1

Group 2b cryptoasset exposures generally need no separate CVA calculation because they already carry the conservative 1,250% risk weight that covers credit, market and CVA risk together. This only changes if a fair-valued, cryptoasset-collateralised transaction's credit risk is calculated some other way, in which case the 1,250% weight is applied specifically for CVA.
rg: Read section 4 in full (pp.44-46); the rest of the module is unchanged general CVA mechanics.

t: CR-L-5 Major Acquisitions and Investments: BELR Part 3
sl: HKMA · CR-L-5 Major Acquisitions and Investments: BELR Part 3 (2025)
s: CR-L-5 explains how HKMA exercises its consent power over an AI's major acquisitions of another company's share capital under Part 3 of the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules. The revision adds a footnote clarifying that a cryptoasset counting as equity ownership is treated the same as ordinary share capital for this consent regime.
w: If the bank ever takes an equity-like tokenised stake in a company, for example a fintech partner, the same 5%-of-Tier-1-capital consent trigger applies as for ordinary shares.
k: A locally incorporated AI needs HKMA's written consent before acquiring, in one go or in stages, 5% or more of a company's share capital measured against the AI's Tier 1 capital.
para 1.1
'Share capital' for this purpose is defined to also include a cryptoasset that conveys the same economic substance as equity ownership, so token-based equity stakes now count toward the 5% threshold.
para 1.1, fn.1
The 5% threshold is measured against how much Tier 1 capital the AI held when it made the acquisition, usually taking the figure from the end of the preceding quarter.
para 2.1.1
Certain small or deemed-consent acquisitions are exempt from needing prior consent, as set out later in the module.
Structure, ss.2.2, 2.4, p.2
rg: Read para 1.1 and its footnote for the crypto-equity extension; the rest of the module (application procedures, exemptions) is standard M&A-consent process detail.

t: Letter to HKAB: Cryptoassets standard: consultation on new and revised SPM modules and code of practice
sl: HKMA · Cryptoassets standard: consultation on new and revised SPM modules… (2025)
s: This is the HKMA Banking Policy Department's covering letter to the Hong Kong Association of Banks (addressed to its then chairperson). It opens formal industry consultation on a package of cryptoasset-related prudential guidance. This package is a brand-new SPM module, CRP-1, on classifying cryptoassets, plus revisions to eight other modules and one code. The stated purpose is to implement, at the Hong Kong level, the Basel Committee's global standard on how banks should treat cryptoasset exposures for capital purposes. It also covers related amendments to the capital, disclosure and exposure-limit rules. The HKMA asked for comments within about a month and noted it sent an equivalent letter to the DTC Association the same day.
w: Gives compliance the authoritative, dated list of exactly which modules and code are in scope of the cryptoasset prudential-standard consultation, useful for tracking which drafts to monitor through to finalisation.
k: The consultation covers a brand-new module, CRP-1 'Classification of Cryptoassets', plus revisions to eight further items. These are CA-D-1, CA-G-5, CR-G-8, CR-G-9, CR-L-5, LM-1, MR-1, MR-2 and the Banking (Exposure Limits) Code.
list of modules, p.1

The revisions implement, at the local level, the Basel Committee's global standard on prudential treatment of banks' cryptoasset exposures. This runs alongside the Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2025, the Banking (Disclosure) (Amendment) Rules 2025 and the Banking (Exposure Limits) (Amendment) Rules 2025.
A separate, related revision to module CA-G-1 (overview of the capital adequacy regime) is being consulted on separately, not as part of this package.
footnote 1, p.1
Comments were requested by 10 October 2025.

t: CR-G-9 Exposures to Connected Parties
sl: HKMA · CR-G-9 Exposures to Connected Parties (2025)
s: CR-G-9 sets out the systems and controls a locally incorporated AI needs to identify, measure, monitor and limit its exposures to connected parties. The statutory cap on such exposures under the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules. It was reissued as part of the same crypto-standard consultation package, but the introductory and structural sections reviewed here contain no crypto-specific wording. Any link to cryptoasset exposures runs through the general BELR valuation cross-references rather than dedicated crypto provisions in this module.
w: This is the general connected-lending control framework the bank already operates under. The pages available here show no dedicated crypto content, so its relevance to crypto business is indirect, through the wider large-exposure/BELR valuation changes rather than this module itself.
k: The module exists to make AIs put in place systems to identify, measure, monitor and control exposures to connected parties, including those falling under Part 8 of the BELR.
Purpose section, p.1
It applies to all locally incorporated AIs in Hong Kong.
Application section, p.1
The module covers the statutory limit on connected-party exposures, board oversight of the connected-party policy, ongoing monitoring, and financial disclosure of these exposures.
Structure, ss.2-4, p.2
This version replaces four earlier editions dating back to a 1999 circular on connected lending.
Previous guidelines superseded, p.1
rg: Read the Purpose and Structure sections for orientation; the bulk of the connected-party control detail (ss.2-4) is unchanged general banking guidance, not crypto-specific.

t: CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process
sl: HKMA · CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process (2025)
s: CA-G-5 explains how the HKMA runs its Pillar 2 Supervisory Review Process (SRP) to set a bank-specific capital add-on on top of the Pillar 1 minimum. Crypto activities and their risks are still new and changing. The revision adds an explicit statement that the HKMA may respond to weak crypto risk management with capital add-ons, provisioning requirements, activity limits, or other measures. These are decided case by case.
w: This is the mechanism by which weaknesses in the bank's crypto risk management can translate directly into a higher firm-specific capital requirement or forced activity limits. It links crypto operational risk straight to the capital plan.
k: Cryptoasset activities and their risks are relatively new and still evolving. Because of this, the HKMA's supervisory response to gaps in an AI's crypto capital or risk management can include capital add-ons and provisioning requirements for foreseeable crypto losses. It can also include activity limits or other mitigation steps.
para 3.6.6
The HKMA's Pillar 2 capital add-on (P2A) is meant to capture material risks not already fully covered by the Pillar 1 minimum requirement.
Structure, s.3.3-3.4, p.2
Before raising or lowering an AI's Pillar 2 capital requirement, HKMA may hold off temporarily to check whether the underlying issue is genuinely resolved or just temporary.
Extra capital is not treated as a substitute for good risk management; HKMA may instead, or in addition, require better systems and controls.
para 3.6.4
Stress tests (sensitivity tests and scenario analyses) run by the AI feed into how HKMA assesses capital adequacy under the SRP.
rg: Read para 3.6.6 (the new crypto-specific supervisory response) and the surrounding 3.6 sub-section on Pillar 2 capital setting first. The legal-framework sections (2.1-2.2) can be skimmed.

t: CA-D-1 Guideline on the Application of the Banking (Disclosure) Rules
sl: HKMA · CA-D-1 Guideline on the Application of the Banking (Disclosure)… (2025)
s: CA-D-1 interprets how AIs should meet the Banking (Disclosure) Rules, which implement Hong Kong's Pillar 3 public-disclosure regime. This revision adds two new items tied to the cryptoassets standard. An annual qualitative disclosure of crypto-related business that creates liquidity risk, and, for larger institutions, a semi-annual quantitative disclosure of liquidity requirements tied to crypto exposures. The rest of the module sets out general disclosure timing, review and exemption rules that already applied to AIs.
w: This creates a standing Pillar 3 reporting obligation about the bank's crypto activities. There is personal criminal liability for directors and managers if it is missed, so compliance needs a dedicated review-and-sign-off workflow.
k: An AI with any cryptoasset exposure must give an annual, mainly qualitative, disclosure of its crypto-related activities that create liquidity risk, using the standard table the HKMA specifies.
para 12.2.4

An AI that is a 'category 1 institution' and has cryptoasset exposures must also give a semi-annual disclosure of the liquidity requirements tied to those exposures. This uses a standard template and is mostly quantitative.
para 12.2.4

Quarterly disclosures are due within 8 weeks of period-end, interim (half-year) disclosures within 3 months, and annual disclosures within 4 months, generally aligned with publication of the related financial statements.
para 9.3.7 (table)
A failure to meet any disclosure requirement is a criminal offence for every director, chief executive and manager of the AI, and can also count against the bank's continuing authorization.

Before publication, the board (or a delegated committee) and senior management must have the disclosures reviewed by staff independent of those who prepared them, to check they are not false or misleading.
Disclosure statements must be lodged with the HKMA before publication and e-mailed to the HKMA's register within 3 working days after publication.

t: CR-G-8 Large Exposures and Risk Concentrations
sl: HKMA · CR-G-8 Large Exposures and Risk Concentrations (2025)
s: CR-G-8 governs how AIs measure and limit large exposures and risk concentrations. This revision inserts a dedicated set of rules, Division 5A, for valuing cryptoasset-related exposures for large-exposure purposes. These are separate from the general rules used for other counterparty-credit-risk and non-counterparty-credit-risk exposures.
w: This determines how much of a client's or counterparty's crypto-linked exposure counts against the bank's concentration limits. That affects how much crypto business the bank can safely do with any one counterparty.
k: Cryptoasset-related exposures are valued for large-exposure purposes under a new, separate set of rules, Division 5A of Part 7 of the BELR. This replaces the general divisions used for other exposures.
Before applying the crypto valuation rules, an AI must first pin down the specific counterparty (or connected group) the exposure relates to.
para 2.8.9

Which specific rule applies to a given crypto exposure depends on how it's defined under the BELR. It also depends on whether the asset is classed Group 1a/1b/2a/2b, and whether it sits in the banking book or trading book.
para 2.8.10
For some crypto exposures, the AI must reuse the valuation figure it already calculated under the Capital Rules rather than doing a separate calculation for large-exposure purposes.
para 2.8.11
Because crypto markets and technology are still evolving, HKMA can give an individual AI written instructions to use a different valuation method for its crypto exposures than the one in the rules.
para 2.8.12

t: CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets
sl: HKMA · CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets (2025)
s: CRP-1 is a new HKMA guideline that sorts a bank's cryptoasset holdings into capital-treatment groups. Group 1 covers tokenised traditional assets and well-backed stablecoins that meet strict conditions, and gets treated like the underlying traditional asset. Group 2 covers everything else and needs much heavier capital backing, with a limited sub-category (Group 2a) recognised for hedging. The module takes effect from 1 January 2026 and sits alongside the Banking (Capital) Rules, which prevail if the two conflict.
w: This module decides how much capital the bank must hold against any crypto exposure it books. It forces a conservative default and an HKMA-notification step for anything new — both are matters compliance must build a process around before 1 January 2026.
k: Cryptoassets split into Group 1 (meets four classification conditions) and Group 2 (does not). Group 1 splits further into 1a (tokenised traditional assets) and 1b (stablecoins with an effective peg mechanism).
The rules and this module start applying from 1 January 2026.
para 1.4.1
Any cryptoasset exposure an AI already holds before that date defaults to the most conservative bucket (Group 2b) until the HKMA agrees a different classification.
para 1.4.2
Before acquiring a brand-new type of cryptoasset, an AI has to tell the HKMA and hold it as Group 2b until the HKMA agrees to a better classification.
para 2.1.2
If a cryptoasset later stops meeting its group's conditions, the AI has to move it straight back to Group 2b.
para 2.1.3

For a stablecoin to qualify as Group 1b, its reserve assets must, even in stress, always be worth at least the total amount holders could redeem. Its reserve assets must also be high quality, liquid, currency-matched to the peg, and independently audited at least once a year.
A stablecoin issued under the HKMA's own stablecoin licensing regime is automatically treated as meeting the extra safeguards needed for permissionless-blockchain assets to qualify for Group 1.
para 2.6.3

To count as Group 2a (limited hedging recognition), a cryptoasset needs deep, liquid markets. It needs an average market capitalisation of at least HKD 78 billion and a 10%-trimmed average daily trading volume of at least HKD 390 million over the prior year.
para 3.1.1
AIs must keep full records of how they classified each cryptoasset and hand them to the HKMA on request.
para 2.1.1
rg: Read paras 1.3-1.4 (classification overview and effective date) and 2.2 (stablecoin redemption/reserve conditions) first; the abbreviations annex can be skipped.

t: Banking (Exposure Limits) Code (draft, consequential and other amendments)
sl: HKMA · Banking (Exposure Limits) Code (2025)
s: This is a draft update to the statutory code of practice under the Banking Ordinance. It guides how AIs apply parts of the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules (BELR), covering large-exposure limits, connected-party rules and related concepts. Despite being bundled into the HKMA's cryptoasset prudential-standard consultation, the drafted text itself covers unrelated topics. These include what counts as a reliable third-party market data provider and what security is acceptable to a prudent banker, including life insurance policies. It also covers how to calculate an employee's annual salary for staff-lending limits, self-use land, and when two counterparties are 'economically dependent' for large-exposure grouping. No cryptoasset-specific provision appears in the text supplied.
w: Bundled procedurally with the cryptoasset package but not itself cryptoasset-relevant. Compliance can note it and deprioritise it against the LM-1/MR-1/MR-2/CRP-1 drafts.
k: A bank should judge a third-party market-data provider's reliability by its market standing, financial strength and service capacity, track record, and back-up arrangements. The bank can also weigh any other factor it considers relevant.
para 3(2), p.1

A life insurance policy can count as acceptable security if written by a Hong Kong-authorized insurer, the insurer or its parent holds at least a BBB- rating (or equivalent). It is valued at the lower of surrender value or 75% of cash value, or a more conservative internal valuation.
para 4(3), p.6

An employee's annual salary for staff-lending-limit purposes should add basic salary, other fixed payments and benefits, and estimated performance-based pay for the year. It should exclude variable bonuses and non-monetary benefits like medical insurance.
para 5(2), p.6

Two counterparties are 'economically dependent', and so grouped for large-exposure limits, if 50% or more of one party's income or spending, or of its output, flows to or from the other. They are also grouped if one has guaranteed the other's exposure to a degree that could cause its own default.
rg: Skim only; no cryptoasset content was found in the supplied text.

t: Supervisory Policy Manual MR-1: Market Risk Capital Charge (V.2 - Consultation)
sl: HKMA · Supervisory Policy Manual MR-1: Market Risk Capital Charge (2025)
s: This is a draft statutory guideline under section 7(3) of the Banking Ordinance for locally incorporated AIs, adding a new section 6 on cryptoasset exposures to the market-risk capital module. It tells banks how to calculate the market-risk capital charge for cryptoasset positions under each of the three approaches the module already covers. These are the simplified standardised approach, the full standardised approach, and internal models. Tokenised assets that mirror a traditional asset (group 1a) and stablecoins referencing traditional assets (group 1b) are generally mapped onto the same risk factors as the assets they represent. This means netting and hedging against the traditional asset is allowed. A separate, harsher, standalone capital charge applies to less traditional 'group 2a' cryptoassets, and internal models cannot be used for them at all.
w: Determines how much market-risk capital a trading or dealing desk must hold against any cryptoasset position, and confirms that holding cryptoassets removes access to the small-book capital exemption.
k: A bank should follow CRP-1 (a separate module) to first classify each cryptoasset into group 1a, 1b, 2a or 2b before applying this module's rules.
footnote 79

For the simplified standardised approach, a group 1 cryptoasset is converted to HKD at the current spot price and mapped to the same risk category as the traditional asset it represents. Hedging and netting between a token and its underlying traditional asset is recognised for group 1a, and between a stablecoin and the asset it references for group 1b.

Under the full standardised (sensitivities-based) approach, a tokenised instrument's risk exposure must be mapped onto exactly the risk factors used for the conventional asset it mirrors. The bank must apply matching sensitivities in doing so.
para 6.1.4
Internal models cannot be used at all for instruments referencing group 2 cryptoassets.
para 6.1.9

Group 2a cryptoassets (which meet a separate hedging-recognition test in CRP-1) get their own standalone capital charge under modified versions of the simplified or full standardised approach. A bank cannot net or offset a group 2a cryptoasset position across different exchanges.

For each group 2a cryptoasset, a bank works out a net long/short position and applies a capital requirement equal to the full value of that net position. Only 65% of any offsetting long-vs-short amount is recognised.
A bank with any cryptoasset exposure cannot use the small-portfolio, de-minimis exemption from market-risk capital rules that would otherwise be available.
footnote 80

Group 2b cryptoassets are not subject to a market-risk capital charge at all. Instead they get the very conservative combined credit/market/CVA-risk treatment (a 1,250% risk weight) under a different section of the capital rules.
footnote 81
rg: Read section 6 in full (pp.152-157); it is the only cryptoasset-specific material -- the rest of the module restates existing non-crypto market-risk mechanics.
