t: Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)3A(I): Divisions A to F and L - Market Risk Capital Charge
sl: HKMA · Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)3A(I): Divisions A to F… (2025)
s: This part of the market-risk return covers the sensitivities-based method (Divisions A-F) and the simplified standardized approach (Division L) for trading-book positions. It adds group 2a cryptoasset positions, broadly stablecoin-type, as a new risk bucket. Banks are instructed to report the highest of three correlation-scenario capital charges for that bucket, regardless of charges elsewhere. They should add a separate curvature-risk charge for price moves in those tokens. Under the simplified method, they should report each group 2a token and its hedges on its own line.
w: For a bank, this is where its trading-book stablecoin-type exposure turns into a specific, separately-tracked capital charge each month. This is on top of whatever the bank already reports for other market risk.
k: Group 2a crypto positions form their own risk bucket. The capital charge reported for it should be the highest of the three prescribed correlation-scenario results, kept separate from charges on other risk types.
para 18, p.10

paras 44-47, p.10
Where a fund (CIS) exposure includes a group 2a crypto slice, that slice's capital requirement should be captured in this same section.
para 48, p.10
Under the simplified standardized approach (Division L), each group 2a token should be reported on its own line, together with its associated hedging positions.
Cryptoasset exposures more generally should also follow the Part 12 crypto rules of the Banking (Capital) Rules in addition to this form's own instructions.

t: Circular to licensed virtual asset trading platform operators on custody of virtual assets
sl: SFC · licensed virtual asset trading platform operators on custody of… (2025)
s: This SFC circular sets minimum custody rules that every SFC-licensed virtual-asset trading platform (VATP) operator and its associated entities must follow. It was issued after overseas custody-related cyber incidents and an SFC review that found some Hong Kong operators fell short. It covers who in senior management is responsible, and how cold wallets should be built and run. It also covers use of outside wallet providers, round-the-clock threat monitoring, and staff training, with sample 'good practice' examples. The rules apply immediately, and will also form the baseline for the coming licensed virtual-asset custodian regime.
w: For a bank, these are custody rules for trading platforms, not a direct bank duty. But compliance should use them as the checklist for vetting any custody partner. This includes offline key generation in a hardware security module (HSM), blocking blind signing, and round-the-clock monitoring, since they also preview the coming statutory custodian regime.
k: A platform operator should put someone in charge of custody matters -- a Responsible Officer or Manager-in-Charge -- for everything this circular covers.
Section I, para 1, p.3
Seeds and private keys should, where practical, be created offline and kept in a secure setting such as a certified hardware security module (HSM).
Section II, para 2, p.2
Cold wallets should avoid smart contracts on public blockchains, to cut down online attack routes.
Section II, para 5, p.3
Once a client withdrawal is signed, its destination address cannot be changed before it reaches the blockchain; cold-wallet transfers need whitelist controls.
Section III, paras 6 & 9, pp.3-4
Seeds and private keys should be created and kept safe on offline (air-gapped) cold-wallet devices.
Section III, para 7, p.4
Blind signing -- approving a transaction without seeing its details -- must be blocked; transaction details must be shown in readable form before anyone signs manually.
Section III, para 11 and footnote 6, p.4
Operators should set up a security operations centre or similar function that watches for threats around the clock, including holidays.
Section V, paras 18 & 24, pp.5-6
Before using an outside wallet provider, operators need to vet it, keep reviewing it, run independent code checks, and test its disaster-recovery plans.
Section IV, paras 12-17, pp.4-5
These rules apply right away and should feed into operators' annual outside compliance and technology review.
'Way forward', p.7
rg: Read Sections I-VI in full (pp.2-7). The 'Good Practice' boxes (pp.4, 6, 7) are illustrative and can be skimmed after grasping the numbered minimum requirements.

t: Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers
sl: HKMA · Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers (2025)
s: This is the HKMA's detailed operating rulebook for licensed stablecoin issuers under the Stablecoins Ordinance, expanding on the minimum criteria in Schedule 2. It sets detailed expectations across several areas. These are: reserve-asset backing, composition, segregation and disclosure; and issuance, redemption and distribution controls. They also cover financial resources, and a full risk-management stack covering credit, liquidity and market risk, technology risk (including detailed private-key and wallet controls), operational risk and reputation risk. They further cover incident management, business continuity and wind-down planning; corporate governance and fitness-and-propriety; and business conduct, including white papers and complaints handling. It distinguishes statutory 'must' requirements from supervisory 'should' expectations throughout. In several places, it also exempts a licensee that is itself an authorized institution (AI) from requirements that would otherwise apply to it.
w: For a bank, this is the operating-level checklist the HKMA will use to supervise any stablecoin issuer, including a bank that becomes one. It also sets the benchmark compliance should use to assess a third-party stablecoin issuer's reserve, custody and redemption practices, before the bank relies on, distributes, or accepts that coin.
k: A licensee must ensure the market value of reserve assets backing each coin type never falls below the par value of coins in circulation. This uses a prudent valuation approach with reconciliation. Even temporarily frozen or restricted coins must remain fully backed.

Eligible reserve assets are limited to a defined list. This is cash, bank deposits of no more than 3 months, and high-quality marketable debt securities of no more than 1 year residual maturity. It also includes overnight reverse repos collateralised by such securities, dedicated investment funds holding only such assets, or other HKMA-acceptable assets. Tokenised versions of these are allowed if the issuer can show they meet the same quality bar.
Reserve assets must generally be held in the same currency as the coin they back, with cross-currency mismatches allowed only with HKMA's prior written approval.

Reserve assets must be held under a trust arrangement backed by independent legal opinion, safe-kept by a qualified custodian, either a licensed bank or an HKMA-acceptable custodian. The issuer stays primarily accountable for their safekeeping, even if a custodian or investment manager is used.
No interest or interest-like return may be paid on coins based on holding period, par value or market value, though non-interest marketing incentives are allowed.

Issuers must submit daily internal statements on reserve composition and coin circulation to HKMA on request. They must report to HKMA and publish key reserve information weekly. An acceptable independent auditor must attest to full backing at least at period-end and one random business day, filed with HKMA within one month.

Valid redemption requests must be honoured within 1 business day, absent HKMA consent to a longer period, without unreasonable fees or unduly burdensome conditions. An independent legal opinion confirming holders' redemption and pro-rata claim rights must be filed with HKMA.

An issuer that engages third parties to distribute its coins must ensure they are 'permitted offerors' where they offer coins in Hong Kong. It must also due-diligence and risk-assess distributors and secondary-market liquidity providers.

Customer on-boarding and account operations must use effective identity verification and, generally, two-factor authentication. Transfers are restricted to pre-registered, customer-named bank accounts and wallet addresses. Controls must guard against VPN-based location spoofing, to prevent unlawful cross-border offering.

Private and seed key management must cover the full lifecycle: generation, distribution, storage, usage, backup, recovery, destruction. It needs elevated air-gapped, HSM-based controls and multi-party authorisation for 'Significant Seeds/Private Keys' tied to contract deployment, role or minter management, or large-scale minting or burning.
Smart contracts must be independently audited at least annually and whenever redeployed or upgraded, and each coin's token standard, ledger and full contract architecture must be documented.
A licensee needs three independent lines of defence (business units, risk/compliance, internal audit), each with adequate authority, resources and a direct Board or senior-management reporting line.
rg: Read section 2 (reserve assets) and section 3 (issuance, redemption, distribution) closely for counterparty due diligence purposes. Read 6.5 (technology and key management) closely if assessing custody quality. Sections 6.6-6.8, 7 and 8 can be skimmed for headings and modal verbs, unless the bank itself is applying for a licence.

t: Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Licensed Stablecoin Issuers)
sl: HKMA · Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (2025)
s: This is the HKMA's finalised, binding AML/CFT rulebook for entities licensed under the Stablecoins Ordinance to issue stablecoins, issued jointly under that Ordinance and the Anti-Money Laundering Ordinance (AMLO). It covers institutional risk assessment. It also covers AML governance, including a compliance officer, money laundering reporting officer, independent audit and training. It covers detailed customer due diligence, including on wallets and third-party distributors, and ongoing transaction and secondary-market monitoring. It also sets a full Travel Rule regime for stablecoin transfers between institutions and to or from unhosted wallets. It further covers sanctions and terrorist-financing screening, suspicious transaction reporting, and record-keeping, generally five years. Compliance is enforced through both the Stablecoins Ordinance and the AMLO, and failures can also jeopardise a licensee's ongoing eligibility under the Ordinance's minimum criteria.
w: For a bank, this is the binding, in-force AML/CFT rulebook for any bank-affiliated stablecoin issuer. Its Travel Rule, wallet-risk and screening standards are also the benchmark compliance should apply when assessing third-party stablecoin issuers, custodial wallet providers and distribution partners as counterparties.
k: A licensee must run an institutional money-laundering/terrorist-financing risk assessment covering customer, country, product/service and delivery-channel risk factors, approved by senior management and kept up to date.
paras 2.2-2.3
AML/CFT systems must include compliance management with a named Compliance Officer and Money Laundering Reporting Officer, an independent audit function, staff screening and ongoing training.

Customer due diligence is required before establishing a business relationship or before any occasional transaction (e.g. issuance/redemption) of HK$8,000 or more, and must identify beneficial owners holding more than 25% control.

Enhanced due diligence, including source of wealth/funds checks and senior management approval, is required for Hong Kong, non-Hong Kong and international-organisation politically exposed persons presenting higher risk.
para 4.23

For customer wallets, the issuer must confirm wallet ownership or control. For custodial wallets, it must run due diligence on the custodian. For higher-risk unhosted wallets, it must screen the wallet address, and may apply enhanced monitoring or transaction limits.

Ongoing monitoring must cover both individual customer transactions and, more broadly, stablecoins already in circulation, using risk-based technology (e.g. blockchain analytics) to trace sources/destinations and flag illicit or sanctioned wallet addresses.

A licensee must prove its screening and monitoring controls are effective against illicit use, particularly for peer-to-peer unhosted-wallet transfers. Otherwise, HKMA expects the identity of every stablecoin holder to be verified. This can be done by the licensee, a supervised institution, or a reliable third party.
para 5.11

The Travel Rule requires an ordering institution to obtain, and securely and immediately transmit, originator and recipient information for stablecoin transfers of HK$8,000 or more. A reduced data set applies below that threshold. A licensee must verify the identity of an originator for transfers at or above that threshold.
A licensee is barred from executing stablecoin transfers where the counterparty institution is a shell bank or a shell virtual-asset service provider.
para 6.39

For transfers to or from unhosted wallets of the licensee's own customers, the licensee must still collect originator and recipient details from that customer. Peer-to-peer transfers between unhosted wallets of non-customers are exempt from this specific requirement, though ongoing circulation monitoring still applies.
A licensee must screen customers and beneficial owners against terrorist/sanctions databases at both issuance and redemption, and screen all parties to a stablecoin transfer before executing it.
para 7.5

Suspicious transaction reports must be filed with the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit as soon as reasonably practicable, once knowledge or suspicion arises. 'Tipping off' a customer about a report, even one raised only internally, is a separate offence.
paras 8.1-8.2
rg: For a compliance head, focus on Chapter 4 (CDD, especially wallet risk paras 4.33-4.40), Chapter 6 (stablecoin transfers/Travel Rule) and Chapters 7-9 (sanctions, STR, record-keeping). Chapter 3's generic governance content overlaps with standard AML guidelines and can be skimmed.

t: LCQ10: Promoting virtual asset development
sl: FSTB · LCQ10: Promoting virtual asset development (2025)
s: A written Legislative Council reply reviews progress across virtual-asset licensing, tokenisation and AML cooperation, in response to questions about licensing speed and international competition. It confirms 11 VATPs are licensed, with 9 more applications pending, and describes the SFC's swift licensing process, introduced June 2024 and expanded January 2025. It notes SFC circulars from November 2023 on tokenised securities, and the 2024 authorisation of a retail tokenised gold product. It also notes the first-in-Asia-Pacific authorisation of three retail tokenised money market funds in Q1 2025. These had grown to over HK$700 million in assets under management by end-March 2025. It also summarises Hong Kong's FATF standing and international AML cooperation channels.
w: For a bank, this confirms two SFC circulars from November 2023 that already govern intermediaries handling tokenised securities and tokenised SFC-authorised products. This is directly relevant if the bank distributes or advises on tokenised funds or securities today.
k: As of early July 2025, the SFC had licensed 11 digital-asset trading platforms and was processing nine further applications.
reply (1), para 2

The SFC issued a 'Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities' and a 'Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products' in November 2023. These guide intermediaries on tokenisation risks.
reply (2), para 2
In 2024 the SFC authorised Hong Kong's first retail tokenised investment product, a gold token offering fractional ownership of physical gold.
reply (2), para 3
In Q1 2025 the SFC authorised three retail tokenised money market funds, the first in the Asia-Pacific region, which held over HK$700 million in assets under management by end-March 2025.
reply (2), para 3
Hong Kong's AML/CFT regime is recognised by FATF as overall compliant and effective, and Hong Kong participates in FATF's Virtual Assets Contact Group.
reply (3), para 2

t: LCQ9: Promoting the establishment of family offices in Hong Kong
sl: Government · LCQ9: Promoting the establishment of family offices in Hong… (2025)
s: This is the written answer from Hong Kong's Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury to a Legislative Council (LegCo) question on 30 July 2025. It describes the family office tax concession and plans to widen it. Family-owned investment holding vehicles (FIHVs) run by a single family office can get a profits tax exemption on qualifying transactions. They must meet a HK$240 million asset threshold and a substantial activities requirement. The reply restates the 2025-26 Budget proposal to add emission derivatives, insurance-linked securities, private credit and digital assets to qualifying transactions. It says the Government aimed to put legislation to LegCo in 2026, applying from 2025/26 if approved. It also cites about 2,700 single family offices at end-2023 and HK$1,551 billion of private banking assets linked to family offices and private trusts at end-2024.
w: It is an official statement that the Government proposed adding digital assets to the qualifying transactions for family-office tax relief. The proposal was not law at the time. A bill on the family-office regime was gazetted in June 2026 (see fca785b80cff).
k: FIHVs managed by single family offices that meet a HK$240 million asset threshold and substance test can get profits tax exemption on qualifying transactions, effective from 2022/23.
Reply, part (1)
The Government proposed in the 2025-26 Budget to add digital assets, among other items, to the qualifying transactions for single family offices.
Reply, part (4)
Industry consultation was complete, and the Government aimed to put legislation to LegCo in 2026, taking effect from 2025/26 if approved.
Reply, part (4)
Multi-family offices are not covered by the FIHV regime, but vehicles meeting the fund definition with transactions arranged by an SFC-licensed corporation can use the unified funds exemption.
Reply, part (4)

An InvestHK-commissioned consultant counted about 2,700 single family offices at end-2023; private banking and wealth assets of family office and private trust clients were HK$1,551 billion at end-2024.
Reply, introduction
rg: Read the introduction and parts (1) and (4) of the reply; parts (2)-(3) are InvestHK statistics.

t: Implementation of regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers
sl: HKMA · Implementation of regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers (2025)
s: The Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers took effect on 1 August 2025. Alongside it, this HKMA press release announces, HKMA published four documents. These are the finalised Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers and its consultation conclusions, the finalised AML/CFT Guideline for Licensed Stablecoin Issuers and its consultation conclusions, plus two Explanatory Notes. These notes cover licensing and application procedures, and transitional arrangements for pre-existing issuers. The attached Supervisory Guideline sets detailed ongoing requirements on reserve assets, issuance, redemption and distribution, financial resources, risk management -- including extensive technology and private-key controls -- corporate governance and business conduct. The AML/CFT Guideline sets customer due diligence, wallet risk management, the HK$8,000 Travel Rule threshold, sanctions screening, suspicious transaction reporting (STR) and five-year record-keeping requirements. The Explanatory Notes define scope terms: stablecoin, regulated stablecoin activity, and permitted offeror. They also cover the application process and minimum criteria. They set the three-month, six-month and closing-down transitional timeline for issuers operating before 1 August 2025. As of the press release date, no licence had yet been issued.
w: For a bank, this brings the Stablecoins Ordinance regime into effect and sets the application timetable. It is directly relevant if the bank is a market participant handling, or considering issuing, licensed stablecoins. It also sets the register the bank should check when doing counterparty due diligence on any stablecoin issuer.
k: The regulatory regime under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) took effect on 1 August 2025. The finalised Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers and the AML/CFT Guideline were both gazetted the same day.
para 1 (main press release)
Parties interested in applying for a licence were encouraged to contact HKMA by 31 August 2025. Those wanting to be considered early were asked to submit applications by 30 September 2025.
paras 5-6
It is an offence under the SO to falsely claim to be a licensee or an applicant. As of the press release date, no licence had been issued.
paras 7-8

A licensee must keep the reserve assets' market value at or above the par value of all outstanding specified stablecoins in circulation, at every point in time. This includes any coins that are frozen or blacklisted. Holding some excess collateral as a cushion is expected.
Supervisory Guideline paras 2.2.1-2.2.3

Reserve assets are restricted to a defined 'eligible assets' list: cash, short-term bank deposits, qualifying marketable debt securities, overnight reverse repos, dedicated investment funds, or HKMA-acceptable equivalents. Tokenised representations of eligible assets can qualify, if the licensee demonstrates no added technology or operational risk.
Supervisory Guideline para 2.3.1-2.3.2

Reserve assets must be held via effective trust arrangements, either an independent trustee or a declaration of trust. They must be segregated from the licensee's own assets, and protected from other creditors, with an independent legal opinion on effectiveness submitted to HKMA.
Supervisory Guideline paras 2.5.1-2.5.2

Valid redemption requests must be honoured, generally within one business day, without unreasonable fees or unduly burdensome conditions. Any delay beyond one business day requires the Monetary Authority's prior written consent.
Supervisory Guideline paras 3.3.3, 6.8.21

A licensee must always hold at least HK$25 million in paid-up share capital, or an HKMA-approved equivalent amount of financial resources. This must be reserved solely for its stablecoin business, and is off-limits for transactions with related parties.
Supervisory Guideline para 5.1.1; Explanatory Note on Licensing para 3.3.2

Significant Seeds/Private Keys are those tied to smart-contract deployment or upgrades, role management, or large-scale minting/burning. For these, the licensee must create, keep and use them inside an air-gapped setup, physically in Hong Kong or another HKMA-acceptable location, never on a system connected to the internet. A cloud-based HSM will not usually meet this bar.
Supervisory Guideline para 6.5.7(iv), (vii); Consultation Conclusions para 2.6.3

The HKMA generally wants at least a third of the Board to be independent non-executive directors (INEDs). This expectation is waived where the licensee is itself a bank, an authorized institution, which instead follows the Banking Ordinance.
Supervisory Guideline para 7.1.3

For stablecoin transfers under the Travel Rule, the HK$8,000 threshold determines the scope of required originator and recipient data, and identity verification. Transfers to or from unhosted wallets of non-customer holders are exempt from the transfer-specific data requirements, but still subject to ongoing circulation monitoring.
AML/CFT Guideline paras 6.5-6.6, 6.41-6.42

Unless a licensee can demonstrate to the HKMA's satisfaction that risk-mitigating measures are effective, the identity of every individual stablecoin holder must be verified, including non-customers. This can be done by the licensee, a supervised financial institution (FI) or virtual asset service provider (VASP), or a reliable third party. This is a notably stricter default than typical VA intermediary AML regimes.
AML/CFT Guideline para 5.11
rg: Read the main press release in full, it is short, then the Supervisory Guideline sections 1-5 (reserve assets, issuance/redemption, financial resources) and 6.5 (technology/key management) closely. AML/CFT Guideline chapters 4-6 (CDD, wallets, Travel Rule) and 9 (record-keeping) are the operational core. The two Consultation Conclusions documents mainly repeat the finalised Guidelines as annexes -- skim only the Q&A sections (paras 2.x) for the HKMA's interpretive clarifications, not the annexes.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Eddie Yue on The Steadfast and Sustainable Development of Stablecoins
sl: HKMA · Eddie Yue on The Steadfast and Sustainable Development of… (2025)
s: HKMA's Chief Executive pushes back on what he calls overhyped and speculative market enthusiasm for stablecoins. He notes many prospective applicants he has met lack concrete use cases or technical capability, and reiterates that only a handful of licences will be issued. He confirms the HKMA consulted the market on both the supervision and AML/CFT implementation guidelines. It was refining them for publication by end of July 2025, expecting the final rules to include tighter AML requirements than the consultation drafts. He also announces that an Explanatory Note on the licence application process would follow the next week.
w: For a bank, this signals that the final AML/CFT and supervision guidelines would be stricter on AML than the May 2025 consultation drafts. It also confirms the exact date from which offering an unlicensed stablecoin to Hong Kong retail investors becomes illegal -- both directly relevant to any group entity distributing or dealing in stablecoins.
k: Many of the dozens of institutions that approached HKMA about stablecoin issuance had only conceptual proposals lacking concrete use cases, implementation plans or risk-management competence.
para 2
HKMA reiterates that only a handful of stablecoin issuer licences would be granted, meaning most applicants will be disappointed.
para 3

The Stablecoins Ordinance commencement on 1 August 2025 would make it illegal to offer any unlicensed fiat-referenced stablecoin to Hong Kong retail investors. It would also be illegal to actively market such an unlicensed coin to the Hong Kong public.
para 3

HKMA had consulted the market on both the supervision guideline and the AML/CFT guideline, following passage of the Stablecoins Bill. It was refining them for publication by end of July 2025, expecting the AML requirements in the final version to be stricter than in the consultation draft.
para 4 (Guarding Against Financial Risks section)
An Explanatory Note on Licensing of Stablecoin Issuers, covering how HKMA would accept and process applications, was announced for release the following week.
final paragraph
