t: Licensing Handbook
sl: SFC · Licensing Handbook (2025)
s: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) Licensing Handbook is a practical guide to licensing under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). It explains who needs a licence or registration, what approval criteria apply and what firms must do once approved. It has a chapter for registered institutions (RIs), meaning banks registered with the SFC. For a bank, it covers executive officer (EO) rules and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) register of bank staff. It also covers the fitness of shareholders and managers, and post-registration filings and fees. Other parts cover continuous professional training (CPT) and notice duties, including for virtual asset services. The virtual asset paragraphs describe the 2019 framework and do not mention the later platform licensing regime.
w: This is the one-stop guide to the bank's SFC registration mechanics: EO numbers, HKMA consent, register entries, notifications and training. It is the practical checklist for adding a digital-asset regulated activity or staffing a new desk.
k: An RI is an authorized institution (a bank, restricted licence bank or deposit-taking company) registered under SFO s.119 for any regulated activity except Types 3 and 8.
para 2.4.1
A bank should appoint at least two EOs to supervise each regulated activity directly, with at least one available at all times.
EOs need HKMA consent under the Banking Ordinance, and the HKMA must refuse unless it is satisfied the person is fit and proper and has enough authority.
para 6.1.4

The SFC expects EOs to meet the responsible officer competence standard. Other bank staff doing regulated work are named on the HKMA register instead of being licensed by the SFC. They are expected to meet the licensed-representative standard, and their fitness is a statutory condition of registration.
The bank's substantial shareholders, directors, chief executive, managers and EOs must all be fit and proper.
para 6.1.8
The HKMA may ask a new or complex registration applicant for an Independent Assurance Report from an external firm it accepts.
para 6.2.3
Under the HKMA's management accountability circular and FAQs, a bank applying for registration should give the HKMA and SFC details of key managers for regulated business and an organisation chart.
para 6.2.6 and fn 26
RIs should send updates on that management information and chart to both regulators within 14 days of a change.
para 9.15.1
ROs and EOs must take two extra CPT hours each calendar year on regulatory compliance.
para 9.13.4
Firms and banks should keep CPT records for at least three years for SFC or HKMA inspection.
para 9.13.9
Intermediaries must notify the SFC before offering trading or asset management involving virtual assets, and are advised to discuss it with the SFC beforehand.
para 9.14.1
Adding a regulated activity to a bank's registration costs HK$23,500 per activity.
para 8.4.1 (table)
rg: For a bank, read Chapter 6 (pp.38-39), paras 8.4 and 9.13-9.15, and the virtual asset paragraphs 1.4.3-1.4.7. Chapters on licensed corporations and representatives are background.

t: Gazettal of banking amendment rules to implement Basel cryptoassets standard
sl: HKMA · Gazettal of banking amendment rules to implement Basel cryptoassets… (2025)
s: The government gazetted three sets of amendment rules -- to the Banking (Capital) Rules, Banking (Disclosure) Rules, and Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules -- implementing the Basel Committee's prudential standard on banks' cryptoasset exposures. The rules take effect 1 January 2026, in line with the Basel Committee's global timetable, and also make other alignment amendments informed by industry feedback. They were tabled at the Legislative Council (LegCo) on 16 July 2025.
w: For a bank, this is a direct, binding prudential obligation as an authorised institution. Capital, disclosure and exposure-limit rules for cryptoasset exposures took effect 1 January 2026 and have applied since then. Risk and finance teams should confirm their calculations and disclosures are already compliant.
k: Three amendment rules sets implement Basel Committee capital, disclosure and exposure-limit standards for banks' cryptoasset exposures.
para 1, p.1
The amendment rules take effect on January 1, 2026, matching the Basel Committee's implementation timeline.
para 2 and closing para, p.1
rg: Read this in full; it is a short notice, but confirms a hard compliance deadline for the bank's prudential treatment of cryptoasset exposures.

t: Gazettal of rules: cryptoassets standard and other updates
sl: HKMA · Gazettal of rules: cryptoassets standard and other updates (2025)
s: This HKMA circular tells all authorized institutions that three rules were gazetted on 11 July 2025. These are the Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2025, the Banking (Disclosure) (Amendment) Rules 2025, and the Banking (Exposure Limits) (Amendment) Rules 2025. These rules put in place the Basel Committee's prudential standard for cryptoasset exposures, plus related changes to disclosure and exposure limits, along with some other minor alignment changes. The Legislative Council (LegCo) was due to receive these rules on 16 July 2025 for negative vetting. Assuming that stage cleared, the rules were expected to start applying on 1 January 2026, in step with the Basel Committee's timeline.
w: For a bank, this marked the formal legal milestone when the crypto capital, disclosure, and exposure-limit rules moved from consultation to gazetted subsidiary legislation. This had a 1 January 2026 start date that has since arrived and passed. The rules are now in force, and banks should already be running the associated reporting and disclosure processes.
k: Three amendment rules were gazetted on 11 July 2025: the Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2025, the Banking (Disclosure) (Amendment) Rules 2025, and the Banking (Exposure Limits) (Amendment) Rules 2025.
bullet list, p.1
The amendments mainly bring in the Basel Committee's capital standard for cryptoasset exposures, along with its related disclosure and exposure-limit requirements.
para 2, p.1
The rules were scheduled for tabling before LegCo on 16 July 2025, to start the negative-vetting process.
para 3, p.1
If that vetting process went through, the rules were expected to take effect on 1 January 2026, matching the Basel Committee's timeline.
para 3, p.1
rg: This is a short, one-page letter; read it in full.

t: Opening remarks by Permanent Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury (Financial Services) at Deloitte's Digital Asset Forum (English only) (with photos)
sl: FSTB · Opening remarks by Permanent Secretary for Financial Services and… (2025)
s: A senior FSTB official's remarks recap the digital-asset policy timeline. This covers the 2022 first policy statement, the June 2023 VATP regime, the Stablecoins Ordinance (effective 1 August 2025), and the LEAP framework from Policy Statement 2.0. They preview details on tokenised bonds and the dealing/custodian consultation. The speech restates already-known facts and figures, with no new binding content.
w: For a bank, this is largely a recap speech. The only new detail is confirmation the SFC has stood up an industry consultative panel on digital-asset regulatory issues, which compliance could seek to engage with.
k: The second batch of tokenised government green bonds was issued in 2024 across four currencies, worth close to HK$6 billion in total. The government describes it as the first-ever green bond issued natively in digital form across more than one currency.
para on RWA tokenisation
The SFC has established a consultative panel on market and regulatory issues, which had held its second meeting the day before this speech.
para on people/partnership section
rg: Skim this. Most content restates facts already in Policy Statement 2.0 and the Budget speech.

t: SFC convenes second Digital Asset Consultative Panel meeting
sl: SFC · SFC convenes second Digital Asset Consultative Panel meeting (2025)
s: This SFC press release reports on the SFC's second consultative-panel meeting with SFC-licensed VA trading platforms. It covers market and regulatory developments under the ASPIRe roadmap's Access and Products pillars, including the VA dealing and custodian licensing proposals and market accessibility and product offerings. It also notes the forum was renamed from 'Virtual Asset Consultative Panel' to 'Digital Asset Consultative Panel', to align with the terminology of Policy Statement 2.0.
w: For a bank, this is a minor engagement-channel update. It is useful mainly to know the Digital Asset Consultative Panel (DACP), a renamed body, exists as an SFC-VATP forum, and that it discussed the dealer/custodian licensing proposals. It contains no new substantive requirements.
k: The SFC held its second engagement session with the Digital Asset Consultative Panel (DACP), made up of SFC-licensed VA trading platforms.
para 1, p.1
The panel was renamed from 'Virtual Asset Consultative Panel' to 'Digital Asset Consultative Panel' to align with terminology used in the Government's Policy Statement 2.0 (issued 26 June 2025).
Note 1
Topics covered included ASPIRe roadmap Pillars A (Access) and P (Products), including the VA dealing and custodian licensing proposals and market accessibility/product offerings.
para 2
The DACP is described as part of the initiative under Pillar Re (Relationships) of the ASPIRe roadmap.
para 4
rg: This is very short; read it in full (1-2 minutes). It is chiefly useful for the naming-history flag: VACP became DACP.

t: Invest Hong Kong strengthens Web3 and fintech ties between Hong Kong and Japan (with photos)
sl: Government · Invest Hong Kong strengthens Web3 and fintech ties between… (2025)
s: InvestHK describes an outbound delegation of 16 Hong Kong organisations to Japan, to build Web3 and fintech business ties. It references the recently issued Policy Statement 2.0 and its LEAP framework as context. It also highlights a few company case studies, including a family office launching a real-estate tokenisation project in Japan. It contains no new regulatory content.
w: For a bank, this is promotional trade-mission news with no regulatory bearing. It is background only.
k: An InvestHK-led delegation of 16 Hong Kong organisations visited Japan to build Web3 and fintech business ties, with one participating family office launching a real-estate tokenisation initiative there.
para 2 and 7, p.1
rg: Skim only. There is no substantive regulatory content.

t: LCQ5: Promoting development of stablecoins
sl: FSTB · LCQ5: Promoting development of stablecoins (2025)
s: In a written Legislative Council reply, the Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury describes government plans to grow stablecoin use cases, attract global issuers, and consider offshore renminbi stablecoins. It confirms the HKMA's stablecoin issuer sandbox, opened early 2024, is not a prerequisite for licensing. Applicants with cross-border use cases must show a comprehensive compliance plan and confirm their business partners hold necessary regulatory approvals in relevant jurisdictions. It also notes the licensing regime allows pegs to different fiat currencies, not only the Hong Kong dollar.
w: For a bank, this confirms it must expect stablecoin-issuer counterparties, and their partners, to demonstrate cross-border regulatory compliance as part of licensing. This is a useful due-diligence benchmark when the bank assesses potential stablecoin partners.
k: Participation in the HKMA's stablecoin issuer sandbox is not a prerequisite for a future licence application.
reply to Q1, para on sandbox
Stablecoin issuer applicants must show adequate setup across reserve-asset management, price-stabilisation, redemption policy, technology security, risk management and AML capability.
reply to Q1, closing para

For cross-border use cases, applicants must also show a compliance plan and demonstrate financial strength. They must also confirm their business partners hold necessary approvals and will comply with regulations in Hong Kong and other relevant jurisdictions.
reply to Q1, closing para
The licensing regime allows an issuer to peg its stablecoin to different fiat currencies, not just the Hong Kong dollar.
reply to Q2, para 2
rg: Read the reply to question 1 in full for licensing expectations. Question 3, on offshore RMB stablecoins, is exploratory and can be skimmed.

t: Fintech Adoption: Progress and Future Directions
sl: HKMA · Fintech Adoption: Progress and Future Directions (2025)
s: This HKMA report presents the results of a January 2025 Tech Maturity Stock-take, covering 56 submissions from 58 authorized institutions, benchmarked against a 2022 baseline. It measures adoption of Regtech, Wealthtech, Greentech, Insurtech, artificial intelligence and distributed ledger technology (DLT). It finds implementation cost, novel-technology risk and integration are the top adoption challenges. It sets out the HKMA's next-phase promotion plan, built around AI, DLT and high-performance computing, underpinned by data excellence and cyber resilience. DLT-specific detail is limited to adoption statistics and general commentary; this is not a rulebook.
w: For a bank, this gives sector-wide DLT adoption benchmarks and the HKMA's stated forward priorities -- risk management and systems integration for tokenisation. It is useful for internal business cases, but is not itself a source of obligations.
k: DLT adoption among surveyed authorized institutions rose from 30% in 2022 to 45% in 2025, with many institutions moving from exploratory pilots to operational use.
One financial institution highlighted in the report uses DLT to provide tokenisation, issuance, distribution and custody services across the digital asset lifecycle.

HKMA's next-phase Fintech promotion names DLT as one of three priority technology enablers, along with AI and high-performance computing. It focuses on risk management, resilient operations and systems integration, as tokenisation initiatives are explored.
Top adoption challenges cited by authorized institutions include implementation cost (75%), risk of novel technology (73%) and integration with existing systems (71%).
rg: Skim Key Observations 1-2 (pp.10-14) for DLT/AI adoption figures, and the Way Forward section (pp.19-22) for the HKMA's stated priorities. Detailed Regtech/Wealthtech figures are not digital-asset relevant.

t: Explanatory Note on Licensing of Stablecoin Issuers
sl: HKMA · Explanatory Note on Licensing of Stablecoin Issuers (2025)
s: This note explains how the HKMA will license stablecoin issuers under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656). It defines a 'stablecoin', a 'specified stablecoin' (currently only fiat-referenced coins), and when issuing or offering one counts as a regulated activity needing a licence. It walks through the minimum licensing criteria in Schedule 2. These cover corporate status, capital, reserve-asset segregation and backing, and redemption rights. They also cover fitness of directors and managers, risk management, AML/CFT, disclosure via a white paper, complaint handling, a ban on paying interest, and recovery or wind-down planning. It also sets out the application process, the HKMA's supervisory powers over a troubled licensee, and the grounds and process for licence revocation or suspension.
w: For a bank, this is the master rulebook for anyone it might deal with as a stablecoin issuer. This also applies to the bank itself, if it or an affiliate ever considers issuing a fiat-referenced stablecoin under its own authorized-institution (AI) status. It sets the baseline the bank's due diligence on any stablecoin counterparty should be checked against, especially reserve segregation, redemption rights, and permitted-offeror status.
k: A stablecoin is a cryptographically secured digital value token. It acts as a medium of exchange or store of value, is transferable electronically, runs on a distributed ledger, and claims to hold a stable value against one or more assets. Central bank money, securities, SVF float and bank deposits are carved out.
Only 'specified stablecoins' - currently those referencing one or more official currencies (fiat-referenced stablecoins) - fall inside the licensing perimeter for now.

Issuing a specified stablecoin in Hong Kong, or issuing one anywhere that is pegged even partly to the Hong Kong dollar, is a regulated activity requiring a licence. Doing so without one, or holding oneself out as doing so, is an offence.

A licensee may only let a defined list of 'permitted offerors' distribute its coins. These are itself, an authorized institution, an SVF licensee, an SFC-licensed VA trading platform, or an SFC Type 1 licensed corporation.
An applicant must be either a Hong Kong-incorporated company or an authorized institution; other foreign entities must set up a local subsidiary to apply.
Non-bank applicants need at least HKD25 million in paid-up capital or MA-approved equivalent financial resources, which cannot be used for dealings with related parties.

Reserve assets backing each type of coin must be segregated, and held under a trust arrangement backed by independent legal opinion. Their value must never fall below the circulating coins' par value, with a buffer for risk. They must be audited regularly by an independent auditor, and disclosed to the public.
Holders have a right to redeem at par, normally processed within one business day, and licensees must publicly disclose fees, conditions, mechanics and timing of redemption.

Chief executives, directors, the stablecoin manager and controllers must be fit and proper, with relevant knowledge and experience. The HKMA looks for at least a third of the Board to be independent non-executive directors. It generally wants to give consent before they take up post. This is not required for an authorized institution's own appointees.

Licensees must run a full risk management programme covering governance, credit/liquidity/market risk, technology risk, operational risk, reputation risk, and incident/business continuity/exit planning.
Licensees must publish a white paper covering the issuer, the coin, reserve management, issuance/redemption mechanics, technology and risks, before offering coins to the public.
Stablecoins must not carry any interest, return or yield tied to holding period, par value or market value.
rg: Read Chapter 2 (definitions and scope) and Chapter 3 (minimum criteria, especially reserve assets 3.4 and redemption 3.5) closely. Chapters 4-7 (process, powers, revocation) can be skimmed except section headings. Annex B's document checklist only matters if the bank itself applies.

t: Appointments to Task Force on Promoting Web3 Development
sl: Government · Appointments to Task Force on Promoting Web3 Development (2025)
s: The government named 20 people, new and returning non-official members, to the Task Force on Promoting Web3 Development. This takes effect 1 July 2025, for a two-year term. The Financial Secretary has chaired the Task Force since it was set up in 2023, and it gives advice on Web3 development. It includes non-official industry members plus regulator and government officials. The notice lists everyone currently on it.
w: For a bank, this is only a personnel-appointments notice, with no regulatory content. It is useful just to know who currently advises the government on Web3 policy.
k: The government named 20 people, as new and returning non-official members, to the Task Force on Promoting Web3 Development, effective 1 July 2025, for a two-year term.
para 1, p.1
rg: Skim the membership list only if tracking who advises the government. There is no substantive content otherwise.

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism (1) FATF Statement on High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action (2) FATF Statement on Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring (3) Outcomes from the Joint FATF-MONEYVAL Plenary, 12-13 June 2025
sl: SFC · licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities -… (2025)
s: This is a routine SFC circular passing on the Joint FATF-MONEYVAL Plenary's June 2025 statements. Countermeasures calls against North Korea (DPRK) and Iran continue. Myanmar remains under enhanced due diligence, with countermeasures to be considered if there is no progress by October 2025 -- five years of limited progress have been noted. The Increased Monitoring list added Bolivia and the British Virgin Islands, and removed Croatia, Mali and Tanzania. The circular also relays several Plenary outcomes. FATF approved changes to Recommendation 16 on payment transparency, published 18 June 2025. It updated Recommendation 1 guidance on financial inclusion, published 23 June 2025. It issued a report on complex proliferation-financing and sanctions-evasion schemes, published 20 June 2025. A global terrorist-financing risk report is forthcoming. And FATF published its 6th Targeted Update Report on VA/VASP implementation, plus Best Practices on Travel Rule Supervision, both on 26 June 2025.
w: For a bank, this is a routine FATF jurisdiction-list update that supersedes the March 2025 circular. It points to the FATF's newly published 6th Targeted Update Report on VA/VASP implementation and Travel Rule Best Practices -- useful primary sources for benchmarking the bank's own travel-rule compliance.
k: FATF countermeasures calls against DPRK and Iran continue (carried forward, Iran's countermeasures suspension remains fully lifted).
Myanmar has shown limited progress over the past five years; FATF will consider countermeasures if no further progress by October 2025.
p.2, para (ii)
Increased Monitoring list updated: Bolivia and the Virgin Islands (UK) added; Croatia, Mali and the United Republic of Tanzania removed.
p.2, section (2)
FATF signed off on revisions to Recommendation 16 and its Interpretive Note, aimed at improving payment-transparency and sanctions detection, with the revised text released 18 June 2025.
p.3, para (a)
FATF published its 6th Targeted Update Report on VA/VASP standards implementation, and Best Practices on Travel Rule Supervision, both on 26 June 2025.
p.3, para (e)
rg: Skim the jurisdiction-list changes (section 2). Note the two virtual-asset (VA) specific FATF publications in section 3(e) as further-reading sources.

t: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Dealing in Virtual Assets
sl: FSTB/SFC · Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Dealing in… (2025)
s: The Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) and the SFC jointly asked for public comment on a revised plan to license providers who deal in virtual assets (VAs). Comments were due 29 August 2025. This replaces the narrower 2024 proposal that only covered VA over-the-counter (OTC) trading. Feedback on the earlier plan showed the industry is far wider than physical coin shops. It includes ATMs, broker-dealers, digital-only platforms, payment firms and card networks, serving both retail and institutional clients. It also flagged a need for custody rules the first proposal lacked. Under the new plan, anyone dealing in VAs as a business -- buying, selling, subscribing, underwriting, or profiting from VA price swings -- would need SFC licensing or registration. This covers everything from simple conversions to complex brokerage, block trading, advice and asset management, whether done in person or online. Banks and stored value facility (SVF) operators would register with the SFC after consulting the HKMA, echoing how banks' securities business is already split between the two regulators. HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers dealing only in their own coin issuance and redemption would be exempt. There is no proposed transition period for existing providers -- the rules would apply fully from day one. So the paper urges firms already in the business to contact the SFC or HKMA early, to avoid having to stop trading.
w: For a bank, this proposal names banks directly. A bank offering VA dealing services would have to register with the SFC, while the HKMA acts as its day-to-day supervisor, mirroring how bank securities business already works. Compliance should keep watching how this consultation turns into law.
k: Anyone dealing in VAs as a business -- buying, selling, subscribing, underwriting, or profiting from price movements -- would need an SFC licence or registration. Banks and SVFs would register with the SFC after consulting the HKMA, which would supervise them day-to-day.
Stablecoin issuers already licensed by the HKMA would not need a separate VA dealing licence for issuing or redeeming their own coins in the primary market.
para 1.10, p.8

The plan covers both simple conversions between VAs or between VA and cash, and more complex work such as brokerage, block trades, advice and asset management, done through shops or platforms. Pure peer-to-peer trades with no middleman are excluded.

A VA dealer that lets a third party hold client VAs on its behalf must use a VA custodian licensed or registered in Hong Kong. This is the topic of a separate, related consultation launched the same day.
para 2.13, p.5

Applicants other than banks must be incorporated or registered in Hong Kong, and keep a permanent local office suitable for record-keeping. They must also name at least two officers -- SFC-approved for most firms, HKMA-approved for banks -- who are personally responsible for compliance.

Proposed capital rules for non-bank applicants: at least $5 million in paid-up share capital. Up to $3 million in required liquid capital, depending on the business model, plus spare liquid capital equal to at least a year's running costs.

Licences would run indefinitely until cancelled, with no transition period for firms already operating. The rules would bind everyone once in force, so existing providers are urged to reach out to the SFC or HKMA early, rather than risk having to shut down.
Firms already vetted and operating with SFC or HKMA approval -- such as existing licensed corporations, registered institutions, or licensed trading platforms -- would get a faster approval track.
Fees would mirror the existing Type 1 securities-dealing fees. Currently $4,740 to apply and renew for a licensed corporation, and $23,500 to apply plus $35,000 a year for a registered institution.

Proposed penalties include up to seven years in prison and civil fines of up to $10,000,000. This is along with licence suspension or cancellation, reprimands and orders to fix problems -- similar to the existing trading-platform regime.
A tribunal modelled on the existing money-laundering review tribunal is proposed to hear appeals against SFC or HKMA decisions.
By end-June 2025, the SFC had licensed 11 trading platforms, with 10 more applications pending, including four operators treated as already licensed during the transition.
para 1.4, p.4
rg: Read Chapter 1 (background and scope, pp.1-9) and Chapter 2 (regulatory requirements, pp.10-26) in full. Skip the FATF/DNFBP footnote boilerplate. The 12 consultation questions, listed at the end, map directly to each subsection and work as a structured checklist.

t: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Custodian Services
sl: FSTB · Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset… (2025)
s: This paper proposes a new SFC licensing regime for virtual-asset custodian services. It defines custody as safekeeping virtual assets, or the private keys that control them, on a client's behalf. Banks, stored value facilities and subsidiaries of locally incorporated banks providing such services must register with the SFC, with the HKMA supervising banks and SVFs. It proposes incidental exemptions for entities whose safekeeping is merely part of another licensed activity, and a full exemption for a stablecoin issuer custodying only the stablecoins it issues. Financial-resource floors, external-assessment requirements, and sanctions mirroring the VATP regime are also proposed. Licensed or registered entities, including fund managers, would be required to use only SFC-licensed or SFC-registered custodians in Hong Kong to safekeep client assets.
w: For a bank, this is the core reference for its own future custody obligations, if it safekeeps client digital assets or private keys. It also sets the standard the bank must use to vet any external custodian it relies on, since regulated entities will be required to use only SFC-licensed or -registered custodians.
k: Providing virtual-asset custodian services as a business - safekeeping VAs, or instruments such as private keys enabling their transfer - requires an SFC licence or registration.
SFC is proposed as licensing authority and standard-setter for VA custodians; HKMA would oversee banks and SVFs directly as day-to-day supervisor of their custodian business.
para 2.12(a), p.9

Regulated entities holding client VAs only incidentally to another licensed activity, and not safekeeping private keys, would be exempt. A stablecoin issuer custodying only its own issued stablecoins is fully exempt, even if it holds the private keys.
Licensed or registered entities, including fund managers, would be required to use only SFC-licensed or -registered VA custodians in Hong Kong to safekeep client assets.
Proposed minimum financial resources: HK$10 million paid-up share capital and up to HK$3 million liquid capital, benchmarked against the SFO Type 13 depositary-licence requirements.
Custodians safekeeping private keys must engage an external assessor, with the SFC as a party to that engagement, before being licensed - mirroring the swift VATP licensing process.
No deeming/grace arrangement is proposed; the regime becomes fully effective from the commencement date of the statutory provisions.
Unlicensed provision or active marketing of custodian services carries a fine of HK$5 million and up to seven years' imprisonment on indictment.
rg: Read Chapter 2 (pages 6-26) in full, especially the definition, exemptions and 'other regulatory requirements' sections. Chapter 1 background can be skimmed.

t: FSTB and SFC launch consultation on legislative proposals for regulating digital asset dealing and custodian services
sl: FSTB · FSTB and SFC launch consultation on legislative proposals for… (2025)
s: FSTB and SFC opened a two-month joint public consultation, to 29 August 2025, on revised plans for two new licensing regimes: digital-asset dealing services and digital-asset custodian services. Both would require a licence or registration with the SFC as standard-setter, with the HKMA supervising banks and stored-value-facility (SVF) licensees offering the services. Dealing covers both simple conversions and complex activities like brokerage and block trading. Custody covers safekeeping of assets, or of private keys that enable their transfer. No deeming (automatic grace-licence) arrangement is proposed, meaning the regimes take full effect from their commencement date. Full detail is in the two attached consultation papers.
w: For a bank, this is the direct forerunner to its own future licensing obligations for any dealing or custody activity in digital assets. It also shapes due-diligence expectations for VATP and custodian counterparties. The full substance is in the two linked consultation papers.
k: Consultation on the two licensing regimes runs from June 27 to August 29, 2025.
para 1, p.1
For both regimes, the SFC will set standards and licence/register providers, while banks and stored-value-facility registrants would be supervised day-to-day by the HKMA.
para 4, p.1
Dealing licensing would cover both simple conversions and complex activities such as brokerage, block trading, and advisory or asset-management activity.
para 6, p.1
Custody is proposed to be defined as safekeeping digital assets, or instruments (including private keys) that enable their transfer, on behalf of clients.
para 8, p.1
Both regimes are proposed to take full effect on commencement, with no deeming/grace arrangement for existing providers.
para 7 and 9, p.1
rg: Read this press release for the summary, then the two consultation papers (f673ef6dcb63 dealing, 30b60438f017 custody) for the detail.

t: FSTB and SFC consult on proposed regimes to regulate virtual asset dealers and custodians
sl: FSTB/SFC · FSTB and SFC consult on proposed regimes to regulate… (2025)
s: This SFC press release announces that the FSTB and SFC jointly launched a public consultation. It introduces licensing regimes for virtual asset (VA) dealing and VA custodian service providers, one day after the Government's Policy Statement 2.0 on Digital Asset Development. It frames the proposals as advancing the 'Access' pillar of the SFC's ASPIRe roadmap, and the 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle. It quotes SFC CEO Julia Leung and FSTB Secretary Christopher Hui, and sets a comment deadline of 29 August 2025.
w: For a bank, this is a consultation announcement, not yet a rule. It signals that VA dealer and custodian licensing regimes are coming, worth tracking for future direct impact on the bank's own VA dealing and custody arrangements. It creates no obligation yet.
k: FSTB and SFC jointly launched a public consultation on licensing regimes for VA dealing and VA custodian service providers.
para 1, p.1
The consultation was launched the day after the Government released Policy Statement 2.0 on the Development of Digital Assets in Hong Kong (issued 26 June 2025).
quote from Christopher Hui, para 6
The two proposed regimes are positioned as advancing 'Access', one of the five pillars of the SFC's ASPIRe roadmap issued 19 February 2025.
Note 1
Comments on the consultation are invited by 29 August 2025.
para 5
rg: Read this short press release in full, 2-3 minutes, as context for the companion consultation paper (25CP7). Skip nothing.

t: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Custodian Services
sl: FSTB/SFC · Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset… (2025)
s: This joint FSTB/SFC consultation paper proposes a new licensing or registration regime for providers of virtual asset (VA) custodian services in Hong Kong. It extends the 'same activity, same risks, same regulation' principle already applied to VA trading platforms (VATPs). It defines VA custodian service as safekeeping VAs, or instruments enabling their transfer such as private keys, on behalf of clients, as a business. It proposes the SFC as licensing authority, with the HKMA as frontline regulator for banks and SVFs. It sets eligibility, fit-and-proper, financial resources (HK$10 million paid-up capital), individual licensing, and prohibition and sanctions provisions modelled on the VATP regime. It seeks views via 17 questions, with comments due by 29 August 2025.
w: For a bank, this directly affects its operating model. Any group entity -- the bank itself, a locally incorporated subsidiary, or an associated entity -- that safekeeps client private keys will need a new SFC/HKMA licence, with no automatic transitional relief. This calls for an entity-mapping exercise now.
k: VA custodian service is defined as, by way of business, safekeeping VAs or instruments enabling transfer of VAs (including private keys) on behalf of clients; self-custody by the client is excluded.

SFC will be the licensing and registration authority and standard-setter for VA custodians. HKMA is the frontline regulator for banks and SVFs providing VA custody, and VA custodians that are subsidiaries of locally incorporated banks are regulated by the SFC.
para 2.12(a)

Associated entities of SFC-licensed VATPs currently providing custody by safekeeping private keys will need to obtain a separate VA custodian service licence under the new regime if they wish to continue.
para 2.21(a)

A licence or registration will also be needed by banks, by subsidiaries of a locally incorporated bank, and by SVFs. This applies wherever they themselves hold the private keys, or similar instruments, that let client VAs be moved. It applies even where that happens as part of VA dealing, or acting as depositary for a fund.
para 2.21(b)

A stablecoin issuer licensed by the HKMA that only custodies the stablecoins it issues is proposed to be exempted from the VA custodian licensing regime. This holds even though it safekeeps private keys, because it is already subject to HKMA supervision.
para 2.19

An incidental exemption is proposed for SFC/HKMA regulated entities, where safekeeping of client VAs is wholly incidental to their principal licensed or registered business. This applies provided they do not safekeep the private keys themselves.
para 2.19

Except for banks and SVFs, an applicant must either be locally incorporated and physically based in Hong Kong, or be a company formed elsewhere but registered here under the Companies Ordinance. It must also name at least two responsible officers (for the SFC) or executive officers (for the HKMA).

Non-bank licensees would need baseline financial resources. These are proposed at a minimum of HK$10 million in paid-up share capital. They also need minimum liquid capital of up to HK$3 million, depending on the business model, modelled on the existing Type 13 (depositary) requirements.
para 2.39(a)

No grandfathering is planned for firms already providing VA custodian services. The licensing regime is meant to apply in full from the day the relevant statutory provisions commence. So firms are encouraged to approach the SFC or HKMA early, for example before applying, to avoid having to halt their business.
para 2.41

VA custodians safekeeping private keys will be required to engage an external assessor for an assessment of systems and controls before licensing or registration. This mirrors the VATP process, with the SFC party to the engagement.
para 2.42

Unlicensed provision, holding out, or active marketing of VA custodian services is proposed to be a criminal offence. On conviction on indictment, this means a fine of $5 million and imprisonment for 7 years. Knowingly advertising an unlicensed provider's services carries a level 5 fine ($50,000) and 6 months' imprisonment.
para 2.51(a)-(b)

Custody technology and security requirements -- private key management, cybersecurity, business continuity, storage ratios -- will be aligned with existing VATP custody requirements. They will be made subject to a further, separate public consultation, alongside SFC exploration of a 'dynamic approach' to custody technologies and storage ratios under the ASPIRe roadmap.
para 2.38
rg: Read Chapter 1 (background, paras 1.1-1.10), then Chapter 2's Scope of Regulation, Definition and Coverage, Eligibility, and Other Regulatory Requirements sections (paras 2.12-2.44). The 17 consultation questions and footnote cross-references can be skimmed after the matching paragraph.

t: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Dealing in Virtual Assets
sl: FSTB · Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Dealing in… (2025)
s: This is the full consultation paper on a proposed SFC licensing regime for virtual-asset dealing services. It replaces the narrower 2024 over-the-counter (OTC) shop proposal, after feedback showed dealing activity is far more varied. Banks and stored-value-facility (SVF) licensees must register with the SFC, in consultation with the HKMA, which remains their frontline supervisor. Licensees must hold client virtual assets with a licensed custodian, and meet financial-resource, AML/CFT, risk-management, conduct and record-keeping requirements. Stablecoins from HKMA-licensed issuers are expected to be an eligible traded asset for retail clients. The paper proposes no deeming arrangement, and heavy sanctions, including fines up to HK$10 million and imprisonment up to ten years for fraud-related offences.
w: For a bank, this paper sets out in detail how it would become a registered digital-asset dealer under HKMA frontline supervision, including the mandatory-custodian rule and proposed financial-resource floors. It also gives compliance the specific consultation questions worth a formal bank response.
k: Any person carrying on a business of dealing in virtual assets in Hong Kong, including simple conversions and complex brokerage/block-trading/advisory/asset-management activity, needs an SFC licence or registration.
Banks and stored value facilities must register with the SFC for virtual-asset dealing activity, with the HKMA as frontline regulator, similar to the existing model for banks' securities business.
para 1.10, p.8

A licensed stablecoin issuer conducting only primary-market offering or redemption of the stablecoins it issues is proposed to be exempt from the dealing licence. This is because it is already supervised by the HKMA.
para 1.10, p.8
Licensees or registrants must hold client virtual assets with a licensed or registered virtual-asset custodian in Hong Kong.
para 2.13 and 2.23, p.13 and 17
For retail clients, tradable virtual assets are expected to broadly follow VATP practice, including large-cap tokens meeting index criteria and stablecoins from HKMA-licensed issuers.
Minimum financial resource requirements proposed: HK$5 million paid-up share capital, up to HK$3 million liquid capital, plus 12 months' operating expenses in excess liquid capital.
No deeming/grace licence is proposed - the regime takes full effect on the commencement date of the statutory provisions.
Operating without a licence while dealing or actively marketing dealing services carries a fine of HK$5 million and up to seven years' imprisonment on indictment.
Fraudulent or deceptive behaviour in virtual-asset transactions carries a fine of HK$10 million and up to ten years' imprisonment on indictment.
rg: Read Chapter 2 (pages 10-25) in full for the substantive regime. Chapter 1 background (pages 2-9) can be skimmed for context on the prior 2024 consultation.

t: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Custodian Services
sl: FSTB/SFC · Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset… (2025)
s: This joint FSTB/SFC consultation document proposes a new statutory licensing regime for providers of virtual asset (VA) custodian services in Hong Kong, applying the 'same activity, same risks, same regulation' principle. It explains the current patchwork of custody requirements: VATP associated entities, and SFC/HKMA rules for intermediaries and funds. It proposes bringing standalone VA custodian services within a dedicated licensing and registration framework, subject to AML/CFT and other regulatory requirements. Comments were invited by 29 August 2025.
w: For a bank, this directly implicates it both as an eligible VA custodian for other intermediaries' clients today. It also implicates it as a prospective SFC registrant, HKMA-supervised, for its own VA custody business under the proposed new licensing regime.
k: Government's October 2022 Policy Statement committed to a comprehensive digital-asset regulatory framework under 'same activity, same risks, same regulation'; a second Policy Statement was promulgated 26 June 2025.
para 1.2, p.2
As of end-June 2025, SFC had formally licensed 11 VATPs, with 10 applicants (including 4 deemed-to-be-licensed) pending.

VATPs are currently required to provide custody through wholly-owned associated-entity subsidiaries. SFC-licensed intermediaries dealing in VAs must custody client VAs with SFC-licensed VATPs, banks, or subsidiaries of locally incorporated banks.
Consultation responses were due by 29 August 2025; the FSTB/SFC may reproduce and publish submissions and contributor names unless anonymity is expressly requested.
Foreword paras 2-4, p.1
Growth drivers cited for a dedicated VA custodian licensing regime include the proposed VA dealing (OTC) licensing regime and growth of VA funds such as SFC-authorised spot VA ETFs.
rg: Read Chapter 1 (Introduction/Background, pp.1-5) in full for the policy rationale. The remaining chapters, not captured in this excerpt beyond p.5, set out the detailed licensing proposal and should be read for implementation specifics before drafting any custody licensing strategy.

t: Second policy statement on development of digital assets issued to scale Hong Kong to new heights of global digital asset leadership
sl: Government · Second policy statement on development of digital assets issued… (2025)
s: The government issued Policy Statement 2.0 on the Development of Digital Assets, building on its October 2022 statement. It sets out the 'LEAP' framework: legal and regulatory streamlining, expanding tokenised products, advancing use cases, and people/partnership development. It confirms the SFC will be the lead licensing authority for digital-asset dealing and custodian service providers. FSTB and HKMA will separately lead a legal review of tokenisation covering bonds and other real-world assets. Full detail, including HKMA's role supervising banks in dealing/custodian activities, is in the attached Annex (package: a29b51bffc6b).
w: For a bank, this press release is the headline announcement of a framework that leads directly to future dealing and custodian obligations. The substantive detail compliance needs is in the attached Annex.
k: The Policy Statement 2.0 organises initiatives under the LEAP framework: legal streamlining, expanding tokenised products, advancing use cases, and people/partnership development.
para 2, p.1

The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) will be the lead licensing authority for digital-asset dealing and custodian service providers. FSTB and HKMA will separately lead a legal review to enable tokenisation of real-world assets and financial instruments.
para 3, p.1
The FSTB and SFC would launch public consultations shortly on licensing regimes for digital-asset dealing and custodian service providers.
final para, p.1
rg: Read this press release for the headline. Then read the Annex (id a29b51bffc6b) for the substance.

t: Policy Statement 2.0 on the Development of Digital Assets in Hong Kong
sl: FSTB · Policy Statement 2.0 on the Development of Digital Assets… (2025)
s: This is the full annex of Policy Statement 2.0. It replaces the term 'virtual assets' with 'digital assets' in government usage. It sets out the LEAP framework across four areas. First, unifying licensing for digital-asset exchanges, stablecoin issuers, and dealing and custodian providers, under SFC leadership. Second, regularising tokenised government bond issuance and clarifying stamp duty treatment for tokenised ETFs. Third, supporting stablecoin payment use cases, including proposals to test licensed stablecoins in government payments. Fourth, expanding talent and cross-border cooperation. It confirms tax concessions for privately-offered funds will be extended to specified digital assets from the 2025/26 year of assessment.
w: For a bank, this is the core policy document compliance should treat as the source of the upcoming licensing structure. It confirms SFC-led licensing, with HKMA as bank supervisor, for both dealing and custody. This frames every later consultation and future obligation for the bank's digital-asset business.
k: The government will use 'Digital Assets' instead of 'Virtual Assets' going forward, to better match international usage.
footnote 1, p.1
SFC will be the lead authority for licensing digital-asset dealing and custodian service providers, while HKMA will be the frontline regulator supervising banks conducting those activities.
FSTB and HKMA will lead a legal and regulatory review of tokenisation, starting with the bond market and covering settlement, registration and record requirements.
para 9, p.4
HKMA is exploring an Ensemble Infrastructure to support interbank settlement of tokenised deposits.
para 11, p.5
Government will clarify that the existing stamp duty waiver for ETFs listed on the stock exchange also applies to tokenised ETFs.
para 14, p.6
Profits-tax concessions for privately-offered funds and family investment vehicles will be extended to cover specified digital assets, subject to LegCo approval, from the 2025/26 year of assessment.
para 15, p.6
The stablecoin issuer licensing regime, commencing August 1, 2025, is described as a cornerstone for enabling licensed issuers to pursue payment and cross-border settlement use cases.
para 16, p.7
Government invited proposals from market participants on how it might test licensed stablecoin usage, including for government payments.
para 16, p.7
rg: Read the LEAP framework list on pages 2-3 and the regulatory-authority paragraphs (5-6, pages 3-4). The talent/partnership section (pages 8-9) can be skimmed.

t: Consultation on revised disclosure templates and tables |  | Annex 1: Standard disclosure templates and tables for making disclosure under the BDR
sl: HKMA · Consultation on revised disclosure templates and tables (2025)
s: The HKMA wrote to industry on 25 June 2025 to consult on revised standard Pillar 3 public disclosure templates and tables under the Banking (Disclosure) Rules (BDR). This annex adds a new Part XII, Cryptoasset exposures. It has Table CAEA: qualitative disclosure on an authorized institution's (AI's) cryptoasset activities, risk profile and classification approach. It also has three templates: CAE1 (cryptoasset exposures and risk-weighted assets (RWAs)), CAE2 (accounting classification) and CAE3 (liquidity requirements, category 1 institutions only). CAE1 requires disclosure, by cryptoasset group (1a/1b/2a/2b), of credit-risk exposure/exposure at default (EAD)/RWA and market-risk long/short exposure/RWA. It requires a total row, and rows for AIs whose group 2 cryptoasset exposure ratio breaches the BCR's 1% or 2% thresholds. Group 1 and group 2 cryptoasset exposures must also be folded into the general disclosure templates that cover equivalent traditional-asset exposures elsewhere in the package. Comments were due 25 July 2025.
w: For a bank, this is separate from the internal prudential returns. It is what the bank must publish externally about its crypto exposures, under Pillar 3. Compliance and disclosure teams, not just regulatory reporting, need to build a public-facing crypto disclosure process alongside the internal MA(BS) returns.
k: A new Part XII, Cryptoasset exposures, is added to the standard public disclosure package, comprising Table CAEA and Templates CAE1, CAE2 and CAE3.
Part XII contents listing, p.9; substantive Part XII section, pp.99-108

Table CAEA requires an AI to describe its cryptoasset-related business activities, how each affects its risk profile, and the scope of its cryptoasset reporting. It must also describe its most significant current and emerging cryptoasset risks, and, for group 1 cryptoassets, how it assesses each of the four BCR section 361 classification conditions.
Table CAEA, pp.99-100

Template CAE1 requires, for each cryptoasset group (1a, 1b, 2a and 2b), disclosure of total credit-risk exposure, exposure/EAD and RWA, plus market-risk long and short exposure and RWA. It also needs a total row, and separate rows for AIs whose group 2 cryptoasset exposure ratio breaches the BCR's 1% or 2% thresholds.
Template CAE1, rows 1-10, pp.101-104

Beyond the dedicated Part XII templates, an AI must also fold its group 1 and group 2 cryptoasset exposures into the general disclosure templates. These cover equivalent traditional-asset exposures elsewhere in the package. For example, Template OV1's row 5c covers cryptoasset credit-risk RWA under BCR section 376, and row 8a covers RWA for the group 2b cryptoasset derivative-contract method.
Template CAE1 Points to note item 2, p.103; cross-referenced rows in Template OV1, p.10
rg: Go straight to Part XII, Template CAE1, around p.363-373. The rest of the annex covers unrelated Pillar 3 templates, which can be skipped for crypto purposes.

t: Robust and Sustainable Development of Stablecoins
sl: HKMA · Robust and Sustainable Development of Stablecoins (2025)
s: HKMA's Chief Executive uses this speech to set expectations around the newly-passed Stablecoins Ordinance. He confirms it would take effect on 1 August 2025, after which HKMA would begin accepting licence applications. He describes stablecoins as a payment instrument, not an investment. He signals that only a small number of licences would be granted at first. Use-case viability and operational readiness would be scrutinised heavily. Joining HKMA's stablecoin issuer sandbox does not guarantee a licence. He references the Financial Stability Board's (FSB) 2023 global crypto-asset framework as a basis for Hong Kong's approach. He also notes HKMA's role coordinating the FSB's review of how that framework is being implemented worldwide.
w: For a bank, this confirms the licensing regime's go-live date and signals a deliberately restrictive, high-bar initial licensing approach. Compliance should factor this into any group decision about applying for a stablecoin issuer licence, or partnering with an applicant.
k: The Stablecoins Ordinance was expected to commence on 1 August 2025, after which HKMA would start accepting stablecoin issuer licence applications.
para 1
HKMA describes stablecoins as a payment instrument, not an investment or speculative asset, and groups them with CBDC and tokenised deposits as alternative emerging payment options.
para 5

Hong Kong's regulatory approach draws on the Financial Stability Board's 2023 global regulatory framework for crypto-asset activities, and HKMA was coordinating the FSB's review of that framework's global implementation.
para 6-7
HKMA expects to grant only a small number of licences initially, and applicants must demonstrate viable use cases and prudent, sustainable operating capability.
para 10 (Licensing regime section)

Applicants need to show capability across reserve-asset management, price stabilisation, redemption, technology security, risk management and anti-money laundering (AML) controls. Cross-border applicants must also show their partners hold the necessary regulatory approvals.
para 11
Participation in the Stablecoin Issuer Sandbox is not a precondition for, or guarantee of, obtaining a licence.
para 13 (Licensing regime section)
rg: Read in full. It is a short piece with no boilerplate to skip.

t: Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return templates |  | Return template: MA(BS)3a Part I

s: This draft form updates Part I of MA(BS)3A, the return of market risk and credit valuation adjustment (CVA) capital charge. It adds group 2a cryptoassets -- unbacked crypto held for trading, treated like equities or commodities -- as a new risk class under the sensitivities-based method (SBM), with its own capital-charge line. It also adds an infrastructure risk add-on for group 1 cryptoasset exposures. A new Division L sets out the simplified standardised approach (SSTM) treatment for group 2a cryptoassets, split into non-option and scenario-approach exposures.

First, the group 1 infrastructure risk add-on (banking book). Second, the redemption-risk add-on for group 1b trading-book exposures. Third, the redemption-risk add-on for stablecoin-linked group 2a trading-book exposures. Fourth, the group 2b risk-weighted amount. Fifth, the group 2 concentration add-on for globally or domestically important banks (G-SIB/D-SIB). The notes describe the same build-up for the output floor in Division B, including separate treatment for trading-book exposures under the standardised (STC) approach.

Third, the redemption-risk add-on for stablecoin-linked group 2a trading-book exposures. Fourth, the group 2b risk-weighted amount. Fifth, the group 2 concentration add-on for globally or domestically important banks (G-SIB/D-SIB).

It covers customer checks on issuance and redemption, extra controls where customers use unhosted, self-custody. Wallets, the Travel Rule for stablecoin transfers, and ongoing monitoring of stablecoins once in circulation. It also flags that the HKMA is separately drafting supplementary AML guidance for other digital-asset activities such as custody. Referencing the securities regulator's existing rules to keep requirements consistent across regulators. The detailed rules were to be finalised in a companion draft Guideline; comments closed 30 June 2025.

And foreshadows a related supplementary guideline on custody and other digital-asset activities that would apply more broadly across the bank. A licensed issuer must run customer checks before issuing or redeeming stablecoins for any transaction of HK$8,000 or more.

Issuers should work out whether a customer's wallet is custodial or unhosted, confirm the customer controls it. And run due diligence on the institution behind a custodial wallet before issuing stablecoins to it.
Where a customer uses an unhosted wallet, the proposal adds extra controls: closer monitoring of those transfers, sending coins only to wallets assessed as reliable, and possible transaction limits.
