The HKMA is drafting separate supplementary AML guidance covering other digital-asset activities. Such as custody services and stablecoin offering by banks and other licensees, drawing on the securities regulator's existing rules for consistency.
para 4.1
rg: Read sections 2 (background and scope) and 3 (proposed requirements) in full; section 5 (next steps) is procedural only.

t: Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Licensed Stablecoin Issuers)
sl: HKMA · Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (2025)
s: This is a draft AML/CFT guideline the HKMA circulated for consultation in May 2025. Meant for entities that hold a licence under Hong Kong's Stablecoins Ordinance to issue fiat-backed stablecoins. It largely mirrors the structure of existing AML rulebooks: risk assessment, governance and staff training, customer checks on stablecoin holders, ongoing monitoring, sanctions screening, suspicious-transaction reporting and record-keeping. Its distinctive chapter applies a travel-rule-style regime to stablecoin transfers, requiring issuers to capture and pass on sender and receiver details above a threshold. The draft was still unnumbered as a Cap.[-] ordinance at the time of publication, confirming it was published ahead of the underlying law being finalised. It has not yet been confirmed as the final in-force text.
w: For a bank, this shows the AML/CFT standard it should expect any stablecoin issuer it deals with. Invests reserve assets alongside, or offers as a product to hold once licensed. Its travel-rule and counterparty-vetting provisions closely track the SFC's VATP guideline, so a bank can largely reuse existing crypto AML controls when assessing stablecoin-issuer counterparties.
k: The guideline would bind anyone holding a stablecoin-issuer licence, covering how they manage laundering and terror-financing risk from issuing, redeeming and otherwise handling their stablecoins.
A licensee must appoint both a Compliance Officer and a Money Laundering Reporting Officer, which can be the same person for a smaller issuer.
An independent audit function with a direct line to senior management and the board must review the issuer's AML controls.
para 3.6
Before transferring stablecoins worth HK$8,000 or more, the sending institution must record sender and receiver identity details and pass them to the receiving institution securely and immediately.

A licensee must vet a stablecoin transfer counterparty's money-laundering or terrorist-financing risk before dealing with it, similar to the counterparty checks other AML guidelines apply to crypto exchanges.
Filing a suspicious transaction report does not close the matter. The issuer must still review the relationship and may need to freeze or burn the stablecoins involved.
para 8.6
Records of customer checks and stablecoin transaction data must be retained for at least five years after the transaction, even if the relationship has since ended.
para 9.3

If a licensee sets up branches or subsidiaries outside Hong Kong, it must apply group-wide AML standards and. Where local law blocks the stricter of the two rule sets, tell the HKMA and take extra risk-mitigating steps.
rg: Read the introduction, Chapter 1, for scope and legal basis, then Chapter 6 for the stablecoin travel-rule mechanics. The customer due diligence chapter (Chapter 4) largely repeats standard AML identification requirements and can be skimmed.

t: Draft Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers
sl: HKMA · Draft Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers (2025)
s: This consultation-stage HKMA guideline spells out, in detail, what a licensed stablecoin issuer must do under the Stablecoins Ordinance to keep its licence. It covers how reserve assets are chosen, valued, segregated and disclosed; how issuance and same-day redemption must work; minimum capital; detailed risk-management expectations including token. Wallet and private-key, cybersecurity and third-party controls; incident, business-continuity and wind-down planning; and corporate-governance and fitness-and-propriety standards for directors and managers. It uses 'must' for statutory duties lifted from the Ordinance, and 'should' for the HKMA's own supervisory expectations layered on top. The consultation closed 30 June 2025; a finalised version was expected to follow.
w: For a bank, this is the core prudential and operational rulebook its stablecoin-issuer subsidiary, or an authorized institution issuing directly, would have to meet. It is also the reference standard compliance should use when assessing any third-party stablecoin issuer the bank deals with as a counterparty, custodian or distributor.
k: An issuer must at all times hold reserve assets whose market value is at least equal to the face value of stablecoins in circulation. With extra buffer, over-collateralisation, built in to cover market-price swings.
para 2.1.1

Reserve assets are limited to short-dated bank deposits, high-quality marketable government or public-sector debt. Overnight reverse repos and dedicated investment funds holding those instruments, or other assets the HKMA accepts.
para 2.2.1

Reserve assets must be held in the same currency the stablecoin references. Segregated from the issuer's own assets and protected from the issuer's other creditors, normally via an independent trustee or trust declaration.
An issuer must not pay interest or interest-like returns to stablecoin holders; any yield on reserve assets belongs to the issuer.
para 2.5.1
Reserve composition and value must be disclosed daily internally, and normally reported to the HKMA and the public weekly, with regular independent attestation of full backing.
Valid redemption requests must be honoured within one business day without unreasonable fees or conditions, unless the HKMA has given prior written consent to a longer period.
para 3.2.3

An issuer must get the HKMA's consent before conducting any business beyond its licensed stablecoin activity. And must show that other business will not put its stablecoin operations or customers at risk; this does not apply to an issuer that is itself an authorized institution.
A non-bank issuer must always hold at least HK$25 million in paid-up capital, or an HKMA-approved equivalent.
para 5.1.1
Issuers should run three lines of defence, business units, risk and compliance, and internal audit, with the risk function reporting directly to the board.

Detailed technology-risk rules require documenting token standards and smart-contract architecture, and multi-signature or similar controls so no single person can unilaterally mint, burn, freeze or blacklist tokens.

'Significant' private keys, governing contract upgrades, role changes or large mint and burn operations. Must be generated and stored offline in an air-gapped, Hong Kong-based, or HKMA-accepted, environment with elevated physical security.
paras 6.5.8(ii),(iv)
Smart contracts must be independently audited by a qualified third party at least annually and on every deployment or upgrade.
para 6.5.5
rg: Prioritise sections 2 (reserve assets), 3 (redemption), 6.5 (technology and key management), 6.6 (third-party risk), 6.8 (incident and exit) and 7 (governance). The glossary (section 9) is reference-only.

t: Government welcomes passage of Stablecoins Bill
sl: Government · Government welcomes passage of Stablecoins Bill (2025)
s: The Legislative Council passed the Stablecoins Bill, creating a licensing regime under the Monetary Authority for anyone issuing a fiat-referenced stablecoin in Hong Kong. Or issuing one pegged to the Hong Kong dollar from anywhere. Licensees must meet requirements on reserve-asset management, client-asset segregation, at-par redemption, anti-money-laundering controls, risk management, disclosure and fitness. Only licensed issuers may offer a stablecoin to retail investors, and only advertisements for licensed issuance are allowed, including during a planned six-month grace period. The press release confirms further consultation on detailed rules, and previews upcoming over-the-counter (OTC) and custodian consultations and the second policy statement.
w: For a bank, this confirms the statutory basis for its later stablecoin obligations: only licensed issuers may reach retail clients. And advertising restrictions apply from day one, so marketing and product teams must not promote unlicensed stablecoin offerings even during the transition window.
k: Anyone issuing a fiat-referenced stablecoin in Hong Kong, or a Hong Kong dollar-pegged one anywhere, will need a licence from the Monetary Authority once the Ordinance takes effect.
para 2, p.1
Licensees must properly segregate client assets, run a robust price-stabilisation mechanism, and process redemption requests at par value on reasonable terms.
para 2, p.1
Only specified licensed institutions may offer a fiat-referenced stablecoin in Hong Kong, and only a licensed issuer's stablecoin may be offered to a retail investor.
para 3, p.1
During the six-month non-contravention, or grace, period, only advertisements for licensed stablecoin issuance are permitted.
para 3, p.1
rg: Read in full; short and directly relevant to the licensing timetable and retail-offering restriction.

t: Government welcomes passage of the Stablecoins Bill
sl: HKMA · Government welcomes passage of the Stablecoins Bill (2025)
s: The Legislative Council passed the Stablecoins Bill, creating a licensing regime for fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers in Hong Kong. Under the resulting Stablecoins Ordinance, anyone issuing an FRS in Hong Kong. Or an FRS claiming to hold a stable value referenced to the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) anywhere in the world, needs a licence from the Monetary Authority (MA). Only specific licensed institutions may offer an FRS, and only a licensed issuer's coin may go to retail investors. At all times, including the six-month transition period, only advertisements for licensed FRS issuance are allowed. The government said it would soon launch consultations on virtual-asset over-the-counter (OTC) and custodian services, and publish a second virtual-asset policy paper.
w: For a bank, as the law bringing in Hong Kong's stablecoin regime, this directly obliges compliance to make sure the bank only markets or offers MA-licensed FRS coins. Including HKD-referenced coins issued anywhere in the world, right from the start of the transition period.
k: Under the Ordinance, anyone issuing an FRS in Hong Kong, or an FRS claiming stable value referenced to HKD anywhere in the world, needs a Monetary Authority licence.
para 2

Licensees must meet requirements on managing and redeeming reserve assets, keeping them separate, using a solid stabilisation method. Redeeming at par value on reasonable terms, AML, risk management, disclosure and audits, and being fit and proper.
para 2
Only institutions holding the right licence may issue an FRS here in Hong Kong, and only that licensed issuer's FRS is allowed to reach retail investors.
para 3
At all times, even during the six-month transition period, only advertisements for licensed FRS issuance are allowed, aimed at stopping fraud and scams.
para 3
The Ordinance was due to take effect later in 2025, with a transition arrangement giving industry time to apply for licences and sort out their business.
para 5
The government said it would soon launch consultations on virtual-asset OTC trading and custodian services, and publish a second policy paper on virtual-asset development.
para 6
rg: Read in full; short but dense with operative rules.

t: SFC’s senior executives visit Abu Dhabi and Dubai to promote collaboration on virtual assets
sl: SFC · SFC’s senior executives visit Abu Dhabi and Dubai to… (2025)
s: The SFC's Executive Director of Intermediaries Dr Eric Yip and Director of Intermediaries and Head of Fintech Ms Elizabeth Wong met regulatory counterparts and Web3 industry stakeholders in Abu Dhabi and Dubai. United Arab Emirates (UAE). These included the Securities and Commodities Authority of the UAE, the Abu Dhabi Global Market's Financial Services Regulatory Authority, the Dubai Financial Services Authority, and Dubai's Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority. They went to exchange virtual asset (VA) regulatory insights and explore cross-border collaboration, in line with the ASPIRe roadmap.
w: For a bank, this signals the SFC's active engagement with UAE VA regulators, including VARA, a jurisdiction many banks' digital-asset units already operate under. Relevant context for a bank tracking potential future mutual-recognition or cross-border cooperation arrangements.
k: The SFC held discussions with four UAE regulators: the Securities and Commodities Authority (UAE). The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of ADGM, the Dubai Financial Services Authority, and Dubai's Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA).
para 2
Discussions centred on evolving VA regulatory approaches and supervisory experience, supporting the SFC's ASPIRe roadmap objective of fit-for-purpose policymaking.
para 2
Industry participants said clear, consistent rules were essential for the sector to grow, and called for balanced regulation that supports growth without letting systemic risks build up.
para 3
rg: Short; read in full.

t: Opening Remarks at MO•MENTS 2025 organised by Ant International on Global Outlook: Unlocking Market Potential through Financial Connectivity
sl: HKMA · Opening Remarks at MO•MENTS 2025 organised by Ant International… (2025)
s: A senior HKMA speaker addresses a payments-industry conference, reviewing Hong Kong's stored value facility and Faster Payment System ecosystems and their cross-border links with mainland China and Thailand. The speech then turns to newer forms of money and value transfer: mBridge, a multi-central-bank wholesale central bank digital currency (CBDC) project, reaching minimum viable product stage. Project Ensemble's work on tokenisation standards and its Sandbox launched with the securities regulator; and the stablecoin licensing law nearing enactment alongside a running stablecoin issuer sandbox. It closes with remarks on fraud risk, cross-border collaboration and operational resilience in payments.
w: For a bank, this gives an early, high-level signal, April 2025, of how close the HKMA was to enacting the stablecoin licensing regime. And of the tokenisation and CBDC infrastructure, mBridge and Ensemble, that the bank's DLT and payments strategy will need to plug into.
k: Project mBridge, a cross-border wholesale central bank digital currency platform co-run by the HKMA and other central banks, reached minimum viable product stage in 2024.
para 21

Project Ensemble's Architecture Community is developing common standards so central bank digital currency, tokenised money and tokenised assets can interoperate. Its Sandbox launched in August 2024 with the securities regulator and private sector.
para 23

The stablecoin licensing law was, at the time of the speech, close to being passed. The HKMA described it as one part of a wider set of rules covering exchange, trading and custody of crypto assets, meant to support a responsible crypto ecosystem.
para 25
A stablecoin sandbox running alongside the legislative process lets prospective issuers test scheme features and controls, and feeds into the HKMA's eventual detailed rules.
para 27
rg: Read the paragraphs on mBridge, Ensemble and stablecoins, roughly the middle third of the speech; the payments-history and fraud sections are background only.

t: Circular on SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets
sl: SFC · SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets (2025)
s: This circular sets the rules the SFC uses to authorise investment funds that put more than 10% of net asset value (NAV) into virtual assets (VA Funds). For public sale in Hong Kong under sections 104-105 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). It replaces the 22 December 2023 circular. VA Funds can get direct, spot, or indirect, for example futures or exchange-traded products, exposure to virtual assets. They must only invest in VA tokens that Hong Kong's public can already trade through SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs). They cannot use fund-level leverage. And any spot VA trading or custody must go through an SFC-licensed VATP or an authorized institution (AI) that meets the HKMA's virtual-asset custody standards. Custody rules require segregated holdings, mostly cold-wallet storage, and Hong Kong-based, access-restricted storage of seeds and keys. New under this version, VA Funds may now stake or do other VA-related activities under the ASPIRe roadmap. As long as they follow guiding principles: fitting the fund's investment strategy. Having strong internal controls, doing due diligence on counterparties, and giving specific disclosures in offering documents and reports. Funds wanting more than 10% VA exposure, or wanting to stake, must first consult the SFC and get its approval.
w: For a bank, this rule applies to SFC-authorised fund providers and trustees, not directly to the bank as an authorized institution. It matters because if the bank's AI or a subsidiary provides VA custody to one of these funds. It must meet the HKMA custody standard referenced here, and staking is now allowed for funds.
k: SFC-authorised VA Funds are limited to holding, whether directly or through another vehicle, VA tokens that Hong Kong retail investors can already trade on an SFC-licensed VATP.
para 10, p.2
At fund level, SFC-authorised VA Funds should carry no leveraged exposure to VA.
para 14, p.2
Transactions and acquisitions of spot VA should be conducted through an SFC-licensed VATP, or through an AI, or a locally incorporated AI's subsidiary, that meets HKMA's regulatory requirements.
para 16, p.2

The trustee or custodian should only delegate VA custody to an SFC-licensed VATP or a qualifying AI, or its subsidiary, that meets HKMA's expected VA custody standards. VA holdings should be kept segregated, mostly stored in cold wallets, with seeds and keys kept securely in Hong Kong. Access restricted, generated non-deterministically, protected by multi-signature controls, and properly backed up.

A fund's offering documents, including the product key facts statements, must spell out VA exposure limits and the key risks: price. Custody, cybersecurity and fork risk for spot VA; roll costs and operational risks for VA futures.

VA Funds may now stake and do other VA-related activities, newly allowed under the ASPIRe roadmap's Pillar P, provided the management company follows guiding principles: fitting the fund's goals. Implementing robust internal controls over risk and conflicts, proper custody, due diligence on counterparties, disclosing VA amounts used in offering documents, and telling investors about material changes.
para 27, p.4-5
Funds wanting VA exposure above 10% of NAV, whether new or existing, or wanting to stake or do VA-related activities, must first consult the SFC and get its approval.
para 30, p.5
rg: Read paragraphs 6-27, the Requirements section, in full; paragraphs 1-5 are background and history.

t: SFC sets out staking guidance for licensed virtual asset trading platforms and authorised virtual asset funds
sl: SFC · SFC sets out staking guidance for licensed virtual asset… (2025)
s: The SFC published two linked pieces of staking guidance. A circular lets licensed virtual-asset trading platforms offer staking services under risk-management and disclosure conditions. And an updated circular lets SFC-authorised virtual-asset funds stake holdings through licensed platforms and authorised institutions, within a cap meant to manage liquidity risk. The SFC framed staking as part of its ASPIRe roadmap, to widen the range of products and services on offer.
w: For a bank, this lets licensed trading platforms and authorised funds offer staking; the bank itself has no direct duty here. But if it distributes such funds or refers clients to platforms offering staking, compliance should confirm those counterparties meet the asset-protection and disclosure standards this guidance sets.
k: SFC-authorised virtual-asset funds may only stake their holdings through licensed trading platforms and authorised institutions, and only up to a cap set to manage liquidity risk.
para 4
The guidance is presented as advancing the 'Products' part of the ASPIRe roadmap, which aims to broaden what platforms can offer.
para 2
Trading platforms should maintain measures to prevent errors in staking services, safeguard staked client assets, and ensure proper disclosure of the risks staked assets may carry.
para 3
rg: Short summary; read companion circulars 50bf95ba3143 (VATP staking) and 353535602a83 (VA Fund staking) for full operative requirements.

t: Provision of Staking Services for Virtual Assets from Custodial Services
sl: HKMA · Provision of Staking Services for Virtual Assets from Custodial… (2025)
s: This 7 April 2025 circular sets the HKMA's expected standards for authorized institutions. And subsidiaries of locally incorporated AIs, that offer staking of virtual assets from their custodial services to clients. Staking here means locking client virtual assets so a validator can take part in a proof-of-stake blockchain, in exchange for rewards distributed back to the client. The circular covers internal controls, required client disclosures, and due diligence over the blockchain protocols and third-party providers used. And asks banks to discuss implementation with the HKMA in advance.
w: For a bank, this is the current, in-force operating standard it must satisfy before or while offering custodial staking to clients. It covers key-control, disclosure and third-party due-diligence expectations, plus a clear signal to talk to the HKMA before launch.
k: This circular covers authorized institutions themselves, plus any subsidiary of a locally incorporated AI, when either offers staking as part of its custodial services for clients. The parent AI must make sure such a subsidiary's conduct, practices and controls also comply.
A bank should maintain possession or control of everything needed to unstake client virtual assets, such as withdrawal keys and any pre-signed exit instructions.
p.2, section A

A bank should maintain policies to catch errors or misconduct in its staking service. Keep staked client assets adequately safeguarded, and have internal controls for operational risk and conflicts of interest.
p.2, section A

A bank should disclose to clients which tokens it stakes, any third parties involved, fees, activation and minimum lock-up periods. How rewards are paid, the unstaking process and its length, uptime performance, what happens during outages, and its custodial arrangements.
p.2, section B

A bank should disclose the extra risks clients face from staking, including slashing, a validator penalty that can reduce staked assets, lock-up risk. Blockchain bugs, hacking, validator inactivity, and legal uncertainty over a client's rights in staked assets, and how losses from these would be handled.
p.2, section B

Before it offers staking on a given blockchain protocol, a bank needs to carry out thorough due diligence and confirm its controls. Technology and infrastructure can handle that protocol and manage the associated risks.
p.2-3, section C

Where staking is outsourced to a third-party provider, the bank should perform proper due diligence and ongoing monitoring. Including checking the provider's track record, technology infrastructure, risk mitigation and security controls.
p.3, section C
Before rolling out staking services, AIs should have suitable policies, procedures, systems and controls in place, and should talk to the HKMA about their plans beforehand.
p.3, Implementation
rg: Read the whole circular, three pages. Sections A-C set the substantive standards; the closing Implementation paragraph sets the expectation of prior HKMA discussion.

t: Circular on staking services provided by virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · staking services provided by virtual asset trading platforms (2025)
s: This circular allows SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs) to provide staking services to clients. Previously prohibited under VATP Guidelines paragraph 7.26(b), which barred VATPs from generating returns on client virtual assets. It does this by modifying VATP licence conditions, subject to the SFC's prior written approval and detailed 'Terms and conditions for providing staking services' in an attached Appendix. VATPs must maintain possession or control of withdrawal mediums, with no third-party custody of staked assets, implement whitelisting and verification controls. Disclose staking terms and risks, such as slashing, lock-up, technical, hacking, inactivity and legal uncertainty risk. Conduct due diligence on blockchain protocols and third-party validators, retain records for at least 7 years. And get SFC approval before including any protocol for retail clients; notification only is needed for professional-investor-only staking.
w: For a bank, this circular binds VATPs, not the bank. But a compliance head assessing a VATP partner's staking offering should use it as the checklist: no third-party custody of staked assets. Mandatory risk disclosure, and SFC approval before retail-client protocols go live.
k: A VATP and its associated entities must keep hold of, or control, every means by which a client's staked VAs could be withdrawn. For instance the withdrawal address's private key and any pre-signed voluntary exit message. They cannot leave that custody to an outside service provider.
para 6, p.1; Terms and conditions para 4, p.1

VATPs should implement systematic whitelist controls, ensuring staking withdrawal addresses are limited to designated whitelisted addresses managed by the client's cold wallet private key. And independently verify staking instructions before broadcast.
Terms and conditions para 6(b), p.2

VATPs should disclose on their website or app: specific VAs staked, third parties involved, fees, minimum lock-up periods, unstaking process and length. Outage and business-resumption arrangements, custodial arrangements, and risks, such as slashing, lock-up, technical, hacking, inactivity and legal uncertainty.
circular para 9-10, p.2; Terms and conditions para 12, p.3-4
Except for institutional or qualified corporate professional investors, VATPs should get a client acknowledgement confirming understanding of staking risks before providing staking services.
Terms and conditions para 13, p.4

VATPs should get the SFC's prior written approval before including any blockchain protocol for retail-client staking, or terminating retail staking services. For professional-investor-only staking, advance written notification to the SFC suffices.
Terms and conditions para 23-24, p.6
Records relating to staking services, staked assets, validators, wallet addresses, dates, returns, protocol-selection rationale, should be kept for not less than 7 years.
Terms and conditions para 10, p.3

VATPs should exercise due skill, care and diligence selecting blockchain protocols and third-party validators. Including reviewing smart contract audits, validator track record, security controls, financial soundness, and insurance for slashing risk.
Terms and conditions para 14-19, p.4-6
rg: Read the 3-page cover circular for the policy shift and background, then the 6-page Appendix, Terms and conditions, for the full operative requirements. Both are needed, as the circular incorporates the Appendix by reference.

t: New speech by Christina Choi: Keynote speech at Hong Kong Web3 Festival
sl: SFC · Keynote speech at Hong Kong Web3 Festival (2025)
s: This is a short SFC news item. It says the regulator has posted a keynote address by Christina Choi, given at Hong Kong's Web3 Festival, about the growth of the city's Web3 and digital-asset sector. Beyond that pointer, this notice gives no further detail.
w: For a bank, this is only a pointer. There is no regulatory substance in the text fetched here, and the actual speech is not included.
k: A keynote address given by Christina Choi at Hong Kong's Web3 Festival, on the growth of the city's Web3 and digital-asset sector, is now available on the regulator's site.
para 1
rg: Six-line stub; nothing further to read here.

t: Four main themes and their corresponding use case categories to be tested on the Project Ensemble Sandbox
sl: HKMA · Four main themes and their corresponding use case categories… (2025)
s: This is a short fact sheet listing the four broad themes being trialled on the HKMA's Project Ensemble Sandbox, a tokenisation testbed run with the securities regulator and industry. The four themes are fixed income and fund products, liquidity management, green and sustainable finance, and trade and supply chain finance, each broken into two use-case categories. It names the banks and other firms taking part as Architecture Community members or Industry Pioneers for each theme, including several major Hong Kong-licensed banks. The list is presented as provisional and subject to change over time.
w: For a bank, this names which banks are already active in the HKMA's flagship tokenisation sandbox. Useful for benchmarking a bank's own DLT and tokenisation ambitions and for due diligence on peers or partners already engaged with the HKMA on tokenised assets.
k: The sandbox groups pilot use cases under four themes: fixed income and investment funds, liquidity management, green and sustainable finance, and trade and supply chain finance.
Eight specific use case categories sit under the four themes, spanning bonds, funds, repo, treasury management, carbon credits, EV charging, supply chain finance and trade finance/payments.

Named participating banks include Bank of China (Hong Kong), Hang Seng Bank, HSBC, JPMorgan Chase Bank and Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong), alongside asset managers, exchanges and technology firms.
The document states the theme and participant list can change, with updates to be posted by the HKMA over time.

t: Speech by FS at Hong Kong Web3 Festival (English only) (with photos/video)
sl: Government · Speech by FS at Hong Kong Web3 Festival (English… (2025)
s: The Financial Secretary's remarks at Hong Kong's Web3 Festival restate the government's pro-innovation stance and recap existing measures. These are the VATP licensing framework, virtual-asset spot exchange-traded funds (ETFs), the near-final stablecoin legislation, and the planned over-the-counter (OTC) and custodian consultations. He references Project Ensemble as a sandbox for tokenised real-world assets, and previews a second virtual-asset policy statement. The speech is promotional in tone with no new binding rules.

k: Stablecoin legislation was described as close to passage, with the licensing regime targeted to start within the year.
speech text, para on stablecoin legislation
The government confirmed plans to consult on licensing for virtual-asset OTC trading and custodian services.
speech text, para following stablecoin mention
Project Ensemble was cited as the HKMA's sandbox letting firms trial tokenised real-world-asset use cases with early regulator feedback.
speech text, para on sandboxes

t: LegCo Subcommittee on Issues Relating to the Development of Web3 and Virtual Assets visits Hong Kong Web3 Festival (with photos)
sl: LegCo · LegCo Subcommittee on Issues Relating to the Development of… (2025)
s: A short notice records that members of a Legislative Council subcommittee toured the Hong Kong Web3 Festival and met industry representatives to discuss Web3 development. It names the attending members and the event themes but contains no policy or regulatory content.
w: For a bank, this is purely a diary item confirming ongoing legislative interest in Web3. It carries no obligations or new facts for compliance.
k: LegCo subcommittee members visited the Web3 Festival to hear about blockchain infrastructure, crypto finance, and Web3 security/compliance, and to discuss Web3 development with industry representatives
para 2-3, p.1
rg: Read in full; one page, no substantive content.

t: The Hong Kong Fintech Ecosystem Report
sl: Other · The Hong Kong Fintech Ecosystem Report (2025)
s: Produced by Invest Hong Kong with the FinTech Association of Hong Kong and HKUST Business School, this market report profiles Hong Kong's fintech sector generally. It includes a timeline of policy milestones, including virtual asset trading platform (VATP) licensing, the stablecoin sandbox. Project Ensemble and spot crypto exchange-traded funds (ETFs), and survey statistics on 130 Hong Kong fintech firms. It is descriptive market research aimed at investors and entrepreneurs, not a regulator publication, and contains no supervisory requirements.
w: For a bank, this is a useful, dated market snapshot of Hong Kong's digital-asset ecosystem size and the regulatory milestone timeline. It is produced by a market-research consortium rather than a regulator, so it should be treated as background context, not an authoritative source for compliance decisions.
k: The digital asset and cryptocurrency sub-sector grew by nearly 30% from 2022 to 2024. 111 digital-asset and cryptocurrency companies were counted in Hong Kong by mid-2024, alongside 175 blockchain application and software firms.

The report's policy timeline lists the SFC's VATP licensing regime taking effect June 2023, the first Bitcoin and Ether futures ETFs (2022) and spot ETFs (April 2024). The stablecoin issuer sandbox (March 2024), Project Ensemble Sandbox (August 2024), and the SFC's five-pillar 'ASPIRe' roadmap for virtual assets (February 2025).
As at February 2025 the report states Hong Kong had 10 SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platforms, with 8 more applications in process.
rg: Read the policy-timeline box (pp.22-23) and the digital-asset sub-sector statistics (pp.12-13); the fundraising and talent-visa sections are not digital-asset relevant.

t: The Hong Kong Fintech Ecosystem Report
sl: Other · The Hong Kong Fintech Ecosystem Report (2025)
s: InvestHK's fintech ecosystem report gives a market overview and a timeline of Hong Kong's fintech and digital-asset milestones from 2021 to early 2025. It counts about 111 companies in the digital-asset-and-cryptocurrency category, notes the sub-sector grew roughly 30% in two years. And lists milestones such as the virtual asset trading platform (VATP) licensing regime taking effect in June 2023. Spot Bitcoin and Ether exchange-traded funds (ETFs) launching in April 2024, and the stablecoin issuer sandbox opening in March 2024. It also describes the SFC's five-pillar ASPIRe roadmap announced in February 2025. The rest of the report is general fintech market and funding statistics not specific to digital assets.

t: Distributed Ledger Technology in the Financial Sector - A Study on the Opportunities and Challenges
sl: HKMA · Distributed Ledger Technology in the Financial Sector - A… (2025)
s: This is a lengthy HKMA research report on distributed ledger technology (DLT) in finance. It describes DLT's architecture and core features, then walks through ten real-world adoption cases, including a hypothetical e-HKD use case. HKEX's Synapse platform and a UBS tokenisation pilot, covering payments, trade settlement and digital identity. It sets out practical adoption challenges such as strategy alignment, novel operational risks and regulatory uncertainty. And gives good-practice guidance for managing risks including third-party reliance, node concentration, smart contracts, key management, cybersecurity, data privacy and interoperability. It closes with the HKMA's own initiatives, the DLT Supervisory Incubator and financial and talent support. And a comparison of how Hong Kong, Singapore, the US and UK support DLT sandboxes.
w: For a bank, this is educational and good-practice material, not a binding rule. It is useful as a risk checklist, covering third-party, node concentration, smart contract, key management, cyber, data privacy and interoperability risk. When a business line proposes a DLT pilot, and points to the HKMA's own sandbox route for engaging supervisors early.
k: The Executive Summary describes the paper's exploration of 10 real-world DLT adoption cases across programmable payments, trade settlement and digital identity. The case studies themselves (Section 3) name platforms such as a hypothetical e-HKD use case, HKEX's Synapse and a UBS tokenisation pilot.
Section 1, p.6 (overview); Section 3, p.17-40 (case detail)

Node concentration risk arises when a party gains control of over half a DLT network's nodes, computing power or staked tokens. Permissioned networks face elevated concentration risk because a fixed, known set of parties already controls validation.
Section 4.1, item 2, p.48-49

Recommended mitigations for node concentration include diversifying node-hosting providers, robust software review and stress testing, contingency plans for non-DLT fallback, and, for permissionless networks, monitoring validator concentration.
Section 4.1, item 2, p.48-49
Smart contracts carry coding-vulnerability and oracle-concentration risks, since bugs can be exploited automatically and at speed, and reliance on a single oracle creates a single point of failure.
Section 4.1, item 3, p.49-50

The paper's practical guidance for banks starting DLT projects (Figure 21) includes developing a firm-wide DLT strategy, centralising efforts with a dedicated DLT team. Delivering fit-for-purpose training, developing mitigation plans for identified risks, and proactively communicating with regulators.
Section 4.2, Figure 21, p.43
The HKMA's own DLT support includes the Supervisory Incubator sandbox, alongside comparable sandbox schemes run by the SFC, its Regulatory Sandbox, and the Insurance Authority, its Insurtech Sandbox.
Section 4, p.58-59
rg: Read the Executive Summary (page 6) and the risk and mitigation guidance in Section 4 (pages 41-59. Especially Figure 21 on page 43 and the risk-mitigation list on pages 48-53). The ten case studies (Section 3, pages 17-40) and glossary and appendix (Section 6) can be skimmed or used for reference only.

t: Distributed Ledger Technology in the Financial Sector: A Study on the Opportunities and Challenges
sl: HKMA · Distributed Ledger Technology in the Financial Sector: A Study… (2025)
s: The HKMA commissioned this study, with input from the SFC, Insurance Authority (IA) and Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) Schemes Authority. After interviewing ten institutions and surveying 113 firms on their DLT projects. It builds on two earlier HKMA circulars: the April 2024 risk-management circular and the January 2025 Supervisory Incubator launch. The paper walks through ten Hong Kong pilot deployments, then sets out adoption barriers and a set of good-practice pointers banks can use when scaling DLT work. It is framed as research and guidance rather than a new binding rule, and it repeats and elaborates several expectations the 2024 circular already set.
w: For a bank, although framed as research, this is the HKMA's fullest current public statement of what it expects banks to have in place for governance. Third-party, node and smart-contract, key-custody, cyber and privacy risk when running DLT. It largely restates the April 2024 circular. Compliance should treat sections 4.1-4.2 as the working checklist examiners are likely to benchmark a bank's DLT risk framework against.
k: Boards and senior management should update governance, technology-risk, business-continuity and outsourcing policies before rolling out a DLT solution. And add safeguards such as dispute handling or a loss-compensation approach where customers interact with it directly.
Section 4.2.1, p.44

A firm should keep enough in-house DLT expertise, echoing the 2024 circular. The paper suggests a centralised team, for example a Centre of Excellence or hub-and-spoke model, blending technologists and business staff to run this.
Section 4.2.2, p.44-45

For outsourced DLT platforms, a bank should vet vendor reliability, security and regulatory standing at every stage. Put performance and data-security terms in the contract, and keep backup vendors or failover plans ready.
Section 4.2.4, item 1 (Third-Party Risks), p.48

Because control of over half a network's nodes, computing power or staked tokens can let an attacker corrupt the ledger. Firms should spread node hosting across providers and locations, and run software review and stress testing to cut shared points of failure.
Section 4.2.4, item 2 (Node Concentration Risk), p.48-49

Smart contracts should not be used for every process; manual override should stay possible. And firms need a governance framework covering suitability review, testing before go-live, and contingency plans if a contract misbehaves.
Section 4.2.4, item 3 (Smart Contract Risk), p.49-50
Because ledger entries are essentially irreversible, firms should build strong upfront data-validation controls, since correcting an error or fraudulent entry after the fact may not be possible.
Section 4.2.4, item 4 (Immutability Risk), p.50-51

A bank holding client private keys as custodian is expected to run tight controls: secure key generation, restricted access, proprietary cold storage, backups and an incident-response plan. The paper flags hardware security modules and multi-party-computation wallets, which split a key into shares, as ways to cut single-key concentration risk.
Section 4.2.4, item 5 (Private Key Risk), p.51-53

DLT platforms still need ordinary cyber defences, for example multi-factor authentication against endpoint attacks and phishing. And firms should track emerging threats such as quantum computing and adjust response plans over time.
Section 4.2.4, item 6 (Common Cybersecurity Risks), p.53

Where a ledger's transparency would expose counterparty or transaction details a firm needs to keep confidential, it should use privacy techniques. Such as stealth addresses, ring signatures and zero-knowledge proofs, and plan for participants who want their data removed from the network.
Section 4.2.4, item 7 (Data Privacy Risk), p.53

The paper repeats the principle that new HKMA rules for DLT-based activity will track existing rules for the equivalent traditional activity rather than create a separate regime. Summarised as 'same activity, same risk, same regulation'.
Section 4.2.5, p.57

Whether a smart contract counts as a binding legal contract in Hong Kong still has no statutory definition. Enforceability turns on ordinary contract-formation tests, agreement, consideration, certainty, intent and formalities, the same approach the paper says Singapore, the US and the UK currently take.
Section 4.2.5, sub-section 1 (Hong Kong), p.57

The HKMA's Supervisory Incubator for DLT, launched January 2025, lets a bank get HKMA feedback and run live trials on its risk controls before fully launching a DLT initiative. The paper also flags the SFC's ASPIRe roadmap, February 2025, 12 initiatives across five pillars, as the parallel securities-side track.
Section 4.2.6, p.58-59
rg: Read pages 41-59, adoption challenges and the six practical-guidance sub-sections. Especially the risk-mitigation list at pages 48-53 and the regulatory-coordination section at pages 57-59. Pages 7-40, the DLT technology primer and ten case studies, are background and can be skimmed.

t: Circular to licensed corporations, SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities Cybersecurity webinar materials
sl: SFC · licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities Cybersecurity… (2025)
s: This follow-up circular attaches the slide deck from the SFC's Cybersecurity Webinar held on 17 and 19 February 2025. It covers findings from the SFC's 2023/24 thematic review of cybersecurity, real incident case studies, and new risk areas. The deck, presented by the SFC's Steve Poon and Markus Au Yeung, reports on a review of 50 licensed corporations. Including on-site checks of 7 internet brokers and talks with 6 licensed corporations that operate globally. It covers cloud security, remote access, managing third-party vendors, retiring old, end-of-life, software, and phishing. Two case studies are given: a ransomware attack that started from a weak VPN gateway and an exposed remote server. And unauthorised trades that followed an attack on an unpatched website using unencrypted data.
w: For a bank, these SFC-documented case studies, a ransomware attack through a VPN gateway, and unauthorised trades through an unpatched web app. Offer lessons it can apply directly to its own digital-asset or brokerage cyber-risk defences. They also show real concentration risk among third-party trading-system vendors.
k: The 2023/24 thematic review looked at 50 licensed corporations, with on-site checks at 7 internet brokers and discussions with 6 licensed corporations running global operations.
deck p.5
The review looked at cloud security, controls on remote access, management of third-party vendors, handling of software that is no longer supported, end-of-life, and phishing.
deck p.5
92% of internet brokers rely on trading systems built by outside vendors. The top 5 vendors hold 70% of that market, and the single biggest vendor holds 30%, a concentration risk.
deck p.6
Mobile apps have overtaken desktop computers as the main way clients trade online: 82% used mobile and 65% used desktop in 2023/24, compared with 80% each in 2019/20.
deck p.7

Between 2021 and 2024, 8 serious cybersecurity incidents were reported to the SFC, including ransomware attacks. A vendor network breach that disrupted back-office services, and account takeovers through weaknesses in network security.
deck p.9

Case study 1: attackers used a weak VPN gateway and an exposed remote server to plant ransomware, which disrupted trading. Settlement, and back-office systems, and forced a halt to online trading and client-money processing. Missing logs made it hard to find the root cause.
deck p.10

Case study 2: attackers exploited an unpatched website that carried unencrypted data and outdated, end-of-life. Database software, letting them break into internal servers, alter the client database, and place unauthorised trades.
deck p.11
Lessons for licensed corporations: strengthen network security, apply software patches, control user access rights, monitor client accounts, keep audit logs, and encrypt data.
deck p.12
Cyber Defender and Scameter, both tools from the Hong Kong Police Force, were highlighted as ways to stay informed about cybersecurity threats.
circular para 3

t: “A-S-P-I-Re” for a brighter future: SFC’s regulatory roadmap for Hong Kong’s virtual asset market
sl: SFC · “A-S-P-I-Re” for a brighter future: SFC’s regulatory roadmap for… (2025)
s: The SFC set out a five-pillar roadmap, named Access, Safeguards, Products, Infrastructure and Relationships (ASPIRe), for developing Hong Kong's virtual asset regulatory regime over the coming years. It opens with market context on institutional versus retail participation, fragmented trading venues, and global regulatory convergence between traditional finance and virtual assets. It then lists twelve forward-looking initiatives, including new licensing regimes for over-the-counter (OTC) trading and custody. More flexible custody and cold-storage rules, staking and lending for professional investors, and better market surveillance. Most items are described as exploratory or under development rather than final rules, so the roadmap signals direction rather than imposing immediate new obligations. It targets custody legislative preparations for completion by end-2025.
w: For a bank, this roadmap previews where SFC rules for VATPs, custodians and OTC desks are heading. Compliance can anticipate new counterparty licensing categories, and start planning for potential custody, staking or product changes among the intermediaries it uses or works with.
k: The SFC will support the government's introduction of a dedicated licensing framework for virtual asset OTC trading desks, applying the same rules that already bind licensed trading platforms.
Pillar A, Initiative 1

The SFC will build a separate licensing regime for virtual asset custodians, modelled on traditional custodian standards for capital. Cybersecurity and asset segregation, with legislative preparation targeted for completion by end-2025.
Pillar A, Initiative 1

The SFC will explore moving away from a fixed mandatory cold-storage ratio, toward outcome-based, technology-neutral custody standards backed by real-time monitoring, audits and cybersecurity controls.
Pillar S, Initiative 3

The SFC will look at professional-investor-only new token listings and virtual asset derivatives trading, at aligning margin-trading requirements with securities-market risk safeguards. And at allowing staking, under custody and operational safeguards, and professional-investor-only borrowing and lending services.
Pillar P, Initiatives 6-8

The SFC will consider straight-through regulatory reporting for digital-asset information. And deploy data-driven surveillance tools such as blockchain intelligence and wallet tracing to detect illicit activity market-wide.
Pillar I, Initiative 9
The SFC will strengthen cross-agency collaboration with local regulators and law enforcement, and promote cross-border cooperation with overseas regulators.
Pillar I, Initiative 10
The SFC will consider a regulatory framework for financial influencers, to address their growing role in shaping investor decisions about virtual assets.
Pillar Re, Initiative 11
rg: Read the Executive Summary for context, then Pillar A, custody and OTC licensing, and Pillar S, custody flexibility, closely, as these most affect bank counterparties. Pillars P, I and Re can be skimmed for direction only, as none commit to firm rules yet.

t: Keynote Speech at ASIFMA Annual Conference
sl: HKMA · Keynote Speech at ASIFMA Annual Conference (2025)
s: This speech covers the growing China-ASEAN trade and investment corridor and Hong Kong's role in it. Touching on trade finance, the internationalisation of the renminbi (RMB), capital markets, and sustainability. The only content related to virtual assets is one line noting the HKMA is trying out tokenisation use cases in trade and supply-chain finance through the Project Ensemble Sandbox. Plus a mention of working with the Bank of Thailand on tokenisation use cases such as trade payments and carbon credits.
w: For a bank, this is a small confirmation that Ensemble Sandbox tokenisation work now covers cross-border trade-finance and carbon-credit use cases with a second central bank, Thailand. It has limited direct relevance to a bank's compliance function.
k: The HKMA said it was trying out tokenisation use cases in trade and supply-chain finance through the Project Ensemble Sandbox. As part of digitalisation work supporting the China-ASEAN trade corridor.
para 19

The HKMA said last October it was teaming up with the Bank of Thailand on Project Ensemble and Project San, looking at tokenisation applications. Covering both payment-versus-payment and delivery-versus-payment models, for uses such as trade payments and carbon credits.
para 22
rg: Skip almost all of this speech, the trade corridor, RMB and sustainability content. Only the two short passages referencing Project Ensemble and Project San are virtual-asset relevant.

t: SFC convenes inaugural Virtual Asset Consultative Panel meeting
sl: SFC · SFC convenes inaugural Virtual Asset Consultative Panel meeting (2025)
s: The SFC held the first meeting of its new Virtual Asset Consultative Panel (VACP). It is chaired by Dr Eric Yip, the SFC's Executive Director of Intermediaries, and made up of senior management representatives from every licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP). The Panel is meant to feed into the SFC's regulatory policy-making and help set priorities for building a sustainable, resilient virtual asset ecosystem.
w: For a bank, this body does not include banks unless they operate a licensed VATP. A compliance head should note it as an indirect policy-influence channel, only available through a bank's own VATP-licensed entity.
k: The VACP is chaired by the SFC's Executive Director of Intermediaries, and comprises all licensed VATPs, represented by their senior management.
para 2
The VACP will contribute to the SFC's regulatory policy-making, and help identify policy priorities for market and regulatory development backed by investor safeguards.
para 2

t: Letter to DTCA: Soft consultation: miscellaneous amendments to the BCR
sl: HKMA · Soft consultation: miscellaneous amendments to the BCR (2025)
s: The HKMA wrote to the Deposit-Taking Companies Association (DTCA) on 11 February 2025, about a second, separate set of Banking (Capital) Rules changes. These are unrelated in subject to the cryptoasset standard, but timed to start alongside it. The main content covers a revised capital treatment for a bank's direct holdings of certain non-capital loss-absorbing-capacity (LAC) liabilities. Plus clarifying edits to existing definitions to better match the Basel framework. Comments were due by 7 March 2025, with an intended effective date of 1 January 2026, the same date as the cryptoasset capital rules.
w: For a bank, this is not itself a crypto rule, but it bundles into the same 1 January 2026 start date as the cryptoasset capital package. So a bank's Basel-implementation project plan for that date needs to track both streams together.
k: The amendments mainly cover a revised capital treatment for a bank's own direct holdings of certain non-capital loss-absorbing capacity (LAC) liabilities.
Other changes are definitional or clarifying edits meant to better line up the Capital Rules with the Basel framework.
The HKMA intends to bring in these changes at the same time as the cryptoasset capital standard, that is, 1 January 2026.
rg: One-page cover letter; the actual amendment text was not part of this attachment set. This is a near-duplicate letter to the one sent the same day to the Hong Kong Association of Banks (id 843b382f9c92).

Plus the same definitional clean-up amendments to the Banking (Capital) Rules. Both are timed for the same 1 January 2026 start date as the cryptoasset capital package. It is sent in near-identical wording to the parallel DTCA letter.

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Cybersecurity Webinar
sl: SFC · licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities -… (2025)
s: This administrative SFC circular announces two Cybersecurity Webinar sessions, on 17 and 19 February 2025, via Zoom. They will share observations from the 2023/24 thematic cybersecurity review of licensed corporations, and raise awareness of emerging cybersecurity threats in Hong Kong. The sessions are free, offer 2.5 Continuous Professional Training (CPT) hours, and enrolment is limited to two representatives per firm via a linked form, due 7 February 2025.

k: Two cybersecurity webinar sessions were held on 17 and 19 February 2025, covering the 2023/24 thematic cybersecurity review findings and emerging cybersecurity threats.
para 1-2
Attendance offers 2.5 Continuous Professional Training (CPT) hours for those attending the whole session.
Who should attend section
Firms may enrol at most two representatives each. The first-named nominee on each firm's submitted form gets priority, first-come first-served, with entries due by 7 February 2025.

t: SFC extends swift licensing process to new virtual asset trading platform applicants
sl: SFC · SFC extends swift licensing process to new virtual asset… (2025)
s: The SFC announced that all new, non-deemed, virtual asset trading platform (VATP) applicants can now use its swift licensing process. This means applicants put in place policies, procedures, systems and controls before a single external assessment, with the SFC as a party to the engagement. This extends the approach already used for deemed-to-be-licensed applicants. The SFC also published its on-site inspection findings the same day, to clarify expected regulatory standards.
w: For a bank, this does not itself bind the bank. But signals a faster regulatory pathway now available if the bank were to sponsor or invest in a new VATP applicant. And points to the same-day inspection findings worth reviewing for expected standards.
k: All new VATP applicants can now seek licences under the swift licensing process. This means putting in place policies and procedures before a single external assessment, with the SFC as a party to the engagement.
para 1-2
This extension follows the effectiveness of the SFC's direct engagement approach, used with deemed applicants during risk-based on-site inspections.
para 3
On 18 December 2024, four VATP applicants received licences from the SFC through the original swift licensing process aimed at deemed applicants.
Note 1
The SFC published its risk-based on-site inspection findings the same day, to provide clarity on expected regulatory standards.
Note 3
rg: Short; read alongside companion circular 2f950979195e and findings circular 0c93d9a066e6, both issued the same day.

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities Findings from inspections on deemed-to-be-licensed virtual asset trading platform applicants and expected standards of conduct for virtual asset trading platform operators
sl: SFC · licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities Findings… (2025)
s: Following on-site inspections of all deemed-to-be-licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP) applicants. Focused on cybersecurity, safeguarding of client assets, and know-your-client (KYC) checks, the SFC published two documents. Appendix 1 sets out 22 detailed 'Expected standards of conduct', labelled A-V, covering cybersecurity, client virtual asset handling and segregation. The 98/2 cold and hot wallet ratio, seed and private key storage, contingency planning, compensation arrangements, client money, and access controls. Appendix 2 lists specific deficiencies found during inspections, mapped to each standard: for example weak or outdated cryptographic algorithms such as AES-ECB and MD5. Manual-only privileged access controls, single-staff-member security operations centres. Mixing of house and client virtual assets, understated hot-wallet calculations breaching the 98/2 rule. Multi-signature keys held partly outside Hong Kong, and bank-account signatory authority given to non-operational staff. All Platform Operators are told to review their policies, procedures and systems, and immediately fix deficiencies.
w: For a bank, this publishes SFC inspection findings showing gaps in VATP applicants' cybersecurity, client-asset safeguarding and KYC processes. Compliance should factor these observations into counterparty due diligence on any VATP relationship, though the circular does not bind the bank itself.
k: Platform Operators should split their networks so critical systems and sensitive data are kept apart from higher-risk network segments. Inspections found some operators allowed direct internet access to trading or custody systems, or unrestricted firewall access between outer and internal networks.
Appendix 1 Std A p.1; Appendix 2 paras 1-2, p.1

Platform Operators should deploy centralised control over privileged access at every level (servers, workstations, network edges), with senior management approving each use. Inspections found manual controls, permanent unreviewed access, and one operator where a single staff member held most administrative accounts.
Appendix 1 Std B p.1; Appendix 2 paras 3-4, p.1-2

Platform Operators should use up-to-date, strong encryption for stored and transmitted data. Inspections found outdated or weak algorithms, such as AES-CBC, AES-ECB and MD5 hashing, and unprotected internal data traffic despite TLS 1.2/1.3 on client-facing channels.
Appendix 1 Std C p.1-2; Appendix 2 paras 5-6, p.3

Under the 98/2 rule, Platform Operators must keep at least 98% of client virtual assets in cold storage. Inspections found miscalculations, such as wrong wallet classification and excluding pending deposits, that let hot wallets exceed the 2% cap.
Appendix 1 Std I-K p.3; Appendix 2 paras 17-20, p.7-8

Seeds and private keys should be kept in Hong Kong in a secure environment, such as a certified hardware security module, and cold wallets should not use smart contracts. Inspections found a hot wallet with 2-of-3 multisig keys split across the US. Singapore and Hong Kong, and a cold wallet using a 3-of-4 multisig smart contract.
Appendix 1 Std L p.3-4; Appendix 2 paras 21-22, p.8

Compensation arrangements should cover 50% of cold-wallet and 100% of hot-wallet client virtual assets, with insurance sufficiency properly analysed, including exclusions and event deductibles. Some operators assumed house funds would cover deductibles without proper assessment.
Appendix 1 Std R p.5; Appendix 2 paras 33-35, p.12-13

Client money should go directly into the associated entity's segregated bank account, not routed via the Platform Operator's own account first. Bank account signatory authority should be limited to staff involved in day-to-day operations.
Appendix 1 Std T-U p.5-6; Appendix 2 paras 38-41, p.13-14

Platform Operators should screen and block access from restricted jurisdictions, those under sanctions or banning virtual asset trading. And detect attempts to bypass this using VPNs or proxies, with documented checks on screening-tool accuracy. Inspections found minimal testing and no formal follow-up procedures.
Appendix 1 Std V p.6; Appendix 2 paras 42-44, p.15
rg: Read the 1-page cover circular for context, then Appendix 1, 6 pages, standards A-V, as the operative checklist. Then skim Appendix 2, 15 pages, for real deficiency examples under each standard, especially cybersecurity, 98/2 custody, and client-money sections.

t: Circular to new virtual asset trading platforms seeking to be licensed – Enhanced licensing process and revamped external assessments
sl: SFC · new virtual asset trading platforms seeking to be licensed… (2025)
s: This circular sets the enhanced virtual asset trading platform (VATP) licensing process for new corporations applying for a licence, as distinct from deemed applicants. It applies to applications submitted after 18 December 2024, and replaces the June 2023 Scope of External Assessment Reports. It collapses the previous first-phase and second-phase assessments into a single external assessment. Done only after the applicant has all systems and controls in place, under a tripartite agreement with the SFC and an External Assessor (EA). This is a direct assurance engagement, under HKSAE 3000 or an equivalent such as ISAE 3000, signed off by a practising accountant (CPA).
w: For a bank, this binds new VATP applicants, not the bank directly. But a compliance head sponsoring or partnering with a bank-backed new VATP should understand the revised single-assessment. Post-deployment sequencing when planning that entity's licensing timeline.
k: Separate first-phase and second-phase assessments are being dropped for VATPs. Going forward, new applicants complete just a single external assessment across the whole licensing process.
footnote 1, p.1

Applicants must submit a licensing application bundle via WINGS, including written policies and procedures, documentation showing a suitable External Assessor has been identified, and that assessor's capability statement.
para 5, p.1

The SFC will assess the applicant's business structure, competence, and fitness of the applicant and its ultimate controllers, owners, substantial shareholders, proposed responsible officers and managers, plus the assessor's capability. It may oppose the assessor or return an incomplete application.
para 6, p.1-2

After acceptance, the applicant must put its systems and controls in place, covering market surveillance. AML and KYC tools, and custody solutions, and fully adapt its policies and procedures before the external assessment.
para 7-8, p.2

The external assessment must be a direct assurance engagement, under HKSAE 3000 or an equivalent standard such as ISAE 3000, signed off by a practising certified public accountant. Its job is to say whether the VATP's policies and procedures were properly designed and put into practice under the VATP Guidelines and AML/CFT Guideline.
para 14, p.2-3
The SFC will pay HK$1 toward the external assessment fees; the VATP applicant pays the balance of all fees, disbursements and expenses.
footnote 5, p.2
As soon as practicable, the applicant must tell the SFC and the assessor about any later material change to its policies and procedures.
para 13, p.2
Once the external assessment is done and any remaining issues, such as a capital top-up. Are cleared, the SFC will issue a licence provided it considers the applicant fit and proper.
para 9, p.2
rg: Read the full 3-page circular plus the 1-page Appendix flowchart, which shows the sequence from application through external assessment to licence approval.

t: Annex 2: Disclosure Requirements in Relation to Cryptoasset Exposures
sl: HKMA · Annex 2: Disclosure Requirements in Relation to Cryptoasset Exposures (2025)
s: This document proposes new public disclosure duties for banks holding cryptoassets, added to the Banking (Disclosure) Rules from 1 January 2026 to match the Basel Committee's cryptoasset disclosure standard. It introduces four new disclosure items: yearly qualitative disclosure of crypto activities and how the bank applied the classification rules. Twice-yearly disclosure of crypto exposures and their risk-weighted amounts. Twice-yearly disclosure of how crypto holdings and liabilities are treated in the accounts. And twice-yearly disclosure of how crypto positions feed into liquidity ratios, for banks that must meet those ratios. It also creates a new defined term, 'cryptoliability', for digital liabilities tied to a cryptoasset.
w: For a bank, this sets the public reporting cadence compliance must run once the bank has any cryptoasset exposure: annual qualitative disclosure of activities and classification methodology. Plus semi-annual quantitative disclosures on exposures, accounting treatment and, for larger banks, liquidity impact.
k: A new term, 'cryptoliability', is added, meaning a digital liability tied to a cryptoasset. It covers a bank's own token issuance liabilities and other digital liabilities linked to cryptoassets.
Item 2(2), p.2

Each year, a bank with cryptoasset or cryptoliability exposures must publicly disclose an overview of its crypto-related business. The risks involved, its risk-management policies, and how it decided whether each Group 1 cryptoasset it holds meets the classification conditions.
new s.16ZQH, p.5-6

Twice a year, a bank must disclose an overview of its cryptoasset exposures broken down by regulatory bucket (Group 1a, 1b, 2a, 2b) and the related risk-weighted amounts. Its operational-risk policies for crypto, the market value and types of crypto it holds in custody for clients, and an explanation of any material change during the period.
new s.16ZQI, p.6-7

The twice-yearly exposure disclosure must break out material individual holdings of Group 1b. Group 2a and Group 2b cryptoassets separately, not just totals; tokenised traditional assets are excluded from this breakdown.
new s.16ZQI(2), p.7
Twice a year, a bank must disclose how it classifies and measures its cryptoasset and cryptoliability holdings for accounting purposes, with a breakdown of carrying values by regulatory bucket.
new s.16ZQJ, p.8

A bank that is a category 1 institution, subject to the full liquidity coverage ratio and net stable funding ratio rules. Must twice a year disclose how its cryptoasset and cryptoliability exposures feed into those liquidity ratio calculations.
new s.16ZQK, p.9

Banks incorporated outside Hong Kong face a lighter version of these rules. Limited to an overview of crypto activities that create liquidity risk and, for category 1 institutions, the classification-conditions disclosure.
new s.103(4B) and s.103AC, p.11-13
rg: Read the four new disclosure sections (16ZQH-16ZQK, pages 5-9) in full. The amendments to existing sections 2, 11 and 91-105 (pages 2-4, 10-14) are mostly consequential cross-referencing and can be skimmed.

t: Annex 1: Prudential Treatment of Cryptoasset Exposures
sl: HKMA · Annex 1: Prudential Treatment of Cryptoasset Exposures (2025)
s: This document sets out the HKMA's proposed line-by-line changes to the Banking (Capital) Rules. These bring in a dedicated capital regime for banks' cryptoasset exposures, copying the Basel Committee's December 2022 standard and its July 2024 amendments, targeted for 1 January 2026. It defines a cryptoasset and a cryptoasset exposure, sorts cryptoassets into four buckets with different capital treatment, and adds new rules for classifying them. Assigning them to the banking or trading book, working out risk-weighted amounts, and capping how much of a bank's capital can sit in the riskiest bucket. A bank must itself decide the bucket for each cryptoasset it holds, based on conditions it must document, and that the HKMA can override.
w: For a bank, this is the draft capital rulebook it must build systems and governance against before 1 January 2026. It fixes how every cryptoasset position gets bucketed, which bucket triggers a punitive 1,250% risk weight. And a hard portfolio limit that forces board-level notification and remediation if breached.
k: A cryptoasset is a digital token representing value that can be used for payment, investment. Or to access a good or service, built mainly using cryptography together with distributed-ledger or comparable technology. A cryptoasset exposure is any on- or off-balance-sheet exposure to one that carries credit, market, valuation-adjustment, operational or liquidity risk.
Item 1, p.2-4

Cryptoassets fall into four buckets: Group 1a, a tokenised version of a traditional asset; Group 1b, a token with an effective mechanism pegging it to a traditional asset or basket. Such as a stablecoin-type instrument; Group 2a, a liquid token with an approved derivative, ETF or ETN referencing it; and Group 2b, everything else, treated as the riskiest bucket.
Item 1, p.4-6
Tokens that run on a fully open, permissionless blockchain cannot qualify for Group 1a or Group 1b. Because the HKMA judges that risk controls for such networks are not yet proven under stress.

A bank decides which bucket each cryptoasset belongs in, on an ongoing basis, against conditions the HKMA sets. It must keep records showing how it met those conditions and hand them to the HKMA on request.

The first time a bank takes on exposure to a cryptoasset it has never held before, it must tell the HKMA immediately. And treat that cryptoasset as the riskiest bucket, Group 2b, until the HKMA is satisfied a better bucket applies.
The HKMA can overrule a bank's own bucket decision for any cryptoasset if it judges that prudent.

Group 1a and Group 1b tokens go in the banking or trading book depending on how the equivalent traditional asset would be booked. Group 2a tokens always go in the trading book; Group 2b tokens always go in the banking book.

For each riskiest-bucket, Group 2b, cryptoasset. A bank must apply a 1,250% risk weight to whichever is bigger: the total of its long positions or the total of its short positions in that token. This one number stands in for credit, market and valuation-adjustment risk together, so none of those are calculated separately for that token.

A bank must work out a Group 2 cryptoasset exposure ratio, its combined exposure to Group 2a and Group 2b tokens, divided by Tier 1 capital. A globally or domestically systemically important bank must keep this at or below 1% at all times, or below 2% if it only occasionally goes over 1%.

If a systemically important bank's Group 2 exposure ratio goes over 1%, it must tell the HKMA in writing. Add extra capital using a set formula, and act quickly to get back under the 1% line. Going over 2% forces the bank to hold capital as if every Group 2 token were in the riskiest bucket.

For a derivative contract on a riskiest-bucket cryptoasset, the exposure used in the capital calculation is the fair value of the underlying token grossed up for leverage. Capped at the most the bank could possibly lose on the contract.

The HKMA can order a bank in writing to hold extra capital. This applies if the bank has sizeable short positions in riskiest-bucket tokens that could lose more than the standard risk weight already covers.
rg: Read Item 1, definitions (pages 2-8), Item 13.3-13.4, classification and book assignment (pages 56-63). And Items 18.4 and 20, risk weight and exposure ratio (pages 97-103), closely. Skim the technical market-risk formula sections in Item 18.1-18.3 (pages 89-97) unless building the trading-book model itself.

t: HKMA launches Supervisory Incubator to foster responsible adoption of distributed ledger technology
sl: HKMA · HKMA launches Supervisory Incubator to foster responsible adoption of… (2025)
s: The HKMA launched the Supervisory Incubator for Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT). A new supervisory arrangement to help banks responsibly adopt DLT and manage its risks, with tokenised deposits as a core initial focus. For an individual bank, it offers a one-stop platform to reaffirm risk-management adequacy before fully launching a DLT initiative. Access to a dedicated HKMA team, and the option of live trials. At the industry level it promotes best practices through supervisory guidance, sharing sessions and research. It was announced at FiNETech4, an event with over 300 professionals from banking, securities, insurance, the Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) sector and technology. Part of the FiNETech series launched in April 2024 and backed by the HKMA, SFC, Insurance Authority (IA) and MPFA.
w: For a bank, this is a direct, bank-facing HKMA supervisory arrangement. A compliance head should treat pre-launch engagement with the Supervisory Incubator as the expected first step before productionising any DLT-based banking service, particularly tokenised deposits.
k: The Supervisory Incubator is a new HKMA supervisory arrangement to help banks manage the risks of DLT adoption. With a particular focus on risks arising as banks bring services such as deposits and loans into production across DLT-based and legacy infrastructure.
para 2
Tokenised deposits are a core focus of the Incubator upon inception.
para 2

At the individual bank level, the Incubator offers a one-stop platform for banks to reaffirm risk-management adequacy before full DLT-initiative launch. With access to a dedicated HKMA team and optional live trials.
para 3
At the industry level, the Incubator promotes DLT risk-management best practices through supervisory guidance, industry sharing sessions and research projects.
para 4

The Incubator was announced at FiNETech4, part of the FiNETech series established in April 2024. It is backed by the HKMA, SFC, Insurance Authority and MPFA, industry associations such as HKAB and the FinTech Association of HK, Cyberport and HKSTP.
para 5, footnotes 1-4

t: Supervisory Incubator for Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT)
sl: HKMA · Supervisory Incubator for Distributed Ledger Technology (2025)
