t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Opening Remarks at FiNETech4 on “Charting the New Frontiers of Finance with DLT”
sl: HKMA · Opening Remarks at FiNETech4 on “Charting the New Frontiers… (2025)
s: These are opening remarks at the FiNETech4 event announcing the launch of the Supervisory Incubator for Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT). A new HKMA arrangement to help banks bring DLT-based banking products and services into production carefully, with risk kept under control. The speech frames DLT's potential across tokenised assets, tokenised money (including tokenised deposits) and tokenised information or data, while flagging legal, technical and regulatory adaptation challenges. It references an earlier Shenzhen-Hong Kong cross-boundary data-verification pilot using blockchain. It signals the Incubator's early focus on products that span DLT-based and legacy banking infrastructure, with tokenised deposits cited as a prime example.
w: For a bank, this establishes a formal, named supervisory channel, the Supervisory Incubator for DLT. That a bank can use to get early HKMA feedback before productionising a DLT-based product. It signals tokenised deposits as the near-term priority area for supervisory engagement.
k: The HKMA launched the Supervisory Incubator for DLT, a one-stop supervisory arrangement offering a dedicated team. Socialisation of DLT-based proposals, supervisory feedback, and live risk-controlled trials for banks.
para 21-22
The Incubator will also provide supervisory guidance, sharing sessions, and forward-looking research to build the banking sector's DLT risk-management understanding and best practices.
para 22

Any bank can bring any DLT-related idea to the Incubator. Though the HKMA flagged it would concentrate at first on offerings that bridge DLT-based and legacy banking systems, with tokenised deposits as the leading example.
para 23

The HKMA said adopting DLT would need a period of adjustment covering technical, legal and regulatory issues. Banks should not have to carry that adjustment burden alone; the HKMA stands ready to help.
para 19-20

The speech points to the Shenzhen-Hong Kong cross-boundary data verification platform pilot, run jointly with mainland authorities, as an example. It uses blockchain and data coding to confirm documents are genuine without moving or storing the original paper copies.
para 11
rg: Focus on the paragraphs where the HKMA head introduces the new Incubator and notes it welcomes proposals from every bank, roughly paragraphs 19-23. The long sailing metaphor earlier can be skimmed, though it has substantive points on tokenised assets, money and information.

t: HKMA launches Supervisory Incubator to foster responsible adoption of distributed ledger technology (with photos)
sl: HKMA · HKMA launches Supervisory Incubator to foster responsible adoption of… (2025)
s: The Monetary Authority launched a Supervisory Incubator for Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT). A new supervisory arrangement to help banks manage the risks of adopting DLT for banking services such as deposits and loans. It gives participating banks access to a dedicated Monetary Authority team for supervisory feedback. And an option to run live trials to check risk-management controls before fully launching a DLT-based service. Tokenised deposits are named as a core initial focus. The Incubator also runs industry-wide initiatives, such as supervisory guidance and sharing sessions, to raise sector-wide DLT risk-management readiness.
w: For a bank planning a tokenised deposit or other DLT-based service, this shows it should engage the Incubator before launch to pre-validate risk controls with the Monetary Authority. This is now the practical supervisory on-ramp for DLT initiatives.
k: The Supervisory Incubator for Distributed Ledger Technology is a new HKMA supervisory arrangement to help banks manage risk when adopting DLT-based services. Particularly where those services cut across DLT-based and legacy banking infrastructure.
para 2
Tokenised deposits are the core initial focus of the Incubator, given strong industry interest in bringing them into production.
para 2

Through the Incubator, banks can check their risk-management safeguards are adequate before rolling out a DLT-based initiative in full. Drawing on a dedicated HKMA team and, if they wish, running live trials.
para 3
The Incubator will also run industry-wide initiatives, including supervisory guidance, sharing sessions and research, to raise sector-wide DLT risk-management readiness.
para 4
rg: Read paragraphs 2-4 for what the Incubator offers and its tokenised-deposits focus; skip the FiNETech4 event background in the later paragraphs.

t: Supervisory Incubator for Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT)
sl: HKMA · Supervisory Incubator for Distributed Ledger Technology (2025)
s: The HKMA announces a new 'Supervisory Incubator'. Giving banks a dedicated supervisory contact point and the option to run live trials of DLT risk-management approaches, under a hands-on, iterative process. Banks accessing the Incubator may be offered a degree of supervisory flexibility, assessed case by case. Similar in spirit to the existing Fintech Supervisory Sandbox, on the understanding they are actively working to manage the risks involved. Where existing rules do not fit distributed ledger technology (DLT) well and the mismatch is inadvertent. The HKMA says it will consider regulatory adaptations consistent with 'same activity, same risk, same regulation'.
w: For a bank, this offers a formal, lower-friction route to pilot DLT projects, including limited supervisory flexibility, in exchange for close HKMA engagement and demonstrated risk management. Compliance should treat Incubator access as a supervised trial, not a compliance exemption.
k: The Incubator gives banks access to a dedicated HKMA team for supervisory feedback on DLT proposals. And the option of live trials, run in a hands-on, iterative and phased manner.

Banks accessing the Incubator may be offered supervisory flexibility, for example on certain supervisory requirements, assessed case by case. Based on factors similar to those used for the Fintech Supervisory Sandbox: boundary setting, customer protection, risk controls, readiness, and monitoring.
p.1, footnote 2
Supervisory flexibility is offered on the understanding that the bank will work to manage the risks of its trial in a way that matches the trial's scale, scope and nature.

Where existing regulatory or legal rules are inadvertently incompatible with DLT adoption, and this conflicts with 'same activity, same risk. Same regulation', the HKMA will consider whether regulatory adaptation or flexibility is warranted, taking account of international standards.

Longer term, the Incubator will run broader industry initiatives building on successful pilots, including further supervisory guidance, industry sharing sessions and forward-looking research on emerging DLT risk areas.
rg: Short 2-page circular; read in full.

t: Circular to virtual asset trading platforms on licensing process and revamped Second-phase Assessment
sl: SFC · virtual asset trading platforms on licensing process and revamped… (2024)
s: The SFC set out its virtual asset trading platform (VATP) licensing roadmap and a revamped Second-phase Assessment. After on-site inspections, deemed applicants get a conditional licence that requires completing a rectification plan. Plus a satisfactory independent penetration test and vulnerability assessment, before operating on a restricted scope of business. VATPs must then engage an External Assessor (EA) under a tripartite agreement with the SFC for the Second-phase Assessment. This is a direct assurance engagement, signed off by a practising accountant (CPA) under standards like HKSAE3000, that checks whether the VATP's policies. Procedures, systems and controls are suitably designed and implemented against the VATP Guidelines and AML/CFT Guideline. Once this is done satisfactorily, the SFC lifts the business-scope restriction.
w: For a bank, this binds VATPs, not the bank directly, but sets the exact assurance bar, penetration test, custody-system analysis. And tripartite external assessment, a compliance head should require evidence of before relying on a VATP's custody and security controls.
k: Deemed applicants get a conditional licence after agreeing a rectification plan with the SFC. As a licensing condition, they must complete rectifications and pass an independent penetration test and vulnerability assessment before operating on a restricted scope of business.
para 5-6, p.1

The vulnerability assessment should include analysis of the custody system's compiled code, including supply-chain libraries, to check production code matches the reviewed version, plus external and internal vulnerability scans.
Vulnerability assessment box, p.2

Penetration testing should check firewalls, servers, databases, wallets, network devices and customer-facing applications (desktop, web, mobile). Tests must cover both the application layer and the network layer.
Penetration test box, p.2
The VATP must engage an External Assessor (EA) under a tripartite agreement with the SFC to conduct the Second-phase Assessment.
para 8, 14, Appendix, p.2-3

The Second-phase Assessment must be a direct assurance engagement, for example under HKSAE3000, signed off by a practising certified public accountant. It assesses whether revised policies, procedures, systems and controls comply with the VATP Guidelines and AML/CFT Guideline.
para 13, p.2-3

As soon as practically possible, the VATP must tell the SFC and EA of any material change to its policies and procedures. And promptly report any material breaches or failures found during the assessment.
para 12, p.2
Once the Second-phase Assessment is completed to its satisfaction, the SFC will lift the licensing condition restricting the VATP's scope of business.
para 9, p.2
The SFC will pay HK$1 toward the Second-phase Assessment fees; the VATP pays the balance of total fees, disbursements and expenses.
footnote 4, p.2
rg: Read the full 3-page circular plus the 1-page Appendix flowchart, which shows the licensing and assessment sequence.

t: SFC licenses virtual asset trading platforms under swift licensing process
sl: SFC · SFC licenses virtual asset trading platforms under swift licensing… (2024)
s: The SFC granted licences to four virtual asset trading platform (VATP) applicants: Accumulus GBA Technology (Hongkong), DFX Labs Company, Hong Kong Digital Asset EX, and Thousand Whales Technology (BVI). This followed the SFC's swift licensing process for deemed applicants, after it finished risk-based on-site inspections of all deemed applicants. They may operate on a limited scope of business until they finish rectification work, plus a satisfactory independent vulnerability assessment and penetration test. The SFC published a matching circular on the licensing process and second-phase assessment the same day.
w: For a bank, this confirms four VATPs were licensed through a fast process only after on-site inspection and remedial work. And only with a limited business scope until second-phase assessment finishes, useful for scoping what a newly licensed VATP counterparty can and cannot yet do.
k: Four VATP applicants were licensed under the swift licensing process: Accumulus GBA Technology (Hongkong) Co. Limited, DFX Labs Company Limited, Hong Kong Digital Asset EX Limited, and Thousand Whales Technology (BVI) Limited.
Note 1

As a licence condition, they may operate on a limited scope of business after finishing rectification work from on-site inspection feedback. Plus a satisfactory independent vulnerability assessment and penetration test.
para 2
The SFC will oversee the whole second-phase assessment through three-way engagement with the VATPs and their outside assessors. And will lift business-scope limits once satisfied the work is done.
para 5
Remaining deemed-applicant applications keep being reviewed under the same swift licensing process. Further guidance for new, non-deemed VATP applicants was expected in early 2025.
Note 1, 4
rg: Short; read in full plus companion circular 6fc7dd34c485 for the licensing-process detail.

t: Hong Kong commits to implementing Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework
sl: FSTB · Hong Kong commits to implementing Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (2024)
s: The government told the OECD's Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information that Hong Kong will implement the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF). CARF is an OECD standard for automatic exchange of crypto-asset account and transaction information between tax authorities, extending the existing Common Reporting Standard model to crypto-assets. The government's initial plan is to have the local legislative amendments in place by 2026. And to start the first automatic exchanges with partner jurisdictions from 2028, on a reciprocal basis with jurisdictions that meet data confidentiality standards.
w: For a bank offering or facilitating crypto-asset services in Hong Kong. This signals it should anticipate future CARF-driven reporting and client due-diligence duties once the local legislative amendments are enacted. Likely feeding into existing tax-reporting and Common Reporting Standard (CRS) processes.
k: Hong Kong committed to the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, an annual automatic exchange mechanism. It covers account and transaction information on crypto-assets, shared between jurisdictions where the account holder is tax resident.
para 1-2

The government's initial plan targets the necessary local legislative amendments by 2026. And the first automatic exchanges under CARF from 2028, run reciprocally with partners meeting data confidentiality and security standards.
para 4
rg: Short press release; read in full for the two dated commitments.

t: LCQ15: Policy on digital assets
sl: FSTB · LCQ15: Policy on digital assets (2024)
s: In a written Legislative Council (LegCo) reply, the Acting Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury set out the government's digital-asset policy. The reply was given in response to questions about a dedicated crypto commissioner and bitcoin as a strategic reserve asset. It describes the government's existing approach: the Task Force on Promoting Web3 Development. The 2022 Policy Statement's same-activity-same-risk-same-regulation principle, and the virtual asset service provider licensing regime. It does not state whether a new department or commissioner will be created. It confirms plans to introduce the stablecoin bill within December 2024. Run a second over-the-counter (OTC) trading consultation in 2025, and introduce a virtual asset custodian licensing regime in 2025. It also states the Exchange Fund does not target crypto-assets, though external managers may hold small amounts. And that the Linked Exchange Rate System is unaffected by virtual asset developments.
w: For a bank, this confirms the government's official policy stance and legislative timetable for digital assets in one statement. It is useful for briefing senior management on the current regulatory approach and how the Exchange Fund and currency peg relate to virtual assets. It does not say whether a dedicated crypto commissioner will be created.
k: The government amended the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (AMLO) to introduce the existing licensing regime for virtual asset trading platforms.
reply para (1)-(2)
The Treasury bureau will introduce the fiat-referenced stablecoin issuer licensing bill to the Legislative Council within December 2024.
reply para (1)-(2)
A second public consultation on regulating over-the-counter virtual asset trading is planned for the following year. And a virtual asset custodian licensing regime will also be introduced that year.
reply para (1)-(2)
The Exchange Fund does not target crypto-assets as an investment class, though its external managers may hold small amounts as part of diversified mandates.
reply para (3)
The Linked Exchange Rate System is described as unaffected by virtual asset market developments, and remains the cornerstone of Hong Kong's monetary stability.
reply para (4)

In November 2023 the SFC issued two circulars: one on intermediaries' tokenised-securities-related activities, the other on how SFC-authorised investment products are tokenised. Both aim to make the regulator's investor-protection expectations clearer.
reply para (4), last paragraph
rg: Read the numbered reply paragraphs (1)-(4); skip the original Legislative Council question, which is speculative framing rather than government policy.

t: Gazettal of Stablecoins Bill
sl: Government · Gazettal of Stablecoins Bill (2024)
s: The government gazetted the Stablecoins Bill. It creates a licensing regime run by the Monetary Authority for anyone issuing fiat-referenced stablecoins in Hong Kong. Issuing stablecoins pegged to the Hong Kong dollar, or actively marketing such stablecoins to the Hong Kong public. The Bill also gives the Monetary Authority supervision, investigation, and enforcement powers over licensees. Officials say it fulfils Hong Kong's Financial Stability Board commitments and applies a same-activity, same-risk, same-regulation approach. The Bill had its first Legislative Council (LegCo) reading on 18 December 2024. And was later enacted as the Stablecoins Ordinance, so this gazettal announcement is now superseded by the enacted law.
w: For a bank, this is the origin point of Hong Kong's fiat-referenced stablecoin licensing regime. A bank that issues, markets, or partners with issuers of HKD-pegged or Hong Kong-marketed stablecoins needs to track this Bill through to the enacted ordinance.
k: A person must be licensed by the Monetary Authority to issue fiat-referenced stablecoins in Hong Kong. To issue stablecoins pegged to the Hong Kong dollar, or to actively market such stablecoins to the Hong Kong public.
para 2
The Bill gives the Monetary Authority supervisory, investigatory, and enforcement powers to run the licensing regime.
para 3
The Bill had its first reading in the Legislative Council on 18 December 2024.
para 6
rg: Short press release; read in full for the licensing trigger activities in paragraph 2.

t: Guideline on the Digital Bond Grant Scheme
sl: HKMA · Guideline on the Digital Bond Grant Scheme (2024)
s: This guideline sets the eligibility and application rules for the Digital Bond Grant Scheme (DBGS), a subsidy announced in the 2024 Policy Address to encourage tokenised bond issuance in Hong Kong. It reimburses 50% of eligible expenses per issuance. This is up to HK$1.25 million (Half Grant, basic requirements only) or HK$2.5 million (Full Grant, basic plus additional requirements), capped at two issuances per issuer group. Eligibility hinges on a Hong Kong nexus (lead arranger or DLT team presence, or issuance on the CMU's DLT platform). For the Full Grant, it also needs independence of the DLT platform provider, and a HK$1 billion minimum issuance size. It further needs at least five unrelated investors, and listing on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong (SEHK) or an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP).
w: For a bank, this gives a concrete cost-recovery incentive and eligibility checklist. Its treasury, debt capital markets (DCM) or digital-assets team should use this when structuring or arranging a Hong Kong digital bond issuance. It explicitly recognises listing on SFC-licensed VATPs as a qualifying route.
k: The DBGS reimburses 50% of Eligible Expenses per digital bond issuance, up to HK$1.25 million (Half Grant) or HK$2.5 million (Full Grant).
An issuer group, counting its associates as one, can draw DBGS support for no more than two digital bond deals.

To qualify at all, the issuance must be half-or-more arranged by Hong Kong-recognised lead arrangers. It must also either have a substantial Hong Kong DLT team, or be issued using the CMU's own DLT platform.

For the Full Grant, the digital bond must also use a DLT platform provider unrelated to the issuer, and be at least HK$1 billion equivalent in size. It must also be issued to five or more unrelated investors, and be listed on SEHK or a licensed VATP.
Eligible expenses include fees to unrelated DLT platform providers, Hong Kong-based arrangers, legal advisers, auditors/accountants/rating agencies, listing fees, and CMU lodging/clearing fees.

For green, social, sustainability or transition digital bonds, the issuer must pick one source for general issuance costs. It is either DBGS or GSF Grant Scheme Track I, capped at HK$2.5 million, not both. The external sustainability review sits separately under Track II, capped at HK$800,000.
Applicants may seek an optional pre-application consultation, then must submit a formal application within three months of the bond's issuance.
The scheme opened for applications on 28 November 2024 for an initial three-year period, and covers bonds issued on or after the 16 October 2024 Policy Address announcement.
p.1, footnote 1
The HKMA keeps full discretion over whether eligibility requirements are met and over the amount of any subsidy granted, and may adjust the scheme's design over time.
rg: Read the whole guideline (six pages); it is short and every section (Overview, Basic/Additional Requirements, Eligible Expenses, Application Process) is operationally relevant.

t: HKMA launches Digital Bond Grant Scheme
sl: HKMA · HKMA launches Digital Bond Grant Scheme (2024)
s: The HKMA launched the Digital Bond Grant Scheme (DBGS), announced in the 2024 Policy Address. It aims to grow Hong Kong's digital securities market and support wider take-up of tokenisation using distributed ledger technology (DLT). Per the attached Guideline, DBGS covers 50% of eligible expenses per digital bond issuance, up to HK$1.25 million (Half Grant) or HK$2.5 million (Full Grant). Each issuer, including associates, may claim for a maximum of two issuances. Basic Requirements include Hong Kong issuance/arranger presence, plus either substantial Hong Kong digital-team presence or issuance on a CMU-operated DLT platform. Additional Requirements for the Full Grant include an independent DLT platform provider, minimum HK$1 billion issuance size, five or more independent investors, and listing on SEHK or an SFC-licensed VATP. Applications opened 28 November 2024 for an initial three-year period, covering bonds issued on or after 16 October 2024.
w: For a bank, this directly matters as a prospective digital-bond issuer: it sets concrete eligibility conditions and a 3-month post-issuance filing deadline. The bank's treasury/DCM and compliance functions must plan around these to capture the HK$1.25m/2.5m grant.
k: Maximum grant per eligible digital bond issuance is HK$2.5 million (Full Grant); Half Grant caps at HK$1.25 million, covering 50% of Eligible Expenses.
Guideline s.1, p.2
Each issuer, together with its associates, can draw DBGS subsidies for at most two digital bond issuances.
Guideline s.1, p.2

Basic Requirements: the bond must be issued in Hong Kong, with half or more of lead arrangers being recognised arrangers. It must also have either a substantial Hong Kong digital team, or issuance on a CMU-operated DLT platform.
Guideline s.2, p.3

Additional Requirements for the Full Grant: the DLT platform provider must not be an associate of the issuer, and minimum issuance size is HK$1 billion equivalent. It must also be issued to five or more unrelated investors, and listed on SEHK or a licensed VATP.
Guideline s.3, p.4
Eligible expenses include DLT platform provider fees, Hong Kong-based arranger/legal/audit/rating fees, listing fees, and CMU lodging/clearing fees.
Guideline s.4, p.5

A green/social/sustainability bond that is also a digital bond cannot claim general issuance costs under both DBGS and GSF Track I. It can claim under only one, up to HK$2.5 million. External sustainability review costs are separately covered by GSF Track II, up to HK$800,000.
Guideline s.4, p.5
Formal application must reach the HKMA no later than three months after the bond is issued; an optional pre-application consultation with HKMA is available.
Guideline s.5, p.6
DBGS applications opened 28 November 2024 for an initial three-year period, eligible for bonds issued on or after 16 October 2024, the Policy Address announcement date.
para 1, footnote 1
rg: Read the press release plus the Guideline sections 1-5 (6 pages) in full — all are operative eligibility/process rules.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Eddie Yue on Project Evergreen: From concept to application
sl: HKMA · Eddie Yue on Project Evergreen: From concept to application (2024)
s: The HKMA Chief Executive reviewed Project Evergreen's progress on bond tokenisation after two successful tokenised government green bond issuances. He announced the launch of the Digital Bond Grant Scheme (DBGS), offering up to HK$2.5 million per eligible digital bond issuance. The article also describes 'EvergreenHub', a new knowledge repository on digital bonds. It sets out forward priorities too: interoperability between DLT platforms and conventional infrastructure, expanding secondary-market and repo use of digital bonds as collateral, and eventually extending tokenised bonds to retail investors. It notes the first-ever repo transaction in Hong Kong using a digital government bond as collateral.
w: For a bank, this sets out the HKMA's stated future direction for bond tokenisation, covering collateral mobility, interoperability, and retail access. This shapes what its markets, custody and collateral-management functions should plan for. It also flags a live grant scheme worth using for any qualifying digital bond issuance.
k: The Digital Bond Grant Scheme, offering up to HK$2.5 million per eligible digital bond issuance, began accepting applications the same day.
para 5
The second Project Evergreen tokenised bond issuance was roughly seven times the size of the first, and helped attract more institutional investors and secondary-market activity.
para 4
Earlier in 2024, two banks executed the first repo transaction in Hong Kong using the Government's digital bond as collateral.
para 4
The HKMA launched 'EvergreenHub', a single online resource pulling together material on digital bond transactions, and will keep adding to its content.
para 5

Forward priorities include interoperability between digital platforms and conventional infrastructure, mobilising digital bonds as repo collateral, and eventually extending tokenised bonds to retail investors.
paras 6-8
Project Evergreen (bond tokenisation) and Project Ensemble (broader tokenisation market infrastructure) are described as complementary and intersecting initiatives.
para 9
rg: Read in full; short article with each paragraph covering a distinct initiative. The DBGS eligibility detail is in the companion guideline (package item), not here.

t: Alert: Misrepresentation and misuse of the word “bank” in Hong Kong by crypto firms
sl: HKMA · Alert: Misrepresentation and misuse of the word “bank” in… (2024)
s: This is a follow-up HKMA alert citing two specific incidents. An overseas crypto firm hosting an event in Hong Kong reportedly called itself a 'bank'. Another firm marketed a 'bank card' product on its website. Neither is a licensed Hong Kong bank. The HKMA repeats that only authorized institutions may use the word 'bank' or carry on banking/deposit business, and that such misuse breaches the Banking Ordinance.
w: For a bank, this is a second HKMA alert (after fcbcbb5d9d99) on overseas crypto firms misusing 'bank' branding at Hong Kong events. It is relevant for customer-protection messaging and verifying counterparty authorized-institution status, not as a direct bank obligation.
k: At a Hong Kong-hosted event, an overseas non-bank crypto firm was reported to have described itself as a 'bank'.
para 2
A second overseas crypto firm marketed a 'bank card' product on its website despite not being a licensed bank.
para 2
Only licensed banks, restricted licence banks and deposit-taking companies may use the word 'bank' or run banking/deposit business in Hong Kong.
para 3
Products or services carrying the word 'bank' are not necessarily provided by a licensed Hong Kong bank.
para 4
rg: Read paras 1-4; the note restates the statutory sections already covered by the September 2023 alert.

t: Misrepresentation and misuse of the word "bank" in Hong Kong by crypto firms
sl: HKMA · Misrepresentation and misuse of the word "bank" in Hong… (2024)
s: The HKMA repeated its earlier caution (from its September 2023 notice on the same theme) about overseas crypto firms describing themselves as 'banks' or their products as 'bank cards' in Hong Kong. It said it had observed two specific instances at Hong Kong-hosted events: one firm representing itself as a bank, another describing a card product as a 'bank card'. It restated that only HKMA-authorised institutions may use 'bank' in their name or hold themselves out as such, under Banking Ordinance sections 97 and 97A. It again pointed the public to the authorized institution / restricted licence bank (AI/RLB) register for verification.
w: For a bank, this is a second, near-identical caution to the one issued in September 2023. It is useful mainly to confirm the concern is recurring rather than a one-off, for brand-protection monitoring purposes.
k: The HKMA observed two specific Hong Kong-hosted-event instances of overseas crypto firms making bank-related representations without authorisation.
para 2

Only a licensed bank in Hong Kong may use the word 'bank', or its letters in sequence, in its business description. The same applies to holding itself out as a bank, under Banking Ordinance sections 97 and 97A.
Note
rg: Skim; content substantially repeats the September 2023 HKMA notice on the same topic.

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism (1) FATF Statement on High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action (2) FATF Statement on Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring (3) Outcomes from the FATF Plenary, 23-25 October 2024
sl: SFC · licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities -… (2024)
s: This is a routine SFC anti-money laundering / counter-financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) circular relaying FATF's October 2024 statements. Countermeasures calls against North Korea (DPRK) and Iran continue; Myanmar remains subject to enhanced due diligence, with countermeasures to be considered if there is no progress by February 2025. The Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring list added Algeria, Angola, Cote d'Ivoire and Lebanon, and removed Senegal. It also relayed FATF Plenary outcomes. There was also a public consultation on proposed revisions to Recommendation 1 (risk-based approach) to support financial inclusion, targeted for finalisation in 2025.
w: For a bank, this is a routine FATF jurisdiction-list update that supersedes the July 2024 circular. It is notable for the addition of four new Increased Monitoring jurisdictions relevant to AML/CFT risk screening.
k: FATF reiterates countermeasures calls against DPRK and fully lifted the suspension of countermeasures against Iran (both carried forward from the prior circular).
Myanmar remains subject to an enhanced due diligence call; FATF will weigh countermeasures if Myanmar has not moved forward by February 2025.

t: Delivering Tax Transparency to Crypto-Assets: A Step-by-Step Guide to Understanding and Implementing the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework
sl: Other · Delivering Tax Transparency to Crypto-Assets: A Step-by-Step Guide to… (2024)
s: This is a general OECD/Global Forum guide for governments implementing the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) worldwide. It covers the legal, administrative and IT groundwork needed, and walks through the due-diligence and reporting rules. It is not Hong Kong-specific, but is the source material the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) points to for background on why CARF exists.
w: For a bank, this is useful only as background on the policy rationale for CARF; it has no Hong Kong-specific obligations for the bank.
k: CARF exists because crypto-asset service providers often sit outside traditional financial-institution reporting regimes, letting tax-relevant activity go unseen.

t: Introduction to HKEX Virtual Asset Index Series
sl: HKEX · Introduction to HKEX Virtual Asset Index Series (2024)
s: This HKEX brochure (November 2024) introduces the HKEX Virtual Asset Index Series. It publishes real-time reference prices and a daily settlement-oriented reference rate for Bitcoin and Ether, aggregated from major exchanges. It explains why an index is useful, since a virtual asset trades at different prices on different venues. It also gives basic market-cap comparisons showing Bitcoin and Ether ranking among the world's largest assets. It is exchange-operator product literature, not a rulebook.
w: For a bank that references HKEX's Bitcoin/Ether reference prices for product settlement or valuation, this background is relevant; it is marketing/product literature, not a regulatory benchmark standard.
k: HKEX's Reference Index updates in real time, giving a volume-weighted spot price over a rolling 24-hour window, built from prices on major virtual asset exchanges.
The daily Reference Rate, meant for settling financial products, is fixed once a day within the 3-4pm Hong Kong time window.
HKEX positions the index series as solving the problem that a cryptocurrency can trade at several different prices across exchanges at once.
By mid-2024 cited data, Bitcoin ranked among the top ten assets globally by market value, alongside gold and major tech companies; Ether also ranked in the top 25.
p.2, market-cap chart

It sets out the government's general approach to encouraging responsible AI adoption while monitoring risk. It has no digital-asset, tokenisation, crypto, or stablecoin content; it is included here only because it is linked from the FSTB fintech overview page alongside digital-asset material.

t: HKEX to Launch HKEX Virtual Asset Index Series

HKEX frames it as supporting Hong Kong's position as a digital-asset hub and as a tool investors can use to price virtual assets.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority partners with Bank of Thailand on Cross-Border Tokenisation Initiatives
sl: HKMA · Hong Kong Monetary Authority partners with Bank of Thailand… (2024)
s: The HKMA said it is teaming up with the Bank of Thailand (BOT) on cross-border tokenisation, joining the HKMA's Project Ensemble with BOT's own initiative, Project San. This builds on a 2019 memorandum of understanding (MoU) and earlier joint work, namely Project Inthanon-LionRock and Project mBridge. The two central banks plan to trial tokenised settlement models, a currency-for-currency exchange method and an asset-for-payment method, in areas such as trade payments and carbon credits. They will also build a proof-of-concept connecting the two projects' distributed ledger technology (DLT) infrastructures. Project San is a BOT-only effort dating from June 2024, building a settlement engine for large-value payments together with ledgers compatible with the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM).
w: For a bank, this confirms Project Ensemble's compatibility testing now reaches EVM-compatible ledger infrastructure through Thailand's Project San. This is relevant for weighing which DLT standards Hong Kong's wholesale settlement ecosystem is converging on.

t: Guideline on Authorization of Digital Banks
sl: HKMA · Guideline on Authorization of Digital Banks (2024)
s: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) issued this guideline under Banking Ordinance section 16(10). It sets the principles the HKMA uses when deciding whether to authorize a digital bank. A digital bank is a bank that serves customers wholly or mainly through the internet or other electronic channels. The guideline replaces the Guideline on Authorization of Virtual Banks. Applicants must meet the usual minimum authorization criteria and must keep a physical office in Hong Kong. The HKMA expects them to be locally incorporated and to have committed, capable owners. The guideline stresses technology risk, a credible path to profit, an exit plan, fair treatment of customers and early discussion of material outsourcing. Digital banks are supervised on the same basis as other banks, with some rules adapted to their model.
w: It sets the entry rules for a bank that operates mainly online. It also shows the HKMA's expectations on exit plans, independent IT assessments and outsourcing for technology-led banks. The guideline does not mention virtual or digital assets.
k: A digital bank applicant must show real substance and a credible business plan, not just a concept riding on new technology.
para 5
Digital banks should not impose minimum balance requirements or low-balance fees.
para 6

The HKMA expects digital banks to be locally incorporated. A holder of more than 50% should normally be a supervised bank or financial institution. Otherwise, the HKMA expects a Hong Kong intermediate holding company with supervisory conditions.
para 8-9
Tech firms and other non-financial groups, as well as financial firms and existing banks, may seek to own a digital bank.
para 9
Digital banks face the same supervisory requirements as conventional banks, with some adapted on a risk-based, technology-neutral basis; boards need relevant technology knowledge.
para 11
Applicants must commission an independent expert review of planned IT governance and systems, and a fuller review before starting operations.
para 15
The HKMA would be concerned by aggressive market-share growth with heavy losses and no credible medium-term path to profit.
para 19
Applicants must provide an exit plan for an orderly wind-down if the business model fails.
para 20
The HKMA's view is that customers should not bear direct losses from unauthorized transactions unless they were fraudulent or grossly negligent.
para 22
Digital banks should discuss plans for material outsourcing with the HKMA in advance. They should show that the principles of the outsourcing module (SPM SA-2) will be met.
para 23

t: Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2023 (Commencement) Notice 2024
sl: Government · Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2023 (Commencement) Notice 2024 (2024)
s: A legal notice fixed 1 January 2025 as the day two sections of last year's banking capital rule changes take effect. This brings Hong Kong's rulebook into line with the Basel Committee's final post-crisis reform package. One section covers how banks measure lending risk, including a floor on how low internally-modelled numbers can go, plus day-to-day operating risk and exposure to weak sovereigns. The other section covers trading-book risk and the extra capital charge for worsening counterparty creditworthiness; the notice itself needed a routine Legislative Council check before taking effect.
w: For a bank, this is the general Basel III capital framework taking effect, not a crypto-specific rule. It uses the same Banking (Capital) Rules that the HKMA's cryptoasset exposure proposals (CP 24.01) will later amend, so compliance should track it as the baseline rule set.
k: 1 January 2025 is fixed as the day the two remaining sections of the 2023 capital rule amendments become law.

body para 2

t: Guidelines on Competence
sl: SFC · Guidelines on Competence (2024)
s: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) issued these guidelines under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), section 399. They explain how the SFC judges whether a firm or a person is competent to carry on a regulated activity (RA). They apply to licensed firms and to banks registered as registered institutions (RIs). They also apply to a bank's executive officers (EOs) and its staff on the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) register. An EO must meet the same bar as a responsible officer (RO). A registered bank employee must meet the same bar as a licensed representative. For firms, the SFC looks at the business model, governance, staffing, controls, independent review, risk and compliance. For individuals, it looks at qualifications, industry and management experience, and a pass in a local regulatory paper.
w: This sets the experience and exam bar for the bank's EOs and front-line staff in any SFO-regulated digital-asset business, including a compliance head who wants EO status. It also tells the RI what records the HKMA may ask for to prove staff competence.
k: An EO of an RI must clear the same competence bar as an RO, and a relevant individual (ReI) on the HKMA register faces the same as a licensed representative.
para 2.2
The RI itself must make sure an ReI meets the competence bar before submitting the name to the HKMA, and the HKMA considers these guidelines when deciding on EO consent.
para 2.2
For ReIs, the RI should keep records showing how each requirement was met and produce them if the HKMA asks.
para 2.5(b)
A firm is judged on its business model, governance, people, controls, independent review, risk and compliance set-up, and on the combined ability of senior management and staff.
para 3.1.1
Supervisory staff in both front and back office should have at least three years of relevant experience plus suitable qualifications.
para 3.2.1, Staff competencies (b)
One element the SFC considers is an operational review function. The function is independent of the business, reports to a high-level independent authority, and assesses risk at least once a year.
para 3.2.1, Operational review (c)-(d)
Firms must stay competent, keep their people competent including on continuous professional training (CPT), and tell the SFC about material changes in business plans, structure or staff.
para 3.1.4
An RO or EO applicant must show they can properly manage and supervise the proposed activity.

Under the standard routes, an RO or EO applicant needs at least three years of relevant industry experience in the past six years. One route instead asks for five years in the past eight. The applicant also needs two years of management experience and a pass in the local regulatory framework paper (LRP).
para 4.2.1.2 (table)
Management experience means hands-on supervision of regulated functions or projects and staff; purely administrative supervision, such as HR or office staff, normally does not count.
Direct experience in a highly innovative technology can count as relevant industry experience. The person must have been key to building or running it, and it must be central to the new firm's RA.
Recognised industry qualifications and the LRP should normally be obtained within three years before the application.
para 4.1.5
rg: Read paras 2.1-2.6 on how the rules apply to banks, then 3.2 for firm-level expectations and 4.1-4.2 for EO requirements. Appendices A and B (sponsors, takeovers) can be skipped.

t: Keynote speech at the Treasury Markets Summit 2024
sl: HKMA · Keynote speech at the Treasury Markets Summit 2024 (2024)

Its only virtual-asset content is a short passage on Project mBridge, a multi-central-bank digital-currency platform. By the time of the speech, mBridge had reached its minimum viable product stage, a tool meant to cut cross-border payment cost and time. t: Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers in Hong Kong
sl: HKMA · Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers in Hong Kong (2024)
s: This is a feature article from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's (HKMA) Quarterly Bulletin, published just after its July 2024 consultation conclusions. It explains in plain language why Hong Kong is regulating stablecoin issuers, covering market history such as the DeFi Summer, the TerraUSD depeg and the FTX collapse. It also covers the proposed licensing requirements and the HKMA's stablecoin issuer sandbox, which launched in July 2024. The first sandbox participants tested payments, supply chain and capital markets uses. Joining the sandbox was not required before applying for a licence. It also warns of scams that falsely claim sandbox or licensed status, and records the HKMA's plan to bring a stablecoin bill to the Legislative Council.
w: For a bank, this is a useful plain-English briefing on why the stablecoin regime exists and how the sandbox worked. Its scam warning is a reminder to check any counterparty's claimed sandbox or licensed status against the HKMA's published list, not the counterparty's own claim.
k: The article groups requirements into four areas: stablecoin stability, reserve safekeeping, issuer governance, and risk management including anti-money laundering controls.
Exhibit 2, p.4
Only stablecoins issued by licensed issuers were intended to be offerable to retail investors, restricting unlicensed issuers to non-retail distribution.
The sandbox, launched July 2024, lets firms test business models and get HKMA feedback; joining it is not required before applying for a licence.
The first batch of three sandbox participants (admitted July 2024) tested use cases in payments, supply chain management and capital markets applications.
Sandbox testing capped user numbers and issuance size and barred customer or public funds at first; HKMA could expand scope later.
HKMA flagged a rising trend of scams where entities falsely claimed to be licensed issuers or sandbox participants, and published a genuine participant list online.
At the time of writing, HKMA planned to bring the stablecoin bill to the Legislative Council before end-2024, ahead of the regime's 1 August 2025 start.
Conclusion, p.7

t: Report on the Review of Virtual Banks
sl: HKMA · Report on the Review of Virtual Banks (2024)
s: This August 2024 Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) report reviews the eight virtual banks (now called digital banks) that launched from 2020. It finds they met the policy aims of promoting fintech, a new customer experience and financial inclusion. They had 2.2 million depositors by end-2023, but none was yet profitable. Six were registered with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) for securities business by July 2024. The HKMA saw no strong reason to license more virtual banks at that time. It said it would remove the rule that virtual banks must mainly serve retail customers, citing their growing dealings with businesses, including the digital asset sector. It says banks' digital-asset activities are supervised on a risk-based, 'same risk, same regulation' basis. The focus is prudential risk, anti-money laundering and financial crime risk, and investor protection.
w: It records the HKMA's position that digital-asset activities at any bank, digital or incumbent, are supervised on the same risk-based footing, and that a risk assessment is expected before starting. It also explains why digital banks may now serve the digital-asset business sector.

t: Consultation conclusions for legislative proposal to implement regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers in Hong Kong released
sl: FSTB/HKMA · Consultation conclusions for legislative proposal to implement regulatory regime… (2024)
s: The Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) and the HKMA jointly released their conclusions on the proposed licensing regime for stablecoin issuers. This followed 108 submissions during the December 2023-February 2024 consultation. Fiat-referenced stablecoins (FRS) in circulation must always be fully backed by reserve assets, with no break at any time. Reserves must generally match the referenced currency, though HKD issuers may hold USD reserves with the Monetary Authority's (MA's) flexibility. Reserve assets must be kept separate and safeguarded through trust or custodian arrangements, usually with licensed Hong Kong banks, and redemption must happen within one business day at par. Paying interest to FRS users is banned, though marketing incentives are not. Minimum paid-up capital is HK$25 million or 1% of FRS in circulation, whichever is higher, down from the 2% first proposed. Non-Hong Kong incorporated issuers, other than authorized institutions, must set up a Hong Kong subsidiary, and only a specified group of licensed entities may offer FRS to the public. A six-month grace period was set, and the bill was to go to the Legislative Council (LegCo) later in 2024.
w: For a bank, this became the blueprint later enacted as the Stablecoins Ordinance. A compliance head should use it to plan the reserve segregation, redemption-timing, no-interest and audit-attestation controls the bank would need to issue an FRS.
k: The full value of FRS in circulation must be matched by reserve assets without exception, at every point in time. Issuers must show the MA that steps such as over-collateralisation are in place to meet this.
para 3.2.3, p.10 (attachment 54aa01e7396e)

Reserve assets must generally be held in the same currency the FRS references; MA prior approval is required for a currency mismatch. HKD-referenced FRS issuers may hold USD-denominated reserves with MA flexibility.

Reserve assets must be kept separate from the issuer's own assets, and safeguarded through an effective trust arrangement, generally safekept with licensed Hong Kong banks. A draft trust deed and independent legal opinion must go to the HKMA for review.
A qualified independent auditor must attest to reserve assets monthly, no matter how large the FRS in circulation is.
FRS issuers must not pay interest to FRS users, whether directly or through a third party. Marketing incentives stay allowed if they do not amount to interest.

Redemption requests must be met within one business day in normal circumstances, at par value in the referenced currency, without undue cost. MA prior approval is needed if an issuer expects difficulty meeting this timeframe.
FRS issuers are banned from lending or financial intermediation. Only activities that support FRS issuance, such as wallet services for their own FRS, are allowed.

Non-Hong Kong incorporated companies, other than authorized institutions incorporated outside Hong Kong, must set up a Hong Kong subsidiary to apply for a licence. Key management, the chief executive and alternate, must be based in Hong Kong.
The minimum paid-up share capital was set at whichever is greater of HK$25 million or 1% of FRS's circulating par value, down from the 2% floor first proposed.

The public may only be offered FRS by a specified licensed entity: an FRS issuer holding an HKMA licence, an authorized institution, a licensed corporation, or a licensed VATP. None needs a separate MA licence to offer FRS, but each must meet its own regime's rules.
A six-month grace period was set for FRS issuers that already existed before the regime started.
The FSTB and HKMA planned to introduce a bill to the Legislative Council later in 2024, with licensing and supervisory guidelines to follow.
rg: Read the Regulatory Framework for FRS Issuers section (pages 8-22) in full; it holds nearly all the operative rules. The Scope and Legislative Approach sections (pages 4-8) and Way Forward (page 29) give context; skip the Annex list of 108 respondent names.

t: Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers in Hong Kong – Consultation Conclusions
sl: FSTB/HKMA · Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin… (2024)
s: Published jointly by the FSTB and HKMA in July 2024, this paper responds to 108 submissions on the December 2023 consultation paper. It confirms the authorities will go ahead with a licensing regime for fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers. It keeps the core proposals: full reserve backing, redemption rights, and HKMA licensing. It clarifies what counts as 'actively marketing' to the Hong Kong public, and confirms HKD-referenced coins issued from outside Hong Kong are still covered. A bill was to go to the Legislative Council (LegCo) later in 2024.
w: For a bank, this shows how the government tightened the stablecoin regime after feedback, including confirming HKD-pegged coins are covered even from outside Hong Kong. This matters for cross-border product screening and checking a stablecoin counterparty's licensing status.
k: The scope was narrowed so the regime targets stablecoins run on distributed ledgers not controlled by a single party, rather than covering privately-run ledgers too.
para 1.4, p.5
Both single-currency and multi-currency referenced stablecoins stay in scope. Multi-currency issuers face rules scaled to the extra complexity of managing reserves in several currencies.
Whether marketing counts as 'active marketing' depends on factors like the language used, whether the audience is Hong Kong-based, and use of a Hong Kong domain name.
An overseas entity issuing a Hong Kong dollar-referenced stablecoin still needs an HKMA licence, even if it operates outside Hong Kong, because of the currency's local importance.
Agents or intermediaries who market a licensed issuer's stablecoin on its behalf do not themselves need a licence, but anyone promoting an unlicensed issuer's coin commits an offence.
The authorities confirmed a bill to bring in the regime would go to the Legislative Council later in 2024, with the HKMA to issue licensing and supervisory guidelines afterwards.
The six-month grace period for existing issuers to apply for a licence was kept, informed partly by experience running the HKMA's stablecoin issuer sandbox.
rg: Read the Introduction (pages 3-4) and the responses under Scope and Coverage (section 1, pages 4-7) and Way Forward (section 12, page 29). You should read it alongside the original consultation paper, which it amends rather than replaces.

t: Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers in Hong Kong – Consultation Conclusions
sl: FSTB/HKMA · Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin… (2024)
s: This paper sets out the FSTB's and HKMA's final positions on the future fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuer licensing regime, after a two-month consultation that drew 108 responses. It confirms the regime covers stablecoins on decentralised distributed ledgers referencing one or more fiat currencies, and requires full reserve backing at all times. High-quality liquid assets must be kept separate from the issuer's own assets. It bans paying interest to holders, requires local incorporation and Hong Kong-based key management, and sets minimum capital at the higher of HK$25 million or 1% of stablecoins in circulation. It also confirms redemption must happen within one business day, and that only specified licensed entities may offer FRS to the public. A bill was to go to the Legislative Council (LegCo) later in 2024.
w: For a bank, this is the direct policy blueprint for what became Hong Kong's stablecoin issuer licensing regime. A bank issuing a stablecoin, partnering with an issuer, offering FRS to clients, or acting as reserve custodian needs every reserve, redemption, capital and offering rule here reflected in its own controls.
k: The definition of a regulated stablecoin was narrowed to those run on a 'decentralised distributed ledger', meaning no single party can unilaterally control or materially change how it works.
para 1.4
Both single-currency and multi-currency fiat-referenced stablecoins (FRS) stay in scope, because both can pose financial stability risk through their links to the traditional financial system.
para 1.6
Stablecoins in circulation must be backed 1:1 by reserve assets at all times; issuers must show steps such as over-collateralisation to keep meeting this on an ongoing basis.
para 3.2.3

Reserve assets must be high quality and highly liquid. Allowed categories include cash and banknotes, deposits at licensed banks, high-credit-quality government or central-bank securities, related overnight reverse repos, and tokenised versions of these assets.
para 3.2.9

Reserve assets must generally be in the same currency the stablecoin references; a currency mismatch needs the Monetary Authority's (MA's) prior approval and may trigger extra rules such as over-collateralisation. HKD-referenced stablecoins may explicitly hold USD-denominated reserves.
para 3.2.10

Reserve assets must be kept separate from the issuer's own assets and safeguarded under an effective trust arrangement. Safekeeping with licensed Hong Kong banks is favoured, though offshore placement may be allowed case by case.
Issuers must get monthly independent auditor attestation of reserve assets, though how often this is disclosed publicly may be reduced from the original proposal after industry feedback.
Issuers may not pay interest to stablecoin holders, though non-interest marketing incentives stay allowed.

Redemption requests must be met within one business day in normal conditions, at par value, without undue cost or unreasonable conditions; issuers expecting difficulty must seek the MA's prior approval.
para 3.2.25
Issuers may only carry out activities that support stablecoin issuance, such as wallet services for their own coin; lending and financial intermediation are explicitly excluded.
para 3.2.28
Non-Hong Kong incorporated applicants, other than authorized institutions, must set up a Hong Kong subsidiary, and key executives, the chief executive and alternate, must be based in Hong Kong.
Minimum paid-up share capital is set at whichever is greater of HK$25 million or 1% of the stablecoins in circulation, valued at par, down from the 2% originally proposed.
para 3.2.33
rg: Read the full body, from Introduction through Way Forward (paragraphs 1-12); the Annex list of respondents (pages 30 onward) can be skipped.

t: Statements issued by the Financial Action Task Force
sl: HKMA · Statements issued by the Financial Action Task Force (2024)
s: This routine circular relays the FATF's June 2024 Plenary outcomes. It confirms extra checks still apply to Iran, North Korea and Myanmar, and points banks to the updated 'Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring' list. It notes the FATF finished a fifth update on virtual asset and virtual asset service provider (VASP) rules, and kept talking about payment-transparency Recommendation 16. This is a periodic list relay, not a new rule.
w: For a bank, this confirms AML high-risk-jurisdiction screening lists stay current. It also flags that FATF's review of virtual-asset AML rules was being updated, relevant to any bank with VASP customers.
k: Banks should keep applying extra checks and countermeasures to Iran and North Korea, under the HKMA's March 2020 circular. They should also apply risk-based extra checks for Myanmar, which stays on FATF's call-for-action list.
At its June 2024 Plenary, the FATF finished a fifth targeted review of how well countries have put its virtual asset and VASP rules into practice, with the full report due later.

Rather than changing payment-transparency Recommendation 16, the FATF agreed to keep talking with stakeholders, given the rules' complexity and possible effect on payment systems; the HKMA will update the industry.
rg: Skim; skip the repetitive country-list boilerplate and read only the VA and Recommendation-16 paragraph on page 2 for crypto relevance.

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism (1) FATF Statement on High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action (2) FATF Statement on Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring (3) Outcomes from the FATF Plenary, 26-28 June 2024
sl: SFC · licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities -… (2024)
s: This routine SFC anti-money laundering (AML) circular relays FATF's June 2024 statements. FATF fully lifted the suspension of countermeasures against Iran, moving from extra checks to a full call for countermeasures. It repeated its call for countermeasures against North Korea (DPRK), and kept Myanmar under a call for extra checks, warning countermeasures will be considered if there is no progress by October 2024. The 'Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring' list added Monaco and Venezuela, and removed Jamaica and Turkiye. It also relayed FATF's fifth annual update on VASP standards, published 9 July 2024, which found implementation still lagging globally, and noted continued talks on proposed Recommendation 16 changes.
w: For a bank, Iran's move from extra checks to a full countermeasures call raises the AML bar for any Iran-linked exposure. It also confirms FATF's own view that global VASP rule implementation still lags.
k: FATF fully lifted the suspension of countermeasures against Iran, calling on members to apply effective countermeasures, because Iran has not brought the Palermo and Terrorist Financing Conventions into force as required.
p.2, Iran section
FATF repeated its call for countermeasures against North Korea (DPRK), given continued AML deficiencies and proliferation-financing risk.
p.1-2, DPRK section
Myanmar stays subject to a call for extra checks; if there is no further progress by October 2024, FATF will consider countermeasures.
p.2, para (ii)
The Increased Monitoring list was updated: Monaco and Venezuela were added; Jamaica and Turkiye were removed.
p.2, section (2)

FATF's fifth annual update on jurisdictions' progress on virtual asset and VASP standards was published 9 July 2024. It found implementation still lagging globally, despite some progress since June 2023.
p.3, para (a)
FATF agreed to keep talking with public and private sector bodies before finalising proposed Recommendation 16 changes, given their complexity and possible impact.
p.3, para (b)
rg: Focus on the Iran escalation (page 2) and the jurisdiction-list changes (page 2, section 2). The DPRK and Myanmar wording is largely carried over from the earlier circular.

t: SFC warns public of seven entities for suspected virtual asset-related fraud

t: SFC warns public of Tokencan, VBIT Exchange and HKD.com Corporation for suspected virtual asset-related fraud and/or unlicensed activities
sl: SFC · SFC warns public of Tokencan, VBIT Exchange and HKD.com… (2024)
s: The SFC warns of three unlicensed operators. Tokencan gave the SFC false information and falsely claimed it had filed a licence application; investors were later locked out of their accounts. VBIT Exchange falsely claimed to be regulated by overseas authorities. HKD.com Corporation copied the name and logo of another VATP; its victims deposited funds into bank accounts and then could not withdraw them. Police blocked the related websites.
w: For a bank, this shows a range of unlicensed-operator tactics to watch for: lying to the regulator, and copying a licensed platform's brand.
k: Tokencan gave the SFC false information and falsely claimed to have filed a Hong Kong licence application.

'VBIT Exchange' bullet

'HKD.com Corporation' bullet

t: Collaboration between BDF and HKMA Unlocks New CBDC Cross-border Opportunities
sl: HKMA · Collaboration between BDF and HKMA Unlocks New CBDC Cross-border… (2024)
s: The Banque de France (BDF) and the HKMA announced they will work together on wholesale central bank digital currency (CBDC). The HKMA is taking part in Wave 2 of the European Central Bank's Eurosystem exploratory work, as a major central bank outside the Eurosystem. The two institutions will study how BDF's DL3S platform and the HKMA's Project Ensemble Sandbox can work together. The focus is real-time cross-border, cross-currency (HKD-EUR) settlement, where payment and delivery happen at the same time.
w: For a bank, this is background only. It records an HKMA-Banque de France agreement to explore cross-border tokenised HKD-EUR settlement, and creates no obligation at this stage.
k: The HKMA is taking part in Wave 2 of the ECB's Eurosystem exploratory work, a notable step as a major central bank outside the Eurosystem.

t: SFC briefs virtual asset trading platform applicants on regulatory expectations after transition period ends
sl: SFC · SFC briefs virtual asset trading platform applicants on regulatory… (2024)
s: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) held a briefing for more than 60 people, including consultants and firms treated as 'deemed-licensed' applicants to run a virtual asset trading platform (VATP). It covered what the SFC expects and how to apply for a licence, and introduced a new on-site inspection programme. It repeated that the transition period under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (AMLO) ended on 1 June 2024. From that date, every VATP operating in Hong Kong must hold an SFC licence, or qualify as a deemed-to-be-licensed applicant under AMLO Schedule 3G.
w: For a bank, this confirms the SFC began active on-site inspections of deemed-licensed VATPs right after the transition cutover in June 2024.
k: The SFC briefed over 60 people -- deemed-to-be-licensed VATP applicants and their consultants -- on what skills it expects and how to apply for a licence.

t: LCQ9: Promoting development of stablecoins and virtual assets
sl: Government · LCQ9: Promoting development of stablecoins and virtual assets (2024)
s: The government gave this written reply to the Legislative Council (LegCo) about stablecoins and virtual assets (VA). It said consultations on licensing stablecoin issuers and VA over-the-counter (OTC) service providers were both done, with bills to follow. The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) let VA spot exchange-traded funds (ETFs) apply from December 2023, and six such ETFs launched within months. It also gave an update on the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's (HKMA) e-CNY pilot with mainland China's central bank.
w: For a bank, this confirms the stablecoin and VA OTC licensing regimes are moving from consultation to law. It is useful for regulatory planning, not for immediate action.
k: Public consultations on licensing stablecoin issuers and VA OTC service providers were both completed, with bills to go to LegCo soon.

reply para (3)

t: Project mBridge reaches MVP stage
sl: HKMA · Project mBridge reaches MVP stage (2024)
s: Project mBridge reached 'minimum viable product' (MVP) stage, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) announced. This cross-border payment platform is run by four founding central banks, working with the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub. Each founding bank ran its own network node, and commercial banks in all four places made real payments on the platform. The Saudi Central Bank has now joined as a full member, and private firms can propose new uses.
w: For a bank, this shows a live cross-border central bank digital currency (CBDC) settlement platform is working, with commercial banks already making real payments on it.
k: Project mBridge reached MVP stage, with each of its four founding central banks -- HKMA, the Bank of Thailand, mainland China's central bank, and the UAE's central bank -- running its own network node.

t: SFC statement on the end of non-contravention period for virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · SFC statement on the end of non-contravention period for… (2024)
s: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) said the grace period under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (AMLO) for virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs) ends on 1 June 2024. From that date, every VATP in Hong Kong must be SFC-licensed or a 'deemed-to-be-licensed' applicant, since unlicensed operation is a criminal offence. A deemed-to-be-licensed applicant is NOT formally licensed, must not market to or onboard new retail clients before showing effective controls, and must keep Mainland Chinese residents from accessing services. The SFC will run on-site inspections focused on client-asset safeguarding and know-your-client (KYC) checks, and will swiftly refuse licences where key investor-protection rules are breached.
w: For a bank, the key check is that 'deemed-to-be-licensed' is not the same as licensed. Such VATPs must also block Mainland China access, before the bank treats a VATP counterparty as durable.
k: From 1 June 2024, all VATPs in Hong Kong must be SFC-licensed or deemed-to-be-licensed applicants under the AMLO; unlicensed operation is a criminal offence.
para 1
Firms on the deemed-to-be-licensed applicant list do not hold an actual SFC licence, and the SFC may still turn down their applications.
para 3, Note 2
The SFC does not expect deemed-to-be-licensed applicants to market services or onboard new retail clients before showing effective controls and becoming formally licensed.
para 4
VATPs and their ultimate owners must stop Mainland Chinese residents from accessing virtual-asset services, and ensure related parties do the same.
para 5
Any non-compliance with key investor-protection regulatory requirements by a deemed-to-be-licensed applicant will result in swift refusal of its licence application.
para 6
The SFC will run on-site inspections of deemed-to-be-licensed applicants, focused on client-asset safeguards and KYC processes, feeding into licence decisions.
para 7
Deemed-to-be-licensed applicants must hire a qualified external assessor to check how well their controls have actually been implemented, under the scope the SFC set out in June 2023.
Note 3

s: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) confirmed that from 1 June 2024, all virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs) in Hong Kong must be SFC-licensed or 'deemed-to-be-licensed' applicants. t: CG-6 Competence and Ethical Behaviour
sl: HKMA · CG-6 Competence and Ethical Behaviour (2024)
s: This Supervisory Policy Manual (SPM) module is version 4, dated 23 May 2024. It is non-statutory guidance from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) on how authorized institutions keep all staff competent and ethical, not only those who need HKMA consent. It links staff competence to the Banking Ordinance (BO) criterion that a bank's business is run with integrity, prudence and professional competence. The board is ultimately responsible. The board should review manpower action plans, with measurable targets, at least once a year. Banks are strongly encouraged to use the Enhanced Competency Framework (ECF) as a benchmark. Banks should not launch new products until staff understand the products, markets and rules.
w: Before a bank offers any digital-asset product, this module expects staff to understand the product and the rules, and the board to have a talent and reskilling plan. It gives the compliance head a basis to require training sign-off before launch and to escalate competence failures to the HKMA.
k: The expectations cover staff at every level, beyond directors, CEs, EOs, s.72B managers and SFO relevant individuals.
para 1.5
Banks that are RIs should ensure relevant individuals meet the SFC's initial competence requirements, as also noted in SB-1.
para 1.5, fn 2
The board is ultimately responsible and should embed a culture of competence and ethics, with recruitment and appraisal weighing competence and integrity.
The board should set direction for manpower development; senior management should propose talent plans with measurable targets, which the board reviews at least once a year.
para 2.4
Banks are strongly encouraged to use the ECF as a benchmark for staff competence and to support staff to gain ECF certifications.
Staff who are not yet competent should not do the work without close supervision; reviewing output after the event is unlikely to be enough supervision on its own.
para 3.5
A bank should not launch new products or activities unless satisfied staff know the products, markets and applicable rules.
para 3.7.4
Competence should be monitored regularly and reflected in appraisal and variable pay, drawing on audit, compliance findings and complaints.
Where staff incompetence causes significant losses or likely serious reputational damage, the bank should tell the HKMA promptly and discuss remedial steps.
para 4.1.3
Banks should assess how technology changes job roles and keep a long-term reskilling plan with measurable targets approved by the board.
para 4.2.2
Where work is outsourced, the bank should check and keep monitoring the provider's competence using staff with the right expertise.
para 2.9
rg: Read sections 2 and 3.7 (competence criteria including new products) and 4.1.3 (HKMA notification); section 5 covers ethics expectations.

t: Expanding the cross-boundary e-CNY pilot in Hong Kong
sl: HKMA · Expanding the cross-boundary e-CNY pilot in Hong Kong (2024)
s: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and the People's Bank of China (PBoC) widened the cross-border e-CNY trial in Hong Kong. Hong Kong residents can now open e-CNY wallets with just a local mobile number and top them up through the Faster Payment System (FPS) at 17 participating retail banks. The HKMA called this the world's first link between a real-time payment system and a central bank digital currency (CBDC). e-CNY wallets support cross-border retail spending but not transfers between individuals, and now also work in mainland pilot zones beyond the Greater Bay Area.
w: For a bank, this shows a cross-border e-CNY and FPS link that some retail banks already support as a top-up channel. It creates no new duty for the bank itself.
k: Hong Kong residents can open a personal (tier-4) e-CNY wallet at one of four wallet operators using only a Hong Kong mobile number.
Annex 1/2, p.1
Retail customers can top up e-CNY wallets through FPS at 17 Hong Kong banks; some of these let users convert HKD to RMB directly.
Annex 1, p.1

para 1, p.1

Annex 2, Usage, p.2
Tier-4 personal wallets cap balances at RMB10,000, transactions at RMB2,000, daily totals at RMB5,000, and yearly totals at RMB50,000, though operators can set tighter limits.

t: Expanding cross-boundary e-CNY pilot in Hong Kong
sl: HKMA · Expanding cross-boundary e-CNY pilot in Hong Kong (2024)
s: Hong Kong widened its trial of China's digital yuan (e-CNY), in partnership with the mainland central bank, letting residents set up a wallet with just a Hong Kong phone number. They add funds through the local instant-payment rail, the Faster Payment System (FPS), via a set list of retail banks. para 2.2.4

t: Risk management considerations related to the use of DLT
sl: HKMA · Risk management considerations related to the use of DLT (2024)
s: This Annex lists ten non-binding considerations the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) applies when reviewing a bank's distributed ledger technology (DLT) projects. They are grouped under governance, application design and development, and ongoing maintenance and monitoring. Key themes include board-level ownership of DLT risk, careful choice of network type, smart-contract governance and audit, and legal-risk awareness around settlement finality. Other themes are third-party and node-operator due diligence, interoperability, cybersecurity matching traditional systems, secure private-key management, data-privacy compliance on unchangeable ledgers, and DLT-specific contingency planning.
w: For a bank, this is the HKMA's working checklist for any DLT proposal -- tokenised deposits, custody platforms, settlement systems. Technology and compliance teams should map each planned DLT initiative against these considerations before HKMA submission, since supervisors will actually probe them.
k: A bank's board and senior management are fully responsible for adopting DLT and managing its risks. This includes updating risk, continuity and outsourcing policies, and ensuring enough in-house DLT expertise and staff training.
Annex, item 1 (Governance)
Where a DLT solution is customer-facing, the bank should review whether DLT-specific consumer education, dispute handling, redress and compensation mechanisms are needed.
Annex, item 1

DLT network-type choice (permissionless, private- or public-permissioned) affects security, stability, scalability and resilience. The HKMA expects the bank to justify its choice against the risk profile, with compensating controls for higher-risk designs.
Annex, item 2
Permissionless networks are not always the best fit for moving sensitive data. But they need not be ruled out if the bank shows mitigations like zero-knowledge proofs or hybrid on/off-chain designs.
Annex, item 2

Where smart contracts are used, the bank must manage the operational, third-party and legal risks, with governance covering suitability assessment, due diligence, design controls, upgrades, and audits before deployment.
Annex, item 3

Because settlement finality and legal standing under DLT can be less clear than under traditional systems, banks should identify these grey areas, seek professional advice where needed, and build in mitigations.
Annex, item 4

Banks must assess whether a DLT network's node operators are trustworthy, reliable and diverse enough. They should avoid permissionless networks, where node operators may be pseudonymous, for critical functions unless adequate controls exist.
Annex, item 5

Banks should design DLT systems to work with traditional and other DLT systems where practicable. That way a tokenised deposit is not confined to the issuing bank's own network, while interbank links stay secure.
Annex, item 6

DLT applications must have cybersecurity as strong as traditional systems. This covers DLT-specific threats such as 51% attacks and common threats such as DDoS, with response plans updated for risks like quantum computing.
Annex, item 7

Banks acting as custodian of client digital assets should apply stricter private-key security: secure generation, storage, backup, access controls and cold storage, cross-referencing the HKMA's separate custody circular.
Annex, item 8, footnote 3

Banks must keep complying with data privacy rules whether data sits on a centralised system or a DLT ledger. This means addressing issues like data retention on an unchangeable ledger, confidentiality on transparent ledgers, and data localisation.
Annex, item 9
For DLT used in critical functions, business continuity plans should include DLT-specific test scenarios -- common cyberattacks, key loss or theft, forking -- and backup options for DLT outages.
Annex, item 10
rg: Read all ten considerations (pp.2–6); each is short and none is boilerplate.

t: HKMA launches Phase 2 of the e-HKD Pilot Programme
sl: HKMA · HKMA launches Phase 2 of the e-HKD Pilot Programme (2024)
s: The HKMA announced Phase 2 of the e-HKD Pilot Programme. This builds on Phase 1, completed October 2023, which studied domestic retail use cases such as programmable payments, tokenised-asset settlement and offline payments. Phase 2 will go deeper into selected Phase 1 pilots, such as programmability, tokenisation and atomic settlement, plus new use cases. It is supported by an enhanced e-HKD sandbox built on the wCBDC sandbox under Project Ensemble. Applications to participate were due by 17 May 2024.
w: For a compliance head, this is informational. It confirms e-HKD pilot infrastructure and Project Ensemble's tokenised-deposit sandbox are technically converging. This is useful context for the bank's digital-asset roadmap, but not a source of any obligation.
k: The e-HKD Pilot Programme's first phase wrapped up in October 2023, covering programmable payments, tokenised-asset settlement, and offline payments.
para 2, p.1
Phase 2 will explore selected Phase 1 pilots more deeply (programmability, tokenisation, atomic settlement) plus new use cases.
para 2, p.1
An enhanced e-HKD sandbox, leveraging the wCBDC sandbox under Project Ensemble, will support Phase 2. It will study interoperability and interbank settlement between e-HKD and other tokenised money.
para 3, p.1
Organisations interested in Phase 2 should submit applications by 17 May 2024.
para 5, p.1
