t: HKMA launches Phase 2 of e-HKD Pilot Programme
sl: HKMA · HKMA launches Phase 2 of e-HKD Pilot Programme (2024)
s: The HKMA launched Phase 2 of its e-HKD (retail central bank digital currency) pilot. This builds on Phase 1's findings on programmable payments, tokenised asset settlement and offline payments. Phase 2 would go deeper on programmability, tokenisation and atomic settlement, using an enhanced sandbox linked to the Project Ensemble wCBDC sandbox. It would explore interoperability between e-HKD and other tokenised money. Applications to participate were due by 17 May 2024.
w: For a bank, this is still a research pilot with no compliance obligations. But it signals the infrastructure, such as atomic settlement and tokenised money interoperability, that could later underpin mandatory retail payment rails.
k: Phase 2 builds on Phase 1 use cases (programmable payments, tokenised asset settlement, offline payments) and adds a deeper focus on programmability, tokenisation and atomic settlement.

t: SFC warns public against unlicensed virtual asset trading platform Bybit
sl: SFC · SFC warns public against unlicensed virtual asset trading platform… (2024)
s: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) warns that Bybit is not licensed for any regulated activity in Hong Kong. Bybit offers many derivative-like and yield crypto products across global markets, and these can count as futures contracts or securities under Hong Kong law. So marketing or dealing in them to Hong Kong investors needs a licence, unless an exemption applies. A similarly named Hong Kong firm, Spark Fintech Limited, which runs a '.com.hk' website, is not related to Bybit's products.
w: For a bank, this warning shows that crypto derivatives, staking and lending products can count as futures or securities under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). A compliance head should apply that classification check to any platform a client mentions.
k: No entity in the Bybit group holds an SFC licence or SFC registration for any regulated activity in Hong Kong.
para 3
Bybit's products listed include futures, options, leveraged tokens, dual-asset products, liquid staking, lending and wealth management.
bullet list

para 4
Issuing related advertisements to the Hong Kong public without SFC authorisation is also an offence.
para 5
A separate, similarly-named Hong Kong-incorporated company (Spark Fintech Limited, bybit.com.hk) is not involved in offering these products.
Notes, note 1

t: Stablecoin Issuer Sandbox
sl: HKMA · Stablecoin Issuer Sandbox (2024)
s: The HKMA announced the launch of a sandbox for firms planning to launch stablecoins pegged to fiat currencies in Hong Kong. This follows a December 2023 consultation paper on a future licensing regime. The sandbox lets the HKMA communicate supervisory expectations and gather feedback from participants testing stablecoin business models, in a limited, risk-controlled way. Admission requires a genuine plan to issue stablecoins, a concrete testing plan, and a reasonable prospect of meeting future rules. Sandbox status is not a licence, and does not guarantee a future licence. The HKMA warned the public to watch for scams using the sandbox's name.
w: For a bank, this marks the start of direct HKMA engagement with prospective stablecoin issuers, ahead of the eventual Stablecoins Ordinance. A bank considering issuing or partnering with a sandbox participant should check the published participant list, rather than rely on a counterparty's own claims.
k: Applicants must show genuine interest in, and a workable plan for, launching fiat-referenced stablecoins from Hong Kong. They must also have a concrete sandbox participation plan, and a reasonable prospect of eventually complying with the proposed rules.
section 'Eligibility for accessing the sandbox', para 11
Sandbox testing will run on a limited scale, and will not use members of the public's money at the initial stage. The HKMA can adjust the scope as testing goes on.
section 'Testing in the sandbox', para 15
Sandbox participants who break the terms can have their participation ended by the HKMA.
para 17
Being admitted to the sandbox does not mean the HKMA or any other regulator endorses or regulates the firm. A separate licence application will still be needed once the regime is in force.
para 17
Sandbox applicants should not reveal their application before admission. Admitted participants should seek the HKMA's agreement before making public announcements about their status.
section 'Staying alert to virtual asset scams', para 21
The HKMA will post the names of sandbox participants online and update the page regularly so the public can check claims.
para 21

t: HKMA launches stablecoin issuer sandbox arrangement
sl: HKMA · HKMA launches stablecoin issuer sandbox arrangement (2024)
s: The HKMA launched a sandbox for firms with a genuine interest in launching fiat-referenced stablecoins from Hong Kong. It is tied to the ongoing consultation on a stablecoin issuer licensing regime. The sandbox lets the HKMA communicate supervisory expectations and gather feedback on the proposed rules before the regime is finalised. Admission does not amount to HKMA endorsement or a licence. A separate application will be needed once the regime is implemented.
w: For a bank, if it or an affiliate wants to issue a stablecoin in Hong Kong, this sandbox is the pre-licensing route. It lets a firm shape and test compliance expectations before the regime is legally binding. For banks not issuing, it signals which counterparties may soon carry an HKMA-recognised sandbox status worth checking in due diligence.
k: The sandbox is for parties with genuine interest and a reasonable business plan to issue fiat-referenced stablecoins in Hong Kong; it is not itself a licence or an endorsement.

Annex, Objectives bullet 3

t: HKMA launches the stablecoin issuer sandbox arrangement
sl: HKMA · HKMA launches the stablecoin issuer sandbox arrangement (2024)
s: The HKMA launched a sandbox arrangement for parties with a genuine interest in launching fiat-referenced stablecoins from Hong Kong. It is tied to the ongoing consultation on the proposed stablecoin issuer regulatory regime. The sandbox lets the HKMA communicate supervisory expectations and gather industry feedback before the regime is finalised. Per the attached Annex, applicants register interest via a dedicated HKMA email. Admission is not an endorsement or a guarantee of eventual licensing. Participants must seek HKMA agreement before making public statements about their participation, and can be withdrawn for non-adherence or voluntary exit.
w: For a bank, this establishes the sandbox through which prospective stablecoin issuers, including banks, could engage with the HKMA before the licensing regime was finalised. It is relevant mainly if the bank is or becomes a sandbox participant or issuer applicant.
k: The sandbox is intended to support virtual-asset ecosystem development, communicate supervisory expectations, gather feedback on proposed requirements, and develop good practices (reserves management, governance, user protection, AML/CFT, data transparency).
Annex, Objectives, p.1
Admission to the sandbox does not mean HKMA endorsement or that the participant is qualified for future regulation.
Annex, Objectives, p.1
Sandbox participants wishing to apply for a licence after the regime is implemented must submit a separate application to the licensing authority.
Annex, Objectives, p.1
Applicants should demonstrate genuine interest, a reasonable stablecoin issuance plan, a concrete sandbox participation plan, and a reasonable prospect of complying with proposed requirements.
Annex, Factors for Consideration, p.1
Before admission, no applicant should make announcements about application status. After admission, any announcement about sandbox participation should first get HKMA agreement.
Annex, Others, p.2
A participant is deemed withdrawn if HKMA finds it fails to adhere to its anticipated operation, or if it voluntarily exits with advance notice.
Annex, Others, p.2

t: HKMA unveils Project Ensemble to support development of Hong Kong tokenisation market
sl: HKMA · HKMA unveils Project Ensemble to support development of Hong… (2024)
s: The HKMA announced Project Ensemble: a wholesale central bank digital currency (wCBDC) programme meant to back interbank settlement of tokenised money. The initial focus is tokenised deposits issued by commercial banks. These would use the wCBDC as a settlement foundation for tokenised asset transactions, such as green bonds, carbon credits and trade documents. A wCBDC Sandbox and an industry Architecture Community, including banks and technology firms, were planned to test use cases and set standards.
w: For a bank, tokenised deposits are a bank-issued product. So if the bank's treasury or digital-asset unit wants to participate, compliance should track evolving expectations on tokenised deposit issuance and custody arising from this initiative from the start.
k: Project Ensemble is a wholesale CBDC initiative to enable interbank settlement of tokenised money, initially focused on bank-issued tokenised deposits.
body para 2
A wCBDC Sandbox would test tokenisation use cases including settlement of green bonds, carbon credits, aircraft, EV charging stations, e-bills of lading and treasury management.
body para 3

body para 4

body para 6

t: HKMA unveils Project Ensemble to support the development of the Hong Kong tokenisation market
sl: HKMA · HKMA unveils Project Ensemble to support the development of… (2024)
s: The HKMA announced Project Ensemble: a wholesale central bank digital currency (wCBDC) effort meant to back Hong Kong's tokenisation market. It will initially focus on tokenised deposits (a digital representation of commercial bank deposits) as the settlement asset for tokenised real-world-asset transactions (e.g. green bonds, carbon credits, aircraft, EV charging stations, e-bills of lading, treasury management). A wCBDC Sandbox is planned to launch later that year, supported by a wCBDC Architecture Community of banks, digital-asset firms, tech companies and the CBDC Expert Group. The HKMA said it may conduct a 'live' wCBDC issuance later if the sandbox garners sufficient industry interest.
w: For a bank, no compliance obligation attaches yet. But a compliance head should track Project Ensemble as the origin of the tokenised-deposit infrastructure the bank may be asked to connect to. This carries governance and control implications once real transactions begin.
k: Project Ensemble will explore new financial market infrastructure enabling interbank settlement of tokenised money via a wholesale CBDC (wCBDC).
para 2, p.1
Initial focus is tokenised deposits — a digital form of the deposits that commercial banks issue and offer to the public.
para 2, p.1

para 3, p.1

t: SFC reminds public VATP application period has ended under transitional arrangements
sl: SFC · SFC reminds public VATP application period has ended under… (2024)
s: The SFC reminded the public that the 29 February 2024 deadline for virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs) operating in Hong Kong to submit licence applications had passed. This was under the AMLO Schedule 3G transitional arrangements. VATPs that did not apply by that deadline must close their Hong Kong business by 31 May 2024. Continuing to operate unlicensed is a criminal offence. Investors were urged to check the SFC's lists of licensed VATPs and VATP applicants, and to close accounts with, or transfer away from, platforms not on either list.
w: For a bank, this is a counterparty-due-diligence checkpoint, not a bank obligation. After the cutover date, compliance must verify any HK VATP counterparty is licensed or a listed applicant, since operating unlicensed is now a criminal offence for that platform.
k: VATPs operating pre-1 June 2023 that missed the 29 February 2024 licence-application deadline must close down their Hong Kong business by 31 May 2024 under AMLO Schedule 3G transitional arrangements.

t: The 2024-25 Budget
sl: Government · The 2024-25 Budget (2024)
s: In the digital finance and Web3.0 sections of the 2024-25 Budget speech, the Financial Secretary reported on the HKMA's e-HKD pilot. It had wrapped up the first phase and was moving into the second. He said Project mBridge cross-border central bank digital currency settlement was progressing. He announced expansion of the e-CNY pilot in Hong Kong. He confirmed the government had issued a second, larger multi-currency batch of tokenised government green bonds. He said the government had consulted on a stablecoin issuer licensing regime, and that the HKMA would soon launch a stablecoin issuer sandbox. He also referenced the SFC's existing VA trading platform licensing regime and the new OTC trading consultation.
w: For a bank, this speech is a policy roadmap, not a binding rule. But it signals where regulators will next legislate, on stablecoins and VA OTC. It also previews infrastructure, such as e-HKD, tokenised deposits and mBridge, that the bank's product and treasury teams may need to plan for.

t: Provision of Custodial Services for Digital Assets
sl: HKMA · Provision of Custodial Services for Digital Assets (2024)
s: This cover letter introduces the HKMA's expected standards, set out in the accompanying Annex, for banks that safekeep clients' digital assets. This applies whether as part of virtual-asset intermediary activity, tokenised-product distribution, or standalone custody. It applies to banks and to subsidiaries of locally incorporated banks. It covers 'digital assets' broadly: virtual assets, tokenised securities, other tokenised assets, and the private keys used to access them. It requires banks already offering such custody to confirm compliance with the Annex's standards within six months.
w: For a bank, this sets the trigger date compliance must track. Any bank already custodying client digital assets as of February 2024 had a firm six-month deadline to self-certify compliance with the detailed standards in the Annex. Any new custody launch needs pre-clearance with the HKMA.
k: The circular applies to 'digital assets' broadly: virtual assets as defined under the AML ordinance, tokenised securities, and other tokenised assets. It expressly extends to the means of accessing them, meaning private keys, seeds and their backups.
footnote 1, p.1
The circular does not apply to custody of a bank's own proprietary digital assets that are not held on behalf of clients.
footnote 1, p.1
Banks should apply the expected standards whether the digital assets are received while acting as a virtual-asset intermediary, distributing tokenised products, or providing standalone custody.
A bank planning to launch digital asset custody should talk to the HKMA before doing so, and satisfy the HKMA that it meets the expected standards.
Implementation, p.2

Banks already providing digital asset custody should review and, if necessary, revise their systems and controls. They should notify the HKMA confirming compliance with the Annex within six months of the circular's date.
Implementation, p.2

t: Guidance on Expected Standards on Provision of Custodial Services for Digital Assets by Authorized Institutions
sl: HKMA · Guidance on Expected Standards on Provision of Custodial Services… (2024)
s: This Annex sets the HKMA's detailed, numbered expected standards for a bank's custody of client digital assets. It covers governance, segregation, safeguarding of keys, delegation/outsourcing, disclosure, record-keeping, AML/CFT and ongoing monitoring. Core requirements include client-asset segregation from the bank's own assets, and board-level risk oversight before launch. They include a written key-management policy covering generation through destruction, a numeric cold-storage floor, and insurance/compensation floors for virtual assets specifically. They also include strict limits on who a bank may delegate custody to. The standards are risk-based for most digital assets, but become prescriptive, effectively mandatory, minimums for virtual assets.
w: For a bank, these are the concrete, numeric custody minimums it must satisfy: 98% cold storage, 50%/100% compensation cover, and a permitted-delegate list. They also set the segregation, key-management and disclosure controls an examiner will test against. This is one of the most operationally binding documents in the batch for a custody-offering bank.
k: Before launching digital asset custody, a bank must complete a comprehensive risk assessment, and put in place policies and controls. The board and senior management must exercise effective oversight, both before launch and on an ongoing basis.
Annex, para 1

A bank must allocate adequate resourcing and expertise to custody activities. It must ensure staff and control-function personnel have the necessary knowledge and skills, kept current through ongoing training given the pace of change.
Annex, paras 2–3

A bank must have clear accountability, roles, responsibilities and reporting lines for custody. It must have adequate policies to identify, manage and mitigate conflicts of interest, for example between the bank's own activities and its affiliates.
Annex, para 4
A bank must hold client digital assets in accounts, including wallet addresses, segregated from its own assets. This protects them from the bank's creditors on insolvency or resolution.
Annex, para 6

A bank must not transfer, lend, pledge, re-pledge or encumber client digital assets. Exceptions are to settle transactions or fees owed by the client, with the client's prior written consent, or as required by law. The bank must have controls to stop client assets being used for its own account.
Annex, para 7

A bank must have effective controls that cut the chance of client digital assets being lost to theft, fraud, negligence or misappropriation. These controls must also stop access being delayed or lost.
Annex, para 8

A bank may take a risk-based approach to safeguarding controls generally. But where client digital assets are virtual assets, the detailed controls in paragraph 11 are 'generally required', not merely risk-based options.
Annex, para 11

Required key-management controls include generating and storing seeds and private keys, and backups, in tamper-resistant environments such as a hardware security module (HSM), ideally offline. They include generating, storing and backing them up in Hong Kong. They include strict need-to-know access with multi-factor authentication and audit trails. And they include splitting keys among multiple authorised personnel (key sharding) to avoid a single point of failure.
Annex, para 11
For client virtual assets under custody, a bank should keep 98% of the total safely offline in storage with no internet connection. This applies unless there is good reason to do otherwise.
Annex, para 11, footnote 6

For client virtual assets under custody, a bank should maintain compensation or insurance covering at least 50% of the virtual assets held in cold storage. It should cover 100% of those in hot or other storage.

Deposits and withdrawals of client digital assets should only be allowed through wallet addresses confirmed to belong to the client. This can be verified, for example, by message signing or a micropayment test, and the addresses whitelisted.
Annex, para 11
As a general rule, for virtual assets a bank can hand its custody role only to another authorized institution, or its subsidiary, or an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform.

t: Sale and distribution of tokenised products
sl: HKMA · Sale and distribution of tokenised products (2024)
s: The HKMA sets out its expectation for when a bank sells a 'tokenised product' to customers. A tokenised product is a digital wrapper around a real-world asset, excluding securities-law-regulated tokens and stablecoins. The same consumer-protection rules that already apply to the underlying non-tokenised product apply equally to its tokenised form. Banks are expected to do enhanced due diligence on issuers and technology vendors, and disclose tokenisation-specific risks to customers. They must put proper risk-management and custodial controls in place before launching such sales. The circular does not create a new licensing regime; it layers tokenisation-specific expectations on top of existing product rules.
w: For a bank, this confirms that selling a tokenised product does not escape existing suitability, disclosure and conduct rules. Compliance must extend, not replace, its existing product-governance and disclosure controls to cover tokenisation-specific risks. It must also pre-clear new tokenised offerings with the HKMA.
k: The circular covers tokenised digital representations of real-world assets, such as structured investment products and precious metals. It does not apply to instruments already regulated under the Securities and Futures Ordinance, or to stablecoins.
Coverage section, footnote 1, p.1

As a general rule, the existing supervisory and investor-protection requirements for a traditional product also apply to its tokenised version. This is because the tokenised form carries the same terms, features and risks as the underlying asset, apart from tokenisation-specific risk.
General principle, p.1

Tokenisation can change a product's substance; for example, fractionalised tokenised interests may become a collective investment scheme. Because of this, banks should independently evaluate the terms, features and risk of each tokenised product, and use professional judgment on which legal regime applies, seeking outside advice if unsure.
Before selling a tokenised product, banks should have adequate systems, controls and additional internal controls addressing the product's specific tokenisation risks.

Banks should perform ongoing due diligence on the tokenised product itself, on its issuer, and on any third-party technology vendor, such as the tokenisation platform. This includes their track record and systems for managing ownership and technology risk.
Section A, p.3

Due diligence should specifically cover private-key management, safeguards against theft, fraud or hacking, and technology audits, including smart-contract audits where used. It should also cover contingency plans for DLT network failure or loss of private keys.
Section A, p.3–4

Before offering a tokenised product, banks should disclose tokenisation-specific risks to customers, in plain, non-technical language. These include DLT network risk, cybersecurity vulnerability, transfer restrictions, smart-contract risk, legal uncertainty on ownership or settlement finality, and custodial risk.
Section B, p.4–5

A bank issuing a tokenised product itself should apply the same due-diligence expectations to its own issuance. It should consider the most appropriate custodial arrangement, with extra care for permissionless public tokens.
Banks providing custody of tokenised products should separately meet the HKMA's expected standards on digital asset custody (the companion custody circular).
Section D, p.6
Banks intending to engage in tokenised-product activities should discuss their plans with the HKMA in advance of launch
Implementation, p.6
rg: Read the General principle and Sections A–D (pp.1–6) in full; the circular is short and has no skippable boilerplate.

t: Government launches consultation on legislative proposals to regulate over-the-counter trading of virtual assets

It applies the same anti-money-laundering standard already used for licensed VA trading platforms. The full legislative proposals are set out in the attached consultation paper.

t: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposals to Regulate Over-the-Counter Trading of Virtual Assets
sl: FSTB · Public Consultation on Legislative Proposals to Regulate Over-the-Counter Trading… (2024)
s: This paper proposes a new licensing regime for businesses that buy and sell virtual assets for cash over the counter (OTC), including physical shops and digital platforms. It would be run by the Commissioner of Customs and Excise (CCE), rather than the SFC or HKMA. Licensees would only be able to trade VA-for-money, and transfer coins to wallets the customer can prove they own. They could only offer tokens already tradable by retail investors on an SFC-licensed platform, or stablecoins issued by an HKMA-licensed issuer. Authorized institutions, licensed corporations and licensed VA trading platforms providing such services would be exempt from the new regime, because they are already regulated. The paper proposes fines up to HK$1 million and up to two years' imprisonment for operating without a licence.
w: For a bank, it would itself be exempt from this specific licensing regime if it provides VA OTC-type services. But its retail and private-banking teams should know that, once enacted, sending client funds to an unlicensed OTC shop becomes a criminal offence for the counterparty. This is relevant to fraud-typology monitoring and customer education.
k: A VA OTC licence would be required for anyone conducting spot VA-for-money trading as a business, whether through a physical outlet, ATM, or digital platform.
para 2.6, p.6
Licensees could not offer VA-to-VA conversion trades; customers wanting that would need to use a licensed VA trading platform instead.
para 2.12, p.9
Licensees could only offer tokens that retail investors can already access via an SFC-licensed VA trading platform, or stablecoins from an HKMA-licensed issuer.
Authorized institutions (banks), licensed corporations and licensed VA trading platforms providing OTC services would be exempt from the new regime, since they are already regulated by the HKMA/SFC.
Operating an unlicensed VA OTC business would be an offence carrying a fine of HK$1 million and up to two years' imprisonment.

CCE would gain powers to inspect premises, investigate, arrest, and impose sanctions including licence suspension or revocation, plus a proposed power to block websites of unlicensed or fraudulent operators.
Proposed transitional period is six months, during which pre-existing operators must apply for a licence within the first three months to keep operating.
rg: Read Chapter 1 (background, paras 1.1-1.6) and Chapter 2's scope, eligibility and sanctions sections (paras 2.6-2.30); the 15 consultation questions can be skimmed.

t: Cryptoasset Exposures — Consultation Paper CP 24.01
sl: HKMA · Cryptoasset Exposures — Consultation Paper CP 24.01 (2024)
s: The HKMA proposes to bring the Basel Committee's December 2022 global standard on banks' cryptoasset exposures into Hong Kong's capital, liquidity, leverage and large-exposure rules. It targets an effective date no earlier than 1 July 2025. Cryptoassets are split into Group 1 (tokenised traditional assets and stablecoins meeting four strict conditions) and Group 2 (everything else). Group 2 gets far more punitive treatment. This includes a 1,250% risk weight and, for systemically important banks, a hard cap of 1-2% of Tier 1 capital. Banks must self-classify every cryptoasset they hold on an ongoing basis, document the assessment, and tell the HKMA before acquiring a new type. The HKMA can overrule the bank's classification. The paper also sets out liquidity, leverage, large-exposure, operational-risk, disclosure and risk-governance expectations. A 2025 letter to the industry shows the HKMA has since moved to a soft consultation on draft rule text. So this paper is the original blueprint, not the current in-force wording.
w: For a bank, this is the master blueprint for how much capital, liquidity and large-exposure headroom it will need to hold against any cryptoasset business. It sets a hard ceiling on speculative (Group 2) exposure for systemically important banks. Compliance needs classification, documentation and pre-notification processes in place well before the rules bite, even though the exact commencement date has since moved.
k: The HKMA does not plan to bring the new capital rules into effect any earlier than 1 July 2025. Rule-gazetting and Legislative Council tabling are expected in Q2 2025.
para 11

Banks must continuously assess whether each cryptoasset they are exposed to meets the four classification conditions. They must keep full documentation available to the HKMA on request, and must tell the HKMA before acquiring a new type of cryptoasset.
para 14
The HKMA can override a bank's own classification of a cryptoasset if it disagrees with the bank's assessment.
para 15

Cryptoassets fall into two broad groups. Group 1, tokenised traditional assets and cryptoassets with an effective stabilisation mechanism such as certain stablecoins, gets treatment close to the underlying traditional asset. Group 2, everything failing those tests, gets much harsher capital treatment.
para 17

To qualify as Group 1, a cryptoasset must pass four cumulative tests on an ongoing basis. It must confer the same legal rights as the traditional asset, or have an effective peg. All rights must be clearly and legally enforceable, and transfers final. The token's network and functions must not create material added risk. And every entity performing key functions, such as redemption, custody or settlement, must be regulated or subject to appropriate risk standards.

A stablecoin only meets condition 1 if its reserve assets equal or exceed the aggregate redemption value at all times, including under stress; where risky, it must overcollateralise. Reserves must be of minimal market or credit risk, held in matching currencies, and independently audited at least annually, with daily value and weekly composition disclosure.
para 23
A cryptoasset arrangement only meets condition 2 if full redemption can happen within a five-calendar-day window from the time it is requested, at all times.
para 26

A bank adopting the basic approach must risk-weight almost all Group 1a and Group 1b cryptoassets at 1,250%, meaning it must hold capital equal to the exposure. It cannot use them as collateral, unless they are issued by the HKSAR Government or a designated public sector entity.
paras 36, 40 n.10

Systemically important banks (G-SIBs and D-SIBs) must cap their total Group 2 cryptoasset exposure at no more than 1% of Tier 1 capital as a normal ceiling. They must never exceed 2%. Breaching 1% requires prompt notification to the HKMA and rapid rectification. Any exposure above the limit is treated at the harsher Group 2b rate in the meantime.
paras 130–133

A Group 2 cryptoasset defaults to the harshest (Group 2b) capital treatment. This applies unless the bank proves to the HKMA's satisfaction that it meets the Group 2a hedging-recognition tests. These tests are: a regulated derivative or ETF exists, the asset is highly liquid, and sufficient price and volume data exists.
paras 68–69

Banks must maintain a monitoring framework to verify at all times that a stablecoin's peg-stabilisation mechanism is actually working. They must document the evidence used, including for newly launched coins where data is thin.
para 22

Operational risk from cryptoasset activity must be captured through the standard operational-risk framework (Business Indicator and Internal Loss Multiplier). If that is insufficient, the HKMA will act through the supervisory review process.
para 109
rg: Read paragraphs 1-23 (scope, timeline, classification conditions) and paragraphs 130-145 (exposure limits, risk management, disclosure) closely. The credit and market-risk RWA mechanics in paragraphs 31-100 can be skimmed, unless the bank runs a trading desk in tokenised instruments.

t: HKSAR Government’s Digital Green Bonds Offering
sl: HKMA · HKSAR Government’s Digital Green Bonds Offering (2024)
s: The HKSAR Government announced the successful offering of roughly HK$6 billion in multi-currency Digital Green Bonds (HKD, RMB, USD, EUR) under the Government Green Bond Programme. It builds on the HKMA's 2021 Project Genesis proof of concept.

t: Cryptoasset Exposures - Consultation paper | CP 24.01
sl: HKMA · Cryptoasset Exposures - Consultation paper (2024)
s: The HKMA sets out how it plans to apply the Basel Committee's global capital rules for banks' cryptoasset holdings in Hong Kong. It sorts cryptoassets into Group 1 (tokenised traditional assets and well-backed stablecoins that pass strict tests) and Group 2 (everything else, including most crypto). Each group gets very different capital, liquidity and large-exposure treatment. It also caps how much of a systemically important bank's capital can sit in Group 2 cryptoassets. The paper invited comments by 6 May 2024 and targeted an effective date no earlier than 1 July 2025.
w: For a bank, this is the rulebook that will decide how expensive it is to hold, trade or provide derivatives on any cryptoasset once finalised. Compliance needs to track classification of every crypto exposure now, since misclassification carries capital, liquidity and reporting consequences.
k: Cryptoassets fall into Group 1 (tokenised assets or stablecoins that meet four strict tests) or Group 2 (everything else). Only Group 1 gets treatment close to the underlying traditional asset.

A stablecoin's stabilisation mechanism only meets classification condition 1 if its reserve assets equal or exceed the peg value at all times. They must also be minimal-risk and currency-matched, and externally audited at least annually, with value disclosed daily and composition disclosed weekly. A separate condition (condition 2) requires full redeemability within five calendar days.
Banks must assess and document classification of every cryptoasset on an ongoing basis, and tell the HKMA in advance before acquiring a new type. The HKMA can override a bank's own classification.
Group 2 cryptoassets that fail hedging tests get a punitive 1,250% risk weight, meaning a bank must hold capital equal to the full value of the position.

A cryptoasset can only count as a high-quality liquid asset if it is a Group 1a tokenised version of an asset that already qualifies. The tokenised and traditional forms must both meet the same eligibility tests.
para 112, p.35

Only systemically important banks (G-SIBs/D-SIBs) face a formal ceiling. Group 2 cryptoasset exposure should generally stay under 1% of Tier 1 capital, and must never exceed 2%. Breaches must be reported to the HKMA as soon as practicable.

Banks must fold cryptoasset risk into existing risk-management frameworks: board-approved risk appetite, and operational resilience per SPM OR-1/OR-2. They must tell the HKMA about their actual and planned cryptoasset activities.
Banks must give qualitative and quantitative public disclosures on cryptoasset business activities, risk management and exposures, following the SPM CA-D-1 disclosure principles.
Planned local timeline: preliminary consultation in H2 2024, draft rule consultation in Q1 2025, gazetting in Q2 2025, with revised rules taking effect no earlier than 1 July 2025.
Table 1, para 11, p.6
rg: Read paragraphs 1-20 (scope and classification conditions) and paragraphs 129-145 (large exposures, Group 2 limit, risk management, disclosure) first. The detailed market-risk formulas in paragraphs 71-100 can be skimmed unless the bank trades Group 2a instruments.

t: SFC urges investors to check regulatory status of virtual asset trading platforms as transition period will end soon

t: A new phase in virtual asset regulation
sl: FSTB · A new phase in virtual asset regulation (2024)
s: In this blog post, the Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury restates that Hong Kong's approach to virtual assets (VA) is risk-based. It follows the principle 'same activity, same risk, same regulation'. It recaps the VASP (virtual asset service provider) licensing system that began operating on 1 June 2023, and notes two licensed platforms could then offer Bitcoin and Ethereum trading to retail investors. It sets out the transitional-arrangement deadlines for VASPs operating before licensing began. These VASPs had a 29 February 2024 deadline to apply for a licence. Those not treated as licensed must wind down by 31 May 2024, or within three months of a 'No-deeming notice' (a notice that a VASP will not be treated as licensed). It also flags an imminent consultation on regulating OTC virtual asset venues, and reminds the public that the stablecoin issuer consultation with the HKMA was closing that same month.
w: This blog is a useful contemporaneous regulator statement of the VASP transitional deadlines, and of the pipeline for OTC-venue and stablecoin-issuer regulation. Both are directly relevant to how a bank should screen VA counterparties and anticipate upcoming regimes. The specific 2024 deadlines are now historical, though, and should be checked against the final rules that followed.
k: Existing VA service providers operating before the licensing regime must have submitted a licence application by 29 February 2024, to be considered for treatment as a licensed provider ('deemed-licensed' status).
para 4
The SFC will issue a 'No-deeming notice' to applicants it considers unable to meet the transitional arrangement's requirements.
para 4
Existing service providers that miss the 29 February 2024 deadline, or receive a No-deeming notice, must cease operations by 31 May 2024, or within three months of the notice -- whichever applies.
para 4

para 5

The government intends to bring OTC (over-the-counter) virtual asset venues -- physical shops and online platforms -- under regulation, and will launch a public consultation on this shortly. This is partly because OTC venues played a role in some fraud cases involving unlicensed VA platforms.
para 6

A joint HKMA/FSTB public consultation on a legislative proposal for a stablecoin-issuer licensing regime was due to close at the end of February 2024. It covered all qualified fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers.

t: Disciplinary Proceedings at a Glance (for regulated persons under Part 5B of AMLO)
sl: SFC · Disciplinary Proceedings at a Glance (2024)
s: This SFC guide explains, in plain terms, how the SFC disciplines regulated persons under Part 5B of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (AMLO). These are virtual asset trading platform (VATP) licensees, their responsible officers, and managers. It sets out the criteria the SFC weighs before taking action and setting sanction levels. It also lists the available sanctions, up to licence revocation and fines up to HK$10 million or three times profit gained or loss avoided. It also sets out the step-by-step process, from investigation through to a Notice of Proposed Disciplinary Action, representations, and a decision notice. It ends with rights of review before the Review Tribunal, and appeal to the Court of Appeal.
w: For counterparty due diligence on VATPs, this is the SFC's own roadmap of what triggers enforcement, what sanctions can follow, and how public the outcome will be. A bank should treat a VATP's history of Notices of Proposed Disciplinary Action (NPDAs), decision notices, or public reprimands as material to its ongoing due diligence and monitoring of that platform.
k: The SFC can only discipline 'regulated persons': licensed VATP operators, their licensed representatives, responsible officers, and individuals involved in management. This includes directors and those serving as Managers-in-Charge of Core Functions.

Factors the SFC weighs include the nature and seriousness of conduct, and the impact on market integrity or Hong Kong's reputation. They also include losses caused, whether conduct was intentional or negligent, prior SFC guidance on the conduct, and the degree of cooperation shown.

Available sanctions include licence revocation or suspension, and prohibition from applying for a licence or to be a responsible officer. They also include a fine of up to HK$10 million or three times the gain made or loss avoided, whichever is larger, plus reprimand and remedial action orders.
Except for a private reprimand, all SFC sanctions are announced publicly by press release.
A regulated person that receives a Notice of Proposed Disciplinary Action is normally given 30 days to make representations, extendable on reasonable request.

If the person does not apply for a review, the SFC's decision takes effect once the 21-day review-application window, from service of the decision notice, expires. An application for review suspends the decision until the Review Tribunal rules.
A person dissatisfied with the Review Tribunal's determination may ask for leave to bring the matter before the Court of Appeal. This must be done within a 14-day window from that determination.
rg: Read pages 3-9 (English) in full; the Chinese-language section from page 10 onward duplicates the same content and can be skipped for an English-reading audience.

s: This SFC presentation explains its 'see-through' approach to tokenised SFC-authorised investment products. It treats them as fundamentally traditional products, wrapped in tokenisation technology. It sets out extra safeguards product providers must apply for primary dealing, flags secondary trading as needing more caution, and requires prior SFC consultation for new or changed tokenised products.
w: If the bank distributes or manufactures tokenised SFC-authorised funds, this sets the disclosure, custody, staff-competence, and prior-consultation checklist compliance must apply before launch. It also clarifies that outsourcing tokenisation technology does not shift legal responsibility away from the manager or distributor.
k: The SFC treats tokenised products as traditional products with a technology wrapper, applying existing product rules plus extra safeguards for the new risks.
Secondary trading of tokenised fund units needs more caution than primary dealing because of 24/7 trading and market-infrastructure readiness challenges.
Product providers/fund managers must remain ultimately responsible for the tokenisation arrangement and ownership record-keeping, even if a technology provider is engaged.
Products should not use public-permissionless blockchains without extra controls, such as a permissioned token layer.

Offering documents must clearly disclose token ownership rights, and whether settlement is on-chain or off-chain and final. They must also disclose transfer limits, smart-contract audit status, and associated cybersecurity and legal risks.

Distributors of tokenised funds must be SFC-licensed for Type 1 regulated activity, and follow suitability and onboarding rules. They must also choose a custodial arrangement suited to the product's ownership and technology risks.

Prior consultation with the SFC is required both for new tokenised products seeking authorisation, and for adding tokenisation to an existing authorised fund. Adding a further, substantially similar tokenised share class to the same fund does not need fresh prior approval.
rg: Read pages 10-16 (SFC guidance section); the introduction and global-adoption comparison (pages 3-8) are useful context but not obligations.

t: Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers in Hong Kong – Consultation Paper
sl: FSTB/HKMA · Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin… (2023)
s: The FSTB and HKMA jointly issued this paper in December 2023. It set out the proposed licensing regime for issuers of fiat-referenced stablecoins (FRS) -- tokens that try to hold a steady value against one or more currencies. It proposed that anyone issuing an FRS in Hong Kong, issuing an HKD-pegged stablecoin, or actively marketing FRS to the Hong Kong public would need an HKMA licence. It set out detailed licensing conditions covering reserve backing, redemption rights, capital, governance, and AML controls, plus who could offer FRS to the public, and the HKMA's supervisory, investigation, and enforcement powers. This proposal was later enacted; the analysis below reflects the original proposal stage, some of which was refined in the July 2024 conclusions paper.
w: For a bank's compliance function, this is the original blueprint for Hong Kong's stablecoin issuer licensing regime, and it must be mapped against. It shows which licensing conditions apply differently to banks (as authorized institutions) versus non-bank issuers, and it sets the baseline for due-diligence questions to any stablecoin issuer counterparty.
k: Any company issuing an FRS in Hong Kong, issuing an HKD-referenced stablecoin, or actively marketing FRS issuance to the Hong Kong public would need an HKMA licence.
A licensed FRS issuer must keep reserve assets worth at least the full value of coins in circulation, at all times. Coins backed only by algorithms or arbitrage would not qualify for a licence.

Reserve assets must be held separately from the issuer's own assets. They would normally sit with a licensed bank or an HKMA-approved custodian, under a trust structure that protects holders if the issuer becomes insolvent.

Issuers must let holders redeem coins at face value in the referenced currency, promptly and without unreasonable conditions or fees. They must also keep a contingency plan for orderly redemption if the issuer runs into trouble.

A minimum paid-up capital was proposed at whichever is higher: HK$25 million, or 2% of the coins in circulation. This, and three other criteria, would not apply to issuers that are already authorized institutions (that is, banks).

Only licensed FRS issuers, banks, licensed securities dealers, and licensed virtual asset trading platforms would be allowed to offer FRS to the Hong Kong public. Unlicensed-issuer coins could only be offered to professional investors, and must be clearly labelled as such.
para 7.2, p.24
HKMA would get powers to intervene in a struggling issuer's management, gather information, conduct on-site inspections, investigate suspected offences, and apply for search warrants.

Proposed criminal penalties for unlicensed issuance reached a HK$10 million pecuniary penalty, or three times the profit or loss avoided, whichever is higher. Lower fines, and up to seven-figure fines with prison terms, applied for specific offences under the wider financial-crime framework the paper draws on.

Pre-existing stablecoin issuers with a real Hong Kong presence would get a 6-month grace period to keep operating. This was conditional on applying for a licence within the first 3 months after the regime starts; those who did not apply in time would have to wind down by month 4.
rg: Read the Executive Summary (paras 1-4, pp.8-9), then section 6.2's licensing criteria (pp.16-22) and section 7 on offering (p.24). Skip the Foreword, the Personal Information Collection Statement, and the repeated consultation-question call-out boxes.

t: Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers in Hong Kong (Consultation Paper)
sl: HKMA/SFC · Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin… (2023)
s: In this joint consultation paper, the FSTB and HKMA set out a detailed legislative plan for licensing fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers. It builds on the HKMA's January 2022 discussion paper and its January 2023 conclusions. It proposed a new stand-alone ordinance. Under it, the Monetary Authority (MA) would licence anyone who issues an FRS from Hong Kong, or issues any stablecoin pegged to the Hong Kong dollar. The same would apply to anyone who actively promotes FRS issuance to people in Hong Kong. Licensing criteria covered full reserve backing, par-value redemption rights, restricted business scope, and Hong Kong incorporation and management presence. They also covered minimum capital, disclosure (a 'white paper'), governance, risk management, audit, and AML/CFT controls. It proposed that only licensed FRS issuers, authorized institutions, licensed corporations, and licensed VATPs may offer FRS in Hong Kong, with unlicensed-issuer FRS restricted to professional investors. This 2023 consultation was the direct precursor to what became Hong Kong's Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656). By 2026 the regime it proposed has been substantially enacted, so this paper itself is superseded as a proposal, though historically important.
w: This is the founding text of Hong Kong's stablecoin licensing regime. It defines who may issue and who may offer or distribute an FRS, including that authorized institutions, licensed corporations, and licensed VATPs are the permitted offering channels. It sets the reserve, redemption, custody, and AML standards a bank should expect of any FRS issuer it deals with. It also previews the sanctions regime the MA can apply -- essential due-diligence criteria for any stablecoin custody, settlement, or distribution relationship.
k: A company would need a Monetary Authority licence if it issues an FRS in Hong Kong, or issues a stablecoin pegged to the Hong Kong dollar. The same applies if it actively promotes FRS issuance to the Hong Kong public.
para 6.1.1

An FRS issuer must ensure reserve assets are at all times at least equal in value to the par value of FRS in circulation ('full backing'). Algorithmic or arbitrage-only stabilisation would not be licensable.
para 6.2.1

Reserve assets must be high-quality, highly liquid, and generally held in the referenced currency. They must be segregated, through an effective trust arrangement, in accounts with licensed banks or MA-approved custodians, protected against theft, fraud, and misappropriation.
FRS issuers may not pay their FRS users any interest; income or losses on reserve assets belong to the issuer, not the holder.
para 6.2.6

FRS users have a right to redeem at par value without undue cost or unreasonable conditions. This includes direct redemption from the issuer if an intermediary channel becomes unavailable, backed by a contingency redemption plan.

FRS issuers may only conduct FRS issuance and closely ancillary activities (e.g. wallet services for their own FRS); lending, financial intermediation and other regulated activities (SFO, MPF, insurance) are off-limits.

Non-bank FRS issuers must be Hong Kong-incorporated with a registered office. Their chief executive, senior management, and key personnel -- heads of operations, IT, finance, risk, compliance, and internal audit -- must be based in Hong Kong. This requirement, plus restricted business scope and minimum capital, does not apply to issuers that are already authorized institutions.
Proposed minimum paid-up share capital for a non-bank issuer is the higher of HK$25,000,000 or 2% of the par value of FRS in circulation.
para 6.2.15
Issuers must publish an MA-notified white paper disclosing the stabilisation mechanism, reserves management, technology and risks, and must disclose redemption policy, fees and timeframe.

Total FRS in circulation and reserve asset value must be disclosed at least daily, and reserve composition at least weekly. An independent auditor must attest to reserve adequacy and issuer compliance at least monthly.
para 6.2.5

Only licensed FRS issuers, authorized institutions, licensed corporations (holding a Type 1 licence permitted to deal in virtual assets), and licensed VATPs may offer FRS in Hong Kong. FRS from unlicensed issuers may only be offered to professional investors by these entities, and must be clearly labelled as not issued by a licensed issuer.
para 7.2

People who control, direct, or run an FRS issuer as chief executive must meet fit-and-proper standards. The MA's prior consent is needed for any change in ownership, controllers, or senior management.
para 6.2.19, para 9.1.2
rg: Read section 6 (licensing criteria, p.16-22) and section 7 (offering, p.23) in full, as the substance of the proposal. Sections 9-12 (supervisory/investigation powers, offences) are useful for context but largely procedural. Skip the Personal Information Collection Statement (p.6-7).

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Eddie Yue on Stablecoins – Regulating issuers to accord protection to users
sl: HKMA · Eddie Yue on Stablecoins – Regulating issuers to accord… (2023)
s: This is Eddie Yue's public explainer, published the same day as the FSTB/HKMA joint public consultation paper on a legislative proposal for regulating fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers. It explains what stablecoins are, and why unregulated stablecoin failure risks harm to users and financial stability. It summarises the proposed regime at a high level. This covers an HKMA licence requirement for FRS issuers, local incorporation and management presence, and financial resources rules. It also covers an effective par-value redemption mechanism backed by high-quality liquid reserves held in proper custody, AML/CFT compliance, and a planned supervisory sandbox. It states only licensed issuers' stablecoins may be offered to retail investors. The full technical proposal is in the attached consultation paper (id 41a8fe3f0ec7).
w: This is the public-facing summary of what became Hong Kong's stablecoin licensing regime (later the Stablecoins Ordinance, Cap. 656); a bank should track this as the origin of rules on which stablecoins it may safely custody, distribute or accept from clients.
k: The HKMA proposes that any entity issuing a fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) in Hong Kong must hold an HKMA licence. It must also be locally incorporated, with local management presence, and meet financial resources requirements.
para on proposed regime
Only stablecoins issued by HKMA-licensed issuers may be offered to retail investors; unlicensed-issuer stablecoins are implicitly restricted to non-retail channels.
para on proposed regime

Licensed issuers must maintain an effective stabilisation mechanism. This is generally a pool of high-quality, highly liquid reserve assets in matching currencies, with proper custody, so users can redeem at par.
para on proposed regime
The HKMA plans to launch a supervisory sandbox to communicate expectations to firms interested in issuing stablecoins in Hong Kong, with details to follow separately.
closing paras
rg: Read this for the plain-English framing, then go to the attached consultation paper (id 41a8fe3f0ec7) for the detail that actually applies. Skip the historical section on 1935 Hong Kong banknote silver-token redemption, which is colour only.

t: Consultation on legislative proposal to implement regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers and announcement on introduction of sandbox arrangement
sl: FSTB · Consultation on legislative proposal to implement regulatory regime for… (2023)
s: The FSTB and HKMA jointly launched a public consultation, running 27 December 2023 to 29 February 2024. It covered a proposed licensing regime for issuers of fiat-referenced stablecoins (FRS) in Hong Kong, to be administered by the Monetary Authority (MA). The consultation paper proposes a new standalone ordinance requiring FRS issuers to be licensed. It sets licensing criteria: full backing, segregation, redemption at par, no interest payment, minimum capital, physical presence, and disclosure. It also restricts who may offer FRS, and proposes MA supervisory and investigation powers, offences, and a transitional arrangement. A parallel sandbox arrangement was announced for prospective issuers.
w: This consultation is not yet binding, but a compliance head should read it as the draft blueprint for the MA licence the bank would need to issue a stablecoin itself. Note that authorized institutions (AIs) are proposed to be exempt from several non-prudential licensing criteria that would otherwise apply to non-bank issuers.
k: Any entity issuing an FRS in Hong Kong, or issuing an HKD-referenced stablecoin, would need an FRS issuer licence from the Monetary Authority. The same would apply to any entity actively marketing FRS issuance to the Hong Kong public.
FRS reserve assets must at all times be at least equal in value to the par value of FRS in circulation (full backing). Issuers deriving value from arbitrage or algorithms would not be licensed.
FRS issuers may not pay their FRS users interest earned on reserve assets.
Proposed minimum paid-up share capital: the higher of HKD 25,000,000 or 2% of the par value of FRS in circulation.

The FRS issuer must be Hong Kong-incorporated with a registered office, with key personnel based in Hong Kong. This, and the business-restriction/financial-resources criteria, do not apply to authorized institutions.

Only licensed FRS issuers and authorized institutions may offer FRS in Hong Kong or market it to the Hong Kong public. Licensed corporations (with a Type 1 licence permitted to deal in VA) and licensed VATPs may do so too. Non-MA-licensed FRS may only be offered to professional investors.
Proposed maximum pecuniary penalty: HKD 10,000,000 or 3x the profit gained/loss avoided, whichever is higher, plus criminal offences for unlicensed issuance/marketing.

Proposed transitional arrangement: the regime would start 1 month after gazettal. Pre-existing FRS issuers with a meaningful Hong Kong presence would get a 6-month grace period (a 'non-contravention period'). This is conditional on lodging an application with the MA during the regime's first three months.
Consultation period ran from 27 December 2023 to 29 February 2024, alongside a new HKMA sandbox for prospective FRS issuers.
press release para 3, 6
rg: Read the Executive Summary and section 6 (licensing criteria) first; skim the Foreword/PICS and the consultation-question call-outs, which are procedural, not substantive.

t: Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities | Appendices: Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities (2023)
s: This is the full appendix set behind the 22 December 2023 joint circular. It gives the client-knowledge test criteria, and the list of jurisdictions whose regulator-approved crypto funds qualify for lighter treatment. It also gives a decision flowchart for classifying crypto-linked products, and a fund due-diligence checklist. It gives model risk-disclosure wording too, plus the current dealing/advisory licence conditions, with a redline against the earlier version. It also gives a separate, standalone set of conditions for firms managing crypto-invested funds or mandates. That last piece, Appendix 7, is effectively its own rulebook for crypto fund managers, covering custody, capital, valuation, record keeping, and reporting -- distinct from the dealing and advisory conditions covered elsewhere.
w: For a bank, Appendix 7 is the key rulebook if its asset-management arm ever runs a mandate meant to hold crypto, or one that could cross the 10% threshold. It sets a hard capital floor, custody and insurance expectations, and a fast notification clock the bank must be able to meet. The rest of the appendices supply the working detail -- the due-diligence checklist, risk wording, and product-classification flowchart -- behind the main December 2023 circular.
k: A firm counts as a knowledgeable client if it has had crypto training, has worked with crypto, or has traded crypto before. Any one of the three is enough.
Appendix 1
Twelve named jurisdictions' regulator-approved retail crypto derivative funds and exchanges qualify for the lighter selling regime; anything else defaults to the stricter complex-product path.
Appendix 2

A fund counts as a 'Virtual Asset Fund Manager', bound by the Appendix 7 conditions, if it is meant to invest in crypto. It also counts if its manager intends to put 10% or more of its value into crypto.
Appendix 7, Interpretation, 'de minimis threshold'

A licensed corporation acting as such a fund manager, and holding crypto for its funds, must at all times keep liquid capital of at least HK$3 million. It must instead hold its variable required liquid capital if that figure is higher.
Appendix 7, para 3.1

The fund manager should use a custodian independent of itself. If it self-custodies, it should show the crypto is legally ring-fenced from its own assets -- for example, by a declared trust over the wallet and keys -- and carry adequate insurance.
Appendix 7, para 4.1(a), 4.4-4.6

Choosing a third-party custodian calls for documented diligence on its crypto track record, regulatory status, asset segregation practices, and financial and insurance strength. The manager should also think about spreading assets across more than one custodian.
Appendix 7, para 4.7 and accompanying note

The fund manager should tell the SFC, and the HKMA if it is a registered institution, at least 7 business days before any significant change to its business. It should report material non-compliance as soon as practicable.
Appendix 7, para 7.1-7.2
Fund investors should be told the fund's key crypto risks up front. For example, most trading venues and custodians are still unregulated, and self-custody and hot-wallet use carry loss risk.
Appendix 7, Schedule 4

Appendix 6 restates the dealing/advisory licence conditions current as of this circular. Appendix 6a marks up exactly what changed from the earlier version, mainly the retail exposure-limit and knowledge-test wording.
Appendix 6a
Appendix 3's flowchart is the reference tool for working out whether a given crypto-linked product is a complex product and which selling rule therefore applies.
Appendix 3
rg: Read Appendix 7 (crypto fund-manager conditions, especially custody in section IV and reporting in section VII) closely if the bank runs, or is considering, any crypto-invested mandate. Appendices 1, 2, and 5 are short reference lists that can be skimmed. Appendix 6/6a largely duplicates id 8401e273511f/bc97c16bac5e's dealing conditions, plus a redline.

t: Circular on SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets
sl: SFC · SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets (2023)
s: This SFC circular sets out the conditions under which the SFC will authorise investment funds with more than 10% of net asset value exposed to virtual assets (VA). Such funds can then be publicly offered in Hong Kong under sections 104-105 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). It covers eligible underlying VA, investment strategy limits, transaction and custody channels, custody standards (cold storage, key management), valuation, disclosure, and prior-consultation requirements. It supersedes the October 2022 VA futures ETF circular, and cross-refers to the companion Joint Circular on intermediaries.
w: If the bank's Registered Institution (RI) arm manages, distributes, or provides custody for SFC-authorised funds with virtual-asset exposure, this circular sets binding requirements. These cover custody segregation, cold storage, key management, disclosure, and prior SFC consultation before exceeding the 10% NAV threshold.
k: SFC-authorised VA Funds may invest more than 10% of NAV in virtual assets, directly (spot) and/or indirectly (e.g. futures, other exchange-traded products).
para 1, 5
This circular supersedes the 31 October 2022 circular on Virtual Asset Futures ETFs.
para 2
Underlying VA must be limited to tokens the Hong Kong public can already access for trading on SFC-licensed VATPs.
para 10
SFC-authorised VA Funds must not carry leveraged VA exposure at the level of the fund itself.
para 14
Spot VA transactions/acquisitions must go through SFC-licensed VATPs or HKMA-compliant AIs (or subsidiaries of locally incorporated AIs).
para 16
Custodian may only delegate VA custody to an SFC-licensed VATP or an AI meeting HKMA's expected VA custody standards.
para 19

Custody standard: most VA holdings must be stored in cold wallets, with hot-wallet amounts and duration kept to what is needed for subscriptions and redemptions. Seeds and private keys must be stored in Hong Kong, with access tightly restricted and resistant to speculation or collusion. This can be done, for example, using multi-signature approval or key sharding, and copies must be backed up.
para 20(b)-(c)
Valuation of spot VA must use an indexing approach based on trade volume across major VA trading platforms (a benchmark index from a reputable provider).
para 21
Funds seeking VA exposure above 10% of NAV (whether new or existing) require the SFC's prior consultation and sign-off.
para 29
rg: Read paras 1-2 (scope/supersession) and the custody section (paras 19-20) first; skim footnotes and the disclosure/service-provider paragraphs (22-27).

t: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities (2023)
s: This joint SFC/HKMA circular updates the conduct rules for intermediaries doing virtual asset (VA) related distribution, dealing, advisory, and asset-management work. It treats most VA-related products as complex products that can only be sold to professional investors, after a suitability check. A VA-knowledge test is also required. It carves out exceptions for exchange-traded derivatives and SFC-authorised funds. It also limits VA dealing to omnibus accounts held with SFC-licensed VATPs (virtual asset trading platforms), and applies RA9 (Type 9, asset management) terms and conditions to VA fund managers. It replaces the October 2023 and January 2022 joint circulars.
w: This is a core, directly binding circular for the bank as a Registered Institution. It sets the capital buffer, custody, VA-knowledge-test, suitability, and platform-partnering rules the bank must meet for any VA dealing, advisory, or asset-management work.
k: VA-related products are 'very likely' complex products, so -- with limited exceptions -- they should go through a suitability check and be sold only to professional investors.
para 5-6.1

Apart from institutional and qualified corporate professional investors, intermediaries should check a client's VA knowledge before any VA-related transaction (a one-off check is acceptable). If a client lacks that knowledge, the intermediary may proceed only after providing adequate training.
para 6.2

VA futures or derivative funds traded on specified exchanges, or authorised in listed jurisdictions, skip the professional-investor-only and suitability rules if there is no solicitation. The same applies to SFC-authorised VA funds traded on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong (SEHK). They still need the VA-knowledge test.
para 7, 9.1

The SFC and HKMA see a clear need for intermediaries to deal only with SFC-licensed VA trading platforms for VA dealing, using an omnibus account or introducing-agent model. Intermediaries should provide such dealing services only to clients approved for Type 1 regulated activity.
para 17-18

Under the omnibus-account terms and conditions, a licensed corporation must keep excess liquid capital in Hong Kong equal to at least 12 months of actual running costs, on a rolling basis. This is on top of the SF(FR) Rules requirements.
Appendix 6, Part I, III para 3.1

Client virtual assets should be held on trust in separate VA Segregated Accounts, either at an SFC-licensed platform or an HKMA-compliant authorized institution. The intermediary should not give clients financial accommodation (margin or leverage) to acquire virtual assets.
Appendix 6, Part I, VII para 7.1(a); IV para 4.4

Advice and recommendations offered to retail clients must be limited to large-cap VA. That VA must appear on at least two acceptable indices from two independent providers, and be available for retail trading on SFC-licensed platforms.
para 28; Appendix 6, IV para 4.9

Asset managers count as VA fund managers, and so must follow RA9 terms and conditions, if the fund's stated goal is to invest in VA. The same applies if the fund plans to put 10% or more of its gross asset value into VA -- what the circular calls the 'de minimis threshold'.
para 23; Appendix 7, I
Type 1 intermediaries offering VA dealing only as a side service, using their own discretion, may put less than 10% of a client portfolio's value into virtual assets.
para 24
The transition period for intermediaries already serving non-qualified or individual professional-investor clients ended 20 January 2024.
para 30
Intermediaries are reminded to give the SFC (and HKMA where relevant) advance notice before starting or changing any VA-related activity.
para 31
rg: Read the main circular body (paras 1-31) first for the policy. Then read Appendix 6 Parts I-II (dealing/advisory terms and conditions) and Appendix 7 (RA9 asset management terms) for the conditions that actually apply. Skip Appendices 1, 2, 4, 5, and the marked-up redline appendices (6a, 7a), unless comparing to the prior version.

t: Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities (2023)
s: This is the current SFC/HKMA rulebook for how banks and brokers may distribute crypto-linked investment products, and offer crypto dealing, advisory, and asset-management services to clients. Most crypto-linked funds and derivatives are treated as complex products that only professional investors can buy. Narrow carve-outs apply for exchange-listed futures ETFs and SFC-authorised funds sold under extra safeguards. Firms must test a client's crypto knowledge, size their exposure against net worth, and route any actual dealing only through SFC-licensed trading venues. It folds in seven detailed appendices, covering due diligence, risk wording, and standalone conditions for dealing, advisory, and fund-management activities, and it fully replaced the two earlier joint circulars.
w: This is the single rulebook that currently governs a bank's crypto distribution, dealing, advisory, and asset-management business in Hong Kong. Every product-shelf and onboarding decision for crypto exposure should trace back to it. It sets the boundary between what needs professional-investor-only treatment and what can go to retail, and it dictates which platforms and custodians the bank may use.
k: Products whose value comes mainly from crypto - funds, ETPs, structured notes - are presumed complex and, unless specifically carved out, can only be sold to professional investors.
para 5-6.1
Before any transaction in a crypto-linked product, the firm must run a one-off knowledge check on the client. It can then proceed, train the client first, or decline.
para 6.2
Exchange-listed crypto futures and SFC-approved futures ETFs escape the professional-investor-only rule when there's no solicitation, but the knowledge check still applies.
para 7, 9.1

Distributing a crypto fund the SFC has not authorised calls for extra due diligence, on the fund manager, the fund itself, and its trading and custody counterparties. This follows a checklist in Appendix 4.
para 12.3

Actual dealing in crypto for clients may only run through an SFC-licensed trading venue, either as an introducer or via a shared (omnibus) account. It is only for clients already approved for securities dealing.
para 17-18
Retail dealing clients need a knowledge check, and a net-worth-based exposure cap that is disclosed to them. Their access is limited to coins the partner venue allows retail investors to trade.
para 20(a)
Client coins from dealing clients must sit in a segregated account either at the partner venue or at a bank meeting the HKMA's custody standard.
para 20(b)

A fund manager whose fund is meant to invest in crypto must instead follow the separate fund-manager conditions in Appendix 7. The same applies if the fund is expected to hold 10% or more of its value in crypto.
para 23
Firms already serving non-qualified and individual professional-investor dealing clients had until 20 January 2024 to meet the new standard.
para 30
Firms must tell the SFC (and HKMA where relevant) in advance before starting any crypto-related activity, or before materially changing one already running.
para 31
rg: Read paragraphs 1-31 in full -- it is only 9 pages. Do not skip section E (Implementation) at the end, which carries the transition deadline and the advance-notification duty.

t: attachment of: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · attachment of: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities (2023)
s: This SFC-hosted PDF exactly matches the combined appendix set behind the 22 December 2023 joint circular, already logged under id 0027a8747112. That set covers the client-knowledge test, exempt-fund jurisdictions, a complex-product flowchart, a fund due-diligence checklist, warning wording, current dealing/advisory licence conditions, and the separate portfolio-manager terms.
w: No separate action is needed. The obligations that apply are already captured in the fuller entry for this appendix set (id 0027a8747112).
k: The text is identical to the already-logged combined appendix set for the 22 December 2023 joint circular.
rg: Do not read separately - see the fuller entry 0027a8747112 for locators and analysis.

t: SFC warns public of LonShiX and Bitbank (Global) Financial Holding Group for suspected virtual asset-related fraud
sl: SFC · SFC warns public of LonShiX and Bitbank (Global) Financial… (2023)
s: Routine SFC scam alert about two schemes. LonShiX used a fake Hong Kong address and social-media 'advisors' posing as bank-authorised professionals to lure investors. Bitbank (Global) Financial Holding Group copied the name of a genuine Japanese exchange and falsely claimed SFC licences plus a pending VA service provider application. Both were blocked by police at the SFC's request and listed on the SFC's alert list.
w: Routine; note the recurring pattern of scammers falsely claiming bank-authorised staff status, relevant to customer-education messaging.
k: LonShiX gave a fake Hong Kong address and used fake 'bank-authorised' advisors on social media to recruit investors.
'LonShiX' section
Bitbank (Global) copied the name of an unrelated Japanese crypto exchange and falsely claimed SFC licences and a pending VA licence application.
'Bitbank...' section
Both entities' websites and related social accounts were blocked at the SFC's request.
para after the two sections
rg: Skim; standard template.

t: SFC warns public of HongKongDAO and BitCuped for involvement in suspected virtual asset-related frauds
sl: SFC · SFC warns public of HongKongDAO and BitCuped for involvement… (2023)
s: The SFC warned about two entities, HongKongDAO and BitCuped, suspected of virtual-asset fraud. It said it had asked police to block their websites, and it issued cease-and-desist letters. HongKongDAO issued a token and was accused of falsely claiming SFC licences and a stake in the government's planned digital-currency exchange licence. BitCuped was accused of falsely naming two senior Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) figures as its chairman and CEO, with no actual affiliation. The SFC repeated its general caution about social-media-driven investment scams and unlicensed promoters.
w: A routine named-fraud alert; useful only as a specific negative screening reference if a customer or counterparty is connected to either name.
k: HongKongDAO's claims of holding Type 4 and Type 9 SFC licences were stated by the SFC to be untrue. So was its claim of applying for a licence in July 2022.
para listing three false claims
BitCuped falsely named two HKEX senior figures as its chairman and CEO on its website; neither has any affiliation with the firm.
para on BitCuped, Notes 3-4
Both entities already appeared, before this warning, on the SFC's list of suspicious virtual-asset trading platforms (HongKongDAO 24 Nov 2023, BitCuped 10 Nov 2023).
Notes 1-2
rg: One-page notice; read in full, it is short.

t: SFC warns public of HongKongDAO and BitCuped for involvement in suspected virtual asset-related frauds

t: AN ASSESSMENT ON THE BENEFITS OF BOND TOKENISATION
sl: HKMA · AN ASSESSMENT ON THE BENEFITS OF BOND TOKENISATION (2023)
s: This is a staff research memorandum, not a policy or supervisory document. It empirically studies whether tokenised bonds deliver measurable benefits versus conventional bonds. The authors use data on 28 tokenised bonds issued globally since 2018 (total US$3.9bn by March 2023, about 70% from Asian issuers), matched against similar conventional bonds from the same issuers. They find tokenisation is associated with lower underwriting fees, lower yield spreads, tighter bid-ask spreads, and improved liquidity in the matched conventional bonds too. The paper states the views are the authors' own, not HKMA policy, and cautions the sample is still small.
w: This is HKMA staff research, not supervisory guidance, but it is the empirical basis regulators and market participants cite for tokenisation's cost and liquidity case. It is useful background if the bank is weighing participation in tokenised bond issuance, underwriting, or custody, but it creates no obligations.
k: By end-March 2023 total global tokenised bond issuance reached US$3.9 billion across 28 deals from 23 issuers since 2018, about 70% issued by Asian institutions.
Key points / Section 2
Tokenised bonds in the sample had underwriting fees averaging 0.22 percentage points of par value lower than matched conventional bonds, a 25.8% relative reduction.
Section 3a

Tokenised bonds had yield spreads averaging 0.78 percentage points lower than matched conventional bonds, a 23.9% relative reduction, i.e. investors accepted lower compensation for tokenised issuance.
Section 3a
Tokenised bonds showed bid-ask spreads 5.3% tighter than matched conventional bonds on average. This rose to 10.8% tighter when the tokenised bond was open to retail investors.
Section 3b
After an issuer's tokenised bond launch, that issuer's comparable conventional bonds also saw bid-ask spreads tighten by about 8.5%, suggesting a price-discovery spillover effect.
Section 3c
The paper explicitly disclaims that findings represent HKMA views and flags the sample as still small, so results should be read with caution.
disclaimer, p.1; Section 4
rg: Read the Key Points box (p.1) and Section 3 findings (p.7-10); the Annex regression methodology (p.14-17) can be skipped by a compliance reader.
