t: Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities
sl: SFC · intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities (2023)
s: The SFC sets out guidance for intermediaries engaging in Tokenised Securities-related activities. It applies a 'same business, same risks, same rules' approach. Tokenised securities stay subject to existing securities law, but intermediaries must also manage new ownership and technology risks from using DLT (distributed ledger technology). Tokenisation itself does not change a security's complex-product classification; the SFC uses a 'see-through' approach based on the underlying security. The circular also lifts the prior mandatory professional-investor-only restriction from the 2019 Statement, for tokenised securities that are fundamentally traditional securities. It formally supersedes the 2019 Security Token Offerings Statement, and distinguishes 'Tokenised Securities' from broader, more bespoke 'Digital Securities' (which remain presumptively complex products).
w: This circular directly binds the bank as a Registered Institution. It sets the classification test, and the disclosure and prospectus obligations, for any tokenised bond or fund the bank deals in, advises on, or distributes. It also confirms the outdated 2019 professional-investor-only mandate no longer applies.
k: This circular formally supersedes the SFC's 29 March 2019 Statement on Security Token Offerings.
para 21
Whether a Tokenised Security counts as a 'complex product' is assessed by looking through to the underlying traditional security's complexity, not the tokenisation wrapper itself.
para 24

The 2019 Statement's mandatory professional-investor-only restriction on security tokens no longer applies. Tokenised Securities are, at their core, ordinary securities carrying a tokenisation wrapper.
para 26

Publicly offering Tokenised Securities still requires compliance with the prospectus regime. This sits under the Companies (Winding Up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance (C(WUMP)O), and the Part IV Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO) offers-of-investments regime. Otherwise, the offer must be restricted to professional investors, or an exemption must apply.
para 27
Intermediaries that issue, or are substantially involved in issuing, Tokenised Securities remain responsible for the tokenisation arrangement even if they outsource it to third-party vendors.
para 13

A separate rule, the 'de minimis threshold', applies only to virtual assets under AMLO s.53ZRA. This is the small-amount test for when a fund manager must follow the VA fund manager Terms and Conditions. It does not apply to Tokenised Securities, unless the portfolio also separately meets that VA threshold.
para 28

Virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs) must maintain an SFC-approved compensation arrangement for security tokens under Guidelines paragraph 10.22. They may apply, case by case, to exclude certain Tokenised Securities from that required coverage if loss risk is otherwise mitigated.
para 30-31
Digital Securities that are not Tokenised Securities (more bespoke/novel structures) will likely be treated as complex products given heightened legal uncertainty.
para 33
rg: Read the full 7-page circular. The Appendix (Parts A and B) gives detailed due-diligence and custody factors; it is useful reference but can be skimmed once you grasp the main body's classification logic.

t: Keynote at the Hong Kong FinTech Week 2023
sl: HKMA · Keynote at the Hong Kong FinTech Week 2023 (2023)
s: Eddie Yue's keynote reflects on the HKMA's seven-plus years of fintech policy. He uses the Faster Payment System's slow-burn adoption as a case study for long-term commitment, then argues fintech is inherently interdisciplinary and needs collaboration. On virtual assets, he notes the HKMA has worked with the SFC to roll out investor-protection measures, so intermediaries, including banks, understand their responsibilities when distributing digital asset products. He previews a cross-border FPS-PromptPay QR link with Thailand, launching 4 December 2023. He also flags tokenisation, stablecoins, and tokenised deposits as accelerating trends, alongside open questions on how tokenised securities will be defined and whether delivery-versus-payment can be achieved on-chain.
w: This signals that the HKMA expects banks distributing virtual asset products to be clear on their investor-protection responsibilities, working from SFC/HKMA joint guidance. It also flags tokenised deposits and stablecoins as near-term growth areas a bank's digital-asset strategy should track.
k: The HKMA and SFC have jointly rolled out investor-protection measures. This helps intermediaries, including banks, understand their responsibilities when distributing or offering virtual asset products and services to clients.
para on cross-sector collaboration

Yue expects accelerating tokenisation of assets and wider use of blockchain-based ways to pay, including stablecoins and tokenised deposits. He flags unresolved questions on the legal definition of tokenised securities and on-chain delivery-versus-payment.
closing paras
A new FPS x PromptPay QR payment link with Thailand's central bank was announced, to launch on 4 December 2023. It lets Hong Kong FPS users pay at PromptPay merchants without pre-converting currency.
para on cross-border collaboration
rg: Short speech; read in full, no technical detail to skip.

t: Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products
sl: SFC · tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products (2023)
s: The SFC sets out requirements under which it would consider allowing tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products offered to the public in Hong Kong. It permits primary dealing -- subscription and redemption -- of tokenised authorised products, where the underlying product meets all existing authorisation requirements plus additional tokenisation safeguards. Secondary trading of such tokenised products is treated with more caution and remains under SFC review. Product Providers must retain full responsibility for the tokenisation arrangement, avoid unrestricted public-permissionless blockchains, and satisfy disclosure, staff competence, and prior consultation/approval requirements.
w: For a bank distributing or considering issuing tokenised authorised funds or bonds, this sets the gating condition: primary dealing is permitted, but secondary trading is not yet. It directly shapes product launch timing, and requires prior SFC consultation before tokenising any existing fund.
k: Primary dealing (subscription/redemption) of tokenised SFC-authorised products is permitted if the underlying product meets all applicable authorisation requirements plus additional tokenisation safeguards.
para 5
Secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised products is not yet generally permitted; the SFC will continue to engage with the market on appropriate safeguards.
para 6-7
Product Providers must not rely on public, permissionless blockchain networks unless extra controls are added, e.g. imposing a permissioned token.
para 13
Product Providers remain fully responsible for the tokenisation arrangement's management and operational soundness despite any outsourcing.
para 10
Prior consultation with the SFC is required for new products with tokenisation features seeking authorisation, and for tokenising existing authorised products (which may also require prior approval).
para 20-21
Products should not be issued in bearer form; distributors must be regulated intermediaries complying with existing suitability/onboarding rules.
para 11 (footnote 2), 18

t: HKMA publishes the “e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 1 Report”
sl: HKMA · HKMA publishes the “e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 1 Report” (2023)
s: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has published the Phase 1 Report on its e-HKD Pilot Programme. e-HKD is a possible digital Hong Kong dollar issued by the HKMA. The report covers 14 pilots run by 16 participating firms. It finds three areas where e-HKD might add real value: programmability (payments that follow set conditions), tokenisation (representing assets digitally), and atomic settlement (completing a trade instantly). The HKMA cautions these were only small-scale trials in a controlled setting. The HKMA still has no timeline or firm plan to launch e-HKD. Its next phase will explore new use cases and dig deeper into some Phase 1 pilots.
w: For a bank, this is a short HKMA announcement of early, exploratory e-HKD pilot findings. It creates no obligation for the bank. For the fuller detail -- the six use-case categories, the e-HKD/stablecoin/tokenised-deposit comparison table, and the DLT (distributed ledger technology) design discussion -- see the full report (id 9f8886b0fb21).
k: The e-HKD Pilot Programme's Phase 1 covered 14 pilots run by 16 participating firms, as this report describes.
para 1
The pilots point to three areas where e-HKD might add value: programmability, tokenisation, and atomic settlement. The HKMA cautions these were only small-scale trials in a controlled environment.
para 2
The HKMA has still not decided whether, or when, it will introduce e-HKD. Its next phase will explore new use cases and go deeper into select Phase 1 pilots.
para 3
rg: Short press release (4 paragraphs); read in full. For full technical detail (case studies, comparison table, Way Forward section) see the attached full report (id 9f8886b0fb21).

t: Experimenting with a multi-CBDC platform for cross-border payments (Project mBridge Update)
sl: BIS · Experimenting with a multi-CBDC platform for cross-border payments (2023)
s: This is a joint update from the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub, the HKMA, and three other central banks on Project mBridge. mBridge is an experimental platform letting several central banks' digital currencies (CBDCs) settle wholesale cross-border payments. Its goal is to shorten correspondent-banking chains by letting banks settle directly with each other in central bank money. The platform runs on a custom, permissioned distributed ledger called the 'mBridge Ledger'. It is built to work like Ethereum and uses its own Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus method to agree on transactions. It protects privacy with masked addresses and encrypted transaction details. Governance runs through a Steering Committee and four subcommittees: compliance, technology, legal, and policy. The platform remains experimental only, with no live, production use of real money, and the report outlines a roadmap toward a Minimum Viable Product.
w: For a bank, mBridge is a wholesale, central-bank-led settlement system, not a retail product. Any Hong Kong bank with cross-border correspondent-banking exposure should track it as a possible future settlement channel. Customer checks and anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) compliance stay with participating commercial banks, handled off the platform -- the key point for a compliance head to note now.
k: Project mBridge aims to let central banks and commercial banks settle cross-border payments directly in central bank money (CBDC), bypassing multi-hop correspondent banking chains.
p.2, 'What is Project mBridge?'

Each central bank stays the only body that can issue or redeem its own CBDC on the platform. Only domestic commercial banks may request issuance or redemption of their local CBDC, which preserves currency sovereignty.
The platform is built on a custom permissioned, EVM-compatible DLT ('mBL') using the Dashing Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus protocol and ISO 20022-based APIs for interoperability.
p.4, 'Technology'

Privacy is protected by masked ('pseudonymous') addresses and encrypted payment details. Only four parties can decrypt those details: the two commercial banks in the transaction, each bank's own central bank, and the central bank that issues the CBDC being used.
Governance runs through a Steering Committee plus four subcommittees (Compliance, Technology, Legal, Policy); banks remain responsible for KYC/AML/CFT compliance off-platform ('off-bridge').

The mBridge Platform Terms form a single contract binding the administrator, each central bank, and each central bank's own commercial-bank participants. Separate, jurisdiction-specific Issuance and Redemption terms, plus a Platform CBDC Instrument, sit alongside this main contract.

At the time of the report, four central banks had founded the project, and more than 25 further members were observing it. The next stage aims to build a Minimum Viable Product, but the platform stays explicitly experimental, with no live-value transactions yet.
p.1 (footer disclaimer), p.10-11
rg: Read pages 2-3 (goals and principles) and pages 8-9 (governance and legal) for the compliance-relevant framing. You can skim the technical architecture on pages 4-6 if you are not technical.

t: HKMA publishes "e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 1 Report"
sl: HKMA · HKMA publishes "e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 1 Report" (2023)
s: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has published the e-HKD Pilot Programme's Phase 1 Report. e-HKD is a possible digital Hong Kong dollar. The report covers 14 pilots run by 16 participating firms, exploring possible retail e-HKD use cases. The pilots pointed to three areas of possible added value: programmability, tokenisation, and atomic settlement. The HKMA has not yet decided whether, or when, to issue e-HKD. Phase 1 findings will feed into a next phase examining further use cases. The full report and a participant annex are both attached.
w: For a bank, this is a market-development signal, not a rule. It shows the HKMA is still exploring e-HKD use cases, including tokenised deposits, which several banks piloted, without committing to issuing e-HKD. No new bank obligation arises yet, but banks already involved in tokenised-deposit or central bank digital currency (CBDC) pilots should track the next phase.
k: The e-HKD Pilot Programme's Phase 1 covered 14 pilots run by 16 firms, the report says.
press release, para 1
The HKMA identifies three fields where e-HKD could add value: programmability, tokenisation, and atomic settlement.
press release, para 2
The HKMA has not made a decision on whether or when to issue an e-HKD.
press release, para 3
rg: This press release is a short summary; go straight to the attached full report (attachment 9f8886b0fb21) for substance. The Annex (attachment ce1acbba8be0) is just a participant list.

t: e-HKD Pilot Programme • Phase 1 Report
sl: HKMA · e-HKD Pilot Programme • Phase 1 Report (2023)
s: This is the HKMA's detailed writeup of the first round of its e-HKD Pilot Programme. It launched in late 2022 as part of a three-rail plan toward a possible retail central bank digital currency. Sixteen firms ran 14 pilots across six use-case areas. These included ordinary retail payments, conditional or smart-contract payments, and payments made without a network connection. They also included bank deposits represented as digital tokens, using e-HKD to settle transactions in the Web3/crypto space, and settling other digitally-represented assets. The report walks through case studies and survey feedback, and a table contrasting e-HKD against stablecoins, stored-value wallets, and digital deposit tokens. That table compares who issues them, what backs them, how transferable they are, whether they carry deposit insurance, and how they can be redeemed. It repeats that no call has been made on issuing e-HKD, and describes plans for a further pilot round.
w: For a bank, especially one already piloting or considering digital deposit tokens, this Table 2 comparison should get close study. It is the HKMA's own framing of how such tokens differ from e-HKD and stablecoins on backing, deposit protection, and redemption -- useful for internal product classification and disclosure work. The report's note that these products sat outside a settled legal framework at the time is a prompt to check how far that has since changed.
k: Sixteen firms ran 14 pilots across six use cases: fully-fledged payments, programmable payments, and offline payments. The other three use cases were tokenised deposits, settling Web3 transactions, and settling tokenised assets.
Executive Summary, p.6

The HKMA identifies three areas where e-HKD could bring something new. These are programmability (payments that carry conditions), tokenisation (representing assets digitally), and atomic settlement (settling transactions instantly and simultaneously).
Executive Summary, p.6
Hang Seng Bank, HSBC and Visa piloted tokenised deposits with wholesale-CBDC settlement, testing on-us and cross-chain payment atomicity.
Case Study 4, p.19

A comparison table sets out that digital deposit tokens sit on a commercial bank's own balance sheet. They are generally covered by the Deposit Protection Scheme unless excluded, and are repayable in ordinary currency. This is unlike e-HKD, which is backed by the central bank's statutory authority. It is also unlike stablecoins, which the table describes as generally backed by assets and issued by largely unregulated private entities.
Table 2, p.29
The report cautions that, at the time of writing, neither stablecoins nor digital deposit tokens sat within a settled legal or regulatory framework in Hong Kong.
Table 2 note, p.29
The HKMA says no call has yet been made on whether, or when, an e-HKD might actually be issued.
Executive Summary, p.6
The report flags that a DLT is not a prerequisite for a CBDC, and the HKMA remains open to both DLT and non-DLT designs.
section 4.2, p.32
Fubon Bank and Ripple piloted using tokenised real-estate liens as collateral for a home equity line of credit settled in hypothetical e-HKD.
Case Study 6, p.21
rg: For a head of compliance, read the Executive Summary (p.6), Case Study 4 on tokenised deposits (p.18-19), Table 2's comparison (p.29), and section 5's Way Forward (p.33). You can skip the individual case-study narrative detail for payments and loyalty use cases unless it is relevant to a specific product line.

t: The Chief Executive's 2023 Policy Address
sl: Government · The Chief Executive's 2023 Policy Address (2023)
s: This is the Chief Executive's annual policy speech. It covers the whole of government, not virtual assets specifically. It mentions blockchain only twice: using it to issue and check certain licences and certificates online, as part of a wider digital-government programme. A separate paragraph on Fintech (financial technology) covers only a green-Fintech subsidy scheme and finance co-operation with Guangdong, with no virtual-asset content. The speech does not mention virtual asset trading platforms, stablecoins, tokenised securities, or e-HKD anywhere.
w: For a bank, this speech has almost no direct relevance to virtual-asset compliance. It shows the government's continuing interest in blockchain for e-government use, but sets no new licensing, prudential, or market-conduct rule for banks.
k: From 2024 the government will roll out over a hundred digital-government initiatives. One of these uses blockchain technology to issue and check certain licences and certificates electronically.
para 41, p.20
A companion annex repeats this as a tracked target: 110 fresh initiatives for digital government and smart cities in 2024-2025, including blockchain-based licence and certificate verification.
Annex II, item 5, p.98
A separate Fintech mention only covers a new green-Fintech proof-of-concept subsidy scheme launching in the first half of 2024, unrelated to virtual assets.
para 72(iv), p.34

t: Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities (2023)
s: The SFC and HKMA updated their policy on intermediaries carrying out virtual-asset (VA) activities. This covers distributing VA-related products, VA dealing services, VA asset management, and VA advisory services. It sets investor-protection measures: selling restrictions, a VA-knowledge test, suitability requirements, and specific terms and conditions imposed as licensing or registration conditions. Intermediaries may only partner with SFC-licensed VA trading platforms for dealing services. They must use segregated VA accounts for client deposits and withdrawals. The circular supersedes the 28 January 2022 joint circular. It includes detailed Appendices setting out terms and conditions for dealing, advisory, and asset-management (RA9) activities.
w: For a bank, as a registered institution it is directly bound by this joint circular's selling-restriction, platform-partner and custody rules for VA dealing, advisory and asset-management activities. The HKMA is its frontline supervisor for these. But compliance must confirm current requirements against the superseding 22 December 2023 version, since this text itself carries a supersession notice.
k: VA-related products count as complex products, other than certain exchange-traded derivatives. They must generally be offered only to professional investors. Other clients need a VA-knowledge test first.

A limited suite of exchange-traded VA derivative products, traded on specified exchanges, and authorized or approved VA ETFs, are exempt from the professional-investor-only restriction. They remain subject to derivative-product and VA-knowledge-test requirements.
para 8
Intermediaries providing VA dealing services may only partner with SFC-licensed VA trading platforms, whether via introducing agent or omnibus account arrangements.
para 16
Client virtual asset deposits/withdrawals must go through segregated accounts maintained with SFC-licensed platforms or authorized financial institutions meeting HKMA custody standards.
para 19(b)
A three-month transition period applies for intermediaries already serving existing clients before full implementation of the updated requirements.
para 29
Intermediaries must hold excess liquid capital worth at least 12 months of actual operating expenses. This applies when conducting VA dealing under omnibus account Terms and Conditions.
Appendix 6, Part I, para 3.1
For discretionary VA asset management, RA9 Terms and Conditions apply once there is a stated objective to invest in VA. They also apply once 10% or more of gross asset value is intended for VA.
Appendix 7, para I (de minimis threshold definition)

VA Fund Managers must select the most appropriate custodial arrangement: an independent custodian, or self-custody using hot or cold wallets. They must document their reasons. Self-custody requires functional segregation of custody and management functions, and adequate insurance.
Appendix 7, para 4.3-4.6
Recommended virtual assets for retail clients must be 'eligible large-cap' virtual assets included in at least two acceptable indices from two independent index providers.
para 27(a) / Appendix 6 para 4.9(i)

t: HKMA signs MoUs with five local universities to foster collaboration on CBDC research
sl: HKMA · HKMA signs MoUs with five local universities to foster… (2023)

t: Terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions which manage portfolios that invest in virtual assets
sl: HKMA/SFC · Terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions… (2023)
s: Known as the RA9 Terms and Conditions, this is the clean October 2023 text of licensing conditions applied to firms whose managed fund or discretionary account invests in virtual assets. It applies once the fund either aims to invest in virtual assets, or holds 10% or more of its value in them. It covers custody of the fund's virtual assets, including standards for self-custody versus an independent custodian. It also covers segregation of client cash, record keeping, and appointment and oversight of an auditor able to verify virtual-asset holdings. It sets counterparty and cybersecurity risk-management standards, and a duty to report material breaches or business changes to the regulators. A separate schedule adds extra rules for firms running discretionary accounts rather than pooled funds.
w: For a bank, any discretionary account or fund with material virtual-asset exposure faces the actual custody, disclosure and reporting standard the SFC and HKMA hold it to. Compliance needs these terms to build custodian due diligence, disclosure and change-notification processes.
k: The extra rules bite once a fund's stated goal is to invest in virtual assets, or once it intends to hold 10% or more of its value in them. A fund is not automatically caught just because price gains alone push it briefly above 10%, as long as the firm takes steps to bring it back down.
s.I, definitions, p.3-4

Before choosing between self-custody and an independent custodian, a firm must document its reasoning. It must weigh accessibility against the security of key handling, and the custodian's ability to compensate for any loss.
s.IV, para 4.3, p.6-7

If a firm chooses self-custody, it must keep the custodial function independent from the fund-management function internally. It may formalise this split, for example by placing a legal declaration of trust over the fund's crypto wallet and keys.
s.IV, para 4.4-4.5, p.7

Firms must document why they picked a given independent custodian. This covers its track record with virtual assets, regulatory oversight status, segregation of client assets, and insurance cover. Firms should prefer a custodian that is itself subject to regulatory oversight, where possible.
s.IV, para 4.7 and Note, p.7-8

If more than 10% of a fund's assets sit with one custodian, or in self-custody, that concentration and its risks must be disclosed to fund investors. Any significant later changes must also be disclosed.
s.IV, para 4.11, p.9

The fund's independent auditor must understand how it verifies the existence and ownership of virtual-asset holdings, and the reasonableness of their valuation. This information must be made available to fund investors on request.
s.IV, para 5.6, p.10-11

A firm must tell the SFC, and HKMA for a registered institution, of any significant change to its business. It must give at least 7 business days' notice before that change takes effect, and report any suspected material breach as soon as practicable.

When vetting a virtual-asset trading platform as a counterparty, a firm should weigh its track record, regulatory status, and governance. It should also weigh custodial arrangements, market-surveillance controls, cybersecurity measures, and its financial ability to cover client losses.
Schedule 3, s.B, p.19-20
rg: Read section IV (Custody, pages 5-9) and section VII (Reporting, pages 11-12) in full. Schedule 2 (discretionary accounts) applies only if the firm runs discretionary VA mandates rather than pooled funds. Schedule 3 (risk controls) is a useful due-diligence checklist for vetting VA counterparties.

This covered senior-management oversight, an independent compliance function, and best-execution and cross-trading rules. The 2023 version drops this duplicated text, and instead cross-references the Fund Manager Code of Conduct for the same points.
s.II para 2.1-2.13 and s.III para 3.1-3.21 (struck through), p.5-16

The custody-of-fund-assets section, covering self-custody versus independent custodian and disclosure of concentration, carries over largely unchanged in substance from the 2019 text into the 2023 version.

t: Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions providing virtual asset dealing services and virtual asset advisory services
sl: HKMA/SFC · Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for… (2023)
s: This is the full standalone conditions document referenced by the 20 October 2023 circular, split into a dealing-services part and an advisory-services part. It fixes how firms must onboard, disclose to, and safeguard assets for clients trading or being advised on crypto. It was itself superseded on 22 December 2023 by an updated version bundled in the Appendices package (id 0027a8747112). That version tightened the retail exposure-limit and knowledge-test wording. The redline is in that package's Appendix 6a.
w: For a bank, this was the operating rulebook it had to build its VA dealing and advisory controls against for about three months. It is no longer current. But its structure, onboarding tests, exposure limits, custody segregation, and monthly statements, carried forward almost unchanged into the December 2023 version.
k: A firm dealing under an omnibus account structure must keep the account with a licensed venue. It can execute trades only if the client's balance already covers them, with no running a negative balance.
Part I, para 4.1 and 4.3
Where a client lets the firm trade both securities and crypto at its discretion, crypto exposure in that mandate must stay under 10% of account value.
Part I, para 4.8
Firms must charge fees that are transparent, fair and clearly tied to order type, trade size and coin type.
Part I, para 4.10
A monthly statement is required whenever a client had a contract note that month, a non-zero balance, or held any coins. It must reach the client within 7 business days of month end.
Part I, para 6.12(g)-(h)
Firms must tell clients how compensation would work if a partner venue is hacked or otherwise loses client coins. They must also explain how forks or airdrops on held coins will be handled.
Part I, para 7.9(c)-(d)

A licensed corporation's yearly audit must state whether it had adequate custody controls. It must also state whether the firm complied with custody and record rules, and met the financial soundness rule.
Part I, para 9.1(a)-(c)
A firm cannot make markets in crypto on the very venue where it also deals for its own clients.
Part I, para 10.1
For advisory clients, the same virtual-asset knowledge test and liquidity screen for retail recommendations apply as on the dealing side.
Part II, para 3.1 and 3.5
rg: Read Part I sections IV, VI and VII (operations, dealing with clients, custody) closely; Part II largely cross-refers back to Part I so can be skimmed.

t: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities (2023)
s: This joint circular sets updated ground rules for banks and brokers dealing in virtual assets. It covers selling virtual-asset investment products, running dealing, advisory or discretionary asset-management services, and letting clients deposit and withdraw virtual assets. It replaces the January 2022 version, widening retail access under new safeguards rather than tightening the earlier professional-investor-only stance. Most such products must still be treated as complex products, requiring a suitability check and a virtual-asset knowledge test. But a narrow set of exchange-traded derivative products, tracked on approved exchanges, is carved out of the professional-investor restriction. Firms offering dealing services may only route trades through SFC-licensed trading platforms. Any client deposits or withdrawals of virtual assets must run through segregated accounts, held either with those platforms or with banks meeting HKMA's custody standards. A three-month transition period applied from the issue date for firms already serving clients under the old rules.
w: For a bank, this is the core standing instrument for any AI or RI conducting virtual-asset dealing, advisory or asset-management business with clients. It sets the licensed-platform-only routing rule, the custody channel for client deposits and withdrawals, and the pre-notification duty. Compliance must build these into onboarding and change-management processes.
k: Firms distributing products that mainly track the value of virtual assets must treat them as complex products. They must apply the SFC's usual suitability checks, unless the product is one of the narrow exchange-traded derivative types carved out.
para 5

Before letting a client trade virtual-asset products, a firm must confirm the client understands the risks. A one-off knowledge test is acceptable. The firm must also confirm the client has enough net worth to bear potential losses, unless the client is an institutional or qualified corporate professional investor.
para 7.2

A defined list of overseas venues qualifies as 'designated jurisdictions'. Certain exchange-traded derivative funds tracked there can be offered without the professional-investor-only limit. The full list sits in Appendix 2 (separate entry, id bf255e1026f4).
para 8, footnote 10

Firms may only provide virtual-asset dealing services by routing client business through platforms licensed by the SFC. This can be by introducing clients to those platforms directly, or by running a pooled (omnibus) account with them.
para 16

Where a firm lets clients deposit or withdraw virtual assets, this can only happen through segregated accounts. These must be held with its partner SFC-licensed platform, or with a bank (or that bank's subsidiary) that meets HKMA's published custody standards.
para 19(b)

A firm managing a portfolio is only pulled into the extra virtual-asset rules once the fund's stated goal is to invest in virtual assets. It is also pulled in once it intends to hold 10% or more of its assets in them.
para 22-23

Before recommending any specific virtual asset to a retail client, a firm must check it is highly liquid. This means it is included in at least two recognised market indices. The firm must also check it is actually tradeable by retail clients on the licensed platform.
para 27

Firms already offering dealing services to certain professional-investor clients before the circular's issue date get a three-month grace period. This lets them bring their systems and controls up to the new standard. New entrants must comply from day one.
para 29

A firm must tell the SFC, and HKMA where relevant, in advance. This applies before starting, or materially changing, any dealing, advisory or asset-management activity involving virtual assets or tokenised securities.
para 30
rg: Read paragraphs 1-30 in full. The numbered footnotes carry operative definitions, such as 'virtual asset' and 'SFC-licensed platform', that matter for scoping. The five enclosures (Appendices 1-7a) are logged as separate registry entries. You should read the relevant one alongside the section, dealing, advisory, or asset management, a firm is assessing.

t: Appendices 1-5 to the Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Appendices 1-5 to the Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual… (2023)
s: These five short appendices flesh out the main joint circular. Appendix 1 lists simple, non-exhaustive tests a firm can use to decide if a client already knows enough about virtual assets. Appendix 2 names twelve overseas markets whose exchange-traded virtual-asset derivative funds can be sold without the usual professional-investor-only limit. Appendix 3 is a decision flowchart for classifying a given virtual-asset product as complex or not. Appendix 4 lists the due-diligence checks a firm should run before distributing a virtual-asset fund that the SFC has not itself authorised. Appendix 5 gives model wording for the risk warnings firms must hand clients.
w: For a bank, these appendices supply the working checklists it needs day to day: a client-knowledge test, a jurisdiction list, product classification, fund due diligence, and risk-disclosure wording. The front line and compliance function need them to apply the main circular's requirements.
k: A client can be treated as having virtual-asset knowledge if they have taken relevant training, or have related work experience. This also applies if they have previously traded virtual assets or related products.
Appendix 1, p.1

Twelve markets qualify as 'designated jurisdictions'. This lets firms offer certain exchange-traded virtual-asset derivative funds there without the professional-investor-only restriction. The markets are Australia, France, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Taiwan (China), Thailand, the UK and the US.
Appendix 2, p.2

The Appendix 3 flowchart routes a virtual-asset product first by whether it is a derivative, and whether it trades on a specified exchange. It then lands on whether professional-investor-only and suitability rules apply.
Appendix 3, p.3

Before distributing an SFC-unauthorised virtual-asset fund, a firm should scrutinise the fund manager's background and internal controls. It should also check whether portfolio management, risk, valuation and custody functions are properly segregated.
Appendix 4(A)(a)-(b), p.4
Fund due diligence should also cover the fund's custody arrangement, including how assets are split between exchanges, custodians, hot storage and cold storage.
Appendix 4(B)(d), p.5

Diligence on the fund's counterparties should check their regulatory status for custody or trading of virtual assets, and their track record. It should also check IT and cybersecurity robustness, and financial soundness including insurance cover.
Appendix 4(C), p.5-6

Model risk-disclosure wording for clients must cover legal uncertainty over whether a virtual asset counts as 'property'. It must also cover valuation difficulty, price volatility, and weak or absent regulation of most trading and custody venues. It must flag the particular danger of loss when assets sit in a 'hot wallet'.
Appendix 5, p.7
rg: Read Appendix 4 in full if distributing unauthorised VA funds. Read Appendix 5 in full for client disclosure wording. Appendices 1-3 can be skimmed once the underlying criteria are understood.

t: Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions providing virtual asset dealing services and virtual asset advisory services
sl: HKMA/SFC · Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for… (2023)
s: This is Appendix 6a to the joint circular. It is the full text of the licensing and registration conditions imposed on firms that run virtual-asset dealing or advisory services, shown with tracked changes against the January 2022 version. Part I covers dealing services, split between two models. Under the introducing-agent model, the firm never holds client assets, and simply refers clients to a licensed trading platform. Under the omnibus-account model, the firm pools client trades through its own account with a licensed platform. Part II covers advisory services. Both parts carry detailed rules on know-your-client checks, disclosure, and custody of client virtual assets and money. They also cover record keeping, an independent auditor's opinion, anti-money-laundering controls, conflicts of interest, and a duty to report material breaches to the regulators.
w: For a bank, these are the actual binding licensing and registration conditions it signs up to when running VA dealing or advisory business. Compliance needs them as the checklist for custody segregation, client disclosures, AML controls, conflict-of-interest limits, record retention, and the auditor's annual sign-off.
k: Under the introducing-agent model, the firm must not relay client orders itself, and must not hold any client money or virtual assets at all. A written client agreement must spell out that the firm provides no dealing, financing, settlement or custody service.
Part I, condition (a)-(c), p.3-4

Under the omnibus-account model, a firm may only trade client virtual assets through an account it holds with an SFC-licensed platform. Retail clients may only be given access to virtual assets that platform itself makes available to retail investors.
Part I, para 4.1, p.7-8

A firm must never let clients withdraw or transfer virtual assets from its own account. Clients may only deposit and withdraw fiat currency through their segregated account, never virtual assets directly.
Part I, para 4.3, p.7
A firm must not offer any financing to help a client buy virtual assets. It should also try to stop other companies in its own group from doing so.
Part I, para 4.5, p.8

Firms must hold client virtual assets on trust in a segregated account. This must be kept either with the SFC-licensed platform itself, or with a bank meeting HKMA's custody standards. Access to move those assets must be tightly restricted to authorised staff.
Part I, para 7.1, p.19-20

Firms must tell clients up front how they would be compensated if the licensed platform or its affiliate were hacked, or otherwise caused a loss of client virtual assets. They must also notify clients promptly of events like hard forks or airdrops affecting their holdings.
Part I, para 7.9, p.24

A licensed corporation's yearly audit must include the auditor's opinion on whether its systems adequately ensured compliance with the custody and record-keeping requirements. It must also state whether the firm met the minimum liquid-capital rule.
Part I, s.IX, p.28-29

Firms must build anti-money-laundering controls specifically for virtual-asset dealing. This includes reviewing red-flag indicators against Financial Action Task Force (FATF) guidance before launching new products or technologies.
Part I, s.X, para 10.1, p.28-29
A firm may not run virtual-asset market-making activity on the same licensed platform through which it services its own clients' dealing business. This is to avoid a conflict of interest.
Part I, s.XI, para 10.1, p.29
Any actual or suspected material breach of these conditions must be reported to the SFC. For a registered institution, it must also be reported to the HKMA, as soon as practicable.
Part I, s.XII, para 11.1, p.29-30

For advisory services, a firm must confirm a client's virtual-asset knowledge and risk tolerance before advising them. When recommending a virtual asset to a retail client, it must confirm the asset is highly liquid, listed on two independent indices, and actually tradeable on a licensed platform.
Part II, s.III, para 3.1 & 3.5, p.34-35
rg: Read Part I sections IV (Operations), VII (Custody), IX (Auditors) and X (AML/CFT) in full for a bank running dealing services. Read Part II section III in full for advisory services. Definitions in section I, and the Schedule of cross-referenced codes, can be skimmed.

t: Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities | Enclosure 2: Appendix 6
sl: HKMA/SFC · Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities (2023)
s: This annex was the first set of licence and registration conditions telling brokers and banks how they could deal or advise in crypto tokens. It let firms either introduce clients straight to a licensed trading venue or run client trades through one shared account at that venue. It laid down client vetting, custody, record and reporting duties for that business. A newer version issued two months later, on 22 December 2023, replaced it in full, so day-to-day compliance work should follow entries bc97c16bac5e and 0027a8747112 instead.
w: This is the version that started imposing binding custody, suitability and reporting mechanics on VA dealing and advisory business, but it has already been fully replaced. Compliance should treat this only as a historical baseline and confirm live procedures track the December 2023 package instead.
k: A firm acting purely as an introducer may only steer clients toward opening their own account at a licensed trading venue. It cannot pass on trade instructions itself, or hold any of the client's coins or cash.
Part I, licensing condition (a) and (c)
Firms running trades through a shared (omnibus) account may only use venues that hold an SFC trading-platform licence. They can spread business across more than one such venue.
Part I, Terms and conditions para 4.1
Firms cannot lend or extend credit to clients so they can buy crypto, and should try to stop group affiliates doing the same.
Part I, Terms and conditions para 4.4

Coins pushed to retail clients must sit in at least two well-run market-cap indices from separate providers. They must also be listed for retail trading on the partner venue before a firm can recommend them.
Part I, Terms and conditions para 4.9(i)-(ii) and Note 1-2
Before serving a client, the firm must check whether the client understands crypto risk. If not, it can still proceed, but only after giving that client proper training.
Part I, Terms and conditions para 6.1-6.2
Each client needs a personal crypto exposure ceiling set against their net worth, told to them, and reviewed from time to time.
Part I, Terms and conditions para 6.4

Clients must be warned that coins may not count as legal property, and are not covered by the Investor Compensation Fund. They must also be warned that a lost or wrongly sent coin usually cannot be recovered.
Part I, Terms and conditions para 6.10(b)-(f)
Client coins must be kept on trust in a ring-fenced account. This must be either at the partner trading venue, or at a bank meeting the HKMA's custody expectations.
Part I, Terms and conditions para 7.1(a)
Any real or suspected serious breach of these conditions has to go to the SFC (and the HKMA for a registered institution) without delay.
Part I, Terms and conditions para 11.1

The advisory half of the annex mirrors the dealing rules. It requires assessing the client's crypto knowledge, sizing a suitable exposure, and only recommending coins that meet the same liquidity bar.
Part II, Terms and conditions para 3.1, 3.3, 3.5
rg: Skip the BRDR catalogue boilerplate in the parent page; go straight to the attachment's Part I (dealing) and Part II (advisory) terms and conditions, pages 3-32.

t: HKPF and SFC establish joint working group on VATPs
sl: SFC · HKPF and SFC establish joint working group on VATPs (2023)
s: Following a senior-level meeting on 28 September 2023, the SFC and the Hong Kong Police Force (HKPF) set up a joint working group. Its job is to strengthen cooperation on watching for, and investigating, illegal virtual-asset trading platform (VATP) activity. It draws on three HKPF units: the Commercial Crime Bureau, the Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau, and the Financial Intelligence and Investigations Bureau. It also draws on the SFC's Enforcement and Intermediaries Divisions. Together they share intelligence on suspicious activity, assess risk at VATPs, and coordinate investigations.
w: For a bank, this is background only. It confirms formal SFC-Police cooperation exists on investigating trading-platform fraud. This matters when deciding whether and how to escalate a suspicious virtual-asset counterparty, though it creates no direct duty for the bank.
k: A dedicated SFC-HKPF working group was set up after a senior meeting on 28 September 2023. Its goal is to strengthen how they cooperate on spotting and investigating illegal trading-platform activity.
main text, para 1-2

The group brings together three HKPF units: the Commercial Crime Bureau, the Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau, and the Financial Intelligence and Investigations Bureau. It also includes the SFC's Enforcement and Intermediaries Divisions.
main text, para 2
Its job is to share intelligence on suspicious platform activity and breaches. It will build a way to assess how risky a suspicious platform is, and improve coordination between investigations.
main text, para 3
rg: Read in full; brief press release, no boilerplate.

t: SFC publishes lists of virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · SFC publishes lists of virtual asset trading platforms (2023)
s: The SFC formally published the promised suite of VATP lists on its website. These are the List of licensed VATPs, and a new List of VATP applicants. A companion List of removed VATP applicants covers those returned, refused or withdrawn. There is also the List of closing-down VATPs, and the List of deemed licensed VATPs, effective 1 June 2024. Finally, there is an enhanced dedicated list of suspicious VATPs. The SFC stresses that appearing on the applicants list does not mean SFC licensing or compliance. It warns investors risk losing their entire investment on an unregulated VATP, with limited legal recourse.
w: For a bank, this gives compliance an authoritative, regularly updated source: the licensed, applicant, removed, closing-down, deemed-licensed and suspicious VATP lists. Use it to check any virtual-asset trading platform counterparty, before or during a relationship.
k: The List of VATP applicants sets out operators whose licence applications have not yet been approved. Entities on it are not licensed, and may not comply with SFC requirements.

A companion List of removed VATP applicants shows names removed because applications were returned, refused, or withdrawn, including for substandard/incomplete applications.
main text, Note 3 & para after item list

Investors are warned they may risk losing their entire investment if an unregulated VATP ceases operation, collapses, is hacked, or misappropriates assets. This includes a VATP on the applicants list. Legal recourse against a VATP without a Hong Kong link may be difficult.
main text, final Note

t: SFC steps up information dissemination and investor education on VATPs
sl: SFC · SFC steps up information dissemination and investor education on… (2023)
s: In direct response to the JPEX incident, the SFC announced measures to strengthen how it shares VATP information and educates investors. It will publish a 'List of licensed VATPs', a 'List of closing-down VATPs', and a 'List of deemed licensed VATPs'. It will also publish a new 'list of VATP applicants', and an enhanced dedicated list of suspicious VATPs. It will also run a public anti-fraud awareness campaign with the Investor and Financial Education Council (IFEC). It will strengthen intelligence gathering and enforcement. It will explore a dedicated information-sharing channel with the Police.

t: Statement on JPEX
sl: SFC · Statement on JPEX (2023)
s: The SFC issued this statement in response to public interest in JPEX, a virtual-asset trading platform. It says JPEX has been unregulated and under SFC scrutiny since March 2022, over suspected false representations and unlicensed activity. JPEX was placed on the SFC Alert List in July 2022. The SFC confirms JPEX never applied for, or discussed, a Hong Kong VATP licence with it, contrary to JPEX's own claims. It states JPEX unlawfully published confidential SFC correspondence, breaching secrecy provisions in the SFO and AMLO. The SFC says it has referred the matter to the Police, amid suspicion of fraud, with investigations ongoing.

t: Misrepresentation by crypto firms using word "bank"
sl: HKMA · Misrepresentation by crypto firms using word "bank" (2023)
s: The HKMA warned the public that some crypto firms call themselves things like 'crypto bank' or 'digital asset bank'. Some also label client funds as 'deposits' and market 'savings plans'. This may breach the Banking Ordinance. Only HKMA-authorised institutions, meaning licensed banks, restricted-licence banks and deposit-taking companies, may use the word 'bank' or take deposits in Hong Kong. Using the word, or holding out as a bank, without authorisation is a separate criminal offence under sections 97 and 97A. So is deposit-taking without authorisation, under sections 11, 12 and 92. The HKMA reminded the public that unauthorised crypto firms are not HKMA-supervised. Their funds are not covered by the Deposit Protection Scheme. It pointed to the register of authorized institutions (AI) and restricted-licence banks (RLB) for checking a firm's status.
w: For a bank, this confirms the statutory basis, Banking Ordinance sections 11, 12, 92, 97 and 97A, that an authorized institution (AI) can point to. This applies when a non-bank crypto counterparty or brand uses bank-like naming. It is useful for brand-protection and misrepresentation monitoring.
k: Only HKMA-authorised institutions may use the word 'bank' in their name/description or represent themselves as carrying on banking business in Hong Kong.
Note 1, s.97/s.97A Banking Ordinance
Only an authorized institution may carry on banking business or a deposit-taking business in Hong Kong.
Note 2, ss.11-12 Banking Ordinance
Funds placed with unauthorised crypto firms are not protected under the Hong Kong Deposit Protection Scheme.
para 4
The public can verify authorisation status via the HKMA's register of authorized institutions and restricted-licence banks.
para 5, register link

t: Warning statement on unregulated virtual asset trading platform
sl: SFC · Warning statement on unregulated virtual asset trading platform (2023)
s: This is the SFC's warning on JPEX, a platform that marketed heavily to Hong Kong retail investors. It used social-media promoters and over-the-counter shops. JPEX has never been licensed by, or applied for a licence from, the SFC. This is despite website claims of overseas licences, which the SFC says are untrue. The notice lists suspicious features: unusually high advertised yields, client withdrawal problems, and a claimed tie-up with a listed company. That tie-up had actually already ended, with no money ever invested. The SFC told promoters to stop marketing JPEX. It warns that fraud and misrepresentation offences under the anti-money-laundering ordinance can carry heavy penalties.

t: Warning statement on unregulated virtual asset trading platform
sl: SFC · Warning statement on unregulated virtual asset trading platform (2023)
s: The SFC named the platform JPEX in this warning. JPEX was promoted in Hong Kong through social-media influencers and over-the-counter (OTC) money-changer shops. No entity in the JPEX group was licensed, or had applied for a licence. The SFC said JPEX falsely claimed local and overseas regulatory approval. It offered unusually high yields, up to 21% APY on some products. Users could not withdraw funds, or found altered balances. A claimed partnership with a listed company had already ended, with no investment actually made. The SFC cited offences under the anti-money-laundering ordinance (AMLO) for fraudulent conduct and misrepresentation in virtual-asset (VA) transactions. It said it had told promoters to stop. It repeated that unlicensed platforms carry the risk of total loss, with little recourse, especially where they have no genuine Hong Kong link.
w: For a bank, this is the SFC's public account of the JPEX case. It is a reference point for red flags, such as unverified licence claims, high fixed yields, and false partnership claims, that counterparty and customer-activity screening should watch for in VA platforms.
k: No entity in the JPEX group was licensed by the SFC to operate a VATP in Hong Kong. None had even applied for one.

JPEX claimed savings-product yields as of 12 September 2023 of 21% APY on ETH, 20% on BTC, and 19% on USDT. This level was flagged as a suspicious feature.

t: HKMA publishes joint report on Project Sela (with photos)
sl: HKMA · HKMA publishes joint report on Project Sela (with photos) (2023)
s: The HKMA, the Bank of Israel, and the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre jointly published 'Project Sela – An accessible and secure retail CBDC ecosystem'. This proof-of-concept report studies a retail central bank digital currency (CBDC) design that would let non-bank payment firms connect directly to a central bank's CBDC ledger. The press release confirms the HKMA still has not decided whether or when to launch e-HKD, and says Project Sela's findings will feed into that ongoing study. The full technical report is a separate registry entry.
w: For a bank, this shows the HKMA is actively studying retail CBDC designs that could let non-bank firms take over certain customer-facing CBDC services without going through banks. This structural shift is worth watching for future disintermediation risk.
k: Project Sela is a joint experiment by the HKMA, the Bank of Israel, and the BIS Innovation Hub. It tests a retail CBDC design featuring a new kind of non-bank intermediary that connects straight to the central bank's ledger.

t: HKMA publishes joint report on Project Sela
sl: HKMA · HKMA publishes joint report on Project Sela (2023)
s: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the Bank of Israel (BOI) and the BIS Innovation Hub (BISIH) Hong Kong Centre jointly published this report on 12 September 2023. It was launched in Tel Aviv. It is a proof-of-concept study of a possible retail central bank digital currency (rCBDC) design, in which the central bank runs settlement directly. A new type of firm, called an "Access Enabler" (AE), handles all contact with customers. It never holds or controls users' rCBDC funds, and needs no balance-sheet liquidity of its own. This design could open the door to a lower regulatory bar and lower entry barriers for non-bank payment firms. The project does not reflect any policy decision by the HKMA on an e-HKD, or by the BOI on a digital shekel.
w: For a bank, this is horizon-scanning, not a rule. Project Sela shows a possible rCBDC design where non-bank 'Access Enablers' could avoid bank-style regulatory requirements. This is worth tracking as a disintermediation risk. But it creates no HKMA obligation for banks today.
k: Project Sela showed it is technically possible for non-bank payment firms ('Access Enablers') to connect directly to the central bank's CBDC ledger.
press release para 2

Access Enablers (AEs) handle all customer-facing rCBDC services. But they never hold or control customers' rCBDC funds, and need no balance-sheet liquidity of their own, since the central bank settles directly.
report para (Legal workstream), Section 1
This design could let AEs meet a lower regulatory bar and face fewer entry barriers than existing payment-ecosystem firms. Other requirements, such as security and governance, could still apply.
report Section 1, footnote 6
The central bank runs the rCBDC platform and ledger, and gives users pseudo-anonymous accounts. End users control their own rCBDC using self-generated private cryptographic keys.
report Section 1
Project Sela does not reflect any HKMA policy decision on a possible e-HKD. Nor does it reflect any Bank of Israel decision on a possible digital shekel.
report Section 1, footnote 5

t: Project Sela – An accessible and secure retail CBDC ecosystem
sl: HKMA · Project Sela – An accessible and secure retail CBDC… (2023)
s: This joint report by the HKMA, the Bank of Israel and the BIS Innovation Hub describes a proof-of-concept (PoC) for a retail central bank digital currency (rCBDC) system. The central bank runs the settlement ledger directly. A new type of firm, called an "Access Enabler" (AE), handles all contact with customers. This includes onboarding, know-your-customer and know-your-business checks (KYC/KYB), anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) screening, and payment routing. An AE never holds customer funds or private keys. Existing banks, called "Funding Institutions", keep the job of converting deposits and cash to and from the CBDC. The report argues AEs could face lighter rules than banks, covering systems, governance and operating capital, but not client-money capital rules, since AEs never hold customer funds. A legal analysis, based on UNIDROIT digital-asset principles, concludes that neither the AE nor the central bank legally "controls" the CBDC; the end user does. The report also sets out cyber-security design principles. These include key management using hardware security modules (HSMs) and trusted execution environments (TEEs), and limits on central-ledger programmability. This lets wider access coexist with strong security. The report is exploratory. It states it does not reflect any HKMA or Bank of Israel policy decision on issuing an actual CBDC.
w: For a bank, if Hong Kong ever adopts an Access-Enabler-style rCBDC design, non-bank firms could gain a lighter-touch route into payment services. This would run on the central bank's own ledger. This is a potential competitive and disintermediation risk to a bank's payments and deposit business. Compliance should track it, even though this remains purely exploratory research.
k: A new type of firm, the Access Enabler (AE), performs all customer-facing rCBDC services: onboarding, KYC/KYB, compliance and payment routing. Unlike a bank, an AE never holds customer funds or private keys.
Section 2, p.8
Funding Institutions, meaning banks, keep the job of managing customer deposit accounts and ATMs, and converting between rCBDC and bank deposits or cash.
Section 2, p.8
The report proposes that AEs handle AML/CFT customer due diligence and transaction screening, freeing the central bank from that role. It leaves detailed rules to individual countries.
Section 3.5, p.21

Legal analysis under UNIDROIT's digital-asset control test concludes that end users, not AEs or the central bank, legally control their rCBDC. This is because AEs cannot access private keys or move funds.
Section 4.2, p.25-26
The report proposes a lighter, tailored regime for AEs, covering systems and controls, governance, and a minimum operating-capital buffer. This replaces client-money capital rules.
Section 4.3, p.26-27

The cyber-security design deliberately keeps programmable functions at the AE layer, not on the central ledger. It relies on hardware security modules (HSMs) and trusted execution environments (TEEs) to protect keys.
Section 5, p.29-30
The project is explicitly exploratory. It does not reflect any policy decision by the HKMA on introducing an e-HKD, or by the Bank of Israel on a digital shekel.
Introduction, footnote 5, p.5
rg: Read the Introduction and Conclusion (pages 5-11 and 55-56) for the core design and findings. Skim the cyber-technical sections (5.1-6.2, pages 29-53) unless you are assessing implementation detail. The glossary on page 4 is reference only.

t: Keynote speech at the Treasury Markets Summit 2023

t: A Bridge to the Future: Hong Kong Fintech Promotion Roadmap
sl: HKMA · A Bridge to the Future: Hong Kong Fintech Promotion… (2023)
s: The HKMA, working with the SFC and the Insurance Authority, commissioned outside consultants to review how far banks, brokers and insurers have taken up fintech. It set out a forward plan under a four-part framework it calls PACE (Propagate, Assess, Connect, Equip). Distributed ledger technology (DLT) sits alongside artificial intelligence (AI) as one of two cross-cutting technologies, layered onto three business areas the regulators want to see grow. The document restates known milestones, such as virtual bank and VATP licensing, rather than announcing new rules. It closes by flagging that firms still find blockchain hard to explain internally, and lack a clear business case for it. It is strategic background, not a source of new obligations.
w: For a bank, this report signals where HKMA's attention and future guidance are headed for distributed ledger use, but it creates no binding duty by itself. A compliance head should read it as context for where thematic reviews or new circulars may follow, not as a source of controls to implement.
k: The regulators group emerging technology into five priority areas for the industry. Three are business lines: wealth and investment tech, insurance tech, and green tech; two are cross-cutting layers: artificial intelligence and distributed ledger technology.
Executive Summary, p.4

Blockchain-based tools are described as most promising for cross-border payments, tokenising financial assets, and building a shared, tamper-resistant record shared between institutions rather than a single central database.
p.3 (foreword) and p.9

The report recaps a short timeline of past regulatory steps: eight virtual bank licences from 2019, and an opt-in regime for security-token trading platforms from 2019. A further licensing regime followed in 2023, covering platforms trading non-security tokens.

The consultants found firms still struggle to separate the technology itself from the digital-asset market associated with it. They cite unclear rules across different countries as a brake on wider blockchain adoption.
High upfront cost and a weak return-on-investment case are named as the leading practical obstacles firms raise for both AI and blockchain projects.
Staff lacking hands-on blockchain expertise is flagged as the single most common technical obstacle firms report when trying to roll out DLT projects.
By 2025 the survey expects firms to be actively trialling blockchain for central bank digital currency work, clearing and settlement, credit scoring, asset tokenisation and trade finance.
rg: Read the Executive Summary (p.4-11) and section 3.5 on technology-overlay challenges (p.43). Skip the detailed initiative-by-initiative descriptions in section 2, and the event timeline appendix, which are promotional rather than substantive.

sl: HKMA · Bond Tokenisation in Hong Kong (2023)
s: This is a detailed HKMA report documenting the design, legal and technology choices made in Project Evergreen's inaugural tokenised government green bond. It is meant as a reference for market participants considering their own digital bond issuances. It covers the technology platform: private permissioned blockchains, node-hosting versus API access, and data visibility choices. It also covers deal-structuring questions and forward-looking priorities. The deal-structuring questions cover whether Hong Kong securities and companies law require any particular legal form for a bond, and 'native' versus 'non-native' tokenisation. They also cover on-chain versus off-chain payment, investor access via self-custody or custodians, and credit rating considerations. The forward-looking priorities include cross-platform interoperability, using digital bonds as repo collateral, and extending tokenised bonds to retail investors.
w: For a bank, this is the HKMA's own working reference on how tokenised bonds map onto existing Hong Kong securities, companies and payment law. It sets out concrete expectations for KYC and custody roles, business-continuity planning and platform-technology risk. A bank should apply these when structuring, custodying, or rating a digital bond, or when assessing a DLT platform provider as a counterparty.
k: Project Evergreen used a 'non-native' issuance: the bonds existed first as conventional book entries in the CMU's securities database. Beneficial interests were then recorded on the digital platform in tokenised securities accounts, rather than being created directly on-chain.
para 26, p.11

Neither the Securities and Futures Ordinance nor the Companies Ordinance, nor the Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance, prescribes a particular physical or paper form for debt securities. So a distributed ledger entry can satisfy existing Hong Kong law without new legislation for this kind of issuance.

For a Hong Kong-incorporated corporate issuer, digital bonds are treated as 'debentures' under the Companies Ordinance. This still requires a Debenture Holders Register that can be printed out in hard copy, even if kept electronically.
para 28(b), p.12

The Notes were distributed only to 'professional investors' under the SFO. The existing SFO licensing regime for regulated activities, such as dealing, advising and automated trading services, applies to digital bond issuance in the same way as to conventional bonds. So do the securities offering rules.
paras 23-24, p.11

Investors can hold digital bonds either by self-custody, directly controlling their own digital wallet and, where applicable, private keys, or through a custodian. Self-custody gives more control but exposes the investor to the risk of losing keys or suffering a security breach, with full responsibility on the investor.
para 42, p.15

Where investors are on-boarded directly to the DLT platform, the platform operator, and any custodian, is expected to carry out know-your-customer checks and enable AML/CFT compliance. Where investors instead access the bond only through a custodian, KYC is the custodian's responsibility.
para 44, p.16

In Project Evergreen, only custodians that are CMU participants and are on-boarded to the digital platform can open tokenised securities and cash-token accounts. Non-participant investors instead hold their interest through an off-platform custody relationship, recorded in the custodian's own books and records. This is structurally similar to indirect participation in a conventional clearing system like Euroclear or Clearstream.
para 45, p.16

The Notes were credit-rated on par with the Government's conventional green bonds. The report flags that digital bond ratings should factor in additional risks from largely untested DLT platform technology. It recommends a documented business continuity plan covering platform disruption, cyberattack, and database migration to an alternative platform.
paras 46-47, p.17

The digital platform used two private, permissioned blockchains, Hyperledger Besu as Layer 1 and Canton as Layer 2, with Daml smart contracts, rather than a public blockchain. This prioritised security and data privacy over the openness of a public chain.
para 12, p.8

Participants can access a DLT platform either by node-hosting, running their own copy of the ledger, or via a standard API/user interface, a lower technical burden. Node-hosting costs more and carries higher operational and cyber-risk exposure. Project Evergreen participants used a graphical user interface.
paras 15-16, p.9

Payments in Project Evergreen were made on-platform using 'Cash Tokens' minted by the CMU, each representing a claim on the HKMA equal to one Hong Kong dollar. These settled atomically with the transfer of tokenised securities balances, meaning a delivery-versus-payment transaction either completes fully or not at all.

Other digital bond transactions may instead use payment tokens not issued by a central bank. The report flags these as carrying higher counterparty, credit, operational, volatility and liquidity risk than central-bank-backed cash tokens.
para 34, p.14
rg: Read Sections I (Overview), III (Deal Structuring Considerations, especially applicability of securities regulations, investor access and custody arrangement, and credit rating) and IV (Unlocking the Potential of DLT) in full. Section II (Technology and Platform Design) can be skimmed for the network-type and participation-model choices, unless the reader needs the technical architecture detail.

t: Report on Bond Tokenisation in Hong Kong
sl: HKMA · Report on Bond Tokenisation in Hong Kong (2023)
s: This is the HKMA press release announcing publication of the report 'Bond Tokenisation in Hong Kong' (24 August 2023). It sums up the Government's inaugural tokenised green bond, Project Evergreen: HK$800 million, February 2023, the first tokenised green bond any government worldwide has issued. It used distributed ledger technology (DLT) for primary issuance, secondary-trading settlement and coupon payment, with maturity redemption to be tested later. The press release describes the report as a blueprint for future issuances, covering technology and platform design and deal-structuring considerations. It flags next steps: further use cases, addressing platform fragmentation, and enhancing the legal and regulatory framework. The report's own detailed content is covered in its own registry entry (a0b44be27c40).
w: For a bank, this reports on the Government's first tokenised green bond, and outlines next steps for Hong Kong's bond-tokenisation market. It creates no obligations, but is useful background if the bank later takes part in tokenised bond issuance, settlement or custody.
k: Project Evergreen issued HK$800 million of tokenised green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme in February 2023, the first such bond any government worldwide has issued. It used DLT for primary issuance, secondary-trading settlement and coupon payment, with maturity redemption to be tested later.
press release, para 2
Bond tokenisation was one of the pilot projects announced in FSTB's October 2022 Policy Statement on the Development of Virtual Assets in Hong Kong.
press release, para 2

The report is described as a blueprint for similar future issuances, covering technology and platform design and deal-structuring considerations. It flags further use cases, platform-fragmentation issues, and legal and regulatory enhancements as next steps; the HKMA says it will work with Government and industry on further tokenised issuances.
press release, para 3

For the report's detailed technical, legal and deal-structuring content (platform design, settlement finality, custody, credit rating, next steps), see the full report, which is a separate registry entry.
attachment a0b44be27c40
rg: This is only the short press-release announcement; read the full report entry (a0b44be27c40) for the substantive technology, legal and deal-structuring detail.

t: Warning: Virtual asset trading platforms engaging in improper practices
sl: SFC · Warning: Virtual asset trading platforms engaging in improper practices (2023)
s: The SFC describes patterns of bad behaviour it has seen among unlicensed VATPs during the new licensing regime's transition period. Some falsely claim to have already applied for a licence. Others set up new entities in anticipation of the transitional rules, or keep launching products, such as virtual-asset 'deposits' or 'savings', that the new regime does not allow. The SFC says such conduct will count against a platform's fitness and properness when it does apply for a licence. It repeats that operating in Hong Kong without a licence is a criminal offence.
w: For a bank, this warning does not bind it directly. But its red flags are exactly what a compliance head's VATP counterparty due-diligence checklist should test for before any referral or distribution partnership. These are false licence claims and impermissible deposit-style VA products.
k: Some unlicensed VATPs falsely claim to have already applied to the SFC for a licence.
heading 'Falsely claiming...', para 1
Making a fraudulent or reckless misrepresentation to induce virtual-asset trading is itself an offence.
heading 'Falsely claiming...', para 2
False licence-application claims will be weighed against the platform when it later seeks an actual licence.
heading 'Falsely claiming...', para 2
Platforms operating in Hong Kong before 1 June 2023 got a transitional window, but the SFC can still refuse to treat them as 'deemed licensed' if it doubts they can meet requirements.
heading 'VATPs which do not comply...', para 1
Products like virtual-asset 'deposits', 'savings' or 'earnings' offered to retail clients are not allowed under the new VATP regime.
heading 'VATPs which do not comply...', para 4
Established unlicensed entities already doing VA business in Hong Kong must apply for a licence or shut down that business.
heading 'Unlicensed VATPs' established entities...', para 1
Operating an unlicensed virtual-asset business in Hong Kong is a criminal offence.
heading 'Unlicensed VATPs' established entities...', para 1
rg: Read the four subheadings in order; the closing 'Warning to investors' section repeats points already made.

t: Warning: Virtual asset trading platforms engaging in improper practices
sl: SFC · Warning: Virtual asset trading platforms engaging in improper practices (2023)
s: The SFC warned that some unlicensed VATPs were falsely claiming to have applied for an SFC licence. It said this is itself a criminal misrepresentation offence under AMLO section 53ZRG, and will count against future fitness-and-properness assessments. It also flagged VATPs setting up new entities, or continuing under existing ones, to launch products the new licensing regime does not allow. These include retail-facing VA deposits, savings or earnings arrangements. The SFC said any past non-compliant conduct, and whether it could reasonably have been avoided or is being genuinely unwound, will feed into licence decisions. It reminded the public that most currently accessible VATPs are unlicensed, and that trading on them carries a risk of total loss with limited recourse.
w: For a bank, this gives concrete red flags for VATP counterparty due diligence. Unverified licence-application claims, and any retail VA 'savings' or 'earnings' style products, signal a platform the bank should treat as materially higher risk or non-compliant.
k: Falsely claiming to have submitted an SFC licence application is a criminal misrepresentation offence and will be weighed in any later fitness-and-properness assessment.
para on 'Falsely claiming to have submitted an application', Note 1
VA 'deposit', 'savings' or 'earnings' arrangements offered to retail clients are not permitted under the new VATP regime.
para 'For example, they may... launch certain virtual assets... virtual asset deposits, savings or earnings'
The SFC will consider whether past non-compliant activity could reasonably have been avoided, and whether the firm shows genuine intent to unwind it, when assessing licence applications.
para beginning 'Where there have been past non-compliant activities'
Established entities of unlicensed VATPs already operating in Hong Kong must either apply for a licence or close their Hong Kong business; unlicensed operation is a criminal offence.
para 'Unlicensed VATPs' established entities operating in Hong Kong'
Firms that were providing VA services before 1 June 2023 could continue without breaching the licensing requirement only during the 1 Jun 2023 to 31 May 2024 non-contravention window.
Note 2
rg: Read the 'falsely claiming' and 'VATPs which do not comply' sections in full; the closing 'warning to investors' section repeats the SFC's standard risk language and can be skimmed.
