t: Frequently Asked Questions on streamlined approach for compliance with suitability obligations when dealing with sophisticated professional investors
sl: SFC · Frequently Asked Questions on streamlined approach for compliance with… (2023)
s: This is a seven-question FAQ explaining how intermediaries should apply the SFC's streamlined suitability approach for sophisticated professional investors (SPIs). It covers evidencing SPI status, using a representative's investment knowledge, and categorising products, with virtual assets and VA-related products as their own category. It also covers what a Product Category Information Statement should cover, and setting and reviewing a streamlining threshold. Other topics are monitoring that threshold, including via designated sub-accounts, and handling leveraged or margin transactions under the approach.
w: For a bank, this confirms that virtual assets sit in their own ring-fenced Product Category, even for sophisticated clients under the lighter streamlined suitability regime. It sets concrete, auditable criteria, five trades in three years, that the bank's product-categorisation and threshold-monitoring controls must be built around.
k: An SPI's requisite knowledge or experience can be shown by qualifications, work experience, or by having executed at least five transactions in the same product category within the past three years. This includes transactions made via power of attorney or joint accounts.

Intermediaries should create Product Categories such as accumulators/decumulators, insurance-linked-securities funds, loss-absorption debt instruments, virtual assets, and VA-related products, keeping each separate from the others.
An SPI may specify their own streamlining threshold appropriate to their financial situation, and the intermediary is required to keep records of the rationale supporting that threshold.

Intermediaries are not expected to force-unwind a client's exposure just because it later exceeds the streamlining threshold. But they may restrict further top-ups or execute new trades outside the designated account instead.

Intermediaries may execute leveraged or margin trades on behalf of an SPI using the streamlined approach, so long as these stay within the SPI's specified Product Categories and threshold. But they must put in place effective systems and controls that keep the gross leveraged exposure at or below that threshold.
rg: All three pages are relevant; read in full.

It repeats the FATF's ongoing call for countermeasures against Iran and North Korea, and enhanced due diligence on Myanmar (the High-Risk Jurisdictions list). It notes the addition of Cameroon, Croatia and Vietnam to the Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring list, and sums up June 2023 FATF Plenary outcomes. t: Task Force on Promoting Web3 Development established
sl: Government · Task Force on Promoting Web3 Development established (2023)
s: The Government announces it has set up the Task Force on Promoting Web3 Development. The Financial Secretary chairs it, with 15 non-official members from market sectors and official members including the heads of the HKMA, SFC, Insurance Authority and Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX). Members' two-year term starts 1 July 2023. This body follows up on the October 2022 VA Policy Statement and the 2023-24 Budget announcement. It is tasked with recommending how to develop Web3 in Hong Kong sustainably and responsibly, balancing regulation and industry growth.
w: For a bank, this identifies the cross-regulator body, with the HKMA, SFC, Insurance Authority and HKEX all represented, that will shape future digital-asset policy direction. It is useful for tracking where forthcoming rule proposals may come from.
k: The Task Force is chaired by the Financial Secretary and includes 15 non-official members plus official members from the HKMA, SFC, Insurance Authority, HKEX, Cyberport and InvestHK.
para 1, membership list
Non-official members' term runs from 1 July 2023 for two years.
para 1
The Task Force's mandate is to provide recommendations on sustainable and responsible Web3 development, balancing appropriate regulation with promoting development.

t: Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism for Licensed Corporations and SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers
sl: SFC · Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism for… (2023)
s: This is the SFC's seventh-edition AML/CFT rulebook for licensed corporations (LCs) and SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform operators, in force since June 2023. Most of its chapters cover generic bank-style controls: risk-based assessment, customer checks, ongoing monitoring, sanctions screening, suspicious-report filing, record-keeping and staff training. Chapter 12 adds virtual-asset-specific rules binding on LCs and SFC-licensed VASPs, including a Hong Kong version of the international travel rule. This rule requires firms to collect and pass on sender and receiver details for crypto transfers. It also requires counterparty due-diligence duties, and extra checks for transfers to wallets not held by a regulated firm. A bank does not follow this Guideline directly for its banking business, which the HKMA's own AML/CFT Guideline governs. Only a bank's SFC-registered institution (RI) arm must have regard to specific cross-referenced parts of this Guideline. These are the customer definition, the correspondent-relationship provisions, Chapter 12, and the illustrative suspicious-indicator appendix. Otherwise, the bank meets this Guideline only as a due-diligence benchmark for its VATP or LC counterparties.
w: For a bank, this Guideline binds its SFC-licensed VATP and LC counterparties directly. Its Chapter 12 travel-rule and counterparty due-diligence content sets the benchmark a compliance head should check any such counterparty against. It does not bind the bank's own banking business directly. For the bank's own AML/CFT programme, the governing text is the HKMA's AML/CFT Guideline. The bank's RI arm need only 'have regard to' the customer-definition, correspondent-relationship, Chapter 12 and suspicious-indicator parts of this Guideline (para 1.6). It need not comply with it as an SFC licensee would.
k: The guideline is legally grounded in the anti-money-laundering ordinance and the securities law. A firm's failure to follow it can count as misconduct affecting its fitness to hold a licence. It applies to SFC-licensed corporations and SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers. A bank's RI arm is required only to have regard to specific cross-referenced parts, see para 1.6: the customer definition, correspondent-relationship provisions, Chapter 12, and the suspicious-indicator appendix. It need not follow the whole Guideline.

Chapter 12 covers both virtual assets as legally defined and any tokens that count as securities under the securities law. It applies to firms that hold an SFC VASP licence, and to LCs when carrying out VA-related or ML/TF-risk-relevant business.
Before moving crypto worth HK$8,000 or more, the sending firm must capture and record both the sender's and the receiver's identifying details, including an account or wallet reference.
The sending firm has to pass that sender/receiver data on to the receiving platform securely and before or at the same time as the transfer itself.

A firm should vet any platform it transacts with on the other end of a crypto transfer. This covers its licensing status, ownership, and whether its AML controls and data-security practices are adequate.
Deals with a counterparty that is a shell entity with no real presence and no group oversight are banned outright.

For transfers to or from a wallet not controlled by a regulated firm, the firm should still gather comparable sender and receiver information from its own customer. It should also assess whether the wallet looks trustworthy before proceeding.
Firms' screening mechanisms should also cover every party in a crypto transfer against sanctions and watch lists before the transfer goes through.
para 12.8.1
Sender/receiver data collected for a crypto transfer, and records tied to occasional transactions above the threshold, must be kept for at least five years.
Deposits or withdrawals routed through a third party's crypto wallet get extra scrutiny, and firms are encouraged to pre-approve a whitelist of wallets belonging to clients or vetted third parties.
rg: Go straight to Chapter 12 (p.140-189). Skim Chapters 2-9 only for cross-references Chapter 12 points to, such as paras 4.20 on correspondent relationships. Skip the generic securities-sector CDD detail not tied to virtual assets.

t: SFC Disciplinary Fining Guidelines (for regulated persons under Part 5B of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance)
sl: SFC · SFC Disciplinary Fining Guidelines (2023)
s: These guidelines are made under section 53ZSS(1) of AMLO Part 5B. They explain how the SFC decides whether and how much to fine a regulated VATP operator or its staff found guilty of misconduct or unfitness. The maximum fine is HK$10 million, or, if larger, three times the profit gained or the loss avoided, and can be assessed per affected person. The guidelines list general factors that make conduct more or less serious, then detailed specific factors the SFC will weigh. These cover the nature and impact of the conduct, whether it was intentional or negligent, cooperation and self-reporting, remedial steps, prior disciplinary record, and consistency with past cases.
w: For a bank, this sets out the fining framework its counterparty VATPs, and any bank entity itself licensed under AMLO Part 5B, face for AML/CFT or fitness-and-properness breaches. It is a useful benchmark when assessing the enforcement risk of a VATP relationship.
k: Maximum fine under s.53ZSP(3)(c) is HK$10 million or three times the profit gained/loss avoided, whichever is greater, and may be multiplied by the number of persons affected.
SFC will not impose a fine where facts warrant only a public reprimand, and will publicise all fining decisions as policy.
Intentional or reckless conduct, conduct damaging market integrity, or conduct facilitating money laundering/terrorist financing is treated as more serious.
p.3, General considerations
Timely self-reporting to the SFC, full disclosure, cooperation and remedial action (including client compensation) are mitigating specific considerations.
p.4, Specific considerations
A fine should not be set so as to place a firm or individual in financial jeopardy, save where financial distress is deliberately engineered to avoid a fine.
rg: Read pages 2-5 in full, the whole substantive text; skip nothing, it is short.

t: Guidelines for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators
sl: SFC · Guidelines for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators (2023)
s: These are the SFC's detailed operating rules for VATP operators licensed under the SFO or the AMLO, or both. They cover fitness-and-properness, competence and training of staff, financial soundness, token admission, client dealing, custody of client assets, governance, cybersecurity, conflicts of interest, record keeping, auditors and ongoing reporting duties. A VATP must hold client assets through a separate Associated Entity, and must keep 98% of those assets in cold storage. Retail clients may only trade large-cap tokens that meet strict listing criteria. The guidelines set the baseline a bank should expect any licensed VATP counterparty in Hong Kong to meet.
w: For a bank, this is the primary rulebook against which it must due-diligence any Hong Kong VATP it partners with, refers clients to, or banks as a customer. The cold-storage, compensation, segregation and reporting thresholds here are the benchmarks compliance should check the VATP actually meets. It also frames the SFC's expectations on suitability and disclosure that a bank distributing or facilitating access to VATP services should mirror.
k: A VATP must be either an SFC Type 1/Type 7 licensed corporation or hold an AMLO virtual asset service licence. It should keep client assets on trust for those clients, held through a separate, wholly-owned Associated Entity that does no other business.
para 1.1 (definitions), para 10.1

Directors, responsible officers and licensed representatives must meet fitness-and-properness and competence tests, including recognised exam papers, minimum industry experience and continuing training hours.
Part II-IV, paras 2.1, 3.16, 4.14

A VATP must at all times maintain HK$5,000,000 minimum paid-up capital and liquid capital above a required threshold. It should keep at least 12 months of operating expenses in liquid non-crypto assets in Hong Kong.
paras 6.1-6.7

A token admission and review committee, including compliance, risk and IT heads, should set and enforce criteria for listing, suspending and delisting tokens, and report to the board at least monthly.
paras 7.1-7.5

Before listing any token the platform should run documented due diligence covering the project team, legal status, liquidity, technical design and money-laundering risk, and commission an independent smart-contract audit.
Tokens offered to retail clients should not be securities (unless a prospectus is used) and should be included in at least two independent, IOSCO-aligned large-cap indices.
paras 7.7-7.8

Platforms should not offer algorithmic trading, virtual asset futures or derivatives, or financial accommodation (margin) to clients to buy tokens, or yield-generating uses of client tokens. They should not engage in proprietary trading or market making on own account.

Clients (other than professional/institutional investors) should be assessed for virtual-asset knowledge, risk profile and a personal exposure limit before trading, and complex products need extra suitability checks and warnings.

At least 98% of client virtual assets should be held in cold storage, such as HSM-based storage. Strict controls apply to private-key generation, multi-person access, and Hong Kong-based storage of seeds and keys.
para 10.6(c), para 10.8(e)
A VATP should maintain an SFC-approved compensation arrangement (insurance, ring-fenced funds, or bank guarantee) covering 50% of cold-storage and 100% of hot/other-storage client virtual assets.

Client money should be paid into segregated accounts with a Hong Kong authorized institution, or an SFC-agreed overseas bank, within one business day. It may only be used for client-authorised purposes.
The platform should run an independent market-surveillance system from a reputable provider, reviewed at least annually, and notify the SFC promptly of any suspected manipulation.
paras 8.1-8.4
rg: For a bank compliance head, the core due-diligence checklist for a VATP counterparty has four parts. These are Part X (Custody, p.62), Part VI (Financial Soundness, p.36), Part VII (Token admission, p.40) and Part XVI (Reporting, p.94). The Fitness, Competence and training detail in Parts II-IV (p.7-35), and Schedule 4's application forms, can be skimmed.

t: Virtual asset trading platform operators - FAQs on licensing related matters
sl: SFC · Virtual asset trading platform operators - FAQs on licensing… (2023)
s: This SFC webpage indexes frequently-asked-questions (FAQs) on licensing-related duties for virtual asset trading platform (VATP) operators, cross-referencing the VATP Guidelines. Topics indexed include the meaning of "actively markets" under section 115 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO) and section 53ZRB of the AMLO, and competence requirements for individuals. Other topics are keeping to notification requirements, doing business outside Hong Kong, external assessment reports for licence applications, senior-management accountability measures, premises and record-keeping, and the SFC Regulatory Sandbox. As with the conduct FAQ page, only the topic index was captured, not the underlying answer text.
w: For a bank, the "actively markets" topic is central to assessing whether an offshore VA platform soliciting the bank's Hong Kong clients is operating without an SFC licence. The full answer text should be pulled from the live SFC page before relying on it.
k: The FAQ page defines the scope of what counts as "actively marketing" VA services to Hong Kong investors under s.115 SFO / s.53ZRB AMLO, as a distinct topic. This determines when an offshore platform needs an SFC licence.

t: Circular on transitional arrangements of the new licensing regime for virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · transitional arrangements of the new licensing regime for virtual… (2023)
s: The SFC set out transition rules under the AMLO for virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs) trading non-security tokens, as the new licensing regime began on 1 June 2023. A 'non-contravention arrangement' lets VATPs already genuinely present in Hong Kong before 1 June 2023 keep operating for 12 months, until 31 May 2024, without breaching licensing rules. A 'deeming arrangement' lets qualifying existing VATPs that file a complete licence application by 29 February 2024 be treated as licensed from 1 June 2024, while the SFC finishes its review. VATPs that were not doing business in Hong Kong before 1 June 2023 get none of this relief and must be licensed before starting up. Platforms trading both security and non-security tokens need licences under both the SFO and the AMLO.
w: For a bank, this sets the AMLO transition and deeming timetable, which decides whether a VATP counterparty was legitimately operating, deemed-licensed, or required to shut down. That is essential for reviewing any VATP relationship active in 2023-2024.
k: The transition rules apply only to VATPs trading non-security tokens; there is no transition period for meeting SFO (security token) rules.
para 3

VATPs genuinely doing business in Hong Kong before 1 June 2023 may keep operating from 1 June 2023 to 31 May 2024. This is a 12-month non-contravention window, and does not breach AMLO licensing rules.
para 6

To count as 'genuinely present,' factors include being incorporated in Hong Kong, having a physical office, and running central management from Hong Kong. Other factors are Hong Kong-based key staff, real trading activity, and other supporting evidence. A shell company is not enough.
para 7-8

To qualify for deeming, treated as licensed automatically from 1 June 2024, an existing VATP must file a complete WINGS application between 1 June 2023 and 29 February 2024. It must also meet further conditions on confirmations and evidence.
para 12

VATPs with no Hong Kong footprint before 1 June 2023 cannot use these transition rules. They must not start business or actively market to Hong Kong investors until formally licensed; doing so unlicensed is a criminal offence.
para 10
An existing VATP must submit at least two Responsible Officer (RO) applications with its licence application. At least one RO must live in Hong Kong, to meet the minimum RO condition for deeming.
para 26
Applications filed after 29 February 2024 cannot qualify for deeming, and the SFC cannot extend this statutory deadline.
para 20
VATPs trading both security and non-security tokens should apply for licences under both the SFO and the AMLO through one combined application.
para 30-33
rg: Read paras 1-20 (eligibility, non-contravention, deeming) and 26-33 (responsible-officer requirements, dual licensing). Skip repeated footnote cross-references to AMLO schedule sections. The Appendix timeline graphic (attachment 273818ad4232) is a useful one-page summary.

t: Police Force engages in Metaverse exploring threats and opportunities of Web3 (with photos)

t: Consultation Conclusions on Proposed Amendments to Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Authorized Institutions)
sl: HKMA · Consultation Conclusions on Proposed Amendments to Guideline on Anti-Money… (2023)
s: The HKMA sets out what banks said about its draft changes to the AML/CFT Guideline, and how it responded. The changes carry out the 2022 amendments to the Anti-Money Laundering Ordinance (AMLO), which brought in VASP licensing and updated customer-checking (CDD) definitions. On virtual assets, the HKMA confirms banks stay under its own Guideline rather than the SFC's, with registered institutions (RIs) pointed to the SFC text via footnote 1. It also states banks may carry out VA transfers for customers if the statutory section 13A conditions are met. Other responses cover digital ID, trust beneficiaries, former politically exposed persons (PEPs), bearer shares, and applying new rules to existing customers.
w: For a bank, this is the HKMA's clearest statement that it may execute VA transfers for customers if section 13A of Schedule 2 is met. It also confirms the bank answers to the HKMA Guideline, with SFC Chapter 12 relevant only through footnote 1.
k: Following the AMLO amendments gazetted on 16 December 2022, the HKMA consulted banks from 18 January to 8 March 2023 and received comments from four industry associations.
Part I, paras 1 and 3, p.3

The SFC's AML guideline, with its new virtual asset chapter, covers SFC licensees and SFC-licensed VASPs. Banks, including RIs, keep following the HKMA Guideline; footnote 1 was updated so RIs and AI associated entities have regard to the SFC text.
Part II, para 4.2, p.7

The HKMA states the AMLO does not bar banks from carrying out VA transfers for customers, provided section 13A of Schedule 2 is met. Banks should keep following HKMA circulars of 28 January 2022 and 27 April 2023, and may raise questions with the AML & Financial Crime Risk Division.
Part II, para 4.3, p.7

Private-sector remote-onboarding tools are not 'recognised digital identification systems' under Schedule 2; iAM Smart is. Existing remote onboarding practice under earlier HKMA circulars continues to apply.
Part II, paras 1.2-1.4, pp.4-5

For trusts, where beneficiaries are a class, banks may gather enough information to identify them at payout. A new para 4.4.13 lets banks verify beneficiaries using trustee-provided information on a risk basis.
Part II, para 2.3, p.6
Senior management approval is no longer required to stop applying EDD to a former PEP, but banks need sound internal controls and oversight for that decision.
Part II, para 3.2, p.6
Updated CDD rules can be applied to existing customers through normal periodic or trigger reviews. High-risk ones, such as non-Hong Kong PEPs, should be updated at or before their next review.
Part II, para 6.3, p.9
The revised Guideline was to be gazetted on 25 May 2023 and take effect on 1 June 2023.
Part III, para 1, p.10
rg: Read Part II section 4 (p.7) first, then 6.3 (p.9) and Part III (p.10). Sections 1-3 and 5 are background for non-VA changes.

t: Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Authorized Institutions) (Revised May 2023)
sl: HKMA · Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For… (2023)
s: This is the HKMA's binding AML/CFT rulebook for all banks (authorized institutions), including those registered with the SFC. The May 2023 revision came into force on 1 June 2023, alongside the 2022 AMLO amendments that created the VASP licensing regime. Its virtual-asset content is thin and targeted. It has a HK$8,000 trigger for customer checks (CDD) on occasional VA transfers, matching record-keeping, and a cross-reference to section 13A of Schedule 2. It also has correspondent-style due diligence for overseas VASPs, and a footnote pointing RIs to the SFC guideline's VA chapter. Everything else a digital-asset business line touches, such as risk assessment, new-product assessment, CDD, monitoring, sanctions screening, suspicious-transaction reports and records, is governed by the generic chapters. It has nothing specific on stablecoins, unhosted wallets or VA red flags.
w: For a bank, this, not the SFC guideline, is its own AML/CFT rulebook. SFC Chapter 12 reaches the bank only for its RI or associated-entity business, via footnote 1. The VA-specific rules are few: the HK$8,000 VA transfer trigger, the section 13A cross-reference, and overseas-VASP correspondent measures. So most digital-asset controls must be built from the generic risk-assessment, new-product, CDD, monitoring and record-keeping chapters.
k: The Guideline is the HKMA's AML/CFT rulebook for every Authorized Institution (AI), including AIs that are also SFC Registered Institutions (RIs). It is issued under the AML/CFT Ordinance (AMLO, Cap 615) and the Banking Ordinance; breaches can lead to disciplinary or other action under either law.
paras 1.1, 1.3, p.3 (printed p.1)
Both 'must' and 'should' in this Guideline denote a mandatory requirement, so 'should' is not optional wording for an AI.
para 1.6, p.4 (printed p.2)

Virtual-asset (VA) cross-reference: RIs, and AIs that are associated entities of SFC licensees, must additionally have regard to the SFC's AML/CFT Guideline for Licensed Corporations and SFC-licensed VASPs. This includes its Chapter 12 on virtual assets. This reaches only AIs acting as RIs or associated entities; it does not import SFC Chapter 12 for a bank's general banking business.
Chapter 1, footnote 1 (to para 1.3), p.3 (printed p.1)

Non-compliance can count against the Seventh Schedule authorization criteria under the Banking Ordinance, on adequate systems of control. Courts and the HKMA take the Guideline into account when judging Schedule 2 breaches.
paras 1.7-1.8, p.4 (printed p.2)

Penalties: an AI that knowingly breaches a specified AMLO provision faces up to 2 years' jail and a HK$1m fine, or 7 years if intent to defraud. Staff and managers who cause a breach face the same. The HKMA can also impose a pecuniary penalty up to HK$10m, or three times the profit gained or cost avoided, whichever is higher.
paras 1.16-1.18, p.7 (printed p.5)

Each AI should run a documented institution-wide ML/TF risk assessment covering customers, customer and operating jurisdictions, and products, services, transactions and delivery channels. Senior management approves the results, and it is refreshed at least every two years and on material trigger events.

Before launching a new product, business practice or delivery mechanism, or using a new or developing technology, the bank should first weigh the ML/TF risks involved and put mitigants in place. This is the hook for assessing any VA, tokenisation or stablecoin-related service before launch.
paras 2.10-2.11, p.12 (printed p.10)

The board, or a delegated committee, and senior management must understand the bank's ML/TF risks and receive timely management information. Senior management appoints a management-level Compliance Officer (CO) and a senior Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO), normally based in Hong Kong and independent of business lines as far as size allows.
paras 3.6-3.9, pp.15-16 (printed pp.13-14)

A Hong Kong-incorporated AI should apply these standards group-wide to overseas branches and subsidiaries doing financial-institution business, and apply the higher of home or host rules. It should tell the HKMA if host law blocks compliance.
paras 3.15-3.19, pp.17-18 (printed pp.15-16)

The four core customer due diligence (CDD) steps are: identify and verify the customer, and identify the beneficial owner and take reasonable steps to verify them, including understanding ownership and control. The other two steps are: understand the purpose of the relationship, and verify anyone acting for the customer and their authority.
para 4.1.3, p.19 (printed p.17)

VA transfer threshold: for a walk-in (occasional) customer, an AI must complete CDD before executing a virtual asset transfer of HK$8,000 or more. This applies whether done in one go or split into operations that appear linked. The same trigger applies to wire transfers, while other occasional transactions use HK$120,000.
para 4.2.1(b)(iii), p.20 (printed p.18)

Footnote 15 points AIs to section 13A of Schedule 2 to the AMLO for virtual asset transfers. The Guideline itself gives no further VA transfer (travel rule) detail, so the statutory text of s.13A is the operative source for a bank's VA transfer obligations.
para 4.2.1, footnotes 14-15, p.20 (printed p.18)
rg: Read fn 1 (p.3) and paras 2.10-2.11 (p.12) first. Then read 4.2.1-4.2.5 with fn 14-15 (pp.20-21) and 8.4 (p.71). Next read 11.6-11.25 (pp.81-86), then Chapters 5 and 6 for monitoring and screening. Chapter 12 (private banking) and the PEP detail can be skimmed for VA purposes.

t: SFC concludes consultation on regulation of virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · SFC concludes consultation on regulation of virtual asset trading… (2023)
s: The SFC released Consultation Conclusions on the Proposed Regulatory Requirements for VATP Operators, following 152 written submissions. A significant majority of respondents supported allowing licensed VATPs to serve retail investors, subject to robust protections (suitability onboarding, governance, enhanced token due diligence, admission criteria, disclosures). The resulting Guidelines for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators took effect 1 June 2023, alongside related AML/CFT guidelines and Disciplinary Fining Guidelines gazetted 25 May 2023. The SFC noted that, as of commencement, it had not yet approved any VATP to serve retail investors, and most platforms accessible to the public remained unregulated.
w: The retail-access decision and 1 June 2023 commencement date here bind VATPs, not the bank directly. A compliance head needs it mainly to confirm which VATP-facing instrument set (VATP Guidelines plus AML/CFT Guideline) now governs any VATP the bank refers clients to or partners with.
k: 152 written submissions were received; a significant majority supported allowing licensed VATPs to serve retail investors.
main text, para 2-3

The VATP Guidelines -- formally titled Guidelines for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators -- became effective 1 June 2023. They cover keeping client assets safe in custody, keeping client assets segregated, avoiding conflicts of interest, and cybersecurity.
main text, para 4 / Note 2
Despite the regime starting on 1 June 2023, the SFC had not yet approved any VATP to serve retail investors. Most VATPs open to the public remained unregulated by the SFC.
main text, para 5

On 25 May 2023 the SFC gazetted the VATP Guidelines, the AML/CFT Guideline for LCs and SFC-licensed VASPs, and the Prevention of ML/TF Guideline for Associated Entities. It also gazetted the Disciplinary Fining Guidelines.
Note 2-3
Operators unwilling to meet SFC standards should proceed to orderly closure of their Hong Kong business.
main text, para 6
rg: Read main text in full; Notes give the exact list of gazetted instruments and dates, useful as a citation index.

t: Consultation Conclusions on the Proposed Regulatory Requirements for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators Licensed by the Securities and Futures Commission
sl: SFC · Consultation Conclusions on the Proposed Regulatory Requirements for Virtual… (2023)
s: The SFC finalises the rulebook for platforms it licenses to trade virtual assets, after a public consultation that drew 152 submissions. It allows retail investors onto licensed platforms, subject to knowledge and risk checks, exposure limits, and a narrow list of large, index-listed tokens eligible for retail trading. It sets custody, insurance, financial soundness and cybersecurity standards for platform operators. It also folds virtual-asset anti-money-laundering rules, including a Travel Rule for virtual-asset transfers, into the SFC's AML Guideline. The finalised texts, annexed as appendices, took effect on 1 June 2023, with a 12-month transition for firms already licensed.
w: For a bank, this is the baseline SFC rulebook to measure any licensed virtual-asset trading platform it deals with, partners with, or, if the group runs one, operates. It covers custody, capital, AML, Travel Rule and disciplinary exposure.
k: Licensed platforms may serve retail clients, but only after assessing each client's virtual-asset knowledge, risk tolerance and personal exposure limit. A client is treated as knowledgeable once they have made five or more virtual-asset trades in the past three years.
paras 12, 18, 21; Appendix A para 9.4 Note 2
Stablecoins cannot be offered to retail investors until Hong Kong's own stablecoin regime is in place. The SFC sees unresolved run and redemption risk in unregulated stablecoins.
para 51

A retail-eligible token needs a track record of at least 12 months, except for security tokens. It must appear in at least two independent large-cap indices, one of which follows IOSCO benchmark standards. The SFC will not publish its own eligible-token list.
paras 47-49; Appendix A para 7.8

Every platform must run a token admission and review committee, drawn from senior managers for the core business, compliance, risk and IT lines. This committee sets and enforces listing and delisting rules, and reports to the board at least monthly.
Appendix A paras 7.1-7.5

Before listing any token, the platform must complete due diligence covering the team, regulatory status, liquidity, technical security, governance and legal risk. For retail-eligible tokens, it must also confirm the token is not a security under the Securities and Futures Ordinance.
Appendix A paras 7.6-7.7

The SFC dropped its original plan to require platforms to file a lawyer's written opinion confirming a token is not a security, citing cost. Platforms still have to satisfy themselves of this before retail listing.
para 39
Token listings need an independent smart-contract audit for security flaws. The platform may rely on an audit the token issuer itself commissioned, rather than always ordering its own.
para 38; Appendix A para 7.10

Client virtual assets must be split 98% cold storage and up to 2% hot or other storage. They must be held through a dedicated, wholly owned custody subsidiary, called the Associated Entity, with keys generated and kept in Hong Kong.
Appendix A para 10.6(c); para 71

Platforms need a compensation arrangement -- insurance, ring-fenced funds, virtual assets, or a bank guarantee, alone or combined. It must cover 50% of cold-storage client holdings and 100% of hot or other-storage holdings, checked daily against the actual value held.
Appendix A paras 10.22-10.23

Proprietary trading in virtual assets by the platform itself stays banned. But the SFC relaxed the original blanket ban, so other group companies (affiliates) may trade or market-make, as long as it does not go through the licensed platform.
para 84; Appendix A para 7.26
Platforms may not offer deposit-taking, lending, borrowing or yield/earn-type products alongside their trading service; their role is limited to matching client orders.
para 86; Appendix A para 7.26

A platform must keep a minimum paid-up share capital of HK$5 million at all times. It must also hold liquid capital of at least HK$3 million, or the Financial Resources Rules basic amount if higher. On top of that, it needs 12 months of operating costs in liquid, non-virtual-asset form, held in Hong Kong.
Appendix A paras 6.1-6.3
rg: Read the Executive Summary (paragraphs 1-7) first. Then read the retail-access, custody, compensation and AML/Travel Rule discussion (paragraphs 8-119), and the Implementation timetable (paragraphs 151-154). These give the SFC's authoritative final position in plain prose. You can skim or skip Appendix E, the list of respondents. The same goes for the general AML/CFT chapters in Appendix B/C (Chapters 1-11), which restate standard requirements not unique to this rulebook.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Opening remarks at the commencement event of e-HKD Pilot Programme

s: This speech launches the e-HKD Pilot Programme, the second of three 'rails' in the HKMA's approach to a possible retail central bank digital currency. t: Consultation Conclusions on Proposed Amendments to Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Authorized Institutions)
sl: HKMA · Consultation Conclusions on Proposed Amendments to Guideline on Anti-Money… (2023)
s: The HKMA sets out what banks said about its draft AML/CFT Guideline changes and how it responded. The changes implement the 2022 AMLO amendments, which introduced VASP licensing and updated CDD definitions. On virtual assets, the HKMA confirms banks stay under its own Guideline rather than the SFC's, with RIs referred to the SFC text via footnote 1. It also states banks may carry out VA transfers for customers if the statutory s.13A conditions are met. Other responses cover digital ID, trust beneficiaries, former PEPs, bearer shares and applying new rules to existing customers.
w: It is the HKMA's clearest statement that a bank may execute VA transfers for customers if s.13A of Schedule 2 is satisfied. It also confirms the bank answers to the HKMA Guideline, with SFC Chapter 12 relevant only through footnote 1.
k: Following the AMLO amendments gazetted on 16 December 2022, the HKMA consulted banks from 18 January to 8 March 2023. It received comments from four industry associations.
Part I, paras 1 and 3, p.3

The SFC's AML guideline, with its new virtual asset chapter, covers SFC licensees and SFC-licensed VASPs. Banks, including Registered Institutions (RIs), keep following the HKMA Guideline instead. Footnote 1 was updated so RIs and AI associated entities take into account the SFC text.
Part II, para 4.2, p.7

The HKMA states the AMLO does not bar banks from carrying out VA transfers for customers, provided section 13A of Schedule 2 is met. Banks should keep following HKMA circulars of 28 January 2022 and 27 April 2023 and may raise questions with the AML & Financial Crime Risk Division.
Part II, para 4.3, p.7

Private-sector remote-onboarding tools are not 'recognised digital identification systems' under Schedule 2; iAM Smart is. Existing remote onboarding practice under earlier HKMA circulars continues to apply.
Part II, paras 1.2-1.4, pp.4-5

For trusts, where beneficiaries are a class, banks may gather enough information to identify them at payout. A new para 4.4.13 lets banks verify beneficiaries using trustee-provided information on a risk basis.
Part II, para 2.3, p.6
Senior management approval is no longer required to stop applying EDD to a former PEP, but banks need sound internal controls and oversight for that decision.
Part II, para 3.2, p.6
Updated CDD rules can be applied to existing customers through normal periodic or trigger reviews. High-risk ones, such as non-Hong Kong PEPs, should be updated at or before their next review.
Part II, para 6.3, p.9
The revised Guideline was to be gazetted on 25 May 2023 and take effect on 1 June 2023.
Part III, para 1, p.10
rg: Read Part II section 4 (p.7) first, then 6.3 (p.9) and Part III (p.10); sections 1-3 and 5 are background for non-VA changes.

t: SFST's speech at Aspen Digital Web 3 Investment Summit (English only)
sl: Government · SFST's speech at Aspen Digital Web 3 Investment Summit (2023)

t: 2023-24 Budget Speech

s: In the 2023-24 Budget Speech, the Financial Secretary sets out government support for Web3 and virtual asset (VA) development. He references the October 2022 VA Policy Statement, and announces a new Task Force on VA development plus HK$50 million to grow the Web3 ecosystem through events and youth workshops. t: Consultation Paper on the Proposed Regulatory Requirements for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators Licensed by the Securities and Futures Commission
sl: SFC · Consultation Paper on the Proposed Regulatory Requirements for Virtual… (2023)
s: This SFC consultation paper (20 Feb 2023) proposed the regulatory requirements for VA trading platforms ahead of the AMLO VASP licensing regime commencing 1 June 2023. This sits alongside the pre-existing SFO regime for platforms trading security tokens. It set out a draft version of Guidelines for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators (below, VATP Guidelines), plus a new AML/CFT Chapter 12 for platform operators. It also proposed Disciplinary Fining Guidelines, and transitional arrangements (deeming and non-contravention periods) for pre-existing platforms. Central proposals included allowing retail investor access for the first time, subject to knowledge assessment, suitability, and token admission safeguards. Other proposals were a token due-diligence and 'eligible large-cap virtual asset' framework for retail-available tokens, and 98% cold storage with detailed custody/key-management controls. A flexible compensation-arrangement requirement would replace the old insurance mandate. Licence applicants would also need a two-phase external assessor report. The paper also proposed removing several prior SFO licensing-condition requirements (e.g., the 'security token' admission criterion, mandatory voting-rights facilitation, legal opinion for all tokens) as the regime evolved. Comments were due 31 March 2023. The finalised VATP Guidelines were later issued, dated June 2023 per the draft appendix cover. This consultation paper is now a superseded, historical proposal document. But it remains the primary explanatory source for the final Guidelines' rationale and numbering.
w: For a bank, this consultation paper binds virtual asset trading platforms and SFC-licensed intermediaries, not the bank as an AI. Its lasting value for a compliance head is as the source of the custody, cold-storage and Travel Rule benchmarks to test any VATP counterparty against. The bank's own AML/travel-rule duties are governed separately, by the HKMA AML/CFT Guideline for AIs.
k: The AMLO VASP regime (non-security-token VA trading platforms) commenced 1 June 2023. It runs alongside the existing SFO regime, which already covers platforms offering at least one security token. Dual licensing is required if a platform's token mix spans both.
Part I, para 1-2

The SFC proposed for the first time to allow retail investor access to licensed VA trading platforms, subject to robust investor protection measures (knowledge assessment, suitability, exposure limits).
Part III, para 27, Question 1

Under the proposed rule, a platform operator, together with its Associated Entity, should keep 98% of client virtual assets in cold wallets, with only limited, SFC-approved exceptions. That is a stricter bar than the roughly 95% cold-storage benchmark cited elsewhere in the same paper for existing SFO licensees.
Appendix A (VATP Guidelines), para 10.6(c)

Seeds and private keys must be stored in Hong Kong, generated in a non-deterministic or random manner. No single person may hold the entirety of seeds, keys or backup passphrases, and distributed backups must mitigate single points of failure.
Appendix A, para 10.8(a)-(e)

The prior mandatory insurance requirement (full coverage for hot storage, substantial e.g. 95% coverage for cold storage 'at all times') is replaced by a flexible SFC-approved compensation arrangement that may combine third-party insurance and/or trust-segregated own funds.
Appendix A, para 10.22; main body para 53-55

'Eligible large-cap virtual assets' for retail trading must be included in at least two 'acceptable indices' from independent index providers. At least one index provider must be experienced in traditional (non-VA) financial markets.
Appendix A, para 7.6, Notes 1-3

Licensed platform operators must maintain minimum paid-up share capital of HK$5,000,000. They must also hold required liquid capital of the higher of HK$3,000,000 or the Financial Resources Rules basic amount, plus 12 months of operating expenses in liquid HK assets.
Appendix A, para 6.1-6.3
Platform operators are barred from offering, trading in, or dealing with virtual-asset futures or related derivative contracts, and from providing algorithmic trading services to clients.
Appendix A, para 7.23-7.24

Virtual asset transfers of HK$8,000 or more trigger mandatory Travel Rule originator/recipient information collection. The ordering institution must obtain and record originator and recipient details -- name, account or wallet, and address or ID number -- before executing the transfer. A reduced dataset applies below that threshold.
Appendix B (AML Guideline), Chapter 12, para 12.11.5-12.11.6

Transfers to or from unhosted wallets require the financial institution (FI) to obtain and record originator and recipient information from its own customer, since the counterparty institution cannot be relied upon. Risk-based mitigating measures, such as enhanced monitoring or transaction limits, must also apply.
Appendix B, Chapter 12, para 12.14.1-12.14.3

Pre-existing VA trading platforms -- those already operating in Hong Kong with a meaningful, substantial presence before 1 June 2023 -- had until 29 February 2024 to submit a licence application. This let them qualify for the deeming arrangement. They could continue operating penalty-free under a non-contravention arrangement until 31 May 2024. Any platform not licensed or deemed licensed by 1 June 2024 is in breach and subject to enforcement.
Part IV, para 74, 79(b), 82; Appendix E timeline

The SFC proposed to publish four public lists: licensed, deemed-licensed, closing-down, and unlicensed VA trading platforms. It explicitly warned that appearance on the 'deemed licensed' list does not mean the SFC has vetted the platform's fitness and properness.
Part IV, para 86-87
rg: Read the Part I Executive Summary (p.6) and Part III retail-access/custody/insurance sections (p.10-24) first, for the policy rationale. Then read Appendix A Chapters VI, VII, X and XII (Financial Soundness, Operations, Custody, Cybersecurity, p.64-109), for the operative requirements. You can skim the generic AML/CFT boilerplate in Appendix B outside Chapter 12. The same goes for the fitness-and-properness and competence chapters in Appendix A Parts II-IV, which largely restate standard SFC licensing conditions.

t: SFC consults on proposals to regulate virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · SFC consults on proposals to regulate virtual asset trading… (2023)
s: The SFC launched a consultation on proposed requirements for operators of centralised virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs), ahead of a new licensing regime taking effect 1 June 2023. The proposals are based on the SFC's existing 2019 regulatory framework for VATPs trading at least one security token. They are benchmarked to the standards already applied to licensed securities brokers and to automated trading venues. A central question is whether licensed VATPs should be permitted to serve retail investors, and if so what additional investor-protection measures (suitability, token admission) would apply. Pre-existing platforms were told to start preparing to comply; those not intending to apply should prepare for orderly closure. Comments were due 31 March 2023.
w: For a bank, this consultation previews the mandatory VATP licensing regime taking effect 1 June 2023. It creates no bank obligations directly. But it flags that any VA-trading-platform counterparty needed to prepare for licensing or wind down.
k: A new licensing regime for centralised VATPs carrying on business in or actively marketing to Hong Kong was to take effect 1 June 2023.
para 2 (main text)

Proposed requirements are benchmarked to the existing SFO rules that apply to licensed securities brokers and to automated trading venues, following the SFC's 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle.
main text, para 3
The SFC specifically sought views on whether to allow licensed VATPs to serve retail investors, and what extra protections (e.g. suitability in onboarding and token admission) should apply if so.
main text, para 4
Pre-existing platforms intending to apply for a licence should begin reviewing and revising systems and controls; those not applying should prepare for orderly closure of their Hong Kong business.
main text, para 6
A platform counts as 'pre-existing' if it already had a real and substantial footprint operating in Hong Kong before 1 June 2023.
Note 6

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Eddie Yue on Tokenised Bond: Huge Potential to be Unlocked
sl: HKMA · Eddie Yue on Tokenised Bond: Huge Potential to be… (2023)
s: This article by the HKMA's Chief Executive marks the world's first tokenised green bond issued by a government. The Hong Kong Government issued it using distributed ledger technology (DLT). It explains that HKD cash tokens, similar to a wholesale central bank digital currency (CBDC), were minted by the HKMA so banks could settle the deal on-platform. This cut settlement time from five business days to one. It flags that custody arrangements will need to be upgraded so custodians can hold digital securities on investors' behalf. The HKMA will publish a white paper on lessons learned, to guide future issuers.
w: For a bank, this is the HKMA's own account of a landmark tokenised bond deal, which points to future custody expectations for digital securities. Compliance should track the promised white paper, since it will likely set out legal-certainty and custody-upgrade expectations for any digital-bond custody or agency role the bank takes on.
k: The Hong Kong Government's tokenised green bond is described as the world's first tokenised bond issued by a government, using distributed ledger technology (DLT).
para 1

HKD cash tokens, similar to a wholesale CBDC, were created by the HKMA when banks handed over fiat cash. They were used to settle the primary issuance, secondary trading, coupon payment and maturity redemption on-platform.
para on cash-token minting
Settlement time was cut from the conventional five business days (T+5) to one day, using tokenisation instead of separate bond and cash settlement channels.
para on operational improvement
Existing custody arrangements may need to be upgraded so custodians can hold digital securities for investors. Banks acting as agents may take on new on-platform tasks.
para on non-technological challenges

The HKMA states it is writing a white paper on lessons from this issuance, to guide future tokenised issuers. It will also set out its thinking on legal certainty for digital securities created natively on DLT.
closing paragraphs

The tokenisation approach builds on Project Genesis, a 2021 proof-of-concept co-sponsored with the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub. It also draws on the cash-token mechanism built for the mBridge cross-border CBDC platform.
paras on Project Genesis and mBridge synergy

t: HKSAR Government's Inaugural Tokenised Green Bond Offering
sl: HKMA · HKSAR Government's Inaugural Tokenised Green Bond Offering (2023)
s: The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) Government offered a HK$800 million, one-year tokenised bond, as green debt under the Government Green Bond Programme. It is billed as the first tokenised green bond issued by any government worldwide. A four-bank syndicate distributed the bond. It was cleared and settled through the HKMA's Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU), using Goldman Sachs' GS DAP tokenisation platform. The initial issuance settled delivery-versus-payment, swapping security tokens for HKMA-issued cash tokens on a private blockchain. The HKMA said records on that private blockchain would be the legally final record of ownership, and that CMU settlement enjoys statutory finality under Hong Kong law. The HKMA also said it would publish a paper summarising lessons learned and offering a blueprint for future tokenised bond issuance in Hong Kong.
w: For a bank, this is a market precedent, not a rulebook: it shows a real Hong Kong-law tokenised bond settling on-chain through the CMU with statutory finality. It is relevant if the bank later joins a similar deal, but creates no ongoing compliance duty.
k: The tokenised green bond -- HK$800 million, in Hong Kong dollars, one-year term -- is the first tokenised bond any government has issued anywhere. It is also the first one governed by Hong Kong law.
para 1, p.1

Settlement ran delivery-versus-payment: security tokens stood for a beneficial interest in the bond. These were swapped for cash tokens standing for a claim on Hong Kong dollars owed by the HKMA, completed one business day later (T+1) on a private blockchain network.
para 3, p.1

The bond clears and settles through the HKMA's CMU, which under Hong Kong law carries statutory finality for settlement. The HKMA describes records on the private blockchain as the legally final record of ownership.
para 4, p.1
This offering was one of the pilot projects flagged in the Government's October 2022 policy paper on developing virtual assets in Hong Kong.
quote from Secretary Christopher Hui, p.1

As the Government's representative under the Green Bond Programme, the HKMA said it will publish a paper on lessons learned and next steps. This paper will act as a blueprint for future tokenised bond issuance in Hong Kong.
para 8, p.1
The deal builds on Project Genesis, a joint effort the HKMA finished with the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre in 2021.
quote from Eddie Yue, p.1

The bond paid a 4.05% coupon, settled on 16 February 2023 (T+1), and was rated A-1+/F1+ by S&P and Fitch. Bank of China (Hong Kong), Credit Agricole CIB, Goldman Sachs and HSBC acted as joint global coordinators, lead managers and bookrunners.
Summary terms and conditions table, p.2
rg: Read the first five paragraphs and the summary terms table (pages 1-2) for the main facts. You can skim the quotes from officials and bank executives (paras 6-13) and the US securities-law disclaimer at the end; these are largely promotional.

t: LCQ11: Tokenised green bonds
sl: Government · LCQ11: Tokenised green bonds (2023)
s: In a Legislative Council written reply, Hong Kong's Acting Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury confirms the HKMA plans a pilot tokenised green bond under the Government Green Bond Programme. It is aimed at institutional investors, and is meant to test Hong Kong's legal and market systems for tokenised issuance. The reply explains that tokenisation may cut issuance cost and settlement time. The HKMA will publish a project report afterwards to guide future issuers, and the government will explore using blockchain to track green-project data for bondholders.

Reply (1)
HKMA will publish a report on the pilot after issuance to guide future issuers on the process, including issuance, settlement, coupon payment and redemption.
Reply (2)
Government will separately explore blockchain-based tracking of green project performance for green bond reporting.
Reply (3)

t: Conclusion of discussion paper on crypto-assets and stablecoins
sl: HKMA · Conclusion of discussion paper on crypto-assets and stablecoins (2023)
s: The HKMA published its conclusion to the January 2022 discussion paper on crypto-assets and stablecoins, summarising 58 submissions received and its response. It confirmed it will bring certain stablecoin-related activities into a mandatory licensing regime, starting with fiat-referenced stablecoins, with flexibility to scope in other structures later. Key regulated activities are governance, issuance, stabilisation/reserve management, and wallets. Both Authorized Institutions (AIs) and non-AIs may be licensed to issue stablecoins. The HKMA targeted implementation of the regime in 2023/24, with a more detailed consultation to follow.
w: For a bank, this signals the HKMA's intent to bring stablecoin issuance under regulation, with implementation expected in 2023/24. Treat it as an early-warning marker for the licensing regime that later took shape, not as a source of present-day duties.
k: Certain stablecoin-related activities will fall under a new mandatory licensing regime run by the HKMA. It starts with stablecoins that claim to track one or more fiat currencies.
para 1.4, p.3

Four categories of key regulated activities: governance, issuance (issuing/creating/destroying), stabilisation/reserve management, and wallets (custody of cryptographic keys enabling access to stablecoin holdings).

A licence is required for an entity that conducts a regulated activity in Hong Kong, or actively markets one to the Hong Kong public. It is also required for anyone dealing in a HKD-referenced stablecoin, wherever they are based, or where the HKMA decides regulation is needed in the public interest.

Reserve assets must fully back outstanding stablecoins at all times, and must be high quality and highly liquid. Holders should be able to redeem at par within a reasonable period, and algorithm- or arbitrage-based stabilisation will not be accepted.

Both Authorized Institutions (AIs) and non-AIs may be licensed to issue stablecoins, under a 'same risk, same regulation' rule that fits requirements to the issuer type. The HKMA rejected a rule limiting issuance to AIs only.

A 'principal business' rule applies to licensees -- for example, wallet operators must not engage in lending. This rule does not apply to an in-scope AI, because AIs already face similar or stricter deposit-taking rules.
para 4.33(iii) and footnote 9, p.18

Tokenised deposits of AIs, closed-loop limited-purpose stablecoins, and possibly central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) or settlement tokens, are candidates to be excluded from scope. Separately, the HKMA will work out how tokenised deposits should be regulated, as a distinct question from stablecoin issuance.
para 4.15 and footnote 10, p.14, 23

The HKMA sees local incorporation as a strong aid to effective supervision and enforcement, such as segregating and seizing assets to protect users. But the HKMA said it would look further at other measures respondents raised instead.

The HKMA flagged possible overlap between its proposed stablecoin regime, the SFC's VASP licensing regime, and the stored value facility (SVF) regime. It said it will work with other regulators to avoid arbitrage and close any gaps.

The target date to start the stablecoin regime is 2023/24. A more detailed consultation will follow, including whether to use new stand-alone legislation or amend existing laws, before any draft bill.

Draft legislation is expected to define which structures and activities are regulated or excluded, and to give the HKMA powers to run the regime and set key requirements. It would also give the HKMA a way, using published 'guiding factors', to bring more stablecoin structures or activities into scope later.
para 5.4, p.27
rg: Read the Executive Summary (paragraphs 1.1-1.8, pages 3-6) and the HKMA's answers under each heading Q1-Q8 in Chapter 4 (pages 13-26) for the main policy positions. Skim Chapter 3 and Annexes 1-3; they are mostly background.

t: Conclusion of Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins
sl: HKMA · Conclusion of Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins (2023)
s: This paper closes out the HKMA's January 2022 discussion paper on crypto-assets and stablecoins, after 58 submissions. It sets firmer proposed terms for the coming stablecoin licensing regime, shaped by the 2022 collapse of TerraUSD and the FTX bankruptcy. It commits to a risk-based regime starting with fiat-referenced stablecoins. Governance, issuance, stabilisation/reserve management and wallet custody are named as the core licensable activities. Key principles are full backing, redemption at par, and a 'principal business' restriction, which is waived for Authorized Institutions (AIs). It also records Hong Kong's parallel move to bring virtual asset exchanges under an SFC licensing regime from June 2023. It notes the government's October 2022 Policy Statement on virtual asset development.
w: For a bank, this shows how the TerraUSD and FTX failures shaped the full-backing, par-redemption and 'principal business' rules it now operates under. It also confirms why Authorized Institutions get lighter treatment on some points, which is useful context for explaining the current rules to internal stakeholders.
k: HKMA confirmed it will prioritise regulating fiat-referenced stablecoins first, while building in flexibility to bring other stablecoin structures into scope later.

Four activities were named as core to the coming licensing regime. They are governance of the stablecoin arrangement's rules, issuance (minting or burning), stabilisation and reserve management, and wallet custody of users' cryptographic keys.
para 1.4 table, p.4

A licence would be required for an entity conducting a regulated activity in Hong Kong, or actively marketing one to the Hong Kong public. It would also be required for stablecoins referencing the Hong Kong dollar, or where the HKMA decides regulation is needed in the public interest.
para 1.4 table, p.4

Core proposed principles were full backing and redemption at par at all times, and ruling out algorithm- or arbitrage-based stabilisation. A 'principal business' restriction would stop regulated entities straying outside their licensed activity -- wallet operators, for example, could not lend. This restriction is waived for Authorized Institutions, given their existing prudential rules.
para 1.4 table, p.4-5
The target implementation date for the regime was reaffirmed as 2023/24, and HKMA was still weighing new standalone legislation against amending existing law.
para 1.4 table, p.5

The May 2022 depegging of TerraUSD, then the largest algorithmic stablecoin, and Tether's brief drop to USD 0.95, were cited as evidence of weak governance, stabilisation and disclosure. The November 2022 FTX collapse was cited too, reinforcing the case for regulation.

Separately, Hong Kong's Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (AMLO) was amended in December 2022 to require an SFC licence for operating a virtual asset exchange, from 1 June 2023. This is a parallel but separate regime from the stablecoin issuer licensing later created by the Stablecoins Ordinance.

Consultation respondents were divided on whether stablecoin licensees should have to incorporate locally. This foreshadowed the requirement that later appeared in the Stablecoins Ordinance for non-bank issuers.
para 4.5(iii), p.12
rg: Read the executive summary table (para 1.4) for the proposed regime terms, and paras 3.2-3.3 for the TerraUSD/FTX context. You can skim the question-by-question summary in Chapter 4, since the later ordinance is the authoritative source.

t: Web 3.0 in Hong Kong – from crypto to blockchain

t: Prudential treatment of cryptoasset exposures
sl: HKMA · Prudential treatment of cryptoasset exposures (2022)
s: The HKMA relays the Basel Committee's final global standard on the prudential (capital) treatment of banks' cryptoasset exposures, issued 16 December 2022. Cryptoassets are split into two groups. Group 1 (qualifying tokenised traditional assets and stablecoins) generally gets the existing Basel risk-based capital treatment. Group 2 (everything that fails the Group 1 tests) gets more conservative treatment, with limited hedging recognition and an exposure limit as a guardrail. The standard adds an infrastructure risk add-on for Group 1 assets and a redemption-risk test for stablecoins to qualify for Group 1. The Basel Committee set a global deadline of 1 January 2025 for banks to apply the standard. The HKMA said it intends to implement it locally on that timetable, and will consult the industry on local details.
w: For a bank, this is the capital-charge framework it must plan for on any cryptoasset exposure. It shows which exposures could qualify for lower-capital Group 1 treatment via the redemption-risk test for stablecoins. Other exposures get the stricter Group 2 treatment, ahead of local HKMA implementation.
k: Group 1 cryptoassets (qualifying tokenised assets and stablecoins) generally receive the existing risk-based Basel capital treatment.

Group 2 cryptoassets (everything that does not meet the Group 1 conditions) get more conservative capital treatment. Only limited hedging is recognised, and an exposure limit caps how large Group 2 holdings can grow in a bank's portfolio.
Only stablecoins issued by supervised, regulated entities with robust redemption rights and proper governance can pass the redemption-risk test needed for Group 1 qualification.
The Basel Committee's global deadline is 1 January 2025. The HKMA intends to implement the standard locally on that timetable, and will consult the industry on local details in due course.
rg: Two-page circular; read in full.

t: Statement on virtual asset arrangements claiming to offer returns to investors
sl: SFC · Statement on virtual asset arrangements claiming to offer returns… (2022)
s: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) warns investors about virtual asset (VA) platforms offering 'deposit', 'savings', 'earnings' or 'staking' products. These products are unregulated, are not the same as a bank deposit, and can carry a big risk of loss, as recent VA platform collapses showed. The SFC reminds firms that such products may count as an unauthorised collective investment scheme (CIS). Under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), advertising or distributing one to Hong Kong investors without authorisation is an offence.
w: For a bank, this shows how the SFC may treat VA yield or staking products as an unauthorised CIS, after major 2022 VA platform collapses. It matters if the bank refers clients to, or partners with, a third-party VA yield platform.
k: VA 'deposit', 'savings' and 'staking' arrangements sit outside regulation and work nothing like a bank deposit; investors get no protection.
para 4
Such VA products may count as an unauthorised CIS if investors lack day-to-day control and their VA is pooled and managed together for returns.

Inviting people in Hong Kong to join an unauthorised CIS is an offence under SFO section 103. The maximum penalty is a HK$500,000 fine and 3 years in prison.
Note 5

Promoting or selling a CIS to Hong Kong, or targeting the Hong Kong market, without an SFC licence is an offence under SFO section 114. The maximum penalty is a HK$5,000,000 fine and 7 years in prison.

t: Statement on virtual asset arrangements claiming to offer returns to investors
sl: SFC · Statement on virtual asset arrangements claiming to offer returns… (2022)
s: The SFC warns the public about platforms offering virtual asset (VA) "deposit", "savings" or "staking" products that promise high or fixed returns. It explains these arrangements are unregulated, carry no protection like a bank deposit, and can fail if the platform or its lending counterparties collapse or are hacked. The SFC notes such arrangements may count as an unauthorised collective investment scheme (CIS) under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). Promoting or distributing one in Hong Kong without authorisation or a licence is a criminal offence.

t: Passage of Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Bill 2022
sl: HKMA · Passage of Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Bill… (2022)
s: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) tells banks that the Legislative Council passed the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Bill 2022 on 7 December 2022. The amended law brings virtual-asset service providers (VASPs) under a licensing regime and sets up a two-tier registration system for dealers in precious metals and stones. It also updates several rules to match Financial Action Task Force (FATF) standards, including a new definition of politically exposed person (PEP) and a risk-based approach to former PEPs. It also lets banks use recognised digital ID systems for customer checks, and widens who counts as a beneficial owner of a trust. The changes take effect on 1 June 2023, and the HKMA says it will consult banks on related changes to its AML/CFT guideline.
w: For a bank, this law is the legal basis for the mandatory VASP licensing regime: from the effective date only licensed VASPs should count as compliant counterparties. It also updated the AML/CFT Guideline that the bank's own anti-money-laundering (AML) programme follows.
k: The amended ordinance brings virtual-asset service providers under a licensing system.
point (a), p.1
The changes take effect on 1 June 2023, giving the industry time to get ready.
A recognised digital ID system can now be used for customer due diligence, including when a customer isn't physically present.
point (c), p.1

t: LCQ4: Promoting development of virtual assets market
sl: FSTB · LCQ4: Promoting development of virtual assets market (2022)
s: This is a reply the Acting Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury gave in the Legislative Council (LegCo), days after a major overseas virtual asset (VA) exchange collapsed. It sets out planned investor-protection safeguards for Hong Kong's coming licence regime for virtual asset service providers (VASPs), to be overseen by the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC). These include segregated client assets, a one-year expense buffer, a ban on proprietary market-making, and audited accounts sent to the SFC. SFC powers to inspect and direct exchanges are also proposed, and the reply confirms the VASP Bill reached LegCo in July 2022.
w: For a bank, this is the clearest checklist yet of what a licensed VA exchange counterparty must meet. Compliance can use it now for counterparty due diligence once the licensing regime takes effect.
k: A licensed VA exchange must keep client assets in a separate account, inside its own wholly owned subsidiary, apart from its own assets.

A licensed VA exchange must meet financial-resources rules and keep on hand enough funds to cover a full year of its actual running costs.

The SFC will be able to enter a licensed VA exchange's premises, inspect and investigate it, demand records, and direct how it runs its business.
para 6
The VASP Bill reached the Legislative Council in July 2022. Anyone running a VA exchange business must apply to the SFC for a licence.

t: An Event Study on the May 2022 Stablecoin Market Crash
sl: HKMA · An Event Study on the May 2022 Stablecoin Market… (2022)
s: This HKMA staff research memo studies the May 2022 collapse of the algorithmic stablecoin TerraUSD (UST), and why some other stablecoins faced less redemption pressure than others. Studying 18 stablecoins that existed at the time, the authors estimate the fair value of each one's reserve assets. They find that stablecoins with stronger reserve backing suffered smaller falls in market value. Crypto-collateralised stablecoins absorbed the biggest shock from the Terra crash. Among those, stricter collateral rules gave more protection against redemption runs.
w: For a bank, this staff research explains, with data, why reserve strength and collateral ratios matter for stablecoin resilience. That is directly relevant background if the bank is assessing counterparty or custody risk from any stablecoin exposure, including an algorithmic or crypto-collateralised stablecoin.
k: TerraUSD (UST), an algorithmic stablecoin, failed to maintain its US$1 peg in May 2022, triggering widespread crypto sell-offs across the market.
Key points, para 1
Looking across 18 stablecoins, the ones with bigger reserve backing saw, on average, smaller drops in market value during the crash.
Key points, para 2
Crypto-collateralised stablecoins were the primary shock absorbers of the Terra crash, given their role providing leverage within crypto markets, and faced extra redemption pressure as a result.
Key points, para 2

Among crypto-collateralised stablecoins, the ones with tougher lending terms (i.e., needing more collateral per coin) held up better against redemption pressure, showing the benefit of a bigger safety margin.
Key points, para 2

t: An assessment of the volatility spillover from crypto to traditional financial assets: the role of asset-backed stablecoins
sl: HKMA · An assessment of the volatility spillover from crypto to… (2022)
s: This HKMA staff research memo studies whether volatility in crypto-asset markets can spill over into traditional finance through asset-backed stablecoins, focusing on Tether. It finds that when Tether adjusts its reserves, this makes volatility spillover from crypto assets into money-market instruments worse. That creates a channel through which stablecoin reserve fire-sales could hit traditional markets. The authors, writing in a personal capacity, suggest regulators consider standard reserve-asset disclosure rules for asset-backed stablecoins. They also suggest stronger liquidity-management rules, including limits on reserve makeup and clear redemption rights.
w: For a bank, this is HKMA staff research, not an official HKMA policy view. But it explains the reserve-disclosure and liquidity-management reasoning that later shaped Hong Kong's stablecoin issuer regime. It is useful for understanding why reserve transparency and redemption terms matter when assessing a stablecoin issuer counterparty.
k: The study finds that Tether's reserve adjustments amplify the spillover of crypto-asset volatility into money-market instruments, indicating a channel through which crypto risk can reach the traditional financial system.
Key points, bullet 2

t: Opening Keynote at the Hong Kong FinTech Week 2022
sl: HKMA · Opening Keynote at the Hong Kong FinTech Week 2022 (2022)
s: In this keynote, the HKMA Chief Executive looks back at Hong Kong's fintech journey and addresses crypto, stablecoins, decentralised finance (DeFi) and non-fungible tokens (NFTs) directly. He says the HKMA is building a proportionate rulebook, sized to risk, for payment-related stablecoins. He says the SFC is putting together rules to bring digital-asset trading venues under licensing.
