t: Embracing Innovation, Regulation and the Future of Finance — Keynote address at Hong Kong FinTech Week 2022
sl: SFC · Embracing Innovation, Regulation and the Future of Finance —… (2022)
s: In this keynote, SFC Deputy CEO Julia Leung reviews the SFC's approach to virtual assets after the 2022 'crypto winter' (the collapse of Luna/Terra, Three Arrows, and crypto lenders freezing withdrawals). She explains that since 2018 the SFC has regulated virtual asset trading platforms and fund managers under a 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle. She cites a January 2022 joint circular with the HKMA that lets banks and brokers offer virtual asset dealing if they partner with an SFC-licensed exchange. She announces plans to review the professional-investor-only restriction, and previews a same-day circular authorising Bitcoin and Ether futures exchange-traded funds (ETFs). She explains that tokenised securities will generally be treated like their traditional equivalents, with due diligence and smart-contract audits expected. She confirms a coming VASP licensing consultation once the enabling Bill passes.
w: For a bank, this is directly relevant to its own or partnered virtual asset dealing. It confirms the legal condition for banks to offer VA dealing: partnering with an SFC-licensed exchange under the joint circular. It also previews the product-classification and due-diligence expectations that would shape the bank's product approval and suitability processes.
k: The SFC has regulated virtual asset trading platforms and fund managers since 2018 under a 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle, combining investor protection and market integrity requirements with AML controls.

Under the January 2022 SFC-HKMA joint circular, banks and securities brokers can only offer clients virtual asset dealing services if they team up with an SFC-licensed exchange. They also need to satisfy other regulatory conditions.
p.2, footnote 2

As of the speech, the SFC had approved 8 virtual asset fund managers and 1 virtual asset exchange, with another approved in principle. It had also approved 2 brokers to trade virtual assets for clients under omnibus account arrangements.

The SFC intends to consult on relaxing the 'professional investor only' restriction for SFC-licensed platforms, STOs and virtual asset funds, given four years of market maturing since the 2018 framework.

The SFC would issue a circular that day authorising virtual asset futures ETFs for public offering. At first this is limited to funds tracking Bitcoin and Ether futures dealt on the CME (Chicago Mercantile Exchange).

Tokenised plain-vanilla securities, such as a tokenised bond, will generally be treated as 'non-complex products' under existing distribution rules. But tokens with novel or complex features and no legal wrapper will likely be treated as 'complex products', restricted to professional investors.
Licensed firms distributing security tokens are expected to carry out sensible due diligence and have the smart contracts audited before offering the tokens to clients.
Following passage of the AML/CTF Amendment Bill (then before LegCo), the SFC will consult publicly on detailed VASP licensing requirements, including whether retail access should be permitted.
rg: Read in full (5 pages). The opening anecdote on page 1 is scene-setting and can be skimmed.

t: Circular on Virtual Asset Futures Exchange Traded Funds
sl: SFC · Virtual Asset Futures Exchange Traded Funds (2022)
s: This SFC circular sets out when the SFC will authorise exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that get virtual-asset exposure mainly through futures contracts (VA Futures ETFs). Once authorised, they can be sold to the public in Hong Kong under sections 104-105 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). It allows, for the first time, VA Futures ETFs to be authorised, at first limited to those tracking Bitcoin futures and Ether futures traded on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange. It sets track-record rules for the manager, limits on investment strategy and net derivative exposure, and disclosure duties. It also confirms that distribution must follow the Code of Conduct and the January 2022 Joint Circular, including the VA-knowledge test.
w: For a bank, this circular has now been replaced. But it set the original distribution gate, the VA-knowledge test and complex-product disclosure, that a bank's distribution desk had to apply to VA Futures ETFs. A compliance head must check current controls now point to the successor circular.
k: SFC is willing, for the first time, to accept applications to authorise VA Futures ETFs for public sale in Hong Kong.
para 6
At first, only Bitcoin and Ether futures dealt on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange qualify as underlying futures.
para 12
A VA Futures ETF's manager must have a good compliance track record and at least three years of proven ETF-management experience.
para 10
A VA Futures ETF's net derivative exposure must not go above 100% of the fund's total net asset value.
para 14
The product key facts statement must clearly disclose upfront the large roll costs and operational risks -- such as margin risk -- specific to VA futures.
para 15
Selling VA Futures ETFs must follow the Code of Conduct and the Joint Circular, including the mandatory VA-knowledge test, even when the sale isn't a solicitation or recommendation.
para 16
rg: Read in full; it is short (3 pages).

t: Government issues Policy Statement on development of Virtual Assets in Hong Kong
sl: FSTB · Government issues Policy Statement on development of Virtual Assets… (2022)
s: This press release announces that the Government has published a Policy Statement on the development of virtual assets (VA) in Hong Kong. It sums up the statement's four themes. First, a facilitating regulatory vision for VA. Second, moves toward a VA service provider licensing regime and an SFC consultation on retail investor access and VA exchange-traded funds (ETFs). Third, openness to reviewing property rights for tokenised assets. Fourth, pilot projects on NFTs, green bond tokenisation and e-HKD. It notes a coming HKMA announcement on stablecoin regulation next steps. The full statement is attached as an annex and is captured as a separate registry entry.
w: For a bank, this is the Government's first combined statement of intent across VASP licensing, stablecoins and tokenisation. It gives compliance a single reference point for the direction of travel that later concrete rules, the AMLO Part 5B licensing regime and the stablecoin ordinance, would follow.
k: The Government is preparing a licensing regime for VA service providers and will invite global VA exchanges to establish in Hong Kong.
section 2, para 2
The SFC will consult on how much access retail investors should have to VA, and Hong Kong is open to VA exchange-traded funds.
section 2, para 3
The Government is open to reviewing property rights for tokenised assets and the legal status of smart contracts.
section 2, para 4
The HKMA will announce consultation outcome and next steps on stablecoin regulation in due course.
section 2, para 5
The named pilots are: tokenising a green bond, testing the e-HKD, and issuing NFTs for Fintech Week 2022.
section 3
rg: Short press summary; read it in full, then read the attached Policy Statement (id f587b828e3fa) for the substantive detail.

t: Policy Statement on Development of Virtual Assets in Hong Kong
sl: FSTB · Policy Statement on Development of Virtual Assets in Hong… (2022)
s: This is the Government's founding policy statement setting Hong Kong's regulatory direction for virtual assets (VA). It commits to a 'same activity, same risks, same regulation' principle, and confirms an opt-in VA exchange licensing regime already exists. It also confirms guidance had already gone to banks and financial institutions on distributing, dealing in, or advising on VA. It announces work on a mandatory VA service provider licensing regime, plus an SFC consultation on retail access and VA exchange-traded funds (ETFs). It flags stablecoins as a priority, given their growing links to mainstream finance, references an earlier HKMA discussion paper, and says outcomes would follow. It also opens the door to reviewing property-rights law for tokenised assets and smart contracts. It describes three pilot projects: NFT issuance, green bond tokenisation, and e-HKD, describing e-HKD as a bridge between legal tender and virtual assets.
w: For a bank, this sets the regulatory principle, 'same activity, same risks, same regulation', that later concrete rules for VASPs, stablecoins and VA distribution would follow. It also confirms banks were already expected to follow guidance when distributing or dealing in VA-related products, making this the policy anchor for a bank's whole VA compliance programme.
k: The Government commits to a 'same activity, same risks, same regulation' principle for regulating virtual asset activities.
para 4

A licensing regime for VA exchanges already existed on an opt-in basis, and guidance had already gone to banks and financial institutions. It covered distributing VA-related products, and dealing in or advising on VA.
para 5

The Government is preparing a new mandatory licensing regime for VA service providers, which would align VA exchanges' AML/CTF and investor-protection requirements with those applied to traditional financial institutions.
para 6
Once licensed, VA exchanges would be able to partner with banks and financial intermediaries offering VA dealing services to clients, subject to meeting regulatory conditions.
para 6
The SFC would consult on how much retail investors should be allowed to access VA once the new licensing regime is in place. It would also separately publish a circular on VA exchange-traded funds.
para 7
The Government is open to reviewing Hong Kong property-rights law to better cover tokenised assets, and the legal status of smart contracts.
para 8

Stablecoins were flagged as a priority, given growing links with traditional finance and payment systems. The HKMA had already issued a discussion paper before the 2022 'Crypto Winter' and would announce next steps in due course.
para 9

Three named pilot projects were: NFT issuance for Fintech Week 2022, tokenisation of a Government green bond for institutional investors, and e-HKD. e-HKD is described as a potential price-stable bridge supporting future security token offerings.
paras 10-11 and Annex
e-HKD work would proceed via a three-rail approach covering technology/legal foundations, use cases and design, then a launch timeline.
Annex para 6
rg: Read the main body (paras 1-11, p.1-6) in full. The Annex (p.7-9) gives useful pilot-project detail on NFTs, green bond tokenisation and e-HKD, but is lower priority.

t: Project mBridge: Successful CBDC project for real-value cross-border payment and foreign exchange transactions
sl: HKMA · Project mBridge: Successful CBDC project for real-value cross-border payment… (2022)
s: The HKMA published 'Project mBridge: Connecting economies through CBDC', together with the BIS Innovation Hub (BISIH) Hong Kong Centre. Other partners were the Bank of Thailand, the People's Bank of China's (PBoC) Digital Currency Institute, and the Central Bank of the UAE. It reports on a six-week trial moving real value across borders using central bank digital currencies (CBDCs). Twenty banks across four jurisdictions ran more than 160 payment and foreign-exchange (FX) trades, worth over HK$171 million (US$22.1 million), the biggest cross-border CBDC trial so far. The project will keep building toward a Minimum Viable Product and, eventually, a system ready for production use.
w: For a bank, this is useful context: it shows a working real-value cross-border CBDC trial. It is worth watching as a possible future alternative to correspondent banking settlement, but it requires no action from the bank today.
k: 20 banks across four jurisdictions -- Hong Kong, Mainland China, the UAE, and Thailand -- ran more than 160 payment and foreign-exchange (FX) trades, settled payment-versus-payment (PvP). These totalled over US$22.1 million during a six-week trial.
para 2
This project was among the earliest multi-CBDC efforts to complete actual cross-border payments for corporate clients.
para 2
HKMA and the project team will keep building the mBridge platform toward a Minimum Viable Product and, eventually, a system ready for production.
para 3
rg: Read the press release in full. See the full report (947fa49606ab) for pilot statistics, key lessons, and legal and policy analysis.

t: The Chief Executive's 2022 Policy Address
sl: Government · The Chief Executive's 2022 Policy Address (2022)
s: The 2022 Policy Address is the Chief Executive's annual wide-ranging policy statement. Only one paragraph, in the International Financial Centre section, deals with digital assets. It confirms the Government had already tabled a bill to bring virtual asset service providers under a legally binding licensing regime. It also confirms the HKMA was reviewing market feedback on stablecoin regulation, aiming to align the eventual regime with international standards and local conditions. Separately, it confirms the HKMA had begun preparatory work on issuing e-HKD, and was working with Mainland institutions on cross-boundary testing of e-CNY. This paragraph is a high-level government commitment, not a technical rulebook.
w: For a bank, this is the clearest top-level government confirmation, as of October 2022, that a VASP licensing bill and a stablecoin framework were both actively coming. It gives compliance functions an official basis to start planning for both regimes ahead of their formal launch.
k: The Government had tabled a bill that would bring virtual asset service providers under a legally binding licensing system.
para 37(vi)
The HKMA was examining market feedback on stablecoin regulation and intended to align the eventual regime with international recommendations and Hong Kong's local context.
para 37(vi)
The HKMA had begun preparatory work on issuing e-HKD and was working with Mainland institutions to expand cross-boundary testing of e-CNY in Hong Kong.
para 37(vi)
rg: Only paragraph 37(vi), on printed pages 15-16 (International Financial Centre section, Fintech bullet), is digital-asset relevant. Skip the rest of this 190-plus page speech, which mostly covers housing, healthcare and other sectors.

t: Project mBridge: Connecting economies through CBDC
sl: HKMA/SFC · Project mBridge: Connecting economies through CBDC (2022)
s: This BIS-authored report, dated October 2022, covers the first real-value pilot of mBridge, a shared blockchain platform letting four central banks issue their own digital currencies for cross-border settlement. Twenty commercial banks from Hong Kong, mainland China, Thailand and the UAE took part over six weeks in mid-2022. They moved over US$12 million of digital currency and settled more than 160 payment and foreign-exchange trades for corporate clients. The report explains how the platform keeps transaction details private, except to the two counterparties and their central banks. It describes the legal contracts used to give the pilot legal certainty, and sets out where each participant's own bank ran its anti-money-laundering and sanctions checks. A dedicated section covers unresolved legal questions, including how to classify the digital currency itself and who should run the platform, based on external legal advice the project team got.
w: For a bank, this is the clearest evidence that mBridge, even at pilot stage, put screening duties on each bank itself, not on the platform. This covers anti-money-laundering (AML), counter-terrorist-financing (CTF) and sanctions screening. That is exactly the control gap a bank's compliance function would need to confirm and own before any live use. If the bank is ever asked to connect to mBridge or a successor platform, this report is the primary source for what to expect. It covers the legal paperwork, screening duties and data-visibility limits.
k: In a six-week live pilot from mid-August to late September 2022, twenty commercial banks issued over US$12 million of digital currency onto the platform. They settled more than 160 payment and foreign-exchange trades worth over US$22 million for their corporate clients.
s.1 Executive Summary, p.4

Before the pilot, participants signed three sets of legal documents. One covered each central bank's role, one set platform-wide rules, including when a payment counts as final, and one covered each digital currency's own terms of use.
s.5.1 Preparation and setup, p.16

Every payment on the platform required each bank to carry out its own anti-money-laundering, counter-terrorist-financing and sanctions screening before sending or confirming a transaction. The platform itself does not run these checks.
s.6.5.2 Payment and PvP, p.30

Sensitive transaction details, such as the identities of payer and payee and the amount, are visible only to the two transacting banks and their own central banks. Other participating central banks or banks cannot see them.
s.6.4 Privacy controls, p.28

The pilot deliberately excluded certain transaction types, such as domestic payments in a foreign digital currency. This was because of the risk that a jurisdiction's own currency could be displaced, or its monetary-policy control weakened.
s.7.1.2 Foreign and domestic use of CBDC, p.32

External legal counsel reviewed over 200 pages of analysis across four jurisdictions on unresolved questions. These include whether the digital currency should count as currency, a claim on the central bank, or a form of debt.
s.7.2 Legal and regulatory considerations, p.34

Only banks that are domestically licensed in a given jurisdiction may request new issuance or redemption of that jurisdiction's digital currency. Foreign banks can hold and transact in it, but not create or redeem it directly.
s.7.1.1 Measures to preserve monetary sovereignty, p.31-32

Fewer currency-exchange trades took place than simple one-way payments during the pilot, partly because pricing for currency exchange happened off the platform beforehand, adding time and complexity to each trade.
s.5.4 Key lessons, p.22

The pilot ran on a single, centralised cloud environment hosted in Hong Kong for simplicity. The project team flagged this as a data-privacy and governance point still to be revisited before wider rollout.
s.7.1.3 Data privacy and governance, p.33
rg: Read the Executive Summary (p.4-5), section 5.4 Key lessons (p.22) and all of section 7, Policy, legal and regulatory considerations (p.31-34). The technical chapters on consensus algorithms (p.24-30) can be skimmed.

t: e-HKD - Charting the Next Steps
sl: HKMA · e-HKD - Charting the Next Steps (2022)
s: This is the full HKMA position paper following two rounds of e-HKD market consultation (75 responses in total). It sums up the feedback (Annexes 1-2) and sets out the HKMA's three-track plan for getting ready in case e-HKD is eventually launched. Rail 1 builds the technology, starting with the wholesale layer, and identifies which legal changes are required for legal-tender status. Rail 2 runs deep-dive research and pilots, including Project Sela, e-wallet access pilots, and settling tokenised securities. Rail 3 covers an eventual launch, timed to how Rails 1 and 2 progress. The HKMA says e-HKD's usual reasons, such as financial inclusion, competition and resilience, matter less for Hong Kong. Its payment market is already diverse, unlike places that have launched a retail CBDC (Bahamas, Nigeria) or piloted one (China, Eastern Caribbean).
w: For a bank, no binding rule attaches yet. But a compliance head should track this roadmap for early sight of possible bank participation, such as Project Sela or settlement pilots. It should also track the legislative-amendment step that will eventually create e-HKD-specific duties.
k: Rail 1 will first build the wholesale interbank layer, expected to take at least 2-3 years to reach production grade, subject to resources. The retail layer design comes after, since it may change based on further deliberation.
Rail 1 section
Early legal analysis found the current laws would not give enough certainty to support issuing a digital version of legal tender; changing the legislation would be needed.
Rail 1 section
The HKMA is inclined to give e-HKD legal tender status. By law this would make it valid for paying a debt unless otherwise agreed, but merchants could not be forced to accept it, just as with cash.
Annex 2, Q11 HKMA response

Of the retail CBDCs launched worldwide so far, only the Bahamas' Sand Dollar and Nigeria's eNaira were actually up and running. Mainland China's e-CNY and the Eastern Caribbean's DCash remained at pilot stage.
Charting the next steps section

Consultation respondents generally favoured a two-tier distribution model, an unremunerated e-HKD, offline payment support, and cross-border interoperability (including potential e-HKD/e-CNY convertibility).
Responses received section
Rail 2 pipeline includes Project Sela (cybersecurity), e-wallet app access pilots, DvP settlement of tokenised securities, and studying CBDC as an on/off-ramp for DeFi.
Rail 2 section
A tiered-account structure (different transaction/holding limits and anonymity levels based on KYC level) was broadly supported by respondents to balance privacy and AML/CFT compliance.
Annex 2, Section 2
rg: Read 'Charting the next steps' (p.8-12) in full for the three-rail plan. Skim Annexes 1-2 (consultation feedback tables) for stakeholder positions relevant to the bank's own submission strategy.

t: HKMA's policy stance on e-HKD
sl: HKMA · HKMA's policy stance on e-HKD (2022)
s: The HKMA released a position paper, 'e-HKD: Charting the Next Steps'. It sets out its policy stance after two rounds of market consultation, a technical paper and a policy paper, with 75 responses in total. Respondents broadly supported e-HKD. The HKMA will follow a three-rail approach. Rail 1 lays the technology and legal foundations, including legislative changes needed for legal-tender status. Rail 2 runs deep-dive research and pilots at the same time. Rail 3 covers the actual launch, timed to how Rails 1 and 2 progress.

The HKMA will use a three-track plan. Rail 1 covers technology and legal groundwork, Rail 2 runs deep-dive research and pilots in parallel, and Rail 3 covers eventual launch, timed to how Rails 1 and 2 progress.

t: Circular Issued by the Securities and Futures Commission to Licensed Corporations on Review of Online Brokerage, Distribution and Advisory Services | Enclosure 1: SFC circular of 31 Aug 2022
sl: HKMA · Circular Issued by the Securities and Futures Commission to… (2022)
s: The HKMA forwards to banks an SFC circular that summarises findings from a review of online brokerage, distribution and advisory platforms run by licensed corporations, including a 50-firm survey. Key issues found include weak non-face-to-face client onboarding, contract clauses that appeared to exclude suitability duties, and weak product due diligence, including for virtual asset (VA)-related products. Other gaps found: poor client risk profiling, weak monitoring of platform content, and cybersecurity gaps. The full findings and expected standards sit in an attached report (Enclosure 2).
w: For a bank, this surfaces a real, enforcement-relevant finding: an inspected firm sold VA-related products through overseas OTC markets to retail clients without following the VA Circular's selling restrictions. That is a concrete example of the product-due-diligence gap the bank's own controls must avoid.
k: The SFC surveyed 50 licensed corporations and found 96% of new accounts over a 12-month period were opened through non-face-to-face onboarding.

t: FSTB and SFC and Invest Hong Kong exchange viewpoints with industry leaders to foster digital asset industry development in Hong Kong (with photo)

Among the gaps, it names one licensed corporation that sold virtual asset (VA)-related products, traded on overseas over-the-counter (OTC) markets, to retail investors through its online platform. It did this without meeting the required investor-protection safeguards: the selling limits and the VA-knowledge check set out in the 2022 joint VA circular.

k: One inspected licensed corporation offered VA-related products, traded on overseas over-the-counter markets, to retail investors through its online platform. It did not follow the required selling restrictions or the VA-knowledge test.

t: Developing the CMU to reinforce Hong Kong's status as an IFC
sl: HKMA · Developing the CMU to reinforce Hong Kong's status as… (2022)
s: In this article, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) Chief Executive describes plans to grow the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU), Hong Kong's central securities depository. The goal is to build it into a major international depository over three years. It covers a new collateralised lending service, fee waivers to attract issuers, a new CMU platform planned for 2025, and more cross-border links, especially with Bond Connect. It has no content on virtual assets, stablecoins or tokenisation. But the CMU it describes later became the platform now called CMU OmniClear, which hosts tokenised bond activity covered elsewhere in this corpus.

t: SFC reminds investors of risks associated with non-fungible tokens
sl: SFC · SFC reminds investors of risks associated with non-fungible tokens (2022)
s: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) warned investors about non-fungible token (NFT) risks. NFTs can be hard to sell, prices can swing wildly, pricing is often unclear, and there is a risk of hacking and fraud. The SFC says an ordinary collectible NFT usually falls outside its rules. But an NFT split into tradeable pieces that acts like a security, or that gives investors a stake in a collective investment scheme (CIS), can trigger SFC licensing and authorisation duties.
w: For a bank, this sets the SFC's test for when an NFT-linked product it might sell or design counts as a regulated security. Is it a genuine collectible, or does it act like a security or a CIS stake?
k: A genuine collectible NFT -- one representing a unique image, artwork, song or video -- generally falls outside SFC rules.

t: LCQ10: Promoting development of metaverse in Hong Kong

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Eddie Yue on Four essential Q&As for e-HKD
sl: HKMA · Eddie Yue on Four essential Q&As for e-HKD (2022)
s: This article, by the HKMA's Chief Executive, explains in question-and-answer form why the HKMA is studying a retail central bank digital currency (e-HKD), beyond the earlier technical whitepaper. It announces a new discussion paper on e-HKD's policy issues, open for feedback until 27 May 2022. It discusses design trade-offs, such as privacy versus AML/CFT traceability, programmability, and impact on bank deposit funding. It states no decision has been made on whether e-HKD will be launched.
w: For a bank, this is background on e-HKD policy design, not a rule. The key point for compliance is the flagged risk to bank deposit funding if e-HKD adoption is large. It also confirms that any e-HKD design would preserve AML/CFT traceability rather than full anonymity.
k: A new discussion paper on the policy issues of e-HKD was released the same day, inviting feedback by 27 May 2022.
closing 'Invitation for comments' section
If e-HKD were made fully anonymous, it would fall short of international AML/CFT requirements. Some degree of transaction traceability is described as inevitable in any design.
answer to Q3 on challenges
If large volumes of bank deposits were converted into e-HKD, this could affect banks' funding. Safeguards such as maximum account balances and daily transaction limits are being considered.
answer to Q3 on challenges
The HKMA states it has not yet decided whether to introduce e-HKD and intends to give a policy stance later in 2022 after analysing consultation responses.
answer to Q4 and closing section
The HKMA is exploring whether e-HKD should be 'programmable' only at the wallet level, rather than embedded in the currency itself. It cites risks such as bugs and cybersecurity.
answer to Q3 on challenges

t: e-HKD: A Policy and Design Perspective
sl: HKMA · e-HKD: A Policy and Design Perspective (2022)
s: This HKMA discussion paper sets out the policy and design issues in introducing e-HKD, a retail central bank digital currency. It weighs benefits, such as more usable central bank money and readiness against stablecoins, against challenges such as bank funding disintermediation, cyber risk, and reliance on power and networks. It sets out design choices, including issuance mechanism, interoperability, privacy and legal treatment. It states three possible issuance routes, with the HKMA leaning toward a 'Coins approach' run through agent banks. It stresses that no decision has yet been made on whether or when to launch e-HKD, and lists twelve questions for public and industry comment.
w: For a bank, e-HKD would compete with, and could partly substitute for, bank deposits. Compliance and treasury functions should track this exploratory work. It could affect deposit funding, AML/KYC design for a new payment rail, and the likely role of banks as distribution and KYC agents.
k: e-HKD would be fully backed by USD assets in the Exchange Fund under the Currency Board system, just like existing Hong Kong dollar cash.
Executive summary, p.4

If deposits shift into e-HKD at scale, banks could face higher funding costs or reduced lending capacity. But the HKMA judges the bank-run risk from e-HKD to be very low, given the Deposit Protection Scheme and prudential oversight.
Section 4.1, p.20-21
Safeguards such as maximum e-HKD account balances and daily conversion or transaction limits are being considered to manage the risk of deposits moving out of banks.
Section 4.1, p.22

HKMA favours the 'Coins approach'. Designated agent banks submit USD to HKMA in exchange for e-HKD, then distribute it to customers. This is favoured over a banknote-style or Aggregate-Balance-based issuance route.
Section 5.1, p.32
e-HKD needs to meet the requirements of the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance. Complete anonymity is not an option, since e-HKD has to support AML/CFT compliance.
Section 5.3, p.34-35
HKMA envisages a tiered wallet design giving more anonymity to low-value holdings and more traceability to higher-value ones, similar to other central banks' approaches.
Section 5.3, p.35
Financial institutions distributing e-HKD would likely be tasked with customer due diligence and record-keeping under a two-tier distribution structure.
Section 5.4, p.36
A review of existing ordinances, including the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance, would be needed. This would give e-HKD a clear legal-tender and AML footing.
Section 5.4, p.36

Smart-contract programmability of e-HKD is being considered, but carries risks from coding bugs and unreliable external data feeds (oracles). HKMA leans toward building programmability into wallets, rather than into e-HKD itself.
Section 3.3, p.14
No cybersecurity study of the e-HKD distribution infrastructure had been done as of this paper. HKMA says a rigorous assessment, for example using the STRIDE framework, would be needed.
Section 4.2, p.27
HKMA had not yet decided whether or when to introduce e-HKD; comments on twelve discussion questions were invited by 27 May 2022
Section 7, p.39-40
rg: Read the Executive Summary (p.3-5) and Section 5 design considerations (p.29-36) for the substance. Section 3 (benefits) and Section 4 (challenges) give context. The footnoted academic references can be skipped.

t: Letter to forerunners of the virtual asset industry: embracing regulation, development, tradition and innovation

t: LCQ10: Trading of digital assets
sl: Government · LCQ10: Trading of digital assets (2022)
s: This is a Legislative Council written reply covering NFTs and virtual-asset crime trends. It confirms government plans for a mandatory virtual-asset service provider (VASP) licensing regime under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (AMLO). This was targeted for introduction to LegCo in Q2 2022. It reports sharply rising police-recorded VA-related crime: 360 cases in 2019, 494 in 2020, and 1,397 in 2021. It confirms the HKMA's January 2022 discussion paper on stablecoins. It also explains that NFTs are not separately defined, but are assessed case-by-case against the FATF's functional virtual-asset definition.
w: For a bank, this confirms the timetable for the mandatory VASP licensing bill that became the AMLO Part 5B regime. Banks now rely on that regime to vet VATP counterparties. It also shows the crime-trend backdrop that motivated it.
k: The government aimed to introduce a virtual asset service provider licensing bill to LegCo in Q2 2022, following consultation conclusions published in May 2021.
para 2

para 2

reply (3)
Closed-loop, non-transferable tokens such as airline miles or credit-card rewards, and central bank digital currency, are proposed to be excluded from the VA definition.
reply (3)

t: Regulatory approaches to Authorized Institutions' interface with Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers
sl: HKMA · Regulatory approaches to Authorized Institutions' interface with Virtual Assets… (2022)
s: This is the HKMA's core policy circular on banks' interface with virtual assets (VAs) and virtual asset service providers (VASPs). It is organised around three pillars: prudential supervision, anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) and financial crime, and investor protection. The HKMA says it does not currently intend to stop banks taking financial exposure to VAs, provided risk controls and senior-management oversight are adequate. But it expects proper due diligence, prudent exposure limits, conservative loan-to-value ratios on VA collateral, and capital set aside for residual risk. It requires banks to discuss any VA activity with the HKMA and get feedback on their risk controls before launch. It also references the same-day joint circular on intermediaries' VA-related activities for investor-protection detail.
w: For a bank, this is the HKMA's central, current-in-force policy statement on how far it may go with virtual-asset exposure, and what controls it must have. It is the reference point for any proprietary crypto exposure, VASP banking relationship, or new VA product proposal.
k: The HKMA does not currently plan to stop banks taking financial exposure to virtual assets. This is conditional on banks having adequate risk-management controls and senior-management oversight.
Prudential supervision section, p.3
Banks should carry out proper due diligence on any virtual asset they gain exposure to. This includes its legal and technical structure, and the background of the parties running it.
Prudential supervision section, p.3
Banks should set prudent limits on their overall virtual-asset exposure and use conservative loan-to-value ratios when accepting virtual assets as loan collateral.
Prudential supervision section, p.3
Where residual risk remains after mitigation, banks should hold sufficient capital against their virtual-asset exposures.
Prudential supervision section, p.3

Banks should watch for customers who transfer funds frequently to or from virtual-asset platforms. They should lodge a report with the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit whenever the pattern looks suspicious.
AML/CFT section (a), p.3-4

When banking a VASP, banks should assess the risk of that specific VASP. This includes its business model, licensing status and AML/CFT controls. Banks should apply due diligence like that used for correspondent banking relationships.
AML/CFT section (b), p.4
Investment products linked to virtual assets are considered complex products because retail investors are unlikely to understand their risks, and additional investor-protection measures apply.
Investor protection section, p.5
A bank intending to engage in any virtual-asset activity should discuss it with the HKMA first. It should get feedback on the adequacy of its risk controls before launching the product or service.
AIs' VA-related proposals section, p.5
rg: Read pages 3-5 in full: Prudential supervision, AML/CFT and financial crime risk, Investor protection, and AIs' VA-related proposals. The international/local-background section on pages 1-2 can be skimmed.

t: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities (2022)
s: This is the joint SFC/HKMA circular updating investor-protection rules for intermediaries distributing virtual-asset (VA) products, offering VA dealing services, or giving VA advice. VA-related products are treated as complex products and generally restricted to professional investors. Other clients need a mandatory virtual-asset knowledge test, except for a narrow set of exchange-traded VA derivatives on specified exchanges in designated jurisdictions. Intermediaries providing VA dealing services may only partner with SFC-licensed VA trading platforms. They must keep client fiat currency and virtual-asset holdings segregated, and must not offer any financing to buy virtual assets. A six-month transition period applied from the circular's date. Intermediaries must notify the SFC, and the HKMA where relevant, before starting VA-related activities.
w: For a bank, its Type 1/Type 4 securities business, as a registered institution, is directly bound by this circular. It applies whenever it distributes VA-related products, deals in VAs, or advises on them. Its detailed conduct requirements sit in Appendix 6, read separately.
k: VA-related products are normally complex products and, other than a limited set of exchange-traded derivatives, should only be sold to professional investors.
para 7.1, p.2

Before letting most clients trade a VA-related product, an intermediary should first check the client understands virtual assets. It should offer training if the client doesn't already have that knowledge.
para 7.2, p.2
An intermediary should be cautious about lending money to clients to invest in virtual-asset products. It must be satisfied the client can meet the obligations even in a worst case.
para 13, p.4
Intermediaries providing virtual-asset dealing services may only partner with SFC-licensed virtual-asset trading platforms and must serve professional investors only.
para 17, p.5
Clients may only deposit or withdraw fiat currency, never virtual assets directly, from accounts used for VA dealing services.
para 20, p.6
An intermediary offering discretionary account management that intends to invest 10% or more of a portfolio in virtual assets must follow the additional RA9 terms and conditions.
para 22, p.6
Intermediaries already doing VA-related business get a six-month transition period to update systems and controls before the new requirements fully apply.
para 27, p.7
An intermediary must tell the SFC (and the HKMA where relevant) in advance if it intends to start VA-related activities.
para 28, p.7
rg: Read all seven pages; every paragraph sets a distinct rule. Appendices 1-6 (id 8b6e24229e9e) carry the operational detail and should be read alongside this.

t: Appendix 1 - 6 to the Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Appendix 1 - 6 to the Joint circular on… (2022)
s: These are the six technical appendices to the joint SFC/HKMA circular on intermediaries' virtual-asset activities. Appendix 1 covers criteria for judging whether a client has virtual-asset knowledge. Appendix 2 lists designated jurisdictions for exchange-traded VA derivative funds. Appendix 3 is a decision flowchart for whether a VA product counts as complex. Appendix 4 is an extra due-diligence checklist for unauthorised VA funds. Appendix 5 gives example client warning statements. Appendix 6 sets full licensing and registration terms and conditions for VA dealing (omnibus account) and VA advisory services. It covers client agreements, disclosure, custody of client assets, record-keeping, auditors, AML/CFT and ongoing reporting.
w: For a bank, Appendix 6 is the operational rulebook its registered-institution arm must follow if it offers VA dealing or advisory services. Client money and asset segregation, custody, record-keeping, auditor attestation, and ongoing SFC/HKMA reporting duties all live here. This makes it essential for building the bank's actual compliance monitoring programme.
k: A client counts as having virtual-asset knowledge if they have executed five or more virtual-asset transactions in the past three years, or have relevant training or work experience.
Appendix 1, p.1

The professional-investor-only rule does not apply to VA derivative funds that are exchange-traded and dealt on specified exchanges. These funds must also be authorised in one of twelve listed jurisdictions, including the UK, US and Switzerland.
Appendix 2, p.2

Distributing an unauthorised virtual-asset fund requires extra due diligence on the fund manager, the fund itself, and the fund's counterparties. This includes checking cold/hot storage allocation policy and counterparties' insurance coverage.
Appendix 4, p.4-6

An intermediary offering VA dealing services under an omnibus account must hold client virtual assets on trust, in a segregated account with the SFC-licensed platform. It must restrict access to authorised personnel only.
Appendix 6, Part VII, para 7.1, p.16
An intermediary must maintain at least 12 months of operating expenses in excess liquid capital in Hong Kong, on a rolling basis, to provide VA dealing services.
Appendix 6, para 3.1, p.7
An intermediary must not provide financial accommodation for clients to acquire virtual assets and should try to ensure no group company does so either.
Appendix 6, para 4.5, p.7
An intermediary must not run virtual-asset market-making activity on the same SFC-licensed platform it uses to serve its own VA dealing clients.
Appendix 6, para 11.1, p.22
Records related to VA dealing activities generally must be kept for at least seven years, with some records (contract notes, receipts, order records) kept for at least two years.
Appendix 6, paras 8.7-8.8, p.21
Records related to VA dealing activities generally must be kept for at least seven years. Some records, such as contract notes, receipts and order records, must be kept for at least two years.
Appendix 6, para 9.1, p.21-22
The intermediary must fully disclose to clients that virtual assets are not protected by the Investor Compensation Fund and that transactions may be irreversible.
Appendix 6, para 6.8(d),(f), p.10
rg: Appendices 1, 2, 3 and 5 are short reference tables/flowcharts (pp.1-3, 7). Read Appendix 4 (pp.4-6) and Appendix 6 (pp.8-33) in full for the substantive due-diligence and conduct rules.

t: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities (2022)
s: This joint SFC/HKMA circular updates guidance for intermediaries wishing to distribute virtual asset (VA)-related products, or provide VA dealing or advisory services. It replaces the 2018 professional-investors-only restriction with a more detailed regime. Most VA-related products remain restricted to professional investors as complex products. But a limited suite of exchange-traded VA derivatives on specified exchanges may be offered to retail investors. So may authorised exchange-traded funds (ETFs) in designated jurisdictions, subject to a VA-knowledge test and derivative-product requirements. It also sets conduct requirements for VA dealing services, which are only via SFC-licensed platforms and for Type 1 clients only. The same applies to VA advisory services, for Type 1/Type 4 clients who are professional investors only. A six-month transition period applied. Appendix 6 sets detailed licensing and registration terms and conditions.
w: For a bank that is a registered institution (RI), it reaches this circular through the HKMA as its frontline regulator. The circular sets the suitability, knowledge-test, selling-restriction and SFC-licensed-platform-only requirements that govern any distribution of VA funds or provision of VA dealing services. Note it was later superseded; see the banner, and id d5ebca32c92b for updates.

t: Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins
sl: HKMA · Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins (2022)
s: The HKMA set out its early thinking on regulating crypto-assets, in particular payment-related stablecoins, and invited industry feedback by 31 March 2022. Payment-related stablecoins are pegged to a fiat currency and likely to be used for payments. The paper explained why these pose distinct monetary, financial-stability, settlement and user-protection risks compared with other crypto-assets. It proposed that any entity carrying out core stablecoin functions be licensed by the HKMA. Core functions include issuance and redemption, reserve management, key custody, transaction validation, or fund transmission. A licensed entity would need to be incorporated in Hong Kong; a branch would not qualify. It would also need to meet prudential, governance, anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) and disclosure requirements. The HKMA targeted introducing the new regime no later than 2023/24. It confirmed it would issue separate guidance to banks on their crypto-asset customer interface, separately from this paper. This paper is the direct forerunner of Hong Kong's stablecoin issuer licensing regime under the Stablecoins Ordinance.
w: For a bank, this sets out the regulatory logic and licensable-activity list that became Hong Kong's Stablecoins Ordinance. It is directly relevant to a bank's due diligence on any stablecoin issuer, custodian or reserve manager it deals with. It also matters to any bank considering issuing or supporting a stablecoin itself.
k: HKMA proposed to prioritise regulating payment-related, asset-linked stablecoins pegged to a single fiat currency, over algorithm-based stablecoins, at the initial stage. It planned to keep flexibility to expand scope later.
Discussion question 1 answer, Section 5.3

Seven categories of stablecoin-related activity were proposed for licensing: issuing/destroying stablecoins, managing backing reserves, validating transactions, storing private keys, facilitating redemption, transmitting funds, and executing transactions.
Discussion question 2 answer, Section 5.3

Any entity carrying out a licensable stablecoin activity in or targeting Hong Kong must be a Hong Kong-incorporated entity holding an HKMA licence. A mere branch or office of a foreign company would not qualify.
Discussion question 5 answer, Section 5.3

Proposed requirements for licensed stablecoin arrangements include authorisation, prudential capital and liquidity rules, and fit-and-proper checks on controllers and management. They also include reserve adequacy, legal clarity of holder claims, sound risk management (including anti-money-laundering controls), redemption robustness, and disclosure to regulators and users.
Discussion question 3 answer, Section 5.3

The existing proposed VASP licensing regime for VA exchanges does not cover most core stablecoin functions, like issuance, redemption, custody and reserve management. This leaves a regulatory gap that this paper aims to fill.
Section 4.1
HKMA aimed to introduce the new stablecoin licensing regime no later than 2023/24.
Discussion question 8 answer, Section 5.3

Banks distributing VA funds not authorised by the SFC should target only professional investors, assess client VA knowledge, ensure suitability, and give prominent risk warnings. This follows the SFC's November 2018 circular referenced here.
Section 4.3
AIs intending to provide VA-related investment services must notify HKMA and SFC in advance.
Section 4.3

The article announces same-day publication of a Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins, open for comment until 31 March 2022, targeting a new stablecoin regime no later than 2023/24. It also flags that the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) are jointly developing supervisory expectations on AIs' crypto-related intermediary services. A circular giving detailed guidance on AIs' crypto exposure will follow.

It also puts AIs' crypto-asset relationships on formal notice, since a dedicated circular on AI-crypto exposure was promised. This meant the bank's compliance function should have expected new binding guidance to follow shortly after this date.

t: Fit and Proper Guidelines
sl: SFC · Fit and Proper Guidelines (2022)
s: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) made these guidelines under section 399 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). They list what the SFC normally looks at when deciding whether a person is fit and proper. They cover licensed firms and staff, and banks registered with the SFC as registered institutions (RIs). They also cover bank staff on the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) register and executive officers (EOs) of RIs. The four tests come from section 129(1) of the SFO: money and solvency, qualifications and experience, ability to act competently, honestly and fairly, and reputation and integrity. The guidelines are not law, and the SFC may still accept a person who misses an element that is not material. Firms and people must stay fit and proper after approval.
w: These are the standards an RI, its EOs and every person on the HKMA register must meet before and after taking up a digital-asset dealing, advisory or custody role. A compliance head uses them to design hiring checks and ongoing fitness reviews, and to judge their own eligibility as an EO.
k: The guidelines name banks that apply for or hold SFC registration. They also cover staff on the HKMA register kept under section 20 of the Banking Ordinance (BO), and EOs of an RI given consent under BO section 71C.

s: SFC Deputy CEO Julia Leung reviewed three years of the Securities and Futures Commission's (SFC's) virtual-asset regulatory journey and previewed change. She described growing bank and broker interest in offering virtual assets to private-bank and professional-investor clients. This interest often came via introducing-agent or omnibus arrangements. She flagged unresolved questions on whether platform-style obligations, like knowledge assessments, should extend to intermediaries who merely introduce clients to VA platforms.

t: mBridge - Building a multi CBDC platform for international payments
sl: HKMA · mBridge - Building a multi CBDC platform for international… (2021)
s: This is a brochure describing the mBridge project. It is a multi-jurisdiction wholesale central bank digital currency (CBDC) platform. It involves the central banks of Hong Kong, mainland China, Thailand and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), supported by the BIS Innovation Hub. It lists 15 private-sector business use cases identified with 22 participating financial institutions, spanning trade settlement, tokenised bond issuance, foreign-exchange (FX) transactions, and wealth-connect settlement. It reports early trial figures on international trade settlement testing. It also sets out a step-by-step roadmap from pilot toward a production-ready platform from 2022 onward.
w: For a bank, several major banks it may compete with or partner with were early mBridge participants. This brochure gives useful context on cross-border CBDC settlement infrastructure. That infrastructure could eventually intersect with the bank's own payments and trade-finance business, though nothing here creates an obligation.
k: mBridge is a collaboration among the central banks of Hong Kong, mainland China, Thailand and the UAE, supported by the BIS Innovation Hub. It tests whether CBDCs can speed up cross-border payments and cut their cost.

Twenty-two private-sector participants across the four jurisdictions -- 19 financial institutions, two banking associations and one exchange -- identified 15 potential business use cases for the platform.

Named participants proposing use cases included Bank of China (Hong Kong), DBS Bank (Hong Kong), Goldman Sachs (Asia), HKEX, HSBC, Societe Generale-FORGE, Standard Chartered, and UBS. Their use cases covered tokenised bond settlement, programmable trade finance, and FX derivatives settlement.

Test transactions on the trial platform for international trade settlement covered four jurisdictions and 11 industries. The combined tested value included 10 billion Thai baht, 1 billion RMB, 2 billion Hong Kong dollars (HKD) and 2 billion UAE dirhams (AED).

The roadmap moves from the 2019 Inthanon-LionRock proof-of-concept, through the Q4 2021 mBridge trial platform. It then moves to a pilot minimum viable product and a production-ready system from 2022 onward.
Implementation considerations flagged for the next phase include a minimum viable legal framework, legal governance, and policy and regulatory compliance requirements.
rg: Read pages 2-3 for the platform overview and page 7 for the roadmap. The use-case list on pages 4-5 can be skimmed for named participants only.

t: e-HKD: A technical perspective – Request for Comments
sl: HKMA · e-HKD: A technical perspective – Request for Comments (2021)
s: This is a technical discussion paper, prepared with the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub. It explores possible designs for a Hong Kong retail central bank digital currency (e-HKD). The paper is part of a wider e-HKD feasibility study, alongside a separate legal and policy study. It proposes a two-tier model: the central bank issues and redeems e-HKD at a wholesale layer, while commercial banks distribute it at a retail layer. It also sets out seven open research problems: privacy, interoperability, performance, cybersecurity, compliance, operational resilience, and technology-enabled features. The paper states the design is not a blueprint or a decision on e-HKD, only a basis for further dialogue. It invited written comments by 31 December 2021.
w: For a bank, this is a non-binding, now-superseded technical research paper. It shows the HKMA's early thinking that any future e-HKD design would still require banks to run standard KYC/AML onboarding. It would also preserve some transaction traceability for compliance purposes. This is relevant background if the bank's payments or treasury teams engage with later e-HKD pilots.
k: The HKMA's CBDC research runs on two tracks: wholesale CBDC work that became Project mBridge, and this separate retail CBDC (e-HKD) track begun in June 2021.

The paper proposes a two-tier architecture. A wholesale system is where the central bank issues and redeems e-HKD. A retail system is where commercial banks distribute and circulate it, or a CBDC-backed e-money form.

The paper builds on the BIS Innovation Hub's Project Aurum, which is separately developing a basic prototype implementing parts of the architecture described here.

t: Inthanon-LionRock to mBridge: Building a multi CBDC platform for international payments
sl: HKMA/SFC · Inthanon-LionRock to mBridge: Building a multi CBDC platform for… (2021)
s: This September 2021 report covers the second phase of a joint central bank blockchain project. The project was rebuilt on new technology and expanded beyond the original Thailand-Hong Kong pairing. It records the point when mainland China and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) joined, and the project was renamed mBridge. The upgraded prototype cut cross-border transfer times from days to seconds. It could also lower several cost components tied to using correspondent banks. The group adopted three guiding principles going forward: do no harm to other currencies; comply with each jurisdiction's laws, including anti-money-laundering rules; and stay interoperable with existing systems. The report also describes a new governance structure, with a steering committee and four specialist subcommittees. One subcommittee is dedicated to legal issues and is chaired by the Hong Kong authority. It lists a work plan of legal, policy and technical gaps still to be closed.
w: For a bank, this report is where the project commits to following local anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) law, and sets up a dedicated legal workstream. This is the clearest early sign that a bank later connecting to mBridge would face jurisdiction-specific AML/CFT and legal-certainty requirements, not just a technical integration. It remains background, not a current instrument, since the platform has since moved on to the pilot and later stages covered in later reports.
k: The prototype moved from days-long settlement to a matter of seconds and pointed to potential cost savings compared with routing payments through a chain of correspondent banks.

t: Warning statement on unregulated virtual asset platforms
sl: SFC · Warning statement on unregulated virtual asset platforms (2021)
s: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) flags that Binance is offering so-called stock tokens elsewhere and worries these could reach Hong Kong investors. No Binance entity holds an SFC licence. The SFC's view is that these tokens are likely to count as securities under Hong Kong law. They track the price of real overseas shares in fractional form. So selling or promoting them here would need a licence or an exemption. It warns that unregulated platforms may not verify that the tokens are genuinely backed, and that investors could struggle to recover money if the platform fails.
w: For a bank, this warns that no Binance entity is SFC-licensed. Unlicensed 'stock token' platforms may be operating illegally in Hong Kong. This is relevant mainly as a name to screen out of any client referral, custody or counterparty relationship.
k: No Binance group entity is licensed to carry out any regulated activity in Hong Kong.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Opening remarks at HKAB Fintech Seminar: Next Phase of Hong Kong's Fintech Journey – 'Fintech 2025'
sl: HKMA · Opening remarks at HKAB Fintech Seminar: Next Phase of… (2021)
s: This speech by an HKMA Deputy Chief Executive launched the Fintech 2025 strategy. It is a four-part plan to push banks toward full digitalisation, build data infrastructure, grow fintech talent, and expand sandbox funding. One strand covers central bank digital currency (CBDC) work. This includes continuing wholesale CBDC research with the Bank of Thailand, and starting a new study into a retail CBDC for Hong Kong, later named e-HKD. No virtual-asset or stablecoin rules are announced here; the speech is a strategy launch, not a binding instrument.

t: HKMA unveils "Fintech 2025" strategy
sl: HKMA · HKMA unveils "Fintech 2025" strategy (2021)
s: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), which supervises banks, launched Fintech 2025. This is a five-year plan pushing banks toward full digital adoption. It covers five areas. First, every bank should use financial technology (fintech) everywhere, checked by a new Tech Baseline Assessment. Second, Hong Kong will prepare for central bank digital currencies, including a study on e-HKD, a possible digital Hong Kong dollar. Third, the HKMA will build shared data systems, such as a Commercial Data Interchange and a credit-data platform using distributed ledger technology (DLT). Fourth, the plan aims to grow fintech skills. Fifth, it gives funding and policy support, including a bigger Fintech Supervisory Sandbox for testing new ideas.
w: For a bank, this sets the HKMA's five-year direction for fintech, including work on e-HKD and DLT-based data sharing. That work later produced supervisory guidance banks must follow.
k: HKMA will run a Tech Baseline Assessment of banks' current and planned fintech adoption to identify gaps needing supervisory support.

t: The HKMA Unveils "Fintech 2025" Strategy
sl: HKMA · The HKMA Unveils "Fintech 2025" Strategy (2021)
s: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) unveiled its 'Fintech 2025' strategy, aiming to get Hong Kong's financial sector to broadly adopt financial technology (fintech) by 2025. It has five focus areas. Focus area 1: getting all banks into fintech, including a Tech Baseline Assessment of how far banks have already adopted it. Focus area 2: preparing Hong Kong for central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), including starting a study on e-HKD and continuing wholesale CBDC and e-CNY cross-border testing. Focus area 3: building next-generation data infrastructure, such as a Commercial Data Interchange, digital corporate identity, and credit-data sharing based on distributed ledger technology (DLT). Focus area 4: growing the fintech-skilled workforce. Focus area 5: nurturing the wider ecosystem through a new Fintech Cross-Agency Coordination Group and an upgraded Fintech Supervisory Sandbox.
w: For a bank, this policy sets the HKMA's expectation that it fully embraces fintech. That includes a future Tech Baseline Assessment, plus CBDC and data-infrastructure work that later shapes the bank's digital-asset plans directly.

t: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposals to Enhance Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Regulation in Hong Kong – Consultation Conclusions
sl: FSTB · Public Consultation on Legislative Proposals to Enhance Anti-Money Laundering… (2021)
s: Published by the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) in May 2021, this paper concludes a late-2020/early-2021 consultation. It confirms the government would proceed with a licensing regime for virtual asset service providers (VASPs, essentially exchanges) under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance. It also confirms a separate registration regime for dealers in precious metals and stones. It set the design later enacted: the SFC as licensing authority, professional-investor-only trading, a 180-day transition window, and specific criminal and civil penalties. This regime has since taken effect and been expanded by SFC guidelines, so this paper is now historical background rather than a current rulebook.
w: For a bank, this is the design document behind today's VASP/VATP licensing regime that any exchange the bank deals with, for custody, trading, or referral, must hold. It is a useful reference for why VATPs are currently professional-investor-only by default.
k: Anyone operating a virtual asset exchange in Hong Kong would need an SFC licence as a VASP. The exchange definition catches any platform that takes custody or control of client money or virtual assets at any point.
Peer-to-peer platforms that only post buy/sell listings without ever holding client funds or assets fall outside the VASP licensing definition.
para 2.5, p.5
A licensed VASP could at first only serve professional investors, despite over 40% of respondents wanting retail access; the government kept the restriction given the sector's risk and volatility.

VASPs would need to be incorporated in Hong Kong, or hold Companies Ordinance registration as a non-Hong-Kong company here. They must also keep a permanent local place of business, giving the SFC a local entity to supervise.
Applicants and at least two designated responsible officers must pass a fit-and-proper test covering past convictions, compliance history, experience and financial integrity.
A 180-day transition period was set after the regime started, letting existing operators keep running while their licence application was processed.
Marketing a virtual asset trading service to the Hong Kong public without a VASP licence, from Hong Kong or elsewhere, would be banned.

Maximum proposed criminal penalties included a HK$5 million fine and 7 years' imprisonment for operating unlicensed. Lower fines and 2-year terms applied to false statements, AML/CFT non-compliance, or fraud to induce a trade.
rg: Read Chapter 2 (VASP proposals, pp.4-15) in full; Chapter 3 covers precious-metals dealers and can be skipped. Chapter 5 (Conclusions, p.27) gives the implementation timeline.

t: LCQ19: Virtual asset trading platforms

It confirms the regime only applies to platforms offering at least one securities-type token. It describes the fit-and-proper vetting criteria: custody, cybersecurity, AML, market-abuse controls, and product due diligence. It states that the SFC had by then received four formal licence applications and granted its first VATP licence in December 2020.

t: Joint statement on Multiple Central Bank Digital Currency (m-CBDC) Bridge Project
sl: HKMA · Joint statement on Multiple Central Bank Digital Currency (m-CBDC)… (2021)
s: The HKMA announced two new members for a joint central bank digital currency (CBDC) project with Hong Kong and Thailand. It is supported by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub in Hong Kong. It would build a proof-of-concept using distributed ledger technology (DLT) to let central banks settle real-time cross-border foreign-exchange payments around the clock. The aim is to cut cost and complexity in cross-border transfers.

t: SFC licenses first virtual asset trading platform
sl: SFC · SFC licenses first virtual asset trading platform (2020)
s: The SFC announced that Hong Kong now has its first SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP), granted under a voluntary opt-in scheme. The licence covers two regulated activities: dealing in securities (Type 1) and running automated trading services (Type 7). Only professional investors may use the platform, and it must follow the Terms and Conditions written for VATP Operators, echoing rules already used for securities brokers and trading venues. This grant follows the SFC's Position Paper of 6 November 2019. The release separately notes a November 2020 government consultation proposing SFC oversight of every centralised virtual-asset exchange, even non-security-token ones.
w: For a bank, this marks the first working SFC-licensed VATP. When checking whether a trading-platform counterparty is properly licensed, compliance can confirm it holds Type 1 and Type 7 licences and follows the professional-investor-only limit.
k: The licensed platform may serve professional investors only, matching the definition used in the SFO's Professional Investor Rules.

t: Terms and Conditions for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators
sl: SFC · Terms and Conditions for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators (2020)
s: This SFC document sets out detailed, binding Terms and Conditions. The SFC imposes them as a licensing condition on virtual asset trading platform (VATP) operators licensed under the voluntary opt-in regime (Types 1 and 7). It covers financial soundness, token admission checks, market manipulation prevention, and client dealing (know-your-customer (KYC) checks, suitability, disclosure, contract notes). It also covers custody of client assets (trust structure through an Associated Entity, cold storage, private key management, insurance). It further covers risk management, cybersecurity, conflicts of interest, record keeping, auditors, AML/CFT, and ongoing reporting. It applies only to platforms serving professional investors and offering at least one security token.
w: For a bank, this document does not bind the bank directly. But its 98% cold-storage and Hong Kong-key-storage rules are the origin of the custody standard a compliance head should still expect any VATP counterparty to be measured against.
k: A Platform Operator should hold liquid own assets in Hong Kong at all times, worth at least a year's actual running costs. These can be cash, deposits, treasury bills or certificates of deposit, but not virtual assets.
para 3.1, p.5
A Platform Operator and its Associated Entity are expected to hold client assets so that at least 98% sit in cold storage, capping hot-wallet holdings at 2%.
Under the Platform Operator's key-management controls, cryptographic seeds and private keys for client assets are kept within Hong Kong.
para 7.6(e), p.22
An insurance policy should cover client virtual assets in hot storage (full coverage) and cold storage (substantial coverage, for example 95%).
A Platform Operator should not offer clients any financial help, such as margin, to buy virtual assets.
para 4.8, p.7
A Platform Operator should not trade for its own account or make markets on a proprietary basis.
A client counts as having enough knowledge of virtual assets once they have made five or more virtual-asset transactions in the past three years.
para 6.7, p.11

Records should generally be kept for at least seven years. Some records, such as contract notes, receipts and audit logs, need only two years, and system design papers two years after the system retires.
A Platform Operator is expected to tell the SFC within seven business days of a planned change to its scope of services, controlling persons, or authorisation status.

A token that qualifies as a 'security' can only be admitted for trading if it is backed by assets and approved or registered with a comparable overseas regulator. It should also have a track record of at least 12 months since issuance.
para 4.3(i), p.6

t: Departmental Interpretation and Practice Notes No. 39 (Revised) - Profits Tax: Digital Economy, Electronic Commerce and Digital Assets
sl: IRD · Departmental Interpretation and Practice Notes No. 39 (Revised) -… (2020)
s: This Inland Revenue Department (IRD) practice note explains how the IRD applies profits tax to e-commerce and, in paragraphs 41 to 52, to digital assets. It sorts tokens into payment, security and utility tokens. It says their tax treatment follows their nature and use, not their label. Profits from selling digital assets held as long-term investments are capital and outside profits tax. Hong Kong-sourced profits from crypto trading, exchange or mining are taxable. Tokens from airdrops or forks received in a crypto business count as business receipts, and crypto salaries are taxed at market value. The note states the IRD's view of the law as at March 2020, and taxpayers' rights to object and appeal are not affected. Its statement in paragraph 43 that Hong Kong has no specific digital-asset law is out of date.
w: This is the IRD's published practice note on how profits tax applies to crypto activity. It matters when a bank's virtual asset dealing, custody or own-account line earns income, and when staff are paid in tokens. Its paragraph 43 description of the law dates from March 2020.
k: The IRD treats payment tokens such as Bitcoin as virtual commodities, not legal tender in Hong Kong.

Tokens are grouped as payment, security or utility tokens, and profits tax treatment turns on the token's nature and use.
para 42

For an initial coin offering (ICO), the substance of the token's rights decides its treatment, not the issuer's stated intention. Proceeds from equity-like tokens are capital. Proceeds from utility tokens are prepayments for future goods or services.
para 44-45

Profits from selling digital assets bought as long-term investments are not taxable. Whether an asset is capital or trading stock depends on the facts, including the badges of trade and the intention at purchase.
para 46
Hong Kong-sourced profits from crypto trading, exchange or mining are chargeable, with source decided by where the profit-generating operations took place.
para 47
Whether crypto activity is a business depends on frequency, degree of organisation and profit motive.
para 48
New tokens from airdrops or forks received in a crypto business are treated as business receipts.
para 49
Crypto businesses are required to keep proper records of their crypto transactions under s.51C of the Inland Revenue Ordinance.
para 50
Payments made or received in crypto are valued at market value on the transaction date, and crypto salaries are taxed at market value when they accrue.
para 51-52

t: Inthanon-LionRock: Leveraging Distributed Ledger Technology to Increase Efficiency in Cross-Border Payments
sl: HKMA/SFC · Inthanon-LionRock: Leveraging Distributed Ledger Technology to Increase Efficiency in… (2020)
s: This is the joint report by the HKMA and the Bank of Thailand on the first phase of their shared blockchain experiment for cross-border payments, published January 2020. It describes a working prototype, built with technology partner R3. The prototype lets participating Thai and Hong Kong banks move funds and make foreign-exchange (FX) deals directly with each other, rather than through a chain of correspondent banks. The prototype cut settlement layers and supported same-time payment-and-FX settlement, while also trying to build in local regulatory compliance checks. It closes by naming unresolved legal, regulatory and operational gaps that would need further work; this is the earliest, now-superseded phase of a project family that later grew into mBridge.
w: For a bank, this superseded, proof-of-concept-stage report creates no obligation today. It is useful background on the origins of mBridge and Ensemble, and shows regulators flagged AML and legal-certainty gaps as open problems from the start, a theme continuing in later reports.
k: The prototype linked Thailand's and Hong Kong's own blockchain payment networks, so participating banks could transfer funds and swap currencies directly, cutting out extra middle banks.
s.01 Executive Summary
Ten commercial banks took part in total, eight based in Thailand and two in Hong Kong, working alongside the two central banks and blockchain vendor R3.
s.01 Executive Summary
The prototype let a currency swap and its matching payment settle together, so neither side of the trade completes without the other.

t: Managing ML/TF Risks Associated with Virtual Assets (VAs) and Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs)
sl: HKMA · Managing ML/TF Risks Associated with Virtual Assets (VAs) and… (2019)
s: This circular formally replaces the HKMA's 2014 virtual-commodity letters, updating guidance to match the Financial Action Task Force's (FATF) 2019 rules on virtual assets (VAs) and virtual asset service providers (VASPs). It tells banks to apply a risk-based approach when banking VASPs, doing extra due diligence in proportion to risk. This includes understanding the VASP's business, checking if it is licensed or registered, and assessing its anti-money-laundering controls. It also says banks must run a money-laundering risk assessment before launching any new VA-linked product.
w: For a bank, this circular is the direct predecessor of the AML/CFT due-diligence checklist still used today for onboarding and monitoring VASP customers.
k: Banks should assess and differentiate the money-laundering risk of each VASP customer individually rather than applying one blanket approach, since VASP business models vary widely.
Extra due diligence on a VASP customer should include understanding its business, checking its licensing or registration status, and assessing its own anti-money-laundering controls.
Before launching any new banking or investment product linked to virtual assets, a bank should carry out a money-laundering risk assessment and put in place measures to manage the risks found.
This circular replaces the two 2014 letters on virtual commodities.
rg: Two-page circular; read in full, note the supersession line on p.2.

t: Managing ML/TF risks associated with virtual assets (VAs) and virtual asset service providers (VASPs)
sl: HKMA · Managing ML/TF risks associated with virtual assets (VAs) and… (2019)
s: This circular is addressed to all Stored Value Facility (SVF) licensees. It passes on the Financial Action Task Force's (FATF) June 2019 update to Recommendation 15 and its risk-based guidance on virtual assets (VAs) and virtual asset service providers (VASPs). It tells SVF licensees to apply extra, risk-based due diligence before starting a business relationship with a VASP. This includes checking whether the VASP is licensed or registered and AML/CFT-supervised. It also means running a money-laundering risk assessment (per para 2.11 of the AML/CFT Guideline) before launching any new VA-related product. It signals that more VASPs would become licensed in Hong Kong and elsewhere as FATF-aligned regimes took hold.
w: For a bank, this is an early, direct HKMA instruction. Any bank-affiliated SVF licensee must treat VASP counterparties as a distinct AML/CFT due-diligence category, the template later intermediary and custody guidance builds on.
k: SVF licensees must apply a risk-based approach when starting or keeping a relationship with a VASP, tailoring due diligence to that VASP's own risk rather than one fixed check.
p.1, para 4

Due diligence on a VASP counterparty should cover understanding its business and checking, from public information, whether it is licensed and AML/CFT-supervised. It should also assess the VASP's AML/CFT controls, scaled to the risk found.
p.2, para 1
Before rolling out any new VA-related product, an SVF licensee must first carry out a money-laundering risk assessment and put in place measures to manage the risks found.
p.2, para 2
SVF licensees are expected to keep watching international and local VASP developments and keep applying a risk-based approach on an ongoing basis, not just at onboarding.
p.2, closing para
rg: The whole two-page circular is short enough to read in full; the FATF Guidance it references is external and not part of this text.

t: Hong Kong Fintech Week spotlights digital asset regulation, virtual banking, future technologies and FintechHK Global Competition final (with photos)
sl: Government · Hong Kong Fintech Week spotlights digital asset regulation, virtual… (2019)
s: This is a general recap press release for Hong Kong FinTech Week 2019, covering virtual banking, blockchain trade finance, and other fintech themes. It briefly notes that the SFC's Chief Executive Officer (CEO) used the event to announce new rules letting virtual-asset trading platforms apply for an operating licence. The new rules are restricted to professional investors and call for insurance against loss or theft of client assets. Most of the release covers unrelated fintech topics: virtual bank licensing numbers, the Faster Payment System, and a China-Hong Kong trade-finance blockchain pilot.
w: For a bank, this is a media recap of marginal value. The substantive rule content is fully covered by the SFC's own position paper and speech from the same week.
k: The SFC announced new rules letting virtual asset trading platforms apply for an operating licence, restricted to professional investors and requiring insurance for lost or stolen assets.
para 10 (SFC section)
rg: Skim only for the SFC paragraph; rest is general fintech-week publicity, not regulatory content.

t: Position paper: Regulation of virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · Position paper: Regulation of virtual asset trading platforms (2019)
s: In this 2019 position paper, the SFC set up a voluntary licence path (Types 1 and 7) for a centralised platform that trades at least one security token. Licensed platforms sit in the SFC's regulatory sandbox for close oversight. The SFC said it had no legal power over platforms trading only non-security tokens, so many venues could stay unregulated. Still, it judged that regulating this smaller group served the public good while broader legislation was pending. Appendix 1 gives the full terms and conditions for platform operators, covering custody and know-your-customer (KYC) checks. It also covers anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) controls, market monitoring, accounting, risk management, and conflicts of interest.
