w: For a bank, this paper set the original custody and insurance benchmarks, such as 98% cold storage and insured, trust-held client assets. Compliance can still use these to check how well a virtual-asset platform counterparty protects client assets, even though the paper is now superseded.
k: Under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), only 'securities' or 'futures contracts' fall under SFC authority, so the SFC cannot license or supervise a platform that trades only non-security tokens.
para 4, p.1-2
To fall under SFC rules and need a Type 1 and Type 7 licence, an operator must run a centralised online trading platform based in Hong Kong. It must also list at least one security token.
para 32, p.7
The SFC will not license platforms that only provide a direct peer-to-peer marketplace, or that just route client orders without running automated trading services themselves.
para 33, p.7
Every virtual-asset trading activity marketed to, or carried out in, Hong Kong must sit under a single SFC-licensed company.
para 39, p.8

Client virtual assets should be held on trust by an Associated Entity that is incorporated in Hong Kong, holds a Trust or Company Service Provider (TCSP) licence under Cap. 615, and is wholly owned by the licensee.
para 47, p.10
At least 98% of client virtual assets must sit in cold wallets (kept offline), capping hot-wallet holdings at 2%.
para 50, p.10
Insurance must cover custody losses: full coverage for assets in hot wallets, and substantial coverage, around 95%, for assets in cold storage.
para 53, p.11
Licensed operators must hire an independent professional firm to review them each year, with the first report due within 18 months of getting the licence.
para 40(f), p.9
From 6 November 2019, operators running a centralised platform that plans to list at least one security token can apply for a licence, though approval may take longer than usual.
paras 82-84, p.15
rg: Read Part I (paras 1-12) for the regulatory approach, and Part III (paras 30-81) for the licensing, custody, KYC and AML standards. The appendix duplicates content already covered in the standalone Terms and Conditions document (id 9c2042fde962), so it can be skipped.

t: SFC issues warnings on virtual asset futures contracts
sl: SFC · SFC issues warnings on virtual asset futures contracts (2019)
s: The SFC warned that virtual-asset futures contracts, for example on Bitcoin, are high-risk. The underlying assets are volatile, hard to value, and traded on largely unregulated venues, some of which have changed trading rules mid-contract or halted trades to investors' harm. A Hong Kong platform offering such futures without a licence may breach the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). Such contracts could also count as unlawful gambling under the Gambling Ordinance unless expressly authorised. The SFC said it had not licensed any such platform, and said it would be unlikely to do so, though it excluded certain already-authorised US-regulated Bitcoin futures from this warning.
w: For a bank, this confirms unlicensed VA-futures venues carry both SFO licensing risk and a possible illegal-gambling risk in Hong Kong. It is a useful screening flag if customers reference such platforms, or the bank considers a product linked to VA derivatives.
k: Offering VA futures trading in Hong Kong without a licence or authorisation under the SFO may itself be an offence.
para beginning 'In Hong Kong, any trading platforms or persons...'
Depending on structure, VA futures contracts can also count as contracts for differences, making them potentially unlawful gambling unless separately authorised.
para on Gambling Ordinance definition
As of this warning, the SFC had not licensed or authorised anyone to offer or trade VA futures contracts in Hong Kong, and said a grant was unlikely given the risk profile.
para 'The SFC has not licensed...'

US-regulated Bitcoin futures already authorised for automated trading services (ATS) and covered by a 2017 circular to licensed corporations and registered institutions are excluded from this warning.
footnote 1
rg: Read the two risk paragraphs and the SFO/Gambling Ordinance paragraphs; skip the footnote detail on the 2017 ATS exclusion unless relevant to a specific product.

t: Position paper: Regulation of virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · Position paper: Regulation of virtual asset trading platforms (2019)
s: The SFC finalised its opt-in licensing framework for centralised virtual asset trading platforms. A platform only falls under SFC jurisdiction once it lists at least one security-type token. Once caught, all its virtual-asset business, security and non-security tokens alike, must sit in one SFC-licensed company holding Type 1 (dealing) and Type 7 (automated trading services) licences. The attached Terms and Conditions set detailed, legally binding rules covering custody (98% cold storage, key management, insurance) and know-your-customer (KYC) checks. They also cover suitability, anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) controls, market surveillance, conflicts of interest, record-keeping, and SFC notification duties. Services are restricted to professional investors only, and this framework was the direct forerunner of Hong Kong's later mandatory VATP licensing regime.
w: For a bank, this is the core rulebook to benchmark any Hong Kong virtual asset trading platform (VATP) counterparty against for custody, AML, KYC and governance standards. A mandatory regime later replaced it.
k: A platform only becomes subject to SFC licensing once it offers at least one security-type token; a platform trading only non-security tokens stays outside SFC jurisdiction entirely.
All of a licensed platform's virtual-asset trading activity marketed to, or run in, Hong Kong must sit under one licensed company, so the SFC can oversee the whole business.
para 39
Client virtual assets must be held on trust through a separate, wholly-owned Associated Entity, with 98% kept in cold storage and no more than 2% in hot wallets.
Terms and Conditions para 7.1, 7.5(c)

Seeds and private keys for client assets must be created and stored in Hong Kong, with backups kept in different places. Strict internal access controls must stop any single person controlling a full key.
Terms and Conditions para 7.6
An insurance policy must cover client virtual assets in hot storage in full, and in cold storage substantially (the SFC's benchmark example is 95%), at all times.
Terms and Conditions para 7.17
Platform operators must only serve professional investors, and must assess and record each client's virtual-asset knowledge before onboarding, or provide training first.
Terms and Conditions para 6.4, 6.7-6.8

Platform operators must run written AML/CFT systems and apply extra checks to tainted wallet addresses, mixing services, and high-anonymity assets. They must unmask or reject clients using masked IP addresses (for example, VPNs) where needed.
Terms and Conditions para 13.1
Operators must tell the SFC about serious non-compliance, system failures, and various operational changes, usually within seven business days or immediately, and file monthly business reports.
Terms and Conditions para 14.1-14.4

A licensed platform operator should not trade for its own account or make markets on a proprietary basis, and must have written policies restricting and monitoring staff's personal virtual-asset dealing.
Terms and Conditions para 10.2-10.3
Platform operators cannot offer clients financing to buy virtual assets, and cannot offer or trade virtual asset futures or related derivatives at all.
Terms and Conditions para 4.8-4.9
rg: Read Part I (paras 1-12) for the policy summary. Then read the Terms and Conditions on Custody (Part VII), Dealing with Clients (Part VI) and AML/CFT (Part XIII) for the operative rules.

t: Keynote Speech at Hong Kong Fintech Week 2019
sl: HKMA · Keynote Speech at Hong Kong Fintech Week 2019 (2019)
s: This 2019 Fintech Week keynote by the then HKMA Deputy Chief Executive reviews three years of the HKMA's Fintech Facilitation Office. It covers the Faster Payment System, virtual bank licensing, open APIs, and a blockchain-based trade finance platform, and previews upcoming AI-governance circulars. Virtual-asset content is minimal. It mentions a joint HKMA and Bank of Thailand blockchain-based central bank digital currency (CBDC) research project, and a trial trade-finance link with the we.trade platform. It is a motivational conference address, not a supervisory or policy document.
w: For a bank, the virtual-asset content here is minimal and non-binding. Its only relevance is as early context for the HKMA's blockchain-based CBDC research, which later grew into the e-HKD and mBridge work streams.
k: The speech confirms the HKMA and the Bank of Thailand had a joint research project exploring blockchain-based central bank digital currency (CBDC) for cross-border payments.
para on cross-border trends

It states the HKMA had recently issued two circulars on banks' use of artificial intelligence (AI): one on risk-management principles, one on consumer protection. Both were deliberately non-prescriptive given how new the area was.
para on AI circulars
rg: Only the short passage on the Bank of Thailand CBDC research and the we.trade blockchain pilot is relevant to digital assets; skim the rest for context only.

t: Fintech: a regulatory strategy for a dynamic industry - Keynote speech at Hong Kong FinTech Week 2019 (Ashley Alder)
sl: SFC · Fintech: a regulatory strategy for a dynamic industry -… (2019)
s: SFC Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Ashley Alder announced, in this speech, the launch of the SFC's new opt-in licensing framework for virtual asset trading platforms. The SFC issued a separate investor-warning statement on VA futures the same day. He explained the 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle, and why the SFC chose an opt-in route rather than waiting for new legislation. He also noted the framework's built-in limit: it only catches a platform once it lists one security-type token, so platforms trading only non-security tokens stay unregulated. He discussed rising international concern about stablecoins after Facebook's Libra proposal.
w: For a bank, this explains, in the regulator's own words, why pre-2023 VA platforms in Hong Kong were mostly unlicensed by design. It is a key fact when checking the regulatory history of a long-established platform counterparty.
k: A platform is only caught by the new framework once it offers at least one token that is legally a security; once caught, all its operations become subject to SFC rules.
page 5
Licensed platforms must hold insurance against loss or theft of virtual assets.
page 5
Licensed platforms may only serve professional investors who can show enough virtual-asset investment knowledge.
page 5
A platform that keeps all its traded tokens outside the legal definition of securities can simply stay unregulated.
page 6
The SFC issued a separate statement the same day warning that offering virtual-asset futures to the public may be illegal under securities or gambling law.
page 6
rg: Read pages 4-6 for the VATP framework announcement; pages 2-3 (stablecoin/Libra commentary) are useful context but not action items.

t: SFC adopts new approach to virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · SFC adopts new approach to virtual asset trading platforms (2019)
s: This press release announces the SFC's 6 November 2019 Position Paper, 'Regulation of virtual asset trading platforms', moving from the conceptual November 2018 framework to an actual licensing regime. Platforms operating in Hong Kong that trade at least one security token can now apply for an SFC licence (Types 1 and 7). Licence conditions require serving professional investors only and checking that clients know enough about virtual assets. They also set strict rules on which virtual assets a platform can admit, and place the platform in the SFC Regulatory Sandbox for close supervision. The SFC still has no power to license or supervise platforms trading only non-security tokens, and a companion statement warns investors about unregulated virtual asset futures contracts.
w: For a bank, this is the historical bridge from the 2018 conceptual framework to actual VATP licensing. A compliance head mainly needs it to understand where today's custody and liquidity rules came from, since this Position Paper itself has since been superseded.
k: Platforms operating in Hong Kong that trade at least one security token can now apply for an SFC licence (Types 1 and 7 regulated activities).
Position Paper, para 82, p.15
A Platform Operator must run all group virtual-asset trading business (Relevant Activities) under one company licensed by the SFC.
Position Paper, para 39, p.8
Licence conditions require the licensee to serve only professional investors and follow the attached Terms and Conditions.
Position Paper, para 40(a)-(b), p.8-9
A Platform Operator and its Associated Entity must hold 98% of clients' virtual assets in offline (cold) storage.
Terms and Conditions, para 7.5(c), p.21-22
Insurance must fully cover virtual assets held in hot storage, and cover most of those in cold storage (for example, 95%) at all times.
Terms and Conditions, para 7.17, p.25-26
Seeds and private keys for client virtual assets must be kept physically in Hong Kong.
Terms and Conditions, para 7.6(e), p.23
A Platform Operator must hold liquid financial resources equal to at least 12 months of operating expenses.
Terms and Conditions, para 3.1, p.6
The SFC has no power to license or supervise a platform that trades only non-security virtual assets, since those do not count as 'securities' or 'futures contracts' under the SFO.
Position Paper, para 4, p.1

A Platform Operator must not trade on its own account or make markets for itself. It must not offer leverage for clients to buy virtual assets, and must not trade virtual asset futures or derivatives.
Terms and Conditions, paras 4.8-4.9, 10.2-10.3
Only security tokens backed by assets, approved or registered with comparable regulators, and with a 12-month track record after issuance, should be allowed for trading.
Position Paper, para 80(i), p.14
Licensed Platform Operators sit in the SFC Regulatory Sandbox for close, intensive supervision, including monthly reporting.
Position Paper, paras 10, 85, p.2, p.15
rg: Read the press release for the headline shift, then Position Paper Parts I and III (paras 1-12, 30-44) for the rationale and licensing regime.

t: Terms and Conditions for Licensed Corporations which Manage Portfolios that Invest in Virtual Assets
sl: SFC · Terms and Conditions for Licensed Corporations which Manage Portfolios… (2019)
s: This short SFC circular announces that the standard Terms and Conditions for 'Virtual Asset Fund Managers' are now published on the SFC website. 'Virtual Asset Fund Managers' are licensed corporations that manage, or plan to manage, portfolios with a stated virtual asset investment goal. This also covers firms that plan to invest 10% or more of gross asset value (GAV) in virtual assets, as first announced in the SFC's 1 November 2018 Statement. The SFC will impose these terms as licensing conditions on all such managers, subject to minor firm-specific changes.
w: For a bank, this confirms the November 2018 virtual asset portfolio manager framework became real, published terms. These are the legal text a bank's Type 9-licensed asset management arm would follow if it manages virtual asset portfolios.
k: The standard Terms and Conditions for Virtual Asset Fund Managers, referenced in the 1 November 2018 Statement, are now published on the SFC website.
The SFC will apply these terms as a standard licensing condition on every Virtual Asset Fund Manager, subject only to minor firm-specific changes.
rg: One-page announcement. The full terms and conditions sit in a separate linked document not captured in this record's text.

t: LCQ15: Application of blockchain technology
sl: Government · LCQ15: Application of blockchain technology (2019)
s: This is a Legislative Council (LegCo) written reply describing early government use of blockchain technology. It covers the bank-consortium trade-finance platform eTradeConnect, a planned cross-border link with Singapore, and blockchain pilots in four government departments. It reports that the Innovation and Technology Fund backed 18 blockchain and distributed ledger technology (DLT) research projects. It has no virtual-asset regulatory content; the focus is public-sector blockchain adoption, not virtual assets.
w: For a bank, this is background on eTradeConnect, the trade-finance DLT platform some banks already use. It does not itself drive any compliance action.
k: eTradeConnect, a 12-bank blockchain trade-finance platform helped by the HKMA, was still at an early operational stage in mid-2019.
reply (1)
The HKMA and the Monetary Authority of Singapore were working to connect eTradeConnect with Singapore's trade platform through a 'Global Trade Connectivity Network'.
reply (1)
The Innovation and Technology Fund had backed 18 blockchain and DLT projects worth about HK$67.2 million over the prior three years.
reply (4)
rg: Skim only; general blockchain-in-government background, not virtual-asset regulation.

t: LCQ20: Regulation of virtual asset investment activities
sl: Government · LCQ20: Regulation of virtual asset investment activities (2019)
s: This is a Legislative Council (LegCo) written question-and-answer from the government, covering virtual assets (VAs). It gives police enforcement statistics on VA fraud and money laundering, and asks whether VA goods like mining rigs count as trade description law. It also covers how profits tax applies to VA transactions, and the government's plan to keep monitoring VA regulation. The government confirmed VA transactions are already taxable under ordinary profits-tax rules, and that police handled hundreds of VA-related crime reports in 2018.
w: For a bank, this shows that as of 2019 Hong Kong still had no dedicated VA licensing law; taxation and enforcement relied on general statutes. It is useful context for how far the regime has since moved.
k: Police recorded 324 virtual-asset-related crime reports in 2018, up from 50 in 2016 and 67 in 2017 (Bitcoin-only figures for those years).
reply (1)
Existing profits tax rules apply equally to virtual-asset transactions; there is no VA-specific tax regime.
reply (3)-(5)
The government said the SFC and the HKMA would keep studying whether to increase regulation of virtual-asset activities.
reply (6)
rg: Skim; mainly of historical/statistical interest, no compliance obligations for banks.

t: Circular to intermediaries Statement on Security Token Offerings
sl: SFC · intermediaries Statement on Security Token Offerings (2019)
s: This circular sends out the SFC's 28 March 2019 Statement on Security Token Offerings (STOs), reminding firms of the legal rules for STOs. It confirms security tokens are likely 'securities' under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), so marketing or distributing them needs a Type 1 licence. From July 2019, the Code of Conduct treats security tokens as 'complex products', triggering extra investor-protection steps. It also sets selling limits, due-diligence duties, and client-disclosure rules, similar to the November 2018 rules for virtual asset funds. It tells firms to talk to the SFC first.
w: For a bank, this 2019 circular binds SFC-licensed corporations, not the bank itself as an authorized institution (AI). It matters for counterparty due diligence if security tokens are distributed through a group licensed corporation (LC).
k: Security Tokens are likely to be 'securities' under the SFO, so Hong Kong securities laws apply to them.
Marketing or distributing Security Tokens needs a Type 1 (dealing in securities) licence unless an exemption applies; unlicensed activity is a criminal offence.
From July 2019, the Code of Conduct (para 5.5) treats Security Tokens as 'complex products', adding extra investor-protection steps.
Firms marketing or distributing Security Tokens must hold a Type 1 licence and should only offer them to professional investors.
(A) Selling restrictions, p.1
Firms should check the STO issuer's background and financial soundness, and the rights attached to backing assets, and read whitepapers and marketing materials closely.
(B) Due diligence, p.1-2
Firms are told to consult the SFC before starting any STO-related activity.
p.2, footnote 5
rg: Read the 2-page attached Statement in full; the transmitting circular itself is a 1-line cover note.

t: Statement on Security Token Offerings
sl: SFC · Statement on Security Token Offerings (2019)
s: The SFC reminded firms that security token offerings (STOs) are almost always 'securities' under Hong Kong law. These are digital tokens structured like traditional securities and backed by real assets or revenue rights. Anyone marketing or distributing them needs a Type 1 dealing licence and must treat them as complex products. They must also check the issuer and the token's backing before offering them, normally only to professional investors. A November 2023 circular later superseded this statement.
w: For a bank, this sets the baseline: most tokenised-asset offerings a bank might distribute or facilitate count as securities, needing full licensing and suitability compliance, not a lighter VA-specific regime.
k: Security tokens are likely to count as securities under Hong Kong law, so distributing them needs a Type 1 licence.
para 4-5
Firms distributing security tokens must apply existing suitability rules and treat the tokens as complex products, adding extra investor-protection steps.
para 6
Firms must check the issuer's and management's soundness and the rights attached to the backing assets, including reading the whitepaper closely.
para (B)
Firms are expected to talk to the SFC before starting any STO-related activity.
para (footnote 5 / final para under selling restrictions)
rg: Short document; read in full. It was formally superseded by a 2 November 2023 circular, so treat it as background, not current guidance.

t: BCBS Statement on Crypto-Assets
sl: HKMA · BCBS Statement on Crypto-Assets (2019)
s: The HKMA passes on a March 2019 statement from the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), setting out risk expectations for banks' crypto-asset exposures. It says crypto-assets do not reliably act as money, are not legal tender, and are not backed by any government. It warns that growth in crypto trading platforms could raise financial-stability and bank-risk concerns. The HKMA tells banks planning crypto-related activities to discuss this with the HKMA first and show they have proper systems and controls.
w: For a bank, this is an early, direct statement that the HKMA expects prior discussion before the bank takes on any crypto-asset exposure, if it does plan such activities. This same expectation repeats in every later HKMA virtual-asset circular.
k: Crypto-assets do not reliably work as money, the Basel Committee says, and no government or public authority stands behind them.
A bank planning crypto-asset activities should discuss this with the HKMA in advance and show it has adequate systems and controls to manage the risks.
rg: Two-page circular; read in full.

t: Circular to intermediaries Distribution of virtual asset funds
sl: SFC · intermediaries Distribution of virtual asset funds (2018)
s: This circular sets expected standards for SFC-licensed intermediaries (Type 1/Type 9) distributing virtual asset funds. It confirms distribution of a fund investing in virtual assets triggers Type 1 licensing regardless of whether the underlying assets are 'securities'. For funds not authorised by the SFC with more than 10% of gross asset value (GAV) in virtual assets, it imposes selling restrictions. These include limiting sales to professional investors, a client knowledge assessment, and concentration limits. It also requires due diligence on the fund, its manager and counterparties, plus mandatory client risk disclosures. The document itself states it was superseded and updated by a circular dated 28 January 2022.
w: For a bank, this circular is now superseded, but it is the direct ancestor of today's virtual-asset (VA) fund distribution controls. Those controls cover professional-investor-only sales, a knowledge test, concentration limits, and counterparty due diligence. Compliance can use this mainly to check which of those requirements have since been tightened or replaced.
k: Distribution of a virtual asset fund in Hong Kong requires Type 1 licensing/registration regardless of whether the virtual assets are 'securities' or 'futures contracts'.
p.1 (Background section)
For unauthorised virtual asset funds with stated VA objective or >10% GAV in virtual assets, intermediaries should only target professional investors and assess client knowledge unless institutional.
Intermediaries should ensure aggregate client investment in unauthorised virtual asset funds is reasonable relative to net worth, to avoid concentration risk.
Intermediaries should conduct due diligence on the fund manager, the fund, and counterparties (custodians/exchanges) before distribution.
Custody arrangement of fund assets across exchanges/custodians/hot/cold storage should be understood as part of due diligence.

Intermediaries should provide prominent warning statements to clients on volatility, manipulation, lack of secondary markets, unregulated custodians, counterparty risk, hot-wallet loss risk, and cyber risk.
Failure to comply may affect fitness and properness and result in disciplinary action.
rg: Read the banner notice on p.1 first (supersession), then sections (A)-(C); skip footnote definitions unless needed for precision.

t: SFC sets out new regulatory approach for virtual assets
sl: SFC · SFC sets out new regulatory approach for virtual assets (2018)
s: This press release announces the same-day Statement on regulatory framework for virtual asset portfolio managers, fund distributors and trading platform operators. It explains that firms managing or distributing virtual asset funds will face new licensing conditions from the SFC. It also explains that the SFC will use its Regulatory Sandbox to test whether platform operators can be brought under supervision and eventual licensing. It quotes CEO Ashley Alder on investor protection goals and the sandbox pathway.
w: This is the SFC's founding 2018 policy statement. It does not bind the bank directly, but it explains the professional-investor-only starting point and the sandbox concept. Both later hardened into the licensing regimes that the bank's counterparties operate under today.
k: SFC will impose licensing conditions on firms managing or intending to manage portfolios investing in virtual assets, regardless of whether the assets are 'securities' or 'futures contracts'.
para 2, p.1
Within the SFC Regulatory Sandbox, the SFC will test whether trading platforms dealing in virtual assets could be brought under a licensing regime.
para 5, p.1
If found appropriate, the SFC would grant a licence and place platform operators under close supervision. Alternatively, it could decide no licence should be granted.
para 6, p.1
Many virtual assets do not meet the SFO definition of 'securities'/'futures contracts', so managing funds solely investing in such assets is not itself a regulated activity.
Notes, p.1
rg: Short release; read in full, then cross-reference the full Statement circular for operative detail.

t: Fintech: Meeting the regulatory challenges - Keynote speech at Hong Kong FinTech Week 2018
sl: SFC · Fintech: Meeting the regulatory challenges - Keynote speech at… (2018)
s: In this speech, the SFC's then-CEO previewed the SFC's first structured virtual-asset framework. This included new conduct standards for fund managers and distributors dealing in crypto assets, and an opt-in sandbox pathway for exploring regulation of virtual-asset trading platforms. It explains the SFC's reasoning for why it could only reach parts of the crypto market given the legal definition of 'securities'.
w: For a bank, this speech is the origin point for the fund-manager and distributor conduct standards, and for the VATP sandbox-to-licensing pathway that later hardened into today's SFC regime. It helps compliance understand why certain thresholds exist, such as the 10% portfolio trigger, and why the regime started with professional investors only.
k: SFC-supervised managers putting more than 10% of a mixed portfolio into virtual assets would need to meet new standards, initially limited to professional investors only.
'Virtual asset portfolio managers and distributers' section, p.5
Firms distributing funds with crypto exposure, already required to be SFC-registered/licensed brokers, would face new specific guidance on distribution standards for such funds.
'Virtual asset portfolio managers and distributers' section, p.5
VATP regulation would start as an opt-in sandbox: interested platforms would explore a conceptual framework with the SFC, with no formal licence granted during that sandbox stage.
'Exploring regulation of platform operators' section, p.5-6

The SFC's jurisdiction is legally limited to virtual assets that qualify as 'securities' or 'futures contracts' under the SFO. Assets and platforms outside that definition fell outside its regulatory perimeter at the time.
'The regulatory regime for virtual assets' section, p.4
Sandbox-stage platforms would be expected to serve professional investors only and meet standards at least as high as existing automated trading services the SFC already supervises.
'Exploring regulation of platform operators' section, p.6
rg: Read 'The regulatory regime for virtual assets' through 'Exploring regulation of platform operators' (p.4-6). The opening remarks on general Fintech regulation (p.1-3) are less relevant to digital assets specifically.

t: Circular to intermediaries Statement on regulatory framework for virtual asset portfolios managers, fund distributors and trading platform operators
sl: SFC · intermediaries Statement on regulatory framework for virtual asset portfolios… (2018)
s: This SFC circular, dated 1 November 2018, sends out an attached Policy Statement to intermediaries. The Statement sets Hong Kong's first regulatory approach for firms that manage or distribute virtual asset (VA) portfolios and funds. It also proposes a voluntary, opt-in idea to test in the SFC's Regulatory Sandbox: whether VA trading platforms might one day be regulated. It lists core rules the SFC might apply to a future licensed platform operator, such as a single company, professional investors only, and 98% cold storage (assets kept offline).
w: For a compliance head, this 2018 circular is historical background. It shows where today's virtual asset trading platform (VATP) custody and professional-investor rules first came from, but it does not itself bind the bank (status: historical, superseded).
k: A Type 9 or Type 1 licensed firm managing a portfolio aimed at virtual assets must be licensed and follow SFC terms and conditions. This also covers firms investing 10% or more of gross asset value (GAV) in virtual assets.
Statement, Section I(a), p.4-5
Only professional investors, as defined in the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), may invest in these virtual asset portfolios.
Statement, 'Type of investors and disclosure', p.5
A licensed firm holding non-securities virtual assets for managed portfolios must keep at least HK$3 million in liquid capital, or more if a higher amount applies.
Statement, 'Liquid capital', p.6-7
A future licensed Platform Operator should run all its virtual-asset trading business through one single SFC-licensed company.
Appendix 2, Core principle (1), p.3
A Platform Operator should serve only professional investors.
Appendix 2, Core principle (3), p.4
A Platform Operator should only allow ICO tokens to trade from 12 months after the ICO ends, or once the project turns a profit, whichever comes first.
Appendix 2, Core principle (4), p.4
Clients must fully fund each trade in advance; a Platform Operator should not offer margin financing, leverage, or virtual-asset futures or derivatives.
Appendix 2, Core principle (5), p.4
A Platform Operator is expected to keep most client virtual assets not needed at short notice, for example 98%, in cold storage (kept offline).
Appendix 2, Terms and conditions (11), p.11
A Platform Operator should insure client assets fully in hot storage (kept online) and substantially, for example 95%, in cold storage.
Appendix 2, Terms and conditions (2), p.7-8
The SFC's approach was an opt-in Sandbox exploratory stage: no licence would be granted at first, and the SFC could still decide not to regulate platforms at all.
Statement, Section II, p.6-7
At this exploratory stage, the SFC would not consider licensing platform operators trading virtual assets that are 'futures contracts' or 'structured products'.
Appendix 2, footnote 4, p.2
rg: Read the Statement (pages 1-7) in full for the policy framework. Then read Appendix 1 (portfolio manager terms) and Appendix 2 (platform operator core principles, pages 3-4) closely.

t: Statement on regulatory framework for virtual asset portfolios managers, fund distributors and trading platform operators
sl: SFC · Statement on regulatory framework for virtual asset portfolios managers,… (2018)
s: The SFC, Hong Kong's securities regulator, set out how it would bring virtual asset (VA) fund managers and fund distributors under its licensing rules. Most VAs are not legally 'securities' or 'futures contracts', so the SFC used licensing conditions instead of new law. It listed investor-protection risks in VAs, such as valuation, custody, market integrity, money laundering, and fraud, and set standard licensing terms for managers running VA portfolios. It also opened a non-binding sandbox exploration of whether VA trading platforms could one day be licensed.
w: For a bank, this is the founding document of Hong Kong's opt-in VA regime. It explains why, before 2023, most VA trading platforms a bank might deal with were unregulated by design.
k: A firm distributing a fund that invests in virtual assets in Hong Kong needs a Type 1 dealing licence and must follow existing suitability rules.
Section I(b)
A licensed asset manager whose portfolio puts 10% or more of gross asset value (GAV) into non-security virtual assets is treated as running a VA portfolio and gets extra licensing conditions.
footnote 6, Section I(a)(i)
Firms already managing, or planning to manage, any VA portfolio must tell the SFC, even below the 10% threshold.
Section I(a)(iii), footnote 9
If a firm will not accept the SFC's proposed terms and conditions, the SFC refuses its licence application, or the firm must wind down any existing VA portfolio.
Section I(a)(iii)
VA portfolios may only be sold to professional investors, with a small-amount exception (de minimis carve-out).
Section I(a)(ii)
The SFC will use its Regulatory Sandbox to watch selected VA trading platform operators run live before deciding whether platforms can be licensed at all.
Section II
rg: Read Section I in full for the manager and distributor rules. Section II is superseded by the 2019 position paper, so skim it for background only.

t: False News Report Claiming HKMA’s Investment in Crypto Products
sl: HKMA · False News Report Claiming HKMA’s Investment in Crypto Products (2018)
s: A fabricated news item, attributed to an international news agency, claimed the HKMA had put money into crypto products through a dedicated trading venue. The HKMA rejects this and says it has no holdings and no intention to acquire any. It again points victims of any related fraud to the police.
w: Shows fake HKMA-endorsement scams using crypto as bait predate the licensing regime; a recurring pattern a bank should recognise when advising customers.
k: HKMA denies the claim that it invested in crypto products via a trading platform.
para 1
HKMA says it has no current plans to invest in crypto or related assets.
para 1
Members of the public who believe they were scammed should contact the police.
para 2
rg: Short; read in full.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Keynote Speech at Treasury Markets Summit 2018: “Crypto-assets and Money”
sl: HKMA · Keynote Speech at Treasury Markets Summit 2018: “Crypto-assets and… (2018)
s: In this 2018 keynote, the then Deputy Chief Executive set out the HKMA's early public position on crypto-assets. Bitcoin-style crypto-assets fail all three classic tests of money — medium of exchange, store of value, and unit of account. The HKMA said they should therefore be called crypto-assets, not crypto-currencies. The speech also covers the Financial Stability Board's early view that crypto-assets were not yet a systemic risk, but needed monitoring. It flags money-laundering and investor-protection gaps on unregulated trading platforms. It also references a 2014 HKMA circular that reminded banks to apply KYC and AML controls when dealing with crypto-assets. It closes by noting HKMA research into DLT-based trade finance, and an early, cautious look at central bank digital currency (CBDC).
w: For a bank, this is the HKMA's earliest public statement that it does not treat crypto-assets as money. It also reminds banks that ordinary KYC and AML duties apply whenever the bank deals with crypto-assets, or with clients connected to them. This remains the baseline expectation behind all later, more detailed guidance.
k: The speech concludes that Bitcoin-style crypto-assets do not meet the tests of money: medium of exchange, store of value, or unit of account. The main reasons are slow, costly transactions and extreme price volatility.
paras (a)-(c) analysis, mid-speech

It reports the Financial Stability Board's contemporaneous assessment that crypto-assets were not yet a material threat to global financial stability given their small size, but that ongoing monitoring was warranted.
para on FSB assessment

It says anonymous, cross-border transfers of crypto-assets make it hard for banks and regulated firms to meet KYC and source-of-funds rules. It recalls that the HKMA issued a circular in 2014 telling banks to apply KYC and AML controls to crypto-asset dealings.
para on illicit-activities risk
It flags that most crypto-asset trading happens on unregulated platforms, creating gaps in investor protection and exposure to market manipulation and platform security failures.
para on investor protection/market integrity
The speech confirms the HKMA and Hong Kong banks were about to launch a DLT-based digital trade finance platform, plus a bilateral DLT link with Singapore.
para (d) on DLT applications
It discloses that the HKMA was studying the technical feasibility of a wholesale central bank digital currency, describing the work as still early-stage.
para (f) on CBDC
rg: Read the three-part money-attributes analysis and the three risk categories (financial stability, illicit activity, investor protection); the DLT and CBDC closing remarks are brief context and can be skimmed.

t: Speech by FS at "Innovative Blockchain-based Remittance Solution to Enhance Financial Inclusion" press conference (English only) (with photo/video)
sl: Government · Speech by FS at "Innovative Blockchain-based Remittance Solution to… (2018)
s: These are the Financial Secretary's remarks launching a blockchain-based Alipay remittance pilot to the Philippines. They showcase the HKMA's Fintech Supervisory Sandbox, and the growth of the stored value facility (SVF) e-wallet market since the 2015 Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance.
w: Background only: shows how HKMA used the sandbox mechanism for blockchain-based payments/remittance before any dedicated virtual-asset licensing regime existed; not a source of current obligations.
k: The HKMA's Fintech Supervisory Sandbox had, by mid-2018, supported 22 new technology products/services through to market launch over two years.
Speech body, p.1
SVF account numbers rose 15.4% year-on-year to 46.7 million by end-2017, with transaction value up 27.7% to over HK$38 billion.
Speech body, p.1
The Faster Payment System (FPS), launching September 2018, would connect banks and SVF operators for real-time transfers.
Speech body, p.1
rg: Skim; mostly promotional remarks with a few statistics of historical interest.

t: LCQ5: Issuance of cryptocurrency
sl: Government · LCQ5: Issuance of cryptocurrency (2018)
s: This is a 2018 LegCo (Legislative Council) written reply. It summarises the SFC's ICO and crypto enforcement actions to date, including letters to exchanges and issuers, and a Bitcoin-futures licensing reminder. It reconfirms the September 2017 ICO securities test. It also states that the HKMA had no plan to issue a retail central bank digital currency (CBDC) at that time, given Hong Kong's already efficient payments infrastructure.
w: For a bank, this is historical confirmation of the SFC's early enforcement approach and its reasoning against a retail CBDC. It is largely superseded by e-HKD work since, but is useful background on how the regime moved from warnings toward licensing.
k: In February 2018 the SFC sent letters to cryptocurrency exchanges and ICO issuers connected to Hong Kong, warning against trading unlicensed securities-type tokens. Most complied, by delisting tokens or ceasing Hong Kong offers.
Reply (1), p.1

The SFC's December 2017 reminder treated dealing in, or relaying/routing orders for, Bitcoin futures contracts as a regulated activity requiring an SFC licence, regardless of where the business is based.
Reply (1), p.1

The HKMA stated it had no plan at that stage to issue a central bank digital currency, given Hong Kong's already efficient payment infrastructure, but would keep monitoring international developments.
Reply (3), p.2
rg: Read replies (1) and (3); reply (2) on offshore digital-currency hub ambitions is less relevant to compliance.

t: A Golden Opportunity for Hong Kong’s Bond Market
sl: HKMA · A Golden Opportunity for Hong Kong’s Bond Market (2018)
s: This is a 2018 HKMA Insight article by the then Deputy Chief Executive. It argues that Hong Kong should keep developing its conventional bond market, alongside its equity and loan markets. It covers the government's new Pilot Bond Grant Scheme, tax incentives, the CMU settlement system, Bond Connect, and a planned government green-bond programme. It contains no mention of virtual assets, tokenisation, stablecoins or DLT. It is commentary, not a rule or supervisory statement.
w: This has no digital-asset content and creates no obligation; a compliance head can treat it purely as historical policy background on conventional bond-market development, unrelated to the digital-asset mandate.
k: The piece describes a new grant scheme and expanded tax exemptions announced in the 2018-19 Budget meant to attract more corporate bond issuance to Hong Kong.
para on Budget measures, p.1 (mid-page)
It explains that the Central Moneymarkets Unit, the HKMA's clearing and settlement utility for debt securities, held about HK$2 trillion of securities and had around 200 members at the time.
para on CMU, p.1
It announces a planned Green Bond Issuance Programme with a HK$100 billion government borrowing ceiling, with the HKMA running the offering and promotion.
para on green finance, p.1
rg: Not essential reading for a digital-assets compliance function; skip unless researching the HKMA's general capital-markets-development history.

t: Crypto product alleged to be launched by the HKMA
sl: HKMA · Crypto product alleged to be launched by the HKMA (2018)
s: The HKMA responds to a public query about a rumoured crypto investment product supposedly launched by the regulator itself. It states plainly that it has never started, and will never start, such a scheme, and that crypto investment products sit outside its supervisory scope. Anyone who thinks they have been defrauded is told to report to the police.
w: A minor early data point that impersonation of the HKMA for crypto scams is a recurring problem long before the VA regime existed.
k: HKMA denies ever launching or planning to launch a crypto investment product for the public.
para 1
HKMA says such crypto products are not something it regulates or supervises.
para 1
Suspected fraud victims are directed to the police's Commercial Crime Bureau.
para 2
rg: One short paragraph; read in full, nothing to skip.

t: Circular on BCBS Sound Practices Implications of Fintech Developments for Banks and Bank Supervisors
sl: HKMA · BCBS Sound Practices Implications of Fintech Developments for Banks… (2018)
s: The HKMA forwards a February 2018 Basel Committee paper on how fintech may reshape banking, without adding Hong Kong-specific rules. It flags that new technologies such as artificial intelligence, distributed ledger technology and open banking-style interfaces could create new strategic, operational, cyber and compliance risks. Senior management is expected to assess this strategic risk and, for locally incorporated banks, bring the assessment to the board. The HKMA says it had already begun talking to major banks' senior management about their fintech plans.
w: For a bank, this is background policy tone-setting, not a rule. But it is the document that first put fintech (including DLT) strategic-risk assessment on the board's agenda, a theme that later hardened into specific HKMA supervisory expectations.
k: Distributed ledger technology and other fintech tools may create new strategic, operational, cyber and compliance risks for banks, alongside opportunities.
Bank senior management is expected to assess the strategic risk fintech poses to their institution and build a monitoring plan.
For locally incorporated banks, that strategic-risk assessment should go to the board of directors.
rg: Two-page letter; read fully, it is short.

t: SFC warns of cryptocurrency risks
sl: SFC · SFC warns of cryptocurrency risks (2018)
s: This press release reports that the SFC sent warning letters to seven cryptocurrency exchanges connected to Hong Kong. It advised them not to trade cryptocurrencies that are 'securities' without a licence, and separately wrote to seven ICO issuers. Most recipients confirmed compliance or ceased relevant activities. The SFC restates that it may lack jurisdiction where there is no Hong Kong nexus, or where products are not 'securities' or 'futures contracts'. But it can refer fraud cases to the police. It warns investors of volatility, hacking and fraud risk.
w: For a bank, this is background only. It shows the jurisdictional gap that the 2023 VATP licensing regime was later built to close, and is not itself a source of any current bank obligation.
k: SFC sent letters to seven cryptocurrency exchanges in or connected to Hong Kong warning against trading 'securities'-type cryptocurrencies without a licence.
para 2, p.1
Most exchanges confirmed no trading of such cryptocurrencies or took rectification measures (e.g., delisting).
para 3, p.1
SFC also wrote to seven ICO issuers; most confirmed compliance or ceased offering tokens to HK investors.
para 4, p.1
SFC may lack jurisdiction over exchanges/issuers with no Hong Kong nexus or not dealing in 'securities'/'futures contracts'.
para 8 (Notes area), p.1
Where fraud is suspected, the SFC may refer cases to the Police.
para 8, p.1
rg: Read in full; short release; the notes at the end explain the jurisdictional nexus limitation.

t: Public education campaign on risks associated with initial coin offerings and "cryptocurrencies" jointly launched by FSTB and Investor Education Centre (with photo)
sl: FSTB · Public education campaign on risks associated with initial coin… (2018)
s: This announces a joint public-education campaign by FSTB and the Investor Education Centre (a subsidiary of the SFC). It warns retail investors about ICO and 'cryptocurrency' risks, using MTR ads, TV and radio spots, and the Chin Family investor-education website.
w: For a bank, this is retail investor education, not a rule. Regulators expect firms to reinforce, not undercut, this risk messaging when marketing crypto-linked products to retail clients.
k: The campaign's core message is that cryptocurrencies are volatile, unbacked virtual commodities, not real currencies, and unsuitable for everyone.
Quote from IEC Chairman, p.1
rg: Short release; read in full.

t: SFC issues reminder on cryptocurrency-related products and derivatives
sl: SFC · SFC issues reminder on cryptocurrency-related products and derivatives (2017)
s: This press release announces the SFC's circular of 11 December 2017. It cautions investors about Bitcoin futures and other crypto-linked investment products, and reminds financial service providers of licensing rules when targeting Hong Kong customers. It quotes SFC officials warning that unlicensed order routing may be a criminal offence and that risks of volatility and illiquidity may be magnified by leverage. It restates the licensing categories (Types 1, 2, 5, 9) triggered by various Bitcoin futures activities.
w: Public-facing companion to the same-day circular; shows the SFC's early public messaging tone on crypto derivatives that set the stage for later formal guidance.
k: Dealing in or routing orders for Bitcoin futures contracts for Hong Kong investors requires an SFC licence regardless of where the business is located.
para 2, p.1
SFC quotes: parties routing orders without a licence may be committing a criminal offence.
para 3 (quote), p.1
Client assets have in the past been taken through theft or misappropriation from crypto exchanges, some of which later failed.
para 4, p.1
rg: Short press release; read in full alongside circular 17EC79 issued same day.

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations and Registered Institutions on Bitcoin futures contracts and cryptocurrency-related investment products
sl: SFC · related investment products (2017)
s: This circular reminds SFC licensees and registered institutions of the legal and regulatory requirements applicable to Bitcoin futures and other crypto-linked investment products. It explains that Bitcoin futures traded on regulated exchanges are 'futures contracts' under the SFO. Dealing, advising, or fund marketing and management activities linked to them trigger Type 1, 2, 5 or 9 licensing requirements. It also notes some cryptocurrency products may separately be 'securities'. It closes with a warning to investors about risks of unregulated exchanges.
w: For a bank acting as a Registered Institution (RI), it must map any Bitcoin-futures-linked dealing, advisory or fund activity onto the correct SFO licence category. It must also apply the right suitability rules before offering it to clients. It must not route client orders to SFC-unauthorised exchanges.
k: Bitcoin futures traded on SFC-authorised exchanges are 'futures contracts' under the SFO even though the underlying asset is unregulated.
Dealing in Bitcoin futures, including relaying/routing orders, requires a Type 2 licence unless exempt.
The SFC expects intermediaries to strictly observe the suitability requirement (Code of Conduct para 5.2) and the conduct requirements under paras 5.1A and 5.3.
para referencing Code paras 5.1A, 5.2, 5.3, p.1
Marketing a fund investing in Bitcoin futures is normally Type 1; managing such a fund may be Type 9; advising may be Type 5.
A party providing regulated-activity services relating to Bitcoin futures needs a licence regardless of location, so long as it targets the Hong Kong public.
Other cryptocurrency-related products (options, swaps, CFDs) may be 'securities' under the SFO, triggering licensing, conduct and authorisation requirements.
Engaging in these activities without a licence/authorisation may be a criminal offence under the SFO.
rg: Read the full 2-page circular; footnotes provide detail on regulated activity definitions but are optional.

t: LCQ15: Regulation of offering and trading of digital tokens
sl: Government · LCQ15: Regulation of offering and trading of digital tokens (2017)
s: This is a 2017 LegCo written reply restating the SFC's newly issued ICO statement, and the government's early position. Digital tokens are not currencies, ICO regulation varies globally, and existing AML/CFT laws apply to virtual-commodity businesses even without a dedicated crypto regime. It also states that virtual commodities were not seen as posing a systemic risk to Hong Kong at that time.
w: Historical confirmation that AML/CFT duties toward virtual-commodity counterparties predate and are separate from the later VATP licensing regime; useful only as background trajectory context now.
k: The government reiterated that digital tokens are a type of virtual commodity, not currency, and are not guaranteed by any issuer.
Reply para 1, p.1
AML/CFT statutory customer due-diligence and record-keeping duties applied to financial institutions dealing with virtual-commodity operators even without crypto-specific rules.
Reply para 3, p.1
At the time, virtual commodities were judged unlikely to pose a systemic risk to Hong Kong's financial system given their limited circulation as a means of payment.
Reply, closing paragraph, p.1
rg: Read the reply's middle paragraphs on AML/CFT and systemic-risk assessment; skip the preamble restating the question.

t: Whitepaper 2.0 on Distributed Ledger Technology - Annex
sl: HKMA · Whitepaper 2.0 on Distributed Ledger Technology - Annex (2017)
s: This is an annex to HKMA's 2017 whitepaper 2.0 on distributed ledger technology (DLT). It holds seven contributions from outside firms and academics, not from HKMA itself. Topics include trade-finance and digital-identity pilots, a mortgage-loan case study, a governance framework, a security paper, a legal note, and an academic paper on blockchain liability. It is background reference material only, and predates Hong Kong's current virtual-asset and stablecoin regimes.
w: For a bank, this is useful mainly as background, not as HKMA's own rule. It explains the governance choices a bank faces when joining a shared DLT platform with other firms: a consortium, a joint venture, or a statutory body.
k: Deloitte names governance, law and regulation, and technical standards as the three factors that most affect banks adopting private DLT platforms.
Annex D, sec 1, p.39
It compares three ways banks could govern a shared DLT network: an informal consortium, a joint-venture company, or a government-run statutory body.
Annex D, sec 1.1, p.39-41
Deloitte cites a 2016 Goldman Sachs estimate of about $2 billion in savings for banks from blockchain use in transaction monitoring and account onboarding.
Annex D, sec 1.1.1, p.40-41
PwC's security paper flags confidentiality, network scalability and availability, and key security as the main technical risks DLT must manage to meet accepted security standards.
Annex E, intro, p.57
The Law Society of Hong Kong asks whether personal data should sit on a DLT ledger directly, or only as an off-ledger hash. Ledger data is hard to delete once written.
Annex F, 'Data protection', p.75

An academic paper by Zetzsche, Buckley and Arner warns that courts could treat a multi-bank DLT project as a joint venture. This spreads legal liability across every owner and operator of the ledger, in the authors' view.
Annex G, abstract, p.98

Bank of China (Hong Kong)'s mortgage-loan pilot shows how a bank, valuers and the Land Registry could share one DLT platform. It covered property valuation, ownership checks and mortgage-count checks.
Annex C, p.33 onward
rg: If time is limited, read Annex D (governance models, pp.38-56) and skim Annex F and G for legal framing. The trade finance, digital identity and mortgage loan case-study annexes (A-C) are illustrative examples, not compliance guidance.

t: Whitepaper 2.0 on Distributed Ledger Technology
sl: HKMA · Whitepaper 2.0 on Distributed Ledger Technology (2017)
s: This is HKMA's second whitepaper on distributed ledger technology (DLT), following its 2016 whitepaper, and was released around HKMA Fintech Day in October 2017. It updates the earlier technology overview, then works through compliance issues (AML/CFT, systemic risk, technology risk, reporting, governance and legal issues) that a bank should think about when deploying DLT. As of this review, it carries only historical or reference value. It predates Hong Kong's virtual-asset licensing regime, its stablecoin regime, and the HKMA's later DLT circular. But its governance and key-management principles were echoed almost unchanged in the 2025 study.
w: For a bank, this whitepaper is now superseded by the HKMA's later DLT circular and 2025 study. But it is the origin of governance and key-management expectations — hardware security modules (HSM), multiple signatures, and key-recovery agents — that the HKMA continued to apply. It is useful background for understanding why those expectations exist.
k: AML/CFT rules are not disapplied for DLT. A bank using a permissioned DLT platform must still design customer-onboarding and transaction-monitoring controls that satisfy its existing AML/CFT obligations. This includes obligations under the AML Ordinance for Hong Kong financial institutions.

Using an unpermissioned (public, anonymous-participant) DLT platform for mainstream banking is flagged as carrying substantial money-laundering/terrorist-financing risk because participant anonymity is unresolved.

Deploying DLT for outsourced or cloud-based functions triggers HKMA's existing Supervisory Policy Manual modules. These include Outsourcing (SA-2), General Principles for Technology Risk Management (TM-G-1), and Business Continuity Planning (TM-G-2).

Regulators or auditors could in principle be given direct, near-real-time access to DLT ledger data through a 'supervisory node'; institutions should consider this possibility in solution design and related agreements.

Three governance models are set out for permissioned DLT platforms shared between banks: a consortium, a joint venture, and a statutory organisation, each with different cost, flexibility and control trade-offs.

New members joining a shared DLT platform should go through AML-aligned due diligence and a cybersecurity/internal-control check, and sign a binding end-user agreement. Ongoing monitoring and re-certification follow after onboarding.

Key management (authentication and access control) and smart contracts are singled out as the two areas needing the most further work, recommending hardware security modules, multiple signatures, and key revocation/recovery agents.

Concentrating on a small number of third-party DLT service providers raises outsourcing concentration risk. This risk could become systemic if a widely-used provider fails, so banks should prepare contingency and recovery plans with their providers.

The Hong Kong Electronic Transactions Ordinance gives digital signatures the same legal status as handwritten ones, for most purposes. But it excludes certain categories, such as assignments and mortgages. A bank should check this before relying on DLT signatures for those document types.
rg: Read Chapter 5 (Compliance Issues, pp.25-29) and Chapter 6 (Governance and Control, pp.29-40) for the compliance content; skip Chapter 4's technology-platform survey (Hyperledger, Corda, Bitcoin, Ethereum comparisons).

t: Whitepaper 2.0 on Distributed Ledger Technology
sl: HKMA · Whitepaper 2.0 on Distributed Ledger Technology (2017)
s: This is a technical annex to the HKMA's second DLT whitepaper, made up of seven contributed papers from banks, consultants, a research institute and lawyers rather than from the HKMA itself. It records the outcome of five 2017 proof-of-concept projects on trade finance and digital identity, done with five banks. It also covers a live mortgage-valuation platform BOCHK built afterwards. It adds think pieces on blockchain governance, network security, Hong Kong data-privacy law, and legal liability on a shared ledger. It is descriptive and educational, aimed at helping banks weigh up DLT adoption; it sets no rules and creates no obligations. Much of the technical detail (choice of protocol, consensus thresholds, cloud hosting) is now dated.
w: For a bank, this is HKMA-hosted but externally written background reading, not supervisory guidance, so it creates no obligations. Its main value today is the still-relevant reasoning on DLT governance models, key-management risk, exposure under the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance (PDPO), and third-party liability. Later HKMA custody and tokenisation expectations build on this reasoning.
k: Five Hong Kong banks and Deloitte ran a proof-of-concept trade-finance DLT platform, built on a private fork of Ethereum. It let them share purchase-order, shipment and invoice status data, and cut duplicate-financing fraud.
Annex A, s.1-2, p.5-9
The pilot's own estimate was that banks could cut trade-finance operating costs by roughly 15% to 60% by removing manual reconciliation and forged-document risk.
Annex A, s.3.4, p.11

Deloitte set out three possible ways to govern a shared bank DLT network: an informal working group, a jointly funded private company, or a hybrid body with government involvement. Each option trades off speed of decisions against IP ownership.
Annex A, s.3.5, p.11-15

ASTRI's digital-identity pilot let a client be onboarded once, by one bank. Only cryptographic hashes of the KYC (know-your-customer) documents, not the documents themselves, were shared on the ledger. This let a second bank confirm authenticity without collecting the paperwork again.
Annex B, s.1-2, p.21-24

BOCHK's live mortgage-valuation platform, built on the earlier pilot, treats the network as workable once at least two-thirds of its nodes are online. It relies on a rolling node-to-node backup, instead of a separate disaster-recovery site.

BOCHK found that day-to-day governance needed a designated central coordinator, even though the ledger itself has no single owner. This covers patching, onboarding new members, and agreeing who is obliged to act as another node's backup.

Deloitte's control-principles paper frames DLT adoption around three linked themes banks should address together: choice of governance model, the legal/regulatory environment (including whether smart contracts are enforceable), and technical standards.
Annex D, s.1, p.39

Writing to a blockchain requires a transaction signed with a private key. Because of this, the paper flags Hardware Security Modules as a necessary control for key generation and storage, alongside the usual network credentials for read access.
Annex D, s.2.1, p.45

Deloitte recommends keeping personal or commercially sensitive data off-chain, and putting only a minimal, permissioned set of fields on the ledger itself. It also recommends building in data-retention and key-destruction plans from the start.
Annex D, s.1.2, p.42-43

The Law Society's contribution concludes that Hong Kong's Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance still applies to DLT data, even when only a hash is stored. This is true if the transaction details let someone work out who the parties are.
Annex F, Data protection s.1, p.74-75

It also flags that moving data outside Hong Kong over a DLT network engages the Ordinance's cross-border transfer restriction, which had not yet commenced at the time. Written consent from the data subject is the most workable way to comply.
Annex F, s.2, p.76-77

The academic liability paper (Zetzsche, Buckley, Arner), not PwC, cites well-known losses on public crypto networks: the Mt.Gox and Bitfinex exchange thefts, and the Parity wallet bug. It uses these as evidence that distributed ledgers do not, by themselves, remove custody and legal risk.
Annex G, Introduction, p.99
rg: Skip the diagrams and vendor-specific architecture detail. Read Annex A s.3.4-3.5 for governance options, and Annex D s.1-2 for control principles and key management. Annex F and G, on data privacy and liability, are also still useful for today's custody and governance thinking.

t: Management Accountability at Registered Institutions
sl: HKMA · Management Accountability at Registered Institutions (2017)
s: This Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) letter to all authorized institutions sets out its expectations on management accountability at banks registered with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC). Such banks are called registered institutions (RIs). For this purpose, management means chief executives and their alternates, directors approved by the HKMA under Banking Ordinance (BO) section 71, and managers notified under BO section 72B. It also covers executive officers (EOs) and anyone else who manages regulated-activity business. The detailed guidance sits in an attached set of frequently asked questions (FAQs). The HKMA expects RIs to send it and the SFC details of the senior people mainly responsible for regulated business, with an organisation chart. The letter adds no new approval steps or legal liabilities. It reminds banks that these managers are regulated persons under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO).
w: This is the bank-side counterpart to the SFC's Manager-In-Charge regime. It decides which senior bankers are on record as accountable for SFO-regulated digital-asset business, and it puts those people within reach of SFC discipline.
k: For this guidance, management covers CEs and ACEs, BO s.71 directors, s.72B managers, s.71C EOs and any other person involved in managing a regulated activity (RA) business of the RI.
p.1, para 3
The guidance should be read with SPM module SB-1, and CG-1 and CG-2 are also relevant; the SFC's December 2016 MIC circular is noted as useful reference.
p.1, para 3 and fn 2
The HKMA says the guidance neither duplicates BO governance rules nor changes approval or reporting rules for CEs, directors, managers or EOs.
p.1-2, para 4

The HKMA gave RIs six months to prepare and expected them to file the management information and organisation chart by 16 April 2018. From the same date, applicants for registration or for an added activity should file it too.
p.2, para 5
Anyone involved in managing a bank's RA business is a regulated person under SFO Part IX and can be disciplined by the SFC.
p.2, para 6 and fn 3
rg: Two short pages; read in full, then go to the FAQs (Annex 1) for the operative detail.

t: Management Accountability at Registered Institutions - Frequently asked questions
sl: HKMA · Management Accountability at Registered Institutions - Frequently asked questions (2017)
s: These 15 frequently asked questions (FAQs) explain how a bank registered with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) should name the senior people accountable for its regulated-activity business. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) expects the bank to name at least one person for overall management, normally the chief executive (CE). It also expects one named person for each business or function in the Banking Ordinance (BO) Fourteenth Schedule, paragraphs 2 to 8, where it involves regulated activities. The HKMA expects these people to be CEs, alternate CEs, directors approved under BO section 71 or managers notified under BO section 72B. The FAQs also cover executive officer (EO) seniority, outsourced functions, temporary cover and updates within 14 days.
w: If the bank adds a virtual asset dealing, advisory or custody-related regulated activity, the HKMA expects it to name who is principally responsible and to meet the EO seniority expectation. It also expects updated filings within 14 days of changes. The head of compliance may be the person named for the compliance function.
k: RIs should name at least one person principally responsible for the whole business, generally the CE, and for each Fourteenth Schedule business or function that involves regulated activities.
Q1/A1
Non-executive and independent directors are not treated as management here, although the board remains ultimately responsible.
Q2/A2
Not every CE, ACE, director or s.72B manager must be an EO, but those who directly supervise a regulated activity should be appointed EOs for it.
Q3/A3; SB-1 para 3.1.13
For each regulated activity, at least one EO should be a CE, alternate CE, director or section 72B manager. Any other EO should be no more than one rank below that level.
Q3/A3

The HKMA treats control functions such as compliance, risk and internal audit as just as important as front-office roles. It expects the bank to name the senior person who covers compliance for regulated business.
Q4/A4
A named person need not be an RI employee (for example a group employee), but an outside provider of an outsourced function cannot be named; bank management keeps accountability.
Q9/A9
Fitness of named persons is already covered by HKMA approval under BO s.71 and the bank's own controls over s.72B managers.
The registered institution (RI), not the individual, files the information. The RI should make sure each named person has acknowledged their responsibilities.
Changes in named persons, their particulars, their responsibilities or reporting lines should be filed with the HKMA and SFC within 14 days, usually with a new organisation chart.
Banks applying for registration, or to add a regulated activity, should file the same information with their application from 16 April 2018.
rg: Read Q1, Q3, Q4, Q9 and Q14 first; Q5-Q8 and Q10 handle edge cases.

t: Statement on initial coin offerings
sl: SFC · Statement on initial coin offerings (2017)
s: This is the SFC's founding statement on initial coin offerings (ICOs). It establishes that digital tokens issued in an ICO can be 'securities' under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), depending on their features. For example, tokens can count as securities if they carry share-like, debt-like, or collective-investment-scheme-like rights. Anyone dealing in, advising on, or managing funds in such tokens needs an SFC licence, regardless of location, if they target the Hong Kong public.
w: For a bank, this remains the foundational test for deciding whether a token is a 'security' under Hong Kong law. That decision in turn decides whether dealing, advising, or fund activity around the token needs an SFC licence.
k: Tokens giving shareholder-like rights (dividends, surplus on winding up) may be treated as 'shares' under the SFO.
'Offering of securities' section, p.1
Tokens acknowledging a debt with fixed repayment or interest may be treated as a 'debenture'.
'Offering of securities' section, p.1
Pooled token proceeds invested for a share of returns may be treated as an interest in a 'collective investment scheme', also a form of security.
'Offering of securities' section, p.1
Dealing in, advising on, or marketing a fund in tokens that are securities needs an SFC licence. This applies wherever the firm is based, if it targets the Hong Kong public.
'Engaging in regulated activities' section, p.1
The SFC flags that ICO tokens' anonymity creates inherent money-laundering and terrorist-financing risk and points licensed firms back to its 2014 AML circular on virtual commodities.
'Cautionary statement' section, p.2
rg: Read the whole (short) statement; the footnotes give the exact SFO definitions used for 'shares', 'debenture' and 'collective investment scheme'.

t: LCQ16: Application of blockchain technology
sl: Government · LCQ16: Application of blockchain technology (2017)
s: This is a 2017 Legislative Council written reply. It describes the government's early, exploratory stance on blockchain: possible public-service uses and an HKMA proof-of-concept study. It also confirms Hong Kong then had no targeted rules for 'virtual commodities' like Bitcoin. It also confirms an early-stage HKMA study into a wholesale central bank digital currency.
w: This is a historical marker showing how far the regime has moved since 2017; useful only for understanding the starting point of HK's digital-asset policy trajectory, not for any current obligation.
k: The government said Hong Kong had no rules specifically for virtual commodities, treating them as unbacked and not legal tender.
Reply (3), p.1
The HKMA had begun a first-phase study, with three note-issuing banks and others, into central bank digital currency for wholesale interbank and securities settlement use.
Reply (3), p.1
No government department had a concrete plan to use blockchain for public services like tax filing or land registration at that time.
Reply (1), p.1
rg: Read reply part (3) only, which is the crypto/CBDC-relevant answer; parts (1),(2),(4),(5) concern general e-government blockchain use and are not digital-asset regulatory content.

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations Regarding Measures for Augmenting the Accountability of Senior Management
sl: SFC · Licensed Corporations Regarding Measures for Augmenting the Accountability of… (2016)
s: This Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) circular created the Manager-In-Charge (MIC) regime for licensed corporations. It says senior management includes directors, responsible officers (ROs) and MICs. It names eight core functions, and each should have at least one MIC. All senior managers, licensed or not, can be disciplined as people involved in management. They may also be criminally liable for company offences under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO) that they consented to or caused by recklessness. The SFC generally expects the MICs for overall management oversight and key business lines to be ROs. It expects firms to file MIC details and an organisation chart, and to report changes within seven business days.
w: The MIC regime is addressed to licensed corporations, not banks. It applies to any SFC-licensed subsidiary the bank sets up, and it shapes how licensed brokers and managers the bank deals with are run. A compliance head who moves into an MIC role at such a firm takes on the personal regulatory exposure described here.
k: Senior management of a licensed corporation includes its directors, its ROs and its MICs; one person can hold all three roles.
para 5-6
The eight core functions are: overall oversight; key business lines; operations control and review; risk; finance; IT; compliance; and anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing (AML/CFT).
para 7; Annex 1
Each core function should have at least one MIC, though one person may cover several functions and several people may share one.
para 8

Whether someone is an MIC depends on their real or apparent authority over the function, such as decision rights, budget authority or representing the unit. The SFC generally expects MICs to report to the board or to the overall-oversight MIC.
para 9-10

MICs may sit overseas and need not be employees, but they are not outside service providers. The SFC does not approve MICs who are unlicensed, but it expects the firm to make sure they are fit and proper.
para 12-13
Every senior manager is a regulated person because they take part in management. The SFC can discipline them for the firm's misconduct that results from their consent, connivance or neglect.
para 17-18
Officers can also be criminally liable where a corporate offence under the SFO resulted from their consent, connivance or recklessness (SFO s.390(1)).
para 22
MICs of overall management oversight and key business lines are generally expected to be ROs; other MICs are not.
para 23
A long-serving head of a control function, such as compliance or risk, may be approved as an RO for the oversight role. The SFC usually adds a condition to work alongside a fully competent RO.
para 24
The board should approve a formal document setting out the management structure and each MIC's duties, and each MIC should acknowledge their appointment.
para 28-29
Changes in MIC appointments or particulars should be notified to the SFC within seven business days, with an updated organisation chart where relevant.
para 33
rg: Read Parts C, E and F (paras 7-25) first, then Part G on the board and para 33 on notifications. Annex 1 describes each core function with example job titles.

t: Whitepaper On Distributed Ledger Technology
sl: HKMA · Whitepaper On Distributed Ledger Technology (2016)
s: This is HKMA's first whitepaper on distributed ledger technology (DLT), issued 11 November 2016 at HKMA Fintech Day. It introduces DLT's technical building blocks. It then walks through operational, identity-theft and conduct risks, plus early regulatory-compliance questions. It also covers security, privacy, legal issues, and two bank-led pilots on mortgage-loan applications and trade finance. At the time, the HKMA said DLT's compliance with regulatory requirements remained largely unexplored. It treated the paper as a starting point for further study, not as settled guidance. As of this review it is historical background: it predates Hong Kong's virtual-asset and stablecoin licensing regimes.
w: For a bank, this is the founding document behind the HKMA's later DLT and custody-related expectations — cold storage of keys, AML/KYC on DLT platforms, and data-privacy handling. It is useful only as background, since the HKMA's 2024 circular and 2025 study now state its own current expectations.
k: DLT platforms could be misused for money laundering, illegal-goods payments or receiving ransom payments if a platform lacks Know-Your-Client (KYC) checks and transaction monitoring.

Owners of DLT-recorded assets are responsible for safeguarding their own private keys; HKMA notes that 'cold storage' (keeping keys offline, e.g. on a hardware security token) gives better protection than online key storage.

HKMA states that, at the time of writing, regulators had issued little formal guidance on DLT. It remained unclear whether a traditional regulatory approach could adequately address DLT's risks and legal issues.

In permissioned DLT networks, member identities can be kept private from other members through pseudonymous transaction credentials, with only authorised auditors able to link a credential back to a real identity.

Under Hong Kong's Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance, personal data placed on a DLT ledger must still be properly notified to customers, and consented to by them, and kept no longer than necessary. This is hard to reconcile with DLT's immutability (its records cannot be changed or erased). The paper suggests deleting an encryption key, rather than the record itself, as a workaround.
sec 10, 'Legal implications in relation to data privacy', p.55-56

An unpermissioned DLT network has no central administrator. Because of this, HKMA flags that it may be hard for a harmed participant to identify anyone legally accountable for a loss caused by a coding defect.
sec 10, 'Litigation and legal disputes', p.56

A five-bank working group ran a trade-finance DLT pilot. The group included Bank of China Hong Kong, Bank of East Asia, Hang Seng Bank, HSBC, and Standard Chartered. It tested whether DLT could cut duplicate-financing fraud in trade finance.
Annex, trade finance PoC intro (also summarised at sec 11.2)
rg: Read section 8 (Risk Management and Regulatory Compliance, pp.44-47) and section 10 (Legal considerations, pp.54-57) for the compliance content. The technology chapters (sections 4 and 6) are a generic 2016-era primer and can be skipped.

t: Risks Associated with Virtual Commodities
sl: HKMA · Risks Associated with Virtual Commodities (2014)
s: A short follow-up letter to banks after press reports of more virtual-commodity exchanges appearing in Hong Kong. It repeats the January 2014 warning and reminds banks that filing a suspicious-transaction report with the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit applies equally to virtual-commodity-related dealings.
