It also points banks to a government public warning on virtual commodities issued in March 2014, and gives named HKMA contacts for questions.
w: For a bank, this shows the HKMA reinforcing its January 2014 controls only months later. Banks were meant to apply those controls continuously, not just at onboarding. It also shows that statutory suspicious-transaction reporting already covered crypto-linked activity, a decade before licensing regimes existed.
k: Banks should keep using stronger due diligence for customers linked to virtual-commodity businesses. A customer's full activity may only become clear after the account is already open.
The statutory duty to report suspected money laundering or terrorist financing to the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit applies just as much to virtual-commodity dealings as to any other business.
Banks should stay on top of official warnings and news about virtual commodities, including the government's March 2014 public alert.
rg: One-page follow-up; read in full, skip nothing.

t: Risks associated with virtual commodities
sl: HKMA · Risks associated with virtual commodities (2014)
s: The HKMA's Banking Regulatory Document Repository (BRDR) catalogue page for a short letter sent to all banks in January 2014 about Bitcoin-type virtual commodities. The letter warns banks to be careful about money-laundering risk when dealing with firms that run virtual-commodity schemes. It tells banks to check that such customers have solid anti-money-laundering controls before opening or keeping an account for them. It also says a bank must tell the HKMA before launching any product linked to a virtual commodity. This circular was later replaced by a 2019 letter on virtual assets.
w: For a bank, this is the founding document in Hong Kong's crypto oversight of banks. It set the first prior-notification expectation, and the customer due-diligence mindset, that every later HKMA virtual-asset circular builds on. This circular has since been superseded.
k: Banks must step up vigilance before starting or continuing a relationship with a customer that runs a virtual-commodity exchange, brokerage or transfer service.
para 1, p.1
Banks should weigh whether the operator of a virtual-commodity scheme already has real anti-money-laundering controls when judging the money-laundering risk of that customer.
para 1, p.1
Before offering any new product tied to a virtual commodity, a bank should notify and discuss it with the HKMA.
para 2, p.1-2
rg: Read the one-page attachment in full; the catalogue page itself is navigation boilerplate.

t: CG-2 Systems of Control for the Appointment of Managers
sl: HKMA · CG-2 Systems of Control for the Appointment of Managers (2002)
s: This Supervisory Policy Manual (SPM) module is a statutory guideline issued under section 16(10) of the Banking Ordinance (BO). It tells every authorized institution (AI) how to make sure the managers it appoints are fit and proper. A manager is someone below director or chief executive (CE) level who is principally responsible for a business or function listed in the BO's Fourteenth Schedule. Examples are a business line, risk controls, anti-money laundering controls, IT, internal audit and compliance. The module lists fitness factors and the control systems an AI should run. It also covers notifying the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) of manager appointments and changes within 14 days under BO section 72B. The version read is version 1, dated 24 May 2002.
w: The head of a digital-asset business line, and the head of compliance, may themselves be s.72B managers. This module sets how the bank vets, appraises and notifies such appointments, and the HKMA may test these controls on-site.
k: An AI must have adequate controls so that each manager is fit and proper; this is one of the BO's minimum criteria for authorization (Seventh Schedule, para 5A).
para 1.2
Functions needing a manager include business lines and any other material business, accounts, risk controls, anti-money laundering controls, IT systems, internal audit and compliance.
para 2.2.1
Materiality of an unlisted business can be judged by its share of income or profit, assets or capital, or operating costs.
para 2.2.3
Signs of being principally responsible include accountability for targets, a direct line to a director or CE, decision rights, budget authority and representing the unit.
para 2.3.3
The aim is to capture the layer of management just below the CE. The AI may need to go further down, for example where a broad division has separate retail and corporate heads.
para 2.3.5
A manager may be a group employee or an outside party, and managers can be personally accountable for many BO breaches.
Fitness rests on three pillars: honesty and good name; skills and track record; and sound finances free of conflicting ties. It applies at and after appointment.
Any doubt about a candidate or serving manager should be investigated, documented and cleared before they start or continue.
para 3.1.3
Performance appraisal of managers should not lean too heavily on financial results and should also weigh compliance with internal rules and regulation.
para 4.1.7
Internal audit should periodically review the AI's controls over appointing managers.
para 4.1.12

The module says AIs should notify the HKMA of new appointments, departures and changes of responsibility within 14 days, by a letter signed by the CE. AIs should also report removals for fraud, dishonesty or malpractice as soon as practicable.
Genuine temporary cover of up to a few months is exempt from notification, but becomes notifiable within 14 days if made permanent.
rg: Read sections 2.3 (who is a manager), 3 (fitness factors), 4.1 (controls) and 6 (notification). Section 5 on HKMA powers is short background.

t: Stablecoin Review Tribunal
sl: FSTB · Stablecoin Review Tribunal
s: This is FSTB's short webpage on the Stablecoin Review Tribunal. This appeal body was created under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) to hear challenges to certain HKMA decisions on stablecoin issuer licensing. It names the current chairman and six members. Their term runs from 1 November 2025 to 31 October 2028. The page explains that a person who disagrees with a decision has 30 days to ask the Tribunal to review it. This confirms the ordinance and its appeal mechanism are already operating, not merely proposed.
w: For a bank, this confirms the Stablecoins Ordinance appeal mechanism is live, with a sitting Tribunal. This matters if the bank itself becomes a licensed FRS (fiat-referenced stablecoin) issuer, or needs to understand a stablecoin counterparty's recourse against an adverse HKMA decision.
k: The Tribunal reviews specified HKMA decisions made under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656).
para 1
A person unhappy with a qualifying HKMA decision has 30 days to ask the Tribunal to review it, or longer if the Tribunal allows.
para 3
The Tribunal only convenes when needed, not on a fixed schedule.
para 3
rg: The whole page is short (under 40 lines); read it in full.

t: Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau (CSTCB) — HKPF
sl: Other · Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau (CSTCB) — HKPF
s: This is a short page describing the Hong Kong Police Force's Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau (CSTCB). CSTCB investigates cyber and technology crime, carries out computer forensics, and coordinates with other agencies. It contains no digital-asset-specific policy content.
w: This is the police unit that would investigate crypto-related fraud or hacking affecting the bank's customers; it is background context rather than a source of obligations.
k: CSTCB has treated combating technology crime as an operational priority since 2012, covering public awareness, inter-agency cooperation, and proactive investigation.
Body text, p.1
rg: Whole page is short; no skipping needed.

t: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers in Hong Kong
sl: FSTB · Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory…
s: This is FSTB's webpage index for the joint FSTB/HKMA public consultation on licensing fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers. It links to the December 2023 consultation paper and the July 2024 consultation conclusions paper. Both linked documents are analysed as separate registry entries below. The underlying consultation fed into the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656), which has since come into force, so this consultation stage is now historical.
w: Use this only as a pointer; the compliance-relevant content sits in the two attached documents in this package.
k: The page is purely a links index to the two substantive PDFs; it carries no independent regulatory content.
whole page
rg: No independent content to read; go straight to the consultation paper and conclusions paper.

t: HKEX Virtual Asset Index Series
sl: HKEX · HKEX Virtual Asset Index Series
s: This is HKEX's own webpage for its Virtual Asset Index Series. It covers the same Bitcoin/Ether reference index and daily reference rate as the companion brochure in this batch. It adds an FAQ on how constituent exchanges are chosen, based on ratings, licensing, and USD trading pairs, plus details of the semi-annual constituent review and the Index Oversight Committee. It names CCData as the index administrator. It is exchange product/marketing content, not a regulatory publication.
w: For a bank, this explains the governance behind HKEX's crypto reference prices: how constituent exchanges are vetted, and the oversight committee. A bank would want to understand this before relying on the index for product settlement. It is product literature, though, not an SFC-recognised benchmark standard in itself.
k: Constituent exchanges must be rated 'AA' or 'A' in the latest two Exchange Benchmark Reports, be licensed and regulated, and offer USD direct trading pairs to be eligible.
FAQ, 'How is a constituent exchange selected'
The top five eligible exchanges by rating become constituents, reviewed every six months (June and December), with an extra quarterly review in March and September if fewer than five qualify.
FAQ, 'How is a constituent exchange selected'
An Index Oversight Committee, including HKEX and the index administrator, oversees index maintenance and must endorse any methodology changes.
FAQ, 'What kind of oversight'
CCData, described as a UK-registered benchmark administrator, calculates and administers the index series for HKEX.
'Methodology Overview' section
rg: Read the 'About the Index Series' and FAQ sections; skip the long HKEX site-navigation menu that makes up most of the fetched page.

t: MPFA — no dedicated virtual-asset statement located
sl: Other · MPFA — no dedicated virtual-asset statement located
s: This is the Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority's homepage, captured in Chinese, showing routine MPF administration news items (fund prices, savings rates, chairman's blog). It contains no virtual-asset, stablecoin or tokenisation content.
w: Confirms the MPFA currently has no published digital-asset-specific guidance for the bank's retirement-scheme business to track; nothing to action here.
k: The page is general MPF scheme administration content and mentions no digital-asset topic.
Homepage news list
rg: No action needed; this page has no digital-asset content.

t: IRD: Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework page
sl: IRD · IRD: Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework page
s: This IRD webpage explains Hong Kong's plan to adopt the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF), a global tax-transparency standard for crypto-asset transactions. It sets out who counts as a Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Provider (RCASP), what must be reported, and the timeline for new legislation. It links the enabling bill and OECD guidance material as attachments.
w: For a bank, if it or an affiliate deals in crypto-asset exchange or transfer services for customers, it may itself become an RCASP (Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Provider). That would bring new registration, due-diligence, and 6-year record-keeping duties from 2027. Compliance should also flag this framework when assessing crypto-asset-linked counterparties and clients.
k: Hong Kong plans its first automatic exchange of CARF tax data with partner jurisdictions in 2028, conditional on the domestic law being ready by 2026.
Overview section, p.1
The enabling bill was gazetted 22 May 2026 and had its First Reading in LegCo on 3 June 2026.
Overview section, p.1

Subject to the Bill's passage, CARF duties (registration, due diligence, reporting) are due to start on 1 January 2027, for firms meeting Hong Kong's nexus tests. The related, amended Common Reporting Standard duties are due to start on 1 January 2028. As of this review, the Bill has had only its First Reading and is not yet enacted.
Overview section, p.1

A business counts as an RCASP if it runs exchange services between crypto and fiat, between different crypto-assets, or operates a trading platform for customers, including as principal or intermediary.
'Individuals and entities subject to...' section, p.2
An entity can be caught by HK's nexus rules through tax residence, incorporation, place of management, or having a branch or regular place of business in HK.
'Nexus rules' section, p.3

Under the proposed Amendment Bill, RCASPs caught by the nexus rules would need to sign up for an account on the future CARF Portal. They would need to do this by 31 January of the year after they first satisfy a nexus test, whether or not they have anything to report that year.
'Reporting portal and mandatory registration' section, p.4

The proposed Amendment Bill would require RCASPs to retain due-diligence and reporting records for six years from the date the related CARF return was due. This record-keeping duty continues even after the entity dissolves, falling on whoever was a director at the time.
'Record keeping requirements' section, p.4

In the Amendment Bill, the Government proposes penalties for RCASP offences, including an administrative (civil) penalty track as an alternative to prosecution, with a right of appeal to the Board of Review.
'Penalty provisions' section, p.5
rg: Read the Overview and 'Individuals and entities subject to...' sections first to check RCASP status; skip the multilingual navigation boilerplate at the top.

t: Hong Kong Police Force — Press Release listing (JPEX case updates, incl. 16 charged Nov 2025)
sl: Other · Hong Kong Police Force — Press Release listing
s: This is the Hong Kong Police Force's general press-release index page (a year/month archive of all police press releases, crime, traffic, missing persons, etc). The fetched page shows only navigation and archive controls, not the substantive text of any specific JPEX release.
w: For a bank, the JPEX collapse remains a live enforcement matter. Compliance should track the individual charge announcements on this index (not captured here) for AML or fraud red flags relevant to counterparty due diligence. But this listing page itself carries no facts to summarise.
k: The page is an archive index of police press releases by month/year, not a single press release with substantive content.
Archive/filter controls, p.1
rg: Not useful as fetched; a specific JPEX press release URL would need to be fetched separately for substance.

t: The rise of tokenised money market funds (BIS Bulletin No 115)
sl: Bank for International Settlements (BIS) · The rise of tokenised money market funds (BIS Bulletin No 11 (2025)
s: BIS staff describe how tokenised money market funds work, trace their growth since 2023 and show where holdings sit. The funds invest mainly in short-dated US government paper and repo, and a handful of wallets, often DeFi protocols, hold most tokens. The authors flag liquidity mismatch, concentration and AML/CFT risks that could echo those of stablecoins and ordinary money funds.
k: Tokenised MMF total value locked: 0.77 USD bn (2023-12-31, global, 36 TMMFs tracked, reported)
PDF p.6 (Bulletin p.4), 'Market structure' and Graph 2.A
Tokenised MMF total value locked: ~9 USD bn (2025-10-31, global, 36 TMMFs tracked, reported)
PDF p.6 (Bulletin p.4), 'Market structure' and Graph 2.A
Share of TMMF TVL on Ethereum: 50 % (2025-10-31, global TMMFs, reported)
PDF p.6 (Bulletin p.4), Graph 2.B
Holdings concentration, BUIDL and WTGXX: ~90 % of tokens held by top four wallets (2025, two largest-concentration funds, reported)
PDF p.7 (Bulletin p.5), Graph 3.C
Minimum investment, institutional TMMFs: 5 USD m (2025, some institutional-only funds, reported)
PDF p.6 (Bulletin p.4), 'Operational model' continued
rg: Authors' own dataset of 36 TMMFs built from rwa.xyz, company filings, iMoneynet and on-chain data; descriptive statistics, no model. Staff views, not an official BIS position. TVL covers funds on public blockchains only; permissioned-ledger funds are outside the sample. Global figures; no Hong Kong breakdown.

t: Tokenisation of government bonds: assessment and roadmap (BIS Bulletin No 107)
sl: Bank for International Settlements (BIS) · Tokenisation of government bonds: assessment and roadmap (BI (2025)
s: BIS staff build a dataset of tokenised bonds and compare them with ordinary bonds from the same issuer, currency and coupon type. They find tighter bid-ask spreads, similar issuance costs and much lower minimum tickets for the tokenised versions, while stressing the sample is small. Hong Kong SAR is named among sovereign issuers, and the paper argues legal and regulatory uncertainty, not cost, is the main brake.

t: Holdings of Cryptocurrencies (IAS 38 Intangible Assets) - agenda decision, June 2019
sl: IFRS Interpretations Committee (IFRS Foundation) · Holdings of Cryptocurrencies (IAS 38 Intangible Assets) - ag (2019)
s: The Committee explained how existing IFRS Standards apply to holdings of unbacked cryptocurrencies that create no contract with any issuer. Such a holding is not cash and not a financial asset, but it is an intangible asset. It falls under IAS 2 Inventories when the entity holds it to sell as part of normal business (with fair value less costs to sell available to commodity broker-traders), and under IAS 38 otherwise. It lists the disclosures that follow.
k: Scope: a cryptocurrency here means a crypto asset on a distributed ledger, secured by cryptography, issued by no authority or other party, and giving no contract with another party.
page 1, opening paragraphs (a)-(c)
A holding of such a cryptocurrency is an intangible asset because it can be separated and sold, and carries no right to a fixed or determinable number of currency units.
page 1, 'Nature of a cryptocurrency'
It is not a financial asset under IAS 32 and is not cash, because no cryptocurrency is used widely enough as a medium of exchange and pricing unit.
page 2, 'Financial asset' and 'Cash'
IAS 2 applies when the entity holds the coins to sell in its normal business; broker-traders consider IAS 2 paragraph 3(b) fair value less costs to sell; otherwise IAS 38 applies.
page 1, 'Which IFRS Standard applies'; page 2, 'Inventory'
Disclosures: IAS 2 or IAS 38 disclosures, IFRS 13 where fair value is used, IAS 1 judgements, and IAS 10 material non-adjusting events such as later value swings.
page 3, 'Disclosure' items a-d
rg: Agenda decision of the IFRS Interpretations Committee; explains existing requirements rather than adding new ones. Treated as international_official because the IFRS Foundation is the global standard setter (it is not a regulator). HKFRS mirrors IFRS, so the analysis is directly relevant in Hong Kong. Covers only unbacked cryptocurrencies; stablecoins with redemption rights and tokenised securities may be financial assets and need separate analysis. Does not address issuers, custodians, or client assets held by a bank.

t: Virtual Assets and Related Activities Regulations 2023
sl: Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA), Dubai · Virtual Assets and Related Activities Regulations 2023 (2025)
s: VARA's core rules for virtual assets in Dubai (all zones except the DIFC). Anyone doing a listed VA activity as a business in the Emirate needs a VARA licence for each activity, unless exempt. Schedule 1 lists the licensable activities: advisory, broker-dealer, custody, exchange, lending and borrowing, management and investment, transfer and settlement, and Category 1 issuance. Activities tied to a UAE central bank digital currency stay with the Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE). This version is dated 19 May 2025; VARA's rulebook site shows it as effective from 19 June 2025.
k: Registration threshold for large proprietary traders: 250000000 USD (2025-05-19, Dubai, reported)
Part IV.A.7.a, p.13
No firm may conduct a VA activity by way of business in Dubai unless VARA has licensed it for that activity, it is an employee of a licensee, or it is an Exempt Entity.
Part III.A.1, p.10
A separate licence is needed for each VA activity a firm will carry on in the Emirate.
Part IV.A.1, p.12
Exempt Entities are federal or Dubai government bodies and their public or non-profit entities. They still need VARA's no-objection before starting VA activity. The definition does not list banks.
Part IV.A.6, p.13; Schedule 4 'Exempt Entity', p.46
VA activities relating to UAE central bank digital currencies remain solely under CBUAE oversight. VASPs must also follow CBUAE rules, for example on payment token services.
Part III.A.4, pp.10-11
A licensee operating outside Dubai must meet VARA standards there too, applying whichever regime is stricter.
Part IV.A.4, p.12
Issuing anonymity-enhanced cryptocurrencies, and any VA activity involving them, is banned in the Emirate.
Part II.C.1, p.9
A Custody Services licence is only open to firms that keep each client's assets in its own separate wallet, unless the Custody Rulebook allows otherwise.
Schedule 1 'Custody Services', p.37
rg: Primary regulation, captured from VARA's official rulebook site (the current version's download link). Dubai only. Does not cover the DIFC (regulated by the DFSA) or ADGM. VARA can amend the rules at its discretion, so check the rulebook site for the latest version.

t: Custody Services Rulebook
sl: Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA), Dubai · Custody Services Rulebook (2025)
s: This rulebook applies to VASPs licensed by VARA for Custody Services. It adds to the general Regulations and to the client-asset provisions of VARA's Compliance and Risk Management Rulebook. Where the two conflict, this rulebook prevails. Its main themes are asset segregation, a separate legal entity for custody, wallet and key controls, client agreements, monthly statements and audit trails.
k: Assets held in custody are not the custodian's own assets or deposit-type liabilities.
Part III.B.1, p.10
Rehypothecating custodied assets is banned, even if the client consents. Custodians must not ask clients for such consent.
Part III.B.2, p.10
Each client's assets must sit in separate wallets that hold only that client's assets.
Part III.B.3, p.10
The custodian must be a separate legal entity from group companies that run other VA activities. A narrow exception allows it to add transfer and settlement services.
Part III.B.5-6, pp.10-11
The split between hot, cold and warm storage should rest on a risk-based analysis. Transfer mechanisms between wallet types are subject to independent third-party audit.
Part III.C.1, p.11
Key and seed backups must be kept apart from the primary keys. Mnemonic seed phrases must be split into at least two parts.
Part III.C.2.c, p.12
Clients get a statement at least monthly, and on request. A transaction audit trail is kept for at least eight years.
Part III.D.4-5, p.15
rg: Binding VARA rulebook, captured from the official rulebook site. Dubai (excluding DIFC) only. The rulebook also has parts on staking from custody and on collateral wallets, which are not summarised here.

t: Exchange Services Rulebook
sl: Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA), Dubai · Exchange Services Rulebook (2026)
s: This rulebook sets extra rules for VARA-licensed exchanges. It covers board and disclosure requirements, a participant code of conduct, market surveillance, system resilience and settlement timing. Separate parts deal with margin trading and exchange-traded derivatives (ETDs), including leverage limits for retail investors and insurance funds. This is the 31 March 2026 version.
k: Maximum leverage for retail investors on exchange-traded derivatives: 5:1 ratio (2026-03-31, Dubai VARA-licensed exchanges offering ETDs, reported)
Part V.G.8, p.29
Settlement deadline for exchange trades: 24 hours (2026-03-31, Dubai VARA-licensed exchanges, reported)
Part III.D.1, p.12
Exchanges must publish and enforce a code of conduct for trading participants, with a range of disciplinary powers.
Part III.A.1-3, p.10
Exchanges must share surveillance information with VARA and report suspected market abuse. Their fee structures must not reward disruptive order behaviour.
Part III.B, p.11
Final settlement is due within 24 hours of execution, subject to factors outside the exchange's control.
Part III.D.1, p.12
Firms offering ETDs must keep an insurance fund, unless VARA agrees otherwise.
Part V.I.1, p.30
rg: Binding VARA rulebook, captured from the official rulebook site. Dubai (excluding DIFC) only. Hong Kong treats virtual asset derivatives differently, so do not compare them directly without checking the Hong Kong position.

t: Broker-Dealer Services Rulebook
sl: Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA), Dubai · Broker-Dealer Services Rulebook (2025)
s: This rulebook applies to VASPs licensed by VARA for Broker-Dealer Services. That activity covers arranging, dealing as principal, market making and placement or distribution for issuers. The rulebook sets a best-execution duty, conditions for principal dealing, a route for adding advisory services, margin trading rules and duties for Licensed Distribution Services.
k: Broker-dealers must use reasonable diligence to get the best price for clients in current market conditions, taking account of costs, speed, likelihood of execution and settlement, and order size. A narrow carve-out covers some quote requests from other VASPs and professional clients.
Part II.A.1-2, p.7
Dealing as principal, including riskless principal, is allowed but subject to best execution. Client money and client VAs may not be used except as the client-asset rules permit.
Part II.B.1-2, p.10
A broker-dealer may also give advice if it meets the extra capital requirements and follows the Advisory Services Rulebook.
Part II.C.1, p.10

A firm distributing VAs for issuers is responsible for the quality of those issuers and assets. This includes consumer protection, FATF and sanctions compliance, and fair markets. VARA can order distribution suspended or stopped.
Part IV.A.3 and IV.B.1-2, pp.17-18
rg: Binding VARA rulebook, captured from the official rulebook site. Dubai (excluding DIFC) only.

t: Virtual Asset Issuance Rulebook
sl: Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA), Dubai · Virtual Asset Issuance Rulebook (2025)
s: This rulebook sorts VA issuance in Dubai into three groups. Category 1 needs a VARA licence and covers fiat-referenced VAs (FRVAs, i.e. stablecoins) and asset-referenced VAs. Category 2 needs no licence but must be distributed through a licensed distributor. Exempt VAs have no prior requirement. Annex 1 sets the FRVA rules: full reserve backing, redemption at par, monthly independent audits and capital. Stablecoins that reference the UAE dirham (AED) are excluded and remain with the CBUAE.
k: FRVA issuer minimum paid-up capital (fixed element): 1500000 AED (2025-05-19, Dubai VARA-licensed FRVA issuers, reported)
Annex 1 Part III.F.1.a, p.37
FRVA issuer capital (variable element): 2 percent of value of available FRVA supply (2025-05-19, Dubai VARA-licensed FRVA issuers, reported)
Annex 1 Part III.F.1.b, p.37
Redemption deadline: 1 working day (2025-05-19, Dubai VARA-licensed FRVA issuers, reported)
Annex 1 Part III.C.2, p.36
Issuing an FRVA or an asset-referenced VA is a Category 1 activity that needs a VARA licence. Other issuances need no licence but must be placed through a licensed distributor.
Part I.C.1, p.8
VARA will not approve a stablecoin that tracks the AED under these rules. Such tokens fall solely under CBUAE regulation.
Schedule 2 'FRVA', pp.23-24; Annex 1 Part I.B.4, p.30
FRVAs must be backed at all times by reserve assets worth at least 100% of the tokens in circulation.
Annex 1 Part III.B.1, p.34

Reserves must be in the reference currency. Eligible assets are cash or cash equivalents, government or central bank debt with 90 days or less to maturity, repos of 7 days or less backed by that debt, and short-term government money market funds.
Annex 1 Part III.B.2, pp.34-35
Reserves must be kept with suitably licensed firms, legally segregated from the issuer's own assets and protected from creditors. They must not be rehypothecated or pledged.
Annex 1 Part III.B.3-4, pp.35-36
Holders have a legally enforceable right to redeem at par. Redemptions must be completed within one working day and without fees.
Annex 1 Part III.C.1-3, p.36
An independent audit of tokens in circulation and reserve composition is needed every month. Marketing must say the tokens are not covered by deposit guarantee or investor protection schemes.
Annex 1 Part III.D.1 and III.E.2, p.37
rg: Binding VARA rulebook, captured from the official rulebook site. Covers only non-AED stablecoins issued in Dubai (excluding DIFC). The CBUAE Payment Token Services Regulation, which governs AED stablecoins, could not be captured because centralbank.ae returned HTTP 403.

t: Market Conduct Rulebook
sl: Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA), Dubai · Market Conduct Rulebook (2025)
s: This rulebook applies to all VARA licensees. It covers marketing, client agreements, complaints, investor classification, public disclosures, insider lists and own-account trading. Investors are sorted into Retail, Qualified and Institutional, and a licence may limit which types a VASP can serve. VASPs are generally barred from actively investing their own or their group's portfolio.
k: Qualified Investor net-asset threshold: 3500000 AED (2025-05-19, Dubai VARA licensees, reported)
Part IV.A.3.a.i and b.i, pp.10-11
Qualified Investor income alternative: 700000 AED per year (2025-05-19, Dubai VARA licensees, reported)
Part IV.A.3.a.ii, p.11
VASPs may serve only the investor types VARA permits, within the limits in the rules, their licence conditions and any other VARA conditions.
Part IV.A.1, p.10

An Institutional Investor includes any entity regulated by a competent financial regulator (the CBUAE among others), any VASP, central-bank-type institutions, and some governments and multilateral bodies.
Part IV.A.4, pp.11-12

VASPs must publish their licence number, licensed activities and responsible individuals, plus a risk statement. The statement must cover loss of value, irreversible transfers, illiquidity and fraud or hacking.
Part V.A-B, p.13
VASPs may not actively invest their own or their group's portfolio. Prudent treasury and liquid-asset management is allowed if records are kept for eight years.
Part VII.A.1-2, p.17
rg: Binding VARA rulebook, captured from the official rulebook site. Dubai (excluding DIFC) only. Retail access depends on each licence's conditions, which this rulebook does not list.

t: Compliance and Risk Management Rulebook
sl: Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA), Dubai · Compliance and Risk Management Rulebook (2025)
s: This rulebook applies to all VARA licensees. It covers compliance management, AML/CFT including the FATF Travel Rule, client money and client VA rules. Client fiat money must be held in 'Client Account' accounts at third-party banks outside the VASP's group, and money for UAE clients must be at UAE banks. Client VAs must be kept apart from the VASP's own assets and reconciled daily.
k: Client money must be held in a designated client account. It is not the VASP's property and stays outside its estate on insolvency.
Part IV.B.2-3, p.37

Client money must reach a client account within one calendar day. Money for UAE clients must be held at banks in the UAE. Money for non-UAE clients may start at a foreign bank but must be moved to UAE banks, with the move started within 24 hours.
Part IV.B.5, p.38
Client accounts may only be kept at deposit-taking banks that are properly authorised and not in the VASP's group.
Part IV.C.1, p.40
Client VAs must be kept in wallets separate from the VASP's own assets and held one-to-one. Rehypothecation needs the client's explicit prior consent and the right licence.
Part V.B.2-4, p.44
Proceeds such as airdrops and staking gains go to the client unless agreed otherwise. VASPs must meet VARA's proof-of-reserves requirements and reconcile client VA balances daily.
Part V.B.5, C.1, D.1, p.45
rg: Binding VARA rulebook, captured from the official rulebook site. Dubai (excluding DIFC) only. The Custody Services Rulebook takes precedence for licensed custodians where the two conflict.

t: MAS Finalises Stablecoin Regulatory Framework
sl: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) · MAS Finalises Stablecoin Regulatory Framework (2023)
s: MAS's finalised rules for regulating single-currency stablecoins (SCS) that are pegged to the Singapore dollar or a G10 currency and issued in Singapore. Issuers meeting the framework's reserve, capital, redemption and disclosure requirements can apply to have their token recognised and labelled an 'MAS-regulated stablecoin'; misusing that label can bring penalties. The framework followed an October 2022 public consultation and took the feedback received into account.
k: Redemption deadline for MAS-regulated stablecoins: 5 business days (2023-08-15, Singapore, reported)
para 3, bullet 'Redemption at Par'
SCS issuers must hold reserve assets that meet MAS requirements on composition, valuation, custody and audit, so as to give users confidence that the coin's value will hold steady.
para 3, bullet 'Value stability'
SCS issuers are required to keep a floor of capital and liquid holdings on hand, to lower the chance of going insolvent and let the business be wound down in an orderly way if that happens.
para 3, bullet 'Capital'
SCS issuers must give holders back the par value within the stated deadline after a redemption request.
para 3, bullet 'Redemption at Par'
SCS issuers must tell users how the token's value is kept stable, what rights holders have, and the results of reserve-asset audits.
para 3, bullet 'Disclosure'

Only issuers meeting every requirement of the framework may apply for their stablecoin to be labelled an 'MAS-regulated stablecoin'. Falsely using that label can lead to financial penalties, imprisonment for an individual, or a listing on MAS's Investor Alert List.
para 4
rg: Official MAS media release, captured from mas.gov.sg. Covers only single-currency stablecoins pegged to SGD or a G10 currency and issued in Singapore; other tokens stay under MAS's separate digital payment token regime. A later legislative-amendment consultation, referenced in a related-news link on the same page, was not captured here.

t: Guidelines on Consumer Protection Measures by Digital Payment Token Service Providers [PS-G03]
sl: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) · Guidelines on Consumer Protection Measures by Digital Paymen (2024)
s: MAS guidance under the Payment Services Act on how a digital payment token (DPT) service provider should look after customers' assets. A provider is expected to keep customer holdings apart from its own, in a trust account it runs itself or through an outside party it has vetted. The guidance also covers risk controls, a cold-storage minimum, conflict-of-interest handling and where the staff who move customer assets should be based.
k: Minimum share of customer assets kept in cold storage: 90 percent (2024-04-02, Singapore DPT service providers, reported)
A provider is expected to keep customer assets in a trust account kept separate from its own assets, whether it runs that account itself or through an outside safeguarding person.

Before placing assets with an outside safeguarding person, a provider should weigh that party's legal protections, financial standing, regulatory status, and whether spreading assets across more than one safeguarding person would help.

Providers are expected to put controls in place so that no single staff member can authorise and carry out a transfer of customer assets alone, and to control transfers between their own storage systems.
Staff and senior managers who control customer-asset movements should be based in Singapore, so they can help return those assets if MAS or a court orders it.
rg: Binding MAS guideline issued under section 101 of the Payment Services Act 2019. Captured as the PDF linked from MAS's guidelines page; the PDF itself is dated 2 April 2024 and states it takes effect on 4 October 2024, while MAS's guidelines page shows the current version as last revised on 19 September 2024. A guideline, not a statute: MAS supervises against the spirit of the document rather than applying it as a fixed rule with set sanctions. Earlier amendment notes listed on MAS's guidelines landing page were not separately captured.

t: MAS Clarifies Regulatory Regime for Digital Token Service Providers
sl: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) · MAS Clarifies Regulatory Regime for Digital Token Service Pr (2025)
s: MAS media release narrowing the scope of its Digital Token Service Provider (DTSP) regime, which sits within the Financial Services and Markets Act passed in 2022, following its 30 May 2025 response to consultation feedback. From 30 June 2025 a licence is needed only by firms serving customers solely outside Singapore; MAS says it expects to grant very few such licences given the money-laundering risk and the limits on its ability to supervise overseas-only business. Firms already serving Singapore customers keep their existing status under other Acts.
k: From 30 June 2025, a DTSP providing digital-payment-token or capital-markets-token services solely to customers outside Singapore needs a licence.
para 2

MAS has set a high bar for that licence and says it will generally decline to grant one, pointing to higher money-laundering risk and its limited ability to oversee firms whose regulated activity sits entirely offshore.
para 2

A firm already serving customers in Singapore stays regulated as before, under the Payment Services Act 2019, the Securities and Futures Act 2001 or the Financial Advisers Act 2001, and may keep serving overseas customers alongside its Singapore ones without extra impact.
para 3
A provider dealing only in tokens used for utility or governance purposes falls outside the DTSP licensing regime altogether.
para 4

A DTSP that today serves only customers outside Singapore must wind that activity down once the regime starts on 30 June 2025. MAS says it has found only a handful of such firms and has already contacted them.
para 5
rg: Official MAS media release, captured from mas.gov.sg. Covers the announcement text only; the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022 provisions, regulations and notices referenced in its Annex were not separately captured.

t: Project Guardian (Guardian) overview
sl: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) · Project Guardian (Guardian) overview (2025)
s: MAS's overview of Guardian (originally launched as Project Guardian), a cross-border sandbox pairing regulators, central banks and financial firms to trial asset tokenisation in funds, fixed income and foreign exchange. Its Policymaker Group sits MAS alongside other regulators, including the UK's FCA, Japan's FSA, the IMF and the World Bank; its Industry Group runs named workstreams with banks, asset managers, custodians and market bodies. A linked grant scheme funds digital bond issuance in Singapore.
k: The Policymaker Group brings MAS together with other regulators and central banks, among them the UK Financial Conduct Authority, Japan's Financial Services Agency, the IMF, the World Bank, Banque de France, Deutsche Bundesbank and Swiss FINMA, to work on common standards and cross-border interoperability for digital assets.
'Members' section, 'Policymaker Group'
Named firms lead each Industry Group workstream: Schroders for Asset and Wealth Management, ICMA for Fixed Income, and Ant Group together with ISDA for Foreign Exchange.
'Members' section, 'Workstream Leads'
A Global-Asia Digital Grant scheme was set up to help fund the issuance of digital bonds in Singapore, to encourage wider take-up of digital bonds in the market.
'Funding' section
rg: Live MAS scheme page, captured on the capture date; the page header itself shows a Published Date of 12 November 2025. A point-in-time snapshot: the membership list and the set of linked publications change as the initiative develops. The page now labels the initiative simply 'Guardian', though it remains widely known by its original name, Project Guardian.
